talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Sylvester Tremmel - [EN] APT Down and the mystery of the burning data centers.
talks.summary:
Journalists on the APT Down Dump

Sylvester Tremmel and colleague Christopher Kunz summarize c't reporting on a leaked workstation belonging to threat actor Kim, likely linked to North Korea's Kimsuky APT, while urging researchers to explore the dump themselves.

What the Dump Contains

Researchers shoulder-surfed Kim using Deepin Linux VMs, capturing messy desktops with Cobalt Strike beacons, Ivanti webshells, rootkits, phishing results against South Korean targets, and a previously unknown Linux rootkit.

Attribution Clues

Kim may be a Chinese national working North Korean hours, using Chinese fonts and struggling with Korean OCR. Tremmel stresses Kim is a cybercriminal, not a hobby hacker.

Burning Data Centers Mystery

The talk title references follow-on reporting about destructive attacks on data centers tied to the broader APT Down investigation, with Korean translation and document-format challenges complicating analysis.

talks.title: Anita Przybył - The Secret Weapon in Your IT Career [JDD2025]
talks.teaser: Shows IT specialists practical soft skills for working with their team, business stakeholders and their own emotions.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with everyday IT scenarios: a colleague who keeps postponing a task, a junior who asks the same question again and again, and a product owner who wants an old system rebuilt but more intuitive. The speaker, who has worked around IT for about seven years and has coached leaders and developers on interpersonal skills for many years, argues that soft skills increasingly appear in competency models and decide promotions. She cites 2024 recruitment figures compared with 2023: applications per position rose by 37% for mid-level and 23% for senior roles, with an average of 44 applications per job.

She groups the soft skills into three areas: the team, business stakeholders and oneself. For a team conflict she introduces transactional analysis and its parent, adult and child ego states. A judgmental message tends to draw a rebellious reply, while a factual message that describes what happened and how it affects the team invites a constructive response. For business contacts she contrasts closed, leading questions with open clarifying ones, and shows how a stakeholder who is motivated by avoiding problems needs a different framing than one who is motivated by reaching goals.

For the personal area she discusses naming emotions, referring to research in which labelling feelings reduced activity in the amygdala. She recommends building a richer emotional vocabulary, letting feelings pass rather than suppressing them, and examining the beliefs behind a reaction. Her closing point is that soft skills do not guarantee career success, but they can make working in an organisation easier and relationships better.

talks.title: Bartosz Olejniczak - How to find joy (and purpose) in your work again? [JDD2025]
talks.teaser: Shows how IT workers can reshape tasks, relationships and their outlook to find more meaning and energy in daily work.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with survey figures on burnout and disengagement among IT workers, then invites the audience to rate their daily energy from 1 to 10 and track it over weeks. The speaker argues that meaning at work is not handed down by an employer and has to be built by each person. He ties this to the PERMA well-being model and to a 2018 Harvard Business Review study in which 70% of respondents said meaning mattered more than pay.

He explains the hedonic treadmill, where raises and promotions give only short-lived satisfaction, and introduces job crafting. The idea comes from a 2002 hospital study of cleaning staff, where engaged workers reshaped their tasks, such as rearranging a bedridden patient's room or scheduling visits to patients with few visitors. The talk outlines three levers: changing tasks, changing relationships and changing how one sees the work. It also describes three orientations toward work (job, career and calling) and a sticky-note exercise for sorting tasks by the energy they give or drain.

Examples from workshops follow, including a colleague who shared learning resources with the team, people who scheduled demanding work for their peak energy hours, and a team that set aside a weekly slot to celebrate wins. The speaker stresses self-awareness, proactivity and autonomy, and suggests 10 to 15 minutes of energizing activity each day, especially during hard periods. The closing message is that no permission or new qualifications are needed to start, only a first step toward the work one can influence.

talks.title: Grzegorz Sztandera
talks.teaser: Surviving operational "Chernobyl" explores Grzegorz Sztandera.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Grzegorz Sztandera (introduced phonetically as Jagger Stander) discusses the realities of managing mission-critical production systems and operating a 24/7 DevOps competence center in Poland. Using personal travel photographs from Chernobyl as a visual backdrop, he examines 14 real-world production incident cases. The presentation highlights the high stakes of production operations—such as life-saving aviation ground communications and emergency eCall automotive response systems handling millions of incidents on AWS—where downtime can have life-or-death consequences. Sztandera frames the talk around a post-mortem game comparing how many incidents stemmed from his own DevOps team versus external factors, developers, or other teams.

### Key Topics
- **Incident Preparedness and Documentation:** Sztandera emphasizes the necessity of maintaining comprehensive operational documentation, step-by-step troubleshooting manuals, Confluence runbooks, disaster recovery tests, and post-incident root cause analyses (RCA).
- **High-Stakes Production Operations:** Managing 24/7 mission-critical architectures like emergency eCall automotive telemetry and aircraft-to-ground communication, where missing 100 calls an hour can cost lives.
- **SLA Management and Escalations:** Dealing with rigid operational SLAs, ticket automation breaches, and organizational challenges when dependencies across external teams impact response metrics.
- **Cross-Team Failures vs. DevOps Ownership:** Walking through 14 production case studies, culminating in a 2 to 12 score showing that the vast majority of severe production outages originate outside the direct control of the DevOps team.

### Technical Details
Sztandera walks through several specific outages and operational failures:
- **eCall Interface Glitches:** After a deployment, emergency call center agents were unable to hang up because a frontend deployment omitted the end-call button. A fallback procedure (automatically retrying three calls) prevented complete failure, but highlighted testing gaps.
- **Authentication & High Availability Outages:** An outage occurred when an upstream team’s two-factor authentication (2FA) service failed. The DevOps team used a configuration toggle to temporarily disable 2FA for emergency agents. In another case, primary and secondary firewalls failed sequentially at 3:00 AM, and an on-premise datacenter experienced a half-day blackout when maintenance crews cut the active power line while servicing the redundant one.
- **Cloud Automation and CI/CD Collisions:** A central cloud team introduced automated Terraform scripts that repeatedly wiped custom AWS configurations. Another ongoing challenge involved unreliable shared and dedicated Jenkins instances, which caused dozens of deployment incidents and demonstrated the need to practice manual deployments.
- **Performance and Capacity Bottlenecks:** Examples included missing database pagination causing list-of-refunds pages to take 2.5 minutes to load, a missing database index slowing down end-to-end (E2E) testing pipelines, and hitting 100% thread/queue limits during message processing.
- **Security Incidents (Log4j):** When the zero-day Log4j exploit surfaced, the team took six hours to patch and deploy. Potential reconnaissance on an internet-facing E2E testing stage occurred 16 minutes after notification, prompting a complete snapshot, database dump, and clean redeployment.
- **External and Human Factors:** One prolonged Docker container restart loop on production was traced to unoptimized queries and rogue internal testing servers hammering the live environment with invalid GET requests resulting in constant 404 responses. Another global three-hour 'critical outage' investigation occurred simply because a remote call center user experienced local office network issues and went to lunch without answering notifications.

### Takeaways
Sztandera concludes that production failures are inevitable; the key is proactive preparation through disaster recovery drills, automated monitoring, and clear operational context. Organizations must maintain tested manual fallback procedures and root-cause documentation to avoid rediscoveries during off-hours emergencies. Finally, software engineers and product teams must write code with operational awareness, recognizing that negligence or poor architecture directly impacts the on-call engineers answering alerts at 3:00 AM.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Marcin Dudek, Piotr Zarzycki - From Zero to AI Pentester
talks.teaser: Shows how two researchers used LLM agents to scan WordPress plugins and web apps, including hallucinations and limits.
talks.summary:
Two speakers from CERT Polska and Orange describe how they went from no AI background to using LLM agents for web vulnerability testing in roughly a month. They were motivated by AI-focused events where offensive uses of AI were common, and by a practical problem at Orange: thousands of web applications produce large numbers of low-severity findings that no person can review by hand.

Early experiments were mixed. Claude Code quickly listed the known flaws in a deliberately vulnerable application, but that came from the model's training knowledge rather than from testing the target. A local model gave weak reports, and another agent invented an SQL injection in a source file that did not exist. Token costs pushed the team toward a flat-rate Codex subscription, which had no API, so they ran it headless from scripts with JSON output. They estimated that the same work through the API would have cost about 4,000 dollars. In a comparison on a blog generated by several models, GPT-5.1 and Gemini 3 Pro found all three planted remote code execution flaws with no false positives, while repeated runs of one prompt gave inconsistent results. Safety refusals were easily bypassed by framing the request as a CTF exercise.

Scaled across 860 WordPress plugins, the pipeline produced 87 findings, with roughly a fifth estimated as false positives. Seventeen were reported with proof-of-concept code, and one report earned a reward above 4,000 dollars. The speakers' takeaway is that LLMs work best as a partner that catches things humans miss, but they hallucinate, so every result must be verified. Prompt structure matters a great deal, and sensitive internal code calls for on-premise models, which were weaker in their tests.

talks.title: Piotr Zarzycki - I'm Still a Dietitian: Fake Reviews, Fake Experts, and the Real Internet
talks.teaser: Shows how scraped public doctor reviews on a Polish booking portal expose clusters of fake reviews and fake credentials.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Piotr Zarzycki delivers a follow-up to his 2023 talk on fake online reviews, social proof manipulation, and platform moderation. Zarzycki begins by demonstrating how easily industry vanity credentials can be manufactured, detailing how he acquired an international "40 under 40 in cybersecurity" award and magazine cover feature with minimal effort and no technical vetting. He then transitions to a large-scale investigative analysis of the Polish medical booking platform ZnanyLekarz, examining how fake and copied reviews persist despite regulatory penalties and platform moderation promises.

### Key Topics
- **Manufactured Industry Accolades**: Zarzycki shares how discovering a "40 under 40 in cybersecurity" listing led him to contact the publisher (*Top Cyber News Magazine*). By submitting an article and a photograph, he secured a spot on the magazine cover and an official "Top International Forty Under Forty" certificate without undergoing a rigorous evaluation.
- **The Fake Review Economy**: Highlighting U.S. and Polish (UOKiK) studies showing that over 90% of consumers rely on and trust internet reviews, Zarzycki reviews the commercial black market for reviews. Despite UOKiK fining review-selling entities like Opinie.pro, these services continue to operate. Similar services advertise via Google Ads or coordinate cheaply on Discord, where reviews are purchased for as little as 2–4 PLN via BLIK.
- **ZnanyLekarz Evolution & Scrutiny**: Comparing data from 2023 to the present, Zarzycki notes ZnanyLekarz grew to 300,000 doctors and 25 million appointments, while backing down from claiming "100% verified reviews" to stating that opinions are moderated according to internal rules.
- **Becoming a Verified Specialist**: To test onboarding verification, Zarzycki legitimately completed three online courses from the Polish Institute of Dietetics (Polski Instytut Dietetyki) over a few days for 2,400 PLN, received official diplomas, and successfully set up a verified dietitian profile on ZnanyLekarz.

### Technical Details
- **Scraping Methodology**: To gather platform-wide data, Zarzycki inspected ZnanyLekarz's XML sitemaps (`sitemap_doctor.xml`, etc.), uncovering 110,407 unique doctor profile URLs after deduplication. To capture profiles missing from the sitemaps, he systematically mapped specialization and city index pages with pagination.
- **Overcoming Protections**: Scraping additional review pages required replaying the asynchronous JavaScript requests triggered by the "see more" button. When rate limiting, CAPTCHAs, and Cloudflare challenges halted simple requests, Zarzycki distributed the load using virtual machines running commercial VPNs, rotating IP addresses whenever CAPTCHA thresholds were reached.
- **Dataset Statistics**: The final scrape yielded 138,000 profiles, over 4 million reviews across 97,000 reviewed doctors, and nearly 4 GB of raw text spanning from 2007 to May 23.
- **Exact & Fuzzy Duplicate Analysis**: Exact-string matching identified identical reviews spanning up to 190 profiles (such as identical paragraphs applied interchangeably to urologists and gynecologists). For near-duplicates, Zarzycki implemented a normalization pipeline: lowercasing, stripping Polish diacritics, unifying titles (e.g., all to "doktor"), standardizing gender references, replacing numbers with placeholders, collapsing whitespace and repeated characters, stripping emojis, and filtering reviews under five words. The normalized text was tokenized, candidate pairs were filtered based on shared tokens and length constraints (within 10 words, max 300 candidates per review), and text similarity was evaluated.
- **ZnanyŚciemniacz**: Zarzycki published a public tool, `znanyściemniacz.pl`, enabling users to input a doctor's profile URL to detect matching or near-duplicate reviews across the platform.

### Takeaways
While ZnanyLekarz reported detecting 1,000 to 2,000 suspicious reviews monthly using 24 risk factors and flagged potential account suspensions, Zarzycki found that identical copy-pasted reviews highlighted during his 2023 presentation remained live years later—including identical reviews duplicated on the exact same doctor profile. Paradoxically, the platform promptly wiped the reviews written on Zarzycki's own profile ahead of the talk. Zarzycki closes by highlighting the persistent vulnerability of crowd-sourced rating ecosystems and the need for independent scrutiny.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Michał Błaszczak - Hack The Knowledge
talks.teaser: A roadmap maps free labs, certs, and communities for red-team and blue-team learners amid noisy paid course markets.
talks.summary:
The session opens on why cybersecurity demands constant learning as attacks, tools, and compliance rules shift quickly. The speaker frames four hurdles newcomers face: vetting trustworthy material, navigating crowded offerings, picking a coherent path, and avoiding stagnation that can sideline careers.

Most of the talk contrasts red-team and blue-team roles, then walks through parallel learning channels for each side. For offense, the presentation points to certifications such as OSCP-style tracks, Hack The Box machines and pro labs, PortSwigger Web Security Academy, CTF discipline by category, and careful use of writeups. For defense, it highlights SOC and incident-response skills, Hack The Box Sherlock log challenges, emerging Threat Range team exercises, Cyber Defenders blue-team tasks, and certification choices screened against hiring filters and marketing hype.

The closing sections stress cheap or free sources—GitHub awesome lists, documentation, threat-intel feeds, conferences, and personal blogging—and habits such as measurable goals, fundamentals, and networking. The speaker presents Not the Hidden Wiki as a community-run, open-source link aggregator with global chapters, partner programs, and initiatives offering free penetration tests and résumé-building experience. The takeaway is to blend theory with regular lab practice, tailor paths individually, share knowledge, and start with free resources before committing to expensive training.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Michał Kłaput- Akuku, Mam Cię! - Jak Namierzyć Operatora Drona w Sercu Wojny - vol. 2
talks.teaser: Explains how drone radio links, GPS and fiber-optic control can be detected, and why hunting the operator matters.
talks.summary:
Michał Kłaput opens with how small drones moved from hobby filming and parcel-delivery pilots into military use. He then turns to the war in Ukraine, citing a figure that 80% of battlefield losses come from drone weapons. His argument is that a trained operator is hard to replace, so finding the pilot can matter more than shooting down each drone.

He recounts a September incident in which drones entered Polish airspace, leading to airspace closures and Polish and Belgian fighter jets being scrambled. He compares a roughly 4 million dollar missile with a far cheaper drone, and describes a house that was hit during the incident. He then covers the drone's links: the control and video radio link, detection on the 58 GHz band, and GPS jamming near the Hel Peninsula that disrupted consumer drones. He also explains fiber-optic drones, which emit no radio signal and are hard to detect. Finally, he describes how DJI's return-to-home feature and its Aeroscope tool relate to finding an operator.

He closes with a live demonstration in which a software-defined radio was used to try to receive a drone video signal, though tuning proved unreliable. He points the audience to a follow-up talk on building interception hardware.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Piotr Głaska - MaaS, traffers, infostealers.
talks.teaser: Maps the infostealer ecosystem, from DNS pivots and domain brokers to affiliate teams spreading fake apps and click-fix lures.
talks.summary:
The talk maps how infostealer malware reaches victims, focusing on the ecosystem around it rather than the code itself. The speaker starts from a lure domain found while hunting an AI video-editing theme, then pivots through passive DNS to a neighbouring domain on the same IP address, and from there to a fake game page that offers a ClickOnce installer. That installer pulls a loader, which fetches a stealer. The macOS path instead asks the victim to run a script in Terminal, and the stealer is tied to a separate operator who sells it as a service.

Further cases show how the roles divide. Traffer teams buy stealers as a service, recruit individual workers, and give each one a tracking code so payments can be attributed. Fake sites check user agents and referrers to hide from analysts. A GitHub-hosted campaign used a click-fix prompt to paste a base64-encoded command into a shell. A fake recruiter interview hid a payload behind an intentional bug in a candidate's test project, running only when the error handler fired. The speaker also reported more than 40,000 domains registered through one broker, and described sitting-duck hijacking, where abandoned domains still delegated to name servers can be reclaimed by anyone.

The practical takeaway is to treat domains from brokers as suspicious, since the speaker had not seen a legitimate one among them, and to block shared infrastructure at the network layer before a lure is used.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Adam Paciuszkiewicz
talks.teaser: Agent QR Code broadcasts again details OMH 2025: Adam Paciuszkiewicz.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from OMH 2025, Adam Paciuszkiewicz (Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego) provides a follow-up to his previous year's physical QR code experiment in Warsaw. He explores how physical QR stickers persist in public spaces and presents new hands-on investigations into real-world cyber fraud, including task-based phishing/money laundering schemes on Telegram and WhatsApp, and romance/investment scams originating on Tinder.

### Key Topics
- **Physical QR Code Lifecycle & Tracking:** Observations on previously placed QR stickers across Warsaw, including stickers surviving on InPost Paczkomat parcel lockers and appearing on InPost's official website imagery, generating 20–30 scans weekly.
- **New QR Campaign & Seasonal Impact:** Deploying posters and stickers (e.g., offering Telegram contacts for illicit substances or directing to WOŚP charity fundraisers) to test public scanning behavior. Paciuszkiewicz noted significantly lower engagement in winter compared to summer due to cold weather, collecting modest data into CSV files before stopping to avoid legal and personal data processing liabilities.
- **Task Phishing & Money Muling (Telegram/WhatsApp):** An interactive dive into task scams where participants perform minor actions (liking videos, adding items to Allegro shopping carts, favoring Booking.com listings) for small payouts (40 PLN, 20 PLN). When transitioned into paying into the scheme to receive larger returns, he identified the broader money laundering and structuring mechanism.
- **Romance & Investment Scams (Tinder to WhatsApp):** Creating a Tinder profile ("Michał") to track romance baiting leading to WhatsApp chats, TikTok shop investment offers, fashion arbitrage portals, and deceptive application installs.

### Technical Details
- **Campaign Architecture:** QR codes linked to personal Telegram accounts (not bots) configured to reply with WOŚP donation links. Incoming user messages and metadata were logged into CSV files.
- **Laundering via Task Scams:** The author earned over 100 PLN across multiple task groups ("świecące światło", VIP groups) managed by personas like "Alice" and "Małgorzata". Tasks involved sending screenshots back to managers for manual or pseudo-automated review. When required to deposit 70 PLN to receive 100 PLN, specific personal recipient bank account details were supplied, illustrating how fragmented funds circulate between participants across different service rings (Booking, Instagram, Allegro, YouTube).
- **Testing Verification with Generative AI:** The speaker tested scam validation pipelines by asking ChatGPT to generate fake bank transfer confirmations. Low-quality transfer receipts received automated rejections ("payment not received"), while a realistic generated confirmation was rejected over metadata discrepancies (July vs. November dates).
- **Bot vs. Human Operators:** When interacting with romance and investment scam profiles, prompt injection and logic tests suggested an AI or automated system operating initially, followed by a switch to manual human handling when unexpected prompts or broken links were introduced.

### Takeaways
- **Environmental Factor in Physical Phishing:** Physical QR phishing campaigns depend heavily on seasonality and user physical comfort; freezing temperatures drastically reduce scan rates.
- **Legal Boundaries in Security Research:** Taking active roles by transferring funds alters legal liability from passive research to active participation in money laundering; managing collected personal communication also risks data privacy violations.
- **Scam Hygiene:** Financial and romance scams heavily mix automation with manual social engineering. Defense requires critical thinking ("heart and mind"), particularly before clicking unknown links or moving off dating apps to encrypted messengers.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Maciej Krzyżaniak
talks.teaser: Traces how fake CAPTCHA lures evolved into FileFix and JPEG-hidden payloads, and which controls stop them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an unusual comparison: kite fighting in Indian cities, where glass-coated lines cut rivals' kites and sometimes injure bystanders. The speaker uses it to frame how a harmless-looking idea can have serious side effects. The main subject is ClickFix, also called fake CAPTCHA, which first appeared in August 2024. Victims reached a lure page through search results or compromised sites, were told to press Win+R, paste a copied command and run it. That launched PowerShell, which fetched further stages, typically infostealers. The speaker follows how the technique was copied and extended by other researchers, including a variant where compromised WordPress sites pulled staged JavaScript from a blockchain smart contract, and a check that confirmed each victim had completed the steps.

The middle section covers FileFix, a variant that abuses the File Explorer address bar. It allows about 2048 characters, compared with 260 in the Run dialog, and the browser becomes the parent process, which matters for monitoring. The speaker then describes a later technique that hides a .NET payload in the APP1 metadata of a JPEG served from a website. The browser caches the image, and a PowerShell one-liner reads it from the cache, decrypts the payload and loads it in memory without writing it to disk. A lab demonstration showed the chain running from Edge. Late in 2025 a fake Windows update lure appeared on adult-content sites, and it looped PowerShell to add Defender exclusions and deliver several payloads.

The closing advice is practical. Block access to the blockchain-based staging domains if the business has no need for them, and restrict mshta and PowerShell launched from browsers. Use WDAC, constrained language mode and monitoring of the RunMRU and TypedPaths registry keys. Disabling the Run dialog is suggested, though the speaker notes it is hard to deploy in practice.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Jarosław Jedynak - Detecting malicious files But what's so difficult about it?
talks.teaser: Explains how a CERT team builds a public file-scanning service that gives non-technical users a clear malicious-or-not verdict.
talks.summary:
Someone receives an email attachment and wants to know if it is malicious. The usual advice, such as not opening suspicious files, asking the sender through another channel, or reporting every file to a CERT, is hard to apply at scale. Uploading samples to VirusTotal answers the question but makes the file visible to researchers and can expose private data contained in it. The speaker describes a public, automated alternative aimed at non-technical users.

Detection combines several kinds of signals: matches on known malware, campaign-specific rules such as file names or HTML phishing forms, and recursive lookups on contacted IPs or domains. Uploads go to an analysis backend that combines the MWDB malware repository with an open-source sandbox using VM introspection to watch behaviour. Observed behaviours are mapped to ATT&CK techniques, with a student extending an existing mapping tool to work with the sandbox output. The hardest part, the speaker argues, is combining weak indicators into one verdict without naive scoring that flags a packed, benign program as malware.

The closing section weighs the project's value: it gives Polish users a free verdict, improves local visibility into campaigns, and keeps samples out of commercial clouds. The speaker admits the implementation is still changing and asks the audience whether the service is worth building.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Wojciech Reguła - Kogo obchodzi gdzie jest Wally. Nieautoryzowany dostęp do lokalizacji
talks.teaser: Explores macOS location privacy and ways attackers bypass authorization to read a user's position.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by framing macOS privacy through Transparency, Consent, and Control, stressing that System Integrity Protection must stay enabled for those controls to matter. It explains how location permissions are stored separately from classic TCC in locationd’s Ward plist database, what fields are recorded, and why only the code-signing team identifier is meaningfully enforced in practice.

The middle walks through several paths to unauthorized location access: hijacking an authorized app via an older Firefox build and library injection, abusing Electron apps with debug tooling, trivial Weather widget and cache leaks, TLS trust and authorization-database tweaks, CFNetwork diagnostic logging, and privileged plugin abuse in iMovie and GarageBand to extract Find My tokens. The speaker contrasts these with red-team alternatives that avoid burning zero-days, including Selenium against Chrome and Safari Web Archive tricks.

Practitioners should treat granted browser and Electron permissions as shared assets, watch for downgrade-to-old-signed-binaries patterns, and monitor Endpoint Security events such as suspicious environment variables. Auditors should verify SIP fleet-wide before trusting any privacy control narrative.

talks.teaser: Explains how to stand up a home security lab on modest hardware, from Proxmox and backups through Wazuh and onward tooling.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a home lab as a personal workshop where security practitioners can experiment without vendor limits or subscription caps. It contrasts domestic setups with cloud and hybrid options, illustrates how varied homelabs can be in size and style, and outlines motivations from privacy and family protection to certification prep and career development.

The speaker describes a practical build path: used servers and mini PCs, Proxmox as the virtualization core, reliable backups, and gradual adds such as UPS, faster networking, and rack gear. For defenders, the core stack includes an open-source SIEM on a VM, DNS filtering, monitoring dashboards, optional self-hosted VPN, and hybrid links to external VPS resources via tunnels. He demos inventory and exposure tooling, Nessus Essentials for home scanning, local threat-intel platforms, IOC enrichment, and workflow automation tied to alerts.

Cautionary notes cover safe power, not over-exposing services, and checking public exposure. Growth paths mentioned include malware sandboxes, IDS on small boards, honeypots, and local LLM projects. The closing emphasis is on community resources and inspiration rather than an exhaustive tool catalog.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Marcin Juszko, Witold Ławacz - Fiszing w erze kłiszingu i ejajszingu
talks.teaser: Explores how AI scales phishing campaigns and how a bank SOC automates triage, enrichment, and analyst workflows.
talks.summary:
Two presenters from a global cyber defense center frame phishing as a still-common initial-access path that is shifting with artificial intelligence, quishing, and far greater campaign throughput. They cite MITRE lateral movement via phish, npm-related fraud that started with stolen credentials, and vendor predictions about AI-written lures, deepfake media, and automated orchestration—including the risk that AI agents could send mail at scale.

The operational core covers first-line SOC pain: user reports are mostly newsletters and noise, gateways face tight delivery SLAs, and nested tricks defeat simple analysis—password-protected archives with out-of-band secrets, HTML smuggling, and QR links buried in ZIP, document, and PDF layers. They reproduce research on AI-linked SVG attachments by tuning VirusTotal hunts, clustering files with DOM similarity and DOMhash, and reading template reuse plus odd encoding mistakes as possible model artifacts.

They finish with a SOAR workflow for reported messages that normalizes multi-vendor verdicts, stores enrichments for threat hunting, weighs malicious verdicts against clicks, uses approved AI prompts as extra signal, and keeps one consistent analyst view with QA on auto-closed cases. They urge planning for automation outages—staffing, priorities, manual tool access—and conclude that defenders should focus on attack outcomes and scale, keep revising architecture, and keep humans in charge of the highest-impact calls.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Kamil Bojarski - Powodzenia, jestem za siedmioma kontraktorami
talks.teaser: Maps private-sector involvement in offensive cyber operations across China, Russia, and Western markets.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that public discourse still treats offensive cyber operations as tasks for militaries and intelligence agencies, while private companies increasingly supply capabilities along three lines: building intrusion tools, operating cyber ranges that double as offensive training, and fully outsourcing break-ins under government contracts.

The middle of the talk walks east to west with case studies. Chinese firms such as i-SOON and Chengdu 404 appear in indictments, leaks, and marketing that borrows penetration-testing language; leaked chats illustrate modest billing, sloppy targeting, and a NATO secretary-general dataset that sponsors reportedly declined to buy. Cyber-range vendors like Integrity Tech tie regulatory push for exercises to attack–defense business models. Russia’s NTC Vulkan leaks point to recon, influence, and OT-focused training platforms tied to multiple agencies. Western examples span long-standing cleared contractors, exploit brokers, and firms that openly recruit offensive researchers.

Practitioners are urged to track contractors like threat actors: map tools, procurement, and victim lists on models such as the diamond model, and resist assuming every high-profile compromise reflects an elite state team when operational mistakes or sales pitches may explain the footprint.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Iwona Prószyńska, Karol Bojke - Mowa jest srebrem, a milczenie złotem
talks.teaser: CERT Poland outlines when silence beats headlines on DDoS and breaches, and rebuts myths that still shape public cyber advice.
talks.summary:
Representatives of CERT Polska’s strategic cyber communication team describe how daily incident work collides with media incentives. From a base of more than 600,000 reports and well over 100,000 classified incidents per year, they argue that what organizations choose to say often differs from what actually threatens operations.

They walk through recurring story patterns: DDoS used mainly for propaganda and brief visibility, ransomware and data leaks that dominate headlines despite lower incident counts, and post-ransomware data theft where notifying only a published “sample” ignores full compromise. They contrast APT persistence with less sophisticated real vectors, note that phishing accounts for over 90% of handled cases, and warn against over-splitting fraud types for the public. Practical communication pitfalls include sweeping breaches under the rug, amplifying combolist panic without guidance, and publishing APT clues before victims can act, while mojecert.pl and deeper advisories serve administrators who need IOCs and patches.

The second half critiques sensational Polish headlines, sponsor-driven surveys that count every phishing mail as an attack, and advice that backfires: “safe sites only,” forced password rotation, blanket fear of public Wi-Fi for encrypted banking, and trust in the browser padlock—CERT logged padlocks on 91,919 of 92,000 listed phishing sites. Practitioners are urged to craft simple, honest messages, assume users will workaround bad rules, and carry verified guidance to family, schools, and employers.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Jakub Ryszkowski, Michał Ciesiński - LLM w rękach hakera od prompt injection do wycieku
talks.teaser: Surveys prompt injection against LLMs, outlines defenses for agents, and shows how criminals use AI for malware and intrusions.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a recap of prompt injection, split into direct attacks, where a user types malicious instructions straight into a model, and indirect attacks, where hidden instructions sit in content the model later reads, such as a web page, email or file. The speakers cite a late 2024 study that reported a 56% success rate across 144 direct-injection scenarios, and describe a recent case where a one-pixel hidden prompt in linked documentation pushed an agent to act on data the user never saw.

For defense, the speakers suggest a separate guard model that screens prompts and responses, isolating the agent from sensitive data, production systems and long-term storage, and logging, monitoring and alerting on suspicious activity such as injection attempts. They stress keeping a human in the loop for consequential actions, because alerts still need judgment and the model should not decide alone.

The second half turns to criminal use. Jailbreak prompts circulate in public repositories, and paid services built on commercial or open models are sold through Telegram with price lists, some offering lifetime access. Attackers use LLMs to iterate and obfuscate malware so each sample differs, to draft pretexts from gathered profile data, and to lower the skill needed for mass campaigns. The talk ends with a reported espionage campaign in which an AI agent, connected to tools such as Nmap, carried out about 80% of the operational work against around 30 entities, with humans setting strategic direction. The takeaway is to treat all model input as untrusted and monitor agents closely.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Tomasz Zieliński - Ile tritów ma trajt i czy to w ogóle ważne?
talks.teaser: Explores how bit counts mislabel classic machines, why bytes need not be eight bits, and how many trits fit in a tryte.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by questioning why familiar machines are called eight-, sixteen-, or thirty-two-bit when registers, buses, and marketing labels often disagree. Walkthroughs of the Zilog Z80 in the ZX Spectrum, the Intel 8088 PC, and the Motorola 68000 in the Amiga show that “bit width” is frequently misleading rather than descriptive.

The speaker contrasts von Neumann unified memory with Harvard-style separation, illustrated through the Apollo Guidance Computer’s ferrite core memory, parity handling, and split addressing for instructions versus data. A long historical thread covers the Intel 4004, Dmitri Grinberg’s Linux/4004 project (MIPS emulation on four-bit hardware, boot times from nine days down to under five days, and a Mandelbrot benchmark taking nine hours), and the emergence of the byte as an eight-bit convention rather than a law of nature.

Balanced ternary arithmetic (−1, 0, 1) leads to the Soviet Setun: a tryte held six trits (729 values), while a machine word used three trytes—eighteen trits total—stored in core memory with two binary bits per trit. The talk closes by linking three-valued weights to neural-network quantization and a playful case for nine-bit bytes, while conceding that eight-bit bytes may still be a happy accident of history.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Łukasz Cepok - The Tale of the Three Little Pigs
talks.teaser: Reverses the DDoSia attack client and its command-and-control logic used by the pro-Russian NoName hacktivist group.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how hacktivist groups, state-linked actors and cybercriminals increasingly overlap, using the pro-Russian NoName group as the central case. It shows how Telegram channels, manifestos and a reward system drew volunteers, and how targets shifted quickly after news about foreign military or financial support. Attribution changed when telemetry from the Bobik malware was matched against the group's targets, moving it from KillNet to NoName.

The middle section reverses the DDoSia client, first a Python tool with hardcoded C2 servers and later a Go version. Login moved from a timestamp that increased by 15 on each request, to base64 encoding, and finally to an encrypted login tied to the system GUID. Downloaded configs defined randomized HTTP parameters and target lists, and the hierarchical C2 setup let a parent server supply configs after lower-tier servers were removed. The speaker also noted a ranking endpoint that accepted forged attack counts and negative values that crashed the server.

The closing part covers the wider operation: some attacks came from infected network devices, targets relied on simple checks to confirm an outage, and a July operation by Europol and several European services led to arrests of members. The main takeaways are that these campaigns are low in sophistication but persistent, and that tracking C2 changes and verifying reported outages helps defenders assess them.

talks.title: OMH 2025: Adam Haertle, Antoni Mróz
talks.teaser: War stories from keeping a Polish security media site online despite WordPress, Cloudflare rules, and spreadsheet chaos.
talks.summary:
The session portrays how Zaufana, a Polish security news and training outlet, stays online while juggling WordPress, podcasts, club subscriptions, and dozens of third-party services. One presenter narrates incidents slide by slide; the other mocks failures from the back row, mirroring how the two operate in production.

The middle catalogs specific breakdowns rather than a single theme: Cloudflare challenge rules treating Przelewy24 webhooks, invoicing callbacks, and SSH as hostile bots; a Castopod database wrecked after a compose file pulled latest images and a backup omitting stored procedures; Klub Bezpiecznika renewals broken by date comparisons and columns misaligned after partial Excel sorts, at times exposing other members’ billing metadata; an in-memory diff that blasted thousands of duplicate course emails; DDoS pressure that knocked out a shared Skyer stack; WordPress quirks that leak site IP through admin errors and oEmbed; and weeks spent negotiating Przelewy24 sandbox cards, Blik notifications, and contradictory API docs.

The closing tone is pragmatic: pin container versions, keep alerts on monitoring, regression-test payment paths whenever CDN bot settings change, and stop treating spreadsheets as the system of record for synchronized membership data.

talks.title: Jeff Moss - [EN] Fireside Chat with Dark Tangent [Confi2026]
talks.teaser: Traces the origins of DEF CON and Black Hat and shares views on government ties, AI-driven patching and open models.
talks.summary:
The conversation looks back at how DEF CON began as an accidental gathering after a planned party fell through, and how Black Hat grew from companies asking for a more professional announcement. Moss contrasts the two: Black Hat addresses corporate security problems, while DEF CON only features tools attendees can get for free. He also recounts early dealings with government, including a Secret Service agent who ignored invitations and then turned up at the first event, and a satellite hacking challenge set up with a military procurement office.

On AI, he argues that open models can deliver much of what restricted frontier models offer, and that AI-assisted bug finding will force faster patching. He expects AI to increase developer jobs rather than reduce them, and sees agents, not generative tools, as the AI use case most likely to hold lasting value.

Audience questions covered legislation on encryption and data sovereignty, which he warns could fragment the internet and raise costs for smaller firms, along with the risk of stolen model weights. He closes by saying conferences last when they balance technical content with community, because technology is both political and social.

talks.title: Aviva Peisach - From Hero to Zero
talks.teaser: Shows how Wix moved from firefighting production incidents to a zero-error culture using monitoring, automation and scoped cleanup.
talks.summary:
Aviva Peisach describes how Wix moved from a hero culture, where a few veteran engineers handled constant production incidents, to a zero-error culture. The platform serves a large share of sites worldwide, with over 4,000 microservices, 600 releases a day and around 750 alerts daily. The early steps added visibility through New Relic and then Grafana dashboards, per-service SLO alerts with default thresholds, distributed tracing, continuous profiling, an alert enricher that suggests root causes, and an AI agent that runs troubleshooting playbooks.

Because these tools only covered production, the team moved earlier into rollout, testing and design. Guidelines were encoded into the internal framework Nile, which generates validation, limits, timeouts and asynchronous communication from a service's protobuf definition. A 1% default error threshold proved misleading at different traffic levels, so they added zero-error alerts, starting with newer services and gradually cleaning up backlogs. Opt-in reached almost all services, and daily errors per service dropped from 1.5 to 0.5.

Legacy services still produced about 7 million errors a day. Focusing on 180 services, just 4% of the total, which caused 98% of errors, the team aimed for 99.999% success and reached 99.995% within three months, cleaning up 80% of errors. The SLO threshold was then tightened to 0.001 to prevent regression. The main takeaway is to zoom in and out to scope improvements, automate repeated fixes, and start the next service at zero.

talks.title: CONFidence 2026: Co można zrobić z radiem bez licencji krótkofalarskiej | Radio Hacking Village
talks.teaser: Surveys what can be received and tried with cheap SDR gear without a ham license, and where transmitting crosses legal lines.
talks.summary:
Jacek Lipkowski, an amateur radio operator for over 30 years, asks what can be done with radio gear without a ham license. He starts with the law: receive-only devices generally need no permit, but gathering information not meant for you can be prosecuted, and people who find flaws in radio systems often do not tell the operators.

The core of the talk is cheap software-defined radio. Dongles built on the RTL2832 chip, costing around 100 PLN and covering roughly 24 MHz to 1.7 GHz, made this hobby accessible. Targets include distant shortwave stations, where digital modes such as FT8 and WSPR decode weak signals; amateur images from the International Space Station; a high-power Alaskan transmitter used to heat the ionosphere; and numbers stations. Aviation yields voice comms and ADS-B positions, which can reveal GPS jamming. Weather radiosondes such as the RS41 can be tracked to help find where they land, and some satellites carry unencrypted voice, data and images. IoT sensors in the ISM bands can be decoded with rtl_433, showing a car tire transmitting a unique serial number that could enable tracking. Meshtastic LoRa radios showed their worth during a blackout in Spain.

The closing advice is to stay away from amateur bands, service frequencies such as aviation, and any commercial or illegal traffic, even when a channel seems quiet. Anyone wanting to transmit legally should get a ham license, which allows higher power and building one's own designs.

talks.title: Michał Leszczyński - [EN] [CVE-2026-9058] Full Authentication Bypass in ZUS, e-Court...
talks.teaser: Shows how flawed server-side checks in Polish government e-signature login let forged certificates authenticate as real citizens.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with a browser plugin used to sign VAT declarations. While the speaker was updating it, the same old 2007 package kept being downloaded. Reversing the native host showed it acts as an updater that fetches code from the internet, and its integrity check was flawed. That let a malicious web page push a payload to the machine, which was reported as a high-severity issue. This raised the question of how the server side of qualified-signature login was handled on Polish public websites.

Those logins sign an XML statement, and the server is supposed to validate the signature and the certificate chain. The speaker first tried a signature with random bytes and a real certificate, using a programmable smart-card emulator. Several services accepted it because they only checked the document structure. A second variant forged the full certificate chain, down to a fake national bank root. One verification library returned a success code while flagging the certificate as fake, and the services relying on that top-level code accepted it. This was rated critical. Affected systems included the social insurance institution ZUS, e-health services, the Ministry of Justice identity module and several other portals. The attacks needed only a victim's name and national ID number.

Disclosure took roughly 50 to 113 days per organisation, and ZUS removed the signature login method entirely. The takeaways are to check the full result of every signature validation, verify the certificate chain against trusted lists, and test authentication integrations rather than trusting the structure of signed data. The speaker stressed that the signature scheme itself was not broken, and that services using the trusted-profile login were not affected.

talks.title: Krzysztof Dębski, Michał Niczyporuk - How (not) to build a startup? [JDD 2025]
talks.teaser: Engineers recount six years of marketplace startup pitfalls, from Magento wraps and scale tests to tech crusades and product misalignment.
talks.summary:
Krzysztof Dębski and Michał Niczyporuk describe joining a small B2B marketplace venture after years at large Polish enterprises such as Allegro. They were hired engineers, not founders, so the talk stays on technology and product rather than funding or corporate structure. The team chased a “dream” stack—cloud-only GCP, microservices, Vert.x, Vue, Kotlin coroutines—while bootstrapping on Magento and soon wrapping and duplicating it, then rewriting core pieces like the shopping cart only months in.

Much of the pain came from habits scaled to the wrong company size: months of linter and REST-style debates, rebuilding CI/CD repeatedly with little customer impact, load-testing product catalogs for millions of items while holding roughly 10,000, vendor-abstraction layers that slowed a move to SNS and SQS, custom OAuth with fixable security flaws, heavy hexagonal layering, and parallel pet projects left at seventy or ninety percent. They nearly went live while ripping out “legacy” Magento and overlooked B2B quoting in favor of a B2C cart model for about a year.

What sustained them included accepting “good enough,” hundreds of small production deploys, pragmatic CI/CD and smoke monitoring, and colleagues who swarm incidents without being asked. They eventually embraced constraints—for example moving from Vert.x toward Spring Boot—and stress that startups rarely die on framework choice or ugly code; misalignment with real customers and business goals does. They close by urging focus on people who have lived failure and on shipping product value over technical vanity.

talks.title: Kamil Banach
talks.teaser: Explains how Java streams run lazily and how custom collectors and Java 24 gatherers extend the Stream API.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short stream pipeline that appears to do nothing, which shows that intermediate operations are lazy and only run once a terminal operation such as collect or count is called. Kamil Banach demonstrates this with peek on a word list, showing each element passing through the filters one at a time. He then compares built-in collectors such as grouping and joining with a hand-written StringBuilder loop that builds a JavaScript-style array, and walks through the Collector interface: supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher and characteristics.

Next come the common pitfalls. Unchecked exceptions terminate a pipeline at runtime, checked exceptions must be handled before the code compiles, and parallel streams share the common ForkJoin pool, which is sized to the machine's processors. A test with 20 one-second calls took about two seconds on a 16-processor machine. Wrapping the stream in a ForkJoin pool with larger parallelism restored the one-second result, though he advises against relying on that implementation detail. He also shows that peek can be skipped when count runs on a sized stream.

The last part covers Java 24 gatherers, which allow custom intermediate operations with mutable state and support parallel execution. Examples include the built-in mapConcurrent, which runs calls on virtual threads, a window-based anomaly check on temperature readings, and a custom distinct-by-length gatherer. He closes with practical advice: check for nulls, prefer method references to lambdas, filter before mapping, and use a plain for loop when it reads better.

talks.title: Ivar Grimstad - The Past, Present, and Future of Enterprise Java [JDD 2025]
talks.teaser: Traces Jakarta EE from J2EE to today and previews upcoming specs, with demos of virtual threads, Jakarta Data and AI.
talks.summary:
The talk traces Jakarta EE from its start as J2EE in 1999, when even a simple enterprise bean needed several interfaces and XML descriptors. It shows how Spring brought XML-based dependency injection in 2004, how annotations simplified EJBs by 2009, and how Spring Boot became dominant after 2014. The platform's move to the Eclipse Foundation and its renaming to Jakarta EE complete the history.

The javax-to-jakarta namespace change in version 9 is presented as a deliberate cleanup that left the APIs untouched, easing migration. Jakarta EE 10 and 11 bring the core profile for microservices, updated test tooling, and a release cadence tied to Java LTS versions. Demos cover virtual threads, switched on by a flag that only takes effect on a runtime that supports them, and Jakarta Data repositories that generate CRUD methods and derive queries from method names.

Planned Jakarta EE 12 items include a higher API level, a shared query specification, and MVC for server-side rendering, while an agentic AI proposal is still in community review. A closing demo connects an OpenAI model to a Jakarta application through LangChain4j CDI using one annotation and a few configuration lines. The takeaway is that Java remains a practical choice for AI work, and that Eclipse Transformer can convert older bytecode with dependencies.

talks.title: 4Developers 2025: Jacek Milewski - "Contract Testing: Spare the Shame."
talks.teaser: Explains how consumer-driven contract tests bound microservice interactions and support safer deploys without company-wide integration rigs.
talks.summary:
The session opens on why large organizations still lean on slow, shared integration environments and heavy end-to-end suites as microservices multiply. Teams lose visibility into who calls their APIs, architecture diagrams drift, and late red builds send developers back to chat instead of code. Contract testing is framed as testing only the edges—HTTP clients and controllers, event publishers and listeners—not databases or full business flows.

The middle walks through consumer and provider roles with Pact-style tooling: consumer tests against a stand-in provider, generated JSON contracts, provider verification against those expectations, and a central broker that maps consumers to providers. The speaker stresses a narrow scope—roughly one happy-path contract per API, loose matching on payloads, provider “state” as capabilities rather than database recipes—and warns against using contracts as functional or pricing-logic tests.

The close shifts from “tests” to coordination: pull-request verification, publishing contracts, and deploy gates that ask whether a service version remains compatible with partners already in production. Practitioners should treat contracts as a compile-time compatibility layer among alternatives such as schemas, SDKs, documentation, end-to-end suites, or versioning—and as a way to shift integration risk left without pretending contracts replace every system test.

talks.title: 4Developers 2025: Michał Sajdak - "Dlaczego hackowanie aplikacji webowych jest proste?"
talks.teaser: Shows real-world web application flaws, from price tampering and reset bugs to authentication bypasses, with live demos.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many web application breaches come from simple logic and input-handling mistakes rather than sophisticated techniques. It opens with a set of publicly reported cases. A fast-food ordering app accepted a client-supplied price field in its JSON cart, so an item could be bought for almost nothing. A car maker's password reset enforced two-factor checks only in the browser, letting a researcher skip them. A code hosting service sent reset emails to an attacker-added address, and a penetration test found a reset API that returned a valid token for an admin account.

The middle section covers live demos against a firewall and an IP camera. On the firewall, a cookie value reached a shell command, and a filter that blocked spaces was bypassed with the shell's field separator. A later firewall flaw bypassed authentication through a path that was decoded twice, because the front-end and back-end servers handled URL encoding differently. On the camera, the NTP server setting was passed to a command run as root, and the request needed the correct content type before the body was parsed. Other cases included a VPN appliance that accepted a crafted session cookie, an ISP API that exposed customer lookups, an open redirect on a trusted domain used to make scam ads look legitimate, SQL injection on a pilot access login, and a WordPress security plugin that logged anyone in as user ID 1.

The closing takeaways are to enforce authorization on the server for every HTTP method, not just the obvious ones, to make front-end and back-end components parse input the same way, to validate parameters against allow-lists, and to avoid building shell commands from user input. The speaker points to OWASP's authentication and forgot-password cheat sheets, CVE Details, CISA's catalogue of exploited vulnerabilities, and public bug bounty reports as further reading.

talks.title: 4Developers 2025: Tomek Ducin - "The many meanings of share and reuse in software architecture."
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding 4Developers 2025: Tomek Ducin - "The many meanings of share and reuse in software architecture.".
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation from 4Developers 2025, Tomek Ducin explores the concept of sharing and reuse across different levels of software engineering and architecture. Through the narrative journey of a fictional developer named Bożydar—who transitions from a bootcamp graduate during the 2020 pandemic to a senior architect and business-focused leader—the talk examines the trade-offs of code reuse, shared persistence, data modeling, architectural decoupling, and business alignment.

### Key Topics
- **Code Reuse vs. Domain Responsibility (DRY vs. WET):** How junior engineers often misinterpret the DRY principle (Don't Repeat Yourself) as a mandate to deduplicate lines of technical code rather than unifying domain knowledge, risking premature abstractions.
- **Monorepos and Universal Patterns:** The pitfalls of blindly adopting trending architectures (e.g., monorepos, reducers everywhere) without defining the actual problem, metrics, or trade-offs.
- **Shared Persistence vs. Database-per-Service:** Evaluating the consequences of a centralized database across services, including tight coupling, deployment synchronization (release trains, code freezes), versus independent data stores.
- **Domain Modeling & Bounded Contexts:** The danger of creating "God Classes" or canonical data models across distinct business subdomains versus separating models using perspectives like being, behaving, and becoming.
- **Microservices, Microfrontends, and Team Topologies:** Determining what should actually be shared (observability, UI design systems) versus what should remain strictly decoupled (state, deployments, data schemas), alongside empowering stream-aligned teams by measuring KPI outcomes rather than task velocity.
- **Business Capabilities and Value Streams:** Viewing software architecture not as an end goal, but as an enabler for business capabilities and strategic business goals.

### Technical Details
- **Integration Patterns:** Clear distinction between Events (facts from the past, declarative statements), Queries (state in the present, questions), and Commands (future intent, imperative instructions that can fail or be rejected).
- **Decoupling Release from Deployment:** Leveraging trunk-based development with feature toggles (boolean flags, scalers, or maps) to support canary releases, rolling deployments, and A/B testing without synchronizing database migrations.
- **Contextual Optimization:** Choosing technical and architectural trade-offs based explicitly on primary business constraints, such as optimizing for time to market (e.g., meeting regulatory deadlines to avoid penalties) versus performance, cost reduction, or complexity isolation.

### Takeaways
- Reuse and sharing always come with a cost, and strict isolation also carries trade-offs; there are no silver bullets in architecture.
- Architectural decisions must be framed around asking the right questions: What problem is being solved, how is it measured, and what context has changed?
- The ultimate maturity in software engineering lies in aligning technical decisions with business capabilities and recognizing that not every problem requires writing software or building in-house solutions.

talks.title: JDD Podcast - episode 3: Piotr Przybył
talks.teaser: A podcast explores how Java evolved over 30 years, why LTS hype may mislead teams, and what recent releases change for production workloads.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with how Java keeps evolving despite recurring claims that it is fading, including its thirtieth anniversary and long-running work on virtual threads compared with Go. The guest argues Java changes by steady evolution rather than revolution: syntax largely stays compatible, while use shifted from embedded ambitions to server backends, with modern idioms like pattern matching and tooling such as Graal for slimmer runtimes.

Much of the middle challenges treating long-term support releases as automatic wins without paid support. The guest cites compact strings in Java 9, unpinned virtual threads in synchronized code from Java 24, and Elastic’s practice of shipping on current JDKs for performance gains from features like the vector API. Versions 22 through 25 add generational garbage collectors, compact headers, JFR updates, and a simpler entry point for beginners than the classic public static main ceremony.

The closing thread ties JDD to the unrecorded “corridor track”: hallway networking, short chats with speakers, and learning from the Java community beyond syntax. Practitioners are nudged to evaluate upgrades on real savings and behavior, not LTS labels alone, and to show up for peer exchange when talks are already online.

talks.title: JDD Podcast - episode 1: Jarosław Pałka
talks.teaser: Explores which skills Java developers need as AI coding tools spread, plus the language's direction and the JVM's recent work.
talks.summary:
Jarosław Pałka, a JDD program council member, discusses how Java developers should adapt as AI tools spread. He argues that architecture, design, refactoring, test automation and understanding business requirements matter more when code is produced by an LLM, since generated code often works but is hard to change later. He also says smaller, focused prompts produce better code, and that developers still need theory such as what a transaction log or consistency model is.

The conversation returns often to the worry about junior developers. Pałka suggests that people who rely on vibe coding skip the mistakes through which experience is built, and that companies will need mentoring to grow seniors. He recalls uninstalling an AI terminal that he felt was dulling his basic command-line habits. He doubts programmers will disappear, pointing to earlier promises such as rule engines and no-code.

On the Java side, the guest argues the language is still worth learning in 2025, citing its large community and library ecosystem and a faster release cadence that has pushed modernization. He highlights the Vector API, foreign functions and memory for calling C code, and garbage collectors such as ZGC and Shenandoah. Choosing between OpenJDK distributions, he says, is mostly about security patch support and vendor accountability, while organizations stuck on Java 8 face migration risk. He closes by recommending JDD for its community.

talks.title: 4Developers Łódź 2024: Maciek Palmowski - Is Astro the ultimate front-end framework?
talks.teaser: Explores Astro's islands architecture, zero-JS defaults, and when it suits content-heavy sites.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from a PHP and WordPress perspective, when headless and static stacks were fashionable and many teams chased speed by swapping dynamic sites for static HTML. The speaker explains why Gatsby-style projects felt overbuilt for that goal, why Next-style app-centric frameworks did not click, and what drew him to early Astro: familiar, include-like components and JavaScript on the front end only when requested.

The core of the talk surveys Astro as a content-oriented framework. Island architecture and client directives let multiple UI libraries coexist while hydration is delayed—for example loading a React carousel only when visible. He contrasts default front-end JavaScript weight with Gatsby and Next, covers image and prefetch tooling, typed content collections and the content layer API for markdown, databases, and external sources, plus CLI ergonomics, integrations, file-based routing, rendering modes, view transitions, multilingual sites, HTMX, Astro DB with libSQL and Turso, and adjunct tools Starlight and Storefront.

He ends by saying no single JavaScript framework is universally best, but Astro is a strong option to evaluate for new content sites, migrations that reuse React or Vue pieces, and CMS-backed projects—supported by adoption trends and features landing in version 5.0.

talks.title: 4Developers Łódź 2024: Dawid Perdek - Testy mutacyjne - trochę teorii i trochę praktyki ze stryker
talks.teaser: Covers mutation testing limits of code coverage and hands-on Stryker workflows on JavaScript projects, with hard-won configuration lessons.
talks.summary:
Dawid Perdek opens by contrasting full code coverage with what it actually proves: lines executed, not assertion quality, edge cases, or whether tests would catch real defects. He positions mutation testing as deliberately changing production code to see if unit tests fail, and introduces Stryker for JavaScript with a borrowed theoretical frame around mutation score and killed versus survived mutants.

The practical half walks through a painful first adoption on a large Angular corporate codebase—misconfigured mutate paths, Karma versus Jest, timeouts, and zero useful mutants—then a cleaner run on Oskar Dudycz’s open-source Emet library. He reports 1863 mutants, about 40 minutes with parallel test runners, a 99.7% mutation score with five survivors, and how HTML reports distinguish killed mutants, timeouts counted as detected, and no-coverage areas. He contrasts mutating test code versus production code, Jest integration versus plain npm test for attribution, runtime cost, equivalent mutants, and non-deterministic results across repeated runs without code changes.

Practitioners should mutate production sources, tune command runners for unit-only speed, aim near 90% rather than 100%, disable noisy mutators or equivalent-mutant hotspots, and schedule runs on CI overnight—not pre-commit. He closes by tying strong tests to safer deploys, living documentation, and sustainable refactoring.

talks.title: 4Developers Łódź 2024: Szymon Chmal - Praktyczny przewodnik po zadaniach, obietnicach i planowaniu
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for 4Developers Łódź 2024: Szymon Chmal - Praktyczny przewodnik po zadaniach, obietnicach i planowaniu.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Szymon Chmal presents a comprehensive guide to understanding JavaScript's task execution model, asynchronous programming, and practical strategies for optimizing long-running operations. The talk addresses common misconceptions about how JavaScript handles asynchronous work and provides real-world solutions for keeping web applications responsive.

## Key Topics

**Event Loop and Tasks**
All code execution in JavaScript—including event handlers, setTimeout callbacks, and synchronous code—is organized as tasks. The event loop manages a queue of these tasks, executing one at a time. Critically, tasks cannot be interrupted; once started, a task must complete before the next task can begin. This single-threaded model means that long-running synchronous tasks can block user interactions.

**Microtasks vs. Macrotasks**
JavaScript distinguishes between macrotasks (regular tasks) and microtasks (created by Promises and MutationObserver). Microtasks use a separate queue that must be completely emptied before the next macrotask begins. This detail matters: wrapping work in a Promise does not run it "in the background" but instead schedules a microtask that still executes on the main thread, blocking interactions during execution.

**Task Splitting and "Yield to Main"**
The speaker demonstrates a practical pattern for breaking long-running work into smaller chunks: the "yield to main" function. This function returns a Promise that resolves after a setTimeout(0), creating a new task. By inserting yields between work chunks, the browser can execute higher-priority tasks (like button clicks or text input) between chunks, maintaining responsiveness. A real-world example: validating a form with 60 nodes and 14 properties per node, originally taking 6 seconds, became responsive by splitting validation into smaller subtasks with yield points.

**Scheduling Constraints and Workarounds**
setTimeout enforces a 4-millisecond minimum delay when nested more than 4 levels deep, limiting control. To bypass this, some libraries (including React 16+) use the Message Channel API, which allows scheduling without the 4ms throttle—though this is an undocumented workaround.

**Modern Scheduler API**
A new Scheduler API (currently supported in Edge and Chrome, behind a flag in Firefox) provides explicit task prioritization: user-blocking (highest), user-visible (default), and background. Tasks include a controller for changing priorities or cancellation mid-execution, and a special yield() method that ensures the current high-priority task completes before lower-priority work resumes.

## Technical Details

**Asynchronous vs. Concurrent**
The speaker clarifies that JavaScript is asynchronous but not concurrent. Without WebWorkers, JavaScript has one thread; asynchronicity refers to the ability to schedule work for later (via the event loop), not to parallel execution.

**Microtask Optimization**
Promise resolution should be used carefully. Receiving 100 API responses that each trigger a microtask can create 100 microtasks in a single event loop cycle, blocking the browser while all are processed. Batching (e.g., 16 microtasks per batch with macrotasks between) reduces perceived jank.

**Frame-Aware Scheduling**
requestAnimationFrame is guaranteed to fire before the browser renders a frame. Wrapping a setTimeout inside a requestAnimationFrame ensures visual updates occur before rendering. requestIdleCallback schedules work during browser idle time, utilizing gaps between frames, but it is not guaranteed to execute if the browser is busy. It accepts an optional timeout to force execution regardless.

## Takeaways

1. **Understand the event loop**: All JavaScript execution revolves around tasks and the event loop; this knowledge is foundational for performance work.
2. **Promises don't run in the background**: Wrapping work in a Promise schedules a microtask on the main thread, not background execution.
3. **Break up long tasks**: Use yield-to-main patterns to insert gaps where the browser can handle user input, keeping applications responsive.
4. **Set deadlines when splitting tasks**: Yield too frequently and context-switching overhead exceeds gains; a 10–50ms deadline per chunk is often reasonable.
5. **Use the right API for the job**: setTimeout for basic scheduling, requestAnimationFrame for visual updates, requestIdleCallback for non-urgent background work, and the Scheduler API for explicit priority control.
6. **Framework behavior**: Frameworks like React use similar task-splitting techniques internally to render large component trees without blocking.
7. **Monitor real-world impact**: Metryki, especially Interaction to Paint, reveal whether optimizations actually help users.

talks.title: 4Developers Łódź 2024: Krzysztof Jędrzejewski - AI - jak nie zrobić sobie krzywdy
talks.teaser: Shows how AI projects go wrong on cost, model choice, hallucinations and legal rules, and how to avoid those pitfalls.
talks.summary:
The talk is about how teams can hurt themselves when building with AI, and it starts with cost. Speaker Krzysztof Jędrzejewski compares vendor APIs, self-hosted open generative models such as Bielik, classical machine learning models and plain algorithmic rules. Each option suits a different data volume, and a rule-based system is often the cheapest when it already performs well.

Benchmarks show that smaller specialised models can match or beat large generative ones. A fine-tuned BERT beat GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on medical terminology extraction, and a fine-tuned RoBERTa roughly matched an open Vicuna model on four tasks. The speaker also lists quantization, serving frameworks, savings plans and batch processing as ways to cut hosting bills. A 1.5-billion-parameter Bielik Mini was presented as small enough to run on phones and Raspberry Pi.

The closing part covers failure modes. A wolf-versus-husky classifier with over 80% accuracy turned out to rely on snow in the background, so explainability tools should be used to check what a model actually relies on. Models also drift as the world changes, which calls for production monitoring. An airline chatbot gave a customer wrong discount advice, and a court ordered the refund. Retrieval from a knowledge base reduces hallucinations, guardrails filter inputs and outputs against jailbreaks, and GDPR and the EU AI Act set legal limits.

talks.title: 4Developers Łódź 2024: Łukasz Pięta - Embracing Clean Architecture in Spring Boot and Kotlin
talks.teaser: The session explains architectural tradeoffs, then refactors a layered Spring Boot Kotlin app toward ports, adapters, and use cases.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing software architecture as the record of decisions over time rather than a fixed blueprint, and by grouping architectural drivers into functional needs, quality attributes, technical constraints, and business pressure such as hard deadlines. It uses a concrete example where added functionality and performance work run into team inexperience with a new library or an immovable release date, often forcing maintainability and readability to suffer.

The middle compares layered, onion, and hexagonal approaches, then links Uncle Bob’s clean architecture to testability and independence from frameworks, databases, and user interfaces. A small Spring Boot and Kotlin service begins with simple product endpoints, then grows to support two discount types and HTTP price calculation while staying in a three-layer layout where JPA entities double as the business model.

The closing live refactor extracts persistence behind a repository port implemented in an adapter, removes API-layer DTOs from domain services, splits pricing into its own service, pushes Spring transactional and bean configuration outward, and adds a dedicated use case so the structure reads clearly. A C4-style diagram summarizes presentation, application, domain, and persistence. Takeaways include judging cleanliness by coupling, test difficulty, mixed concerns, cycles, and uncertainty about where a change belongs.

Sebastian Dąbkowski presents narrative architecture as a documentation storyline that keeps business sponsors, architects, and developers aligned across long projects. Using building metaphors from Sagrada Família to a botched gateway in a wall, he argues that decisions must be explained in linked chapters rather than isolated diagrams.

His pipeline stitches business context, architecture decision records, functional and nonfunctional requirements, event storming, bounded-context components named by behavior, quality attributes, architecture style selection via scoring worksheets, C4 views, deployment sketches, fitness functions, metrics trends, and Team Topologies constraints. Each artifact cross-links forward and back so readers can follow why microservices, monoliths, or stream-aligned teams were chosen.

Dąbkowski cites O’Reilly sources, an Architecture Cata win, and cautions that the approach pays off only when systems keep evolving. The session is a Polish-language software-architecture methods talk for developers who must justify structure to nontechnical buyers.
