talks.title: 4DevelopersWrocław2024: Karol Horosin -Serverless Deployment of Large Language Models on AWS Lambda
talks.teaser: Shows how to package a quantized small language model in a Docker image and run it on AWS Lambda, with timings and cost.
talks.summary:
Karol Horosin walks through running a small language model on AWS Lambda, a serverless runtime normally used for short, small functions with no GPU. The talk argues that compact models and higher Lambda limits make this workable for narrow cases, such as a separate model per customer, privacy-sensitive workloads, or full control over the model. Managed LLM APIs remain the better default for most teams, and the speaker lists alternatives including SageMaker, ECS or Kubernetes, Google Cloud Run and Hugging Face hosted endpoints.

The build starts from a minimal Lambda handler packaged as a Docker image, then adds a quantized small Microsoft model (Phi-2) run through the llama.cpp Python wrapper. A multi-stage Docker build compiles llama.cpp with OpenBLAS, and the model loads outside the handler so warm invocations reuse it. The deployment is a bash script that creates an ECR repository and execution role, pushes an ARM64 image, and creates or updates the function with a Lambda URL. Memory sets the CPU allocation, so the 10 GB setting with six cores was used. Lowering memory to about 3.5 GB made responses slower and raised cost.

Measured results were 17 seconds for a cold run and 9 seconds for a warm one, at about 9.2 tokens per second, with an 8-second load for the image. The speaker compared the cost with GPT-3.5 Turbo and concluded that self-hosting is not cost-effective unless privacy, control or per-customer isolation matter. Practical takeaways are to test memory settings against runtime and cost, and to consider smaller fine-tuned models for specific tasks.

talks.title: 4Developers Wrocław2024: Paweł Zubkiewicz - Optymalizacja kosztów AWS dla zapracowanego dewelopera
talks.teaser: Shows developers where to find easy AWS cost savings, from budget alerts to unused volumes and GP2 to GP3 disk swaps.
talks.summary:
The talk walks developers through the quickest ways to cut AWS spending, starting with what the billing console already shows. Budget alerts, free tier notifications and anomaly detection act as a safety net. The speaker's example was a logging cost that rose from about 4 dollars a day to 94, caused by an error being logged in a loop. Because AWS has no hard spending cap, he recommends reviewing costs regularly, not only when an alert fires.

Next comes Cost Optimization Hub, a free service that must be enabled and gathers recommendations from several places. The speaker sorts savings into waste, misconfiguration, architecture and organization-level discounts, and focuses on the first two because developers can act on them. Waste examples include unattached EBS volumes, which are snapshotted before deletion, idle NAT gateways, and databases with no connections for 14 days. Non-production environments that run 12 hours a day on weekdays can save up to 64 percent. For misconfiguration, switching GP2 volumes to GP3 is about 20 percent cheaper and was shown to cut one client's disk bill from 100,000 to 80,000 dollars a month. In another case, an RDS instance paid for 1000 provisioned IOPS while using about 40.

The talk closes by noting that most Trusted Advisor cost checks need paid support, which the speaker considers not worth buying just for those checks. Developers can find the same problems themselves by reviewing costs and resources. Architecture changes and commitment discounts are left to finance teams.

talks.title: 4Developers Wrocław 2024: Mateusz Nowak - Moc i Magia Domain-Driven Design przez pryzmat Heroes III
talks.teaser: Uses Heroes III mechanics to show how event modeling and Domain-Driven Design reveal business rules before code is written.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that business software is better designed around processes and behaviour than around nouns and database tables. Mateusz Nowak uses the battle and recruitment mechanics of Heroes III as a running model. Two domain experts give contradictory answers about whether a hero always belongs to a player. Making that field nullable would spread extra conditionals and regression risk through the code. Instead, the speaker splits the concept by behaviour, viewing it through being, becoming and behaving, with behaving as the leading lens.

He then shows a workflow: a quick event storming pass to collect events and group them into processes, followed by event modeling, which lays out screens, commands, events and the API the UI needs. Boundaries are drawn where a change in one process must not disturb another. Work is split into command, view and automation slices so developers can build in parallel. Given-when-then examples become tests, and two functions, decide and evolve, implement the domain without requiring event sourcing. Automation links separate modules by reacting to events.

The closing argument is that quality is largely decided during planning, so code review can shift toward checking that the agreed model made it into the code. The speaker notes that open source projects still rely on pull request reviews. The method matters less than the outcome: a shared understanding between developers and domain experts that lets the system change with the business.

talks.title: 4Developers Wrocław 2024: Adrian Bury: Jak sprawić, by frontend i backend stali się przyjaciółmi?
talks.teaser: Shows how dedicated backend-for-frontend layers align web and mobile clients with a lean cron API without bloating the core.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a product team that builds Cron Manager so users can configure scheduled jobs instead of running reports by hand. Frontend mocks call for friendly schedule text and next run times in tables, while the backend team wants a minimal GET contract with ids, status, and raw cron expressions only.

Three paths are weighed: extending the core API, parsing crons in the browser with libraries that add roughly 30 KB to the bundle, or adding a Backend for Frontend that maps core responses server-side. The BFF keeps Cron API stable, drops raw expressions from what the UI receives, and later combines translation calls for localized dynamic fields when the app expands to new markets.

Mobile push notifications and a second client reopen the same tensions. One shared BFF, GraphQL, a dedicated BFF squad, and ad-hoc edits from Kotlin or Swift teams each bring coordination or quality risks. The approach in use splits web BFF and mobile BFF so each client stack owns its mapper layer. Practitioners gain a clear split between business core, presentation mapping, and when extra deployable tiers are worth the cost.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2024: Julia Papée
talks.teaser: Projektowanie dla różnorodności details 4Developers Katowice 2024: Julia Papée.
talks.summary:
The talk defines cross-cultural UX design as understanding cultural differences and letting them shape interfaces. The speaker opens with a personal purchase from an American retailer, where an unfamiliar credit card option and a partial charge caused confusion, and suggests local methods such as BLIK would have helped. Other cases: Amazon's icon was read as a ping-pong paddle in India and fixed with a Hindi label, and a car named Matador meant killer in Puerto Rico.

The middle section looks at how culture shapes layouts, comparing the British and Chinese Firefox sites through a theory of analytic versus holistic thinking. A Dutch travel site adapted for German users added quality certificates, more payment options and fuller trip details. It also covers low and high context communication, cultural intelligence and a cultural dimensions model whose dimensions are now questioned. The exploratory study used 12 participants, five Swedish and seven German, with interviews, usability tests of Volvo and Audi sites and a questionnaire.

Participants split roughly in half on whether interfaces should be adapted or standardised, though all favoured more inclusive design. Swedish participants almost always chose the Swedish version of a site, describing a minimalist look with soft pastel colours, while Germans found a German style hard to define and valued simple navigation. The talk closes with per-country guidance on layout, UX writing, UI design and functionality, plus advice on building cultural intelligence in teams and reviewing existing research before entering a new market.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2024: Nina Westfal, Ola Hantkiewicz–Skuteczny UX writing - moc prostego języka
talks.teaser: Covers plain-language UX rules, readability tools, and empathetic copy for users with mental health and neurodiversity needs.
talks.summary:
Two product designers open by defining plain language as short, familiar wording that helps people read, understand, and act, contrasted with cryptic error screens and jargon-heavy interfaces. Through repeated 404-page exercises they walk through rules such as simple sentences, getting to the point quickly, guiding next steps, clear structure, and unambiguous labels on buttons and links, illustrated with banking, retail, social, and mobile examples.

The second half shifts to measurement and inclusion. One presenter demos Logios fog-index checks on dense banking legalese, AI-assisted drafts with ChatSonic, and Jasnopis simplification workflows. The other ties simple copy to neurodiversity and mental health statistics, warning against shaming or guilt-based nudges in apps like Reddit, Duolingo, and ride-hailing promos, while highlighting progress cues, reassurance, accessibility settings, and safety features from well-known services.

They close with behavioral linguistics: user-centered tone, benefit-focused calls to action, emotional empathy, and A/B testing, plus a brand-appropriate 404 that balances creativity with clarity. Practitioners leave with concrete rewriting habits, tool names to audit readability, and a checklist for inclusive, low-cognitive-load interface text.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2024: Grzegorz Grzywocz - Płynne animacje i przejścia z API View Transitions
talks.teaser: Shows how the View Transitions API animates DOM changes and page navigation with plain CSS, plus framework support and limits.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the View Transitions API, a browser feature for animating changes to a page's DOM and moving between states without a JavaScript animation library. The speaker places it as the newest step after CSS animations and JavaScript libraries, and separates two levels. Same-document transitions, which animate changes within one page, have been available in Chromium browsers for about a year. Cross-document transitions between separate HTML pages of the same origin only reached stable Chrome recently. The speaker says Safari added the feature with a recent iOS release, while Firefox does not support it yet.

The demonstrations cover the basic setup. Matching elements on two pages get the same view-transition-name, so the browser can morph one into the other, even when they are different element types. Transitions are then customised with ordinary CSS animations, such as changing duration, opacity, scale or hue. A small JavaScript clock shows calling document.startViewTransition to wrap a DOM update. Elements that exist on only one page animate in or out alone. Angular's router and Astro's multi-page approach can enable the feature with little code. Limits mentioned include odd SVG scaling, some blend modes not working on images, and the need for a skeleton placeholder when the target page loads data slowly.

The talk closes with case studies: a bus-ticket booking company used transitions to keep animations light for users on old phones or weak connections, and a Japanese media company added them to a news site. The practical takeaways are to respect the reduced-motion setting, provide fallbacks with @supports for browsers without support, and use the feature in moderation, since animating too many properties can hurt performance.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2024: Marcin Krzanicki - Rok 2025. Musisz czy chcesz w dostępność?
talks.teaser: Maps Poland's 2025 accessibility rules, product scope, and why teams should embrace inclusion rather than minimum legal compliance.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a staged “crash” to stress how teams panic when digital services fail, then pivots to Poland’s Accessibility Act entering force on 28 June 2025 as the national transposition of the European Accessibility Act. Where commerce once treated accessibility as optional business cases, covered products and services—from operating systems and smartphones to retail banking, e-commerce, and passenger transport portals—must meet universal design expectations, with WCAG cited as the practical benchmark for digital offerings.

The middle walks through who is actually in scope, who remains exempt (micro-enterprises, legacy hardware already on the market, and public transport covered elsewhere), and enforcement beyond turnover-based fines, including withdrawal of products or suspension of services. US ADA litigation examples and European momentum illustrate the shift. Interactive audience exercises frame accessibility as situational and temporary exclusion, not only wheelchair iconography, and contrast compliance driven by fear with work driven by empathy—illustrated through game accessibility programs, keyboard-first product fixes, Deaf users’ needs beyond captions, and plain-language tooling on public health sites.

The close urges developers to treat guidelines as craft rather than checkbox exams, mentions semantic HTML and frontend framework accessibility comparisons, and shares form-design failures after bereavement alongside UK government research on bereavement benefits. Global disability statistics and shared reading materials reinforce building for future selves and diverse users, not only audit deadlines.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2024: Michał Jagosz - Znajdź siedem różnic.. Czyli o tym "czy to musi tak być?"
talks.teaser: Shows designers and developers how to collaborate earlier using breadboarding, quick sketches and shared benchmarks.
talks.summary:
Michał Jagosz opens with the frustration of comparing a finished product with the design it was supposed to follow, using a spot-the-differences frame. He explains that designers and developers notice different things, that handoffs done one after another leave gaps, and that a waterfall process can persist inside sprints. He also touches on low-code tools, which spread design skills but can set unrealistic expectations about how long real development takes.

The middle of the talk covers working techniques for mixed teams. Breadboarding sketches how a product works and how screens connect, without visual detail, so developers can flag implementation limits early. In one example about adding autopay to invoices, the team moved the feature into the payment flow after spotting problems in the first version. He also recommends rough marker sketches, shared benchmarks, reusable components, and annotated mockups that show interaction states and corner cases.

He closes with research and team habits. Rapid iterative testing and evaluation uses small studies with frequent fixes, ideally late in a cycle on a working prototype, and developers can join sessions as observers or read the reports. He urges teams to discuss what could go wrong, treat tangled code as a sign the experience may be complicated too, use existing analytics to settle defaults, and keep one shared channel open.

talks.summary: A KSAVIA data-engineering lead demos building enterprise chatbots on Amazon Bedrock: foundation-model APIs, content generation versus retrieval-augmented generation with OpenSearch Serverless knowledge bases, citation-backed answers, guardrails that refuse out-of-context queries, and Agents orchestration wiring OpenAPI Lambdas for travel-booking style workflows. He contrasts Opus versus Haiku costs, warns that chat history inflates token bills, and stresses chunking quality as most of real bot engineering time.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2024: Marcin Szeliga
talks.teaser: Shows practical uses of generative AI assistants across data analysis, coding, documents and email, with their limits.
talks.summary:
The session, given in Polish as a last-minute addition to the machine learning track, offers a practical tour of generative AI in everyday IT work. The speaker briefly explains how large language models build on the 2017 Transformer architecture, turn words into embeddings, and learn through pretraining and fine-tuning. Most of the time goes to live demos: Perplexity for research and reading the EU AI Act, Microsoft 365 Copilot summarising a confidential campaign report and a long email thread, and Copilot in Azure Data Studio writing SQL. The first generated query had valid syntax but failed against the real tables, while a later attempt that received the database structure produced a working one.

Further demos cover generated images, presentations built from a plan, drafted emails, and a coding assistant in Cursor that wrote a web client for a scoring script. A résumé-screening test with hidden white-text instructions showed indirect prompt injection, and the model ignored the planted instruction. The speaker stresses hallucinations, the need to check every output, and provider data terms that may let prompts reach training data, with local open models offered as one alternative. Copyright of AI-generated content remains with humans, and the EU AI Act regulates systems by risk.

The takeaway is to verify AI output before using it, read the data terms, and weigh the risks of each tool and model against the task.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2024: Ignacy Szreter - Kiedy sama modularyzacja to za mało
talks.teaser: Maps Eric Evans's large-scale DDD layers onto a .NET payments example as invoices, payroll, and shifting rules outgrow simple modules.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces large-scale structures from Domain-Driven Design as a way to manage organizational and domain complexity when tactical patterns and bounded contexts alone no longer clarify module or team boundaries. The speaker frames the idea around responsibility layers, Conway’s law, and scaling teams, contrasting hype-driven agility with solid engineering habits.

A fictional startup builds an in-house invoice payment flow in .NET: once-only payment submission, five-day delays for software vendors, and doubled delays when company balance is negative. When payroll automation is added, invoice-specific rules break the shared payment model. The walkthrough refactors toward generic payments, anticorruption translators, and application services that hold invoice-specific logic. New demands—AI-driven date shifts, VIP contractors, and state entities—push payment-date rules out of orchestration into a stable operation abstraction, concrete policy transformations, and a factory-like decision layer.

The four layers—capability, operations, policies, and decision support—are checked against dependency direction and everyday language. Practitioners are urged to adopt layers only when complexity truly warrants them, train the team, keep at most about five layers, and treat adoption as a deliberate, reversible organizational choice rather than a dogmatic import from the book.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2024: Dominik Guzy
talks.teaser: Idempotentność API details 4Developers Katowice 2024: Dominik Guzy.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at 4Developers Katowice 2024, Dominik Guzy explores the concept of idempotency in API design and distributed systems. He explains how unexpected network retries or message redelivery can cause unintended duplicate operations (such as double financial transactions or corrupted sports stats) and demonstrates practical ways to implement idempotency using both C#/.NET and TypeScript.

### Key Topics
- **Theoretical & Mathematical Foundation**: Introduced historically by Benjamin Peirce in 1870, idempotency defines operations where applying them multiple times yields the same result as applying them once. Real-world physical analogies include pressing an elevator floor button or a pedestrian crossing button multiple times.
- **HTTP Semantics & Distributed Systems**: While HTTP safe methods (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`) and certain unsafe methods (`PUT`, `DELETE`) are inherently idempotent with respect to server state, methods like `POST` and `PATCH` are not by default. Distributed systems like AWS SQS and Apache Kafka rely on "at-least-once delivery", where failures or timeouts can cause duplicate message processing, necessitating idempotent consumer design. Load-store CPU architectures (e.g., ARM) also handle page faults via idempotent instruction replay.
- **Strategies for Implementation**:
  1. *Server-calculated payload hashing* (e.g., AWS Lambda Powertools pattern with DynamoDB persistence).
  2. *Client-provided idempotency keys* passed via headers (e.g., the pattern popularized by Stripe).

### Technical Details
- **C# / AWS Lambda Powertools Demo**: Implemented via AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model) with a DynamoDB table containing a hash key and a TTL (`expiration`). Instead of hashing the entire request payload (which is brittle), Guzy extracts a specific property (`name`) as the idempotency key with a 10-second TTL. The server checks DynamoDB, sets initial state, processes the handler, records the response, and serves subsequent matching calls directly from the cache.
- **TypeScript / Hono Framework Demo**: Using the Hono framework, an endpoint enforces an `x-idempotency-key` header via a validator. An in-memory cache (JavaScript `Map`) stores responses indexed by the client-provided key. If present, the cached response is returned immediately (reducing response time from ~7 ms to ~3–4 ms), preventing duplicate executions of `POST` actions.

### Takeaways
Idempotency is simple to implement yet vital for preventing severe bugs in systems that handle financial transactions, real-world value changes, event sourcing, or CQRS architectures. Engineers can delegate key generation to the client or compute targeted payload hashes on the server to make endpoints resilient against retries.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2024: Marek Chrapek, Anka Wolańska
talks.teaser: Explains how evolutionary architecture keeps software ready for change through architectural tests and team practices.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a problem: early architecture decisions are hard to reverse, yet teams make them when they know least about the domain. Requirements shift with markets, competitors and key clients, so the speakers propose steering architecture over time rather than fixing it up front. Borrowing the idea of a fitness function from evolutionary algorithms, they argue that architecture is multidimensional. Tests, security, performance, legal constraints and team skills interact, so no single formula declares a system ready for change.

In the middle, the speakers look at team growth through a forming, storming, norming and performing model, showing how expertise rises and falls when key people leave. They recommend encoding rules in tools, such as architectural tests that fail a build when a domain module pulls in a framework, rather than policing people in code review. Other examples cover avoiding both bare-bones designs that pile up technical debt and over-engineering chosen for a CV, recording decisions in architecture decision records, Conway's law, removing feature flags once rollouts finish, and questioning API versioning for internal consumers.

They close by saying the real formula is the whole delivery pipeline, from gathering requirements through releases and incident response. That pipeline, not any single tool, is what keeps an architecture prepared for new features.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2024: Damian Dziaduch–Beyond cronjobs: adopting long running business processes
talks.teaser: The session explains how an e-commerce print platform replaces cron polling with event-driven process managers and tames queue spikes.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining long-running business processes as workflows that spend much of their time waiting on external steps, using automotive assembly as an intuitive analogy. The speaker then describes Printify’s challenge of tracking print-partner order fulfillment: a legacy cron job periodically queried the database for stale orders, fanned out partner status checks through queues, and struggled under holiday-season load despite healthy indexes.

The first case study moves to an event-driven process manager with start, continue, and stop handlers. Work is scheduled forward on delayed jobs instead of scanning for neglected records. Production rollouts exposed gaps when partners reported no status change, a bug that spiked continue logs, and a shift of database load from the orders collection into a MongoDB-backed jobs store—compounded by SQS’s fifteen-minute maximum message delay when ten-hour delays were required. Fixes included a no-change status event, corrected Mongo indexes, observability, and parallel running with the old cron until edge cases were covered.

A second case covers cyclic HTTP health checks for on-prem devices at partner print shops, message buffering when devices fail, and Symfony Messenger routing that accidentally duplicated messages across two SQS queues. Dedicated FIFO queues with content-based deduplication and queue-level delay stabilized scheduling. Practitioners are urged to favor observability, learn platform limits early, and understand framework routing before shipping queue-heavy designs.

talks.title: Piotr Bazydło: Szukanie podatności w Microsoft SharePoint: Case Study | OMH 2024
talks.teaser: Walks through hunting two SharePoint bugs: an XXE caused by URL parsing confusion and a deserialization RCE.
talks.summary:
Piotr Bazydło, a vulnerability researcher at Zero Day Initiative, starts with how he approaches hard targets, long-lived enterprise products where easy bug classes are already mined out. He stresses long-term effort, side projects to stay motivated, studying a product's public history and attack surfaces before reading code, and revisiting old attack surfaces since one code change can reopen them. Deep reading of framework and library code often explains how product features behave.

The first case is an XML external entity issue in SharePoint's data source classes. Several chained reader objects carried different security settings, so a parameter entity still made an outbound request before .NET threw an exception. The secure resolver blocked local host and file access, but SharePoint's own data source parsed a crafted URL as a relative path to a file stored in its database. That parsing mismatch gave an unrestricted policy and a working out-of-band channel.

The second case is a deserialization remote code execution. A type binder meant for a web control allow list guarded a BinaryFormatter path, and one permitted class derived from DataSet, so a gadget chain reached an internal XML serializer. A SOAP WebPart method then deserialized attacker-supplied attached properties, and a live demo ran a calculator on a SharePoint server. The takeaway: check where components disagree and never assume a mature product is exhausted.

talks.title: Wojciech Reguła: Izolacja aplikacji na macOS i jej exploitacja | OMH 2024
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Wojciech Reguła: Izolacja aplikacji na macOS i jej exploitacja | OMH 2024.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Wojciech Reguła presents a deep dive into macOS application isolation and process control mechanisms, debunking the common assumption that macOS behaves like traditional Linux. The talk demonstrates how macOS enforces process isolation even between tasks owned by the same user ID (UID), how mechanisms like System Integrity Protection (SIP) and Hardened Runtime enforce these boundaries, and how architectural oversights or insecure configurations in popular password managers allow attackers to execute code and steal credentials.

### Key Topics
- **macOS Architecture vs. Linux**: macOS is a hybrid kernel combining FreeBSD (POSIX compliance, process management, signals) and Mach (tasks, ports, multitasking, virtual memory). Unlike traditional Unix/Linux where processes with identical UIDs can inspect and control each other, macOS prohibits cross-process control unless explicitly allowed via entitlements such as `com.apple.security.get-task-allow`.
- **System Integrity Protection (SIP) & TCC**: SIP acts as an enforced global sandbox across the operating system (rootless model). Breaking process isolation can allow attackers to hijack entitlements, bypass Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC) privacy prompts, escalate privileges to root, or defeat system protections.
- **Process Injection Requirements & AMFI**: Controlling another process requires acquiring its task port via `task_for_pid`, which is strictly audited by Apple Mobile File Integrity (AMFI) and Taskgated. It is blocked for platform binaries and Hardened Runtime processes unless debugging entitlements exist.
- **Hardened Runtime & Entitlement Exceptions**: Hardened Runtime blocks code injection, `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` (the macOS equivalent of `LD_PRELOAD`), and dynamic library hijacking. However, exceptions such as `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation` allow arbitrary dynamic library loading.

### Technical Details & Case Studies
Reguła analyzes exploitation vectors across various password managers:
- **MacPass**: While Hardened Runtime was active, library validation was disabled to support plugins loaded from `~/Library/Application Support/MacPass`. Attackers can drop an untrusted dynamic library or plugin into this unconfined directory, enable `loadIncompatiblePlugins` in defaults, and execute code inside MacPass to dump the database and master password.
- **Bitwarden**: Distributed via the Mac App Store, where Hardened Runtime is merely recommended rather than enforced by Apple's notarization pipeline. Due to the missing Hardened Runtime flag, standard library injection via `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` succeeded directly, allowing a keylogger to capture the master password.
- **NordPass**: An Electron-based application where Electron debugging fuses were left open (`enable_node_cli_inspect_arguments`). Using the speaker's open-source tool `electronizer`, arbitrary JavaScript was injected via Chrome DevTools protocol over WebSockets to extract the master password.
- **KeePassXC**: Examined in the context of browser integration. While IPC communication uses asymmetric cryptography, the browser extension stores the private communication key in unprotected browser files without sandboxing. An attacker can read the key with a single bash command, spoof the extension, and retrieve credentials.
- **Proton Pass**: Operates purely as a browser extension, keeping decryption and secrets inside the browser's JavaScript runtime. Automation frameworks like Selenium can instrument the browser directly to read decrypted secrets.

### Takeaways & Developer Recommendations
- Always enable **Hardened Runtime** and eliminate dangerous entitlement exceptions like disabled library validation whenever possible.
- Keep **SIP (System Integrity Protection)** enabled across all managed environments (`csrutil status`). Disabling SIP degrades macOS security guarantees.
- Implement macOS App Sandboxing, which prevents unauthorized processes from reading application-specific directories.
- In Electron applications, disable debugging flags and developer inspection fuses in production builds.
- Conduct third-party security assessments rather than relying solely on automated store review mechanisms.

talks.title: Marcin Ratajczyk: Kto to zrobił? I dlaczego (tu wstaw dowolny kraj), ale tylko na 21,37%? | OMH 2024
talks.teaser: Outlines probabilistic cyber attribution, state doctrine, vendor naming, attribution models, and major false-flag case studies.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by defining cyber attribution as assigning responsibility to states, groups, or individuals for hostile activity, always with graded probability rather than certainty. It outlines a practical pipeline from collecting or buying telemetry through clustering incidents, categorizing motives and actors, deciding how far to go beyond naming a country, and choosing whether to publish findings—along with the intelligence, operational, and diplomatic tradeoffs of going public.

The middle surveys how major powers frame cyber in national strategy, maps military and intelligence units to well-known intrusion sets, and explains why different vendors use incompatible group names. It contrasts espionage-heavy network exploitation with rarer destructive attacks, summarizes several published attribution models mixing technical and non-technical evidence, and stresses that individual indicators can be faked even when doing so across an entire operation is harder.

Case studies anchor the narrative: Olympic Destroyer’s misleading artifacts versus GRU/Sandworm accountability, North Korean activity against Poland’s financial regulator with deliberate Russian-language decoys, and the long-running Ghost Writer influence and phishing campaign where industry and government assessments diverged on Belarus versus Russia. The close argues that private organizations gain more from hunting and hardening than from chasing public blame, while state bodies remain the right audience for formal attribution work.

talks.title: Kamil Bojarski: Odstraszanie i strategiczna odpowiedź na operacje cyber | OMH 2024
talks.teaser: Walks through how states use deterrence, sanctions and persistent engagement to respond to cyber operations against private firms.
talks.summary:
The talk moves the question of cyber operations from individual incidents to the level of states. The speaker opens with a thought experiment: a new chief security officer at a heavy-industry supplier in Western Europe or the United States hears in a first briefing about drone reconnaissance, special forces break-ins and air strikes. The point is that private companies can sit in the path of geopolitical conflict. The talk then introduces the state toolkit, covering diplomacy, information, economic measures, intelligence and law enforcement. It recalls how deterrence theory, rooted in nuclear strategy, was adapted by the US Cyber Solarium Commission into layered deterrence: shaping behaviour, denying benefits and imposing costs.

The middle section looks at examples. A 2015 US-China agreement on commercial cyber espionage is assessed using analysis that showed a sharp drop in Chinese activity, though the speaker stresses that causation is uncertain and the effect faded as trade tensions grew. Indictments are presented as strong evidentiary documents that rarely lead to prosecution, and sanctions as a lever whose impact depends on relations between states. European approaches are contrasted, with resilience measures such as sector coordination and new EU legislation.

The final part covers persistent engagement, the idea of continuous offensive activity against adversary infrastructure. Examples include US Cyber Command operations against ISIS and troll farms, and the deployment of teams to partner countries. The takeaway is that state responses are hard to measure, yet they shape the threat environment that private organisations must plan for.

talks.title: Maciej Broniarz: Secret? Midnight? Zamieć? | OMH 2024
talks.teaser: Traces a Microsoft cloud intrusion and its fallout for Polish NGOs, with practical hardening lessons for Microsoft 365 environments.
talks.summary:
The speaker revisits a Microsoft incident, focusing on its effects on victims rather than the technical path. Attackers reached a legacy, non-production test tenant, gained elevated access to production, and stayed inside for a long time. They read mailboxes of security staff and reached source code repositories. Microsoft only later told organisations what data about them was likely exposed.

The main case is a group of Polish non-governmental organisations, some working with Ukrainian refugees, linked by Microsoft to a campaign it calls Secret Blizzard. In one case the timeline ran from detection on 11 January to last attacker activity on 15 January, with notice on 26 January. Seven Polish organisations were taken over in a single day using the same model. Malicious binaries went unflagged by Defender for about a dozen days or more, and Talos helped with analysis. WordPress sites connected to Microsoft 365 sign-in held permissions the attackers could use.

Lessons the speaker draws include enforcing two-factor authentication, locking or switching off workstations overnight, and keeping SSH keys and their passphrases out of plain text. Limit Global Admin rights, review service principals and app permissions, and decide whether users may register their own apps. Logs held the trail but were rarely read; one organisation had a mail rule quietly marking administrators' messages as read.

talks.title: Krzysztof Zieliński, Paweł Piekutowski: Testy TLPT - nowe podejście do realizacji Red Team | OMH
talks.teaser: Explains how DORA's TLPT requirement turns red team testing into a regulated, threat-led exercise for financial institutions.
talks.summary:
Speakers from a Polish financial-sector cybersecurity team explain threat-led penetration testing (TLPT), a new requirement under the EU's DORA regulation that applies from January 2025. They start from the limits of standard penetration tests and code audits, which examine single systems and miss weaknesses between systems, processes and people. Red team exercises close that gap, but they run against production environments and carry real risk, so DORA makes them mandatory for the largest financial entities. The framework builds on TIBER-EU, and the talk walks through the actors: a control team that alone knows the test is running, test managers appointed by the authority, a threat intelligence provider that prepares a targeted report, an external red team, and a blue team that is tested without advance warning.

Preparation may take up to six months and includes a sector threat landscape report, a secret codename, and dedicated communication channels that avoid the IT department. The red team then plans attack scenarios and a schedule of stages, with fallback options such as an internal user with minimal privileges if the initial vector fails. Scenarios cover supply-chain attacks, ransomware on a workstation and hacktivist groups. Afterwards, both teams compare reports and hold a purple team session to rework detection rules. The speakers estimate a full cycle at 12 to 15 months, repeated every three years, and note that finding qualified testers will be a challenge.

talks.title: Marek Zmysłowski, Konrad Jędrzejczyk, Piotr Duszyński: AI Code Generator - przyjaciel czy wróg?
talks.teaser: Surveys business risks of AI-generated code, including security flaws, package hallucinations, licensing and privacy issues.
talks.summary:
This Polish-language talk, presented by Marek Zmysłowski, asks whether AI code generators are a friend or an enemy for businesses that build and sell software. It starts with the appeal: faster delivery, less time on routine code, fewer people to hire, and the claim that generated code can be consistent and easy to scale. The speaker then turns to the downsides.

The middle of the talk covers privacy and data leakage when prompts are sent to online services, unclear ownership and licensing of generated code, and dependence on a single vendor whose terms or availability can change overnight. It also covers maintainability: generated code can be bloated, poorly documented and hard to debug. Two examples show plausible but wrong output. One asks a model for the lyrics of a national anthem, starting from the second verse, and gets invented text. Another asks for a Basic program that draws a Sierpinski triangle and produces calls to functions that do not exist. A package-hallucination case is also shown: a dependency name the model invented was registered by someone else and downloaded tens of thousands of times.

The talk stresses security. Generated code often lacks input validation, output sanitising and authentication checks, and the speaker cites studies in which a large share of generated programs contained vulnerabilities. The takeaway is to treat AI output as untrusted, combine it with testing, code review, audits and coding standards, and set clear company policy and training on when such tools may be used.

talks.title: Paweł Jałowiczor, Damian Kuczaty: Kiedyś | OMH 2024
talks.teaser: Phased municipal roads IT modernization covers monitoring, helpdesk, VPN access, printing, PAM, and continuity planning lessons.
talks.summary:
Staff from the Bielsko-Biała municipal roads administration describe how years of incremental projects replaced reactive firefighting with preventive operations. They began with environmental and service monitoring that delivers SMS and email alerts, then calibrated noise versus signal through alert tuning and false-positive triage. Server-room cooling evolved from inadequate portable units to redundant commercial systems, staged over roughly two years with procurement planning suited to public budgets.

The narrative covers helpdesk and intranet adoption—including priority rules that nudged hallway requests into tickets—individual VPN accounts for more than 80 external technicians, videoconferencing rooms, NFC access and time recording, and centralized secure printing that cut costs by more than half. Privileged access management added session recording and controls, building on earlier contract and identity work. Business continuity moved from paper policies to owned systems, realistic continuity plans with a critical ITS vendor, and weekend failure exercises.

Practitioners hear recurring themes: executive visibility, phased funding, resistance to change, and avoiding exceptions that undermine rollouts. The speakers argue the effort improved sleep more than maintaining the old “someday” posture, while noting ongoing challenges such as MDM and GPS concerns.

talks.title: Michał Kłaput: Hardware Hacking - odzyskiwanie klucza TPM za pomocą retro konsoli | OMH 2024
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Michał Kłaput: Hardware Hacking - odzyskiwanie klucza TPM za pomocą retro konsoli | OMH 2024.
talks.summary: Michał Kłaput retraces how a Polish TV report on a handheld car-unlock gimmick led him to mod an Anbernic emulation handheld into a full Linux platform with USB OTG ports for security experiments. He explains discrete TPM modules, BitLocker expectations, and why Microsoft documents that physical attackers can read keys unless a startup PIN is enforced through Group Policy. TPM 1.2 chips on legacy LPC buses reuse unencrypted PS/2-era low-pin-count signaling, letting a Raspberry Pi Pico sniffer capture frame, clock, and lane traffic during boot. Existing PicoTPM-sniffer tooling reconstructs decryption material that Dislocker can mount on Linux, exposing filesystem secrets despite intact BitLocker branding. TPM 2.0 trials on his board were flaky because single-bit line noise corrupts recovered keys. Mitigations include TPM-plus-PIN unlock, soldered TPMs, and awareness that hotel-room physical access remains a practical theft scenario. He closes urging realistic threat models beyond marketing claims of maximum protection.

talks.title: Anna Wasilewska-Śpioch: Wojna w rosyjskim darknecie | OMH 2024
talks.teaser: Traces how Russian darknet drug markets reshuffled after the Hydra takedown, with rival forums, state links and wartime ties.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at what happened to the Russian darknet after Hydra, the dominant drug marketplace, was taken down. It opens with the April 2022 seizure of its servers in Germany and the bitcoin reported as seized with them, then covers the US sanctions, an indictment naming a suspected administrator, and Russian arrests linked to a hosting company that had ties to the platform. Russian authorities reportedly arrested three people in total, and the speaker questions how much of the case was really about Hydra.

The middle section follows the rival shops that moved in, including Rutor, OMG, Kraken, Mega and Black Sprut, and how they advertised offline, on YouTube and on Telegram. It then describes a feud involving the Solaris shop, a data leak published by a security researcher, and the Killnet activist group, whose payments from a rival market and alleged paid deanonymisation services are presented alongside competing accounts of the same events. Each episode is kept separate, with the evidence available for it.

The closing part covers the current market, with about fifteen shops and nearly 18,000 registered sellers, the drugs most often sold, and seizure figures that rose to 35.6 tonnes in 2022. Most arrests reportedly hit couriers who hide and deliver small parcels, while people at the top of the shops largely kept operating. The takeaway is that no single forum has yet become a clear monopolist.

talks.title: Wojciech Cybowski: Chiński sprzęt sieciowy: ryzyka, potencjał i inżynieria wsteczna | OMH 2024
talks.teaser: Dissects ultra-cheap Chinese routers and Wi-Fi repeaters, uncovers authentication flaws, and ports OpenWrt to them.
talks.summary:
The talk examines some of the cheapest networking equipment available from online marketplaces, including a budget router and several Wi-Fi repeaters sold at very low prices. The speaker opens the hardware and looks at memory layout, flash chips and serial console access. He notes that one router has only a small amount of onboard RAM with little room for alternative software, while the repeaters carry external RAM and easily reachable serial pins. He links the low prices to a recycling-based supply chain, which he connects to the differences found inside units that look identical from the outside.

On the software side, the serial console uses a non-standard baud rate, which a logic analyser makes easy to identify. The web interfaces run without HTTPS, log users out after five minutes, and keep login state on the device, so the login check can be bypassed by setting a flag. Several endpoints return the Wi-Fi password and the full configuration without authentication, passwords can be changed without the old one, and the admin account's login shell can be switched to a working shell. The repeaters also run extra services such as telnet, SSH and a second web server, plus a LuCI interface left over from OpenWrt on another port.

For modification, the speaker replaces the flash chip with a 16 MB part, backs up the Wi-Fi calibration partition, and builds current stable U-Boot and OpenWrt images with fixes he has published in his repository. He argues that factory firmware should not be trusted and that these devices can serve as small, low-power Linux nodes for experiments, such as an access point or a small cluster. The takeaway is that cheap hardware is a practical starting point for firmware work, but its stock software should be replaced.

talks.title: Anna Wasilewska-Śpioch, Adam Haertle: Fejkowe deepfake’i, czyli nie wszystko musi być głębokie | OMH
talks.teaser: Surveys real deepfake and impersonation scams, from a fake French minister's calls to prank hoaxes aimed at world leaders.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining deepfakes and noting that, although the technology has been discussed for years, many reported voice-cloning cases lack any recording to prove them. The speakers then walk through a concrete case: a fraudster posing as the French defence minister phoned business leaders and public figures, asking for millions of euros to be paid quietly to free hostages. Several recipients transferred money, and the trail later surfaced in a separate business email compromise investigation that linked the transfers to the same accounts.

The middle of the talk covers the Russian prank duo known as Vovan and Lexus, who phoned politicians, celebrities and officials while impersonating other people. They cut and edited their recordings to suit their narrative, and one 2021 hoax used a real clip of a Russian opposition figure looped into a video call. The speakers show that simple edits and staged footage often work as well as full synthesis, and they tie several cases to Polish institutions and to investment-scam videos built from recycled or altered material.

The closing section looks at where deepfakes are used today: most are shallow edits, audio is common in political and targeted attacks, and sexual abuse content is the most advanced area. The practical takeaways are to verify unexpected calls through a separate known channel, ask the other party to turn on video or show a profile, and publicly disclose a suspected fake before it is used against you.

talks.title: Tomasz Zieliński: Dostałeś z ministerstwa 10 milionów PDF-ów. Co teraz? | OMH 2024
talks.teaser: Shows how millions of ministry PDFs on court case assignment were parsed and published as a low-cost public website.
talks.summary:
Tomasz Zieliński explains the random case assignment system that Polish courts began using in 2018, which was meant to distribute cases fairly and evenly among judges. Little was public about how it worked, and a ministry algorithm document published in 2021 was the only official description. After a change of government, he filed a public information request for the assignment reports from 2022 and 2023. The ministry asked him to receive the data on a physical storage device, which arrived back by post with the files on it.

The dataset held about ten million PDFs, and he describes the practical problems of working with them. Directories containing very large numbers of files broke ordinary commands, simple listings took minutes, and some conversions were estimated to run for months. Parallel processing on a 16-core machine reduced a job estimated at two weeks to about a day. The extracted records, around 100 million rows, went into a 5 GB SQLite database. The result was a static website with pages for each judge, court and division, built with Hugo and served through Cloudflare Pages and a cheap VPS. He also reported findings: workload indicators in the billions, a ministry specification whose text and diagrams contradicted each other, and a period of about 1.5 years when draws appeared to come from the wrong pool.

He had planned to stop the project until a reader scraped the reports and the portal then published the data as JSON, which made the processing much quicker. The main takeaway is that a public-data project can run cheaply on static hosting, while the assignment system itself still lacked transparency and workload balancing.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2024: Manfred Bjørlin
talks.teaser: Traces how an early-2000s SMS gateway moved from one big SQL script to event-driven messaging, and why that still matters.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the speaker's early-2000s SMS gateway business, which stored every message in a SQL table and ran scheduled T-SQL jobs that made HTTP calls to provider APIs. As traffic grew, congestion on both the inbound and outbound paths made indexing and archiving only a stopgap. The replacement ran as Windows services on one bare-metal server, using Microsoft Message Queuing, an internal thread pool and asynchronous database logging.

The design had clear weaknesses. The queues were not persistent, so a crash could empty them, and the whole setup depended on a single server and a single disk. When that disk failed, most of the data had to be rebuilt from vendor records and other sources. The talk then traces the same idea back through Unix pipes, early subroutine calls and real-time systems, and it reviews the recent debate over modular monoliths versus microservices, with the speaker arguing that the monolith's drawbacks outweigh its benefits as a system grows.

The closing part argues that event-driven designs are approachable today. Small Kubernetes distributions run on modest hardware, and NATS with JetStream adds persistence for edge and IoT setups, with LoRa and ESP32 examples given along the way. The speaker suggests starting with small home projects to learn messaging and clusters, and presents flexibility, scalability and faster deployment as the reasons the approach still matters.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2024: Łukasz Przybył - From NoOps to DevOps and back
talks.teaser: An engineering leader explains how a Heroku-first shop measures swings between NoOps ease and full SRE-backed operations at scale.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames DevOps, NoOps, and site reliability engineering, then ties reliability to measurable signals such as latency, errors, capacity, and throughput, plus recovery metrics like mean time to recover, mean time between failures, and restore time and point objectives for disaster planning.

The speaker describes joining a Ruby on Rails organization that ran almost entirely on Heroku without dedicated cloud administrators, until partner traffic triggered database crash loops and exposed gaps: no on-call rotation, Redis queue overflows that discarded gigabytes of jobs, and per-app monitoring that missed cross-service workflows. After hiring site reliability engineers, the company added unified Datadog observability, moved heavy databases to AWS, tracked per-application cloud spend via APIs, measured end-to-end latency for a high-volume near-real-time alerting pipeline, and scored developer self-reliance with a support-level matrix culminating in Terraform and Atlantis for safer database changes.

The closing argument is that pure NoOps suits early cost-conscious growth until spend and complexity outpace platform knobs alone; keeping NoOps as a long-term aspiration while investing in expertise, business metrics, and replaceable skills made the transformation measurable and worthwhile.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2024: Karolina Ochlik - Templatify the process and have fun
talks.teaser: Shows how teams replace manual, tribal DevOps habits with standards, templates, and quick wins from Backstage and GitHub Actions.
talks.summary:
Karolina Ochlik frames a common IT pattern: teams optimize locally while manual provisioning, inconsistent tooling, hidden dependencies, and slow environments block scale and communication. She argues that “templatifying” work means standardizing first—one repeatable way to build and deliver—then collaborating across team boundaries so knowledge and artifacts can be reused.

The middle of the talk walks through a practical stack. Reusable GitHub Actions workflows cover test, build, package, Docker images, Helm charts, and maintenance across curated languages. A small Python generator spins up a documented API with JWT and CRUD models in hours. Backstage templates scaffold multi-repo setups (backend, frontend, and a coordinating system entity) with permissions, READMEs, and catalog registration. Release flows tie YAML definitions, Jira fix versions, GitHub acceptance gates, image build and promotion, drift correction on clusters, and ServiceNow change records for compliant production releases. She also points to discovery via Backstage and catalog metadata, Crossplane-style infrastructure templates, status pages for transparent health, and automation that can react when services fail.

Practitioners should start small for quick wins, communicate progress openly, begin immediately rather than waiting for perfect tools, experiment continuously, and follow “make it work, then make it good” before polishing structure.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2024: Tomasz Manugiewicz
talks.teaser: Hybrid heroes investigates DevOpsDays Warsaw 2024: Tomasz Manugiewicz.
talks.summary:
Tomasz Manugiewicz, who leads Grant Parade engineers inside Evoke, frames team building as connecting people, processes, and tooling so relationships—not org charts—deliver outcomes. He contrasts component silos, disposable project teams, and dedicated product squads, then shows how finance pressure reintroduces bench billing and talent-pool chaos that erodes ownership.

Remote work data from Buffer, Harvard Business Review, and Vanessa Bohns’s influence research illustrate shorter but more numerous meetings, harder trust building, and executive cyber fears even as almost everyone wants hybrid freedom. Manugiewicz shares Grant Parade’s playbook: nineteen nationalities, quarterly travel gatherings, deliberate onboarding, results-based management, psychological check-ins, and celebrating wins that remote cadences often skip.

He closes with the Harvard Study of Adult Development finding that high-quality relationships dominate happiness, urging engineers to invest emotional energy at work because careers already consume the bulk of adult life.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2024: Eugene Romero - An unpopular opinion: Get rid of Pull Requests!
talks.teaser: Challenges default pull request culture with room polls, merge-time data, and criteria for when review actually helps teams.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a deliberately provocative title, then walks through how pull requests emerged from distributed open-source contribution and were adopted wholesale by companies—including co-located teams—before remote work made them ubiquitous again. The speaker frames the “pull request paradox”: reviews aim to ship good change quickly, yet reviewers and authors are both pulled away from focused work, and hands in the room affirm familiar frustrations such as oversized diffs, rubber-stamp approvals, and blocked urgent fixes.

Industry analyses cited along the way tie size to outcomes. Large changes correlate with multi-day cycle times, long idle periods, and sparse meaningful comments; per-file scrutiny effectively collapses on very wide pulls, feeding LGTM-style approvals, responsibility diffusion between author and reviewer, and follow-on defect work. The middle of the talk is less about abolishing review than diagnosing when it adds value versus when it is ceremony—for example destructive or hard-to-reverse infrastructure and schema edits versus typos, routine dependency bumps, or changes no second expert can judge.

The closing recommendations keep pull requests where they matter but shrink and stack them, favor short-lived branches and toggles, and treat each request like something a colleague would willingly pick up: clear scope, line counts, ticket links, availability, and urgency. Pair programming is offered as an alternative when the real goal is shared understanding. The takeaway is to periodically re-examine team rituals, including standups and review gates, and adapt them to how the project actually works today.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2024: Agnieszka Prędka - The Case of Learning Days!
talks.teaser: Explains how a busy DevOps squad adopted optional hack days and used delivery metrics to prove learning time did not hurt output.
talks.summary:
A Scrum Master at a global software company describes a client-facing DevOps team that ran two-week sprints, frequent releases, and constant support work while engineers reported no time to learn or try new tools. The tension between road map pressure and burnout motivated a deliberate change rather than informal, unplanned study time.

The initiative took inspiration from the Spotify model’s hack-day idea: engineers could optionally reserve one sprint day for work-aligned learning, agree the plan with the team, bank days for certification prep, and keep urgent client work from slipping. Learning days were omitted from capacity metrics. After roughly a year the team credited the program with eight role-related certificates plus courses, spikes, automation experiments, and toolchain exploration, alongside stronger satisfaction and product-side innovations.

To reassure leadership, the speaker paired the cultural change with four measures—epics completed per quarter, epic cycle time, committed-versus-completed sprint percentages in a mid‑80s to mid‑90s band, and production defects versus fixes for an app with about 7,000 monthly users—plus Spotify-style team health workshops and optional company surveys. Closing steps generalize adoption: listen, co-plan, implement, gather feedback, pick metrics, review often, and adjust; recommended reading includes the DevOps Handbook and material on developing leaders.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2024: Pedro Ivo Raimundo - No More Heroes: Why Team Composition is a Big Deal
talks.teaser: Shows how team structure shapes software outcomes, covering Conway's law, team types and the hero anti-pattern.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that the way a company groups its engineers shapes the software it produces, and that poor team composition causes recurring pain: long waits for another team to unblock work, repeated redirection to find an owner, urgent fixes made under pressure, and a constant flood of alerts that need no action. The speaker frames the problem through Conway's law and separates two views of team composition: macro, meaning how teams and organizations interact, and micro, meaning how people work together inside one team.

To make the idea concrete, the speaker uses a party-planning analogy in which three groups each optimize their own part and the result does not fit together. The fix is the inverse Conway maneuver: agree on a shared goal first, then organize teams around the outcomes wanted. The talk then covers the four team types from Team Topologies (stream-aligned, enabling, complicated subsystem and platform teams) and the ways they interact, such as collaboration, facilitation and X-as-a-service. On the micro side it covers cognitive load, the hero anti-pattern and the burnout cycle it feeds, and Dunbar's number as a reason to keep teams small with clear boundaries.

The closing advice depends on role. Leaders are encouraged to study Conway's law, experiment with team splits and rotations, and look for bottlenecks on a team map. Developers can speak up, join hiring interviews and take ownership of problems rather than only shipping features. The speaker stresses that team design depends heavily on context and that changes can be risky if they separate people who work well together.

talks.title: JDD 2024: Native Spring Applications with GraalVM
talks.teaser: Shows how GraalVM compiles Spring applications to native executables, with startup, memory and throughput trade-offs.
talks.summary:
Krzysztof Gonia introduces GraalVM as a JDK extended with its own just-in-time compiler and an ahead-of-time compiler that turns Java code into a standalone native executable with no JVM required. He explains that the build analyses which classes and methods are reachable, so unused parts are left out, and that frameworks relying on reflection need extra support. Native images start faster and use less memory, but they do not reach the peak throughput that JIT-compiled code can.

The focus is on Spring. Spring Boot 3 ships Spring AOT, which generates bean definitions and controllers as Java source during the build, so they are compiled ahead of time. In a live demo of a MongoDB-backed Spring application, the native build took longer than a plain jar, yet the executable started in under a second. Compared with a standard JVM run, the native process used far less CPU during startup and about half the memory, and it responded faster under a simple load test. He stressed that these figures depend on machine, versions and settings, and pointed to profile-guided optimization as a way to recover throughput.

Drawbacks include longer build pipelines, limited JRebel and Java agent support, libraries such as log4j that cannot be compiled, and debugging built images with tools like GDB. Suitable use cases include cloud functions, fast-scaling nodes, short-lived jobs that can run with a no-op garbage collector, command-line tools and desktop apps. His closing advice is to move to Spring Boot 3 before trying native images, and to decide based on how often the app is deployed.

talks.title: JDD 2024: How to transform in a place where everyone says "cannot be done"?
talks.teaser: Explains how a slow, manual corporate engineering process was turned around through standardization, automation and trust.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a familiar corporate problem seen across banks, telcos and pharma: environment requests move through chains of service desk tickets, and turnaround times stretch from weeks to months. Each team keeps its own unwritten rules, steps are done by hand, and knowledge sits with a few long-serving people. Adding more support staff only buys time, because the underlying process stays the same.

The proposed path begins with cataloguing what exists, then standardizing processes so common building blocks can be reused and automated. The speaker recommends repeatedly asking why inherited practices exist, since many were set up for conditions that no longer apply. On the technical side, the team adopted Backstage as a developer portal, describing components in YAML, and used templates to generate repositories with boilerplate workflows. Reusable GitHub workflows handled builds, scans and releases, pulling fixed versions from Jira, generating release notes and registering production changes in ServiceNow automatically. When Argo CD was not approved, the speaker built an in-house YAML-driven deployment tool that acted as a single source of truth, with a nightly teardown and rebuild of environments.

Progress came through quick wins on non-critical applications, then demos and brown-bag sessions that spread the tooling and built a group of supporting leaders. The team grew from two people to about eight over seven months. The main takeaway is that this approach depends on psychological safety and trust: let colleagues explain their reasons before changing how they work.

talks.title: JDD 2024: Leader in the Land of Dilemmas
talks.teaser: Walks through the dilemmas engineers meet when they become leaders, from fairness and rule-bending to toxic top performers.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who now leads developer and DevOps teams, starts with the loneliness of leadership: the role brings doubts and private decisions that no one on the team can share. Each hard call is treated like a black box, where the inputs are the context: urgency, available money, differing viewpoints, seniority, the leader's own style, the type of organisation, and even how rested the decision maker is.

The middle pairs opposing choices. Treating everyone equally can feel unfair, so judge people by the value they add to the team. A 1983 Soviet early-warning case shows that rules serve a purpose: an officer doubted a missile alarm, held back from reporting it, and was right. Group decisions improve quality but cost time, so start democratically and decide alone when stuck. Hiding bad news from a team tends to backfire, so openness usually works better. Squeezing out the last few percent of output leaves no slack for the creative work that improves products. Toxic high performers carry hidden costs, while the square root law suggests a small share of people does half the work, so invest in top performers first.

The closing part covers communication style, acting on incomplete data, and the leader as the link between team and company, where burnout hurts everyone. A weekly four-duck happiness barometer, filled in with timesheets, helps spot trends. Peer groups, intuition and a mirror test for integrity round out the advice to look after your people and yourself.

talks.title: JDD 2024: Hipokamp vs AI - LLM nie potrafi tego co ty
talks.teaser: Shows how recognising generic algorithm patterns like graphs and knapsack helps turn vague business rules into simpler, reusable solutions.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with reflections on why programming once felt like flow and how large business projects, with many constraints on people, equipment and dates, can overwhelm that feeling. The speaker uses a scheduling example: a sorter that orders construction stages by funding and legal conditions. Adding rules one by one leads to a pile of conditionals, while a colleague reframes the requirements as a graph where each link is a constraint, so a topological sort handles them generically.

The middle part explores how to spot the underlying problem class. Listening for bridge words from the business domain, such as cycles or dependencies, points to graph or knapsack problems. The speaker compares this to how the hippocampus reuses the same neural machinery across contexts, so knowing standard solutions helps recognise them in new settings. A taxi dispatch case is then treated as a matching problem, where flipping which side is treated as the container yields a different solution.

The closing advice is that classic algorithms and data structures let you propose features the business values, such as finding which constraints to drop to make a project deliverable. Selling the pain a feature removes matters more than naming the technique behind it.

talks.title: JDD 2024: Porządkowanie chaosu - Structured concurrency
talks.teaser: Shows how structured concurrency and scoped values bring predictable control flow and error handling to Java virtual threads.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the history of structured programming and Dijkstra's criticism of goto. The speaker argues that blocks with one clear entry and exit, built from conditionals, loops and function calls, keep control flow predictable. He notes that Java reserves goto as a keyword, and that exceptions and labeled breaks still stay within the call structure.

He then argues that virtual threads bring back the same problem: once work is forked, its result and failure are lost unless handled by hand. He demonstrates Java's structured concurrency API with a group-dinner example, where a StructuredTaskScope forks one subtask per friend and join waits until they finish. A shutdown-on-failure scope cancels the remaining work when one task fails, and throwIfFailed reports the first exception with a clear stack trace. Further demos cover nested scopes in a tournament bracket and throttling in a pizza-sharing example, using a small library still at version 0.1.

In the last part, he compares ThreadLocal with ScopedValue. He lists ThreadLocal's problems: values can be changed from anywhere through set, leftover values can leak into pooled threads, and inherited values can cause hard-to-find memory leaks. A room-painting analogy shows a scoped value bound for one block and restored afterward. Suggested uses include passing the authenticated user through a framework such as Spring Security and carrying logging context. The takeaway is that bounded lifetimes make concurrent code easier to reason about.

talks.title: JDD 2024: One Does Not Simply Query a Stream
talks.teaser: Compares ways to query event streams in Kafka, from Kafka Connect and Kafka Streams to streaming SQL and OLAP databases.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how a team can query data that lives in a stream rather than in a table. It starts by contrasting transactional lookups of single records with analytical queries that compute aggregates over history, and explains why log-based systems such as Kafka are good at storing ordered events but weak at answering questions directly. Because rebuilding state means replaying the log from the beginning, the speaker argues that the stream has to be materialized somewhere before it can be queried.

The middle section surveys the options. Kafka Connect moves data into databases or caches that already support queries, though its transformation abilities are limited. Kafka Streams lets a Java application keep state and run joins and aggregations, and interactive queries can expose that state, but lookups must use a known key and each use case needs its own topology and deployment. Streaming SQL engines such as Apache Flink SQL, Materialize, RisingWave and ksqlDB, along with cloud data warehouses, data lakes and the Apache Pinot real-time OLAP database, are compared on where they keep data, how they query it and how tightly they depend on Kafka.

The closing advice is that no single tool solves every case. Teams should first check whether an existing database and connector already meet the need, weigh performance and latency for their workload, and draw on community resources when choosing.

talks.title: JDD 2024: Spotting Pure Functions in I/O Driven Code
talks.teaser: Shows how to separate pure logic from I/O in a Scala food-ordering example, making code easier to test and refactor.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a backend engineer at Allegro who works in Scala, argues that defining functional programming as "programming without side effects" never helped him. He describes it instead as programming with mathematical functions, where the same input always gives the same output. Such pure functions are predictable, cacheable, safe to call in any order, and safe to refactor. I/O is never pure, so the useful split is between I/O and pure logic.

Using a food-ordering example, he checks whether a restaurant is open and labels each step as I/O or logic. Reading the clock inside a helper hides a dependency and can cause subtle bugs if the day changes between two reads. Passing the time in as an argument makes the helpers pure, and loading opening hours up front lets the filtering run as pure code that can be tested with table-driven cases. A second endpoint reuses only the pure part, with I/O kept in facades at the edges.

He then explores wrapping I/O in an effect-description type with map and flat map, so that repository methods declare their side effects in their return type and run only at the endpoint. He notes trade-offs: long argument lists, loading data before validation can hurt performance on failure paths, and effect types add complexity. His takeaway is that a plain sequence of pure functions with clear conventions may be enough, and developers should look for pure logic in their own code.

talks.title: JDD 2024: Software Engineering career beyond senior
talks.teaser: Maps the career paths open to software engineers after the senior level, from people management to technical tracks.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at what software engineering careers involve once someone has reached the senior level. The speaker explains how his company came to build its own engineering progression after growing and noticing that engineers at similar contribution levels were rated differently across departments. Their framework grouped expectations into technical skills, delivery and teamwork, and the talk uses that lens to compare the early stages, from intern through junior and mid-level to senior.

Beyond senior, the speaker describes two broad directions. One is people management, running from team lead to engineering manager, director, VP of engineering and sometimes CTO. The other is a technical path that includes tech lead, architect, process expert, domain expert and niche expert roles, with staff, principal and distinguished engineers at the top. Across these, problems become less well defined, scope widens from a single project to the wider organisation, and leadership, communication and relationship-building matter more than raw technical skill. The speaker argues that staying at senior level can be a valid choice for a whole career, and that moving into management and back to a technical role is possible.

The closing advice is to watch how people in the desired role spend their time, build a mentoring network outside the current company because mentors become scarce higher up, understand the business and the people around each project, and accept that promotion can depend on budgets or on whether a suitable role is open. The talk ends with reading suggestions and an offer to share more material with anyone who gets in touch.
