talks.title: JDD 2024: Embracing Clean Architecture in Spring Boot and Kotlin - Łukasz Pięta
talks.teaser: Contrasts layered, onion, and hexagonal styles, then refactors a Spring Boot Kotlin catalog demo toward domain-centric clean architecture.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing software architecture as decisions driven by functional needs, quality attributes, technical limits, and business constraints such as hard deadlines, using examples where performance fixes trade away maintainability. The speaker contrasts layered, onion, and hexagonal approaches, noting ports and adapters as the distinguishing pattern for hexagonal designs, and treats clean architecture as a pragmatic hybrid rather than a universal template.

A small product-listing service grows with percentage and quantity discounts. Starting from a classic controller, service, and JPA repository stack with business logic tangled in persistence models, the walkthrough extracts a repository port and adapter, separates pure Kotlin domain models from Hibernate entities, splits pricing into its own concern, introduces use cases in an application layer, and moves Spring transactional boundaries out of domain services.

The closing diagram stresses dependencies pointing inward toward the domain. The speaker lists symptoms of unhealthy structure—tight coupling, mixed persistence and business code, excessive mocks, circular dependencies, and change that ripples everywhere—and warns against over-engineering when simpler layering suffices. Practitioners are urged to document architectural drivers, apply strategic domain-driven design when boundaries shift, and leave discount campaigns as a possible bounded-context exercise in the public sample repository.

talks.title: JDD 2024: Objects - where do they live, what do they eat and how to observe them?
talks.teaser: Shows how a Java cache of category parameters ballooned in memory, and how heap dumps and deduplication brought it down.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short tour of JVM memory: new objects land in the young generation, survivors move between regions, and G1 handles this by evacuating live objects. The speaker then turns to a production problem at Allegro, where his team builds listing filters from product parameters. Parameters are stored per category, with roughly 25,000 of them, and some category responses weighed over 4 MB.

Growth came from several directions. Translations were added language by language, so each new locale multiplied the stored values, and category managers merged brands into one large brand with around 15,000 to 16,000 values. On startup the service loaded everything into a cache. The application stopped responding and was killed after 5 to 10 minutes, GC logs showed evacuation pauses coming more often, and raising the heap to 24 GB only delayed the failure. A heap dump showed parameter value objects retaining about 19 GB, with translations and empty lists adding much of the rest.

The fix was deduplication: a cache of parameter value objects so identical values across categories reuse one instance. Retained size dropped from 19 GB to about 335 MB, which the speaker related to the flyweight pattern. He closes by warning against optimizing without evidence, such as adding reactive code to a small service or tuning startup time for a deployment done every two weeks, and suggests learning GC logs, heap dumps and profilers before a problem shows up.

talks.title: JDD 2024: Monorepo or Polyrepo: What's the Right Choice for You?
talks.teaser: Explains when a monorepo beats separate repositories, covering dependencies, atomic changes, build costs and team readiness.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the monorepo, a single repository holding many projects, and asks when it makes sense to break the usual one-project-per-repository rule. The speaker compares this to chess, where grandmasters bend textbook principles only when they are prepared. To show scale, he describes a monorepo with about 400 monthly contributors, 100,000 CI builds and 3,000 merged pull requests each month, more than 1,000 projects, and roughly half of its code written in Java.

The main benefits are easier dependency management and coordinated change. Libraries can be consumed from source, and a shared bill of materials lets one version bump fix a vulnerability everywhere. Visibility rules control who may use each library. Atomic commits let interdependent services ship together, so temporary backward-compatibility code is not needed. A Spring Boot upgrade from 2.7 to 3.2 was done in one large change, with code owners helping review it. Shared service templates, a common development environment and one CI setup make it easier for engineers to move between teams.

The downsides are longer build times, weak access control for confidential code, and tooling complexity that can slow individuals even when the organisation gains. Mitigations include caching, parallelization and building only affected projects. The speaker recommends reliable, reproducible tests, starting with a small set of projects, training users and fixing tooling problems quickly. He closes with questions to ask before adopting one: whether code is secret, whether tests are stable, how many languages are used, and whether a dedicated team and a collaborative culture exist.

talks.title: JDD 2024: Krótka historia jednego wycieku? - Opowieść oparta na faktach
talks.teaser: Opisuje dochodzenie w sprawie procesu synchronizacji na Kubernetesie oraz metody analizy natywnej pamięci JVM i tuningu.
talks.summary:
Prezentacja zaczyna się od awarii tygodniowego procesu synchronizacji danych w środowisku testowym na Kubernetesie: pod kończył się kodem 137, co zwykle oznacza zabicie procesu przez kernel z powodu nadmiernego zużycia pamięci. Aplikacja backendowa w Kotlinie, z Ratpackiem i RxJava, działała na AWS; szybkie obejście polegało na zmniejszeniu liczby podów i przeniesieniu zwolnionej pamięci, aby odblokować zależny zespół.

Autor pokazuje, że wykresy heapa i Grafana nie wskazywały klasycznego wycieku na stercie. Kolejne kroki to m.in. jemalloc i jeprof, zrzuty wątków przez jcmd, analiza w IDE oraz native memory tracking, które ujawniło rosnące direct buffery powiązane z Netty używanym przez Ratpack. Omówione są też RSS z /proc, limity requestów i limits w Kubernetesie oraz różnica między pamięcią JVM a samym heapem.

Po eksperymentach z konfiguracją JVM (m.in. MALLOC_ARENA_MAX, ustawienia heapa i direct memory) zużycie poda podczas przetwarzania spadło z około 5,5 GB do około 3,7 GB przy stabilnym przebiegu. Na koniec wspomniane są async profiler i flame grafy do wiązania alokacji natywnych z kodem; autor przyznaje, że nadal nie ma pewności, czy był to wyciek, czy głównie nieoptymalne użycie pamięci natywnej i ustawienia środowiska.

talks.title: JDD 2024: Produkcja nie daje spać, czyli kwartał walki o lepsze jutro - Łukasz Guz
talks.teaser: Traces how a production firefight with native memory growth and blocked workers ended the team's night-time alerts.
talks.summary:
A software engineer from a product team running sponsored offers on a large Polish e-commerce platform describes a production period when alerts disrupted sleep. The first problem was an indexing service feeding Elasticsearch, whose container kept growing toward its memory limit while the JVM heap looked healthy. A heap dump analysed in a memory tool showed native direct byte buffers about nine times the heap, owned by IO dispatcher threads created by the Apache HTTP client. Two data centres each had 30 such threads, so the total reached 60. Cutting the configuration freed roughly a gigabyte.

The second service, an aggregator of campaign statistics, restarted repeatedly and paged on-call staff about every two hours at night. Its metrics were read through gauges that queried the database, so slow queries of around two and a half minutes blocked the Graphite reporter. Removing those metrics did not stop the restarts, because health checks failed when requests queued behind blocked Undertow workers. Separate thread pools for reads and writes, a bulkhead approach, brought database response times down to about 30 seconds. Replacing find-and-save with insert-on-conflict, then moving writes to insert-only models with a periodic update, ended the calls.

The takeaways are practical. Problems do not fix themselves, so every alert needs an owner who fixes it, retunes it or removes it. Alerts nobody can act on should not wake people. A steady reviewer speeds up hypothesis checks, and graphs help persuade the business to fund maintenance time.

talks.title: JDD 2024: The four rules of simple design
talks.teaser: Thomas Sundberg examines JDD 2024: The four rules of simple design.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Thomas, a software developer with over 20 years of experience, presents the four rules of simple design—a set of principles first documented by Kent Beck in his Extreme Programming books (2000, 2004). These rules form a practical foundation for code quality that the speaker argues can replace or complement frameworks like SOLID, KISS, and others.

## The Four Rules

1. **Tests Pass** – Implies the existence of tests; without them, nothing can pass
2. **Reveal Intent** – Make code purpose clear through naming and structure
3. **Remove Duplication** – Eliminate redundant logic
4. **Small** – Keep classes and methods minimal

Thomas emphasizes these rules should be applied sequentially, repeatedly, and somewhat mechanically. The order of rules 2 and 3 can vary, as removing duplication often improves clarity and vice versa.

## Key Technical Demonstration

The speaker demonstrates applying these rules to the tennis kata (created by Emily Bache), a refactoring exercise involving a tennis score calculator with unusual scoring rules (love for 0, 15 for 1, 30 for 2, 40 for 3). Key refactoring steps include:

- Removing unused code identified by test coverage
- Extracting methods to reveal tennis rules (winner, advantage, equal)
- Inlining methods used in only one location
- Converting string equality from `==` to `.equals()`
- Creating a `getPointName()` method to eliminate repeated constants (15, 30, 40, love)
- Simplifying conditional logic by identifying patterns and replacing multiple conditions with unified patterns
- Using a lookup table (array) instead of switch/case statements
- Converting fields to local variables where appropriate

## Critical Principles

- **Fast Test Suite:** Tests must run quickly (under 200ms ideally). Slow tests discourage refactoring and break flow
- **Mechanical Application:** Apply rules consistently and without overthinking, running tests after each small change
- **Small Steps:** The speaker emphasizes tiny, reversible changes to prevent breakage
- **Definition of Done:** Software in production, used by real users—not just written or tested
- **History Matters:** The software community often repeats past mistakes because it lacks historical awareness; these rules have been available for over 20 years

## Takeaways

Thomas demonstrates that by mechanically applying these four rules in small steps with a fast test suite, developers can significantly improve code clarity, reduce duplication, and maintain deliverability. The refactoring shown—starting from a complex, unclear method and ending with smaller, clearer components—proves the approach works without requiring a full rewrite. The speaker notes developers can ship safely at any point if tests pass, making this approach low-risk and pragmatic.

talks.title: JDD 2024: Subiektywnie o liderach w IT
talks.teaser: Lists common leadership traps in IT teams, from delegation and coaching to feedback, and suggests practical ways around them.
talks.summary:
Anita Przybył opens with an experiment in which a large technology company removed its managers and flattened its structure, only to find that some areas needed someone to look after them. She points to the follow-up Oxygen study, which identified ten leader behaviors linked to team results, turnover and satisfaction, and to a Gallup finding that 68% of people leave a manager rather than an organization. Her argument is that leadership matters a great deal in IT.

She then walks through habits she sees in technical leaders. Many keep acting as the team's expert and take over operational tasks, often because they struggle to delegate and need control. Others avoid coaching, or become a buddy after promotion, which makes it hard to give corrective feedback or to react when behavior slips. Recognition is either missing or delivered in a way people read as manipulation. Development is often reduced to a training budget, although daily work with growing challenges and short feedback loops does more. She also sketches two informal leader types, the hidden tiger and the controller, and argues that neither style fits every situation.

In the last part she looks at remote and hybrid work, which removes the informal bonding that offices once provided, so leaders need deliberate ways to build belonging. Team agreements can set working norms together with the team. She suggests a rough pattern of three positive comments for each corrective one at work, presented as a tendency rather than a formula. Her closing message is that leadership is a set of learnable behaviors, and that anyone considering the role should first ask whether they actually like people.

talks.title: JDD 2024: How to NOT get insane when working for 20+ years as a dev
talks.teaser: Explains how emotions act as signals from different parts of the mind, and how developers can use them to cope with burnout.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a developer and architect with more than 20 years in the industry, argues that people with persistent depression or burnout should see a professional, and that a doctor should check for physical causes such as a thyroid problem. He then offers a simple mental model: a single narrating consciousness that explains decisions made by several semi-independent parts of the mind, supported by split-brain and misattribution experiments. The point is that we often do not know why we feel what we feel.

Building on that model, he suggests treating each strong emotion as a signal with a likely source. Sadness can mean something important is missing, anger often means a boundary has been crossed, frustration suggests a strategy is not working, and fear calls for more safety. He illustrates these with work examples: moving from management back to hands-on programming, being micromanaged, estimates demanded without historical data, a noisy open-plan office, and a cloud sales role that clashed with his values. For fear, he recommends continuous deployment, owning observability for your services, and test-driven development to build confidence.

When a company cannot change, he suggests reframing your goal, such as mastering a skill like observability, and using healthy escapism like reading, sport or games to restore stability without replacing real life. Other practices include protected "perfect moments" of uninterrupted rest and setting clear boundaries with colleagues. He closes by urging listeners to notice their own inner conflicts and find methods that suit them rather than copying his.

talks.title: JDD 2024: A Crash Course in Business Thinking for Engineers
talks.teaser: Michał Bartyzel details JDD 2024: A Crash Course in Business Thinking for Engineers.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at JDD 2024, the speaker addresses the persistent divide between engineering (IT) and business stakeholders. Drawing on 20 years of industry experience as a software developer, trainer, consultant, author, and startup founder, the speaker outlines common stereotypes, miscommunications, and mindset gaps that hinder effective collaboration. The goal is to provide software engineers with practical frameworks to understand business perspectives, align language, and transition from mere order-takers to trusted partners.

### Key Topics
- **Client Perspective and Vulnerability**: Clients often feel intimidated when engaging with IT, similar to a patient visiting a doctor or a driver consulting an expensive auto mechanic. They may adopt industry buzzwords (e.g., business intelligence, microservices) without fully understanding them, simply to fit in.
- **Uncovering True Business Needs**: Clients typically describe desired features or visual interfaces rather than their underlying business problems. Engineers must apply coaching techniques to uncover actual business outcomes, as clients pay for solved problems or business value rather than raw features.
- **Scope Definition and the Shift-Left Principle**: Defining what is *out of scope* early in the process helps surface hidden assumptions and expectations before development begins.
- **Differing Conceptions of Priority**: Business often views priorities (1, 2, 3) as a chronological schedule where everything eventually gets completed, whereas IT views priority strictly as a filter (1 is guaranteed, 2 is probable, 3 is tentative). Without upfront alignment, this mismatch creates cumulative backlogs.
- **Avoiding Destructive Habits**: Overwhelming non-technical stakeholders with dozens of technical questions acts as perceived aggression. Similarly, reducing domain concepts to standard CRUD verbs ("skrudawianie czasowników") destroys rich domain rules and hurts system architecture.
- **The Value of Adaptability**: As raw technical IQ has become globally commoditized, flexibility and domain empathy serve as the primary competitive advantage for modern software engineers.

### Technical Details
- **Five Perspectives Framework (Slide 38)**: Value delivery can be viewed across five levels: *Inputs* (resources consumed), *Activities* (tasks performed), *Outputs* (items produced), *Outcomes* (measured value), and *Impacts* (market/behavioral change). IT typically communicates in technical terms (blue language), whereas business communicates in outcomes and financial impact (purple language).
- **Translating Code Quality to Business Metrics**: The speaker cites a case study with Bank Nordea in Poland. When developers wanted to remove legacy code after operations ceased in Poland, the business initially refused a pure refactoring effort. By measuring Cyclomatic Complexity before and after hypothetical dead-code removal, the engineering team demonstrated a 15% reduction in complexity. They directly translated this technical metric into business terms: a 15% reduction in testing effort, saving approximately 30 tester person-days (man-days) per release, which secured business approval.
- **TCP/IP Protocol Analogy for Communication**: Human communication mirrors network packet structure: establishing connection, agreeing on protocol, data transmission, and validation/compensation. Engineers often fail by jumping straight to transmission without first establishing connection and common protocol.

### Takeaways
- Focus conversations on business problems and outcomes rather than technical implementation during early stakeholder meetings.
- Preserve domain language and business verbs instead of reducing domain logic to generic CRUD operations.
- Map technical engineering goals (e.g., refactoring, cyclomatic complexity) directly into measurable business outcomes, such as reduced testing overhead or cost savings.
- Avoid aggressive technical interrogation and unprofessional jargon when communicating with non-technical business partners.

talks.title: JDD 2024: People mental models
talks.teaser: Maps Shu-Ha-Ri and the Dreyfus skill ladder onto developer teams, pathologies, and sharper technical interviews.
talks.summary:
The session argues that leading and growing software organizations works better when managers share concrete mental models for how people learn, instead of leaning on hiring alone or counting years of experience. It situates the topic in large-team leadership experience and a conference track already covering other soft skills, then focuses on learning as the main lever for helping colleagues stay curious and capable.

Two frameworks carry most of the narrative. Shu-Ha-Ri is walked through as protect fundamentals, deliberate practice through katas and retreats, then breaking ingrained habits and finally intuitive mastery. The Dreyfus novice-to-expert ladder is presented as factually imperfect but conversationally powerful, with software examples at each rung: rigid rules and primitives, passionate rule trading among advanced beginners, agonizing ownership at competence, feel-based proficiency, and quiet expert judgment. The middle section spends substantial time on failures such as expert beginners, pattern or technology zeal, missing feedback loops when code never reaches production, and why juniors interviewing seniors or experts interviewing juniors goes wrong.

Closing guidance targets day-to-day practice: separate people from skill level, coach through decisions and consequences, test depth instead of buzzwords, adjust answers to the asker’s stage, and use interviews to explore flexible mental models rather than rule recitation. The speaker also warns that expertise is per-skill, humans have bad days, and superficial “theory of flight” knowledge is common—so verify, mentor patiently, and seek external perspectives through communities and conferences.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2024: Tomasz Manugiewicz - Think like a CTO and master devops transformation
talks.teaser: Explains how executives view DevOps, agile, and culture, and how engineers can earn trust during large-scale transformation.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from an engineering-leadership vantage point at Grand Parade within Evoke, framing DevOps as both toolchain and mindset and as the shared ground between development and operations. It walks through siloed handoffs, environment sprawl, and why tooling alone fails when teams do not align, then describes breaking silos via funded transformation programs and Kurt Lewin’s unfreeze–change–refreeze model, including the friction of merging a smaller Polish software house with a large corporation.

The middle contrasts how executives and engineers talk past each other on strategy, agile ceremonies, structure, and revenue-driven priorities. It stresses mutual trust built on competence and relational openness, cites research that only 4% of operational problems reach top leadership, and illustrates how a trusted engineer can deliver rapid proof-of-concepts for a CTO under board pressure.

The close offers practical guidance: map strategy to team contribution, sustain motivation through change, engage executives without fear, stabilize production systems during transition, study industry transformation stories, and act as a “tugboat” steering organizational movement while keeping services reliable.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2024: Piotr Trębacz - Terraform, day 1001
talks.teaser: Shows how to grow a sprawling Terraform codebase into versioned modules, layered stacks, and guarded CI/CD pipelines.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through refactoring a Terraform codebase that grew out of a tutorial-style repository into one that works for larger teams. Speaker Piotr Trębacz lists the common symptoms: local state and local modules, shared module repositories without version control, slow full-environment changes that time out, and corrupted state that affects large areas. The first fixes are remote, locked and encrypted state split into smaller backends, plus a short study of the cloud provider's account or project structure before changing code.

The middle covers code structure. Terraform should manage slowly changing resources, while tools such as Ansible or Packer handle provisioning steps. Workspaces are discouraged for separating environments, and manual console changes in production should stop, with existing resources imported and tagged to show which repository deploys them. Modules should be small and opinionated, with validated variables and locals acting as guard rails. Stacks are then split per service and environment, versioned, and given separate repositories and access rules for staging and production.

For delivery, the pipeline runs pre-commit formatting and doc generation, validation, TFLint, and policy checks with Open Policy Agent, plus cost estimates to catch expensive deployments. Testing should focus on application integration tests rather than on Terraform or providers. The takeaway is that scalable Terraform is a gradual, multi-year effort, with the speaker's planned path spanning about 1,000 days.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: Anita Przybył - Nie daj się zwariować, czyli co robić gdy psychika szwankuje
talks.teaser: Outlines warning signs of depression, anxiety and burnout in IT, plus crisis care paths and habits that protect everyday mental health.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing mental health as a baseline concern that often sits beneath leadership topics like feedback and delegation. Survey figures cited for IT and Polish populations highlight high rates of self‑rated poor mental health, depression, anxiety, and burnout, including developer community research, and stress that these conditions are common and serious rather than trivial.

The middle section maps when to worry: criteria aligned with clinical references for depression, anxiety disorders, and occupational burnout, with emphasis on duration, functional change, and physical symptoms. It explains how acute stress mobilizes cortisol, dopamine, and serotonin, and how chronic overload can flip those mechanisms toward irritability, anhedonia, slowed thinking, and crisis thoughts. It distinguishes psychologist, psychotherapist, and psychiatrist roles, describes combined psychotherapy and medication, and sketches cognitive behavioral work on automatic thoughts.

The close focuses on prevention and support: body awareness, reframing stress as challenge, emotion labeling, rest versus overstimulation, balanced work and recovery, behavioral activation, and listening without minimizing others’ distress. The practical takeaway is a four‑part framework—recognize symptoms early, understand stress biology, know crisis steps, and maintain ongoing mental hygiene.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: Łukasz Szydło - Czysty kod - to jednak nie takie proste.
talks.teaser: Argues that clean-code heuristics miss the point unless teams measure how fast and safely code accepts future changes.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by questioning how teams recognize “clean” code. Most people lean on a familiar triad: rules such as SOLID, desirable properties like low coupling and tests, and familiar patterns. Through a fictional team that deletes campaign code after a few weeks on production, the speaker shows that piling on best practices can slow delivery without improving outcomes when the software’s real lifecycle does not justify the cost.

The core shift is from static code traits to quality attributes defined by activities. Using phone examples and scenarios with actors, actions, artifacts, and metrics, the talk reframes non-functional needs as testable attributes. It distinguishes modules in source from runnable components, treats changing code as the primary developer activity, and proposes metrics for change cost and resulting defects. Understandability, bottom-up versus top-down reading, and Kent Beck’s coupling model (strength, volatility, distance) connect readability and architecture to modifiability.

Practical takeaways include simulating future changes—such as adding a field under CQRS, DDD, and hexagonal layouts or comparing microservice splits—before committing to patterns. Clean code is defined as code that enables quick, safe modification, with heuristics serving verified quality goals rather than becoming ends in themselves.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: Szymon Chmal - Astro - wyspiarska technologia w imię optymalizacji
talks.teaser: Outlines Astro's island model and selective hydration for content sites, and contrasts JavaScript cost with Next.js-style stacks.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by separating highly interactive applications from sites that mainly deliver text and media, arguing that SPA-oriented frameworks ship JavaScript many visitors never need. It positions Astro as a content-first alternative alongside options such as Gatsby, plain static generators, and mainstream React meta-frameworks, noting real-world adoption examples shown to the room.

The middle walks through how Astro builds pages: components with build-time script, scoped styles, built-in Markdown, typed content collections, and optional UI libraries activated only where interactivity is required. Astro Islands and client directives (load, idle, visible, media, client-only) control when hydration runs. Hybrid static and on-demand rendering, JSON or API-style endpoints, View Transitions, and an optional SPA-style mode are also covered, with brief live-oriented pointers to a sample project rather than a full slide deck.

The close compares framework JavaScript payload sizes, cites business impact of load time on conversion, and lists strong fits—blogs, news, portfolios, landing pages, lighter storefronts, and corporate sites—while stressing that Astro complements rather than replaces Next for deeply interactive products. Developers can start minimal and add complexity only where islands or nested interactive apps demand it.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: Magdalena Sędkiewicz - W multiwersum obłędu - jak dołączyć do projektu i przeżyć
talks.teaser: Outlines tactics for chaotic IT projects: ally-finding, access checks, communication norms, boundaries, and self-care before burnout.
talks.summary:
The talk frames joining a messy commercial IT project as entering a multiverse where survival depends on practical reconnaissance rather than theory. The speaker, a psychologist turned developer, contrasts polished deployments with “recognition by combat” assignments typical for juniors and career changers who must build experience fast.

The core advice is to map the project ecosystem early: compare contracted responsibilities with what managers and teammates expect, note cadences such as investor-driven crunch in software houses, and identify who can decide, mentor, review code, own outages, and explain the repository. Operational habits include validating permissions before deploy pipelines fail silently, skimming the repo before estimating work, requesting walkthroughs, naming blockers promptly, and clarifying ambiguous backlog items so pieces fit together.

Later sections address communication channels, async expectations, core hours, and how dailies really run versus Scrum labels. The conclusion stresses boundaries, ergonomics, outside-community support when no senior is available, documenting facts when conflicts escalate, and recognizing when the only healthy move is to leave—while planning rest so anger does not become the sole fuel for change.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: Paweł Lorenc - Czas na zmianę - obecna i przyszła obsługa czasu w JavaScripcie
talks.teaser: Maps JavaScript Date footguns, real-world timezone rules, and the Temporal proposal developers can try before production rollout.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with everyday product asks—timers, penalties, match countdowns—that expose how brittle time logic is in JavaScript. It walks through `Date` constructor quirks (zero-based months, string parsing as UTC versus local display), `getDay` numbering, and why the 1995 design still fuels complaints about parsing, mutability, leap seconds, Gregorian-only calendars, and daylight saving.

The middle contrasts calendar math (variable month lengths, DST-skewed days) with fixed-duration math, shows why `setMonth` autofill surprises developers, and warns about mixing UTC-stored values with local form input. It introduces TC39’s immutable `Temporal` (stage 3, not production-ready): ISO parsing, time zones, `add`/`subtract` with optional overflow errors, and contrasts popular libraries—Moment’s maintenance stance and mutability versus Luxon, date-fns, and others.

The closing grounds APIs in civil time: UTC versus GMT, leap seconds and the 2035 discussion, IANA zones with fractional offsets and political changes, DST gaps like Poland’s spring forward, `Intl` formatting, and ISO 8601 versus `toISOString` always emitting Z. Practitioners should treat zone and calendar context explicitly, prefer immutable patterns until Temporal ships, and validate edge cases against the IANA database.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: Dawid Stronczak - Unlocking the Power of Remote Teams: Lessons from the Trenches
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for 4Developers 2024: Dawid Stronczak - Unlocking the Power of Remote Teams: Lessons from the Trenches.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at 4Developers 2024, Dawid Stronczak shares insights and practical strategies for optimizing productivity in remote and hybrid teams, drawing from his 13 years in the industry, 9 years as an engineering manager, and 4 years working remotely. Highlighting survey data indicating that roughly 8% of industry professionals work purely remotely, 25% hybrid, and about 80% desire the option to work remotely, he argues that remote/hybrid models will continue to grow in popularity. While remote work theoretically offers better focus and fewer interruptions, poor workplace practices—particularly meeting overload and synchronous interruptions—can quickly erode these benefits.

### Key Topics
- **Remote Work Trends and Perceptions**: Examining the trajectory of remote work from pandemic necessity through return-to-office mandates to a steady resurgence, supported by strong employee preference for remote flexibility.
- **Three Pillars of Remote Work**: Framework consisting of productivity/effectiveness (the talk's primary focus), clarity/consistency, and autonomy/independence.
- **The True Cost of Context Switching**: Differentiating between manager schedules (frequent context shifts) and maker schedules (engineers requiring deep, uninterrupted creative blocks). 
- **Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Workflows**: Replacing unnecessary live meetings with asynchronous collaboration methods like written documentation, knowledge bases, and brief recorded video clips.

### Technical Details
- **Focus Loss and Interruption Penalties**: Stronczak cites research showing that an interruption costs an average of 23 minutes to fully return to deep focus on an abandoned task, generating significant stress and frustration.
- **Centralized Knowledge Base**: Establishing a single, accessible internal knowledge hub containing decisions, rules, and documentation to eliminate repetitive ad-hoc inquiries.
- **Asynchronous Decision-Making and Discussion**: Drafting proposals in shared documents with asynchronous comments or conducting quick polls/Slack discussions to decide matters without live meetings, or using meetings strictly to finalize pre-read proposals.
- **Slack and Chat Hygiene**: Setting explicit communication norms (e.g., establishing a 2-hour response window rather than expecting instant replies) and utilizing screen-recording video clips with commentary instead of scheduling large sync presentations.
- **Optimizing Essential Meetings**: When meetings are unavoidable, teams should establish strict agendas and objectives, respect timeboxes (or end early), invite only essential participants to minimize cumulative time costs, favor recurring over ad-hoc meetings, and batch/group meetings into consolidated blocks.
- **Calendar Restructuring and Focus Days**: Demonstrating a calendar refactoring exercise by eliminating non-essential syncs, replacing ad-hoc meetings with async channels, splitting long grooming/refinements to pair with daily standups, clustering meetings into contiguous blocks, and introducing dedicated "no-meeting days" (which research links to improved employee autonomy).

### Takeaways
To unlock remote productivity, teams must intentionally design their schedules rather than defaulting to synchronous meetings. By establishing a central knowledge repository, shifting decisions to asynchronous documents and chats, grouping unavoidable meetings, and carving out uninterrupted blocks of focus time, software teams can substantially reduce context switching and improve overall engineering performance.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: Krzysztof Jończyk - Personal maps. Czyli jak poznać wirtualny zespół
talks.teaser: Describes async Personal Maps for an 18-person remote team to build trust beyond Zoom faces and job titles.
talks.summary:
After shifting to a fully remote team where members had never met in person, the presenter felt the group had become a task factory: dailies and planning worked, but informal bonds and curiosity about colleagues as people were missing. The talk introduces Personal Maps from Management 3.0—mind-map self-portraits with suggested areas such as work, education, family, hobbies, goals, and values—and argues the classic one-workshop format does not scale for larger or distributed groups.

The approach used was deliberately asynchronous: instructions and an example went on the company wiki, maps were built in Miro with the person at the center, and existing meetings gained five to ten minutes for one map at a time. A teammate—not the map’s owner—facilitated, screenshared, and asked questions. With eighteen people, reviews ran for over a month, maps lived in a shared place (including links and later photos), and the exercise repeated about every six months and when newcomers arrived.

Reported outcomes included seeing peers as individuals with names and shared interests instead of role labels, stronger belonging, and easier trust in a low-meeting remote culture. The presenter notes downsides: a few people never submitted maps and stayed more distant, and letting owners present their own maps would drag. The closing takeaway is that remote teams need engineered substitutes for hallway conversations, and this lightweight ritual can do that without a full-day offsite.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: A. Warsińska & W. Jacaszek - Jak wprowadziliśmy servant leadership w zespole
talks.teaser: Shows how a nonprofit scales volunteer autonomy using servant leadership, staged handoffs, and deliberate trust building.
talks.summary:
The presenters describe the Digital Competency Foundation, which builds websites, applications, and marketing support for other foundations while running an internal community of IT and design volunteers. They frame servant leadership as treating each volunteer or employee like another customer group: understand why people join, tailor the organizational “product” to their needs, and measure satisfaction rather than assuming everyone only wants pay.

They segment volunteers into juniors and mids (portfolio and skills growth), mentors (often soft-skill development while supporting others), and stress a shared need for belonging. Using a ladder from manager-led teams through self-managing, self-designing, and self-governing groups, they explain how they moved step by step—proposing a change, securing explicit buy-in, granting decision rights quickly, then widening scope. Examples include project delivery workflow, choice of web tools, task monitoring, and refining processes.

What helped most was bilateral trust: feedback culture via satisfaction and sync meetings plus everyday clarity checks, paired with a belaying metaphor—neither dumping too much responsibility at once nor hoarding tasks. Practitioners can take away a concrete pattern for growing autonomy without chaos, and the observation that volunteers began actively seeking more responsibility once trust and voice were in place.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: Tomasz Manugiewicz - Hybrid heroes: How to build cross-functional, hybrid teams
talks.teaser: Shows how one international branch builds cross-functional hybrid teams through remote work, trust, and quarterly offsites.
talks.summary:
The session opens by asking why companies build teams at all, then frames “building” as assembling people, knowledge, tools, and processes so information and relationships can flow. It contrasts component teams (vertical silos), product and feature teams, and classic project staffing, including billable project models where people rotate when funding ends—leaving fragile ownership when bugs or questions linger.

Interdisciplinarity is presented as necessary but not automatic autonomy or self-organization; those depend on trust, psychological safety between juniors and seniors, and agreement with decision-makers on delivery and technology choices. Remote and hybrid work after COVID brings survey-backed tensions: most people still want home offices, yet meetings multiplied, context switching hurts, async mail is weaker for persuasion than face-to-face contact, and remote staff can feel overlooked for promotion or boundaries.

The speaker outlines Grand Parade’s Kraków setup: mostly remote and distributed, cross-functional product teams, hybrid touchpoints, and roughly four yearly big-room or team offsites, plus managing multiple video platforms. Takeaways stress inclusive diversity across many nationalities, anonymous feedback channels, clear expectations across cultures, outcome-based management, proactive check-ins, celebrating wins, and investing in high-quality relationships—as echoed in closing references to long-running happiness research.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: Marcin Milewicz - DDD na frontendzie? A komu to potrzebne?
talks.teaser: Explains why strategic domain-driven design matters on large frontends and how bounded contexts improve builds and team focus.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that modern frontends are full business applications, so domain-driven design should not be treated as backend-only guidance. Tactical patterns such as entities and aggregates are set aside in favor of strategic DDD: bounded contexts, explicit boundaries, and vocabulary aligned with the business.

Using a sample HR system with employee management and learning management, the speaker shows how shared employee and course models create cross-context imports, coordination overhead across Scrum teams, and bloated JavaScript bundles when routes lazy-load unrelated code. The alternative is duplicate context-specific models, strict import rules, and file structure that mirrors domains.

The talk walks through an Nx monorepo layout with tagged libraries, ESLint boundary rules, and internal layers (data-access, feature, model-shared, shared UI, core). A heavily coupled codebase reportedly needed about 600 seconds to start locally versus about 28 seconds after the split. Layering and structural typing reduce accidental ties between list and detail features. The closing message is pragmatic: apply these boundaries when complexity and payoff justify the migration cost, not everywhere by default.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: Artur Król - Czy hackowanie swojego mózgu jest możliwe?
talks.teaser: Separates brain-boosting myths from evidence for IT professionals and points toward habits that actually help cognition.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by warning listeners that popular ideas about upgrading cognition clash with what research supports, and that the IT field is especially flooded with products and podcasts promising quick mental gains. The speaker challenges the brain-as-computer metaphor and RPG-style “level up” thinking, arguing that homeostasis, hardwired cognitive biases, and risks such as overtraining in fine motor skills cap how much deliberate “hacking” can help healthy people.

A large middle section teaches how to read enhancement claims critically: results from ill populations are often stretched to healthy users, studies may use tiny or unblinded samples, citations may not match the advertised effect, benefits may be tiny or short-lived, and personal anecdotes confuse placebo, motivation, and missing measurement. Specific tools get similar scrutiny—unregulated supplements, nootropic stacks and microdosing, consumer brain-training games, DIY cranial stimulation, and simplistic dopamine narratives—while medically supervised TMS is noted as promising but not a consumer shortcut.

The close shifts to interventions with stronger backing: paying down sleep debt, modest daily movement, real cognitive rest, shorter sustained work blocks, lowering chronic stress, offloading memory to lists and people, basic diet and social contact, and caffeine where already used. The speaker also notes that undiagnosed ADHD may explain focus struggles for some. The practical takeaway is to stop funding dubious shortcuts and invest incrementally in unglamorous habits instead.

talks.title: 4Developers 2024: Michał Szczepanik
talks.teaser: Koder w „normalnym” życiu analyzes 4Developers 2024: Michał Szczepanik.
talks.summary:
Michał Szczepanik caricatures remote developer Adam who schedules seven-day weeks of meetings yet still codes through weekends. He urges calendar focus blocks, shared meeting windows across time zones, out-of-office bots (including a chatbot impersonating his Lagotto dog), and electronics-free days to reset.

After work he recommends physical cooldown rituals, brain-dump checklists on paper, and passions shared with family so analytical thinking does not hijack evenings. Tips cover one change at a time, internal habit shifts before blaming employers, and protecting small daily solitude without doom-scrolling Slack on phones.

talks.title: 4Developers: Łukasz Reszke - Praktyczne zastosowanie eventów w aplikacji do cashflow managementu
talks.teaser: Four legacy cashflow stories show pragmatic event sourcing for webhooks, ordering, classification, and onboarding.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with event sourcing fundamentals—append-only event logs, streams, and rebuilding current state by replay—then ties them to event-driven processing on a cashflow product for small businesses. Bank data arrives through a middle provider’s webhooks; persisting each payload as an event and handling it asynchronously speeds API responses, scales workers, supports retries, and retains an audit trail, while duplicate keys drop replays.

The first case study tackles out-of-order asynchronous updates to bank balances using timestamp-guarded operations on a bank-account aggregate, pragmatic dual writes to the existing relational model, and streams as the source of truth. A second story uses the event history to diagnose pending transactions that stalled for weeks, then replay processing after a one-line behavioral fix. A third walks through extracting transaction classification from an oversized monolith model: encapsulated rules, testable aggregates, background read-model updates, and a process manager so classification steps run once instead of fanning out redundant rebuilds.

A lighter onboarding flow records step and skip events without heavy invariants, enriches metadata for tenant-wide debugging, and enables analytics or replay when integrations break. The close argues for incremental adoption with familiar queue and Postgres tooling, warns about ordering and long streams, and notes event sourcing is not mandatory everywhere.

talks.title: PLNOG 32 - PANEL DISCUSSION: CEO TALKS
talks.teaser: Polish telecom CEOs debate fiber rollout, 5G core shifts, datacenter growth, and survival strategies for small operators.
talks.summary:
The panel opens on how Poland’s telecom landscape shifted from closed, dedicated gear and textbook firewall rules toward virtualized, cloud-like operator cores—and how integration work now largely determines whether services stay reliable. Veterans recall copper, SDI, ATM, and committee-driven builds fading as fiber and radio took over, including an ironic swap where television moved to cables while everyday data traffic rides cellular radio.

Recent momentum centers on true 5G capacity in the 3.5 GHz band, mass-market fiber with XGS-PON offerings marketed around 10 Gig (about 8 Gbps net), and home Wi‑Fi finally keeping pace so regulators and customers stop arguing over speed tests. Speakers note vendor consolidation, software-heavy 5G cores with REST-style interfaces, and Polish suppliers gaining ground as hardware通用izes. Datacenter operators argue denser facilities remain essential even as edge nodes may move closer to users for ultra-low latency.

Closing remarks stress symbiosis between large and small operators, monitoring and automation as upgrade cycles fragment, upcoming 5G standalone core work, sparse “killer apps” versus vertical B2B needs, and resilience worries if power fails at scale—alongside frank skepticism about marketing hype versus what customers actually need.

talks.title: PLNOG 32 - Quo vadis telekomunikacjo?
talks.teaser: Traces Poland's telecom history from 1990s modems and academic networks to gigabit fiber, framing a panel on the future.
talks.summary:
This opening segment of a PLNOG session looks back at how Polish telecommunications grew before the panel discussion on where the sector is heading. The speaker starts in the early 1990s, when bulletin board systems were popular, computer clubs swapped software on floppy disks, and academic networks carried only a few services over slow links. He describes a university network in Lublin that ran on a 2400 bps modem, the move to 64 kbit/s links, and a trade-fair trial that carried ATM traffic at 34 Mbit over fibre strung on high-voltage line protection wires.

He then traces the commercial phase: dial-up internet providers, a national backbone starting at 622 Mbit with 155 Mbit customer links, and a response from the incumbent operator that quickly upgraded its own core. Fixed broadband offers such as Neostrada brought around two million subscribers to megabit speeds, while early mobile data over GPRS offered only a dozen or so kilobits per second, which made it hard to use in practice.

The talk closes with the present day, where fibre and mobile access now reach gigabit speeds, and the speaker notes how easily that progress is taken for granted. He introduces the four panelists, who will discuss how the market sees the future and where the practical limits lie. The takeaway is that people working in the industry shape this growth and should keep its history in view when judging the next steps.

talks.title: PLNOG 32 - Dyskusja o światłowodach, wojnie i planie ciągłości działania
talks.teaser: A telecom panel weighs fiber risks, cloud backup traps, staffing gaps, and continuity plans amid geopolitical crisis pressure.
talks.summary:
At a Polish telecom industry gathering, operators and infrastructure providers debate whether commercial firms can realistically prepare for extreme geopolitical crises when even large players struggle to fund security talent and tooling. Participants contrast national-level critical-infrastructure duties with local company survival, questioning state support beyond new regulations and fines, and whether mid-sized operators should bear responsibilities meant for governments.

The conversation moves through practical war-game gaps: mobilization rosters draining technical staff, board members unavailable, payroll when banking stalls, evacuations without fuel or working cash, and family plans when networks fail. Speakers warn that crisis-driven cloud scale-out clauses may fail due to provider overbooking, argue for warmed overseas capacity or physical metal backups, and note lessons from ongoing Ukrainian operations and submarine fiber damage that can isolate whole countries for long periods. They also highlight dependence on GPS timing for modern networks and a shrinking pool of young cybersecurity hires.

Closing remarks stress that security means managing risk rather than eliminating it. Panelists judge telecom somewhat ahead of other sectors through self-reliance, yet urge diversification, realistic testing of cut-cable scenarios, and skeptical review of assumptions leadership approves without challenge.

talks.title: PLNOG 32 - PL-5G Project: construction of a private 5G network with national coverage and the pos...
talks.teaser: Describes a Polish university consortium's private 5G testbed, its lab facilities and how industry partners can use them.
talks.summary:
The talk presents PL-5G, a project in which several Polish universities built a shared research laboratory for private 5G networks between 2021 and the end of 2023. The speaker explains the motivation: universities had no way to test 5G equipment on their own, and a large national roadmap budget, around 240 million, made a multi-site build possible. The consortium is led by Warsaw University of Technology, with partners in Poznań, Gdańsk and Wrocław, and the speaker's own institution, AGH in Kraków.

The infrastructure is split into several labs. The 5G lab covers both core and access networks, including standalone mode and an open RAN setup, while the simulation and measurement lab holds a compute cluster for long simulation runs, spectrum analysers and traffic generators. Further labs cover outdoor field testing, an IoT environment and a multimedia lab, and all sites connect over the national Pionier research network. The Nokia-based private network uses network slicing and QoS flows, and the 39 GHz band was licensed for the universities. A campus-wide deployment at AGH is also planned.

The closing part covers access and status. Research units can use the facility without charge, while companies work on commercial terms, and a remote booking portal was close to launch. The speaker notes that terminal support for slicing and millimetre-wave devices was still limited, and that the team had submitted comments on the millimetre-wave rules. The main takeaway is that the shared facility gives researchers and companies a large, flexible testbed for 5G and future 6G services.

talks.title: PLNOG 32 - PIONIER-LAB - Krajowa Platforma Integracji Infrastruktur Badawczych z Ekosystemami...
talks.teaser: Surveys the PIONIER-Lab platform and details the innovative network technologies lab, from flexgrid DWDM to Juniper MPLS cores.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces PIONIER-Lab as part of Poland’s national platform for integrating research infrastructures with innovation ecosystems. The initiative is split into thematic laboratories hosted at 22 centers on academic metropolitan networks, covering network innovation, time and frequency, Smart Campus, ICT-oriented live labs, cloud services, multiscale simulation, training, and pre-incubation. The speaker notes he will not expand every laboratory and instead focuses on the innovative network technologies lab, matching the conference’s networking orientation.

That laboratory supports research on modern teleinformatics with infrastructure that is stable yet open to new protocols and experiments, while linking dispersed sites into one logical research environment so teams can use remote resources without low-level wiring overhead. Described capabilities include optical DWDM services, MPLS-based transport, traditional point-to-point and VPN connectivity, public Internet access where needed, high-speed traffic generation and measurement, data-center IP fabric work, and detailed flow monitoring for validation. A LOFAR-related example illustrates hybrid L2 and point-to-point designs that keep antennas useful when central observation is idle.

Organizationally, the PIONIER network spans five large computing centers and sixteen metropolitan networks on owned fiber, with CDC flexgrid optics, alien-wave exchanges with partners such as SURFnet, OTDR monitoring of spare fibers, and terabit-class transponders including encryption suited to quantum-related research. The packet core uses Juniper PTX and MX platforms with redundancy and latency-aware paths, ACX devices in MANs, Arista fabrics with P4-programmable switches, and Spirent test gear up to 800 GbE. Practitioners see how a national research network scales capacity, supports procurement testing, and hosts cutting-edge experiments including quantum-safe connectivity trials.

talks.title: PLNOG 32 - Sharing experience of deploying IPoDWDM, Segment Routing and EVPN for SP transport...
talks.teaser: A practitioner overview of simplifying carrier transport with segment routing, EVPN, and coherent IP-over-DWDM deployments.
talks.summary:
The session frames how service provider transport evolved from large flat IGP domains with LDP, RSVP, and BGP labeled unicast toward designs that must scale while subscriber bandwidth rises faster than revenue. The speaker walks through why operators split domains, how MPLS labels act as forwarding instructions rather than mere encapsulation, and why vendors push automation-friendly underlays with fewer control protocols.

Segment routing is presented as the underlay foundation: ISIS or OSPF extensions replace LDP for transport, BGP still carries L3VPN services, and EVPN tames Layer-two VPN complexity for dual-homing, MAC distribution, anycast gateways, and flexible cross-connect for broadband hierarchies. The talk covers parallel SR and LDP migration, fast reroute benefits, traffic-matrix visibility from sampled NetFlow on label stacks, and anycast pseudowire use cases.

A colleague’s section contrasts traditional layered DWDM, OTN, and IP stacks with routed optical networking and digital coherent optics in routers. It explains QSFP-DD and roadmap modules, cross-vendor pluggables, moving protection to the IP layer, and operating optical parameters from the routing team. The takeaway is simpler optical plants, integrated IP-over-fiber topologies, and operational models where MPLS engineers also manage DCO modules.

talks.title: PLNOG 32 - Klasyfikacja treści stron internetowych w czasie rzeczywistym
talks.teaser: Explains how web pages get classified in real time into hundreds of content categories using lightweight text features.
talks.summary:
The speaker, from a Polish company, describes a real-time web classification system built for a national educational internet network run by NASK. Static domain lists fail on shared platforms and fast-changing sites, and checks based only on URLs are easy to fool, for example through machine-translated pages. Context also matters: a page about abortion may be informational, medical, or activist, and each needs a different parental-control decision. The category scheme grew from about 80 to roughly 300 categories with subcategories.

The pipeline has three stages: building a labelled dataset, extracting text from HTML, and classifying that text with a model. The speaker calls the manually tagged dataset, which holds more than 2 million tags, the main asset, and says errors found in production led the team to re-review categories. For extraction they used Java and Intel's Hyperscan library to count thousands of regular expressions in one pass. They compared bag-of-words features with BERT-style embeddings and a custom method. Gradient-boosted trees needed too many parameters for 300 classes, so the team moved to a neural network and then a custom architecture. That cut the parameter count about eightfold while keeping accuracy, and it ran on CPU only.

The talk reports about 98 percent of the best result after these changes and an average processing time of around 30 ms. It also gives deployment figures: 1000 HTML requests per second on 16 cores and 32 GB of RAM, use in more than 20,000 schools, and over 5 million users. The main takeaway is that a good labelled dataset and careful engineering at each step matter as much as model choice. The speaker kept some details confidential.

talks.title: PLNOG 32 - Warzymy Piwo: BIER dla Operatorów
talks.teaser: Shows how BIER carries multicast destinations in packet headers so transit routers keep no per-tree state.
talks.summary:
This PLNOG 32 session, given by a solution architect from Juniper Networks, introduces BIER (Bit Index Explicit Replication), a method for carrying multicast traffic across an operator network. The problem it starts from is that conventional approaches such as PIM, mLDP and RSVP-based point-to-multipoint need forwarding state for every multicast tree on transit routers, which strains scalability as the number of trees grows. The beer-themed slides frame the material lightly.

The core idea is to move the destination list into the packet. Each edge router gets a numeric identifier, and a bit string in an added header marks which egress routers should receive a copy. Transit routers read the bits, consult a forwarding table and replicate only where paths diverge. Table size depends on network size rather than the number of trees, so no per-tree state is needed. For large networks the bit string is split into sets, and subdomains confine multicast to part of the topology.

The talk closes with standardisation and interoperability. BIER already has published RFCs and several working drafts. In February the speaker reported a multi-vendor interoperability test run at an independent lab in Berlin, with Juniper, Nokia and Huawei forwarding BIER traffic and a Keysight tester generating it, and captures were decoded to confirm the extensions were read correctly. The practical takeaway is that BIER suits operators facing large numbers of multicast trees, since it trades per-tree state for header overhead.

talks.title: PLNOG 32 - Routing IP w kontekście AI/ML i RoCEv2
talks.teaser: TONY PRZYGIENDA details PLNOG 32 - Routing IP w kontekście AI/ML i RoCEv2.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation examines backend AI/ML training clusters and explores how data center networking is shifting from custom fabrication toward mass production of standardized information processing substrates. The talk contrasts InfiniBand with Ethernet/IP running RDMA over Converged Ethernet version 2 (RoCEv2), evaluating how physical topologies, congestion control, and routing architectures influence the primary performance metric: Job Completion Time (JCT).

### Key Topics
- **Backend Training Clusters and RDMA:** While frontend networks handle administrative duties, backend fabrics handle massive, long-lived, fat flows required for distributed linear algebra. RDMA directly maps memory between systems, bypassing traditional socket overhead (yielding roughly 4x speedups) and placing substantial stress on underlying network substrates.
- **Network Topologies:** Topologies are evaluated by their ability to scale and handle congestion. Folded Clos networks remain the primary form factor (also utilized internally in Nvidia NVLink switches), but as clusters grow and face power constraints (~300 MW substation limits), alternate topologies like dragonfly, dragonfly+, and toroidal meshes (used in Google TPUs) emerge, each presenting distinct routing and recabling tradeoffs.
- **InfiniBand vs. RoCEv2:** InfiniBand uses credit-based flow control, simple 4K packet formats, and centralized Subnet Managers, but faces addressing boundaries (limited to 48k addresses) and proprietary pricing pressures. RoCEv2 wraps InfiniBand in non-fragmentable UDP over IP/Ethernet, relying on DSCP/TOS priority mapping and ECN/PFC (802.1Qbb) for congestion management, though with challenges in entropy and packet misordering.
- **Architectural Principles (CAP & Price of Anarchy):** Designing distributed routing systems involves balancing consistency, availability, and partition tolerance (CAP theorem). Centralized systems achieve resource efficiency under predictable workloads, whereas distributed systems provide rapid fault recovery and availability at the cost of efficiency (the Price of Anarchy).

### Technical Details
- **Adaptive Routing and Out-of-Order Handling:** In standard RDMA fabrics, packet misordering triggers heavy retransmissions that degrade JCT. Vendor libraries such as Nvidia NCCL require specific extensions/hacks to safely handle packet misordering, allowing ECMP and multi-path routing to operate without retransmitting entire 1 GB blocks.
- **Centralized vs. Hybrid IP Routing Approaches:** 
  - *Hyperscale Hybrid Controller (Meta/Facebook model):* Uses BGP/EBGP as an underlying distributed routing base while deploying a centralized controller that interfaces with custom job schedulers and modified NCCL to inject specific longest-prefix-match exception routes, steering traffic away from congested paths.
  - *BGP Next-Next-Hop & Local Flooding:* Combines BGP with localized, one-hop flooding mechanisms to advertise real-time link congestion, allowing weighted ECMP decisions without relying on a centralized controller.
  - *IGP / RSVP-TE & FlexAlgo:* Running traditional link-state protocols with FlexAlgo enables per-prefix constraint computation, though full flooding and scaling overhead become bottlenecks at large cluster scales.
- **Routing on Regular Topologies (RIFT):** Standard shortest-path routing fails on non-Clos fabrics like dragonfly+. Specialized protocols such as RIFT (Routing in Fat Trees) exploit fabric directionality by flooding topology information strictly northbound (southbound remains mostly default routing with selective prefix exceptions), providing loop-free, valley-free non-shortest-path routing at scale.
- **In-Network Computing (SHARP):** Nvidia SHARP establishes in-network multicast trees across intermediate switches to perform mathematical reductions (such as floating-point summations) directly in hardware during packet transit, distributing final aggregated results downstream to worker nodes.

### Takeaways
As AI clusters expand toward hundreds of thousands of accelerators, network design requires balancing the extreme efficiency of centralized scheduling against the rapid fault convergence of distributed IP routing. Emerging protocols like RIFT, alongside hybrid controller-based route injection and in-network computing substrates, represent the ongoing evolution to replace or augment specialized InfiniBand fabrics with scalable IP networks.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2024 - Templating your CICD Workflows
talks.teaser: Shows how a platform team templates CI/CD pipelines and Terraform repositories so developers self-serve safely.
talks.summary:
Lidor Gerstel, a platform engineer at a fintech company, presents an idea for templating CI/CD and infrastructure so teams can self-serve. He begins with the team's culture: everyone reviews and can approve everyone else's changes, mistakes are admitted openly, and blame is avoided. The core stack is GitHub Actions, Argo CD, Terraform and AWS.

The pipeline starts when a developer opens a pull request or merges to main. Service repositories call a central repository of reusable workflows and actions, passing inputs such as the service name and runtime version. Builds produce Docker images or static web assets, and a deployment workflow hands off to Argo CD, which runs one instance per EKS cluster. A separate infrastructure repository creates new GitHub repositories from Terraform templates, so branch rules and required approvals come built in. Terraform plans appear on pull requests for review, and apply runs on merge only for the changed parts, with state kept in S3 per account. The talk ends with the folder layout: modules, root configuration for providers and accounts, then region and service folders that follow naming conventions.

His takeaway is to stop accepting legacy setups and to build a platform that lets developers own their services instead of only reacting to requests. He presents extending the same pattern to data and ML pipelines as his next step, still an idea rather than a working system.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2024 - Test-oriented Cloud Application Architecture
talks.teaser: Wojciech Dąbrowski details DevOpsDays Kraków 2024 - Test-oriented Cloud Application Architecture.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this DevOpsDays Kraków 2024 presentation, the speaker explores test-oriented cloud application architecture, breaking down testing strategies across traditional and cloud environments. Drawing from practical experience leading AWS initiatives, the talk examines why automated testing exists, categorizes test levels using the testing pyramid, and discusses architectural requirements for creating robust, isolated test environments in the cloud.

### Key Topics
- **Purpose of Automated Testing**: Beyond verifying newly implemented functionality, automated tests primarily guard against regression, enable safe refactoring of code and cloud architectures (e.g., migrating from containers to serverless or altering databases), and act as a validation signal for underlying system design.
- **Test Classification & Definitions**:
  - *Unit Tests*: Fine-grained tests evaluating business logic within isolated functions, classes, or methods.
  - *Integration Tests*: Tests specifically focused on verifying communication contracts between components or external APIs/data stores, rather than end-to-end flows.
  - *Component Tests*: Tests that evaluate application logic and flow within a bounded context without integrating real external services, typically utilizing fakes or stubs.
  - *End-to-End (E2E) Tests*: Black-box tests run against deployed environments that validate the complete application flow across real services without test doubles.
- **Test Doubles**: Differentiating test double categories, specifically fakes (functional replacements like in-memory databases), stubs (pre-configured return values), and mocks (verifying invocation counts and payloads).
- **Cloud Testing with AWS Examples**: Implementing tests across a typical cloud pattern (API Gateway, AWS Lambda, Amazon S3, and DynamoDB). Clean code and inversion of control underpin unit testing, while architectural patterns like hexagonal or onion architecture enable effective component testing.
- **Infrastructure as Code (IaC) & Test Environments**: Creating on-demand testing environments requires repeatable, parameterized IaC templates (e.g., AWS CloudFormation or Terraform). Anti-patterns that prevent isolated testing include hardcoded resource names, tightly coupled cross-stack dependencies, and distributed monoliths.
- **Testing Myths & Professional Mindset**: Refutation of common development excuses, including the claim that systems are too unique to test, the belief that MVPs do not need testable architecture, and the habit of writing untested code due to shifting ticket requirements.

### Technical Details
- **Inversion of Control & Clean Architecture**: Keeping core application logic independent of concrete implementation details (such as direct cloud SDK calls to DynamoDB or S3) allows developers to swap real storage engines for test doubles during unit and component testing.
- **IaC Parameterization**: Hardcoding resource names or external service identifiers into CloudFormation stacks or Terraform modules creates collisions that prevent deploying isolated preview or branch-level environments on demand.
- **Distributed Monolith Pitfall**: Microservices that share distributed transactions or lack bounded context autonomy force end-to-end testing across massive, interconnected environments rather than allowing independent component verification.

### Takeaways
- Even in serverless or cloud-native architectures where integration configurations are prevalent, the traditional testing pyramid remains valid, emphasizing fast, maintainable unit tests.
- Code should always be written to be 'test-ready' from the start, as untestable code introduces architectural debt that cannot easily be retrofitted.
- Engineers must understand requirements deeply rather than blindly implementing tickets, ensuring systems are decomposed into testable, loosely coupled boundaries.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2024 - The challenges of Platform teams...
talks.teaser: Explains common platform team pitfalls, from developer experience and lock-in to roadmap alignment, with ways to overcome them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the pitfalls that platform teams commonly run into and how to get past them. It groups the problems into four areas: developer experience, business alignment, technology choices, and the particular pressures that fall on platform teams themselves. Examples include weak user-centred thinking, feedback that is hard to collect from developers, requirements that reach the team second-hand, reactive work that crowds out the roadmap, and lock-in to cloud, identity or observability providers.

For remedies, the talk recommends applying user research and journey mapping to internal users, building self-service developer portals so onboarding needs no manual steps, and using abstraction layers carefully so they do not leak underlying details. It suggests tying the roadmap to business goals over the next few months, favouring vendor-agnostic tools such as Terraform, using default guardrails like blocking public storage buckets, and treating internal platform products as services with defined value, support levels and retirement. Practices borrowed from software delivery, including infrastructure tests, feature toggles for gradual rollouts, and regular demos to stakeholders, are also covered, along with Team Topologies and DORA metrics for measuring success.

The closing takeaway is that platform teams work best when they have technical stakeholders with decision power, clear definitions of done, and a strong feedback loop with the teams they serve. Not every team will reach this maturity immediately, but the talk presents it as a goal every platform team can work toward.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2024 - Maximizing Collaboration: Unleashing the Power of... (Krzysztof Rudek)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of DevOpsDays Kraków 2024 - Maximizing Collaboration: Unleashing the Power of... (Krzysztof Rudek).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from DevOpsDays Kraków 2024, Krzysztof Rudek, a DevOps engineer at IBM, discusses how teams can maximize collaboration and trackability by leveraging simple, pragmatic automation rather than over-engineered AI or LLM solutions. Working alongside approximately 200 developers across 20 to 25 squads managing around 40 microservices, Rudek explains how repetitive tasks, deployment tracking, and cross-team communication can be streamlined using fundamental tools like Git, GitHub webhooks, Jenkins, and Slack.

### Key Topics
- **Demystifying ChatOps:** Defining ChatOps not as advanced AI, but as a conversation-driven interface between humans and automated actions—analogous to state-machine tools like Clippy or IBM Z ChatOps for mainframes.
- **PRs as the Core API:** Using GitHub pull requests and comments as the primary interface between developers and DevOps, avoiding redundant manual requests.
- **Webhook-Driven Orchestration:** Triggering selective test suites (such as BVT) or deployment tasks directly through comment phrases within PR webhooks.
- **Release Trackability and GitOps:** Overcoming visibility loss after moving from RTC to multi-repo GitHub setups by maintaining a single source of truth for microservice versions.

### Technical Details
- **Selective Test Execution:** To prevent two-hour build pipeline delays, developer comments in PRs (such as `BVT`) are intercepted via GitHub webhooks by CI tools like Jenkins (via trigger phrases in Jenkinsfiles) or Tekton/Argo, executing only relevant test suites.
- **The `digest.yaml` File:** IBM bundles roughly 40 microservices into a standalone installer (Red Hat operator case bundle) and weekly cloud deployments. A central `digest.yaml` file tracks each microservice's exact image digest/tag, serving as the single source of truth.
- **Automated Issue Tracking via Git Log and GitHub API:** To link code changes to project management without prematurely auto-closing tickets, developers reference tasks using custom phrases (e.g., `fixes issue #...`). An automated script with two `for` loops traverses the `digest.yaml` file and inspects the `git log` / commit list for each tag using GitHub's API. Once an associated PR/issue is identified, the script automatically comments on the central tracker issue, notifying developers and managers exactly which standalone installer version or deployment contains the fix.

### Takeaways
- True ChatOps does not require complex LLMs, chatbots, or fancy tooling; it can simply be an interactive mechanism inside familiar interfaces like GitHub PRs or Slack.
- Simple, foundational utilities—such as `git log`, webhook parsing, and basic loops—are easier to maintain, implement, and support at scale than complex dashboards or manual status checks.
- Establishing clear APIs and automated feedback loops between developers and DevOps saves time, maintains accountability, and keeps engineering teams and management aligned.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2024 - Driving Efficiency: Harnessing the power of 3rd party... (Maciej Rutkowski)
talks.teaser: Shows how to cut CI/CD cost and build time with agent choices, templated pipelines, lock files and caching.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how to make CI/CD pipelines cheaper, faster and easier to maintain. The speaker frames the work around three goals: the money spent on engineering time and on build infrastructure, time to market, and the amount of repeated code across repositories. He compares hosted and self-hosted build agents on Azure DevOps and GitHub Runners, covering the fixed VM specifications, the software preinstalled on hosted images, the limits on reaching internal resources, and the pricing model.

Using a case study of a .NET application whose CI build failed often and downloaded the same dependencies on every run, he walks through a series of changes. These include choosing a lightweight, recent Ubuntu image, moving variables into template files, and placing shared stages and steps in a central repository that each application references. He also recommends pipeline artifacts over build artifacts when the output does not need to leave the pipeline. For dependencies, he locks packages with lock files and restores in locked mode. A cache task keyed on the lock file hash then lets later runs skip the restore step on a cache hit. Cached data is kept for 7 days, and the same idea applies to GitHub Actions cache save and restore.

He closes by urging teams to keep pipeline changes transparent to developers and operations staff, and to build a shared DevOps mindset rather than new silos.
