talks.title: PLNOG 32 - Watch live IoT hacking! (Michał Sajdak)
talks.teaser: Demonstrates root-level takeovers of cameras, routers and VPN appliances through unauthenticated flaws and command injection.
talks.summary:
Michał Sajdak walks through unauthenticated attacks on widely deployed cameras, routers, VPN gateways and firewalls, combining a live demonstration with screenshots. He opens with a Hikvision camera, where an injection in a language-setting request yields a privileged SSH login, and shows how the ZoomEye search engine can locate exposed cameras, login pages and VPN portals by country and device type.

The middle section surveys other cases. A Palo Alto GlobalProtect flaw lets a crafted session cookie create files that run commands as root. An Ivanti Connect Secure API chain bypasses authentication, and its session IDs can be reused to get past two-factor login. An LG TV pairing weakness lets an attacker create a privileged account and inject commands through a report parameter. A Fortinet admin API accepts spoofed headers, which allows adding an SSH key to an admin account. A Citrix memory leak exposes session IDs, and a Cisco IOS XE path-decoding quirk leads to root. A Juniper web console setting makes PHP read configuration from standard input, so command injection follows.

The closing advice is to keep web management panels off the public internet or protect them with client certificates, and to segment IoT devices from the main network. Two-factor authentication offers little once an attacker already has root. Vendor severity ratings can be inaccurate in either direction, so readers should check what a bug actually allows. Buying used devices is suggested as a way to test such flaws.

talks.title: PLNOG 32 - Automatyzacja sieci: efektywność i oszczędności... (Andrzej Mazur, Mariusz Skwara)
talks.teaser: Outlines how ISP-oriented OSS orchestration cuts costs, ends silos, and scales from small operators to large migrations.
talks.summary:
The session opens with context on PacketFront’s background serving mostly mid-sized and smaller ISPs, plus a Warsaw-based team supporting Polish deployments. The technical segment frames the operator’s challenge as constant change—growth, service variants, and multi-vendor gear—that produces silos, inconsistent documentation, and a “network monster” that resists fast, error-free change.

Orchestration is presented in three layers: centralized management and integration with provisioning and BSS/OSS, a single configuration repository, and automation that coordinates tasks across the network rather than only pushing configs to one box. Benefits are argued across management speed, engineering time freed from repetitive work, and faster productized services. A good platform should pair guided wizards with scripting (including Python), APIs, and GUI; support many hardware vendors; and use topology-oriented interfaces that document the live network.

Adoption is advocated incrementally on a slice of the network, with read-only verification before production changes—illustrated by large and small customer migrations. The close stresses that orchestration sits in critical infrastructure, with NIS2-style expectations, UK TSA experience, and security handled in ongoing product development rather than as an afterthought.

talks.title: PLNOG 32 - Why should access networks be open? (Marcin Kuczera)
talks.teaser: Explores why European FTTH operators should allow subscriber-owned ONTs and routers under EU rules.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that access-network operators should relax restrictions on customer-supplied terminals, separate from the well-known wholesale “open fiber” service model in the EU. The speaker contrasts earlier eras—dial-up and ADSL, where subscribers could attach their own modems and routers—with today’s FTTH practice of mandatory operator CPE, often an integrated ONU and home gateway.

The technical core is GPON architecture: OLT at the central office, splitters, and ONU or ONT at the premises. Many Polish deployments, including large Orange offerings, leave no official way to use a simple L2 ONU or an SFP-based terminal. EU directives on network neutrality and terminal-equipment choice are cited, with QR links to regulations, while implementation varies by country. Germany’s model—fiber ending in a wall socket and subscriber-provided, serial-authorized CPE—is held up as workable. Practical options include small L2 boxes, 2.5 Gbit capabilities on GPON, and SFP ONT modules the speaker’s firm supplies globally, sometimes with industrial temperature ratings for automation and monitoring use cases.

Operators resist openness because of support load, remote OMCI firmware updates, and vendor behavior—notably Huawei licensing that blocks third-party ONUs, versus Nokia’s more permissive stance. The speaker contends integrity fears are overstated compared with physical mischief on a PON branch, and that fighting gray-market serial spoofing wastes effort better spent on certified bring-your-own-device programs. The closing message is that regulation and emerging enterprise demand will push terminal choice, opening markets for bespoke broadband and SDN-style services on fiber.

talks.title: Piotr Zarzycki, Paweł Srokosz: ScamBook | OMH 2024
talks.teaser: Walks through Facebook scams, from fake car-recovery services to fraudulent ads, and tests how the platform responds to reports.
talks.summary:
The talk, presented by two researchers from CERT Orange Polska and CERT Polska, examines scams spread through Facebook. The speakers first created fictional personas to see how fraudsters respond, then followed several scam types. The first case was posts from people whose cars had been stolen, where commenters offered recovery services. One such operator, contacted through a direct message, demanded payment in bitcoin and claimed access to city camera feeds. The speaker kept the conversation going, found inconsistencies in the operator's location and language, and noted that the scam posts were picked up by scanners within hours of the original post.

The middle section covered other cases. Fake airline and airport customer support profiles offered to recover lost luggage for a fee, and a fake obituary post invited visitors to a funeral livestream that required account creation before showing a scam. The speakers walked through Facebook's reporting flow, showing how category and impersonation choices are entered, and noted that many reported profiles remained online. For ads, they described investment scams using fake news pages and celebrity content. Of 122 scam ads reported over a year, about 10 were removed. A test site also showed that the same ad could display different content depending on the visitor's network, so reviewers saw one page while users saw another.

The talk closed with a call for platform operators to take more responsibility instead of relying on users to report abuse. The speakers also noted that their own article about these ads was removed as spam. For practitioners, the main takeaway is to treat unsolicited recovery offers and support chats on social media as suspect, and to expect that reports may not lead to removal.

talks.title: Podcast PROIDEA - Odcinek 1
talks.teaser: The episode explores HackYeah paths for newcomers and winners, from team building and startups to networking and IT career growth.
talks.summary:
The opening frames Pro Idea’s podcast as a place to discuss IT events, with a focus on HackYeah—a 24-hour hackathon in Krakow described as a large stationary marathon mixing technical, social, and innovation challenges. Hosts introduce two guests who share how the event shaped their paths rather than delivering a single technical tutorial.

Dawid Tambor describes arriving without an IT background from traditional showroom sales, joining a team-building session, and leading coordination while teenagers handled code. His group worked on fake-news detection for a partner challenge and did not win, but he kept working with teammates; with Aleksander he pursued a separate startup idea for virtual home staging aimed at real estate agents, contrasted with a Harvard student offering, and now seeks scaling help, mentors, and investors. Jakub Strykowski recounts three HackYeah editions, including assembling an international student team and winning work for Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego on a certification authority demo with PDF signing pitfalls, Dockerized modules, and deliberate task and prize choices. He ties participation to recruitment stories, a raise for a teammate, and later conference speaking.

Practitioners hear recurring themes from event research: communication drives winning teams, cross-team feedback is normal, and many projects ship in the final hour before deadlines. Closing advice urges first-timers to register with low expectations, stay open to people and sponsors, treat the weekend as community and learning—not only prizes—and notes that ticket revenue supports charitable computer access for children.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | Dr Maciej Chrzanowski: Jak wykorzystać narzędzia gen-AI do budowy second brain
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a personal second brain with generative AI tools, folder systems and daily micro-automations.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the claim that people optimise projects, processes and companies but rarely themselves. The speaker estimates how much time small repeated actions cost, such as resizing windows and locating folders, and argues that simple launcher and shortcut tools save seconds that add up over a year. He is sceptical of a recent study that reported large productivity gains from generative AI, pointing out that participants were often handed tools without any training.

The core idea is a "second brain": a system for capturing, organising, filtering and creating information, which he presents as an old concept under new names. He suggests asking how each of those steps works for you and separating incoming material into actionable items and reference material. He shows his folder structure, a PARA-style scheme of projects, areas, resources and archive with numbered folders, and names tools for capture and reading, such as Rewind and a read-later workflow, along with Markdown and Perplexity for writing and research. He notes that a well-organised system saves more time than any single AI tool, and gives a LinkedIn post as an example that takes only minutes to produce from material he has already filed.

He closes by arguing that the foundation is physical and mental: fitness, attention to time and personal memory, and offline reading, so that technology does not quietly take over those roles. For practitioners, the takeaway is to build the system around their own habits, keep tools simple, and treat technology as support rather than the goal.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | Dawid Szałański: Automatyzacja pracy z wykorzystaniem Cognitive Services
talks.teaser: Outlines how a European financial group scales citizen development with Power Platform and Cognitive Services across markets.
talks.summary:
The session describes how Kruk, a financial-services company operating across several European markets, structures no-code and low-code automation as part of digital transformation. The speaker argues that technology, people, and business processes must be balanced together, with labs and centers of excellence coordinating streams while citizen developers deliver most solutions.

The tooling picture combines RPA (including UIPath), Power Automate for everyday workflows, Power Virtual Agents for contact-center bots, Power Apps, and Microsoft Cognitive Services—including tests with chat assistants fed on internal documents. Concrete examples include a Teams-integrated app that standardizes monitoring of B2B contractor availability for managers and HR, and outcomes from an internal AI contest: a photo-driven story generator using vision and chat APIs, an Excel-backed test-scenario creator for business analysts, and a self-built assistant that splits large Excel files without macros.

Practitioners should treat platform capabilities as composable building blocks, prioritize process sense over blind automation, accept fast tool churn, and pair grassroots experimentation with light governance, basic documentation, and deployment practices aligned with IT—so business ideas enter through a single path rather than depending on individual relationships.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | Dominika Bucholc: Rola AI w Transformacji Cyfrowej
talks.teaser: Outlines how companies can plan AI adoption in digital transformation, from business needs to integration, training and measurement.
talks.summary:
Presented at No Code Days 2023, this talk looks at the role of AI in digital transformation strategy from a business consulting perspective rather than a developer's. The speaker traces how forecasts from earlier years misjudged the pace of change, and notes that generative AI moved into everyday use within a short time. She argues that many firms lacked prepared data and clear strategies, and that fear of the technology, among both decision-makers and the public, still shapes how adoption is approached.

The middle section walks through areas where AI is easiest and cheapest to adopt: market analysis with predictive models, customer segmentation and CRM optimisation in sales and marketing, chatbots and voice bots for customer service, product development, and HR tasks such as recruitment. She then lists common blind spots: relying on a single dataset, using off-the-shelf tools without knowing what runs inside them, analysis paralysis from too much data, a poor fit with company culture, and employees using generic tools without privacy controls or a clear purpose.

To close, she recommends starting with business needs rather than tools. That means analysing the market and competitors, mapping processes and organisational structure, and then choosing technology that fits those goals. Integrating AI into systems a company already uses, such as adding an AI feature to an existing CRM, is preferable to replacing them. Changes should be tested in stages and measured, and staff training and evaluation should continue throughout, since the technology keeps changing.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | Łukasz Kuchna: Smart biznes - pracować mniej, a zarabiać więcej?
talks.teaser: A holding company's leader explains no-code stacks, BI, and AI that aim to cut manual work while sustaining rapid revenue growth.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes a re-recorded session originally disrupted by technical problems at the live event. He frames the problem as sustaining roughly 200% annual growth across a multi-company holding with more than 100 people, where traditional methods would mean managing through incomplete data and slower decisions than globally digitized professional-services firms.

The middle walks through their “smart business” model: flexible tooling, Make as integration glue, business intelligence with transactional and analytical stores including BigQuery, dashboards for leaders, and OpenAI-backed assistants over Notion and other knowledge. He sketches a live stack tying sales, accounting, and delivery tools into shared data flows, notes similar architecture at Skanska, and flags obstacles such as poor data collection, silos, and rigid legacy apps. Examples include automated client satisfaction surveys, a compensation calculator tied to revenue and KPIs, and an internal chatbot for policies and prompts.

Practitioners hear that measurable automation and consistent data are meant to free staff from repetitive tasks, speed decisions, and keep scaling without proportional headcount. The close argues quarterly productivity gains, cleaner data, and easier scaling, with room for questions on adapting the patterns elsewhere.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | Karol Maj: Zastosowanie Low-Code w złożonych procesach biznesowych
talks.teaser: Low-code lessons show how teams simplify sprawling business workflows with structured design, Mermaid notation, and AI-assisted modeling.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens with his long career building dedicated enterprise software and the shift toward low-code around 2009, when accelerated delivery mattered for advanced project-management systems. He introduces the Airspace low-code platform for business processes, with administrative configuration, workflows, and object-backed relational storage, alongside other firms he runs that serve education, procurement, and e-commerce clients.

Case work spans universities, the Polish Academy of Sciences, and large student-housing processes affecting thousands of people. He stresses that apparent complexity usually comes from trying to model every stakeholder and domain in one diagram, not from the business itself. Early project work often redraws processes using rules such as keeping diagrams readable on a single A4 page, layering from general to detailed views, and linking related processes. BPMN is the common standard but can be slow in live client workshops; the team uses a Mermaid-based textual notation with custom labels so analysts can draft implementable flows during meetings, illustrated with invoice acceptance and interlinked processes clients can navigate.

He closes on embedding company-specific AI assistants that read the platform API and Mermaid conventions to propose processes such as invoice or document approval, with a roadmap toward assistants that trigger operations and show monitored status, notifications, and linked analytics as work advances.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | Damian Lemczak: Praktyczne zastosowania Low-Code w branży produkcyjnej
talks.teaser: Low-code on Power Platform digitizes shop-floor time logs, boards, receipts, safety reports, and maintenance without full IT projects.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a concise picture of Industry 4.0—cloud, IoT, big data, business intelligence, robotics, digital twins, and cyber-physical links—and why plants struggle with cost, fear of sweeping change, and tiny IT teams that cannot own every improvement. The speaker argues for incremental low-code steps rather than overturning the whole production model at once.

Most of the time walks through Microsoft Power Platform cases from real factory pain: RFID kiosk timekeeping with month-end approval to SharePoint or Dataverse; Power BI boards fed from ERP, planning, quality, and safety data instead of hours on paper; mobile goods receipt with AI Builder document capture and ERP upload, including automatic mail when quantities mismatch; safety and audit forms with photos and Power Automate escalations; a tablet station hub to start ERP orders, view drawings, report missing parts straight to forklift staff, and capture kaizen or 5S ideas; and a maintenance app for barcode parts intake, preventive swap alerts, and replacement logging.

Licensing notes—F3, per-user, per-app, kiosk multiplexing, and premium connectors—appear alongside each pattern. Takeaways: business-built apps can target shop-floor time waste first; connectors tie low-code layers to ERP and logistics; and even rough UX can pay back when it removes paper, delays, and broken handoffs between shifts.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | Arkadiusz Chodorowski & Bartłomiej Pisz: Tame the Mule with point'n'click
talks.teaser: The session covers adopting MuleSoft for enterprise integrations and building Salesforce-to-Slack flows with Composer and Anypoint Studio.
talks.summary:
The presenters recount how GDPR pressure at a large German automotive client drove a Salesforce-centered data migration and integration program. They initially stood up a container-based landscape with heavy Java development, DevOps, and a large permanent team, delivered on time and on budget, then struggled when ongoing maintenance still demanded nearly the same headcount.

After MuleSoft became part of Salesforce, they framed the shift around clear goals, a new delivery mindset, deliberate upskilling, and tight client feedback. They outline Anypoint Platform and Studio for IT-style integrations, Composer for business-side automation, plus RPA and Exchange, and caution that meaningful MuleSoft competence takes weeks rather than a short certification course.

Live demos show Composer alerting Slack when a high-value lead is deleted, synchronizing Google Sheets contracts with Salesforce and Slack-driven approval, and building an Anypoint Studio flow that reads a contact’s coordinates from Salesforce and returns weather from a public Meteo API. The closing message favors reusable connectors and templates so citizen developers can move quickly while IT supplies governance and accelerators.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | Mieszko Rożej: Nie bój się automatyzacji - jak ujarzmić flow
talks.teaser: Shows how Salesforce Flow automates CRM processes, explains variables simply, and demos screen and scheduled flows.
talks.summary:
The session opens with audience questions about daily work with Salesforce and broader automation, then positions Salesforce as a CRM platform that can support many business processes beyond sales, from fleet management to student administration. The presenter argues that Flow is the main low-code tool for tying records, notifications, screen-guided steps, and background jobs together without frightening maintainers with heavy custom code.

Most of the middle demystifies variables as a temporary workspace—like a drawer or scratchpad—where calculations and record edits stay safe until a final step writes results into the live database. Colored building blocks assign values, transform data, and update records; screen flows walk users through data entry, while scheduled and record-triggered flows run without user attention.

After theory, live configuration builds a screen flow to add client branch offices under a parent account for a sample company, then a scheduled flow that nightly flags customers with no revenue in the current year as inactive. Closing guidance favors clear flow descriptions, Trailhead for self-study, and custom development only when scale or complexity demands it, such as millions of records at once.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | Bartosz Sobolewski: Obsługa błędów w rozwiązaniach Robotic Process Automation
talks.teaser: Covers failure modes in unsupervised RPA and practical recovery patterns for dialogs, dirty sessions, and silent application updates.
talks.summary:
The session opens with robotic process automation as software that mimics a human using desktop, web, email, spreadsheet, database, and API interfaces. Attended bots assist an operator on an open workstation; unattended bots run on virtual machines or terminal-server accounts on schedules or triggers, often across many systems, without anyone watching the screen.

Failures are grouped into design mistakes, developer bugs usually caught in testing, and deployment configuration drift between environments. Production pain more often comes from a shifting machine: vendor updates, UI or column layout changes, network or database outages, pop-up dialogs, forced restarts, and human-prepared inputs that break agreed formats or process order. The speaker illustrates recovery after a crash by repeatedly dismissing known message boxes, closing windows, optionally killing stubborn processes, and only then alerting a caretaker if the desktop cannot be cleaned. Robots should prefer a clean start state, though license pooling sometimes forces leaving applications open.

Further mitigations include checking application versions against values the bot was tested on, comparing Excel header rows or table layouts to stored fingerprints before processing, and using state machines so irreversible steps are not duplicated. Reliable unattended automation depends on ongoing coordination between robot authors, IT that owns the environment, and operators who supply data.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | D. Ciurko, W. Mamys: Czy Tosca i podobne rozwiązania są przyszłością testowania?
talks.teaser: Compares Tosca and Cypress on the same job-search flow and asks whether no-code automation can match scripted end-to-end testing.
talks.summary:
The session frames codeless and low-code test automation against staff shortages cited for the EU and Poland, then walks through one scenario on a careers site: open the page, reach job offers, search for a role in Bydgoszcz, and confirm results appear. Two presenters implement the same steps in Tricentis Tosca—project setup, scanning modules, explicit names, and data-driven templates—and in Cypress with Node.js, manual selectors from devtools, intercepts for flaky result loading, and optional Cypress Studio recording.

They contrast browser, desktop, mobile, API, and SAP coverage, scripting requirements, reporting, and when Python or JSON fixtures help scale cases such as Toruń or many cities without copy-paste. Both paths still demand tester judgment, tool familiarity, DOM understanding, and maintainable structure; Tosca is portrayed as faster for click-and-scan work while Cypress stays anchored in JavaScript.

Their takeaway is pragmatic rather than binary: Tosca-class tools belong in the mix and can deliver equivalent checks with less daily coding, but projects, teams, and skills still decide the right blend, and experience in one stack transfers to the other.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | K. Rakowski & P. Rekowski: Zmiany są wszędzie.
talks.teaser: Walks through Kotter's eight-step change model and shows why organizational transformations so often stall and how to lead them.
talks.summary:
Krzysztof Rakowski and Paweł Rekowski argue that change is everywhere, from personal habits to whole-company transformations, and that attempts usually fail when people act on instinct. They cite Kotter's research that about 70 percent of transformations fail, and a recent Harvard Business Review finding that 67 percent of managers had seen changes miss their goals. Their starting point is Lewin's three stages of unfreezing, changing and refreezing, combined with Kotter's eight steps, which they say should not be followed as a strict waterfall.

Leaders should first show urgency by explaining what happens if nothing changes, then build a guiding coalition of people with different roles and personalities, using stakeholder mapping and profiling tests. A clear vision explains what will change and why, and volunteers become change ambassadors. Resisters should get work that suits them rather than being pushed, and barriers such as missing time or budget must be removed. Communication runs throughout, since momentum fades when nothing visible happens.

The closing part covers short-term wins, keeping pace after setbacks, and making change stick. Retiring old procedures matters as much as launching new ones, and behaviour should change before culture does. Adoption should be measured, not just project completion; the speakers gave the example of a Microsoft software suite where only about 5 percent is used. They recommend taking one change, explaining why it matters, and starting with small steps, with Atomic Habits as a useful read.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | Łukasz Zajączkowski: Chcę do IT!
talks.teaser: Offers practical guidance on entering IT through low-code roles instead of traditional programming bootcamps.
talks.summary:
The session opens by polling who already works in IT and who joined within the last five years, then frames career entry from the perspective of someone who became a software trainer with minimal prior knowledge and now helps others change industries. The speaker stresses that IT work is constantly verified: applications either run for users or they do not, which makes the field demanding even when salaries attract newcomers who are unsure which role to pursue.

Using examples from dozens of recruits and trainees over roughly the last three years, he contrasts multi-month programming bootcamps with faster paths into low-code and no-code consulting, project management, training, and related roles. He discusses company expectations such as moving beyond junior level within about 12 months, citizen developers building solutions outside classic IT channels, shadow IT, and the communication needed so business-led tools can grow without breaking production.

He closes with labor-market numbers on application growth and Gartner-cited forecasts, plus three delivery modes—fast low-code builds, assisted fusion development alongside programmers, and full IT delivery where low-code is insufficient. The practical message is to choose technology and role deliberately, build broad communication and documentation habits, and invest time in abstract thinking before assuming senior standing.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | Marcin Zajkowski: Leniwy programista na autopilocie o życiu z LowCode NoCode
talks.teaser: Explores how developers reclaim time through elimination, monitoring, and low-code automation for daily and business workflows.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why IT professionals chase an “autopilot” life: time cannot be bought outright, yet repetitive work and unclear tasks drain weeks that could go elsewhere. The speaker discusses burnout, the Dunning–Kruger curve versus imposter feelings after conference demos, and skepticism toward low-code among experienced developers.

A practical thread follows: quantify small recurring tasks over years, eliminate distractions first, then monitor behavior with tools such as Rize and Opal before defining event–condition–action automations. Examples span browser blockers, Shortcuts, TextExpander, Keyboard Maestro, Make for RSS and YouTube prep, GitHub commits summarized for timesheets, and email rules. Low-code enters for integration platforms and a client MVP evaluated across Bubble, Retool, and Xano with UI built via Tabler.

The closing message is eliminate wasteful habits, automate only defined processes, delegate when automation is not enough, and choose platforms with export and scale in mind—not every shortcut survives multiple product generations.

talks.title: No Code Days 2023 | D. Trzaskowska & M. Nowicka: O psychologii zmiany i „(nie)męskim” świecie IT.
talks.teaser: A panel blends psychology of career change with research on gender stereotypes and barriers women face entering IT.
talks.summary:
Two psychology graduates who moved into low-code consulting host a discussion on przebranżowienie—changing industry and skill set—and why Polish research on the topic is still sparse. They share pre-event survey data on motivations for moving into IT, including pay and passion, then connect gender schemas from childhood through school choices to hiring and leadership patterns in tech.

The middle of the session weaves theory with personal timelines: elective programming sparked satisfaction in building products and teamwork; imposter feelings and a male-dominated image of IT complicated the jump from humanities backgrounds. Practical guidance covers mapping skills on a CV, optional self-discovery tools such as Belbin and strengths frameworks, job-offer comparisons, and reading emotions as signals that a workplace may no longer fit values.

Later segments name recurring obstacles—discrimination in hiring, emotional stereotyping, extra vigilance at work, imposter syndrome, higher proof burdens for women in recruiting, glass ceilings, and pay gaps illustrated by EU equality campaigns. The panel closes by urging listeners to judge fit individually, seek peer support networks, and treat fear as information when planning change.

talks.title: Patryk Hes: Ten things we've learned from running production infrastructure at Google | DOD Warsaw
talks.teaser: Presents ten SRE lessons from running Google's production systems, covering reliability, culture, change management and automation.
talks.summary:
Patryk Hes, a site reliability engineer who has worked at Google for seven years, opens by explaining SRE as an approach that treats running production as a software engineering problem. The discipline began when Google was essentially a single site. SREs sit in a central organization separate from product developers, but work closely with them, and that arrangement lets engineers move between areas and spread good practice. He argues that a healthy team culture matters more than any strategy.

The core of the talk is a sequence of ten lessons. Reliability must have an advocate from the design stage, because fixing an unreliable system later is far more expensive. Standardizing machines and software, rather than treating each server as a unique pet, reduces cognitive load at scale. Incident reviews should assume people act competently and in good faith, so the focus lands on the system and its processes rather than on blame, and people should feel safe reporting problems. Teams should measure what matters against agreed goals, since anything unmeasured tends to degrade. SREs should take part in on-call to learn how systems fail, and heroics should be discouraged because they reward firefighting over prevention. Recurring manual work should be automated before it grows. Change is the leading cause of outages, so releases should be versioned, reviewed and reproducible, with freezes used sparingly. Outages should be mitigated first and investigated later, with written incident notes and shared visibility across teams. Finally, small unresolved problems, or broken windows, accumulate into haunted graveyards, so systems should be kept simple and cared for regularly.

The talk closes on common themes: shared responsibility for production, openness to change, engineering automation to scale, and keeping systems simple. For practitioners, the takeaway is to involve reliability early, measure against clear goals, and automate the work that will not scale by hand.

talks.title: Bartłomiej Pisulak: Embracing Chaos: Breaking Your System to Make It Indestructible | DOD Warsaw
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Bartłomiej Pisulak: Embracing Chaos: Breaking Your System to Make It Indestructible | DOD Warsaw.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at a DevOps conference in Warsaw, Bartłomiej Pisulak (BK), a Senior Manager at Pegasystems, introduces the fundamentals of chaos engineering and argues for its adoption in modern distributed architectures. Drawing a direct connection between mathematical Chaos Theory and modern IT architectures, Pisulak explains that complex, distributed systems are inherently chaotic—where minute fluctuations can trigger massive downstream failures. He outlines the history, core principles, business justification, and practical execution of chaos experiments using cloud tooling.

### Key Topics
- **Chaos Theory Foundations:** The talk reviews Edward Lorenz's work (and early insights by Henri Poincaré), explaining the butterfly effect and how small changes in dynamic initial conditions yield drastically different outcomes, contrasting chaotic systems (which are deterministic if all variables are known) with purely random systems.
- **Origins of Chaos Engineering:** Pisulak traces chaos engineering back to Netflix's 2008 AWS migration after a three-day DVD outage. This spurred the creation of Chaos Monkey, the Simian Army (including Chaos Gorilla and Chaos Kong), and eventually specialized industry tools such as Gremlin and AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS).
- **Core Principles:** Developed at Netflix, the five foundational principles are: building hypotheses around steady-state behavior, simulating real-world events, running experiments in production, automating experiments continuously in delivery pipelines, and minimizing blast radius.
- **Prerequisites for Chaos Testing:** Before introducing chaos, organizations must first fix all known bugs and establish clear observability to define and monitor their system's normal steady-state baseline.
- **The Business Case (Resiliency, Reputation, Money):** Pisulak emphasizes that downtime causes severe human strain (such as 2 a.m. emergency pages) and brand damage, citing user impatience when websites take over 10 seconds to load. Financially, Gartner and other research estimate average downtime costs between $5,600 and $9,000 per minute (averaging around $7,000 per minute), with major historical incidents like Delta Airlines' $150 million loss during a five-hour outage in 2016 and significant cross-service blast radiuses during AWS outages.

### Technical Details
Pisulak demonstrates a basic chaos engineering experiment on AWS using Terraform and AWS Fault Injection Simulator:
- **Infrastructure Provisioning:** Terraform deploys an Application Load Balancer (ALB), target group, security group, and an Auto Scaling Group managing EC2 instances (configured with desired capacity 2, max size 4) labeled with the tag `to_be_destroyed: true`.
- **Observability:** A lightweight Python script (`observe.py`) continuously polls the ALB DNS endpoint, flagging non-200 HTTP responses and recording total downtime seconds.
- **Fault Injection:** In AWS FIS, an experiment template targets running EC2 instances with the designated tag and triggers an instance termination action.
- **Results & Findings:** The termination caused 87 seconds of total website downtime before the Auto Scaling Group restored healthy instances. While the hypothesis was confirmed (the architecture survived and self-healed without manual intervention), the experiment revealed architectural latency and measurable downtime that cost money, prompting engineers to evaluate whether bare EC2 instances are the right architecture.

### Takeaways
- Chaos engineering does not create flaws; it uncovers pre-existing vulnerabilities before they manifest as unplanned customer outages.
- Fixing known defects and implementing robust observability are strict prerequisites before introducing simulated chaos.
- Tools like AWS Fault Injection Simulator make it straightforward to execute controlled chaos experiments against infrastructure.
- The ultimate objective is moving experiments toward production pipelines, reducing human operational stress, protecting revenue, and continuously proving system self-healing capabilities.

talks.title: Karolina Ochlik: Hey engineer - facilitate the change! Implementing lean DevOps | DOD Warsaw 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how lean thinking, reusable CI/CD templates and small mixed teams can fix slow handoffs in large corporate DevOps.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why DevOps is hard to adopt in large, heavily regulated companies, where work is split between business, development and operations teams and the operations side is swamped with manual requests. The speaker walks through a personal case: a developer waited about three months for a development environment and database, passing through paperwork, a security self-review and permission requests, with manual data entry errors along the way. Delays like these make delivery slow, and the setup does not scale when many teams need the same thing.

The proposed remedy borrows from lean manufacturing. Teams should define the value a product delivers, map the value stream, remove steps that add nothing, work in a pull style driven by real feedback, and keep iterating in small steps. Practical moves for an engineer include assessing the current process, asking end users for input, automating repeated tasks such as project creation through an API, and building reusable, parameterized CI/CD pipelines. The speaker mentions reusing one pipeline across six Python projects, and suggests cataloguing services in a developer portal such as Backstage so ownership and APIs are easy to find.

To finish, the speaker encourages engineers to share what they build through brown-bag sessions and innersource contributions, and to measure where time is lost so improvements can be justified. Longer term, the talk proposes merging product ownership and delivery into small BizDevOps teams so that feedback reaches developers quickly. Managers are best persuaded with clear, positive data, presented with green rather than red.

talks.title: Katarzyna Majer, Michał Janusiński: The impact of energy crisis on European data center operations
talks.teaser: European data center growth meets energy crisis fallout: gas-linked power spikes, FLAP-D grid limits, and summer cooling failures.
talks.summary:
The session frames cloud workloads as dependent on physical data centers, then maps the global and European market, including the FLAP-D hubs and how fiber, land, and power shape where capacity concentrates. It walks through data growth drivers such as AI training, IoT, and pandemic-era traffic, and links facility design to steady power, cooling, and the usual 18–27°C operating band.

The middle traces the European energy crisis from TTF gas price history through Gazprom supply cuts and the 2022 spike, showing how electricity costs tracked gas and hit gas-heavy economies hardest. It explains how colocation and hyperscaler buyers use spot, hybrid, or fixed power deals, ESG pressures, and large renewable power purchase agreements, while demand for space and long lead times tightened FLAP-D inventory.

The close turns to city-level consequences: Frankfurt restricting grid access and pushing builds outward; West London hitting power ceilings and suffering redundant cooling losses at Google and Oracle during record heat; Amsterdam blocking large Meta and rumored hyperscaler sites; Paris balancing GDPR-driven demand with Olympic zoning; and Dublin halting new builds until 2028 while Microsoft seeks on-site generation. Practitioners should treat power, water, heat, and permitting as operational risks beside rack economics.

talks.title: Marcin Kwiatkowski - Sposoby migracji aplikacji frontendowych do nowszych technologii...
talks.teaser: Covers when frontend rewrites fail on cost and risk, then three incremental migration paths with live legacy-to-React examples.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting the temptation to rebuild frontends from scratch with the real price tag, using a rough estimate of a year with twenty developers at 15,000 per month per person to illustrate why management often rejects full rewrites. The speaker argues migration is not a universal fix: missing business justification, integration overhead between old and new stacks, the expense of running two systems, mismatched scope, and very small codebases can all favor staying put or rewriting instead. He also warns that greenfield rewrites tend to drop undocumented features and can erode business trust, and cites regulated environments where platform versions carry accreditation constraints.

Before tactics, he recommends documenting technical decisions for rotating teams, investing in design systems (including Storybook), and either porting an existing design system into the new stack or aligning legacy styling with a planned one. The core of the talk is three patterns demonstrated with simple HTML legacy apps and newer React or Next-based pieces: reverse-proxy URL routing on one domain so cookies and auth can be shared; hybrid components that mount new frameworks inside legacy DOM shells, illustrated with AngularJS and React; and iframe-based slices with parent-child communication via postMessage events (and mention of CSP to block standalone iframe use). Live demos show users routes switching stacks while URLs stay familiar, lists reimplemented as React inside AngularJS, and dashboard embeds driving navigation in the parent app.

Practitioners should treat migration as a phased product decision: weigh asset-load costs when users cross stack boundaries, budget build-pipeline work for hybrid repos, and plan explicit cross-app contracts for auth, navigation, and events rather than assuming a seamless single application.

talks.title: Karol Przystalski
talks.teaser: Shows how JavaScript, React Native, and TensorFlow.js deliver commercially deployed skin lesion analysis for dermatologists.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a long-running research effort on melanoma and other skin cancers, starting from an unusably small university image set and growing to thousands of clinical photos gathered over a year in Poland. The speaker outlines why dermatoscopy and pattern-based diagnosis matter more than simple ABCD scoring, and how commercially deployed software now ships inside dermatoscope hardware from a Munich manufacturer.

The middle of the talk contrasts Python’s mature machine-learning stack with JavaScript options such as TensorFlow.js, pandas-js, and React Native for mobile delivery. On-device inference on older iPhones is weighed against networked TensorFlow Serving for retraining and precision. Notebook demos walk through border removal, asymmetry checks, and blue-veil pattern detection, plus the limits of shallow versus deep models and why explainability matters before production.

The close summarizes trade-offs: JavaScript suits phones and quick web pivots while training stays in Python; MLOps tooling in JS remains thin and many npm libraries fail in production. The speaker briefly notes ongoing hair-loss pattern work, resources on GitLab, and related research on coronary imaging and medical explainability.

talks.title: Łukasz Wójcik - Jak okiełznać transakcje rozproszone w Masstransit.
talks.teaser: Covers MassTransit saga patterns, comparing central orchestration with routing-slip choreography through live warehouse demos.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing distributed transactions as a consistency problem that outgrows classic ACID guarantees once work is split across microservices. It sketches familiar transaction properties—atomicity, consistent state, isolation, and durability—and notes that monolithic databases handled these more naturally than today’s service meshes, where choreography and orchestration become the main levers.

MassTransit is introduced as a .NET-oriented distributed application framework: transport abstraction over brokers such as RabbitMQ, publish–subscribe semantics, queue management, retries, scheduling, OpenTelemetry-friendly monitoring, and saga support. The first deep dive is orchestration via a state-machine saga with a central coordinator. A warehouse scenario—accept an item, validate storage, pack, and release—shows how states, events, correlation identifiers, and compensating paths are coded, run against RabbitMQ, queried while in flight, and dropped from storage when marked finished.

The second pattern is choreography built on routing slips and Courier activities, illustrated by renting audio gear for a show: license validation, availability checks, device verification, VIP handling, and localized compensation when a late step fails. The talk closes with a candid comparison: orchestration fits complex, state-heavy flows but concentrates failure risk; choreography scales simpler pipelines with less central control yet can blur observability and introduce cyclic messaging if designed carelessly.

talks.title: Maciej Godek - Czego o architekturze nauczyła mnie praca nad własnym edytorem kodu
talks.teaser: Reviews architecture lessons from iterative Lisp editor prototypes, Emacs-inspired workflows, and unconventional implementation choices.
talks.summary:
The presenter argues that “architecture” is a weak metaphor for the kind of software he builds; evolving programs is closer to inventing a language for what you create. He grounds the story in Lisp and Emacs: prefix notation, homoiconicity, cons lists, and evaluating expressions under the cursor during incremental work.

Three editor prototypes trace that idea. An early version pairs Lisp text with rudimentary graphical “parenthesis” widgets and right-click transforms. A phone-based Java editor turns drawn shapes into s-expressions and supports split panes and factorial play, but fails as a long-term base because Java cannot host Lisp syntax, Android-only deployment hurts, attaching Kawa slows builds, and testing and keyboard editing lag. The current line uses mixin-style extension instead of inheritance, string renderers for tests, shared graphics APIs across clients, terminal and desktop UIs, and visual extensions including buttons and a stepping evaluator.

Late sections treat design problems that look architectural: representing whitespace around cons structure with hash maps and custom definers rather than inheritance, avoiding global state via dynamic scope for cursor moves, and one traverse pipeline—with continuations where needed—for measure, draw, and hit-test. The through-line is how language features and editor affordances co-evolve when you build your own environment.

talks.title: Agnieszka Cent - Event Sourcing dla nieprzekonanych - case study w oparciu o CosmosDb i...
talks.teaser: Walks through event sourcing basics, when to use it, and a production case study on Cosmos DB and Service Bus.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces event sourcing to developers who are sceptical of it. The speaker, Agnieszka Cent, starts with the core idea: instead of overwriting records, a system appends events and rebuilds current state by replaying the events of a stream, usually keyed by an order ID. She separates event sourcing from related terms such as CQRS, event-driven architecture and DDD, and explains where the pattern fits, such as sagas, orchestration and choreography, audit trails, and reports that can be rebuilt by replay. It is a poor fit for simple logic, for workflows that need immediate strong consistency, or for teams with no prior experience.

The case study covers a production setup in which small process services store events in Azure Cosmos DB, with one partition per stream, and publish them through a transactional outbox driven by the change feed. Integration runs over Azure Service Bus. The speaker shares modelling advice: keep streams short, because long-lived streams drove request-unit costs up, and handle event versioning with care. For a high-volume device-data service, Service Bus became a bottleneck, so that load moved to Azure Event Hubs, while older events were moved to cheaper storage.

The main takeaway is that event sourcing gives a strong audit trail and makes replaying failed flows possible, but stream length and storage costs need constant watching. The speaker concludes that Cosmos DB worked well for her team once costs were monitored and limits were set carefully.

talks.title: Bartosz Banachewicz - 3D for everyone with R3F
talks.teaser: Explains how React Three Fiber merges React and Three.js so developers ship interactive 3D configurators in dozens of lines.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the speaker’s path from wanting to make 3D games—months of tutorials before a single triangle appeared—through graphics pipelines, performance, hardware, and GPU driver work at Intel. That long stack of low- and high-level knowledge frames why React Three Fiber feels like a breakthrough: it links React’s declarative UI model with Three.js so teams can import a ready integration instead of building separate abstraction towers.

Live examples anchor the argument. A shoe customizer and a pair of rotating cubes show color pickers, hover and click on 3D meshes, lighting, materials, and roughly 39–76 lines of code. The walkthrough covers Canvas, scene primitives, refs, state, useFrame for animation, raycasting for pointer events, and physically based materials without demanding the math underneath. A commercial angle compares six-figure 3D UX projects with what a React-savvy shop could build for far less.

The closing section treats limits honestly: useFrame can fight React’s render model, memoization still matters, whole-scene GLTF files hinder per-part interaction, and DOM versus 3D trees stay separate unless architects plan for it. Drei helpers, GLTF-to-JSX tooling, and portal-based “tunnels” ease those pains. React scheduling and workers can keep pages responsive under heavy 3D work, and hot reload can swap models in dev like ordinary components.

talks.title: Karol Przystalski
talks.teaser: Attendees learn how JavaScript and TensorFlow.js power a production skin-cancer app used on dermatoscopes and mobile devices.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting skepticism about JavaScript for machine learning with a long-running project to detect skin cancer from dermatoscopic images. He describes gathering thousands of clinic images after starting from a tiny university set, identifying roughly a dozen visual patterns during doctoral work, and partnering with a German dermatoscope manufacturer so the model ships on next-generation clinical hardware.

The middle of the talk walks through stack choices from early hybrid mobile frameworks to React Native, on-device versus server inference, and MLOps concerns such as data preparation, model testing, and explainability for regulators and clinicians. He compares Python and JavaScript ecosystems, highlights libraries that work versus those that break in production, and demonstrates pattern recognition on mole images, including multispectral cues such as blue-gray areas tied to deeper melanoma.

He closes with notebook examples for border removal, asymmetry scoring, and blue-veil detection, argues shallow explainable models often beat opaque neural nets in deployment, and summarizes tradeoffs: JavaScript suits mobile and web delivery while training stays in Python, with thin MLOps tooling in JS despite a large developer community.

talks.title: Marcin Milewicz - Pragmatyczna architektura frontendowa, czyli jaka?
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Marcin Milewicz - Pragmatyczna architektura frontendowa, czyli jaka?.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Prezentacja Marcina Milewicza, Principal Developera i Frontend Architekta w firmie KMD, poświęcona jest pragmatycznemu podejściu do architektury frontendowej. Prelegent odchodzi od czysto taktycznych szczegółów implementacyjnych, skupiając się na architekturze jako procesie podejmowania decyzji projektowych dopasowanych do celów biznesowych tu i teraz, zamiast ulegania zjawisku Hype-Driven Development.

### Key Topics
- **Definicja architektury oprogramowania**: Odwołanie do książki Simona Browna *Software Architecture for Developers*, gdzie architektura oprogramowania stanowi sumę architektury systemowej (komunikacja, interfejsy, backend) oraz architektury aplikacji (wzorce, struktura kodu, komunikacja zespołu). Prelegent podkreśla, że architektura to przede wszystkim zbiór decyzji projektowych powiązanych z realiami biznesowymi.
- **Hype-Driven Development vs. Pragmatyzm**: Zestawienie bezkrytycznego wdrażania nowinek technologicznych (Clean Architecture, DDD, Storybook, pełna piramida testów: unit, integration, E2E w Cypress czy Playwright) z pragmatyzmem, który definiowany jest jako dostarczanie największej praktycznej korzyści biznesowej w danym momencie przy skończonym czasie i budżecie.
- **Specyfika frontendu**: Frontend to aplikacja uruchamiana w przeglądarce (lub środowiskach wyspecjalizowanych, takich jak bankomaty czy aplikacje webowe pokroju Figma i Photoshop w WebAssembly). Nowoczesny frontend przejmuje coraz więcej logiki biznesowej i wymaga bezpośredniej współpracy z interesariuszami.
- **Identyfikacja potrzeb i alternatywy zamiast priorytetów**: W rozmowach z klientem pytanie o pojedyncze priorytety prowadzi do sytuacji, w której „wszystko ma najwyższy priorytet”. Zamiast tego architekt powinien identyfikować potrzeby, przedstawiać alternatywne opcje (np. w postaci ADR – Architecture Decision Records) z jawnym określeniem kosztów oraz ryzyk i pozostawić ostateczną decyzję biznesowi.

### Technical Details & Architectural Drivers
Prelegent omawia kluczowe drivery architektoniczne determinujące wybory techniczne:
- **Zarządzanie danymi i integracje**: Częstotliwość zmian danych, wolumen danych ładowanych do pamięci RAM przeglądarki (np. 150–200 tys. rekordów w systemie bankowym i ograniczenia bibliotek tabelarycznych), architektura API (obecność API Gateway, integracja z mikroserwisami, komunikacja w sieci lokalnej vs. zewnętrznej) oraz konieczność wsparcia trybu offline (Offline First).
- **Analiza backlogu i kontekst biznesowy**: Weryfikacja planów na wyższym szczeblu (np. u CTO). Prelegent przytoczył przypadek wyboru Reacta zamiast Angulara ze względu na dostępność specjalistów na lokalnym rynku oraz wcześniejszy zakup gotowego Design Systemu, a także projekt tworzony na 4 tygodnie bez dalszego utrzymania, gdzie pisanie testów integracyjnych widoków było nieuzasadnione ekonomicznie.
- **Kwantyfikacja atrybutów jakościowych**: Mierzenie wskaźników wszędzie tam, gdzie to możliwe – m.in. metryki wydajnościowe (Core Web Vitals), pokrycie testami i testy mutacyjne, analityka i audytowalność przy użyciu narzędzi takich jak Matomo, Google Analytics czy Faro.
- **Ograniczenia (Constraints)**:
  - *Regulacyjne i prawne (Regulatory & Compliance)*: Ograniczenia geolokalizacji danych (np. zakaz przechowywania danych analitycznych poza krajem lub w Google Analytics w określonych instytucjach publicznych w Niemczech i Rosji).
  - *Technologiczne (In-house Technology)*: Narzucone biblioteki wewnętrzne, wrappery komponentów (np. zmodyfikowany Angular Material ograniczający API), specyficzne mechanizmy renderowania czy niestandardowe biblioteki logujące.
  - *Skalowanie zespołu (Team Scaling)*: Dostępność programistów na danym rynku pracy (np. trudności w rekrutacji programistów Angulara w Anglii czy dominacja programistów C++ we Wrocławiu ze względu na obecność Nokii).
  - *Biznesowe*: Budżet oraz Time to Market, gdzie szybsze wdrożenie na produkcję z dopuszczeniem drobnych błędów może przeważać nad rozbudowanymi pipeline'ami CI/CD.

### Takeaways
- Architektura nie jest wyryta w kamieniu, lecz jest „zbiorem decyzji wyrytym w czasie” i ewoluuje wraz ze zmianami wymagań.
- Decyzje o strukturze (SPA, PWA, SSR, mikrofrontendy, podział na warstwy) powinny wynikać bezpośrednio ze zdefiniowanych wcześniej driverów architektonicznych, a nie od nich zaczynać.
- Zadaniem architekta jest przekładanie kwestii technicznych na język kosztów i ryzyk biznesowych, co umożliwia podejmowanie świadomych decyzji.

talks.title: Mateusz Buczkowski - Vertical video marketing dla developerów: jak tiktoki, szorty i rolki mogą...
talks.teaser: Explains how short vertical videos on TikTok, Reels and Shorts can promote IT services, courses and personal brands.
talks.summary:
Mateusz Buczkowski, a marketer who is writing a book on vertical video for onepress, argues that short-form feeds on TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts and similar platforms have become a serious channel for promoting services, courses and personal brands. He points to audiences that use these feeds as a search engine or as their main news source, and notes that Twitch has adopted the format while Netflix and Spotify are testing it.

He explains that the recommendation logic rewards content that entertains, provokes or is useful, and that viewers save, rewatch or return to helpful videos. Personal brands led by a founder or a single recognisable face tend to outperform faceless company accounts, and regular posting matters because the algorithm learns an audience over time. Authenticity counts for more than polish: a phone recording can beat a studio production, and results rise and fall in a wave-like pattern rather than growing steadily. Examples include a programming channel built on basic tutorials, a video on the most expensive PC buildable from current parts, and a Tricity company, Speednet, with only 14 TikTok followers.

For practitioners, the main takeaway is that the entry barrier is low: a phone and a well-lit room can be enough. One video can be reused across several platforms, evergreen how-to content keeps working for a long time, and paid promotion can boost results. Because few strong Polish-language benchmarks exist, he encourages early testing, since early movers can become the reference point others are measured against.

talks.title: Monika Sałach - Wypalenie zawodowe to nie Twoja wina - naukowo o wypaleniu zawodowym
talks.teaser: Recognize burnout’s warning signs and see how workplace conditions and personal well-being shape the response.
talks.summary: The speaker presents a psychology-based account of workplace burnout, describing its three dimensions: exhaustion, cynicism or distance from work, and a reduced sense of effectiveness. She distinguishes burnout from depression, reviews workplace conditions that can contribute to it, and explains why individual personality traits do not make it the employee’s fault. talks.title: Krystian Rykaczewski - How to test network protocols
talks.teaser: Shows how to capture, replay and malform network protocol traffic with Wireshark, Radamsa and Python.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that network protocol implementations get less testing attention than web or desktop software, even though every layer of the stack parses untrusted input. The speaker contrasts classic functional testing, where valid and invalid values are checked against the RFC or requirements, with fuzzing. Dumb fuzzing sends malformed data without regard to the expected behaviour, while smarter approaches use some knowledge of the protocol's structure. The speaker also describes an internal library that rejected improper input, which led to writing small custom clients instead.

The speaker lists findings in the GoAhead web server, used in embedded devices, including an overflow from an oversized Host header, a memory issue from repeated headers in multipart form data, and a problem with an unclosed IPv6 host bracket. Issues in lower-layer TCP/IP stacks and a DHCP option were also mentioned. The workflow is to record traffic in Wireshark, export the bytes of the relevant layer, and mutate them with Radamsa using a fixed seed so results can be reproduced. In the demos, Burp Intruder is used against a captured HTTP request to test long header values, and Radamsa generates malformed variants of a captured FTP login sequence. The speaker then rebuilds an FTP client in Python, finding that the server sends a banner first and needs a separate connection step before the user and password commands.

The closing point is that this approach pays off most for small embedded devices with custom network services, where full server stacks do not fit and bugs are common. A practitioner should capture real traffic, replicate it exactly before changing anything, and then vary fields such as lengths and format specifiers.

talks.title: Mikołaj Kurkuba - Testowanie wymagań, czyli biznesowy prapoczątek każdego projektu technologicznego
talks.teaser: Shows how to test requirements early, linking user stories to business goals and stakeholders before development starts.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a business analyst who began his career in QA, opens by explaining why requirements matter. He cites research showing that many projects fail because of weak requirements, analysis or management, and he notes that communication problems rank first. His argument is that the cheapest place to catch these problems is the very beginning, so requirements should be checked before any code is written, in line with shift-left thinking.

He then walks through a large set of user stories and acceptance criteria from a workshop with a client. His method is to start from the business goal, identify the stakeholders affected, and only then break the work down into functional requirements, with diagrams and mockups added where they help. Each requirement should trace back to the goal. He also recommends asking what would happen if a feature were not delivered, a question that once revealed nobody would use it. A shared glossary guards against ambiguous terms, and criteria should be phrased positively rather than with negatives. Step-by-step scenarios of user paths, including negative ones, help expose gaps in business logic.

For story quality, he describes a definition of ready agreed before refinement. It covers the business justification, a success path, mockups where relevant, and a size that fits within one sprint. Many acceptance criteria signal that a story should be split. Flow checks show when objects can still be edited or deleted, and event storming helps identify who is responsible and which systems must communicate. The takeaway is to validate requirements with the team early, in plain language backed by visuals.

talks.title: Tomasz Jakóbiec - In the search for Evolutionary Architecture
talks.teaser: Explains how to improve legacy code incrementally using fitness functions and layered architecture.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a case study of a business software product whose engineering team grew sharply across releases while the codebase barely expanded and the cost per line of code rose steeply. The speaker traces this to tangled dependencies between classes and modules, which make changes risky, hard to test and hard for teams to share. Architecture is framed as the set of decisions that let a system support chosen quality attributes such as testability, performance and portability as requirements and technology change.

Evolutionary architecture is presented as resting on four pillars: guided incremental change, fitness functions, architectural coupling and data coupling. Using a hypothetical network communication stack reused across yearly device releases, the speaker shows how a benchmark measuring packets per second or a dependency checker can act as fitness functions. Several such checks should run together in continuous integration, and legacy code is first wrapped into layers and components with stable interfaces, so new work avoids the old internals.

In the organization's own experience, one interface-refinement metric took more than half a year to rise by 10%, while a dependency metric improved slightly even without deep refactoring. The speaker recommends building a group of supporters, agreeing on the target architecture and its rules, and securing management time as a share of team capacity. Progress should be reported with numbers managers understand, plans kept imperfect but moving, and effort focused where it pays off most.

talks.title: Piotr Zarzycki: ZnanySciemniacz.pl czyli jak zostałem dietetykiem i przeanalizowałem 3m komentarzy
talks.teaser: Shows how a mirrored medical review platform exposed copied, paid-looking patient reviews using simple text comparison.
talks.summary:
The talk examines fake patient reviews on Znany Lekarz, a large Polish platform for booking doctor appointments. Survey data shows most people read online reviews and trust them, while the regulator UOKiK fined two companies selling fake reviews, yet one seller kept offering paid comments a year later.

The speaker mirrored the platform's public doctor profiles with a slow, single-threaded scraper that ran for about two weeks, collecting nearly 150,000 profiles and around 2.5 million reviews. Exact copies were common: one review text appeared on 200 profiles and, counting small wording variants, 574 times overall. Near-duplicates differed only by a period, a comma or one word, and some long reviews were reused with names, ages and relatives swapped. A web tool built from this compares a profile's comments with others and flags similarity scores around 90 percent. Publication dates help show which copy came first, though short generic reviews can repeat legitimately.

The speaker also completed quick online dietetics courses to obtain credentials, created a profile, and tried buying reviews, which were only partly posted. The platform's team reviewed the findings, acknowledged that its checks had not targeted duplicate text, and began re-verifying older reviews. The takeaway is that simple text comparison and date ordering can expose copied reviews that more complex checks miss.

talks.title: Kamil Grzela, Maciej Nowak: Samochody w Sieci: Jak Testy Penetracyjne Odkrywają Ukryte Zagrożenia...
talks.teaser: Shows how penetration tests of car telematics units found weak cryptography and an SMS-triggered remote access path.
talks.summary:
The speakers, who work on automotive electronics security, explain that modern cars are networked systems of many controllers rather than purely mechanical machines. Vehicle architecture has moved from a flat bus, through domain clusters, toward zonal designs. The talk focuses on the telematics control unit, which handles cellular and radio links, and groups attack vectors by range: physical ports, short-range wireless, cellular, and cloud or infrastructure links.

Automotive penetration testing follows the V-model and comes in white-box, grey-box and black-box variants, at either component or whole-vehicle level. The first case study concerns a telematics unit that accepted remote commands from a mobile app through a vendor server, authenticated by a challenge-response scheme using a shared secret and a block cipher. The testers found weak randomness, flawed key derivation, and a master key that was either hardcoded in firmware or exposed on the bus. With such a key, an attacker could impersonate the unit and command other components on a flat network. The second case study involved a truck telematics unit that opened a TLS channel to its backend when it received a specially crafted binary SMS. The testers used that path to make the unit connect back to their own server, then injected code into a partly writable partition and sent commands on the vehicle network, with the demonstration run remotely between Tel Aviv and a European city.

The speakers stress that safety must come before security in automotive design, and that security is sometimes dropped under schedule pressure. Most flaws they meet come from implementation or configuration errors, such as missing authentication, homemade cryptography or code produced by AI tools, rather than from broken standards. Their advice is to harden devices, authenticate internal messages, and test before vehicles leave the factory, a step that regulators in the EU and US now require.

talks.title: Jakub Mrugalski: Hosting on Fire - Threats from Hackers to... Users | OMH 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how a shared hosting provider hardens its servers against scanners, abusive tenants and weak passwords with low-cost measures.
talks.summary:
Jakub Mrugalski, who runs the Polish hosting provider Mikrus, explains why a shared hosting platform is much harder to secure than a single server. Mikrus targets developers, yet many production applications run on it, including a glucose-monitoring app for children with diabetes that moved over after a free hosting tier closed. Scanners probe servers hundreds to thousands of times a month for vulnerable web apps, and with mostly beginner customers, one weak application is enough to get in.

Measures described include moving SSH off default ports, blocking traffic from countries with little legitimate use, and placing decoy servers whose contact triggers a network-wide ban. Abuse blocklists are imported into ipset, with a free tier of 10,000 entries and a supporter tier of 20,000, and IPv6 rules must be kept in step with IPv4. For customer apps, the speaker describes default subdomains with automatic HTTPS, a shared reverse proxy, disabled risky PHP functions, unprivileged LXC containers, and password checks against dictionaries, with John the Ripper used to audit weak passwords.

The main takeaway is that hosting security is a balancing act: protections must not break customers' applications, and no configuration is ever finished. The talk also stresses that traffic between tenants needs filtering and monitoring, since any customer can rent a machine and attack its neighbours.

talks.title: Agnieszka Gryszczyńska: Czy ustawa o ograniczaniu niektórych skutków kradzieży tożsamości wpłynie...
talks.teaser: Tests whether Poland's new PESEL restriction register stops real fraud, from SIM swaps to money mules.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether a new Polish law on reducing the effects of identity theft will change how criminals actually operate. The speaker, a lawyer who works on public registers, starts from the point that a PESEL national ID number is already widely exposed, so it is a weak proof of identity. She then traces how the criminal offence of impersonation was reworded by a recent amendment, so that actual harm must now occur, and notes that attempts remain punishable.

The middle of the talk walks through attack scenarios. These include fake identity documents sold online, money mules who collect stolen funds and move them through gold dealers or crypto exchanges, SIM card registrations made in other people's names, and SIM swap fraud that depends on a single human check to fail. Phone scams impersonating police or bank staff, investment fraud, business email compromise, fake online shops rebuilt on expired domains, and takeovers of social media accounts are also covered. For each, she checks whether the new register of PESEL restrictions would help. It would stop some paths, such as a planned 12-hour hold on certain branch cash withdrawals, but not others.

She concludes that the register shifts much of the burden onto citizens, and that its overall impact will be smaller than expected while attackers adapt. The practical takeaway is that restricting a PESEL helps against some fraud paths, but banks, lenders and mobile operators still need to verify who they are dealing with.

talks.title: Piotr Pęsiek: Śmiać się czy płakać, bezpieczeństwo na bazie przykładów z życia wziętych... | OMH
talks.teaser: Real-world security blunders from audits and pentests, from exposed backups to leaked cookies, told with humour and no theory.
talks.summary:
Piotr Pęsiek, a security officer who has worked through help desk, network and system administration, auditing and programming, presents real cases from his day job, audits and penetration tests. He frames the talk as facts rather than theory and stresses that any weakness found should be reported responsibly to the affected organisation. He opens with the growing exposure of everyday technology: smartphones, connected home devices, online shopping, remote education and ride-hailing apps, alongside social engineering and outdated software.

The middle of the talk walks through specific cases. He describes personal data that stayed reachable on a public government health fund website after he reported it in 2021, and a SQL injection he found while testing a site through a public channel. He mentions backup files left accessible to everyone, and a web application firewall that blocked his testing for a minute after a series of unusual requests. He recounts an exposed remote desktop port at a state organisation, a shared network folder holding plaintext passwords, and an encrypted password file stored beside an executable that could decrypt it. Further examples include cloud storage with overly broad permissions, stolen session cookies sold on a closed marketplace that can bypass multi-factor authentication, and a fraud case where a company's network devices pointed to a Vilnius location behind a London virtual office.

He closes with practical lessons: keep systems patched, use multi-factor authentication and strong passwords, monitor events, train staff, and test regularly with penetration tests.

talks.title: Ireneusz Tarnowski: MU74455: Cyberzagrożenia pisane cyrylicą | OMH 2023
talks.teaser: Follows Russian GRU unit 74455, known as Sandworm, through its infrastructure attacks and the attribution methods behind them.
talks.summary:
The talk, delivered in Polish, opens with a short introduction to threat intelligence as the work of understanding adversaries' capabilities, tools and infrastructure so an organisation can use that knowledge. The speaker walks through the diamond model for organising evidence about an actor and explains why attribution is hard. Firm attribution usually depends on a confession, a leak, or direct access to the adversary's infrastructure, and a single shared element such as an IP address is weak evidence. The talk also notes that vendors name the same group differently, so analysts must compare their own data carefully.

The main body follows GRU unit 74455, known as Sandworm, through a series of cases. These include the 2015 power outage in Ukraine linked to malware from the Black Energy family, the NotPetya attack, and a 2018 disruption of infrastructure supporting the Olympics in Korea. In the Korean case, early analysis pointed to several different actors, and later indictments and a detailed analysis of the delivery chain pointed to the same group. The speaker then covers the 2022 attack on a satellite communications operator and the wiper malware used against Ukraine, followed by a 2023 campaign against eleven Ukrainian telecom providers. The talk closes with a 2023 case in Denmark involving Zyxel switches, where the speaker argues the attribution rested on too little evidence.

In the final part, the speaker describes leaked contractor documents that name tools used for reconnaissance and operator training, and argues that the group's growing disregard for collateral damage means each new large operation brings new tooling. Practitioners are advised to track how the group's methods change and to read the recommended books for analysts.

talks.title: Michał Leszczyński: Backdoory w kryptografii asymetrycznej | OMH 2023
talks.teaser: Maps common RSA and ECDSA mistakes—from weak moduli to bad nonces—that let attackers forge signatures or steal private keys.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that asymmetric cryptography is easy to break in practice when protocols and implementations add assumptions the math does not guarantee. It opens with modular arithmetic as the foundation of RSA and elliptic-curve work, then shows how factorable moduli, duplicated primes from poor randomness, and close prime pairs can yield keys that look legitimate yet fall quickly to analysis.

For RSA, the speaker covers duplicate signature key selection in domain-validation flows, homomorphic properties behind padding-oracle abuse, and why detailed error feedback is dangerous. The ECDSA portion emphasizes verification edge cases, including a banking-library case where an all-zero signature verifies universally, hash values taken modulo curve order so one signature can match two messages, and recovering candidate public keys from a single message-signature pair. Further examples include forging plausible signatures from only a public key, MD5 chosen-prefix collisions against a commercial CA, nonce reuse draining private keys from game signing on consoles and mobile stacks, and concerns around standardized elliptic-curve randomness generators.

Practitioners should treat digital signatures as binding only when the exact signed message or its hash is known, enforce robust padding and modern schemes such as EdDSA where possible, and never skip boundary checks or proper entropy for nonces and key generation.
