talks.title: Adam Pietrasiak: Lata porażek i potem sukces - czego nie widać podziwiając udane start-upy.
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Adam Pietrasiak: Lata porażek i potem sukces - czego nie widać podziwiając udane start-upy..
talks.summary:
# Overview
In this talk, Adam Pietrasiak discusses the hidden struggles behind startup success, sharing his journey from 15 years of design, coding, and repeated failures to launching Studio, a product that achieved rapid financial success. Pietrasiak addresses the survivorship bias on social media—where high-revenue posts dominate while the mental health toll, burnout, and depression remain largely unmentioned—and offers practical insights into shifting from romanticized notions of entrepreneurship to sustainable execution.

# Key Topics
- **Social Media Distortion:** How startup platforms amplify revenue milestones while ignoring personal costs like depression, burnout, and relationship strain.
- **The Romantic Approach vs. Reality:** The pitfalls of falling in love with product ideas without direct user feedback, clear utility, or viable business models.
- **Mental Health and Career Burnout:** Pietrasiak's experience changing jobs eight times over five years while attempting side projects, leading to severe mental distress and medication.
- **Acceptance and Focus:** How letting go of the obsessive urge to build a revolutionary startup enabled professional stability, improved productivity, and a healthier mindset.
- **Building in Public:** Utilizing transparency on platforms like Twitter to build momentum, ask for help, and cultivate early adopter trust.

# Technical Details
- **Studio Product Definition:** A software utility designed to capture screen recordings, automatically apply visual effects, smooth cursor movement, and execute intelligent camera zoom-ins, creating promotional-quality tutorial videos tailored for platforms like Instagram without manual animator work.
- **Monetization and Pricing Strategy:** Abandoning freemium models in favor of charging $89 per license from day zero to ensure immediate financial viability with three months of runway.
- **Validation Mechanics:** Early interest was validated when early sales were processed despite public landing page warnings indicating the product was not yet downloadable.
- **Traction Metrics:** Generated 4,000 sales and roughly $500,000 in gross revenue within six months, while the speaker's Twitter following expanded from 170 to over 12,000 across seven months.

# Takeaways
- **Define Value Clearly:** A product must solve an explicit problem—saving time or generating money—expressible in a single sentence.
- **Charge Early:** Validating willingness to pay from day one eliminates ambiguous business planning and tests real market demand.
- **Embrace Persistence and Chance:** Startup outcomes rely heavily on timing and luck, but opportunities require continuous, low-attachment attempts.
- **Protect Mental Well-Being:** Acknowledging personal limits and overcoming comparison culture prevents burnout and preserves health.

talks.title: Agnieszka Świecznik: What's up CSS?
talks.teaser: Surveys recent CSS features like variables, nesting, container queries and content-visibility, with notes on browser support.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys recent CSS features that the speaker, a front-end developer, suspects many working developers have missed. She starts with custom properties, which can be changed to restyle many elements at once and fall back to default values, and with native nesting, which removes repeated selectors. Next come :is(), which shortens long selector combinations, and a note that an unsupported selector in a plain list can cause the browser to drop the whole rule.

The middle section covers layout and typography. Text-box trimming cuts the space above and below text so it can be matched to a designer's exact measurements, the inset property shortens positioning, and object-view-box crops images. Container queries let components adapt to their own width rather than the viewport, and cascade layers define which rules win without reaching for !important. Preference queries for contrast and reduced motion are presented as ways to respect user needs, with a reminder that higher contrast does not have to mean a dark theme.

The closing part looks at rendering performance. Adding content-visibility: auto, together with containment, to sections of a large static test page reduced rendering time from 160 milliseconds to 60 milliseconds, and the speaker expects bigger gains on weaker devices. Unlike JavaScript-based lazy loading, the content stays in the page from the start, so search engines and screen readers still see it. The takeaway is to check browser support for each feature before relying on it, and to follow the specification and community articles she linked.

talks.title: Bartłomiej Miś: Frontendowe optymalizacje wydajności na 2023
talks.teaser: Covers interaction latency, CSS invalidation costs, and HTML-first frameworks for faster real-user performance.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that frontend performance work in 2023 should lean on real-user data rather than chasing high Lighthouse scores alone. Chrome User Experience Report, Search Console, and field monitoring matter because they reflect how pages feel during clicks, form use, and navigation—not only initial load.

Most of the session centers on Interaction to Next Paint and main-thread blocking shown through DevTools recordings. Examples include sluggish buttons, mobile menus, and portal link clicks where analytics or DOM work stalls the UI. Mitigations include immediate visual feedback, deferring heavy JavaScript with scheduling APIs, moving work to web workers, and sending marketing events after navigation. A later segment ties CSS style and layout invalidation to slow interactions, with guidance on selector cost, avoiding read-write thrashing, containment, and content visibility. Back-forward cache behavior and common breakers are summarized briefly.

The closing comparison contrasts hydration-heavy stacks with Astro’s HTML-first, islands, and client directives that load JavaScript only when needed. Practitioners are urged to profile real interactions, watch INP as it matures beyond First Input Delay, and ship less client-side code where static markup suffices.

talks.title: Grzegorz Kocjan: Zen of IT - the secrets of sleeping well at night
talks.teaser: Shares a developer's burnout story and practical habits like clean architecture, frequent small deployments and better monitoring.
talks.summary:
Grzegorz Kocjan describes his own burnout after years of firefighting production incidents and late-night alerts, which led him to quit a job and rethink how he works. He presents the lessons he gathered as practices spanning code, workflow and company level, with sustainable engineering as the goal.

On the code side, he argues for code architecture beneath service-level diagrams, using established design patterns and styles such as clean or hexagonal architecture to postpone decisions and make changes cheaper. He also recommends consistent naming and formatting, avoiding global state, and test-driven development, which he uses as a gauge of how well a codebase is structured. For workflow, he advocates many small deployments, sometimes several per task, separating integration from delivery with feature flags, and refactoring continuously rather than as a separate task. He suggests monitoring staging more closely than production and never ignoring errors.

At company level, he recommends focusing on the one most important thing and checking with customers and usage data whether shipped features are actually used. His closing message is that this is continuous work built from small steps, and that engineers should step away from the keyboard to find root causes in code quality, deployment friction or poor user stories.

talks.title: Jacek Milewski: Testowanie kodu to bajka. Strategia taka, że piszesz unity i integration.
talks.teaser: Presents a layered testing strategy for microservices, covering unit, component, dependency and contract tests and when to use mocks.
talks.summary:
Jacek Milewski, speaking in Polish, starts from the gap between tutorials, which make JUnit and Mockito easy to set up, and the harder question of what each test should cover. In microservices, whole systems are rarely stable enough for end-to-end checks, and mocks can create a false sense that production code is being tested. He proposes a strategy organised around business rules rather than individual methods.

He redefines the test pyramid. A unit is a business capability that enforces invariants, such as refusing to cancel an order once it has been paid for. Micro tests cover validators, parsers and mappers with simple input and output. Component tests exercise a group of units, dependency tests check repositories against an in-memory or real store, and contract tests verify API schemas. Functional API tests sit at the top. For asynchronous flows, he replaces the queue publisher with an in-memory one that runs the handler immediately, and he describes an outbox for consistency. In his own project he reports about one and a half lines of test code per line of production code.

The takeaways are to avoid testing the same rule at several levels, to name tests after the business scenario they cover, and to leave testers with critical end-to-end flows rather than every edge case. Where full staging parity is impossible, he suggests gradual rollouts and synthetic checks in production, with contract tests guarding the interfaces between services.

talks.title: Łukasz Chruściel: Czy SOLID umarł? Porozmawiajmy o projektowaniu wielokrotnie używalnego kodu
talks.teaser: A Sylius maintainer shares architecture decision records and hard-won API design choices from rebuilding admin and shop interfaces.
talks.summary:
The presentation walks through strategic choices made while designing a new API for Sylius, an open-source e-commerce stack paired with API Platform. The speaker anchors the narrative in architecture decision records kept in the repository, so each major fork—context, options, and outcome—can be revisited years later.

Audience members vote through live quizzes on choices the team actually took. REST won over GraphQL in 2020 despite industry hype, partly because admin panels relied on POST-heavy flows and caching mattered. Separating admin and shop surfaces led to prefix-based APIs rather than one unified product resource. Versioning stayed in the URL to honor a twelve-year `/v1` legacy, though header-based versioning and OpenAPI sunset semantics are portrayed as preferable going forward.

Checkout started as UI-shaped verb endpoints and evolved toward a draft cart updated with partial patches, deliberately not mirroring front-end wizards or backend state machines in the HTTP layer. Order cancellation via a URL verb is admitted as imperfect; modeling multi-step work as dedicated operation resources is offered as the better pattern. Closing advice stresses ADRs, REST as a sensible default, resources distinct from database tables, and APIs stable enough not to chase every UI change.

talks.title: Marek Chrapek: Working with legacy code - how to sleep soundly after a production release?
talks.teaser: Offers a practical approach to stabilising inherited frontend code using git history, snapshot tests and incremental refactoring.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a familiar situation: a frontend team inherits a codebase nobody fully understands, after the original architect has left and patches have piled up. Legacy code, the speaker argues, can also arise in a mature system that is still being developed.

To find a starting point, he runs a small script over git history to plot each file's change count against its complexity, splitting the result into four zones. High complexity combined with many changes marks the spot where fixes keep colliding. He warns that a high coverage percentage can hide weak tests, and recommends recording decisions in architecture decision records, linting only changed files, and using snapshot tests to lock structure during refactoring. For frontend code he favours integration tests over unit tests, keeps end-to-end tests for key user paths despite their slowness, and uses Storybook with screenshot tests to review shared components.

He also warns about broken windows, such as a shared utilities folder that keeps growing, and suggests checking which files change together to see whether module boundaries match the domain. The takeaway: evolve code step by step, make each change easy for reviewers to read, and leave the codebase in a state that future maintainers will not resent.

talks.title: Marek Rudziński: Oprogramowanie umysłu, czyli jak działa umysł i dlaczego tak często się mylimy
talks.teaser: Explains how perception filters and cognitive habits create psychological inertia, and why past lessons can block change.
talks.summary:
The talk, given in Polish, looks at why people often get things wrong and why change is so hard. The speaker, a psychologist who has spent about fifteen years coaching IT teams on management, change and product work, opens with a story about a patient who keeps a hand in a hot oven and wants the pain to stop without removing it. He starts from behaviourism and argues that a learned response only works in the context where it was learned, so repeating a past reaction in a new setting produces different results.

He then shows that perception is an active construction built from stored patterns, citing people who regained sight in adulthood and needed years to learn to interpret what they saw. Filters remove, distort or assign meaning to incoming information, and the mind avoids cognitive dissonance. Audience exercises illustrate anchoring with a fear scale, the availability effect in comparing rainfall in Rome and London, and confirmation bias with an image that viewers keep reading as a bee. Beliefs are built in layers, and meta-programs such as proactive versus reactive thinking shape how people act.

The closing case follows an employee who fears losing his job after his manager stops speaking to him. Reframing the meaning he gives to the silence, and listing the choices he actually has, opens new options. The takeaway is to widen what you notice, question the meanings you attach to events, and recognise that contexts change, so a belief that once helped may now limit you.

talks.title: 4DEV TALKS: Radek Wojtysiak - Transformacja zawodowa z programisty w team leadera.
talks.teaser: Explores how a senior developer moved into team leadership, trade-offs, culture building, and leading in a new firm.
talks.summary:
The conversation centers on moving from a long programming career into team leadership. The guest describes roughly ten years of commercial development, reaching senior level, and starting to share practical career guidance on LinkedIn. That outreach clarified that he enjoyed advising peers and nudging their growth, which helped him choose a management path aligned with a written career plan.

He argues that splitting time evenly between hands-on coding and leadership did not work for him: leadership demands current domain and organizational knowledge, while deep daily coding competed with time the team needed from him. He frames the shift as a real career change, not merely a promotion, and notes relief after stepping back from writing code most of the day. Motivation includes shaping team culture, influencing which ideas ship, and working across business and design, not only the codebase.

He contrasts becoming a lead among former peer developers—new hierarchy, confidentiality, and changed relationships—with joining a new company as an unknown leader, which he found easier for building trust from scratch. He highlights listening, openness, and face-to-face communication as core skills, plus willingness to speak up proactively. Recent wins at his current employer include regular team coffee meetings, a quarterly eight-hour team maintenance and ideas day adopted by other teams, and tailored people-management routines. He recommends The First 90 Days for onboarding into leadership and credits a former manager as a mentor, preferring practice and organizational training over self-selected courses.

talks.title: Kuba Barć: Advanced Opentelemetry Magick | DOD Warsaw 2023
talks.teaser: Explains OpenTelemetry's data model and collector pipelines, then shows real processor configs that reshape metrics and traces.
talks.summary:
The talk is a practical walk through OpenTelemetry for people who already run monitoring in production. It starts with the basic signals, metrics, spans and logs, and then explains the data model in layers: a resource, a scope, then metrics or spans, then data points or span events. The speaker stresses that metadata attaches at each level and that processing can only look upward, so an attribute has to be read from the level where it actually lives.

The middle section covers how collectors are assembled. Receivers, processors and exporters are wired into separate pipelines for each signal type, and the order of processors matters because each one hands its output to the next. Counters can be cumulative or delta, which changes how the numbers should be read, and a conversion processor can turn cumulative values into deltas. The logging exporter is recommended for debugging a pipeline, and connectors can bridge data types, such as turning logs into metrics.

Two case studies make this concrete. In the first, a request metric carrying the URL path was too high in cardinality to send to a paid backend. The team copied the metric, extracted only the path and a public key with a regular expression, dropped series that did not match, and reaggregated the copy, leaving the original metric intact. In the second, gateway spans were fixed by setting the service name, the peer service attribute and the client span kind, which stopped a service map from fragmenting. The takeaway is to check where an attribute sits in the data model, use debug output when a filter does not match, and write custom components when no existing one fits.

talks.title: Tomasz Borek: Maven demo dump - just the useful bits | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Walks through practical Maven habits for faster builds, safer dependency updates and cleaner command-line use.
talks.summary:
This live terminal session walks through practical Maven habits for developers, with the speaker working on a demo project as he goes. It opens with searching Maven Central from the command line using the MCS tool, which can list archetypes, artifacts and the projects that use a given class. The speaker then argues that the common habit of running a clean install is usually unnecessary: install copies build output into the local repository, and most core plugins do not need a clean step, so package is often enough.

Further demos cover a build that behaves differently across machines when no encoding is declared, and the pom fix for it. A settings file can map plugin groups so short plugin names resolve, and the build plan plugin lists which plugin runs in each phase. The versions plugin finds and applies newer dependency, property and plugin versions, and OWASP Dependency-Check is pointed to for flagging risky dependencies. Other tips include quieter output flags, an enforcer rule that checks a file's checksum, sorting the pom, the Maven wrapper for pinning a Maven version, and the Maven Daemon for faster builds.

The main takeaway is to automate version checks so that updates, including security fixes, are proposed regularly rather than discovered late. The speaker cautions that faster local flags, such as skipping tests, should never be used on CI, and that CI logs should be kept lean.

talks.title: Konrad Szałkowski: How to make your electrons do more in Java? | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how Java's Vector API and Tornado VM use SIMD instructions and GPUs for faster numeric code, with live benchmarks.
talks.summary:
The talk explains SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) CPU instructions, which process several values in one operation, and why Java has used them little. The speaker recaps how the C2 compiler's superword optimization vectorizes simple integer loops, while floating-point loops are held back to keep results identical. Java 16 introduced the Vector API as a preview, and it became official in Java 21 under Project Panama.

Demonstrations cover vector species, lane-wise operations and reductions, and a summing loop that needs a bounded loop plus a scalar tail for leftover elements. On a 100-million-element benchmark, summing took 29 ms in one version and 21 ms in the Vector API version, finding the maximum took 44 ms versus 22 ms, and solving quadratic equations took 300 ms versus 227 ms. Drawbacks noted were more code to write, incomplete instruction coverage, and reduced accuracy for some SIMD results.

The second half turns to GPUs, surveying earlier attempts such as Sumatra and Rootbeer before introducing TornadoVM, a project from the University of Manchester. Developers mark parallel loops with annotations and build task graphs that move data to the device, and TornadoVM compiles the Java methods into GPU kernels. A ray tracer that used parallel streams on the CPU was shown reaching 60 FPS on the GPU via OpenCL. The speaker also noted that TornadoVM can choose between CPU and GPU based on transfer costs, trading a simple programming model for limited control.

talks.title: Álvaro Sánchez-Mariscal: Unleash the power of your applications with Micronaut & GraalVM | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how Micronaut moves framework work to compile time, and how GraalVM native images cut startup time and memory.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Micronaut, a JVM framework built for microservices, serverless functions and message-driven applications. Its central idea is ahead-of-time processing: dependency injection and framework wiring are generated at compile time through the annotation processing API, so the application avoids runtime reflection, dynamic proxies and classpath scanning that slow startup and add memory use. The speaker contrasts this with frameworks that do much of that work when the application starts.

The speaker walks through the feature set, including declarative HTTP and messaging support, a data layer modelled on repositories where errors such as a mistyped property fail the build, built-in test resources that start containers for tests, and Micronaut 4 changes such as a Java 17 baseline and properties as the default configuration format. He then explains GraalVM, which is both a JDK distribution and a native image compiler that turns reachable code into an operating-system-specific binary. Quoted figures include a hello world starting in as little as six milliseconds, compared with about 250 milliseconds for a regular Java startup.

A live demo builds a small football teams API with Flyway migrations, an H2 database, a repository interface, a controller and a functional test. The test ran in about 300 milliseconds, and the native image started in about 32 milliseconds. The takeaway is that compile-time checks and fast startup suit serverless functions and Kubernetes scaling, where containers need to become ready quickly.

talks.title: Tomasz Janczewski: 365 dni cyber wojny - jakie ataki przeżył mój serwer w ostatnim roku | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: A developer shares one year of honeypot data from a Java server, revealing who attacks, which ports and CVEs are targeted.
talks.summary:
This talk is a one-year case study from a Polish developer who ran a honeypot in front of a Java server styled as a small company's site. The setup logged 756,000 attacks from about 31,000 unique IP addresses, spread across the world, with Iran, Russia and China standing out and India high by volume. The speaker had expected skilled human attackers but found mostly scripts and mass scanners. Tor exit nodes were rare, and a test run from a university server suggested Tor is too unstable for this kind of traffic.

Most traffic aimed at SMB and SQL Server ports, with 445 and 1433 leading and 443 third, rather than the web application itself. Many attacks tried known CVEs, including a remote code execution flaw in Windows SMB and one in SQL Server. Login attempts used default and common credentials such as sa, root and admin, not leaked password lists. The lesson for developers is that automated attacks chase rare, high-severity bugs and default settings, so dependencies and exposed services need regular checks.

The speaker walked through the honeypot stack, a Docker-based bundle that needs roughly 8 to 16 GB of RAM and around 128 GB of disk for logs. Events are written as JSON and shown in Elasticsearch and Grafana dashboards, and they can feed scripts that block offending addresses for a set time or be forwarded to a host-based detection agent. Placing the honeypot behind a web application firewall cuts the visible traffic, so placement is a design choice. A practical takeaway is that exposed services face constant automated probing, and monitoring them is cheap enough to be worth doing.

talks.title: Adam Bien: The Best of Java Shorts Shorts Show: 100 Snippets in 45 Minutes | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: The session delivers a fast live demo reel of overlooked standard-library Java features for everyday backend work.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens as a conference-driven spin on a YouTube shorts series: the speaker has recorded hundreds of minute-long Java clips and uses the slot to revisit favorites live instead of slide-heavy material. The promised migration demo from a prior year is deferred to an existing screencast on the channel, then attention shifts to a numbered parade of small programs run from the command line.

Each segment highlights something in the JDK itself: unconventional entry points and varargs, legacy timers beside schedulers, NIO file watching and built-in diffing, clipboard access, masked console input, custom runtimes via jlink, terminal styling, the platform logger, JDBC driver self-registration, asserts, formatting helpers, filesystem utilities, shebang-style execution, stream-based CLI parsing, minimal JWT payload decoding, and newer language conveniences such as list tail access and record patterns. Corretto, serverless backends, and redirecting standard output in cloud logging appear as recurring motivation.

The through-line is operational: reach for java.* and close third-party gaps only when the standard library truly lacks an answer, partly to shrink patch and supply-chain surface. The hour ends with time exhausted while hundreds of remaining shorts stay online for self-study, plus brief audience questions.

talks.title: Rafał Maciak: Nonviolent Communication in the world of distributed systems | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how contract testing catches breaking API changes between microservices, and why it beats integration and end-to-end tests.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how to make sure microservices keep communicating correctly, both at first deployment and after their APIs change. A monolith's compiler catches a changed method signature, but across services nothing catches it automatically. The speaker walks through the testing pyramid: unit tests do not exercise network communication, integration tests mix business checks with communication checks and rely on teams coordinating by hand, and end-to-end tests are costly, slow and prone to false failures.

Contract testing is presented as the alternative. A contract defines one business scenario, covering the request and the expected response, and both consumer and producer are tested against it, so a breaking change on either side fails a build. Ownership can be consumer-driven or producer-driven, a distinction borrowed from upstream and downstream services in domain-driven design. In a Java demo using the Pact framework, the order service's consumer test generates a contract that is published to a Pact Broker; the payment service's verification first fails because its endpoint is missing, then passes after the fix. A can-i-deploy check then reports whether a given version is safe to release.

The takeaway is that contracts give cheap, isolated checks of communication and serve as living documentation of how each consumer uses an API, which makes it safe to remove unused fields. Drawbacks include maintaining the contracts and getting every team to follow the practice. Spring Cloud Contract is mentioned as another option, and the approach also works for asynchronous messaging.

talks.title: Kamil Rogulski: What really stresses you out at work and why is it not what you think? | JDD
talks.teaser: Explains how thoughts drive workplace stress and shares mental exercises for reframing worries about deadlines.
talks.summary:
Kamil Rogulski, a soft-skills trainer who also runs a psychological support service for employees, opens with an audience poll on workplace stress and beliefs about its harm. He then describes a long-running study of about 300 people. Those who had a lot of stress and believed it was harmful had 43 higher odds of illness and death, while similarly stressed people who did not hold that belief did not. The takeaway is that thoughts about stress can shape the body's response as much as the events themselves.

He explains that stress is a survival mechanism built for short bursts, and that the body reacts the same way to an imagined threat, such as a mortgage that may never come due. He links this to burnout in the IT sector, citing research in which about one in ten respondents were on medication for depression and many more suspected they needed a check-up. He presents emotions as a kind of radar rather than good or bad, and shows how one event, like a colleague asking to see the boss, can trigger fear or curiosity depending on the first thought. He also traces how a single missed deadline can grow into a chain of catastrophic thoughts.

For practical steps, he sorts worries into three circles: things fully within one's control, things partly influenced, and things entirely outside one's influence, arguing that much anxiety sits in the last. He suggests catching automatic thoughts, testing them against evidence, and estimating how likely a feared outcome really is, using a betting question as a calibration tool. He compares this to training for a marathon, where the skill grows with repeated practice and sometimes with professional support.

talks.title: Milen Dyankov: Location transparency (for Java developers) | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how message types like commands, events and queries let components talk without knowing each other's location.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the gap between how software is drawn and how it behaves once it is split up. Breaking a monolith into microservices looks simple on a diagram, but hidden dependencies between components cause problems that often surface only later. The speaker separates coherence from coupling and describes connascence as the dependencies that tie parts of a system together, sorting them into forms such as shared names, types, positions, algorithms and timing.

The middle section focuses on communication between components. Each arrow on an architecture diagram hides a location dependency, since one component must know where another lives, whether that is a direct class call, a REST endpoint or a Kafka topic. The speaker proposes treating messages as commands, events and queries, each with different routing and response expectations. A Java model is sketched in which producers send messages through gateways and consumers register handlers by message type, without knowing where the other side runs.

To close, the speaker argues that bounded groups of objects can stay tightly coupled internally while talking to other groups only through messages. Axon Framework is presented for messaging inside one JVM, and Axon Server for distributing those components across machines, with an HTTP layer for services written in other languages. The takeaway is to design the messages exchanged between components deliberately rather than relying on whichever broker happens to be in place.

talks.title: Jarosław Pałka: Wszystko, czego nie chcesz wiedzieć o współbieżności w JVM | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Maps JVM synchronized, reentrant locks, and atomics via profiling, inflation, and ARM Linux lock slowdowns from database benchmarks.
talks.summary:
The talk stems from a long-running effort to show that a Java graph database is fast and cost-effective on ARM in cloud deployments. Early benchmarks showed faster reads but writes lagging by roughly thirty percent on ARM, with vendors arguing the bottleneck lived in the application. That dispute became a motivation to explain what the JVM actually does with everyday concurrency code.

The presenter lines up synchronized methods, reentrant locks, and atomic operations on the same counter, using profiling views to show when execution stays in Java, invokes JVM monitor machinery, or reaches the operating system. The middle of the session goes deep on object mark words, lightweight versus inflated locks, native object monitors, reentrancy, a monitor cleanup issue between Java 11 and 17, escape analysis and lock coarsening, java.util.concurrent and AbstractQueuedSynchronizer, fair versus unfair locking, and an ARM Linux slowdown in low-level locking addressed in a recent JDK release. Custom benchmarks contrast behavior under light contention versus many readers with a single writer.

The closing message ties lock cost to scalability: parallel work wins only where critical sections stay short, synchronized fares poorly under heavy read contention, and atomics help only where the problem fits single-address updates. Practitioners should match the primitive to contention and measurement, not treat synchronized as the default.

talks.title: Michał Ostruszka: You put out the fire on production, what's next? | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Explains running blameless postmortems after production outages, from timelines to action items that actually get finished.
talks.summary:
The talk covers postmortems, the structured review teams hold after a production failure. The speaker recounts a case where a sudden marketing-driven load spike, roughly 10 times normal, was handled first by scaling every service out, with analysis only afterward. He suggests letting the team recover for a short while, no more than two or three days, before starting the review. He lists triggers for a postmortem, including user-visible downtime, data loss, manual on-call intervention and failures found by hand rather than by monitoring.

The review has three parts: a shared timeline of who did what and when, root-cause brainstorming, and action items. He contrasts the five whys, which follows a single chain, with the fishbone diagram, which groups possible contributors and often reveals several causes. Using the Challenger disaster, he argues that a broader look at the launch decision yielded more useful findings than a materials-only explanation. Analysis can stop when a cause is beyond control or too costly to fix, provided the risk is explicitly accepted.

Action items should be small enough to finish within a sprint or two, have a named owner, and favor automation over extra manual steps. Stakeholder buy-in matters, and including product managers and customer-facing staff helps. Keep the review blameless, focusing on why something happened rather than who, and avoid promising that an incident will never recur. Verify each action against a deadline, tag postmortems so they are searchable, and share lessons through tech talks and game days. Repeated identical failures show a gap in learning.

talks.title: Dominik Szałkowski: Skomplikowane testy jednostkowe - oksymoron, czy smutna rzeczywistość | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Explains how to measure test complexity and when to refactor code instead of forcing unit tests.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a code review where private modifiers had disappeared from constants and fields, raising the question of why. The speaker, a Java developer, argues that hard-to-read tests usually reflect hard-to-read production code. A mandatory SonarQube quality gate then forced his team to add tests to legacy code, and one of the largest classes they examined had a cyclomatic complexity of 147.

He traces cyclomatic complexity back to a 1976 article that used Fortran examples and gave rough thresholds for when code becomes risky to test. He contrasts it with the cognitive complexity metric from the SonarQube team, which better reflects how easy code is to understand. Causes he lists include skipping design work before coding, piling on conditionals to meet new business requests, and not knowing testing features such as parameterized tests. When tests cannot reach private logic, he covers workarounds: reflection, temporarily widening visibility, nested classes, Mockito for private and static methods, and a visible-for-testing annotation paired with ArchUnit rules. He stresses these are temporary.

The lasting fixes, he says, are splitting large methods into smaller parts, writing tests earlier in the process, and using parameterized tests. For test data, he describes builder-style factories, serialized real data with anonymisation where needed, and generated or published test datasets. His takeaway is that testability should be agreed within the team and enforced, not treated as an afterthought.

talks.title: Rafał Grembowski: Multi-regional high availability in AWS cloud | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Rafał Grembowski: Multi-regional high availability in AWS cloud | JDD 2023.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at JDD 2023, Rafał Grembowski, an architect at Huuuge Games, discusses implementing multi-regional high availability in Amazon Web Services (AWS). He outlines the evolutionary steps of application redundancy—from single-machine processes to multiple servers, dedicated data centers, Availability Zones (AZ), and ultimately multi-region setups designed to withstand catastrophic infrastructure failures such as natural disasters or regional blackouts. While multi-AZ deployment handles common failures with reasonable effort, the speaker's organization took on the engineering challenge of an active-active multi-region architecture driven by both team interest and real-world disaster warnings (e.g., hurricane-related blackout risks on the US East Coast).

### Key Topics
- **Active-Active vs. Active-Passive Architectures:** The trade-offs between running hot-standby failover setups and true active-active configurations where traffic and data replication flow across both regions simultaneously.
- **AWS Regional Isolation:** Challenges arising because AWS regions are completely isolated units with separate VPCs, subnets, Kubernetes clusters, load balancers, and security credentials.
- **Traffic Routing and Service Discovery:** Managing public user traffic using AWS Global Accelerator and private server-to-server traffic through internal networking and Route 53 Proximity routing while avoiding DNS caching bottlenecks.
- **Data Replication and Capacity Planning:** Utilizing DynamoDB global tables for bidirectional multi-master replication, handling conflicts (last-write-wins), and factoring cross-region replication traffic into Read and Write Capacity Units (RCU/WCU).
- **Custom Failover Health Checks:** Building custom health check microservices in Python to validate critical dependent services (such as DynamoDB and EC2/Kubernetes) rather than relying on trivial HTTP 200 responses.
- **Cost Implications and Operational Benefits:** Evaluating financial impacts (data transfer, Global Accelerator costs, doubled storage) alongside infrastructural flexibility, canary deployments at the infrastructure layer, and reduced on-call stress.

### Technical Details
- **Kubernetes & Load Balancing:** Kubernetes worker nodes must stay in the same region as their control plane, preventing multi-region clusters. Likewise, AWS load balancer target groups cannot cross regional boundaries, exposing endpoints in multiple places.
- **DNS Limitations & Global Accelerator:** Public DNS caching and long TTL propagation (up to two days across cascades) prevent rapid failover via standard DNS edits. For public client traffic, AWS Global Accelerator provides a static anycast IP that routes transparently to backend endpoints across regions without DNS propagation delay. Internal server-to-server traffic relies on Route 53 with latency/proximity routing over private networks to satisfy corporate security policies.
- **Database Layer:** DynamoDB was selected as the managed storage engine capable of bidirectional cross-region replication. Conflicts are resolved via timestamps (latest write wins). When provisioning RCU and WCU, engineers must allocate capacity for both local application operations and incoming replicated writes.
- **Health Monitoring:** Because AWS does not offer an out-of-the-box regional health score, the team developed a custom Python endpoint. It probes upstream dependencies (e.g., listing DynamoDB tables) before returning healthy status to Route 53 or Global Accelerator. Centralized monitoring was transitioned from regional Grafana/Prometheus/Alertmanager instances to Datadog for unified cross-region metric analysis.
- **Cost Drivers:** Compute (EC2) costs do not simply double if overall traffic is distributed (e.g., 70/30 split), but DynamoDB storage is paid in both regions, and Global Accelerator introduces significant data transfer premiums (roughly 3x to 4x higher standard egress).

### Takeaways
Multi-region active-active architectures require solving significant distributed systems problems—including data synchronization, traffic rerouting without DNS caching latency, and end-to-end health checking. While not necessary for every project due to cost and complexity, multi-region setups offer superior fault tolerance against catastrophic outages, enable infrastructure-level canary releases, reduce user latency via geographic routing, and give on-call engineers high operational confidence.

talks.title: Wojciech Marusarz: Everything Everywhere All at Once | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Compares Spring MVC, Reactor, coroutines and Project Loom for handling I/O-bound web requests, with load-test results.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the JVM concurrency landscape and the question of how threads are used in server applications. It explains that a system thread pairs a context with a scheduler, that CPU-bound work is judged by throughput while server requests are judged by latency, and that the classic thread-per-request model of Spring MVC loses time to blocking I/O and context switching.

The speaker then follows one team's path through Futures, CompletableFutures and Project Reactor, before moving to Kotlin coroutines. The coroutine section shows how the compiler turns a suspending function into a state machine held in continuation objects, and how Netty event loops fit underneath. Project Loom's virtual threads are presented as using the same continuation idea, but implemented at the library level. A test with 100,000 activities, Gatling traffic and two CPU cores compared the four approaches on code readability and 99th percentile response time. Spring MVC degraded as traffic rose, while Reactor, Loom and coroutines performed similarly and coroutines came out best.

The closing advice is to weigh readability and performance together. Teams starting a Java project might try Loom with Spring MVC, while Kotlin teams might pick coroutines with WebFlux. Before changing an existing application, the speaker recommends writing performance tests, and migrating incrementally rather than rewriting everything at once.

talks.title: Andrzej Grzesik, Wojciech Ptak: Avoiding mistakes with events, an event at a time | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Catalogues common mistakes in event-driven systems, covering event IDs, schemas, serialization, delivery guarantees and timestamps.
talks.summary:
Two engineers share recurring mistakes they saw in large-scale event-driven systems. They define an event as a discrete fact that happened at a specific point in time, then warn against both avoiding events where they fit and applying them to everything. Audit tables that try to reconstruct events are flagged as a common trap.

Much of the advice concerns identifiers, schemas and delivery. Time-ordered UUIDs are recommended over sequential integers, which can be enumerated, and UUIDs should be stored in their native binary type rather than as strings. Events should be designed around the use case rather than the broker, and a relational database can serve as a queue. Personal data should be replaced with tokens, since legal retention duties and erasure requests can conflict with immutability. Serialization tests across versions and explicit timestamps also feature.

The closing section addresses distributed behaviour, which is hard to reason about. Teams should ask product owners what a term like straight away actually means, use idempotency keys to avoid repeated processing, and attach correlation IDs to trace flows. Hop counters help catch event loops. Event sourcing and CQRS are worth adopting only where audit or read-model needs justify them, since many systems are fine as a simple API over a database.

talks.title: Bartek Kuczyński: ID, EGO and Super EGO of your entity | JDD 2023
talks.teaser: Uses Freud's id, ego and superego to frame how software entities get identifiers, from JVM object headers to database keys.
talks.summary:
Bartek Kuczyński uses Freud's id, ego and superego as a loose frame for choosing identifiers for software entities. The "id" layer is the low-level view: the JVM allocates memory for an object and finds it through a header, with a mark word used for locking and garbage collection metadata, and a class pointer that tells the runtime how to read the fields. The "ego" layer is how an entity is presented to the outside world. The talk compares plain sequences, UUIDs, ULIDs with a timestamp prefix, and Snowflake-style IDs that embed a machine number, looking at uniqueness, speed, ease of use and sortability.

The "superego" part looks at business and legal constraints. Natural identifiers such as email addresses and the Polish PESEL number run into GDPR limits and data errors, and the speaker notes that PESEL has validation flaws. Invoice numbers must usually be gap-free, which a plain sequence cannot guarantee if a transaction fails after the value was taken. The talk also covers how coordinating sequences across several database instances causes conflicts or extra network traffic, and how identifiers that are random or time-ordered change the behaviour of database indexes and inserts.

The takeaway is that plain sequences are fast and simple but expose internal information and need coordination across nodes. Practitioners should decide which identifiers users will treat as business concepts, and test how the chosen identifiers behave in their own indexes and write patterns before committing to one.

talks.title: Sławek Sobótka: Business Model Archetypes
talks.teaser: Follows a document workflow system's redesign from god classes and shared data toward composable state-based behavior.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a document circulation system built for German healthcare providers, where authors draft medical procedures, reviewers verify them, and staff must read them once published. The first version split the code into technical layers instead of business domains, relied on a few oversized classes, and reused the same data structures across modules. Because those structures were tied to the database, refactoring became hard and duplicated rules drifted apart.

The middle of the talk replays a series of design attempts on a public example repository, a transport-management system with contracts. An approach that hardcoded status checks inside document methods came first. A base-class version whose unsupported operations threw exceptions was called a bad abstraction, and a State pattern with template methods helped only partly. The final version composes each state from predicates that decide which transitions are allowed, with the actions run on a transition assembled separately. State names are kept as data, and the speaker warns that loading such configuration from a database needs type-safe handling rather than string-based reflection.

The closing part argues for defining the questions the system must answer before modelling, and for separating domain models from presentation models. Status changes are treated as events that the catalogue reacts to, and stable behaviour is kept apart from unstable data. The speaker's takeaway is that patterns are worth learning from books, but the trade-offs only become clear through experiments that show the consequences of each change.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2023 - Level up your Infrastructure Skills with your own Compute...(Kerim Satirli)
talks.teaser: Five hands-on learning paths use a home compute cluster to deepen packaging, IaC, secrets, networking, and orchestration skills.
talks.summary:
Operations-minded engineers constantly face new platforms and terminology while the underlying problems—images, provisioning, secrets, connectivity, and scheduling—stay familiar. The presenter frames five skill areas (packaging, infrastructure, security, networking, and orchestration) and argues that deepening them raises career options even for developers who rarely get paged.

The core proposal is a small multi-node lab built from a carrier board that accepts several compute modules (with alternatives such as Raspberry Pi modules or Jetson boards). Around that hardware, the talk walks through layered practice paths: building nearly complete machine images and extending them across local and multicloud targets; finishing the last mile with cloud-init and secret injection; hardening with credential storage, encryption, and identity federation; designing service discovery, health checks, and monitoring; and evolving orchestration from ad hoc deploys to registry-driven pipelines, bin packing, and failover drills—including unplugging network links on real kit.

Each path is expressed as interview-style scenarios drawn from market and customer research rather than copy-paste snippets. The closing emphasis is that infrastructure work is a team sport, that codifying environments beats one-off UI clicks, and that learning in public accelerates growth; listeners are pointed at a public GitHub “workloads” repository for Terraform, Vault, Consul, and related experiments.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2023 - Use the Observability, Luke! (Paweł Piwosz)
talks.teaser: The session shows how to add logs, metrics, and traces on AWS Lambda using X-Ray, CloudWatch, and Lambda Power Tools.
talks.summary:
Operations teams lose ground as workloads move from bare metal and VMs to containers and serverless. The speaker contrasts traditional monitoring with observability: a cultural shift toward structured, consistent telemetry that carries context across microservices, not a single dashboard product.

He frames observability around logs, metrics, and traces, each needing full coverage, automation-friendly shape, and business-relevant collection. Context ties error counts to request volume. He sketches an extension—metrics, events, logs, and automated actions—and turns to AWS Lambda, where default CloudWatch output hides cold starts and latency spikes. Through a small SAM-style template and live console work, he enables X-Ray and enhanced monitoring, turns on API Gateway logging with trace identifiers, and instruments Python handlers with the open-source Lambda Power Tools layer using tracer, metrics, and logging decorators.

The walkthrough shows service maps and traces that pinpoint slow segments, warns about capturing full request payloads in production, and briefly maps instrumentation and visualization options including OpenTelemetry-aligned tooling. The practical takeaway is that meaningful serverless observability can start with a few console toggles and a handful of library decorators.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2023 - A better approach for orchestrating tasks with... (Rafał Bigaj)
talks.teaser: Shows how Tekton custom runs tie Kubernetes pipelines to serverless jobs while cutting idle pod overhead in MLOps workflows.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens in the MLOps domain, where production machine learning needs observability, metrics, and trust—including security-oriented checks such as adversarial robustness monitoring that can be more expensive than training. The speaker contrasts typical sequential CI/CD pipelines with the branched, parallel graphs common in ML workflows and positions Tekton as a graduated CD Foundation project for composing those graphs on Kubernetes, where each standard task maps to pods and containers that become costly when a step only waits on work running elsewhere.

The core problem is illustrated with IBM Code Engine: a Tekton task can submit an external batch job easily, but the cluster still keeps a pod alive for polling until the job finishes. Custom runs are presented as the alternative—a custom resource plus a small controller using a reconciliation loop (often generated with Knative tooling in Go) that reflects external job state in Tekton without dedicating a pod to busy-waiting. Examples include expression evaluation, waiting for artifacts, nested pipelines, and Lambda-style triggers.

Practitioners see a minikube demo with a Code Engine custom task, resource footprints for the controller deployment, and pipeline runs completing in hundreds of milliseconds compared with pod-heavy tasks. The talk also mentions pipeline traceability work spanning pipeline runs, reconciler iterations, and API calls. References point to Medium articles and GitHub examples for readers who want to reproduce the pattern.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2023 - Will Machine Learning take your operations... (Rafał Ligmann, Brajan Fitas)
talks.teaser: Shows how AWS DevOps Guru uses machine learning to find anomalies in monitoring data and link them to root causes.
talks.summary:
The session introduces AWS DevOps Guru, a machine learning service the presenters describe as an AIOps tool for operations teams. It analyses metrics, logs and traces gathered in AWS, including CloudWatch metrics, CloudTrail logs and X-Ray traces, and learns normal application behaviour over time. The speakers note that the service needs about 24 hours of data before it can learn how an application behaves.

The middle of the talk is a live demo based on an AWS workshop: a simple serverless application with an API gateway, a Lambda function and a DynamoDB table. After the baseline was learned, the presenter lowered the table's read capacity units and ran a load test to overload the system. Guru grouped the resulting anomalies into insights, both reactive ones about current issues and proactive ones, and tied them to the capacity change. The service can also check CloudFormation stacks for recent configuration changes that may explain a problem, and alerts can be routed through SNS or EventBridge to external tools.

The closing point is time saved. The presenter argued that tracing a spike of 500 errors by hand could take about half a day, while the correlated event and its cause shown in the demo should take around 30 minutes. The speakers frame the service as a teammate that watches systems continuously, sitting on top of existing monitoring and logging rather than replacing them.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2023 - TDD - Trust Driven Development. How to break... (Tomasz Manugiewicz)
talks.teaser: Connects engineering trust to VUCA, Agile values, and breaking DevOps silos via competence, vulnerability, and shared language.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from a manager’s push to take trust seriously after a career shift from hands-on engineering to leading technical teams. The speaker frames modern software work with a VUCA-style lens—volatile markets, unclear requirements, complex problems, and ambiguous estimates—and argues that trust is what makes collaboration possible in that environment, including the implicit trust woven through the Agile Manifesto.

Two pillars organize the rest of the narrative: cognitive trust built by delivering competently, and emotional trust built through openness, honesty, and emotional intelligence. Examples walk through Dev versus business “buzzword” language, organizational silos across build-test-deploy-run domains, painful release approval meetings in banking, pair programming and code review as moments of vulnerability, and inspiration from Brené Brown on small daily trust-building gestures.

The close ties trust to measurable culture: quoting Charles Feltman on making important things vulnerable to others’ actions, then briefly noting how DORA-style metrics can be gamed when teams fear blame. The practical takeaway is that DevOps and Scrum practices only work when people invest in relationships—teams are groups that trust each other, not merely people who share a backlog.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - Evolution of IT support for WOŚP (Mariusz Aksamit and Łukasz Bromirski)
talks.teaser: Traces two decades of volunteer IT for a Polish charity broadcast, from early Cisco gear to a Kubernetes setup on Google Cloud.
talks.summary:
Mariusz Aksamit and Łukasz Bromirski walk through how the network and IT behind the Polish charity broadcast WOŚP grew over about two decades. They open with a 2001 internal email from the early team and the first vendors involved, Oracle, IBM and Cisco, followed by early hardware installed by interns around 2002 and 2003. One early highlight is a Cisco Catalyst 3550 that could do layer 3 routing in hardware. A 2007 setup needed a network in a TV studio to support a call center, and a live video link from a regional location failed on its first try because of a signal conversion problem.

The middle of the talk follows how demand pushed the design. Over time the team went from a simple internet switch to dedicated VPN links. The bandwidth rose from about 9 megabits per second in 2009 to about 120 megabits in 2010, which led to load balancers being added. In 2011 the firewall ran with access lists, and 10 gigabit ports were sized far above the real peak of roughly 200 megabits. Logs were reviewed by hand with grep and similar tools during the event.

The final part covers the most recent setup. For the 31st final, the platform moved to Kubernetes on Google Cloud, with Terraform scripts, an HTTP load balancer and a web application firewall at the edge, and a fallback plan to rebuild the environment elsewhere. The speakers reported about 270 endpoints and traffic that scaled 233 times from morning to peak, with Google providing engineers during the event. The main takeaways were the value of versioned, reproducible infrastructure and of planning for a load that peaks for only one day a year.

talks.title: PLNOG31- Monitoring & Troubleshooting in Networking Stack (Grzegorz Molenda)
talks.teaser: Shows how a content delivery platform monitors capacity, load balancing and tail latency, and why averages mislead engineers.
talks.summary:
Grzegorz Molenda, a senior manager on a mapping team at a content delivery platform, explains how that platform monitors its network. The mapping system decides in near real time which servers should serve each group of users, so the inputs have to be measured carefully. He argues that many dashboards are built for marketing rather than engineering, and that useful views show distributions and detail instead of smoothed lines.

The talk walks through several cases. Link capacity is read from routers over SNMP, and a target set below the real limit leaves headroom; when a link exceeds that target, part of its traffic moves elsewhere, which he shows happening during evening peaks. Load is compared between router counters and host-side measurements, and retransmissions, which routers cannot see, are sampled on hosts. Users are assigned to regions with a stable-matching algorithm, and oscillating user groups cause costly migrations. For server utilisation, he shows that averages and aggregated graphs hide spikes, while percentiles, histograms and hit maps expose them once aggregation is turned off.

On tail latency, he explains that a page load triggers many requests, so a rare slow response at the 95th or 99th percentile is likely to affect most users. Client mapping relies on resolver addresses, ping points and throughput-based scoring, and a prefix tree built from BGP tables finds the link that serves a given client. The takeaway is to track percentiles and distributions rather than means, and to question how the data was aggregated before trusting a chart.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - Cyberbezpieczeństwo w Grupie MIŚOT: opis produktów... (Marcin Zemła i Maciej Linscheid)
talks.teaser: Explains how new Polish cybersecurity rules affect telecom operators and presents managed security services for small providers.
talks.summary:
This talk, given by two representatives of a Polish group with roots in the telecom sector, looks at what their unit can offer small and medium telecom operators as the regulatory environment changes. The speakers describe an amendment to the national cybersecurity act that draws on a new EU cybersecurity directive and the 5G toolbox guidance. Under the draft, staff in a security operations center would need security clearances from the internal security agency, a process they estimated takes about twelve months. They also cited a fee of 46 500 zł for an industrial clearance valid for five years.

The middle of the talk covers the services and products the group has built or resells. These include monitoring of the network at a peering exchange shared by a cluster of small operators, traffic scrubbing within the bandwidth a customer already pays for, vulnerability checks, endpoint protection against ransomware-style behaviour, and a 24/7 network operations center. The speakers showed a panel where an administrator with basic knowledge of their own network can classify addresses and set protection levels. One pilot operator, they said, had been quoted about 2000 dollars for comparable protection, and their product costs several times less.

The closing part presents compliance as operational work rather than paperwork and proposes a partnership model. Operators could resell the services to their own customers, and staff training and certification preparation are also offered. Early deployments run as barter-style arrangements in exchange for bug reports. The main takeaway for small operators is to treat security as a service they can package, and to check early whether the new clearance and SOC requirements apply to them.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - Rozpalamy GG! (Jarek Rybus)
talks.teaser: Traces Gadu-Gadu from founding to half-million logins, Premium, wallet, business beta, and crowdfunding to co-own the brand.
talks.summary:
The speaker outlines why the Gadu-Gadu team is “reigniting” Poland’s legacy instant messenger after joining the current operator a few months ago. He frames the talk around returning to roots at a telco-oriented event, walks through a quiz on the brand’s 2000 founding, and situates GG beside ICQ, Skype, WhatsApp, and later global chat apps. He recounts early growth on free SMS-style messaging, side products such as Blip and Gadu Radio, the 2007 Warsaw Stock Exchange debut, ownership shifts, and the slide after Facebook and smartphones reshaped habits.

He stresses emotional user attachment—memorable emoticons, famous stunts such as chats with astronauts, and charity auctions for prized GG numbers—and contrasts the 2011 peak of about seven million users with roughly half a million monthly logins today, noting that more than half are young. Under fintechcom he highlights GG Premium near eighteen thousand subscribers, reminders and notification hubs, ruletka meetups, multi-device use, an English build, and fintech plans including GG wallet, QR tipping for creators, and a business edition in beta with organizational structure and segregated security.

Practitioners in telecom or product roles get a clear picture of strategy: rewrite clients across mobile, desktop, and web; add end-to-end encryption after crowdfunding; expand wallet and business offerings toward the EU; and run a community equity campaign that already exceeded four million złoty in declared interest with over a thousand supporters ahead of an autumn round.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - Praktyczne wykorzystanie nowoczesnych mechanizmów routingu (Łukasz Bromirski)
talks.teaser: Demonstrations walk through optimal route reflection and ADD-PATH in operator-scale BGP labs with live configuration changes.
talks.summary:
The session targets mature operator networks with many border routers and varied customer contracts, not simple two-router lab setups. It reviews why classic route reflectors advertise only one best path from their own IGP perspective, and when confederations or reflectors break down at scale.

Most of the time goes to live configuration in an isolated lab. Optimal route reflection ties BGP to link-state and constraint SPF so a chosen provider edge can act as the computation root, changing nexthops and IGP costs on real prefixes. ADD-PATH is configured on PE routers and reflectors to install and signal additional BGP paths for backup and load sharing, including pitfalls when policies on reflectors and edges disagree. The speaker shows nexthop shifts, extra path entries, and what happens when ADD-PATH is torn down on one side only.

ORR and ADD-PATH can run together in production designs. The talk briefly touches BGP labeled unicast for steering traffic in large data centers and closes with a warning that a chart implying falling RPKI coverage in Poland misread incomplete data, while noting full Polish anti-spoofing coverage on a monitoring site.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - How cloud looks like under the hood - hyperscale datacenter story! (Michał Furmankiewicz)
talks.teaser: Explores how hyperscale cloud datacenters are designed, cooled and scaled, from availability zones to GPU clusters.
talks.summary:
The talk takes a tour of how Microsoft builds the hyperscale datacenter regions behind its cloud, drawing on the speaker's experience leading construction of the Polish region. It starts with scale: dozens of operating regions, with each region made of several buildings and at least three availability zones. Each zone has its own power, cooling and network connections, and the zones sit close enough together to keep latency low. The speaker explains how the model has moved from fixed paired regions to letting customers replicate workloads to any region they choose.

The middle section follows the engineering changes. Early sites were mechanically cooled, while later designs used evaporative (adiabatic) cooling that works while outside temperatures stay below 28 degrees Celsius; above that, water is injected into the air, and hotter locations need other cooling methods. Rising power per rack pushes designs toward liquid cooling and, for AI workloads, large GPU clusters linked over high-speed connections. The talk also covers standardised open hardware, custom storage built for archival volumes, drives destroyed on site before they can leave the region, and the many compliance certifications needed across different markets.

The closing section covers energy supply and experimental ideas, including an underwater datacenter trial and glass-based archival storage that is written once and needs no power to hold data. The talk ends with the launch of the Polish region, with three zones around Warsaw and services offering data residency. The main takeaway is that at hyperscale, density, heat and supply decisions shape how cloud services get delivered.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - If not BGP, then what? (Tomasz Mikołajek)
talks.teaser: Explores when enterprises need BGP at the internet edge and when simpler links and static routing meet the same goals.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a consulting problem: BGP is often sold into enterprise designs where a single upstream link would suffice, echoing the trap of treating every problem like the one tool you know best. The speaker limits scope to BGP sessions facing the public internet, not internal dynamic routing inside an autonomous system, and explicitly excludes hype, vendor pitches, and fantasy replacements for inter-domain routing.

The business half walks through decision questions—whether the site shares services externally, how much outage pain is acceptable, whether a second link is truly diverse, staffing to design and operate sessions, and whether owning an AS number delivers real provider independence. When redundancy or traffic control are not real requirements, plain provider connectivity or floating static routes may be enough. Pursuing BGP anyway brings LIR fees, long waits for address assignments, ongoing maintenance, and prefixes that must be announced correctly.

The education half covers operational hygiene: filter what operators send and what you advertise, deploy source-address validation on customer networks, use RPKI and validators to build routing policy, and harden the edge router instead of leaving management and BGP ports exposed. References include MANRS, BCP 194, and NSA guidance, with the reminder that internet-facing BGP must be monitored continuously. The close and Q&A stress that unused BGP—kept only to impress management or pressure an ISP—wastes money, and that teams should match technology to actual need or formally accept residual risk.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - "Quality of Services" nie takie straszne (Artur Gmaj)
talks.teaser: Demystifies QoS concepts for network operators, covering classification, policing, shapers, schedulers, and simple production designs.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by arguing that Quality of Service frightens many engineers because vendor nomenclature piles up, even though switches and routers often ship with QoS already active. The speaker stresses that deep vendor configuration is optional for most careers, yet teams still need literacy when failover concentrates traffic on a link that cannot exceed its line rate and something must be dropped or deferred.

The middle of the session maps the shared building blocks: classifying packets using 802.1Q priorities, IPv4 and IPv6 DSCP fields, and MPLS markings; trusting or overriding those marks at the edge; policing with single- and two-rate three-color token buckets; shaping on egress; and scheduling queues via strict priority, round-robin variants, weighted approaches, and deficit round robin, plus random early drop and remarking on exit. Examples reference committed information rate, bucket depth, policers versus shapers, and why high-priority queues without rate limits can starve everything else.

The close recommends keeping designs modest—often best effort, expedited forwarding, and network control—sizing burst buffers using MTU multiples or short millisecond windows, and aligning behavior on every router because there is no signaling protocol for per-hop behavior. The goal is conceptual clarity so unusual acronyms map to a small set of mechanisms, with pointers to further operator-focused study material.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - Once Upon a DDoS: Who’s behind them, who’s targeted, how they’re done, how much they co...
talks.teaser: Maps the DDoS-for-hire market and hacktivist groups behind recent attacks, and how organisations can defend their infrastructure.
talks.summary:
Paweł Piekutowski, who leads the CSIRT KNF team at the Polish Financial Supervision Authority, explains why DDoS attacks have become a daily problem for the financial sector. Where such attacks once required skilled criminal groups and their own botnets, DDoS-for-hire panels now let almost anyone buy an attack for a modest sum, often ordering it through Telegram. He also describes hacktivist collectives, many of them active since the war in Ukraine began, that coordinate through Telegram channels, vote on targets and reward members who generate the most traffic. KillNet is described as the most active group in Poland, alongside groups such as Dosia, NoName and Legion.

The middle of the talk covers how these attacks work. Volumetric floods saturate bandwidth, while application-layer attacks put a smaller load on heavy functions such as site search and paging. Attackers also abuse reflection through misconfigured NTP, SNMP and MikroTik devices. Activist tooling sometimes contained mistakes, such as a target variable that was overwritten so only the last entry was attacked, and a user agent setting that stayed fixed, which made the traffic easy to filter. Checkhost, a service used to test reachability from other countries, can hint at an upcoming attack because its address pool is known.

The closing section gives practical advice. Organisations should agree on scrubbing and backhauling services with their providers before an incident, and keep the operator's contact details ready. Web application firewall rules can target suspicious user agents, missing SNI values and unusually high request rates from one source. Any country-level geoblock should be preceded by an analysis of which services depend on foreign clients. Administrators also need a way to reach the network out of band, and public statements should stay neutral so they do not amplify the attackers' message.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - Internet measurement tools for the good of the Internet (Alena Muravska)
talks.teaser: Surveys RIPE NCC measurement services that help operators troubleshoot BGP, query internet data, and run active connectivity tests.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces RIPE NCC’s role as a regional internet registry and focuses on three measurement offerings aimed at network operators and researchers. The Routing Information Service has collected BGP routing data from internet exchange peers since 1999, preserving history so incidents can be investigated long after they end and offering a shared view that supports troubleshooting and better visibility into routing risk.

The speaker walks through RIPEstat as an open data platform fed by more than thirty-five sources, including registry records, RIS routing data, and RIPE Atlas measurements. Audience members can look up addresses, prefixes, autonomous system numbers, countries, or domain names, adjust time ranges, and use info cards such as BGP routing history playback, registry versus live routing consistency, upstream visibility, and RPKI-related views, with the same material exposed through a public API.

RIPE Atlas is described as a global fleet of probes and anchors, plus software alternatives, that perform active connectivity measurements; hosts, sponsors, and members can run customized tests using a credit system. The talk closes with preview figures from an forthcoming Central European country report covering Poland, including IPv4 and IPv6 path patterns and top international upstream relationships, and points to RIPE community meetings where operators can engage further.
