talks.title: PLNOG31 - Rozwój technologii w świetle jej skuteczności w walce z... (Dominik Hawryluk)
talks.teaser: Charts attack generations and vulnerability growth driving layered defenses as automation still needs skilled operators.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a reminder that large-scale cyberattacks have reached a fifth generation: organized groups with serious budgets and highly targeted operations. Growth in connected devices and software is tied to rising vulnerability counts and a cybercrime economy measured in trillions of dollars, which in turn fuels more professional attacks.

The speaker walks through parallel evolutions on the defensive side, from early antivirus and perimeter firewalls through IDS, encryption, web application controls, DLP, GRC, next-generation firewalls, EDR, cloud security, behavioral analysis, zero trust, SASE, CASB, and XDR. Firewalls and endpoint stacks are traced in more detail, along with SIEM moving toward next-generation platforms that add intelligence, machine learning, and built-in orchestration. A recurring theme is that even highly effective tools leave dangerous gaps when abuse rides on legitimate, policy-allowed activity, and when teams lack experts who understand both the tooling and the organization.

Regulatory pressure—including Poland’s KSC framework from 2018 and the EU’s NIS2—is framed as another driver of mandatory controls and meaningful incident reporting. The talk closes with context-driven detection and response: dynamic asset roles inferred from logs, tailored automated reactions, scenario chains, and attack-path views meant to support operators rather than replace them. Practitioners are left with the takeaway that advanced platforms help, but judgment, organizational context, and qualified staff remain central.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - Protokoły sieciowe stosowane przez nowoczesne przeglądarki Internetowe (Tomasz Nowicki)
talks.teaser: Compares HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 to show how multiplexing and QUIC cut latency on modern heavy websites.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames today’s web as hypermedia piled onto protocols meant for simple text, citing HTTP Archive averages of dozens of cross-domain requests and many parallel TCP connections per page. He walks through HTTP/1.1’s request–response sequencing, TCP coupling, uncompressed headers, and head-of-line blocking, then contrasts that with real-world sluggish loads when bandwidth or latency is poor.

HTTP/2 is explained as one multiplexed TCP connection with binary framing, HPACK-style header compression, stream priorities, and optional server push, illustrated with side-by-side load demos, waterfall charts, and measured gains such as roughly 10–13% full load time and about one-third faster DOM Content Loaded, with the largest wins on high-latency links. Adoption near seventy percent is contrasted with slow IPv6 uptake. Because TCP still blocks at the transport layer, QUIC moves reliability and encryption into user space over UDP, aiming for resumption-friendly encrypted starts, independent streams, forward error correction, and connection IDs that survive IP changes—leading to standardized HTTP/3 and stalled adoption around twenty-five percent in cited data through 2021.

Practitioners should treat HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 as the default design target: fewer brittle HTTP/1 tricks such as domain sharding, image sprites, and heavy inlining, and more attention to how many small assets parallelize. Secure transports remain the practical gate for HTTP/2 upgrades in common implementations.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - Should only banks follow the example of... (Andrzej Karpiński and Piotr Wojciechowski)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding PLNOG31 - Should only banks follow the example of... (Andrzej Karpiński and Piotr Wojciechowski).
talks.summary:
# Overview

Andrzej Karpiński and Piotr Wojciechowski present DDoS protection best practices for medium-sized enterprises based on Polish Financial Supervision Authority (KNF) recommendations. The presentation demonstrates that telecommunications industry expertise in internet connectivity can protect organizations beyond banking sector institutions.

# Key Topics

## Internet Link Architecture
Proper internet edge design fundamentally determines organizational resilience to DDoS attacks. The KNF guidance categorizes four link types by characteristics:

**International Transit**: Expensive with limited bandwidth, many hops, high latency, high DDoS attack probability. Entire global internet accessible.

**Domestic Transit**: Paradoxically sometimes more expensive than international, fewer hops, lower latency, significantly lower attack probability. Polish networks total approximately 2,000—enabling rapid national-level detection and mitigation of threats.

**Peering Links**: Very low cost (interface and bandwidth fees only), extremely high throughput, zero hops, minimal latency. Organizations control directly connected sources, making DDoS from peered operators impossible.

**CDN/Resource Links**: Local content caching (YouTube, Facebook, Google) improves user experience and reduces load on paid transit links.

## BGP Routing Strategy
Most organizations implement BGP passively—purchasing internet through tenders without understanding routing implications or achieving conscious link management. The presentation advocates strategic BGP management: maintaining full routing tables, selecting operators carefully, implementing community-based filtering, and continuously monitoring prefix changes.

## Operator Selection
Operators are service providers, not integrators. Large operators provide superior infrastructure, multiple presence points, BGP community filters, and DDoS scrubbing services. Smaller local operators often lack proper infrastructure and community filtering, making them unsuitable despite lower pricing.

## DDoS Mitigation Techniques
Black-holing and null-routing via router null interfaces are cost-effective, network-wide mitigation methods. When properly configured across network nodes, these eliminate harmful traffic at the first ingress point, ideally before reaching target organizations.

## Infrastructure Design Principles
Critical services (banking) should operate on dedicated infrastructure separate from general internet connectivity. Physical cable routing documentation and redundancy are essential. Out-of-band management enables recovery during network compromise. Equipment should maintain 10x performance overprovision. Organizations must implement proper device lifecycle management (3-5 year replacement cycles).

# Technical Details

The presentation includes a practical case study testing international disconnect scenarios using BGP communities. Monitoring via University of Portland's BGP prefix tracking project revealed:

- Operators frequently implement community-based filtering inconsistently across their ASes
- Hurricane Electric and similar transit providers commonly cause prefix "leaking" (unintended propagation)
- Standard community exports are not universally accepted despite RFC compliance
- Real-time monitoring reveals operator outages and misconfigurations affecting traffic paths
- Proper operator selection enables visibility into connection quality to remote global resources

The speakers advocate for simplified operator-provided tools—a single "kill external" community command—rather than complex, operator-specific configurations requiring constant manual maintenance.

Advanced monitoring enables comparative operator quality assessment by analyzing BGP path changes, detecting anomalies automatically, and reporting performance differences to specific remote destinations.

# Takeaways

1. Design traffic architecture and failure scenarios before selecting operators or links
2. Implement multiple link types from different operators; single-link systems are inherently vulnerable
3. BGP routing strategy protects against DDoS more effectively than edge scrubbing services alone
4. Organizations should demand simplified community filters and kill-switch capabilities from operators
5. BGP prefix monitoring tools validate whether purchased services deliver advertised protection
6. Physical cable routing, equipment selection, and redundancy design justify specialist consulting
7. Continuous monitoring of prefix changes and operator performance enables rapid incident response
8. Poland's limited network count (~2,000) provides natural advantage for rapid national-level DDoS mitigation

talks.title: PLNOG31 - Od światłowodu do pasma (Michał Wal)
talks.teaser: An operator retraces Poland's fiber rollout, rising access traffic, and the bandwidth upgrades ahead.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames three pillars for fixed-access operators: how Poland reached large-scale FTTH coverage, which construction techniques and cable designs were used along the way, and how demand shifts once fiber is in the ground. It walks from early domestic deployments through roughly ten million households passed, a Pareto-style split between easier and harder builds, and public funding still aimed at closing gaps toward full nationwide reach.

The middle focuses on engineering tradeoffs—legacy high-fiber cables, blown microduct builds, and whether point-to-multipoint PON was the right long-term bet versus denser or point-to-point models—as well as the access-speed roadmap beyond GPON toward XGS-PON and higher aggregation rates. Traffic growth dominates the outlook: steep year-on-year increases, streaming and other big-tech sources cited as the bulk of volume, many devices per home, and average customer speeds that doubled in a few years while operator revenue does not keep pace with bits carried.

Practitioners should expect access upgrades to unlock the next bottleneck in aggregation and core, mandatory CPE and line-card churn with each generation, and sustained capex pressure from video and platform traffic. The closing operational anecdote covers removal of an obsolete Poland–Denmark submarine link, illustrating how long-lived plant outlasts textbook descriptions.

talks.title: PLNOG31 - RIFT: zero config, zero opex IETF standard based IP fabric routing (Tony Przygienda)
talks.teaser: Shows how the RIFT routing protocol builds self-configuring IP fabrics, with a demo on a 30-router lab.
talks.summary:
Tony Przygienda opens by arguing that IP fabrics, the leaf-and-spine style data center networks used by hyperscalers, are spreading to large enterprises and service providers. He says these operators want networks that run without specialist tuning, while designs built on older protocols need many layers of workarounds for addressing, topology visibility and failure handling.

He then presents RIFT as a routing protocol designed around the regular structure of a fabric. Nodes learn their position in a top-to-bottom hierarchy automatically, and topology information flows only north or south, so lower tiers never need a full view of the network. Configuration is largely automatic: link-local IPv6 addressing, IPv4 reachability carried over IPv6 next hops, and optional BFD can all be enabled without manual setup. Traffic is spread across links according to available bandwidth, and failures are handled by pushing topology changes up the hierarchy. He also notes that the implementation is open source and that the work is progressing as an IETF standard.

The talk closes with a demo on about 30 virtual routers. It shows the fabric as seen from the top tier, the level each node assigned itself, overload and link state changes, and a large prefix load converging within seconds. The takeaway for practitioners is that a fabric can be designed to need little configuration and operations effort when the protocol is built for that topology from the start.

talks.title: Dawid Czarnecki: Build a Fuzzing Framework with IAST | CONFidence 2023
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Dawid Czarnecki: Build a Fuzzing Framework with IAST | CONFidence 2023.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Dawid Czarnecki presents a year-long research project on building an Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST) framework called cake-fuzzer, which combines dynamic scanning and static analysis to detect vulnerabilities. The framework was inspired by papers from Miguel Philip Batric and Christof Zion's WP Garlic technique, and was commissioned by Luxembourg Armed Forces.

## Vulnerability Detection Approaches
The presentation contrasts three approaches: dynamic scanning (firing attacks externally and observing behavior), static scanning (analyzing source code), and IAST (combining both with real-time application knowledge). IAST monitors multiple components simultaneously—application responses, log files, file systems, OS processes, and network connections—to detect anomalies that indicate vulnerabilities.

## Technical Architecture
The cake-fuzzer solution has six core components: (1) monitors that observe OS and application behavior; (2) attack queue that executes scheduled attacks; (3) registry storing results in SQLite; (4) configuration strategies (JSON files defining attack scenarios and detection scanners); (5) instrumentation that modifies application and framework code to enable monitoring; and (6) a fuzzer that extracts application information and schedules attacks.

The framework takes a bottom-up approach by targeting specific frameworks (initially CakePHP) rather than broad language coverage, providing detailed knowledge of application internals without pre-configuration. This enables dynamic extraction of routes, endpoints, and parameters during execution.

## Key Technique: Magic Arrays
Following WP Garlic methodology, the solution overrides PHP superglobals (like $_GET) with custom "magic array" objects. These objects detect when user input is accessed by the application and automatically inject attack payloads into the execution flow. This discovers parameters dynamically during actual code execution rather than static analysis, adapting to different execution paths and parameter conditions.

## Instrumentation Process
Instrumentation involves three parts: (1) overwriting function calls to monitor specific operations (e.g., header requests); (2) patching by including application files to extract variables and framework methods; (3) copying files as needed. The approach allows extraction of application routes dynamically—cake-fuzzer discovered 141 paths in its example, scheduling 141 SSRF attacks, 282 LFI attacks, etc.

## Testing Results on MISP
Tested on MISP, a large open-source CakePHP project used by military and governmental organizations, the solution: discovered over 700 vulnerabilities (including duplicates), achieved a 2% false positive rate (15 false positives among findings), scanned 2,000+ paths, scheduled 880,000 attacks, and required approximately 3 hours on AWS EC2. Notably, it detected both known CVEs from previous MISP versions and previously unknown zero-days in the latest version.

## Benefits and Extensibility
The approach can extend to other PHP frameworks and eventually other languages by focusing on framework-level patterns rather than broad language support. It discovers obscure parameters missed by typical scanners, supports manual testing integration (components can run separately), and uses simple JSON-based attack strategy definitions. The tool is open-source on GitHub.

## Challenges
Three major challenges remain: (1) duplicate vulnerability reports (same vulnerability across multiple endpoints, which adds value by showing broader impact but complicates result presentation); (2) complex multi-condition vulnerabilities requiring specific configurations or user states to exploit; (3) increased application errors when scanning deeper due to magic array objects not being understood by some application code, making deeper coverage harder.

talks.title: Michał Sarnowski: ChatGPT - wróg czy przyjaciel | CONFidence 2023
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Michał Sarnowski: ChatGPT - wróg czy przyjaciel | CONFidence 2023.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this CONFidence 2023 presentation, software developer Michał Sarnowski examines the emergence and rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs), focusing on ChatGPT and its dual role in cybersecurity as both a beneficial tool and a potential threat vector. Drawing on his background in low-level C programming, Sarnowski compares the foundational mechanics of neural networks and the human brain, contextualizes the rise of models like ChatGPT compared to earlier or lesser-known LLMs, and analyzes how machine learning reshapes defensive and offensive security paradigms.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Large Language Models**: While industry giants created various LLMs (such as Minerva, PaLM, Pang, Sigma, Galactica, Megatron, and Gopher), ChatGPT achieved mainstream prominence primarily due to its openness and interactive accessibility.
- **Neural Networks vs. the Human Brain**: A structural comparison between biological brains and artificial neural networks, highlighting nodes, connections, dynamic vs. static memory, parameter scaling (from ~100–110 million in GPT-1 to over 175 billion and upwards of several trillion estimated nodes in GPT-4), and massive differences in energy consumption during training versus execution.
- **Societal & Structural Threats**: Non-security risks including the centralization and potential gatekeeping of knowledge by corporate vendors, digital divide escalation, invasive AI-driven surveillance, and communication misalignment (illustrated by incidents like an AI drone simulation where objective-driven systems could act against operators).
- **Offensive Security Applications**: Utilizing ChatGPT to enhance phishing, social engineering, scam generation (e.g., automated creation of fake Nigerian prince personas and multilingual copy), disinformation campaigns, automated exploitation tooling, fuzzing optimization, and vulnerability scanning.
- **Model Tampering & Defensive Applications**: Code review, debugging, and identifying software flaws using LLMs, counterbalanced by risks of model weight manipulation (exemplified by swapping node weights in GPT-2 so the model mislocates the Eiffel Tower to Rome) and the growing attack surface introduced by third-party plugins.

### Technical Details
Sarnowski explains that modern neural network computations fundamentally rest on basic linear algebra and activation functions, but current hardware advances now accommodate the enormous compute needed during training cycles. He contrasts human brain efficiency (~20W) with ChatGPT's runtime inference requirements (500W to 5 kW per request), not including the substantially greater energy demanded during training.

From a security perspective, the speaker demonstrates how quickly scams can be generated: in three prompts, ChatGPT created a fictional persona, localized the text into Polish, and produced a portrait via Craiyon. He also details research on GPT-2 where modifying internal node weights caused the model to conflate Paris with Rome, reliably directing users through Italian streets when prompted for restaurants near the Eiffel Tower. Sarnowski warns that similar fine-tuning or poisoning techniques could be leveraged by adversaries to inject hidden vulnerabilities into suggested code, especially as abstraction layers and third-party plugins proliferate.

### Takeaways
While Sarnowski concludes that AI does not currently possess true consciousness or pose an immediate existential takeover risk, legislative efforts are unlikely to halt competitive AI development. Defensive teams must actively monitor new offensive capabilities—such as automated exploitation, sophisticated phishing, and targeted model poisoning—while leveraging LLMs to automate code review, patch insecure software, and stay ahead of emerging attack methods.

talks.title: Jan Iłowski: How the FBI traces "anonymous" cryptocurrencies | CONFidence 2023
talks.teaser: Traces how stolen cryptocurrency moves through mixers and chain hopping, and how exchange identity checks exposed the launderer.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a copycat scam in which a hacked social media account promoted a fake cryptocurrency giveaway tied to a well-known tech figure, and it explains why such schemes pay off for criminals. It then covers how a public blockchain records every transaction under pseudonymous addresses, and why transfers cannot be reversed, sit outside any single jurisdiction, and can be spent directly on goods or services.

The main case is the theft of about 120,000 bitcoin from the exchange Bitfinex, described as worth roughly $7 billion. The speaker walks through laundering methods: peel chains that move small amounts across many transactions, mixers that pool funds through central or clustered wallets and leave patterns to analyse, and chain hopping through Monero and other coins. He notes that a mixer previously seized by the FBI left its data under federal control, and that one exchange gave authorities the buyer details of a token purchase.

The launderer's downfall came when he cashed out at a regulated exchange, Coinbase, and submitted real identification. The speaker says private keys were found in a Google Drive account under his real name, and that the couple were arrested about a year before the talk. He closes by arguing that KYC rules and risk scoring have reduced illicit crypto use, and that adoption will grow as systems become safer.

talks.title: Julia Zduńczyk: Hacking Access Control Systems | CONFidence 2023
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Julia Zduńczyk: Hacking Access Control Systems | CONFidence 2023.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at CONFidence 2023, Julia Zduńczyk, a penetration tester and red teamer at SecuRing, explains how physical RFID access control systems are targeted and compromised during red team engagements. While highlighting that basic physical bypasses (such as door shimming with plastic cards or coat hangers) should be addressed first, the core focus of the session is examining RFID vulnerabilities, demonstrating cloning techniques using tools like Proxmark, and detailing an end-to-end physical kill chain from low-privilege badge theft to server room compromise.

### Key Topics
- **Physical vs. RFID Access**: Emphasizing that basic door integrity checks should precede investments in expensive RFID security solutions.
- **RFID Fundamentals**: Differentiation between low-frequency (LF) and high-frequency (HF) systems, how passive tags draw power from the reader's electromagnetic field, and identifying frequencies with detector devices.
- **UID-Only Access Systems**: The risks associated with systems that validate access purely via static Factory UIDs, decimal numbers printed directly on cards, or predictable sequential UIDs issued to employees.
- **MIFARE Classic & Cryptographic Failures**: Vulnerabilities inherent in MIFARE Classic cards, including standard/default sector keys (e.g., `FFFFFFFFFFFF`) and broken proprietary ciphers (Crypto-1).
- **The Red Team Lifecycle**: Practical methodologies divided into observation, preparation (selecting antennas, concealing equipment), and execution (social engineering, surreptitious badge scanning).

### Technical Details
- **Card Scanning and Cloning Tools**: The speaker demonstrates the Proxmark device connected via USB and operated in standalone mode with an external power bank and custom concealed antennas hidden inside paper document folders.
- **MIFARE Exploitation**: Demonstrating automated multi-attack tooling that executes default dictionary checks followed by cryptographic attacks such as the Nested attack and Darkside attack to recover non-default keys and dump sector data.
- **Case Study Kill Chain**:
  1. *Observation*: Identified an HID MiniProx LF reader, noticed employees leaving cards unattended in an accessible dining area, and observed staff carrying badges on neck lanyards.
  2. *Scanning*: Used a concealed Proxmark inside a document folder to scan an unattended card and a cleaning worker's badge via pretexting ("lost umbrella").
  3. *UID Analysis & Brute Forcing*: Identified sequential UIDs (~500 apart). Found a staircase reader out of camera range to brute-force valid UIDs, discovering 20 active card numbers in roughly 30 minutes.
  4. *Reconnaissance & OSINT*: Tested discovered UIDs at a badge-authenticated office printer that displayed the user's full name upon login. Cross-referenced the names via OSINT to locate a network administrator's badge number.
  5. *Access*: Cloned the administrator's UID onto a writable badge to open the server room door.

### Takeaways
Securing physical access requires defense-in-depth across technology and personnel:
- **Proper System Architecture & Hardening**: Avoid UID-only access; implement modern cards supporting strong encryption (such as MIFARE DESFire with AES), ensuring the system is actively configured to enforce encryption rather than falling back to unauthenticated modes.
- **Multifactor Authentication (MFA)**: Require two-factor authentication (PIN pads or biometrics) for sensitive zones like server rooms.
- **Auditing & Monitoring**: Log badge activity and set alerts for anomalous access attempts, sequential scanning bursts, or abnormal access hours (time-based policies).
- **Human & Physical Factors**: Employee security awareness to prevent leaving cards unattended on tables or in locks, and distributing anti-RFID protective card holders.

talks.title: Felipe Duarte: Raspberry Robin: Evolution of an advanced malware downloading framework | CONFidence
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Felipe Duarte: Raspberry Robin: Evolution of an advanced malware downloading framework | CONFidence.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Felipe Duarte, Threat Research Lead at Security Joes, examines the architecture and evasion techniques of the Raspberry Robin worm. Raspberry Robin functions primarily as an advanced malware loader and distribution botnet designed to establish stealthy persistence, filter target environments, and deliver high-impact second-stage payloads such as IcedID, TrueBot, or Clop ransomware. Duarte focuses on how the threat actors behind Raspberry Robin actively study analysts and implement deception mechanisms to mislead defenders and automated sandboxes.

### Key Topics
- **Infection and Distribution Vectors:** Duarte details two primary distribution methods. The first relies on infected USB drives using `.lnk` shortcut files that launch command lines directing `msiexec.exe` to download malicious MSI packages from compromised QNAP NAS devices. The second vector utilizes malvertising campaigns delivering ZIP archives that contain encrypted Microsoft JScript (`.jse`) files, which ultimately drop DLLs invoked via `regsvr32.exe`.
- **Abuse of Legitimate Infrastructure:** The operators leverage trusted cloud and web services—including GitHub, Microsoft Azure, and Discord—to stage payloads and collect campaign telemetry, tracking the efficacy of their malvertising operations.
- **Sophisticated Obfuscation:** The loader incorporates extensive anti-analysis barriers, including at least eight distinct layers of shellcode and packers, junk instructions, indirect execution calls via the stack, and a finite state machine (FSM) to obfuscate control flow.
- **Analyst Deception via Fake Payloads:** Rather than merely terminating when sandboxes or debugging environments are detected, Raspberry Robin triggers a decoy downloader payload. This fake payload collects analyst environment data, transmits it to a QNAP C2 server via RC4 encryption, and executes benign or fake files to mislead triage processes.

### Technical Details
- **Execution and Memory Clean-up:** Duarte illustrates an indirect call pattern using the stack: the malware pushes the shellcode address (in `ECX`), pushes the main DLL address (in `EAX`), and executes a `jmp` to the Windows API `VirtualFree`. This alters the return address to transfer execution directly into the shellcode while simultaneously freeing and unmapping the initial DLL from memory.
- **Environment Fingerprinting:** The malware examines the Process Environment Block (PEB) for debugging flags, inspects process paths and file names for analysis strings (e.g., 'sample'), queries CPU details, and checks physical disk product IDs. It also cross-checks current usernames and computer names against a hardcoded blocklist embedded within the binary.
- **Decoy Pipeline vs. Real Payload:** When an analysis environment or sandbox (such as Joe Sandbox) is identified, the malware runs a fake payload that queries display devices via `EnumDisplayDevices`, profiles the host, communicates with a QNAP C2 server over RC4, and downloads a decoy file. This deception trick feeding fake telemetry back to the attackers allows them to profile sandboxes and harvest analyst metadata. Conversely, on a clean, valid target, the real loader communicates exclusively over the Tor network to download shellcode or secondary payloads like IcedID, TrueBot, or Clop ransomware.

### Takeaways
Defenders should maintain targeted threat hunting rules, such as flagging `msiexec.exe` fetching remote files from external URLs, and monitoring `regsvr32.exe` invoking extensionless files out of temporary directories (`\Temp`). Organizations must also closely monitor suspicious outbound Tor connections. Finally, Duarte emphasizes that malware triage must not rely solely on automated sandbox success reports: observed C2 traffic and simple downloader activity may be intentionally staged decoys engineered to deceive analysts and gather intelligence on defensive environments.

talks.title: Jannik Clausen: Schema-as-Code: Developer platforms and database schema changes | DOD Warsaw 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how declaring desired database schemas in code lets CI lint and deploy migrations, using the Atlas tool.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why database schema changes slow teams down once applications are split into microservices, each with its own database and often less database expertise than the old central DBA model. It ties these problems to the four DORA delivery metrics: fear of change pushes teams to batch releases, manual planning and review create bottlenecks, and recovering from a bad schema change is harder than rolling back compute.

The proposed answer is schema as code. Developers declare the desired end state of a schema, and tooling computes the migration needed to reach it. The speaker demonstrates the open-source Atlas tool with a plain SQL schema file, where a new unique index and a hair color enum column are generated as a diff against the existing migration files. A GitHub Action then lints the migration in a pull request and warns that a unique index on a column with existing duplicates could fail in production. After merge, migration artifacts are pushed to Atlas Cloud, and a Kubernetes operator applies them to a local MySQL database in a Minikube demo.

In the questions, the speaker explains that changes are wrapped in transactions, although MySQL's implicit commits can prevent a full rollback, and that the operator runs inside the cluster so database credentials stay local. Looking back at the metrics, the speaker argues that deployment frequency and lead time improve and that recovery gets easier. Future work covers data-dependent checks, data migrations, multi-stage refactorings and online schema changes.

talks.title: Łukasz Pięta: How not to Hibernate? | CodeFrenzy 2023
talks.teaser: Maps JPA lifecycles, cascade traps, lazy-loading limits, and query patterns through a hands-on Spring Data repository walkthrough.
talks.summary:
The session opens by separating JPA, Hibernate, and Spring Data, then walks the entity state graph—transient, managed, detached, and removed—and why flush, persist, and merge behave the way they do under the hood.

Using a small post-and-author example driven by Spring Data repositories and tests, the presenter shows typical failures such as transient references on save, detached authors reused across calls, and eager joins that pull unneeded associations. Fixes include thoughtful cascades versus treating authors as their own aggregate, lazy fetching with clear boundaries, and wrapping access in Spring transactions so proxies can load safely.

Later steps add embeddable value objects, nullability mapping that bypasses Kotlin constructors, and a one-to-many comment model that exposes join-table churn and inefficient deletes until the mapping is owned on the child side. The close covers n+1 selects and JPQL constructor projections as a practical way to fetch shaped data in one round trip, with generated SQL and schema changes traced throughout.

talks.title: Marcin Stożek: Java feat. OpenTelemetry | CodeFrenzy 2023
talks.teaser: Explains how OpenTelemetry collects logs, metrics and traces from Java apps and links them to speed up debugging.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces OpenTelemetry, an open standard for telemetry data, with a focus on using it from Java. The speaker starts with a small gRPC client and server taken from the OpenTelemetry Java documentation. Running the programs with the Java agent attached and the exporter set to logging, without changing any code, prints spans on both sides of the call that share one trace identifier.

The middle section covers the three signals: logs, metrics and traces. Logs record discrete events, metrics are numeric values that change over time, and traces show how a request moves through services as parent and child spans. A worked example follows a request from service A to service B and then to a database, showing where the time is spent. The speaker explains how logs can be tied to a trace through its context, so an error span leads directly to the related log lines instead of a manual search across separate systems.

The closing part describes the OpenTelemetry architecture: a specification, language APIs and SDKs, and a collector that accepts all three signals over one protocol and forwards them to different backends. Semantic conventions standardise attribute names. The Java agent instruments many libraries automatically, can be configured to switch parts off, and supports annotations for custom spans and extensions for in-house code. On Kubernetes an operator can inject the agent into pods. The speaker notes that the logs signal is still marked experimental and points to documentation and workshops for those who want to try it.

talks.title: Johan Bäck: IP / Optical Convergence
talks.teaser: Explores how coherent pluggable transceivers shrink DWDM into routers and abstracted management eases IP-optical convergence.
talks.summary:
Internet growth has depended on explosive gains in optical transport capacity, from early wavelength systems carrying tens of gigabits per fiber pair to modern coherent designs approaching terabit-scale throughput on a single pair. At the same time, equipment that once filled rack rows has shrunk into hand-held QSFP-DD pluggable modules that can carry hundreds of gigabits while using far less power per bit than earlier generations.

That shift enables IP routers and other hosts to host long-reach DWDM optics directly, but operation remains awkward when packet teams must tune analog transport settings through low-speed buses and vendor-specific memory maps that keep changing as features evolve. The talk contrasts that friction with how consumer wireless stacks hide RF complexity, and argues that IP and optical staff should not need each other's domain expertise for every link.

The closing vision keeps routers focused on ports and speeds while a transport domain controller manages wavelengths, power, and modulation wherever pluggable optics appear—from core routers to edge servers or radio access gear. An industry working group has packaged secure, IoT-inspired management for these smart coherent plugs so service providers can adopt IP over optical convergence without breaking SDN-style separation between packet and transport control.

talks.title: Michał Wojtyna: Becoming a Technical Business Partner | CodeFrenzy 2023
talks.teaser: Explains how developers can move beyond writing code by understanding business goals and influencing product decisions.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether developers understand why they build what they build and whether they can influence business decisions. It contrasts software engineers, focused on clean code and architecture, with business-minded people who test whether a product fits the market. A technical business partner combines both. The speaker argues that many developers only conform to decisions handed down from business, and proposes a shared vision instead.

Several steps follow. Keep technical excellence as the base, then apply a test-driven mindset to learning and new ventures: fail, win one small step, reflect, repeat. Model behaviour rather than nouns, question assumptions gradually, talk to domain experts directly rather than through a proxy, and suggest features proactively. Useful tools include a product vision board and business model canvas, context mapping for team and module relationships, and domain experiments that combine knowledge crunching with mob-style "cold storming" on code, with accepted models recorded as decision records. A value evolution map helps decide what to build and what to buy.

The talk ends by urging people to learn business model archetypes so they can spot improvements in their own company, and to try selling something small, such as an online course or ebook, to see how a business really runs. Combining these tools, the speaker says, gives a sense of purpose about what you are building.

talks.title: Michał Guzowski: Jakie cechy powinien mieć lider it w 2023? | CodeFrenzy 2023
talks.teaser: Argues that IT leaders should manage people, not schedules, and offers practical tools for feedback and blame-free team reviews.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who has worked in IT for 12 years, moving from developer to manager and founder of two companies, argues that IT leaders must manage people rather than schedules and reports. He opens with a bonus his team received at his first job: a small amount, split evenly, that showed him money cannot replace respect. He draws on Marcus Aurelius and on the idea that people are a company's most scarce resource.

Next he describes Southwest Airlines in the 1980s, which, facing a crisis of trust after accidents, made open communication central and adopted a just culture in which an admitted mistake is not punished. He notes the airline later carried over 150 million passengers in 2022 and had the fewest customer complaints among US carriers. He introduces colour-based personality types as a way to adapt communication, stressing that people mix colours and that context shifts them, and a perception ladder that explains why the same feedback can feel like an attack. For team conflicts he suggests a four-line exercise covering what each person and the team did well and should improve, focused on behaviour rather than blame.

He criticises sandwich feedback and quarterly reviews as artificial, recommending brief, frequent praise and a team appreciation round. He closes with a message from an employee struggling with depression, arguing that managers should act as a first line of psychological support because work and personal life cannot be fully separated. Motivation, he concludes, comes from meeting people's needs, and a leader should act as an umbrella protecting the team.

talks.title: Zbyszek Tenerowicz - I Run Code from the Internet and What Will You Do to Me? Hardened JavaScript...
talks.teaser: Shows how Lava Mode and Hardened JavaScript limit what untrusted npm dependencies can run during install, build and runtime.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the risk of installing and running code pulled in from npm dependencies. Install scripts can read environment variables and send credentials elsewhere, and a malicious package deep in a dependency tree is easy to miss. The speaker walks through a sample project in which a tampered TypeScript package injects code into the built application.

The defences are shown in layers. First, install scripts are disabled and only an allowlist of trusted packages is rebuilt, with entries matched by their full path in the dependency tree rather than by package name. Next, the speaker shows how package-declared binary commands can be restricted, so a dependency cannot expose a command the project did not expect. Finally, Lava Mode generates a runtime policy during a build and then blocks access to Node built-ins such as https, process and fs that a package never used before. It relies on Hardened JavaScript compartments built on SES to do this.

The closing demo has a later version of a package start making a network request, which the policy blocks. The speaker also shows an experiment in which calls from an obfuscated payload to globals, require and eval are intercepted and answered synchronously at runtime. The takeaway is to restrict what dependencies can reach rather than rely on audits alone, and to consider policy-based runtime controls for production code.

talks.title: Damian Hoffman - Cyber Crime as a Service, czyli gdzie, kto i za ile [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Maps the prices and offerings of cybercrime-as-a-service sellers on the dark web, from exploits to phishing kits.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a small personal investigation from 2019, carried out during a mini audit for a client. A database of Polish users was offered on an open web forum for roughly 10 to 15 euro cents per record, covering about 3,000 users. Tracing the seller's supposed Texas company with simple lookup scripts and street-level imagery led to a different location, which pushed the speaker to look deeper into what is sold on the dark web.

The market has become more granular. Buyers now purchase access, hosting, phishing pages, botnets and software separately, while operators and middlemen run consoles that track clients, payments and chats. For one case, the speaker estimated a return of about 1000% on each dollar invested. Listings covered a web admin portal flaw, a document macro code execution flaw sold for 3500 dollars, card credentials from about 7 dollars, identities around 20 dollars, phishing page generators priced from 50 to 300 dollars, a botnet loader, DDoS-for-hire and hacking-for-hire priced by job size, with a minimum of 250 euros for the smallest job. Quarterly bot-infection statistics placed Poland fourth among the countries shown.

The talk ends with takeaways for defenders. Dark web marketplaces carry a high chance of scams, and many forums require a fee or a vouch from an existing member before access. The speaker recommends monitoring dark web sources for keywords tied to your organisation and running continuous scanning of internet-facing systems rather than treating it as a one-off task, since most items on sale concern exposed services.

talks.title: Michał Leszczyński - Wprowadzenie do NFC - jak działa, które rozwiązania są bezpieczne... [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Explains how NFC cards work and why older systems like MIFARE Classic are easy to break, with practical checks for buyers.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces near-field communication (NFC) and the everyday systems built on it, including building access cards, hotel keys, transit tickets, contactless payment and sensor tags. It then focuses on the MIFARE Classic card, which splits its memory into 16 sectors, each with two keys that carry separate access rights. The speaker says the material compiles previously known weaknesses without new zero-days, and asks listeners to act responsibly.

The central example is why this card fails. Its proprietary cipher, Crypto-1, was kept secret under a security-through-obscurity design, but researchers reverse engineered it and showed it is weak. The Dark Side and Nested attacks can recover keys using a Proxmark 3 device, in some cases offline and within seconds. Developers often leave unused sectors with default keys, so one recovered key can open the rest of the card. Cloning is harder because genuine cards have an unchangeable UID, although certain clone cards with a backdoor allow writing it. A sniffing demo of a reader and card exchange also showed no authentication at all.

For buyers and developers, the advice is to check a card with a phone app to see whether it only exposes its UID, and to treat a product spec that lists only compatibility as a warning sign. Low-frequency 125 kHz fobs are treated as essentially unprotected for access control. Better designs use newer tags with AES-based protection, application-layer encryption and signatures, or JavaCard applets that keep keys on the card. Moving away from weak cards is the strongest fix, though it is often hard in practice.

talks.title: Kamil Bojarski- Smoki i pandy- organizacja chińskiego wywiadu w kontekście operacji cyber [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Maps the structure of China's PLA and Ministry of State Security and how their cyber intelligence units operate.
talks.summary:
The talk examines Chinese cyber operations from an intelligence perspective, focusing on the People's Liberation Army and the Ministry of State Security. It explains why these campaigns are hard to study, given language barriers and limited sources, and starts with the 2013 Mandiant report that tied APT1 to PLA Unit 61398. The intrusions described ran from 2006 and lasted four years and ten months before detection.

Next, the doctrine document Science of Military Strategy is discussed, treated as quasi-doctrine, which presents cyber operations and military-civil fusion as continuous from peacetime to war. The 2015 reform then moved PLA technical units into the Strategic Support Force, grouping information, space and electronic operations under one command. Judging its effect is hard, because activity dropped after a 2015 US-China agreement on industrial espionage. The Ministry of State Security, created in 1983, is shown through US indictments: one group recruited spies, another ran a campaign against dissidents abroad, and a third collected material for a prosecution against a Chinese telecom firm.

Case studies show how structure shapes operations. APT10 was linked to a Tianjin bureau working through managed service providers, and vendors disagreed on whether a related campaign was APT10 or APT31. APT40 was tied to a state security bureau using contractors against maritime targets, with later activity appearing alongside coast guard pressure in disputed waters. The talk closes by urging care with vendor labels and use of open sources such as indictments and PLA publications.

talks.title: Piotr Głaska - Jak atakujący używali DNS w 2021/2022 [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Surveys 2021-2022 malware cases in which attackers abused DNS for command-and-control, exfiltration and DNS-over-HTTPS traffic.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how attackers used DNS across the stages of an intrusion, from reconnaissance and delivery through exploitation, command-and-control and data theft. The speaker explains why operators prefer domain names over fixed IP addresses for their control servers, why some malware generates domains with algorithms instead of storing them, and how DNS queries and answers can carry data in both directions.

The middle of the talk walks through a series of cases from roughly the last two years. A cryptominer aimed at AWS serverless environments resolved its mining pool over DNS-over-HTTPS through public resolvers. Brute Ratel was shown configured to tunnel command traffic over DoH, and a ransomware group used it after getting into a company. The FluBot Android banking trojan combined generated domains with Base32-encoded DNS queries and encrypted TXT replies. An Excel macro tied to an APT34 campaign against a Jordanian government reported each step of its run through DNS queries, and a group linked to Iran used a custom Base32 alphabet that changed from attack to attack. The Orchard botnet derived its domain seed from the balance of a well-known cryptocurrency wallet. A Linux backdoor in attacks on Brazilian banks filtered its own traffic when it detected packet capture tools.

The closing part turns to defence. Blocking known malicious domains at the resolver stops simpler malware, but families that hard-code public resolver addresses or use DoH get around it. The speaker recommends blocking direct outbound DNS except to the trusted internal resolver, blocking port 853 and known public resolver IPs at the firewall, and layering host-based and network-based detection. Encrypted DoH on port 443 looks like ordinary browser traffic, so it is hard to spot without knowing what is inside.

talks.title: Kamil Goryń - Screwedcurity by design, czyli egzotyczne podejście do zapewniania... [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Shows through humorous, real project failures how security requirements and early testing prevent costly flaws.
talks.summary:
Kamil Goryń gives a non-technical, humorous review of software projects that went wrong on security. The talk opens with an audience quiz about the flaws hidden in one project, then walks through several real cases the speaker audited, saw first-hand, or read about publicly.

A mobile app designed to work without cellular coverage copied its full production database onto every installed device, and users who had removed their account could still reach that data while the app stayed installed. Test builds were installed on handsets left at client sites, signed in with private accounts. In a second case, a client ordered a pentest report signed by named people rather than actual testing. The student-facing application had basic SQL injection, and with no staging environment every test ran against live production. The speaker also described a leaked report on Twitter's servers, where roughly 250,000 of 500,000 machines needed updates and sensitive data was poorly protected.

The closing section argues that vague security guidelines can be stretched, while clear legal obligations cannot, so ignoring them invites fines and regulatory trouble. The remedy is to define what security means as a project requirement from the start, just like features, and to use testing mainly to confirm that the worst flaws were avoided. Nothing will be fully secure, but a clear plan can raise the level.

talks.title: Magdalena Wrzosek - Gaming i ćwiczenia sztabowe, czyli jak robić cyberbezpieczeństwo... [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Shows how board games and tabletop crisis drills help technical teams explain incident response and new regulations to management.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that slide decks are a poor way to explain cybersecurity to management, legal teams and non-technical staff. The speaker presents games as an alternative and uses ideas from cultural theory of play to explain why games hold attention. One card game has teams build a security operations centre over three rounds, each representing a year, with a budget of one million in-game currency. Random cards bring malware incidents and events such as a key manager leaving. Teams that tried to shortcut the scoring, for example by outsourcing first, often saw their reputation suffer during incidents, especially when they had not joined sector CERT groups or cooperated with a national CERT. A Monopoly-style board game then walks players through a new directive and shows that some processes depend on specific roles being in place first.

The second part covers tabletop exercises for critical-sector organisations. Instead of a slide quiz, a realistic exercise injects an incident into a factory and follows how it is reported, escalated, translated into production losses, and handled with legal staff, public authorities and simulated media. Planning with the client took about two months. Such drills exposed which processes worked, which roles were missing, and how staff behaved under pressure.

The takeaway is that technical teams and lawyers need a shared language, and that games and realistic drills build that understanding better than presentations do.

talks.title: Paweł Kusiński - Czy persystencja na środowiskach serverless jest możliwa?! [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Shows how an attacker can keep a foothold in AWS Lambda and Google Cloud Functions by hijacking their execution runtime.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether an attacker can maintain persistence inside serverless functions, using AWS Lambda and Google Cloud Functions as examples. The starting assumption is that a function has already been compromised, for instance through remote code execution or a malicious third-party dependency. The speaker explains why these environments are less ephemeral than their name suggests: a warm execution environment is reused between invocations, and a control process hands incoming events to the function through a runtime loop.

The core of the talk is how that loop can be hijacked. On AWS, the payload can recover the current invocation ID from the process stack or memory, or use an undocumented behaviour where the runtime returns the last invocation ID again. With that ID, it starts a replacement bootstrap that forwards every incoming event to an external server, while the original bootstrap waits indefinitely. On Google Cloud, where the same approach is harder, the payload instead patches the Python web application in memory to add a route that sends request data out over sockets. A live demo showed event data from a vulnerable YAML-parsing function reaching the speaker's listening server on both clouds.

For defence, the speaker suggests placing functions inside a VPC and removing internet egress, which stops the callbacks but breaks functions that legitimately need outbound access. Alerting on runtime logs tends to produce noise, so he recommends securing the software supply chain and scanning dependencies before they run. He also mentions two untested ideas, layer integrity checks and flow logs, and points to a GitHub repository with the vulnerable code, the exploits and a reverse shell tool he built that runs over HTTP.

talks.title: Adrian Sroka - Jak wspierać deweloperów w bezpiecznym kodowaniu? [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Presents a five-area framework for helping developers write secure code, from security awareness to building engagement.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that developers are best placed to write secure code, yet in many companies they and the security team work in separate worlds. The speaker says that buying tools or sending staff to one-off training rarely lasts, because deadlines and business demands take over once the workshop ends.

Instead, the speaker presents a five-part framework drawn from experience in several organisations. It starts with making developers aware of which areas matter, such as login, password reset, registration, payments and sensitive data. Next comes decision support: checklists and decision maps for choosing libraries or handling file uploads, so developers do not have to ask security about every choice. Teams also need a place for discussion, such as guilds or chapters, and a Security Champions model where a named person in each team links up with the security group.

The last two parts are regular exposure and engagement. Sharing news about security measures, and even about attacks the company faces, keeps the topic visible, while hackathons and cross-team challenges keep people motivated and let them test their skills. The speaker stresses that the framework is subjective and should be filtered through each company's own situation before adoption.

talks.title: Adam Lange - Jak to robią "zagramanicą" - przegląd ciekawych kampanii ze świata [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Contrasts international cybercrime campaigns with Polish ones across phishing, scams, infrastructure, and analyst-facing differences.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames everyday Polish cybercrime against a wider view from institutions and private tracking. Organized groups and lone operators pursue monetizable data through phishing, malware, fake e-commerce, investment fraud, and business email compromise, often leaning on bulletproof hosting and specialized roles such as infrastructure providers, mules, and brokers who resell data on darknet markets.

A major thread is how scenarios diverge. Polish bank phishing frequently uses freshly registered brand domains and operator panels that guide victims through withdrawals step by step. Abroad, kits targeting institutions such as Chase more often expose simple statistics, email exfiltration instead of server-side storage, and harvesting of full identity bundles (“fulls”) rather than live account takeover. The talk also contrasts hosting tricks (compromised sites and subdirectories versus keyword domains), notes rare Polish BEC volume, and walks through abroad-heavy fraud types: fabricated online banks for 419-style scams, destructive romance scams, gaming and streaming credential theft, multinational fake outlet shops, marketplace phishing, crypto giveaway pages, crisis charity clones, and Poland-specific parcel payment SMS lures now spreading into neighboring countries.

Practitioners should expect overlapping actors globally while local flavors remain distinct. Poorly secured phishing backends that write credentials to flat files can unintentionally aid defenders who map victims, and Polish campaigns increasingly export mechanics that were honed domestically.

talks.title: Tomasz Zieliński - Fidonet - światowa amatorska sieć komputerowa (przed Internetem) [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: The session traces modems, BBS culture, and Fidonet mail routing in Poland before dial-up Internet became widely available.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on life before always-on broadband: acoustic couplers, Bell-era rules that blocked direct modem line taps, and the march from 300 bit/s toward 33,600 bit/s links that still felt painfully slow. It situates Polish users under PRL-era telecom limits—scarce phone lines, expensive long-distance calls, and modems that could be throttled on multiplexed lines—then explains why bulletin board systems mattered for software, games, and the lonely hobbyists who had no local peers.

The middle follows BBS habits: busy signals, upload ratios, conference mail akin to forums, and turn-based multiplayer games when only one caller could be online. From there it describes Fidonet’s 1984 origins with Tom Jennings’s Fido software, the growth past roughly 250 numbered nodes, and the zone/net/region/point addressing model with hub routing that could reach the United States in about seven hops. Polish peaks around April 1997, mandatory overnight mail windows, multi-day netmail round trips, and early gateways that handed traffic to Internet e-mail are spelled out with concrete latency examples.

The close covers Fidonet’s global peak near 30,000 nodes in 1996, how Poland’s nationwide dial-up access number drained BBS appeal, the speaker’s own drift away after 2000, and failed hunts for conference-mail archives contrasted with a personal backup of thousands of echomail messages. The practical takeaway is to keep local copies of content you care about, because community history on ephemeral platforms is easily lost.

talks.title: Michał Trojnara
talks.teaser: A penetration tester surveys crypto failures from XOR and Base64 misuse through key flaws and side-channel risks.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames cryptography through Murphy’s law and long experience in penetration testing and corporate risk work. The intended message is not to design novel cryptography or roll custom implementations when proven libraries suffice, while still treating other people’s crypto as fertile ground for review and testing. The talk is explicitly not a complete checklist of every mistake; many atypical flaws remain beyond the patterns shown.

The core walks through classic property failures with real anecdotes: confidentiality broken by treating XOR or Base64 as encryption, homegrown ciphers, weak or short algorithms, ECB leakage, and stream-cipher keystream reuse as in older Office practices. Integrity is often neglected because ciphertext looks unreadable, yet validity oracles can leak plaintext bits with large numbers of queries. Authentication, password storage, and replay resistance are easy to get partly right but hard to combine. Key management stories cover shared vendor keys, keys “protected” by another weak secret, extraction from binaries or runtime, one key baked into every device, and missing rotation plans. Randomness on constrained IoT, VMs, and the Debian OpenSSL incident illustrate how implementation detail shrinks effective key spaces. Later sections cover conditional-access and white-box designs, trust in SGX and mobile TEEs, browser JavaScript crypto limits, and fault or side-channel attacks on hardware wallets.

The closing guidance favors TLS where networking applies, libraries such as NaCl-style APIs for offline messaging, careful certificate and time handling, and independent cryptographer review separate from whoever built the system.

talks.title: Paweł Krawczyk - Prywatność i cenzura w federacji ActivityPub [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Explains how ActivityPub federation works, where its privacy limits lie, and how moderation and defederation shape the fediverse.
talks.summary:
The talk untangles a common confusion: Mastodon is one open-source application that implements the ActivityPub protocol, while the fediverse is the wider network of many servers and applications that federate through it. The speaker walks through delivery between instances. A post is pushed by HTTP POST to the inboxes of followers' servers, remote content is copied locally, and so one post can exist on several servers at once. Each instance's feeds (local, federated and global) reflect who its users follow, not a recommendation algorithm.

On privacy, the speaker explains that visibility settings only limit distribution, and that receiving and sending servers are the ones enforcing those limits. Messages are not end-to-end encrypted, so server administrators can read them, and the protocol is designed for publishing rather than confidential exchange. Server-to-server requests are signed to prevent spoofing, and public keys are published on user profiles. Moderation is set per instance, with reports that can cross servers. Blocklists of defederated domains, often shared on GitHub, are a growing concern. The speaker also reviewed published vulnerability records for fediverse projects, finding mostly subtle, non-critical issues, plus one cross-site scripting flaw in a customized Mastodon instance.

The takeaway is to treat fediverse posts as broadcasts rather than confidential messages, and to use end-to-end encrypted tools for sensitive material. Choosing an instance also means accepting its moderation policy and its federation choices.

talks.title: Marcin Marciniak - Jak zabić światowy handel czyli zestaw najczarniejszych scenariuszy [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Walks through hypothetical attacks on shipping, ports, GPS and aviation systems that could disrupt global trade.
talks.summary:
Marcin Marciniak presents a fictional worst-case exercise asking how an adversary could disrupt global trade. He starts by breaking trade into its stages: order, production, transfer, payment and additional services. He argues that offshoring and just-in-time supply leave little slack, so a disruption at any one stage could trigger a cascade of failures across the chain.

The middle of the talk focuses on maritime targets. The speaker describes identifying vessels through public AIS data and satellite links, noting that some ships still use older low-bandwidth satellite systems where traffic can be intercepted with inexpensive equipment. He outlines a path from an office network with weakly managed firewalls into the operational networks on board, and explains how an engine failure could be caused on a large container ship. Ports, the Suez and Panama canals, GPS jamming and spoofing, and disruption of aviation landing systems are covered as further scenarios, with the cost estimates he presented for some of them.

The closing section covers ports, aviation and railways, with the speaker saying rail procedures are more resilient than the others. The main takeaway he draws is that unpatched legacy devices, equipment moved between network segments without oversight, unmonitored logs and missing lifecycle procedures are what make these scenarios plausible.

talks.title: Przemek Jaroszewski - Ilu bezpieczników potrzeba do wkręcenia żarówki? [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Shows how blue teams split siloed security roles and align preparation, detection, response, hunting, and lessons learned.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames corporate cyber defense as the “blue side”: protecting crown jewels and running incident management, explicitly not diving into firewall or EDR mechanics or formal risk management. After a military metaphor for preparation—intelligence, layered defenses, rapid response, and visibility—the talk walks through how large firms often silo endpoint, network, cloud, and mail security, and why that granularity can hide kill-chain gaps unless someone maps coverage holistically.

He stacks responsibilities that feed that preparation: threat intelligence filtered to actionable TTPs rather than volatile IOC shopping, detection engineering that translates control telemetry into SOC-ready rules and dashboards, MITRE ATTACK–driven coverage checks, purple-team style validation with red team, vulnerability testing and tabletop exercises, and dedicated lesson-learned and playbook maintenance. Incident response is described as intelligence-driven detective work spanning tier-one alerting, tier-two coordination with business and legal stakeholders, and tier-three deep technical analysis.

A fictional e-commerce crisis—emerging zero-day risk on a critical web platform, then confirmed compromise—shows how CTI, detection engineering, vulnerability assessment, and threat hunting parallel one another while patch urgency collides with business downtime costs. The close stresses that named roles are illustrative, functions can be bought or merged, and staffing should follow asset value and acceptable risk—not a fixed headcount formula.

talks.title: Grzegorz Tworek - Co NTFS Extended Attributes mają wspólnego z security [OMH 2022]
talks.teaser: Explains how NTFS extended attributes hold hidden Windows metadata and how forged cached hashes can fool AppLocker.
talks.summary:
The talk explains what NTFS extended attributes are and why Windows depends on them. The speaker starts with the classic FAT-era file flags such as read-only, hidden, system and archive, then moves to NTFS, where a file is a set of attributes stored in the master file table, and small files can sit inside that table entry. Extended attributes add named metadata with arbitrary values on top of this. Windows components use them as caches, for example for Defender bookkeeping, the catalog location of a file's signature, and a file hash kept by Microsoft's EDR driver.

The middle of the talk covers the kernel-only namespace. Attribute names starting with the kernel prefix can only be created by kernel-mode code, and names containing the purge marker are removed by the driver when the file is modified. The speaker then looks at AppLocker, which stores a hash of each executable in an extended attribute so it does not have to rehash files on every launch. The hash it uses matches the Authenticode-style content hash rather than the SHA-256 that the documentation implies. In a demo on a mounted virtual disk, the speaker edited the binary to rename a kernel attribute into an ordinary name, then planted a forged hash for a blocked program. In audit mode the program was logged as allowed.

The closing point is that a cache is only as trustworthy as its invalidation. Windows Defender Application Control, by contrast, does not use these attributes on non-system drives, computes hashes itself and can clear extended attributes at restart. For practitioners, the takeaway is to treat extended attributes as useful but unverified storage and to check whether a cached value is actually refreshed.

talks.title: Panel Rady Programowej PLNOG - Halo! Co słychać w branży telco?
talks.teaser: Panelists from the PLNOG programme council discuss network engineer skills, hiring gaps, AI tooling and when cloud makes sense.
talks.summary:
The panel from the programme council of PLNOG discusses where the network engineer role stands in Polish industry. The speakers describe a network engineer as someone comfortable from cables and routers up to what protocol output means, and note that few people are growing into that role. They argue that employers often want all-round experts at junior pay, and that niche skills such as BGP are better bought as occasional service work than kept on payroll, since routine upkeep may take only a few hours a month.

The discussion then turns to AI and tooling. Panelists see tools such as ChatGPT as useful for working through large volumes of logs or configuration output, but warn that people who cannot define the task or judge the result may add risk, with generated playbooks and low-quality code cited as concerns. They also stress that engineers must explain technical ideas to non-engineers, comparing it to a house design where users' needs have to be gathered before drawing anything.

The final part covers cloud. The panel weighs whether companies are moving workloads back out of the cloud, noting that Polish firms are still moving in while some large Western enterprises repatriate. Security tooling costs, latency to distant regions, data-location rules and the ability to scale quickly are weighed, and the panel concludes that hybrid models chosen on the numbers rather than ideology will likely matter most. The session closes with four of six prepared topics covered and an invitation for audience questions at a follow-up session.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Explaining annotation magic
talks.teaser: Tomasz Borek analyzes 4Developers 2022: Explaining annotation magic.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from 4Developers 2022, Tomasz Borek sets out to demystify Java annotations and dispel the notion that they rely on impenetrable "dark reflection magic." Explaining that annotations are simply code and metadata used for meta-programming, Borek traces their evolution from early marker interfaces like `Serializable` and `Cloneable` to the formal introduction of annotations in Java 5. The presentation walks through basic mechanics, targeting, retention policies, built-in annotations, runtime reflection, classpath scanning alternatives, code generation via Project Lombok versus Java records, and compile-time annotation processing.

### Key Topics
- **Origins and Purpose of Annotations**: Early Java used marker interfaces with no methods to convey intent or capability. Annotations formalized this as structured metadata that can signal intent, instruct compilers or build tools, or trigger behavior at runtime.
- **Annotation Targets and Retention Policies**: Discussion of `ElementType` targets (classes, methods, fields, parameters, packages, records, etc.) and `RetentionPolicy` levels (`SOURCE`, `CLASS`, and `RUNTIME`), highlighting that only `RUNTIME` annotations remain accessible when an application executes.
- **Standard Built-in Annotations**: Analysis of built-in annotations including `@Override`, `@FunctionalInterface`, and `@SuppressWarnings`. The talk highlights common traps, such as placing `@SuppressWarnings` too broadly or relying on it without checking compiler warnings.
- **Building a Custom Test Runner with Reflection**: Demonstration of building a basic test runner using Java reflection to discover methods marked with custom `@Test` and `@Ignore` annotations.
- **Classpath Scanning vs. Indexing**: How frameworks like Spring scan the classpath (e.g., using libraries like Reflections) and why scanning large classpaths with jars and zip files incurs performance overhead ($O(N)$), contrasted with indexing techniques using the ClassIndex library.
- **Code Generation (Lombok vs. Records)**: Comparing boilerplate reduction using Project Lombok (e.g., `@Value`) against built-in Java records introduced in Java 14.
- **Compile-Time Annotation Processing**: Introduction to writing custom compile-time annotation processors by extending `AbstractProcessor` to inspect elements and generate code or diagnostic messages during compilation.

### Technical Details
- **Targeting**: Demonstrated declaring annotations without `@Target` (which allows them almost everywhere except certain type uses) versus scoping them strictly to `ElementType.LOCAL_VARIABLE` or `ElementType.METHOD`.
- **Retention Behavior**: Inspected bytecode and runtime reflection calls to show that `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.SOURCE)` annotations disappear after compilation, while `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)` annotations remain accessible via reflection methods such as `isAnnotationPresent()`.
- **Reflection Mechanism**: Constructed a runner executing `clazz.getDeclaredMethods()`, filtering methods using reflection streams for `@Test`, checking optional parameters like an `ignore` boolean attribute, and invoking test methods using `Method.invoke()`.
- **Classpath Scanning Performance**: Discussed how Reflections-style scanning inspects packages, archives, and jars on the classpath, contrasting it with compile-time indexing using the Polish library `ClassIndex` to track annotated types without runtime scanning.
- **Package-Level Annotations**: Explained the role of `package-info.java` as a dedicated file to hold package-level annotations and documentation, referencing `java.util.concurrent` as an example.
- **Lombok vs. Records**: Showed how Lombok's `@Value` generates getters, `equals()`, `hashCode()`, `toString()`, and constructors, versus native Java records, noting Lombok provides more customization (such as `@NonFinal` and no-arg constructors).
- **AbstractProcessor**: Outlined the core structure of an annotation processor, including defining supported annotation types, supported source versions, and implementing the `process()` method using `RoundEnvironment` and diagnostic messaging.

### Takeaways
Annotations are not magical constructs but straightforward mechanisms grounded in metadata, reflection, and compiler processing. Developers should understand retention policies to avoid expecting source-level annotations at runtime, scope targeting appropriately, avoid blanket use of `@SuppressWarnings`, and weigh the trade-offs between expensive runtime classpath scanning and compile-time indexing or processing. When choosing between Lombok and Java records, native records are preferable for simple, immutable data carriers, whereas Lombok remains useful when specialized configurability is required.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: TDD - Trust Driven Development
talks.teaser: Shows how team relationships, learning, autonomy, purpose and impact in DevOps work support developer wellbeing.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how wellbeing in software work can be supported by the way teams collaborate. The speaker starts with five everyday wellbeing aspects published by a UK organization: connecting with others, continuing to learn, being active, noticing the present moment, and giving to others. Drawing on several studies of effective development teams, the speaker groups their findings into five themes: relationships, competence and learning, autonomy, purpose, and impact on customers and the world.

The speaker then maps these themes onto the agile manifesto, which emphasises interaction, collaboration and responding to change, and onto DevOps. In DevOps, the speaker argues, the phases from coding and building through testing, deployment, operation and monitoring should not be split into silos; developers and operations people should pick up each other's skills. Pair programming, shared test automation, team meetings and informal get-togethers after work are presented as ways to build relationships and keep learning going, while a finished, delivered product gives a sense of impact. The talk moves from everyday enjoyment at work toward a deeper satisfaction that comes from good relationships.

The closing message is that collaboration between people is the foundation for everything else, including the tools and artifacts a team uses. The speaker suggests that whether the future of work is remote, office-based or hybrid, building relationships and staying in contact matters most.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Dawid Bastek - Jak usprawnić swój projekt mobilny w 1 dzień - poradnik dla każdego
talks.teaser: Shows practical tools like README templates, SwiftLint, Danger and branch protection to improve a mobile project quickly.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a mobile project the speaker joined, where a new iOS app was built from scratch for an English-speaking client while the Android version was already about seven years old. The team struggled with a request for iOS to look like Android, missing documentation, a cross-platform shared-logic setup that part of the team had not used before, and communication gaps across locations.

The speaker then walks through a set of low-effort tools. A README should explain the setup, required tool versions and how to run the project, which helps newcomers and recruiters alike. A pull request template nudges authors to describe their changes. Pinning tool versions is illustrated by a case where a developer lost half a day to a different build tool version than the rest of the team used. For linting, he covers Android Studio's built-in inspections and SwiftLint for iOS, which needs a build phase script and a customised configuration to avoid an overwhelming number of warnings. Danger runs in CI and posts comments on pull requests about lint failures, missing titles or branch names, and very large changes.

To finish, he shows GitHub branch protection rules that can require a review, passing status checks and resolved conversations before merging, with a caution that blocking on Danger can slow developers down. His closing advice is to start with small steps, get the whole team to agree, and treat the tools as serving the team rather than the other way round.
