talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Grzegorz Stolecki - Warsztat inżyniera ML, czyli jak płynnie spiąć R i Power BI
talks.teaser: Shows how R and Python integrate with Power BI for statistical charts, data prep, serialized ML models, and anomaly detection in reports.
talks.summary:
The session addresses a gap many analytics teams hit: Power BI is strong for exploration and standard visuals, but falls short for econometric charts, custom statistical tests, and flexible machine learning workflows. The presenter walks through Microsoft’s R and Python integration in Power BI Desktop, starting with setup, pointing Power BI at a local R or Python install, and using scripted visuals whose graphics are captured from R’s graphical device via a CSV handoff and wrapper code.

The middle of the workshop demos two integration paths. Scripted visuals consume filtered table data from the tabular model (with a 150,000-row cap and one-way filtering from Power BI into R). Power Query runs R or Python during refresh—for web scraping with Python, ARIMA-style forecasting, missing-value imputation with mice, k-means clustering, and isolation-forest anomaly scores added as model columns. Cloud deployment is covered honestly: scripts can run in the Power BI service, but file access, outbound network calls, and R packages are restricted to an approved list of roughly one thousand packages.

For practitioners, the takeaway is when to push computation into the data load versus a visual, how to store trained models as text in tables when binary types are unavailable, and how the same pattern supports operational monitoring—such as flagging slow report executions on a shared reporting server before users complain.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Grzegorz Wątroba - optymalizacja animacji w Unreal Engine 4
talks.teaser: Shows how to cut animation and update costs in Unreal Engine 4 so hundreds of characters keep a steady frame budget.
talks.summary:
Grzegorz Wątroba describes optimising a large crowd of fully animated, procedurally generated characters in Unreal Engine 4. The target is up to 1000 units on a virtual city map, with about 200 drawn on screen at once, and a steady 60 fps at both Full HD and 4K. He argues that developers should track frame time in milliseconds rather than FPS, because a high FPS number hides small differences that matter when setting a per-frame budget.

The talk outlines engine basics such as actors, components and the tick loop, then covers three areas: multithreading through ParallelFor, Async Task and runnables; data-oriented layout with SIMD and an entity-component-system style; and heterogeneous work on the CPU and GPU, including compute shaders and OpenCL. The main case study is the Significance Manager, which scores each object's importance so that distant or off-screen actors tick less often. Action points register with a central subsystem, animation blueprints read data through a thread-safe proxy, and a skeleton mesh budget lowers animation precision automatically to fit a fixed cost.

Rendering techniques close the talk, including LOD, culling and upscaling. The speaker reports that upscaling saved roughly 10 to 30 percent of frame cost depending on the game. He notes that threading adds a fixed overhead, so a single unit can run slower with the optimisations, while large crowds gain. He recommends matching techniques to the game genre, measuring every change with the profiler, RenderDoc and Unreal Insights, and verifying each theory with timings.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Jakub Wawrzyniak - Prognozowanie z wykorzystaniem metod uczenia maszynowego
talks.teaser: Surveys ML forecasting for sales, retail, and industrial failures with explainability, data readiness, and cloud ML tooling.
talks.summary:
The session opens from the perspective of a Poznań consulting firm that combines data platforms, data science, and machine learning for client projects. Forecasting comes up most often for sales, but also for spotting industrial equipment failures, including work on production-line tools such as industrial screwdrivers and an NCBR-backed product direction.

The core of the presentation is five recurring business problems: whether a target is actually predictable, the difference between predicting a value versus proposing one (such as pricing), model explainability instead of black-box output, adapting models when the business environment shifts (including pandemic-era retail unpredictability), and data quality plus organizational readiness—often starting from a data sample before estimating ROI.

The closing portion walks through practitioner workflow on Microsoft Azure Machine Learning (notebooks, visual pipelines, AutoML for time series), Databricks on Azure, and Synapse-style analytics, plus open-source options and libraries such as Prophet. The speaker advocates problem-first, data-first iteration from simple linear regression and visual curve fitting toward richer transforms, using AutoML for quick benchmarks before deeper investment.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Jessica Szarek - Czy matematyka naprawdę jest (nie)potrzebna?
talks.teaser: The presentation weighs when mathematics is essential in game development and when engines and self-study suffice for programmers.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a familiar debate: teachers insist programmers cannot succeed without mathematics, yet many commercial game developers work primarily in engines like Unity without deep formal training. The speaker argues that school-level arithmetic already covers much of what simple games need, while trigonometry, vectors, matrices, statistics, and physics mathematics become important when building 3D spaces, AI opponents, custom engines, or low-level graphics.

A long middle section walks through commercial titles to show where math hides. Angry Birds illustrates trajectories and physics stacks; The Sims uses grids, needs, and event statistics; racing games lean on vehicle physics; Candy Crush relies on grid coordinates and random drops; League of Legends ties ability areas, ranges, and damage formulas to live calculations; Heroes and Command & Conquer repeat placement and resource checks. The speaker also contrasts modern abstractions—Unity helpers such as Lerp, Perlin noise, MoveTowards, Max, Mean, and Vector3.Distance—with writing the same logic from scratch in OpenGL via vertex coordinates.

The closing message is conditional rather than absolute: mathematics becomes necessary when the feature demands it, advanced topics can be learned on the job, but understanding what engines do underneath still aids debugging and growth. Viewers are pointed toward self-study resources and GDC-style material on math for games.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Joanna Zembaczyńska
talks.teaser: QA ma głos. explores 4Developers 2022: Joanna Zembaczyńska.
talks.summary:
Joanna Zembaczyńska coaches testers on surviving their dual role as team insiders and client advocates. She opens with why new QA engineers feel like fault-finders, then walks through day-one exposure: learn names, observe personalities before forcing small talk, document how you test, and state boundaries on off-hours pings.

She recommends mining knowledge silos with backward storytelling and reverse-order questions, capturing client business goals before crunch, and writing reproducible bugs with sane titles and attachments. Assertive four-eyes feedback, aligning with informal team leads, and taking distance from production disasters round out a Polish-language 4Developers talk aimed at human skills rather than tooling.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Kamil Frankowicz
talks.teaser: Shows developers how to fuzz their own code and dependencies, from writing harnesses to wiring fuzzers into CI pipelines.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the state of software security: most modern software is assembled from open-source libraries and their dependencies, which are often patched slowly, and published CVE identifiers have grown about fourfold over the past decade. Memory-corruption bugs such as buffer overflows still top the CWE rankings, and the speaker argues that memory-safe languages do not remove the problem. Coverage-guided fuzzing is presented as a scalable answer, with the speaker citing near-linear scaling as more cores are added.

The middle section is a practical introduction for developers. The speaker defines the core vocabulary: the corpus of test inputs, the dictionary of tokens that help the fuzzer pass basic checks, and the harness, a small piece of code that feeds generated data into a library function and watches for failures. Advice includes starting with a few varied seed files, minimizing corpora to strip redundant bytes, and pairing fuzzers with AddressSanitizer to catch even one-byte out-of-bounds accesses. In-memory fuzzing is contrasted with slower binary-only fuzzing, and example harnesses are shown for C, C++, .NET and Python, along with a GitLab CI integration.

The closing part places fuzzing in the development pipeline, running after build and unit tests and feeding fixes back into the loop. The speaker points to vendor and open-source services, and to the OSS-Fuzz project and its large collection of tested open-source projects. The takeaway is to start small, fuzz a dependency or a personal project early to learn the workflow, and extend fuzzing to the dependencies of dependencies, not only one's own code.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Krystian Zybała - nowe algorytmy GC w Javie
talks.teaser: Walks through Java's low-pause Shenandoah and ZGC collectors, G1 limits, and Kubernetes ergonomic defaults that swap algorithms.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how Java heap generations and classic collectors evolved from Serial GC and Parallel GC through CMS to G1 as the default since Java 9, including stop-the-world phases, region sizing, and the 512 MB humongous region change in Java 18. It highlights operational surprises when small Kubernetes pods trigger JVM ergonomic mode, which can switch collectors away from G1 unless flags force otherwise.

The core compares two low-patience, mostly non-generational designs. Shenandoah from Red Hat (not in Oracle builds) runs on Java 8+ with region-based concurrent compaction, forward-pointer evolution from 1.0 to 2.0, I-U mode, and optional concurrent marking that can shrink pauses to two in favorable cases. ZGC targets sub-10 ms pauses with ambitions toward 1 ms, runs on 64-bit Linux, uses colored pointers and load barriers, relocates with forwarding tables, and can defer or skip phases across cycles.

Practitioners should match collector choice to heap size (both are poor fits near 300 MB heaps), set Xmx for ZGC, avoid misleading microbenchmark pause metrics, and note GraalVM support for ZGC but not Shenandoah, plus upcoming Project Loom/JEP changes to concurrent processing that Shenandoah and ZGC adopted but G1 did not.

talks.summary: The speaker describes how Elixir and Erlang support reliable software through functional programming, lightweight processes, asynchronous message passing, supervision trees and code updates without stopping a server. Attendees learn how these features help isolate failures, use multiple processor cores and keep applications running during changes.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Mariusz Bełtowski - wykończ zadania, zanim one wykończą Ciebie
talks.teaser: Shows how to turn fuzzy to-do items into concrete actions, projects, and a trusted inbox workflow for busy IT leads.
talks.summary:
The presentation follows a fictional IT manager who stays busy yet reactive, drowning in a growing to-do list that mixes reading goals, hiring, reporting, and quarterly planning. The speaker names three structural flaws: entries that are not actionable, multi-step efforts that are really projects, and cognitive overload when too many open loops compete for attention.

Drawing on David Allen’s Getting Things Done and Henry Ford’s idea that a well-stated problem is half solved, the talk contrasts vague items like “recruit a DevOps engineer” with next physical actions and with project lists bounded by a clear definition of done. Research on working memory—often summarized as a limit around four items—motivates a separate inbox for quick capture without immediate sorting.

A simple processing flow decides whether each inbox note needs action, can be done in under two minutes, should be delegated, or belongs on a project list. Practitioners are urged to review the inbox regularly, note deadlines on a calendar, and use whatever note tool they already trust until the habit sticks. The closing message is to stop relying on memory and externalize commitments in a system the mind can believe in.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Mateusz Chrzonstowski non-obvious spring functions 4developers 2022 720p
talks.teaser: Delivers a map of lesser-known Spring features: modular config, JDBC access, projections, hypermedia APIs, and domain events.
talks.summary:
The presenter contrasts the usual Spring stack—JPA, Spring Data repositories, manual entity-to-DTO mapping, and annotated REST controllers—with a sample Boot application whose behavior is switched through versioned modules and configuration properties. Early modules stress package-private types, explicit bean wiring, lazy controller registration, Java records for configuration, and optional Jersey-style JAX-RS controllers so domain code stays plain Java and framework coupling stays at the edges.

Later modules add Bean Validation on records and path parameters, exception handling scoped to controllers or global advice, and Spring Data JDBC on H2 instead of a full ORM. The walkthrough covers derived query methods, native SQL, read-side projections that trim API payloads, and Spring Data REST with paging, sorting, and multiple projection views. A final segment wires repository domain events to an application event publisher, listens in a public service, and uses AOP around handlers mainly to illustrate how Spring wraps beans.

Practitioners get a map of features they may already transitively depend on—such as JDBC support pulled in by common starters—and concrete patterns for modular boundaries, read/write separation, and keeping Spring removable where that matters. The speaker notes that hypermedia repository exporters and some AOP tricks are often better for experiments or narrow read models than as default production architecture.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Marcin Baranowski - CVDD - the pitfalls of succumbing to the bling of new technologies
talks.teaser: A Java-focused speaker maps CV-driven technology choices to failed deliveries and concrete habits for skeptical adoption.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces CV Driven Development as the habit of elevating resume-building and novelty over what a product actually needs, illustrated first through a public-procurement voting-system anecdote and the risks when almost nobody on a team knows the chosen stack.

Through several backend experiences—Kotlin adoption after a lead departure, Spring Data REST with HATEOAS, Redis used as cache for huge payloads, reactive Spring WebFlux paired with a legacy database and immature drivers, over-engineered hexagonal refactoring, and gRPC where documentation said not to—the speaker shows how boilerplate moved between layers while timelines grew. Recurring lessons include training collaborators, aligning with frontend needs, measuring concurrent load rather than total user counts, reading “when not to use” guidance, and fitting tools to constraints such as Kubernetes and browser clients.

The closing argument urges skepticism toward conference hype, makes room for structured evaluation time, and cites developer-satisfaction research linking autonomy and growth to well-being. The session ends with brief audience wellbeing exercises offered as a light counterweight to long conference days.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Michał Mela
talks.teaser: Follows a Java team moving from on-premise servers to Azure Kubernetes, replacing ticket-driven deploys with Terraform.
talks.summary:
The speaker describes how a small group of Java developers took on DevOps work during a company-wide move from on-premise servers to Azure. The DevOps team had been disbanded, no dedicated infrastructure engineer was available for their product, and Microsoft consultants helped them learn the platform. The talk argues against relying on a single DevOps engineer who becomes a bottleneck, and stresses that engineers should understand the business behind their application.

The team compared virtual machines, container services, managed Kubernetes and serverless options, and settled on a managed Kubernetes cluster. Their first Terraform layout parameterized configuration across environments and used Helm for applications. It reached production but became hard to extend whenever a microservice was added. They then rebuilt it with plain Terraform, reusable modules, per-environment directories and Helmfile, keeping secrets encrypted in git before moving to HashiCorp Vault. Observability used a self-hosted monitoring stack built around the four golden signals from the SRE book.

The results included cutting time to production from one to three days down to about half an hour, and a game-day exercise that measured disaster recovery at around two hours. Infrastructure changes that once took weeks became routine, and team members could take vacations without blocking delivery. The practical takeaways are to describe infrastructure as declarative code, keep scripting out of the pipeline, run Terraform through a tool such as Atlantis in CI, and experiment while setting cost alerts.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Magda Stożek - Say goodbye to implicits - contextual abstractions in Scala 3
talks.teaser: Contrasts Scala 2 implicits with Scala 3 given, using, and extension constructs across seven everyday coding scenarios.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens with personal frustration learning implicits in Scala 2: one keyword attaches to many constructs, so working code can fail after a move because a buried import was missing, or break when an accidental implicit conversion slips in via a broad import.

Scala 3 is framed as a rewrite that splits contextual abstraction into focused constructs. Side-by-side examples cover execution context (implicit parameters versus using and given), adding methods to closed types (implicit class versus extension), type classes (implicitly versus summon), conversions (implicit def versus scala.Conversion), import syntax for givens, dropping unused implicit instance names, and compiler diagnostics that name the missing capability and sometimes suggest imports.

The close addresses migration: during early 3.x releases, older implicits and new givens can interoperate, so teams need not wait for every library. The takeaway is that code should express intent—what context or behavior is needed—not the implicit mechanism. Brief Q&A covers production readiness, library support, and finding implicit parameters in IntelliJ.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Roberto Cortez - Developer Joy with Quarkus!
talks.teaser: Shows how Quarkus cuts Java cloud memory and startup costs while preserving familiar APIs, live reload, and Kubernetes-friendly workflows.
talks.summary:
The session opens by positioning Quarkus as an open-source Java stack for cloud-native microservices and more, then argues that container and cloud billing make Java’s habitual memory and CPU use a practical problem compared with lighter runtimes. The speaker contrasts buying fixed on-prem hardware with pay-per-use cloud deployments, where wasted heap across many nodes shows up on monthly bills.

The core technical story is shifting work from runtime to build time: scanning the application during the build to pre-load configuration, shed bootstrap-only classes, and reduce reflection and dynamic proxies so startup stays fast and footprints shrink. Extensions wrap popular libraries so those optimizations apply; GraalVM native image compatibility motivates much of the design. Demos cover dev-mode live reload, continuous testing that runs only affected tests, Dev Services that spin up Postgres and Kafka via Testcontainers, Docker and Minikube deployment from Maven parameters, remote development against a cluster, Spring Web on Quarkus, and a native executable starting in tens of milliseconds.

Practitioners should leave with a concrete picture of when Quarkus pays off (multi-node cloud, serverless-style startup, edge or ARM targets), how to start via code.quarkus.io and extensions, and the workflow tradeoff of developing on the JVM while letting CI produce native images.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Zbyszko Papierski - Add search, you say? Sounds easy!
talks.teaser: Walks through application search from inverted indexes and analyzers to ranking, relevancy metrics and user session data.
talks.summary:
Zbyszko Papierski makes the case that applications should offer their own search instead of relying on outside search engines, since good search keeps users inside the product and suits a specific audience. He starts from a naive database approach using pattern matching, which is slow and misses variants such as plurals or reordered words. He then introduces the inverted index, tokenization, and analyzer chains made of character filters, tokenizers and token filters such as lowercasing, stop word removal and stemming, as used in Lucene-based engines like Elasticsearch and Solr.

The middle section covers retrieval followed by ranking with BM25, and explains precision and recall, noting that the right balance depends on the feature, such as an instant answer versus a list of related questions. Because relevance is defined by users, the speaker recommends collecting click-stream data grouped into search sessions, linking frontend and backend events with a request ID, and reviewing zero-result queries.

The loop he describes is largely manual at first: adjusting strategies offline against judged query sets, running A/B tests, then feeding the analysis back into the process. Machine learning features such as learning to rank and vector search come later and only work once data quality and measurement are reliable. He closes by arguing that search engineering suits developers who want to work across backend, data and user understanding, and points to a book, community channels and Wikipedia dumps for practice.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Anita Przybył - Soft skills for everyone, czyli o miękkich sprawach w twardym świecie
talks.teaser: Explains what soft skills are, why employers value them, and how developers can build communication and assertiveness skills.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a trainer who works mainly with IT leaders and managers, opens by asking whether technical skill alone is enough at work. She explains how psychology defines social competence as learned abilities that make people effective in social situations, and she lists the common, often mocked, views of soft skills. The audience is invited to self-check areas such as self-presentation, handling conflict, active listening and assertiveness.

She then reviews workplace research. A study of 3000 business leaders expected demand for social skills such as empathy and communication to rise by 22% by 2030. A 2019 survey of 5,000 talent specialists in 35 countries found that 92% saw soft skills as equally important as hard ones. A Polish study of 271 programmers linked the group's traits to openness to experience and conscientiousness, and found no more introversion than in the general population. She also covers upbringing and temperament: a democratic parenting style and lower neuroticism were associated with stronger social competence.

For practice, she recommends choosing one small, specific skill, such as active listening, and training it through workshops with expert feedback. She suggests observing colleagues who handle social situations well and asking peers for advice rather than generic feedback. Personality tests can be taken through a psychologist, and introverts can still learn these skills, though it costs them more effort.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Dominik Przybysz - Release the locusts - distributed performance tests
talks.teaser: Engineers learn how massive HTTP load tests combine Locust masters, Java workers, custom load shapes, and Grafana metrics on bare metal.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by defining performance testing as a way to judge responsiveness, stability, reliability, and resource use under heavy HTTP workloads. The speaker’s organization needed distributed traffic approaching seven hundred gigabits per second, multi-step user sessions, stateful clients, custom DNS, and fine-grained control over headers and redirects—requirements that ruled out a single machine.

Locust became the core framework because it is distributed by design and scenario-centric. The described architecture pairs a Python master with workers over ZeroMQ, later swapping default Python workers for Java via locust4j. Headless runs use custom load-shape classes for warm-up and staged ramps. Observability layers on InfluxDB, Telegraf, Jolokia JVM probes, and Grafana; Ansible inventories deploy masters, multiple worker instances per host, and environment locks before tests start. Scaling rules tie worker counts to NIC throughput or CPU when HTTPS is expensive.

Operational lessons include watching for a missing client-ready handshake with large worker pools, accepting Locust’s response-time buckets for sub-second APIs, routing locust4j failures through success records with error suffixes to avoid slow failure reporting, randomizing blended tasks because locust4j starts task groups sequentially, tuning JVM and GC for stop-the-world pauses, and delaying upgrades after patch-zero releases. The close emphasizes Locust as a programmer’s framework that still demands surrounding automation for metrics and fleet management.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Andrzej Dębski - How to avoid common mistakes and misconceptions when working with Java...
talks.teaser: The session covers JVM Lambda cold starts, cost modeling against Fargate, and pitfalls of in-process caching in short-lived instances.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing AWS Lambda as a choice that brings JVM-specific latency and cost trade-offs rather than a drop-in substitute for long-lived application servers. The speaker distinguishes cold start type one (initialization, constructors, and static blocks) from type two (JIT compilation and lazy class loading), illustrates both with timed Hello World and multi-branch handlers, and ties tail latency spikes in production to recycled containers hitting unfamiliar code paths.

The middle section walks through mitigations: provisioned concurrency on aliases, spillover and utilization metrics, constructor pre-warming with caveats for on-demand instances, CodeDeploy traffic shifting, background keep-warm traffic, and alternatives such as Go or GraalVM. Cost estimation uses gigabyte-seconds, invocations, the free tier, and the AWS Pricing Calculator, comparing on-demand and provisioned Lambda against Fargate for steady traffic, small workloads, and a simplified Stack Overflow–scale scenario where Fargate becomes far cheaper at high request rates.

The closing segment explains why Guava or Caffeine in-memory caches often underperform when instances recycle roughly every fifteen to twenty minutes, when the runtime freezes between invocations, and when client libraries assume background threads. Practitioners are advised to favor external caches such as Redis, consider Fargate when cache locality matters, or explore Lambda extensions, while monitoring latency and running numbers before committing JVM services to Lambda for latency-sensitive or high-volume request-reply paths.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Oguzhan Onkal - Rule Evaluations: From Nashorn to GraalVM
talks.teaser: Maps how enterprise rule engines run JavaScript on Nashorn and move those evaluations to GraalVM when upgrading past Java 11.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why a structured-products engineering group needs deterministic rule evaluation to map securitization data onto stock exchanges, clearing houses, and other partners. It contrasts ETL pipelines, hard-coded Java, Spring EL, Apache Commons JEXL, Drools, and an embedded JavaScript engine, noting that no option is universally best.

Most of the talk walks through Nashorn as Java 8’s built-in engine: JJSE on the command line, javax.script’s ScriptEngineManager, eval from strings or files, Invocable for calling JS functions, bindings that inject Java values, and brief mention of calling Java types from script. It then introduces GraalVM and Graal.js—polyglot VM layers, Maven SDK dependencies, the Context API for arrays, functions, and objects, JSON-driven rules over nested product fields, and a legacy ScriptEngine path that mirrors Nashorn for easier porting. A small UI demo defines location and discount rules evaluated against sample product JSON.

Closing advice targets teams still on Nashorn before Java 15 removes it: swap jjs for js in the JDK tools, add GraalJS as a dependency when a full JDK swap is impossible, expect weaker performance without the standalone VM compiler, confirm some GraalJS builds still bundle Nashorn, and use Context.Builder host-access settings if Java interoperability breaks. Pointers to Oracle and Graal migration documentation round out the material.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Krystian Zybała - The newest GC's algorithms
talks.teaser: Surveys modern Java garbage collectors G1, Shenandoah, and ZGC, including pause tradeoffs, barriers, and tuning tips.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing garbage collection as heap cleanup driven by the generational hypothesis, then walks through Serial, Parallel, and G1 as the familiar baseline, including regions, pause targets, Kubernetes ergonomic fallback to Serial GC, and Java 18’s larger G1 regions for humongous objects.

The core compares low-pause collectors. Shenandoah’s concurrent single-generation compaction, forward pointers, load barriers, 1.0 versus 2.0 invariants, and Red Hat tuning flags are contrasted with ZGC’s colored pointers, multi-mapping, Z pages, sub-millisecond pauses, Linux focus, and generational experiments planned for Java 22. Both are related to concurrent marking, evacuation races between application and GC threads, and why concurrent phase time matters when pause metrics look idle.

The close offers practical choice guidance: Shenandoah on supported OpenJDK builds, ZGC when pause bounds and heap scale matter, G1 still viable with recent performance fixes, and Project Loom stack processing tying collectors together. Extra CPU and memory are the price of very low pauses.

talks.teaser: Walks through a city bus servicing system to show how one model can split into several context-specific models.
talks.summary: Łukasz Panek uses shadows, spreadsheet rows, and Romeo lines to argue engineers must establish context before interpreting requirements—what row means in Excel versus theater seating changes every downstream decision.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Marcin Chrost - IntelliJ debugger tips & tricks
talks.teaser: Shows IntelliJ debugger features like conditional, non-suspending and exception breakpoints, plus altering execution at runtime.
talks.summary:
This session is a practical tour of debugging features in IntelliJ, demonstrated on a small console application that stores and searches posts. It opens with a common mistake: starting the program with the normal run button rather than debug mode, which leaves little to inspect. The presenter also argues that a debugger helps when learning inherited code, before writing integration tests and refactoring.

Conditional breakpoints come first. One fires only when a menu action equals the exit option, which exposed a typo in an enum that made a terminal check return false. Non-suspending breakpoints with evaluate-and-log let a sample post be added to the in-memory service without stopping or editing code, and let search results be logged from inside a stream lambda. Exception breakpoints catch a title-length error that a catch-all handler in the run method had been swallowing silently.

Runtime changes come last. A method argument can be edited during a session, though a final field cannot. Force Return from a call stack frame supplies a replacement value, and throwing an exception from a breakpoint skips a method. Side effects already performed, such as a post saved before an exception, are not rolled back. The main takeaway is that these features reduce the need for temporary logging and code changes while investigating a problem.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Philipp Krenn- Learnings from Log4Shell
talks.teaser: Explains Log4j lookup abuse, shaky patches, Elastic-style mitigations, and how honeypots still catch Log4Shell probes.
talks.summary:
The session revisits Log4Shell as a critical remote code execution flaw in Log4j 2 (and related JNDI behavior), sparked widespread disruption around December and often triggered simply by logging attacker-controlled strings such as HTTP headers. It walks through how lookup plugins combine with JNDI LDAP/RMI resolution so a malicious payload can run inside the application, why follow-on Log4j releases still left exploitable paths, and why dependency scanners frequently missed real mitigations like stripping the JNDI lookup class or disabling message lookups.

From an operator’s side at Elastic, the speaker maps Elasticsearch versions against bundled Log4j and JDK combinations, noting where the Java Security Manager blocked logger network fetches, where older stacks remained exposed, and practical fixes including format-message no-lookups flags, build-time removal of JNDI classes, and cautions against disabling logging or swapping whole JARs. A Spring Boot demo shows header-based exploitation with an attacker LDAP server; the talk stresses that exploits stay application-specific rather than worm-like.

Closing themes cover ongoing risk: honeypots logged roughly 1,500 attempts across several regions, targeted actors still hunt for Log4j, and detection should watch uncommon child processes, JNDI lookups in stack traces, suspicious outbound connections, and vulnerable Log4j JARs via tools such as OSQuery. The takeaway is that obscure logging features create outsized blast radius, patching alone is messy, and layered JVM hardening plus vigilant monitoring remain necessary long after the headlines.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Maciej Przepióra - Java memory model for mere mortals
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for JDD 2022: Maciej Przepióra - Java memory model for mere mortals.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from JDD 2022, Maciej Przepióra explores the Java Memory Model (JMM) and how ModernHardware and runtime optimizations affect concurrent execution. While Java developers are generally shielded from low-level execution details by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) and the standard library, understanding memory visibility and instruction reordering is crucial when building concurrent libraries or optimizing high-performance applications.

### Key Topics
- **Instruction Reordering:** Compilers, Just-In-Time (JIT) compilers, and CPU pipelines reorder execution steps and memory writes to optimize speed, bounded by the "as-if-serial" semantics in single-threaded environments.
- **Cache Coherence Protocols:** Multi-core hardware employs snooping on the bus and protocols such as MESI (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) to coordinate state between processor caches and main memory.
- **Limitations of `volatile`:** While `volatile` ensures immediate visibility across threads by preventing cached CPU register values from remaining stale, it does not solve race conditions requiring atomic compound operations like compare-and-swap (CAS).
- **The Java Memory Model & Happens-Before:** Introduced in its modern form in Java 5, the JMM establishes a partial ordering relation (`happens-before`) across program actions to define formal visibility and ordering guarantees.

### Technical Details
Przepióra walks through a classic concurrent example featuring four shared variables (`x`, `y`, `a`, `b`) across two threads to illustrate how instruction reordering and stale memory reads can yield surprising outcomes, including scenarios where both variables evaluate to `0`. Under single-threaded constraints, the JVM guarantees "as-if-serial" semantics, ensuring optimizations do not alter program outcomes. However, in concurrent environments lacking synchronization, compilers and processors can freely reorder independent assignments.

At the hardware layer, processors enforce cache coherence using protocols such as MESI (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) or proprietary vendor adaptations by Intel and AMD. Even with coherent caches, processor registers and memory write buffers can still obscure updates across cores. Rather than requiring developers to manually insert platform-specific memory barriers or memory fences (as in C/C++), the JVM automatically places these instructions based on standard synchronization primitives.

The talk defines specific `happens-before` rules governing thread visibility:
- **Program Order Rule:** Each action within a single thread happens before subsequent actions in that thread.
- **Monitor Lock Rule:** An unlock operation on a monitor happens before every subsequent lock on that same monitor (applying to both implicit monitors and `java.util.concurrent` locks).
- **Volatile Variable Rule:** A write to a volatile field happens before subsequent reads of that same field (with atomic variables sharing volatile semantics).
- **Thread Management Rules:** A call to `Thread.start()` happens before any action in the started thread, and all actions in a thread happen before another thread detects its termination.
- **Interruption and Finalizer Rules:** An interrupt call happens before the target thread detects it, and object constructor completion happens before its `finalize()` method execution starts.
- **Transitivity:** If action *A* happens before *B*, and *B* happens before *C*, then *A* happens before *C*.

### Takeaways
While the underlying mechanics of memory barriers, cache lines, and MESI states are complex, standard Java developers rarely need to manually construct complex low-level synchronization. The JDK provides battle-tested abstractions—such as thread-safe collections and utilities in `java.util.concurrent`—that natively supply transitive happens-before guarantees. Przepióra recommends Brian Goetz's *Java Concurrency in Practice* for mastering concurrency principles, emphasizing that the core memory model fundamentals established in Java 5 remain the foundation of Java concurrency today.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Nicolas Frankel - Chopping the monolith
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning JDD 2022: Nicolas Frankel - Chopping the monolith.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at JDD 2022, Nicolas Frankel challenges the prevailing industry consensus that microservices are universally superior to monolithic architectures. Drawing from his 17 years of experience across software engineering, architecture, and developer advocacy, Frankel argues that organizations often adopt microservices for the wrong reasons—such as resume building or misguided organizational fixes—without understanding the real problems they are trying to solve. Instead of completely decomposing an application into microservices or following a full migration path like the strangler pattern toward a pure microservices end state, he advocates for an alternative pragmatic architecture: keeping the monolith intact and selectively "chopping" out only the specific components that change frequently.

### Key Topics
- **Microservices Definitions and Conway's Law:** Frankel references Martin Fowler's definitions, emphasizing that true microservices require organizing around products rather than short-lived projects with end dates. He also highlights Conway's law and the "reverse Conway's law" (such as AWS's two-pizza teams), noting that layered teams cannot simply adopt microservices purely through technical edicts.
- **Evaluating Microservice Benefits:**
  - *Strong Module Boundaries:* Can be achieved without microservices via Java modules or static analysis rules (e.g., Sonar).
  - *Technology Diversity:* While polyglot databases make sense due to specialized storage needs, having multiple programming languages across services often satisfies developer ego rather than business needs and leaves a maintenance mess.
  - *Independent Deployment and Lead Time:* Accelerating implementation and deployment lead time has historically been approached via release trains, rule engines, or microservices, but each comes with its own trade-offs and organizational bottlenecks.
- **Identifying Variable vs. Stable Components:** Within any software application, certain parts remain stable (e.g., product catalog or delivery integrations), while others change frequently or arbitrarily due to business promotions, marketing rules, or legal shifts (e.g., pricing engines in e-commerce).
- **The "Chopping the Monolith" Architecture:** Rather than breaking everything apart, teams can place an API gateway in front of the monolith and route only the fast-changing endpoint to an isolated service or serverless function.

### Technical Details
Frankel demonstrates this architectural approach using a live coding example of an e-commerce store:
- **Monolith Implementation:** The original sample application ("ChopShop") is written in Kotlin using Spring Boot, containerized via Docker Compose, backed by an SQL database, and fronted by the Apache APISIX API Gateway (which stores its configuration in etcd).
- **Isolating the Pricing Endpoint:** In the initial monolithic state, the application handles catalog browsing, cart operations, and pricing calculation within a single integrated request flow. To chop the component, Frankel first refactors the web layer so that the cart and pricing operations are decoupled into two distinct HTTP routes (version 1.3).
- **Offloading via API Gateway to Serverless:** Using Apache APISIX route configuration, requests directed to the pricing route (`/pricing`) are redirected away from the Spring Boot monolith to an independent Azure Function written in JavaScript. Frankel demonstrates that this allows pricing calculation logic to be modified and deployed independently on serverless infrastructure on the fly without redeploying the core monolith.

### Takeaways
- Teams should understand their application over time before making major architectural decisions; jumping straight into microservices means not knowing which parts are actually stable and which truly need rapid iteration.
- Microservices introduce significant operational complexity; isolating only the few fast-changing, volatile components provides the agility of independent deployment without the burden of maintaining an entirely distributed system.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Andrés Torres Garcia - Friends don't let friends test with In-Memory databases
talks.teaser: Shows how Testcontainers runs real databases in Docker during Java builds, catching issues in-memory H2 tests miss.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how teams test database code in Java services, and why in-memory H2 databases can hide problems that only show up in real environments. The speaker describes a team that had to support several database products, including Oracle, SQL Server and MySQL, and found that tests passing on H2 still failed once deployed. Shared databases and per-developer instances were slow or costly, so the goal was to move database testing earlier, onto developers' machines and into the build.

The solution presented is Testcontainers, a library that starts a real database in a Docker container for the duration of a test and removes it afterwards. In a demo, a Spring Boot test that passed on H2 was shown to break against MySQL 8, because a table named groups conflicts with a reserved word in the newer version. The speaker explained how to switch only the JDBC URL in a simple setup, and covered container lifecycles, the Quarkus dev services that start a database automatically, and running a Spring application against a containerised database. Another team used the same approach to generate database documentation with SchemaSpy on every build.

The closing part described a cloud-hosted execution option that runs containers remotely, useful when laptops cannot run Docker. The main takeaway is that database compatibility checks can run early and automatically as part of normal development, rather than waiting for shared test environments.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Patryk Piechaczek - The Magic of Spring - how does it really work?
talks.teaser: Builds a mini dependency injection framework to show how Spring proxies, transactions and caching work under the hood.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a small plain Java service that saves a company record, with transaction begin, commit and rollback code written by hand. Repeating that pattern across methods leads the presenter to move the logic into a proxy. The session compares JDK dynamic proxies, which need an interface and cannot intercept final methods, with CGLIB, which subclasses the class instead. The presenter notes that classic Spring defaults to JDK proxies, while Spring Boot from version 2 uses CGLIB by default.

Next the presenter builds a simple application context. Classes marked with a custom component annotation are found by scanning the package with reflections, and each bean is created by picking the single implementation of a requested interface. Constructor injection resolves dependencies recursively. A custom transactional annotation is then added: the proxy checks for it on the implementation class, opens a transaction, and commits or rolls back. A similar cache annotation stores results in a map keyed by method and arguments. Scope handling is added as well, with singletons kept in a map and prototypes created on each request.

The most useful case shown is self-invocation. When one annotated method calls another method on the same bean, the call bypasses the proxy, so no new transaction starts. This explains why annotations sometimes seem to be ignored. The presenter stresses that the mini framework leaves out propagation, qualifiers and many other features, so it is a simplified model. Still, it shows that the same proxy mechanism sits behind Spring's annotation behaviour, and the example code is linked in a repository for step-by-step review.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Karolina Strzelczyk
talks.teaser: Shows how IT workers can use job crafting to raise satisfaction without always chasing a new employer.
talks.summary:
Careers in technology can consume on the order of forty thousand working hours, yet many people experience those hours as something to survive until the weekend. The speaker, an organizational psychologist with long experience in IT corporations and startups, argues that treating work as one layer of life—not something parked until “real life” begins—matters for mental health and engagement. She cites low European engagement figures, burnout among developers, and the limits of benefits: perks may attract candidates but rarely sustain motivation compared with meaning, influence, and purpose.

Instead of assuming that changing companies fixes dissatisfaction, the talk centers on job crafting: small, responsible changes to tasks, thinking, and relationships at work. Four familiar IT patterns illustrate the point—leaving only for higher pay while work still feels pointless, complaining about legacy stacks without personal initiative, expecting promotion after a short tenure, or treating a bootcamp as a guaranteed fast track. Crafting at the task level might mean creating onboarding material, negotiating focus time, or choosing mentoring; at the cognitive level, clarifying values before interview marathons; relationally, peer support for managers, mentorship after code review, or social initiatives colleagues initiate themselves.

Amy Wrzesniewski’s orientations toward work as paycheck, career ladder, or calling frame why people craft differently. Crafting increases agency and satisfaction when firms allow autonomy, accept mistakes, and avoid micromanagement, while individuals keep responsibility within their real sphere of influence. Leaders can nurture this through inspiration exchanges, open Q&A, clear expectations, and constructive feedback—including learning from failed projects. The hospital janitor research reminds listeners that the same job description can feel empty or meaningful depending on how it is reframed, and the session closes with reflection on what matters in one’s current role rather than deferring satisfaction.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Nacho Cougil - TDD: seriously, try it!
talks.teaser: The session explains test-driven habits and demos a Java feature built with unit mocks and a Postgres integration test.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by noting how few attendees routinely use test-driven development, then frames the practice through Kent Beck’s origins with xUnit and extreme programming, the classic Chicago versus London approaches, and the familiar red–green–refactor loop. The speaker argues that tests written first guide design, catch regressions early, and act as living documentation, while acknowledging a steep learning curve, team resistance, and the mistake of chasing coverage instead of behavior.

The middle section covers practical habits: start on small personal exercises, pair with a driver and navigator, read recommended books, always see a new test fail before implementing code, keep each test focused on one failure reason, use behavior-oriented names ending in “Should,” and write assertions before scaffolding setup. Pair programming is presented as simultaneous coding and review.

The closing live demo builds a film recommendation service in Java with Gradle, JUnit, AssertJ, and Mockito. A unit test drives a service that depends on a mocked repository returning genre-filtered films ordered by average rating. A separate integration test uses Testcontainers with PostgreSQL, SQL seed data, and JDBC mapping; when the repository implementation completes, both tests pass and most new code sits under test. The recap urges teams to practice persistently despite the upfront cost.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Haim Yadid - “Show Me the Garbage!”, Understanding Garbage Collection
talks.teaser: Explains JVM garbage collection basics, OpenJDK collector choices, and practical production monitoring for mainstream web services.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing garbage collection as a topic many developers avoid, then narrows scope to mainstream web and microservice workloads where occasional stop-the-world pauses of hundreds of milliseconds are often acceptable, rather than high-frequency trading or zero-allocation tuning.

The middle walks through heap terminology, tracing collectors, and core algorithms such as root scanning, marking, sweeping, compaction, and copying, along with generational design. It surveys OpenJDK 17 options including Serial, Parallel, G1, ZGC, Shenandoah, and Azul C4, emphasizing tradeoffs among throughput, concurrency, memory overhead, and pause behavior.

The close shifts to operations: three KPIs (time or CPU overhead, memory overhead, and pause latency), enabling and reading GC logs, tools such as GCViewer and GCEasy, JMX and jHiccup-style pause detection, and diagnosing overhead, latency sensitivity, allocation rate, and G1 humongous-object fragmentation. The speaker urges teams to record heap size, GC overhead, max pauses, live set, and allocation rate for each production service.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Grzegorz Piwowarek - CompletableFuture and its Quirks
talks.teaser: Walks through surprising CompletableFuture behaviours in Java, from cancellation and thread pools to exception handling.
talks.summary:
The talk examines Java's CompletableFuture, a way to receive results from asynchronous work and chain follow-up steps. The presenter argues that its behaviour often surprises experienced developers, so the session skips the basics and focuses on less obvious details. It starts from classic futures, whose get call blocks and whose API offers little beyond waiting, cancelling and polling.

Several pitfalls follow. Cancelling a CompletableFuture does not interrupt the thread running the work, since one future may not map to a single thread, so cancellation must be handled manually. The allOf combinator returns void and keeps waiting while another input has failed, so a short-circuiting version needs an extra future completed by the first exception. Futures without an explicit executor fall back to the shared common pool, which blocking calls can starve; on a machine reporting one processor, the library creates a new thread per task instead. Callbacks such as thenApply may run on the thread that completes the future, blocking the caller, while Async variants still default to the common pool. Finally, applyToEither can propagate an exception even when the other future already produced a valid value.

The takeaways are to pass a dedicated executor for any blocking work, to avoid assuming cancellation reaches running threads, and to test combinators against early failures and edge cases before relying on them. Where library behaviour does not match expectations, small custom helpers are often needed.

talks.title: JDD 2022: Bartosz De Boulangé - Integrate Hibernate with your Elasticsearch database
talks.teaser: Shows how Hibernate Search syncs JPA entities with an Elasticsearch index and runs full-text queries on them.
talks.summary:
The session introduces Hibernate Search, a way to add full-text search to a Java application that already maps its data with Hibernate. It pairs the relational database with a search index, using Apache Lucene on a single node or Elasticsearch across a cluster. Text analysis such as tokenizing and normalizing shapes what gets indexed, and Hibernate keeps the index updated as entities change. The speaker warns that Elasticsearch updates arrive with a short delay and that the two stores can drift apart, with an outbox-style polling strategy still in development.

The setup has five steps: add dependencies, annotate the entities to index, annotate fields as full-text, generic, indexed-embedded or geo-point, and write code for initial indexing at startup. Supported queries include exact, fuzzy, range, wildcard, regex and phrase searches, sorting by relevance score or by field values, and distance sorting based on coordinates. Projections can return index results without querying SQL. Rebuilding the index from scratch is possible but may take minutes or hours for a large database.

The demo used MySQL, Elasticsearch and Kibana in Docker, with books, authors and reviews. A single full-text query matched book descriptions and review text, sorted results by title and returned up to 20 books as database entities. The main takeaway is that changes made through the ORM keep both stores in step, while failures outside a transaction can leave them out of sync.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Mariusz Walczak - Sztuka budowania zespołów - radar mentalności
talks.teaser: A framework maps actor, initiative, discipline, and thinker profiles so project teams hit the right delivery tempo.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the 1939 defense of Westerplatte as an analogy: a small force held out because people were chosen for temperament and role fit, not only résumé strength. From that story the speaker introduces a “mentality radar” inspired by an ethogram—a map of behavior types along four axes: actors who start work immediately, initiative seekers who hunt problems, discipline-oriented people who wait for defined tasks, and thinkers who delay coding until options are weighed.

Different products need different balances on that radar. A short-lived branded contest skews toward actors and light thinking; a long-running e-commerce build sits nearer discipline and thinkers. The speaker maps real colleagues on a current shop project—backend as extreme thinker, himself as actor with initiative, others as discipline or neutral—and shows how opposing styles produce substantive debate yet align the team’s composite point with the project’s target. Short “sprint” pushes remain possible when a flag goes up, at some quality cost; one such push correlated with a week-long regression on their app.

Practical takeaways include staffing all four quadrants, avoiding homogenous teams that repeat the same mistakes, using structured argument (each person defends one option and attacks the rest), and pairing seniors with juniors rather than stacking seniors who enforce one way of working. The Westerplatte close ties the metaphor back to deliberate composition over heroics alone.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Marcin Hankiewicz - Supply chain blunder i ficzery niespodzianki
talks.teaser: Surveys supply chain incidents caused by lone maintainers, sabotage and sloppy releases, and what teams can do about them.
talks.summary:
The talk covers software supply chain failures caused by a single maintainer or a very small group, where the cause is a blunder or a deliberate act rather than a typical criminal attack. The speaker argues that modern projects depend heavily on code written by others, and that many widely used packages, especially in the JavaScript ecosystem, are kept alive by one or two people with little capacity for review.

The incidents range from a USB controller vendor whose certified Windows driver reset the product IDs of counterfeit chips, making those devices unusable, to a developer who broke two of his own popular packages out of frustration with open source. A protest-motivated change to a communication library targeted machines with Russian or Belarusian IP addresses by overwriting files. In another case, a developer unpublished packages after a dispute over a package name, and the registry restored them. Later, a popular package taken over by attackers carried a Monero miner and a password-stealing trojan on Windows until npm blocked it after about four hours, affecting tens of thousands of machines.

The speaker's takeaways are practical: know which packages your projects depend on, check how many people maintain them and how they handle releases, and watch for signals such as unsigned commits or missing two-factor authentication. He suggested holding new versions for review before use, along with software composition analysis, SBOMs and tools such as Dependabot. He expects such incidents to continue, since the long tail of rarely checked packages is largely unseen, and he sees today's tooling for the problem as still early.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Marcin Kuśmierz - Jak powinno wyglądać dobre User Story
talks.teaser: A shared user-story structure bridges empty tickets and oversized docs so teams can implement features with less guesswork.
talks.summary:
Marcin Kuśmierz opens by contrasting two familiar delivery failures: requirements buried in huge documents, or a bare title with no actionable detail. Both extremes slow implementation because teams must hunt for meaning or hold extra meetings before coding can start.

He presents a Jira-ready template developed at TSH and refined across many projects. On a shopping-cart quantity change, he walks through preconditions, post conditions, constraints such as min/max counts and select-based input, main and alternate flows written in plain language with when/then-style steps, and the need for every role to read the same story the same way. A second InPost shipping example highlights data-input tables that specify field types, API-backed sources, validation links, plus a messages table for success, error, and user-facing copy.

He stresses that the layout is not fixed: teams should add, remove, and tune sections, gather answers with short questions, and keep enough detail to act without overload. Practitioners should treat the template as a starting point and adapt it to product context rather than copying it blindly.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Marcin Baranowski
talks.teaser: Explores contract testing for microservices through automotive supply-chain analogies and hands-on Pact workflows.
talks.summary:
Teams building microservices typically lean on fast unit tests and heavier integration tests, but integration suites often pass on a developer machine and fail in continuous integration because of mismatched configuration, scarce resources, or slow, timing-sensitive setups. The talk opens with that pain and reframes it using automotive manufacturing: a finished car depends on tens of thousands of parts from long chains of suppliers, and the industry relies on detailed contractual specifications so independently produced pieces still fit together.

The middle section maps that idea to consumer and provider services communicating over HTTP and JSON. It introduces contract testing styles, focuses on Pact as a multi-language, broker-backed approach supporting REST, messaging, GraphQL, and related patterns, and walks through a dogs-themed demo. The consumer writes unit-style tests that declare expected interactions, emits JSON contracts, and publishes them; the Spring Boot provider verifies against matching provider states and broker-stored contracts without needing the full peer stack running on every laptop.

The closing material places contract tests between unit and integration layers in the test pyramid, outlines a pipeline where can-i-deploy guards releases, and notes trade-offs such as broker infrastructure, product choices between open broker tooling and paid flow features, and the risk that contract tests add little value without deployment checks. It stresses that consumer and provider teams must agree on expectations, not only automate them.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Łukasz Ćmielowski - Czy sztuczna inteligencja jest "fair" ?
talks.teaser: Shows how to measure ML fairness with disparate impact, use the 80% rule, and apply open-source debiasing on trained models.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why bias in machine learning matters for production systems: human prejudice can be baked into training data and amplified at scale. Examples cited include commercial face recognition with far higher error rates for Black women than for white men, skewed demographic composition in training sets, and the well-known Google Photos mislabeling incident, along with growing legal expectations for fairness documentation in hiring and lending.

The core of the session defines what practitioners need to measure fairness: a sensitive attribute, monitored and reference groups, and favorable versus unfavorable outcomes. The speaker walks through disparate impact as a simple ratio of favorable outcome rates, the common 80% rule for calling a model unfair, and additional metrics available from open-source Python libraries, using loan-approval style scenarios. Configuration resembles standard model evaluation, including support for classification and regression.

When metrics fail, the talk surveys mitigation paths without always retraining from scratch: IBM Research packages for metrics and in-processing or post-processing fixes, model-refiner workflows, and runtime monitoring that compares counterfactual predictions (for example swapping gender on otherwise identical records). A German Credit demo illustrates improving disparate impact from 48% to 77% while accepting some accuracy loss. The closing message is that fairness can be instrumented before deployment using accessible open tooling.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Paweł Kierat - Multithreading for human beings
talks.teaser: A Java trainer uses a board game and Petri nets to make multithreading, race conditions, and deadlocks approachable for junior developers.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why multithreading often disappoints in real projects: freezes, crashes, and uncontrolled data changes, especially for developers with only a year or two of Java experience. Dense textbook wording makes the topic worse, so the speaker built a portal-and-pawn board game played for two weeks before anyone hears the word multithreading.

After unpacking game rules—shared platforms, dice-driven turns, activation conditions, and blocking moves—the talk reconnects them to Java’s non-atomic increment, race conditions, synchronization via critical sections, deadlock, and livelock. The game mechanics map directly to Petri nets: places, transitions, tokens, and arcs. That formalism is positioned as a simpler shared language for concurrent systems than BPMN or UML activity diagrams, with mathematical checks for deadlocks, reachability, and livelock, plus open-source simulation tools. Extensions such as colored, timed, and prioritized nets appear, along with roundabout traffic exercises and Java synchronizers modeled visually.

Practitioners teaching concurrency gain a playbook: delay jargon, use play and visuals first, then layer formal models and tooling. Trainees reportedly retained failure patterns from gameplay and found Petri-net thinking easier before diving into heavy mathematical notation.

talks.teaser: OOP revisited details 4Developers 2022: Dominik Przybysz.
talks.summary:
Dominik Przybysz revisits object-oriented programming basics for 4Developers 2022, arguing teams confuse JavaBean getters and setters with true encapsulation. He walks through why returning mutable collections or guessable fields leaks state, how information-expert and tell-don’t-ask rules reshape task APIs, and when dependency inversion and hexagonal ports keep domains isolated from databases and message queues.

The talk connects GRASP patterns such as Creator and Pure Fabrication with SOLID’s Liskov and interface segregation lessons, warns that `sealed` hierarchies can create switch-expression leaks, and advocates composition-backed interfaces over deep inheritance trees. Close takeaways urge designers to hide detail, expose minimal collaboration surfaces, know when to break a rule deliberately, and model classes rather than typing boilerplate.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Dawid Stronczak
talks.teaser: Explores why low-friction collaboration matters and offers three self-check questions for daily engineering work.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens with a workplace memory of a heated code-review dispute over tabs versus spaces, using it as an example of unnecessary high friction: tension, slow progress, and unproductive heat. He contrasts healthy friction—constructive challenge and reasonable disagreement—with excessive friction that slows decisions, fuels emotional arguments, and makes colleagues hard to work with.

He frames daily collaboration through a physics-inspired metaphor, then introduces three questions he uses to audit his own behavior. First, whether he genuinely considers others’ perspectives, knowledge, and intentions before reacting when he disagrees. Second, whether he optimizes for the broader system—team and company—rather than narrow local convenience when pushing a preferred solution. Third, whether a disagreement is worth prolonged conflict or whether it is better to decide, commit, and move on, as with minor style debates.

The closing message is that engineering managers and individual contributors can deliberately choose lower friction by practicing empathy, systems thinking, and selective restraint, so cooperation stays productive without smothering useful debate.

talks.title: CONFidence 2022: DRAKVUF Sandbox: Open source, self-hosted malware..
talks.teaser: Shows how a hypervisor-level sandbox observes and unpacks malware from outside the guest VM, without installing agents.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces DRAKVUF Sandbox, an open-source, self-hosted environment for malware analysis that runs samples in a Windows 7 virtual machine while monitoring them from the hypervisor. The guest stays unmodified and has no agent. The speakers explain why packed samples are hard to study: many packers wrap a small number of malware families, so the goal is to capture the unpacked core through memory dumps taken at the right moment. They also show how in-guest monitoring can be evaded, for example by malware that restores patched code or repeats pointless registry operations until the analysis environment fails.

The middle of the talk covers the techniques behind the approach. Virtual machine introspection rebuilds the guest's process list from raw memory, and breakpoints are placed on system calls in the hypervisor. Page faults are injected to force lazily loaded DLLs into memory so their exports can be hooked, and the call stack is rebuilt by scanning the last few hundred bytes of the stack. User-mode hooks are demonstrated with a host-side interception of a random-number library call, and TLS master keys can be extracted for decryption in Wireshark. Intel Processor Trace is presented as work in progress for recovering dynamically resolved API calls.

The output is structured data, including dumps and metadata in JSON form, that can feed later analysis and automation. The speakers stress that the sandbox does not decide whether something is malicious; it supplies behavioural evidence to analysts. In the Q&A they note that the core is written in C and C++, Python scripting is still limited, and configuration extraction tools can be run alongside it in a Docker-based setup.

talks.title: CONFidence 2022: Jak nie realizować audytów i jak nie reagować na incydenty
talks.teaser: Shows common mistakes made during security audits and incident response that turn small problems into major failures.
talks.summary:
Maciej Jan Broniarz explains how organisations often turn small security problems into serious incidents through their own decisions, not only through technical weaknesses. Drawing on years of incident handling across many industries, he describes clients who skip reporting a data leak, appoint an incident team that never meets, or route around the data protection officer. Staff keeping access tokens on desks and using personal cloud storage to avoid VPN friction also feature.

The middle of the talk walks through concrete cases. A Git directory left behind after a server migration exposed a database with personal records of almost 20,000 people for three or four years. A former administrator kept reaching the company network through a Wi-Fi network bridged to the internal LAN, which the dismissal procedure had not considered. An IPv4 firewall held over a thousand rules while the IPv6 side had three rules that accepted everything. During an audit, staff were found switching off ports to hide systems from scans, and the auditors turned them back on.

He closes with the point that written procedures and checklists mean little unless they are tested and reviewed regularly. Under pressure, a short pause and a question about dependencies often beats rushed shutdowns, since bringing a large server room back up can take two days. Empathy for business, legal and PR colleagues helps incident work, and concealing facts during an audit rarely helps the client.

talks.title: CONFidence 2022: CAR-Hacking 2.0 Protocols and Connectors of Modern Cars
talks.teaser: Surveys in-car buses and connectors, from CAN and LIN to FlexRay and OBD-II, and where attackers can reach them.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through how the networks inside modern cars fit together, starting from the older buses and moving toward software-defined vehicles. The speaker explains that CAN, introduced in 1986 for communication between the engine and transmission, remains the backbone of most cars, and that its two-wire design keeps working even when one wire fails. LIN, a simpler single-wire bus, handles low-speed jobs such as door locks, windows, seats and mirrors.

FlexRay is presented as a fiber-optic option used mainly by some European premium brands, offering higher bandwidth for safety and suspension systems, while Ethernet is described as the likely future for data-heavy features like cameras and infotainment. The speaker then covers the diagnostic port: OBD-II, required in the EU for petrol cars from 2001, sits within reach of the steering wheel and links directly to CAN, and on some electric cars it can be exposed by removing a cover. Event data recorders and an emergency-call SIM are also mentioned as features that new cars carry.

The attack discussion focuses on injecting traffic. Sniffing and then replaying CAN frames is described as the simplest route, while FlexRay is considered harder to reach. A question about security add-ons leads to the view that layers placed on top of decades-old protocols only partly help, with gateways and node checks as partial defences. The talk closes with practical pointers: Japanese cars are easier to work with, Tesla's public technical documentation and the open comma.ai project offer useful access, and the CAN bus is the most practical entry point.

talks.title: CONFidence 2022: Redteaming na zapleczu sklepu
talks.teaser: Borys Łącki examines CONFidence 2022: Redteaming na zapleczu sklepu.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Prezentacja Borysa Łąckiego z firmy LogicalTrust podczas konferencji CONFidence 2022 skupia się na specyficznym teście typu red teaming, łączącym fizyczne wtargnięcie na zaplecze sklepu sieciowego w galerii handlowej z penetracją korporacyjnej sieci IT. Prelegent podkreśla różnicę między klasycznymi testami penetracyjnymi (skupionymi na wyszukiwaniu konkretnych podatności w wyznaczonym zakresie) a działaniami red teamingowymi, które sprawdzają odporność procesów, reakcję zespołów Blue Team/IT oraz procedury bezpieczeństwa w organizacji.

### Key Topics
- **Kwalifikacja klienta i dojrzałość bezpieczeństwa:** Red teaming i dedykowany phishing powinny być wykonywane w organizacjach o odpowiednio dojrzałym poziomie bezpieczeństwa. Bez odrobionych podstaw (np. wcześniejszych testów penetracyjnych, analizy ryzyka i strategii) zaawansowane symulacje ataku są często nieefektywnym wydatkiem.
- **Specyfika galerii handlowych:** Przestrzeń galerii charakteryzuje się obecnością klientów, niestandardowymi układami lokali, obecnością ochrony galerii oraz mapami ewakuacyjnymi na korytarzach, które okazują się cennym źródłem wiedzy o wejściach służbowych i ciągach komunikacyjnych.
- **Faza rekonesansu:** Zbieranie informacji z mediów społecznościowych, rozmów z byłymi pracownikami, opinii w sieci (np. o zachowaniu managerów), raportów firmowych, a także analiza ruchu w sklepach, obecności personelu i kątów widzenia kamer.
- **Metody wejścia:** Wykorzystanie dwóch planów działania — wejście ciche (obserwacja, odczytanie/nagranie kodu z zamka szyfrowego i wejście pod nieobecność pracowników) oraz wejście socjotechniczne na pracownika IT (pretekst inwentaryzacji sprzętu, wydrukowane wizytówki, nawiązanie rozmowy o uciążliwościach nowego systemu informatycznego i żargon techniczny).
- **Penetracja sieci wewnętrznej:** Wykorzystanie fizycznego implantu (np. urządzenia typu LAN Turtle z łącznością GSM) wpiętego do sieci lokalnej w celu uzyskania zdalnego dostępu i eskalacji uprawnień w kierunku zasobów centralnych.

### Technical Details
- **Infrastruktura lokalna:** W sklepach zidentyfikowano typowy podział na 2–3 VLAN-y (dla urządzeń POS/kas, komputerów oraz zarządzania siecią).
- **Początkowy przyczółek sieciowy:** Skanowanie wykazało dostęp do panelu administracyjnego serwera WWW umieszczonego na tym samym porcie co usługi wewnętrzne, gdzie udało się odgadnąć hasło.
- **Eskalacja uprawnień i pivot:** Nadmierne uprawnienia do odczytu plików na serwerze WWW pozwoliły na odczytanie skryptów administracyjnych i przejęcie poświadczeń. Wykorzystano również niezabezpieczone hasłem klucze SSH używane przez administratorów, co umożliwiło skakanie na kolejne serwery w backendzie.
- **Konta Active Directory i bazy wiedzy:** Zdobyte serwisowe konta domenowe posiadały zbyt szerokie uprawnienia i pozwoliły na zalogowanie się m.in. do systemów takich jak Jira oraz wewnętrznych baz wiedzy/Wiki. Zasoby te zawierały niezaszyfrowane dane logowania do innych systemów, środowisk testowych oraz repozytoriów kodu źródłowego.

### Takeaways
- Fizyczny red teaming to dla atakujących operacja wysoce kosztowna i ryzykowna, w realnym świecie stosowana rzadko w porównaniu do phishingu czy ataków zdalnych, jednak doskonale obnaża braki w procedurach i segmentacji sieci.
- Bezpieczeństwo fizyczne zależy w dużym stopniu od czynnika ludzkiego (rotacja pracowników, rutyna, brak weryfikacji tożsamości) i detali technicznych (np. brak osłon na klawiaturach kodowych, odbicia w lustrach, niedomykające się samozamykacze drzwi).
- Kluczowa jest właściwa architektura IT i segmentacja: nawet w przypadku uzyskania fizycznego dostępu do gniazdka sieciowego na zapleczu, odpowiednie reguły firewall, brak współdzielonych kluczy SSH, zasada najmniejszych uprawnień dla kont serwisowych oraz ochrona poufnych danych w wewnętrznych bazach wiedzy uniemożliwiłyby prosty pivot do sieci korporacyjnej.

talks.title: CONFidence 2022: Sherlock Holmes na tropie cyberzłoczyńców - Dominik Hawryluk, Łukasz Barański
talks.teaser: A detective motif links next-gen SIEM correlation, machine learning, and business context to stepwise detections across a staged intrusion.
talks.summary:
The session opens by comparing interdisciplinary detective reasoning to modern security operations, arguing that individual sensors handle local threats well but sophisticated intrusions need correlated context across time and sources. Next-generation SIEM is positioned as the place where firewall, IPS, EDR, and workstation logs meet, using event correlation, anomaly models, and broader log ingestion such as Windows Event Forwarding and Sysmon.

A fictional intruder on a workstation thread is walked through as a sequence of detection tiles. Machine learning flags an unusual VPN login country for a user who normally connects from Poland. Sysmon-driven rules surface suspicious process creation when a hash fails trusted baselines. An EDR finding is elevated when it follows a prior anomaly on the same host and user. Firewall visibility exposes RDP to another machine, lateral movement, high-volume port scanning, and blocked then successful reach toward an invoicing-style business application, with Active Directory group membership supplying authorization context. A Windows Security event captures interactive logon that amounts to privilege escalation from a standard user to an administrator account, after which authorized-looking business traffic is correlated with earlier failed attempts from the same source address.

Practitioners are shown how modular rules drop events into category buckets that later SQL-style correlation can chain without rigid ordering, and how business-process maps plus directory data turn bare network logs into meaningful access decisions. The closing emphasis is that focused detection rules plus correlation engines can reconstruct an entire kill chain for analyst response.
