talks.title: 4Dev2022: Front end technologies for desktop applications: embrace window.open()! Eric Dilcher
talks.teaser: Covers multi-window desktop apps with web stacks, linking parent and child frameworks through window.opener for shared state and views.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that many popular JavaScript-based desktop clients stick to a single window even though native mail, messaging, and IDE apps routinely let users pop content into separate windows. After surveying Electron, NW.js, Neutralino, CEF, and related options, the speaker uses GOG Galaxy as a case study: large game libraries can spawn many edit and configuration windows, and metadata must stay consistent everywhere while backends and local databases update data.

PostMessage-style bridges looked hard to scale, so the team exposes the parent window’s global framework state to children via window.opener. For Angular, the parent injector is published on the global object, child modules re-provide parent services, and NGZone subscriptions keep change detection aligned both ways—including noop runs so updates reach every child. React with Redux shares the parent store through the provider, with simpler automatic view sync. Live counter demos show many child windows staying in step.

Trade-offs include onboarding cost, broken encapsulation, harder unit tests without a real opener chain, severe memory-leak risk, and framework limits when child windows use separate renderer processes. Build tooling needs extra HTML entry points; sample code and an npm helper package are offered. The closing message is to embrace multiple windows on desktop when separate views help users, and to use this pattern to avoid heavy inter-window APIs.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Single Page Applications - was it a good idea?
talks.teaser: Challenges single page applications as the default front-end choice, weighing their performance and complexity costs against their benefits.
talks.summary:
The talk questions whether single page applications should remain the default for front-end work. It starts with a storefront built on Spartacus, an Angular library set for SAP Commerce Cloud, which scored about 20 on a Lighthouse performance check. Even after server-side rendering, caching and asset optimisation, the score only reached 50.

The speaker traces the web's history: HTML was made for sharing static scientific documents, JavaScript was written in about ten days to add interactivity, and the term single page application appeared in 2002 for a proof of concept. Frameworks such as AngularJS and React followed. Their strengths are rich interactivity, fast navigation after loading, component-driven work shared with designers, and separate frontend and backend teams. Drawbacks include a performance ceiling, extra effort for search engines and accessibility, a complex build and test pipeline, rebuilt browser behaviours such as history and scroll restoration, weaker fault isolation, and reliance on third-party scripts.

Newer approaches such as React Server Components, Remix, Islands architecture and a fine-grained lazy-loading framework move work back to the server, which adds backend knowledge to the frontend role. The speaker favours evolving with web standards over inventing a new protocol, and urges teams to treat single page applications as a deliberate choice rather than a given.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Komunikacja w rozproszonym świecie
talks.teaser: Explains how to make service-to-service communication reliable with discovery, retries, circuit breakers and message queues.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a monolith is not automatically legacy, and that splitting an application into distributed services brings new problems, mainly in how services talk to each other. Once calls cross a network, the caller can no longer assume delivery or fixed addresses. The speaker starts with service discovery, where instances register their location in a registry that clients query, and mentions an API gateway as a single entry point in front of internal services.

The middle part covers failure handling. Retries with growing waits address temporary faults, a retry limit stops endless traffic, and a circuit breaker fails fast while a service is down, then probes it again in a half-open state. Because a repeated request can run the same work twice, the talk explains idempotent operations and an inbox table that records processed operation IDs. It then contrasts synchronous HTTP calls with asynchronous messaging through queues, covering direct, fanout and topic routing.

The closing part addresses consistency between a database write and a published message. The outbox pattern stores both in one transaction, and a background job relays pending messages, with a dead letter queue for messages that cannot be processed. Sagas coordinate multi-step flows such as an online order, using compensating actions like refunds when a step fails. The speaker suggests injecting failures during development to test these mechanisms, and notes that message ordering, monitoring and tracing were left for another time.

talks.title: 4Developers2022: From connectivity to simulations - the evolution of Digital Twin
talks.teaser: Traces how digital twins evolve from basic connectivity to simulation, and where low-code and no-code tools fit in.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how digital twins evolved, starting with simulation and telemetry in the Apollo program and moving up a layered pyramid from monitoring to adaptive simulation. The speaker argues that the right layer depends on client value, so teams can start small and focus on behaviour rather than technology. Storage choices are compared, from time series and graph databases to column stores, and matter more at larger scale.

Two client cases illustrate the approach. A UK water and drainage provider with smart meters on a weak LoRaWAN network added network monitoring and map-based GIS context, which let it pinpoint leakage, an emergent benefit nobody had planned for. In a separate factory example with no sensors, workers were given tablets to log recurring machine problems, and analysis of those reports showed which machines caused the most trouble on the production lines.

On low-code and no-code, the talk weighs claims about citizen developers: lower upfront cost and faster innovation against concerns about governance, shadow IT and scalability. Visual modelling and process definition work well for prototypes and small deployments, while maintenance and vendor lock-in remain long-standing complaints. The speaker closes by suggesting low-code suits process definition layered over IoT, that digital twins are starting to resemble master data, and warns against rebuilding an enterprise service bus.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: "Panie, kto tu Panu tak ... - czyli porozmawiajmy o Legacy Artur Skowroński
talks.teaser: Connects legacy inertia to cognitive bias and details a Phoenix proxy path that retired Lotus Notes and ETL for cloud APIs.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing legacy not as shameful technical debt but as an almost unavoidable outcome of success, using the New York City subway’s stalled expansion after early triumphs as a parallel to systems that still run the business but cannot be replaced wholesale. The speaker argues that developers blame predecessors via attribution bias, cites aging-software research from the 1990s, and describes how systems rot both when they are neglected and when they accumulate compromises as people and requirements change.

The core case study walks through a company system born in the 1980s with mainframe-style batch flows, a 1990s Oracle integration hub with quasi key–value tables, and an ETL layer that gradually owned most data movement. In the 2000s, Lotus Notes became a critical but fragile hub on an unmaintained Windows server. Cloud migration started with two years of requirements archaeology, documentation with people who remembered tribal rules, and a deliberate refusal to begin by swapping the database.

Instead the team introduced Phoenix as a communication proxy mirroring Lotus file outputs, shipped a narrow read-only API MVP with clear docs to win first adopters, compared nightly generated files for parity, extended Phoenix to ETL feeds, replicated the human administrator UI, and cut clients over one by one with rollback to Lotus. Lotus and much ETL could then be retired while cloud clients grew. The practical takeaway is to attack interfaces and observability first, earn users incrementally, and treat legacy modernization as controlled strangulation rather than a single heroic rewrite.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: O mniej znanych funkcjonalnościach Chrome DevTools
talks.teaser: Tours lesser-known Chrome DevTools features for web developers, from CSS and animations to accessibility checks and recorded tests.
talks.summary:
Dominika Zając gives a tour of lesser-known features in Chrome DevTools, the developer toolkit built into Google Chrome that needs no installation. After a brief recap of the familiar Elements and Console panels, she shows practical shortcuts: centering an element with flexbox properties from the styles pane, using the angle picker to tune a linear gradient, and inspecting CSS animations in the Animations panel, where a loading spinner can be slowed, lengthened or delayed.

The middle of the talk covers the newer CSS Overview panel, which summarises colours, fonts, unused declarations and media queries and flags low-contrast text. Lighthouse audits score a page from 1 to 100 across categories and link to explanations for each problem. Console messages can be filtered by level, by regular expression or by URL. The Recorder panel turns a coffee-ordering flow into a replayable script that can be edited, extended and measured for performance. The Performance panel, with network and CPU throttling, and an experimental Performance Insights view in Chrome Canary are also demonstrated.

The closing section focuses on accessibility. Lighthouse accessibility audits are a good starting point, though the speaker notes that automated checks find only around 57% of issues. DevTools can emulate colour vision deficiencies, and its contrast checks suggest a nearby colour that meets the AA or AAA standard. The main takeaway is to explore these panels hands-on and use audits as a starting point rather than a complete check.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: W sieci połączeń - Service Mesh
talks.teaser: Shows how a service mesh like Linkerd adds encryption, retries, metrics and canary rollouts between services without code changes.
talks.summary:
Systems that began as one monolith often grow into many services, each with several instances and sometimes written in different languages. The talk explains how hard it becomes to route requests to the right instance, secure the connections between services, and see what is failing, especially when shared libraries are impossible and legacy code is untouchable. It also stresses that the network cannot be trusted to deliver every request, so failures have to be handled somewhere.

The speaker introduces the service mesh as a layer of proxies placed beside each service and managed by a control plane. Traffic between services passes through these proxies, which can encrypt connections, authorize which service may call which, export standard request metrics, and retry failed requests without changes to application code. Using Linkerd on Kubernetes, the demo injects proxies into a namespace, builds a service map from observed traffic, and shows a flaky call reaching full success once retries are enabled. A Flagger-driven canary rollout then shifts traffic in 10% steps against a 95% success threshold, rolling back a faulty version that had received 30% of traffic before a fixed version is promoted. Authorization policies return 403 to unauthorized callers, and a traffic split injects errors to test resilience.

The main takeaway is that a mesh moves networking concerns out of application code and into shared infrastructure, at the cost of extra hops and added latency. Retries need explicit limits on attempts and timing, or they can add load to a struggling network. The speaker encourages trying a mesh on a local cluster before adopting it.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Czego uczy nas system Legacy?
talks.teaser: Shows how working on legacy systems reveals domain boundaries, invariants and business rules that greenfield projects lack.
talks.summary:
The speaker defines a legacy system as one where a small change feels frightening because anything might break, regardless of its age, tooling or test coverage. He argues that developers often prefer to start over on greenfield projects, but an existing system already holds knowledge a new one lacks: business rules, edge cases and invariants that years of production use have exposed.

He describes reading such code to find its domain structure, in the spirit of Domain-Driven Design. Repeated checks that always operate on the same data point to consistency boundaries, which he treats as aggregates. Getters that exist only so data can be copied into a DTO suggest a separate read model, and a service with dozens of dependencies can be split into smaller application services. In one case, a machine-rental system was extended to handle vehicle leasing and became tangled. The team cut the rental module out, rebuilt a leasing model beside it, and used commit history and change coupling to see which parts of the code changed together. Complexity trends over time can also point to places where unrelated concerns were mixed.

His takeaway is that legacy code teaches impact analysis, causal reasoning, careful questioning of requirements and patience, since finding the right boundaries often takes repeated failed attempts. Building a mental model of a system and sharing it with business stakeholders can make a developer a more useful partner, even when the code itself cannot be changed.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Painless / Painful? Własny system rankingowy w Elasticsearch - Łukasz rynek
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a custom Elasticsearch ranking with Painless scoring functions, plus how to debug it.
talks.summary:
Łukasz rynek, a senior PHP developer, describes building a custom ranking layer on top of Elasticsearch for a production search engine. The talk uses a fictional car rental application with sports cars, colours, and add-on services as the case study. The demo stack is PHP 8.1 with Symfony, and OpenSearch 1.3.0 is used for the examples. He starts with the index mapping and a function_score query, and explains why filter clauses do not contribute to the score, so the team chose to score matches against filters explicitly.

The middle of the talk covers scoring factors. Index-time factors are computed when a document is indexed, such as a promotion flag. Context-time factors depend on the query, such as which filters were chosen and how well a document matches them. The colour factor rewards cars whose requested colour is dominant among up to three colours, adds a bonus for exclusive colours, and multiplies a normalised value by a weight. The results are sorted by the combined score, which replaces Elasticsearch's native score. Painless is presented as a restricted, Java-like scripting dialect. The live debugging section shows how hard it is to inspect values, including why array order is lost unless the original source is read, and how the explain output helps.

The closing part covers the trade-offs: custom ranking gives full control but needs careful debugging and attention to performance. He also raises uncertainty about whether Elasticsearch would keep an explain-style feature, which led the team to OpenSearch 1.3.0, where that feature was added. The example code is shared in a repository that needs only a search engine and a Symfony setup.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Dostępność dla każdego
talks.teaser: Shows common HTML and CSS mistakes that block users with disabilities, and how front-end developers can avoid them.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that digital accessibility is often mistaken for a niche add-on for blind users. It sorts disabilities into four groups (visual, hearing, cognitive and motor) and points out that everyone meets temporary limitations, such as a broken arm or a crowded metro, so inclusive design benefits all users. The business case follows: the speaker cites 4-7 million people with disabilities in Poland, the risk of losing customers, and fines or lawsuits, including a case over media that triggered epileptic seizures.

The practical section covers design and markup. Text should meet at least the WCAG AA contrast ratio, checked with an online tool, and colour should never be the only signal, so labels should accompany it. Meaningful images need descriptive alt text, while decorative images keep an empty alt so screen readers skip them. Headings should follow a logical order from a single h1, chosen by document structure rather than visual size. Placeholders should not replace labels, since they vanish once a user types. Removing focus outlines breaks keyboard navigation, and animations can be turned off with the prefers-reduced-motion setting. A visually-hidden CSS class keeps text for assistive technology only, and CSS reordering can pull focus away from the DOM order.

The closing part covers ARIA, which should supplement native HTML rather than replace it. Landmarks, aria-label and aria-labelledby help name navigation and sections, and aria-describedby can explain password requirements. The speaker recommends testing with NVDA or JAWS on Windows and VoiceOver on macOS, and checking element names and roles in the accessibility tree of browser developer tools. The main takeaway is to start with semantic HTML and treat accessibility as an ongoing part of front-end work.

talks.title: 4Developers2022: Event-driven revolutions, or from monolith to event sourcing in practice
talks.teaser: Walks through migrating a CRUD shopping cart to event sourcing in Node.js, one piece at a time.
talks.summary:
Oscar Dudy frames the talk around an online store whose checkout runs on a simple CRUD setup: a React front end, a Node.js service and a Postgres database that overwrites the whole shopping cart on each save. The business wants abandoned-cart and basket analysis, which these flat tables cannot support because they discard what customers added and removed. He proposes moving toward event sourcing gradually, starting with the cart.

To recover business events from legacy code, he suggests looking at status fields, separating fields needed early from those filled later, and running an event storming session. For the cart this gives four events: opened, product added, product removed and confirmed. In his Node.js and TypeScript example, each command loads a stream from EventStoreDB, folds past events into the current state with a "when" function, checks business rules such as only adding products to an open cart, and appends a new past-tense event. Projections subscribe to events and write flattened rows into Postgres.

The payoff is an audit trail, time travel to explain what a customer did, and correlation and causation IDs that link commands to their resulting events. He notes that Kafka lacks a per-stream read API, so it does not serve as an event store. His takeaway is to migrate one module at a time, writing the new model alongside the old and cutting over with the strangler pattern, and to skip event sourcing where history adds little, such as a warehouse core domain.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: Jak przemalować słonia - redesign w dojrzałym produkcie
talks.teaser: Staged design-system work lets a mature live-chat product regain visual and code consistency without freezing releases.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on Tidio, a long-lived live-chat product that accumulated inconsistent visuals because features were designed in isolation, LESS scoping encouraged duplicate components, and past attempts to tame the problem with Bootstrap or stock UI kits only added more variants. Halting delivery for a monolithic redesign was ruled out in a product company where shipping value still mattered.

The middle walks through incremental wins: unified buttons with semantic variants and shared interaction states; colors evolved from hex values to named swatches, design tokens, and role-based semantics that set up believable dark mode; typography was inventoried, reduced, and enforced with typed heading and text components plus review gates. Dropdown work collapsed six implementations into one composable pattern and removed hundreds of lines of styling noise. Modal layouts, tooltip defaults, and bloated icon-button APIs were simplified so the happy path matches current design without manual flags.

Practitioners should leave with a repeatable loop—inventory what exists, standardize variants, ship new pieces with Storybook, adopt them in new or touched surfaces, and retire legacy names instead of stacking version suffixes. Smaller pull requests, dedicated improvement time, and regular front-end knowledge sharing keep migrations reviewable while teams grow.

talks.title: 4Developers 2022: The victory has defeated you
talks.teaser: Karol Rogowski examines 4Developers 2022: The victory has defeated you.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from the 4Developers 2022 conference, Karol Rogowski (Head of Engineering at SoftwareHut and lecturer at Białystok University of Technology) discusses how modern developer convenience and excessive reliance on ready-made frameworks or libraries can lead to skill stagnation. Referencing Bane's quote to Batman—"victory has defeated you"—Rogowski argues that modern tooling, cloud scaling, and code generators like GitHub Copilot often lead developers to ignore fundamental theoretical computer science concepts, creating software without understanding execution costs, algorithmic complexity, or optimal data structures.

### Key Topics
- **Framework Dependency vs. Foundational Knowledge**: The developer ecosystem has changed dramatically over 13–15 years. Whereas developers previously wrote utilities and algorithms manually, modern workflows rely heavily on frameworks (such as Angular, React, Vue) and boilerplates. Rogowski criticizes short bootcamps that produce developers incapable of evaluating code optimality beyond basic framework usage.
- **Data Structures**: Rogowski highlights common data structures and explains why using simple lists or arrays for every problem is suboptimal:
  - *Queues (FIFO)* and *Stacks (LIFO)* allow constant-time retrieval when order dictates access, unlike arbitrary list traversal.
  - *Trees* provide hierarchical organization and allow significantly faster search capabilities than linear collections.
  - *Graphs* model networked relationships and complex connections cleanly through object references.
- **Classical Algorithms**: Developers frequently reinvent the wheel instead of leveraging standard algorithms, such as QuickSort (compared to bubble sort), the Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm for substring matching, Dijkstra's algorithm for pathfinding in graphs, and Breadth-First Search (BFS) vs. Depth-First Search (DFS) for tree traversals.

### Technical Details & Code Demos
- **Understanding Costs (Time and Space Complexity)**:
  - Rogowski points out that cloud environments (like Azure or AWS) encourage complacency through auto-scaling, masking inefficient code that would previously crash on-premise hardware.
  - In a simple `getMax` demo, Rogowski shows that finding a maximum value in an array takes linear computational time $O(n)$ and constant space $O(1)$. He recounts a student who believed calling `Math.max()` eliminated execution loops and costs entirely, emphasizing that built-in methods still execute the underlying operations.
- **Trade-offs: Time vs. Memory Complexity**:
  - Analyzing a technical interview problem (finding the first missing positive number in an array), Rogowski contrasts two distinct approaches:
    1. An in-place approach filtering and sorting the data, which requires no additional memory ($O(1)$ auxiliary space) but incurs sorting computational costs ($O(n \log n)$ or $O(n^2)$ depending on sorting).
    2. A hash-table-based approach that trades memory for speed by allocating a temporary hash map, reducing the time complexity to linear $O(n)$ at the expense of $O(n)$ memory.

### Recommended Resources & Takeaways
- Rogowski recommends practicing problems on platforms like LeetCode (highlighting the "multiply strings" problem as an exercise in algorithmic optimization) and reading Kyle Simpson's work on functional programming without framework reliance.
- The central takeaway is that developers should consciously evaluate theoretical time and space complexity rather than blindly assembling frameworks or library utilities.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Krakow 2022 - Serhat Can - DevSecOps: Shift Left or Right?
talks.teaser: Explores why DevSecOps needs production-side controls beyond pipeline shift-left, covering monitoring, policy-as-code, and on-call.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with DevOps history and culture, then positions DevSecOps as security woven through the whole software lifecycle—not only pre-production checks. Many organizations treat DevSecOps as “shift left,” meaning security tests inside CI/CD such as software composition analysis, static and dynamic testing, container scanning, and configuration management. The speaker agrees that catching issues before release matters and can reduce operational friction, but argues that pipeline gates alone cannot cover manual changes, identity access, or everything running in live environments.

The middle of the talk defines “shift right” as security after runtime: continuous collection of logs, metrics, and assets across cloud providers; security and policy expressed as versioned, testable code; and operational practices borrowed from on-call culture, including centralizing alerts and paging the teams that own affected services. A dedicated security function remains important even when “everyone’s job” is involvement, not abdication.

Five shift-right pillars are walked through in order: continuous monitoring, security as code and policy as code (for example MFA and root-user constraints), improved on-call and escalation discipline for security signals, centralized asset management for sprawling SaaS and multi-cloud estates, and automated compliance evidence instead of manual ticket churn. The conclusion stresses bidirectional shifting: collaborate across dev, ops, and security, automate without blocking delivery, and maintain visibility and response after software is live.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2022 - Marek Śmigielski - SRE's Swiss Army Knive
talks.teaser: Shows how user-journey canary probes alert teams before customers notice outages and reuse the same checks after deploys.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames site reliability needs as knowing whether production works before users complain, validating changes quickly, and measuring how long breaks last. It contrasts reactive Saturday-night boss calls with continuous external checks that page on-call staff and produce outage reports for Monday.

Using an e-commerce journey, the speaker argues that monitoring must reflect what users see—loaded assets, cart actions, and checkout—not merely HTTP status codes. Design principles include reliable probes, execution from outside the stack (often another region or cloud), and maintained automation code with proper abstractions and review practices. Example operations use triggers, serverless runners, dashboards, and paging. Grafana views break journeys into steps with availability history and latency trends that can warn before hard failure, as when a late step slowed for days before Cassandra disk exhaustion.

Limitations remain: failing scenarios rarely identify which microservice broke, and detection still trails some real user impact. Benefits span post-release smoke scripts, staging triage without log debates, spotting unintended deployment gaps, catching slower releases after algorithm changes, rare intermittent errors, and timezone edge cases. The closing message treats canary monitoring as a versatile SRE instrument that complements—not replaces—other observability tools, while cutting stress through predictable alerting.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2022 - Tomasz Dudek - Is the MLOps tooling the same as the DevOps tooling?
talks.teaser: Explains how MLOps differs from DevOps in testing, reproducibility, drift monitoring and team roles.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether the tooling used for machine learning operations is the same as ordinary DevOps tooling. It starts with a short machine learning refresher: training produces a model, which is essentially a set of numbers stored as files. That model is wrapped in a containerized inference server and served on Kubernetes, while teams keep iterating between data processing, model development and monitoring.

A sample AWS platform is shown, built from a multi-account landing zone and Kubernetes with open-source components such as MLflow for experiment tracking and model registry, Kubeflow for pipelines, a feature store and Seldon Core for deployment and monitoring. The speaker then contrasts ML with DevOps. Passing tests only indicate when not to deploy, since a retrained model can behave differently even with the same pipeline. Reproducing results needs versioned code, data and experiment metadata. Monitoring must catch model drift and data drift, not only uptime, and getting a model to run can involve the whole team, sometimes by swapping in a faster algorithm.

The main takeaway is that DevOps principles such as ownership, automation and observability still apply, while the implementation differs. Practitioners should learn enough machine learning basics to understand what their team builds, and avoid choosing tools without consulting the people who will use them.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2022 - Ricardo Castro
talks.teaser: Explains how Network Service Mesh links workloads across clusters and clouds where traditional service meshes fall short.
talks.summary:
Ricardo Castro, lead SRE at Anova, opens with the limits of traditional service meshes. He recaps their usual parts, a data plane of business services with sidecar proxies and a control plane for administration, then explains why they struggle when workloads sit in separate runtime domains. He walks through scenarios where that matters: hybrid and multi-cloud clusters, multi-company extranets, meshes that have to be bridged through gateways, and workloads that span two different meshes.

The middle of the talk introduces Network Service Mesh (NSM), a CNCF sandbox project that connects individual workloads at layer 3 regardless of where they run and works alongside an existing CNI without changing the clusters. He covers its core concepts: network services, clients identified by SPIFFE IDs, endpoints, and the virtual wires that link them. He also describes the request, close and monitor API, including why clients must refresh wires before they expire, and how registries match clients to endpoints using source and destination labels, with separate registry domains distinguished by a domain suffix.

He closes by tying the pieces together: an endpoint registers its services, a client requests a wire, and NSM handles the wiring. He points to advanced topics such as interdomain connectivity and topology-aware selection, along with the NSM tutorial, webinar, roadmap and documentation as places to continue.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2022 - Gabriel Manor - No More Walled Gardens: Removing Barriers with SCM...
talks.teaser: Shows how to harden GitHub source control and CI pipelines with signed commits, branch protection and config-as-code.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a live demo in which a commit is pushed to a public GitHub repository under the name of a well-known cloud-native figure, showing that default settings let anyone attribute commits to someone else. The speaker links this to git phishing: attackers copy popular open source projects into lookalike organisations, plant malicious code and wait for developers who search for a tool to clone it. The talk also cites a coverage tool's CI infrastructure breach, where build secrets were harvested through pipelines that were not locked down.

The middle section works through controls drawn from a CIS supply chain guide. Teams should require signed commits, protect every branch rather than only main, watch repository creation, deletion and forks, decide who may contribute, enforce MFA, and scan infrastructure as code and third-party components. For pipelines, the talk recommends a central CI repository so projects can only use approved workflows, scanning of build images, and restricted outbound network access on build workers. Managing GitHub settings with the Terraform GitHub provider lets a single service account be the only identity able to create, configure or invite into the organisation.

To close, the speaker introduces open source tools. chain-bench from Aqua Security runs these checks automatically, and the speaker has not seen any user score 100 out of 100. Step Security adds an egress firewall to CI runners, reporting blocked outbound connections so runs can be narrowed to what they need. The main takeaway is to start with one tool and one control rather than treating the whole task as too big.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2022 - Paweł Piwosz - Plan CI/CD on the Enterprise level!
talks.teaser: Shows how organizational structure, process and governance shape enterprise CI/CD design, beyond the choice of tools.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by Paweł Piwosz at a DevOpsDays event, looks at planning CI/CD for a large enterprise from the organization and process side rather than from the tooling side. The speaker starts with Conway's law, arguing that how teams communicate shapes the systems they build, and that who delivers CI/CD to whom matters as much as the pipeline itself.

He presents a checklist-style framework covering branching strategy, delivery strategy, artifact management, SDLC, quality gates, releases and rollbacks, KPIs, monitoring, value streams, tools and security. Examples show how mismatches cause trouble: three teams storing artifacts in three different places, one team using blue-green deployments while another rolls out gradually, and one team rolling back while another rolls forward. He also separates continuous delivery, which keeps a manual approval step, from continuous deployment, which has none. For measurement he points to DORA metrics and value stream mapping as ways to find waste and bottlenecks.

The framework is treated like a set of non-functional requirements, so architects, business stakeholders, engineers and security staff can discuss CI/CD using a shared vocabulary, which he calls a Rosetta Stone. He describes a mind map he has used with customers, still evolving, and offers to share it. The practical takeaway is to define the organizational and process context before choosing tools.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2022 - Paweł Sawicki
talks.teaser: Walks through defining a service, SLI, SLO and alert in Google Cloud Operations using a sample e-commerce demo.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how Google's site reliability engineering approach turns user happiness into measurable targets. The speaker defines a service level indicator as a point-in-time measure of how a service is performing, and a service level objective as a target evaluated over a time window and set below the service level agreement. The starting point is a critical user journey, with checkout used as the example because it ties most directly to revenue.

The demonstration runs on an open source learning environment, a microservices e-commerce app on GKE with Istio. An availability indicator is built as the proportion of good HTTP requests to checkout measured at the service mesh, counting server errors as bad while excluding most 300 and 400 responses. The speaker then creates a service in Cloud Operations, adds the indicator, sets an objective and window, and configures alerts for breaches and error budget burn.

The key takeaway is to understand the application before choosing indicators, and to set achievable targets based on historical trends, with windows long enough to guide decisions. The steps follow a set order: define the service, define the indicator, set the objective, then add the alert.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Po co nam te wszystkie Petabajty danych z kosmosu... (Marcin Kowalski)
talks.teaser: Shows how a Poland-based cloud hosts and processes tens of petabytes of open satellite data for climate, agriculture, and civil use.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces a Poland-based organization that built large public and project clouds devoted to Earth observation rather than generic hosting. The speaker argues that EO workloads treat multi-petabyte collections as normal, rely on open data and open-source stacks such as OpenStack and Ceph, and split the market into archival catalog services versus heavy on-demand processing for corrected satellite products.

He walks through Copernicus-era constellations, multispectral and radar products, and portals where anyone can browse or query scenes through APIs. Examples include chlorophyll and pollution layers for the Baltic, ocean currents, land-cover maps used under agricultural subsidy programs, flood and change-detection alert feeds, and an EU-backed effort to estimate Ukrainian harvests and forest loss before official statistics arrive. The infrastructure picture covers roughly 30 PB per major site, seasonal compute spikes when vegetation projects start, and why maintaining very high resolution archives across many years is physically unrealistic at public-EO scales.

Operations at this scale dominate the closing message: weak tenant isolation on stock OpenStack, simultaneous science jobs exhausting RAM, hard geographic diversification inside Poland, multi-tenant abuse, Ceph and NFS limits, missing multitenancy-safe SDN, and alert storms during network failures. The speaker expects vertically specialized clouds, simple pricing, API-first delivery, and full automation of deployment and capacity planning as the durable business model.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Jak budować usługi by ich nie pogubić
talks.teaser: IP Anycast praktycznie (Łukasz Bromirski) investigates PLNOG30 - Jak budować usługi by ich nie pogubić.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Podczas 30. edycji konferencji PLNOG Łukasz Bromiński przedstawił prezentację poświęconą architekturze Anycast i technikom równoważenia ruchu (load balancingu) w nowoczesnych sieciach IP. Prelegent nawiązał do swojego wystąpienia z 2011 roku, w którym udowadniał możliwość skutecznego działania Anycastu dla protokołu TCP oraz zastosowania blackholingu w obronie przed atakami DDoS. Celem sesji było omówienie ewolucji mechanizmów sieciowych, fizycznych ograniczeń sprzętu (krzemu) oraz zaprezentowanie praktycznych metod inżynierii ruchu przy wykorzystaniu BGP, ECMP, tunelowania i Add-Path.

### Key Topics
- **Ewolucja Anycast i ochrona usług**: Historia wykorzystania Anycastu do skalowania DNS (od root serwerów po instancje u polskich operatorów) oraz mitigacji ataków DDoS i przeciążeń.
- **Krzem vs. oprogramowanie**: Przesunięcie balansu między programowym przetwarzaniem ruchu (np. Squid, proxy aplikacyjne) a sprzętowym load balancingiem w ASIC routerów i przełączników w warstwach L2–L4.
- **Wyzwania enkapsulacji i tunelowania**: Trudności z haszowaniem i polaryzacją ruchu w tunelach (np. ruch GTP w sieciach mobilnych 4G/5G, MPLS, VXLAN, GRE) oraz problem braku entropii w nagłówkach.
- **ECMP i UCMP w złożonych topologiach**: Równoważenie ruchu o równym (ECMP) i nierównym koszcie (UCMP) w rzeczywistych sieciach produkcyjnych, w których idealne symetrie znane ze slajdów rzadko występują.
- **Tunele i nakładki (Overlays)**: Omijanie ograniczeń skomplikowanych metryk sieci podkładowej (underlay) poprzez tworzenie sieci nakładkowych i tuneli (np. RSVP, BGP, Segment Routing).
- **BGP Multipath i Add-Path**: Wymuszanie na procesie BGP instalowania i rozgłaszania wielu alternatywnych ścieżek do tego samego prefiksu anycastowego.

### Technical Details
- **Skalowanie DNS i wydajność**: Wdrożenia Anycast na tanim sprzęcie pozwoliły polskim operatorom osiągać wydajność rzędu 80 milionów zapytań DNS na sekundę w testach laboratoryjnych, zastępując pojedyncze serwery Sun/Solaris.
- **Haszowanie w sprzęcie**: Wykorzystanie krotek warstw L3/L4 (m.in. losowy wysoki port źródłowy UDP/TCP wybierany przez klienta DNS odpytującego port 53) do stabilnego rozrzucania ruchu pomiędzy różne instancje za pomocą ECMP.
- **BGP Multipath w laboratorium**: Demonstracja na wirtualnych routerach z demonem DNS NSD na adresie `123.9.53.53/32`. Domyślnie BGP wybiera jedną najlepszą trasę (np. na podstawie Router ID). Włączenie `maximum-paths` (np. do 4 lub więcej) pozwala zainstalować wiele ścieżek w tablicy routingu (RIB/FIB) routera brzegowego (R1).
- **BGP Add-Path w architekturze z Route Reflectorem**: Demonstracja bardziej złożonej topologii asymetrycznej (prefiks `33.56.53.53/32`). Zastosowanie rozszerzenia BGP Add-Path na Route Reflectorze (R4) oraz routerach klienckich (R5), aby router odbijający trasy przekazywał wszystkie ścieżki do klienta (R7), zamiast ukrywać trasy alternatywne i wysyłać tylko jeden „best path”.

### Takeaways
- Anycast w połączeniu z ECMP zapewnia efektywne i bezpłatne narzutowo skalowanie usług, pod warunkiem zachowania symetrii metryk lub odpowiedniego przygotowania protokołów routingu.
- W skomplikowanych środowiskach produkcyjnych, gdzie zmiana metryk IGP grozi awarią wielu usług, standardowym rozwiązaniem problemu asymetrii jest budowa sieci nakładkowej (overlay) za pomocą tuneli o ujednoliconym koszcie.
- BGP w sieci wewnętrznej jest elastycznym narzędziem do inżynierii ruchu, a mechanizmy takie jak BGP Multipath i BGP Add-Path są kluczowe, aby zapobiec monopolizacji ruchu anycastowego przez jedną instancję wybraną wyłącznie przez mechanizm tie-break (np. niższy Router ID).

talks.title: PLNOG30 - SDN. W tajnej służbie jej biznesowej mości (Piotr Wydrych)
talks.teaser: Examines SDN from a business angle: what it is not, how software steers BGP and DC traffic, and pitfalls when algorithms stay confidential.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by separating software-defined networking from conference clichés such as OpenFlow, rigid north–south architectures, or Kubernetes deployments that remain effectively static. For him, SDN means software continuously deciding how the network behaves with only limited administrator intervention, and he draws on Akamai-style traffic estimation and engineering built largely from in-house algorithms on open-source building blocks.

Most of the talk maps business problems onto outbound and inbound traffic engineering. On egress he contrasts default routes, transit plus peering, and full tables, including TCAM limits on the order of 128 thousand IPv4 prefixes and the cost gap between high-port switches and carrier routers. Programmatic prefix choice can stretch cheaper hardware between a default and a full table, react when a peer is congested, or prefer transit when peering is not automatically cheaper. Similar logic applies to deaggregation, live responses to overload or partial DDoS pressure, and where to place virtual network functions when power or site cost matters more than peak performance.

He closes on organizational and legal friction: build versus buy, running routing software around the clock, single points of failure, and routing intelligence treated as confidential intellectual property. Practitioners should treat SDN as an iterative development loop tied to business metrics, not a one-time policy write, and should expect hiring and operations models that blend network engineers with developers.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Transformacja wewnętrznego IT w erze multi-cloud (Maciej Lelusz)

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Dlaczego samolot leci? (Wojciech Ścigała)
talks.teaser: Traces ground-to-air data flows, coordination, and redundancy behind routine European passenger flights for operators-minded listeners.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with tongue-in-cheek answers to why an aircraft flies, then frames air traffic control as balancing safety against throughput—the same tension network engineers know from capacity planning. The engineering half walks a typical commercial trip weeks before wheels-up: AIRAC publications and aeronautical information products, route restriction spreadsheets, NOTAM streams without severity sorting, standardized flight plans, weather bulletins, delay and cancellation messages, and European flow management with calculated takeoff slots, including knock-on delays when French controllers strike.

It continues through transponder code assignment, flight activation, fused multiradar tracking (and why continental controllers distrust ADS-B positions from the aircraft), electronic coordination between units, dedicated ground telephone meshes, VHF coverage engineering, controller–pilot data link, and Warsaw-specific arrival metering that nudges timing minutes early for smoother approaches. It closes on retention of voice, radar, and message traffic, then a business view of national ATC as costly, long-lived critical infrastructure: limited human backup after years of training, KVM-style failover and simulator halls used for live fallbacks, hybrid vendor strategies, multi-decade service contracts, and procurement constraints on state operators.

Practitioners hear parallels to telco-grade systems—legacy message formats beside IP, partial automation with humans in the loop, and why duplicated hardware alone does not survive correlated failures or untested disaster paths.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Czarne dziury Internetu operatorskiego i jak do nich nie wpaść (Rafał Broda, Filip Glock)
talks.teaser: Engineers explain operator-network blind spots, rising DNS abuse, and practical DDoS defenses for Polish transit providers.
talks.summary:
The session frames “black holes” on operator networks as places where missing process and overloaded critical services quietly erase availability. A swimming-pool analogy stresses that raw connectivity is never safe by itself; operators need lifeguards, policy, and tooling layered on top of cables and routers.

Much of the material centers on DNS as the first critical layer users hit and attackers love. Recent global outages at major platforms are tied to DNS failures. Industry statistics show DNS reflection and amplification in DDoS climbing sharply over a decade, while multi-vector floods replace a single dominant UDP style. DNS appears throughout typical intrusion chains, including command-and-control and data theft, and the speakers argue malware campaigns lean on it heavily. They explain why the protocol is brittle: it answers first, responds even to junk, and stays open on port 53.

On DDoS, they compare common operator choices—waiting out short attacks, blackholing, costly on-prem scrubbers, cloud scrubbing with regulatory friction, and upstream mitigation aligned with transit economics—and note that passive approaches often let attackers win. Remediation guidance stresses capacity planning for spikes, fast caching, clear management interfaces, continuous monitoring, curated threat feeds with regional relevance, and behavioral DNS analytics for novel abuse. The close urges awareness, network understanding, monitoring, and treating DNS as the usual weakest link in a repeating security cycle.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - CDN 3.0 - dokąd zmierza rynek? (Przemysław Frasunek)
talks.teaser: See how distributed content delivery can bring streaming and application processing closer to users.
talks.summary: The speaker traces how content delivery networks evolved, from basic HTTP caching to platforms that can process applications close to users. The talk explains streaming delivery, traffic routing, caching, and the provider’s distributed architecture, then considers edge computing and ways operators can improve content delivery and offer new services.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Burzymy silosy infrastruktury IT (Robert Ślaski, Krzysztof Załęski)
talks.teaser: A narrative contrasts siloed and collaborative network operations, covering automation, documentation, and outage analytics.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a scripted dialogue about engineers stuck in comfortable silos while business demands faster delivery, then introduces two presenters who frame years of client work in network and data-center orchestration. They argue that impatient business units, opaque requirements, and separate technical and organizational silos stall projects such as a fictional Lifestyle Premium service.

Through the contrasting personas Stefan and Roman, the talk walks the project lifecycle: Stefan deepens chaos with one-off VLANs, copy-paste configs, orphaned data, and siloed scripts, while Roman pushes why-oriented questions, agile-style requirements, an automation lens, structured data for repeatability, and documentation of logical services rather than device screenshots. They show how duplicated infrastructure “donuts,” blurred ownership, and fear of deleting config create long-term operational debt.

The close covers day-to-day change tickets, starting automation with low-risk reporting and compliance checks, building a single source of truth for port and service data, and using shared analytics to shorten mean time to repair and “time to innocence” during outages. The presenters stress grassroots culture change, treating create and modify as one pipeline, and sharing failures openly so automation becomes an ongoing process rather than a mythical megaproject.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - IP w IT - Mieć ciastko czy/i zjeść ciastko? (Adrianna Pilecka)
talks.teaser: Explains how copyright, patents, design rights and trademarks apply to software, and how contracts decide who owns the code.
talks.summary:
The talk focuses on protecting and selling what an IT team builds. Copyright arises automatically without registration, but it covers only how an idea is expressed, such as code or architecture, not the methods or functions behind it, and its existence can be challenged in court. Patents can cover functionality, but software is generally excluded in Poland and Europe unless it is part of a system tied to a device. The speaker cited about 150 granted Polish patents out of more than 300 filings from 2016 to 2020, and a 60% success rate at the European Patent Office. Industrial designs and trademarks are presented as other tools.

Ownership also depends on contract structure. In Polish law an employer usually acquires software copyright from an employee automatically, so the speaker advises an explicit clause to keep the tax-deductible author's costs available. Job duties should describe creative work, since a manager's output may fall outside the role. With contractors, written agreements must name the rights and fields of use, and source code delivery needs a clear clause, because courts have confirmed it is not owed by default. Licensing lets a vendor keep the product and serve many clients.

The closing part noted that creators can later seek extra pay if a commercialised invention earns large profits. A planned copyright amendment may add a right to sales information, and AI authorship was touched on, which current law does not allow because an author must be a natural person. The takeaway: put ownership, scope and source code terms in writing before work starts.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Telemetria i monitoring sieci dla nowoczesnego sieciowca (Marek Zbroch)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding PLNOG30 - Telemetria i monitoring sieci dla nowoczesnego sieciowca (Marek Zbroch).

talks.title: PLNOG30 - BGP Community w sieci ISP i końcowej (Tomasz Mikołajek)
talks.teaser: Covers BGP communities for ISP and customer routing: informational tags, triggered policy actions, and filtering pitfalls.
talks.summary:
The presenter introduces the BGP Community attribute from RFC 1997 as an optional, transitive 32-bit tag operators attach to prefixes. He contrasts well-known communities such as no-export and graceful shutdown with locally defined schemes, and frames two roles: carrying metadata and driving routing policy when a neighbor’s filters match a tag.

Informational communities can encode peering versus transit versus customer relationships, geographic POPs, or upstream identity so export rules need fewer prefix lists. Action communities let peers request local preference changes, AS-path prepending, selective re-announcement, or next-hop manipulation; remote blackholing is shown as a practical DDoS response, with cautions about no-export, conflicting local preference, and strict prefix acceptance. Real numbering plans and published registries illustrate how large operators label customer routes.

The closing section treats communities as a possible attack surface when tags propagate widely, citing research on cross-AS effects on AS-path prepending and blackholing. Practitioners should filter communities on ingress and egress, publish active action codes, offer looking-glass visibility, strip only locally originated tags with vendor-specific care, and treat peering agreements as the reliable scope rather than assuming end-to-end tag survival.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Biometria behawioralne - Święty Gral rozwiązań... (Andrzej Karpiński)
talks.teaser: Describes how a national credit bureau deploys behavioral biometrics to detect account takeover during live banking sessions.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the role of BIK, Poland’s statutory credit information bureau owned by banks, and how shared credit data reduced fraud and stabilised lending after fragmented 1990s abuse. Most records are positive payment histories; the bureau also supplies indicators, credit scoring, query alerts, voluntary credit blocks, and stolen-document flags consumers can manage online.

The core shift is passive behavioral biometrics through the BIK-owned Digital Finger Prince platform. Banks profile how users type, move a mouse, or interact with a phone across sessions rather than only at login. A zero-to-1000 similarity score rises when behavior diverges; pilots on more than a million customers reportedly reach about 96% recognition accuracy. Examples include phishing with stolen credentials flagged within seconds, remote-desktop investment fraud visible through quantized input, and concurrent logins from different cities.

Practitioners hear that consent is collected despite arguments the signals are not personal data, with sector-wide rollout and cooperative banks in view. BIK Hub offers aggregated regional credit statistics without exposing individuals. The close targets telecom operators: behavioral checks on portals and mail, resale of alert-style value-added services, credit checks on high-risk handset orders, and help provisioning proper DDoS-resistant peering after KNF guidance.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Diagnozowanie sieci w Google Cloud Platform (Sebastian Grabski, Przemysław Sroka)
talks.teaser: Explains why cloud networks behave differently and how Google Cloud's native diagnostics help troubleshoot them.
talks.summary:
The talk, given at PLNOG30 by two Google Cloud engineers, opens with a simple demo: two virtual machines in one subnet ping each other, yet their ARP tables are empty. The speakers use this to show that Google Cloud networking is fully software-defined, built on their own SDN stack, and does not rely on broadcast or multicast, so many habits and tools from traditional networks do not carry over directly.

The presenters then walk through a classic troubleshooting approach: check connectivity, routing and filtering step by step. They note that ping and traceroute still help, but not every endpoint answers traceroute. They also cover the console, the API, router views, firewall rule logging and VPC Flow Logs. The second speaker presents Network Intelligence Center, which combines a topology view with six weeks of hourly history, a performance dashboard for packet loss and latency, and connectivity tests that mix static configuration analysis with probe packets. Firewall Insights flags shadowed or unused rules, and a network analyzer, in public preview, raises alerts when a configuration change breaks a path.

The closing part covers limits and roadmap. Connectivity tests only see the Google Cloud part of a path, so a third-party appliance in the middle is a blind spot. Planned work includes an API and scheduled tests, DNS resolution simulation, IPv6 support, and a shift from VPC peering toward Private Service Connect. The main takeaway is that cloud troubleshooting needs a configuration-based view alongside traditional probing.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Jak dosięgnąć chmur? (Tomasz Jarlaczyk)
talks.teaser: Reviews Azure and GCP connectivity from on-premises sites, covering peering, VPN, partner interconnects, costs, and failover design.
talks.summary:
Allegro operates hybrid infrastructure that mixes data centers with multiple public clouds, and the presentation treats “reaching the cloud” as a connectivity and economics challenge rather than picking a single vendor. It opens by walking through access patterns—public peering, VPN tunnels, and partner or dedicated interconnects—and stresses why control over ingress and return paths, spare capacity on alternate routes, and the billing category for each flow matter as much as headline port speeds.

Most of the session draws on Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud work in Poland: standing up public peering as an inexpensive failover when carrier outages pinned traffic, comparing partner metro interconnect pricing models and the gap between promised redundancy and single-port reality, using Express Route local circuit where it eliminates egress, and living with Google tunnel “software task” restarts. Audience puzzles underline that terabyte-scale egress quotes are meaningless without knowing which link carries the bytes, that checksum checks after migration can force full re-downloads, and that slowing backup jobs can shrink costly interconnect sizing.

Later sections scale the problem to hundreds of cloud projects, VPC peering limits, multi-region hubs for many endpoints, and reference hub designs with environment separation. The closing advice is to read granular cloud invoices, keep steering options you can actually use under failure, question paper-perfect redundancy, and plan bandwidth changes over quarters—without assuming one cloud wins every workload or acquisition scenario.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Neuroróżnorodność w IT i Security (Andrzej Gab, Marek Madej)
talks.teaser: Shows how a security team hired neurodivergent engineers and how the wider group adapted.
talks.summary:
At PLNOG 30, Andrzej Gab and Marek Madej described neurodiversity in IT and security and how a Polish cybersecurity team set out to hire neurodivergent specialists. They explained that neurodiversity is natural variation in how human minds are wired, covering autism spectrum traits, ADHD, Tourette syndrome, dyslexia and dyscalculia. Prevalence estimates vary, and many adults never receive a diagnosis.

Traits common in the spectrum, such as attention to detail, pattern recognition, visual thinking and deep focus on a special interest, were presented as well suited to security work. The team's effort started after a business contact linked to a US neurodiversity centre suggested the idea. With a foundation that runs neurodiversity recruitment, they moved 38 applicants through several stages, including their own cybersecurity test, to a shortlist of 13 and interviewed each one. They hired four candidates and offered a fifth a challenge: close specific skill gaps first, with no guaranteed job. Existing staff were trained beforehand, and the first hires shared one team for mutual support.

The speakers highlighted lessons from the first year: remote work was essential for some colleagues, and direct communication about needs was valuable even when it felt blunt. Hyperfocus helped some newcomers absorb project documentation within weeks. Balancing equal expectations with individual adjustments requires continuous effort. By autumn the team had six neurodivergent colleagues, after two departures and two new hires. Their advice was to prepare the team first and treat each neurodivergent person as an individual.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Jak rekrutować, aby nie wybrać odpowiedniego pracownika i... (Piotr Wojciechowski)
talks.teaser: Surveys IT hiring failures, turnover drivers, and engineer-led practices that improve recruitment for infrastructure teams.
talks.summary:
An infrastructure-oriented engineer presents recruitment and career development as a shared problem for employers and technical specialists, not as generic HR doctrine. Labor-market data cited in the session highlight how hard IT hiring remains, how long onboarding can run before a hire pays back, and how mismatched expectations drive rotation within months. Interactive prompts and published surveys align on pay and role fit, while ranking micromanagement—accentuated by remote and hybrid models—ahead of salary among reasons people quit.

The discussion links generational shifts to hiring outcomes: younger workers emphasize mental health, work-life limits, ethical employers, pay equity, and feedback over brand prestige or unpaid career chasing. The speaker contrasts reasons to stay in a comfort zone—corporate benefits, equity vesting, quiet quitting—with barriers to change such as financial pressure, home ownership, and relocation. A step-by-step example of layered agencies on an international B2B engagement illustrates how a headline contractor day rate can shrink sharply before it reaches the engineer.

Closing guidance is operational for infrastructure hiring: stop bloated job ads and nine-stage gauntlets; define the real operational scope and core technologies; disclose contract type and salary bands; prefer engineer-led screening, reference calls, and practice-based interviews over random certification trivia; and treat candidate Q&A as a two-way filter. Job seekers are encouraged to research targets, stay honest in CVs, and join recruitment processes occasionally to learn market rates even when they do not plan to move.

talks.title: PLNOG30 - Cyberbezpieczeństwo wodnej infrastruktury krytycznej (Płk Dr Piotr Potejko)
talks.teaser: Shows why water utilities are exposed to cyberattacks, from phishing and outdated Windows systems to weak resilience planning.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at cybersecurity of water infrastructure, both in Poland and abroad. The speaker, who spent years on physical protection of critical infrastructure, argues that a facility can be disrupted remotely without anyone touching it. He recounts cyber attacks linked to the conflict in Ukraine, which he traces back to 2015, that hit banks, a rail network and public institutions. He also describes a case near Poland's eastern border where a large water supply network lost access to all control systems for a full day, which he says caused serious problems beyond drinking water, for example for industrial users.

The middle section covers weaknesses he has seen in Polish utilities and municipal bodies. He says many sites lack sensors, data transfer and analytics, and that some institutions still run mostly Windows 7 systems that no longer receive support. In his own tests, a phishing mail with a CV attachment was the most effective lure, and staff opened it even with an empty body. He notes that breaches are often found only long after they start, and that boards tend to see security as a cost. To make the case, he estimated the losses from a single day of downtime at one chemical production site, which he put at 21 million, and used that figure to argue for investment.

He closes by urging a shift from pure security toward resilience, covering incident management, data governance and the protection of infrastructure. He credits the government's alert levels with prompting many organisations to review their exposure. He hopes for a national overview of audit findings and offers to share attack statistics afterwards.

talks.title: PLNOG ONLINE 3: Improving the Reaction to IPv6 Stateless Address... (Fernando Gont)
talks.teaser: Covers IPv6 flash renumbering failures on SLAAC hosts and layers operational tweaks, CE router rules, and IETF protocol work.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames IPv6 renumbering as either planned, with graduated prefix lifetimes, or flash, where old configuration must be invalidated immediately. Flash events are poorly served when hosts miss router multicast signals and then cling to stale prefixes until RFC 4861’s default seven- and thirty-day lifetimes expire, which can silently break IPv6 while dual-stack happy eyeballs masks the failure on IPv4.

A detailed walkthrough covers the common home and enterprise pattern: DHCPv6 prefix delegation to a customer edge router, a hard power-cycle, a new delegated prefix, and LAN hosts retaining obsolete addresses. Related cases include CE routers that announce LAN lifetimes longer than the ISP lease, VMs moved between subnets without link-down cues, and daemons that fail to zero lifetimes or lose invalidation multicasts.

Mitigations span three tiers. Operators and ISPs can favor stable prefixes where feasible and shorten preferred and valid lifetimes. Published customer edge router requirements address automatic DHCPv6 release on reboot, matching WAN-to-LAN lifetimes for all delegated data, persisting leases when possible, signaling flash events with zero lifetimes, and conservative SLAAC defaults. Longer term, ongoing IETF work aims to tighten SLAAC behavior and add host-side heuristics for flash renumbering.

talks.title: PLNOG ONLINE 3: BGP/OSPF with 100Mpps on amd64... (Pim Van Pelt)
talks.teaser: Compares kernel routing with VPP and DPDK, then shows BGP and OSPF sustaining high packet rates on commodity amd64 hardware.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting general-purpose kernel forwarding with userspace data planes built on DPDK pull-mode drivers and Vector Packet Processing. It explains how VPP batches packets into vectors, walks a directed graph once per vector, exploits CPU caches and SIMD, and scales roughly linearly with worker threads rather than paying per-packet interrupt and context-switch costs.

The middle section covers a Linux Control Plane plugin that mirrors VPP interfaces into Linux via TUN/TAP and Netlink so operators can configure routes and addresses with familiar tools and run suites such as BIRD for BGP and OSPF while transit traffic stays in VPP. Load testing uses Cisco TRex with single-thread cycle measurements and RFC-style ramp tests across Netgate, Supermicro, and Ryzen platforms, comparing kernel paths on pfSense and Ubuntu against VPP on IMIX, tiny 64-byte floods, and hardest single-flow 64-byte cases, plus energy per switched packet and PCIe limits on dual 100G NICs.

The close highlights production use at a small Swiss ISP, SNMP exposure for monitoring, and configuration examples for L2 cross-connects, QinQ tag rewrite, VXLAN and Geneve tunnels, bridge domains with a routed BVI, and LACP bonds—often at tens of millions of packets per second per core on tunnel endpoints.

talks.title: PLNOG 3 ONLINE: SONiC oraz Dell Enterprise SONiC (Emil Kacperek, Valerio Martini)
talks.teaser: Covers SONiC networking, Dell Enterprise SONiC features, and Ansible-driven datacenter fabric builds in minutes.
talks.summary:
A Dell network engineer opens by noting that a co-presenter could not attend and that the hands-on segment appears as a recorded walkthrough. He frames the shift from monolithic vendor boxes toward disaggregated hardware and software, then describes SONiC as a containerized open network operating system born from hyperscale needs, with routing and management split across services, Redis-based state distribution, and hardware abstraction that scales across many switch platforms.

The middle contrasts community SONiC with Dell Enterprise SONiC: familiar management interfaces, validated EVPN and related data-center features, extensive interoperability testing with optics and observability stacks, commercial support, and a choice of Dell switches running SONiC or legacy OS10. He outlines reference designs such as BGP leaf-spine fabrics, EVPN overlays, routing on the host without traditional Layer 2 domains, and optional third-party containers on switches for bare-metal integration or monitoring agents.

The close moves to operations: Fabric Design Center for graphical topology design, generated Ansible inventories and playbooks, version control, and AWX-driven deployment against a small virtual lab. The recorded segment shows importing a fabric bundle and pushing configuration until switches converge. Practitioners should leave with a picture of when enterprise SONiC adds value over raw open builds and how free design and automation tooling can shorten large fabric turn-up.

talks.title: PLNOG ONLINE 3: RIPE NCC & RIPE Update (Piotr Strzyżewski)
talks.teaser: Summarizes RIPE NCC strategy, registry workload, Atlas measurement, sanctions compliance, and community funding for operators.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with RIPE NCC’s 2020–2026 strategy and how it translates into operational priorities: keeping the registry accurate, strengthening core systems, improving organizational security and compliance, and deepening community outreach. The speaker stresses multistakeholder internet governance, including work on European policy such as NIS2, partner forums, and dialogue with governments and other bodies.

The middle section turns to concrete services and pressures on the registry. IPv4 transfer demand has surged, increasing staff load and affecting service quality, while sanctions at international, EU, and Netherlands levels add checks that also touch banking relationships. The talk describes DNS anycast offerings, RIPE Atlas scale (on the order of eleven thousand probes across many countries and autonomous systems), public measurement portals, routing views, training and IPv6 certification paths, localized community support, and RIPE Labs content including Internet Measurement Day events.

It closes with governance mechanics—revised acceptable-use guidance, ongoing RIPE Database policy review, and consensus-based policy development on mailing lists—with emphasis on registry neutrality under geopolitical stress, updated board positions on sanctions tied to the invasion of Ukraine, and an invitation to the hybrid RIPE meeting planned for Berlin in May. Practitioners gain a picture of where RIPE NCC is investing, which operator-facing programs to use, and how compliance and politics now shape day-to-day registry work.

talks.title: PLNOG 3 ONLINE: Measuring RPKI ROV adoption with NetFlow (Doug Madory)
talks.teaser: NetFlow analytics reveal how much live traffic reaches RPKI-valid routes compared with BGP route-signing statistics alone.
talks.summary:
The talk frames RPKI as the Internet’s practical line of defense against accidental BGP hijacks and leaks, and explains why both creating ROAs and validating routes on receipt must reach scale. Public monitors from NIST and RIPE Stat show rising valid prefix counts and tiny persistent invalid fractions, but those metrics describe BGP announcements and address space rather than carried traffic.

The presenter traces work by NTT engineers who extended the open-source pmacct tool to tag NetFlow with RPKI state so operators could quantify customer impact before dropping invalids, and describes Kentik’s adoption of the same idea for opted-in aggregate data. A one-week analysis finds most bits headed to valid or unknown destinations, with invalid traffic negligible; regional and country breakdowns show large U.S. eyeball and content networks driving much higher valid-traffic shares than raw signing percentages imply. Time-series views correlate with national deployment jumps such as Poland’s late-September shift and illustrate Taiwan’s validator outage reclassifying traffic as unknown for about a day without visible disruption.

Operators are encouraged to reject invalid routes while measuring local impact through pmacct or NetFlow trials, and warned that globally adjusting local preference or communities from validation state can amplify risk if validators fail.

talks.title: PLNOG ONLINE 3: Plany ciągłości działania (Marcin Marciniak)
talks.teaser: Maps business continuity from disaster scenarios and critical apps through replication, testing, and people, power, and connectivity.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames business continuity as coordinated actions whose goal is to keep the organization’s main business lines running, not merely to restore infrastructure. It walks through likely disruptors—datacenter fires such as the OVH incident, local facility losses, floods, technical failures, conflict-related stress, malware, and human error—and argues that each event needs rated probability and impact from hardware and applications up through business services, partners, and customers, across short and long time horizons.

From there it ties revenue-critical processes to application stacks, explains why superficial health checks mislead, and stacks local dependencies such as power, cooling, site access, virtualization, and shared hardware failure. It connects continuity planning to risk management practice, then contrasts classic backup-centric recovery with horizontally scaled, standardized, automated designs using replication, snapshots, and golden images, including when synchronous failover still loses in-flight work.

Practitioners are urged to test plans deliberately with documented success and failure criteria, exercise manual workarounds, and treat failed drills as plan input rather than organizational defeat. The closing stresses that continuity spans knowledge retention, workplaces, remote access, utilities, and wide-area connectivity—lessons reinforced by recent European crises—and invites audiences to review and modernize their own plans along that full chain.
