talks.title: PLNOG ONLINE 3: Jakie błędy popełnił Facebook, Cloudflare, Google i inni wielcy...(Łukasz Bromirski)
talks.teaser: Walks through real BGP and DNS outages at Facebook, Google, Cloudflare and others, and what operators should change.
talks.summary:
Delivered in Polish at PLNOG Online, this talk reviews real routing and operations failures at large internet companies and carriers. The speaker treats each case as a lesson and argues that teams should avoid blaming individual staff when a failure comes from a knowledge gap or a product bug.

Facebook's outage comes first: withdrawn BGP routes left its DNS servers unreachable once cached records expired after about a minute, and even building badge systems failed because they depended on the same network. In 2008 Pakistan Telecom announced a more specific route to a YouTube prefix, and its upstream carrier did not filter it, so the bogus route spread worldwide. Later, a Nigerian operator leaked about 500 Google prefixes, and two large carriers failed to filter them. Cloudflare's 2013 incident came from a configuration push that crashed BGP processes on edge routers. A 2006 Cisco demo with a mistyped prefix blackholed the company's own corporate network.

The recommendations include filtering customer and peer announcements against expected origins, rejecting unusually specific or overly long prefixes, registering your own prefixes and monitoring them, and testing routing changes on a lab network before production. The speaker also urges organisations to run chaos experiments, as Netflix popularised, and to outsource commodity operations where a provider does them well.

talks.title: PLNOG ONLINE 3: Podstawy sieci w Kubernetes (Piotr Jabłoński)
talks.teaser: Explains how pod, service and ingress networking works in Kubernetes, from node addressing to traffic exposure.
talks.summary:
The session walks through networking basics in Kubernetes, starting with how the orchestrator creates a pod and how the network plugin assigns addresses on each node. The speaker explains that containers inside one pod share a single IP address, and that pod address ranges are usually local to a node rather than stretched across the cluster. On managed cloud clusters the provider handles much of the routing, while self-built clusters may add an overlay, BGP routing or encryption depending on the plugin.

The middle part covers services, which give a stable virtual address in front of a changing set of pods chosen by labels. Three service types are compared: ClusterIP for access inside the cluster, NodePort for exposing a port on each node's address, and LoadBalancer for external traffic. Kube-proxy programs iptables rules on every node to translate the service address to backend endpoints. By default traffic can be spread to pods on other nodes, which can be limited to local endpoints. Ingress is presented as the layer for HTTP and HTTPS routing by host name and path, handled by a separate controller.

The closing part argues that these layered abstractions make workloads more resilient, since losing one pod only removes one endpoint and scaling adds endpoints without reconfiguring clients. The trade-off is that troubleshooting a distributed setup is harder. For network and infrastructure engineers, the practical advice is to expose services through a load balancer or ingress rather than raw node ports, and to understand how kube-proxy rules shape traffic.

talks.title: PLNOG ONLINE 3: Dlaczego wkrótce będziemy zajmować się migracją firmowej telefonii (Paweł Marciniak)
talks.teaser: Explains why businesses are moving phone systems to the cloud and what features, costs and partner options come with it.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why business telephony is moving from traditional on-site exchanges to cloud-hosted voice services. The presenter, speaking for a European cloud telephony provider, argues that the pandemic sped up adoption of remote communication tools, and that fixed telephone lines are being phased out by operators. Hardware exchanges are described as costly to maintain, hard to scale and limited in the services they can offer.

The middle of the talk covers practical features. Caller identification links an incoming number to a CRM record so staff see the caller's history before answering. Call queues can route calls by time of day, language or other rules, and callers hear the same prompts across locations. Calls can be answered on desk phones, computers, mobile apps, conference speakers or older analogue phones through a converter. Integration with Microsoft Teams lets users call external numbers. Pricing is subscription-based, paying only for the lines in use, which suits businesses with seasonal peaks. Examples from a plumbing firm, which routes callers by postcode, and from a hotel chain, where room status is updated from phones, illustrate these workflows.

The presenter said customer data is encrypted and hosted in German data centres spread across three sites within the EU, with critical data replicated elsewhere. The talk ends with a partner programme offering tiered status, recurring commissions on subscriptions, setup fees and free vendor training. The practical takeaway for IT managers is that cloud telephony removes exchange maintenance and offers scalable continuity, while the commercial details were aimed at prospective resellers.

talks.title: OMH 2021: Prototype pollution - czyli jak zatruć aplikację XSS-em
talks.teaser: Shows how prototype pollution can change application logic and bypass DOMPurify to achieve XSS in browser code.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the JavaScript prototype chain. When an object lacks a property, the engine searches its prototypes, so changing a shared prototype such as Object.prototype affects every object. The speaker shows that the in operator also walks the chain, so an injected property can flip a simple admin check from false to true.

The main case is a rich text editor that sanitizes HTML with DOMPurify and a custom allow-list. The demo used a URL query parser that turns bracketed parameters into objects without guarding the __proto__ key. Polluting Object.prototype with an extra allowed attribute made the sanitizer keep an onerror handler, which gave XSS. The speaker stresses that the sanitizer itself is not the flaw; the risk comes from combining a polluting parser with code that reads the polluted property, called a gadget. He also showed that setting document.mode to 9 through the prototype makes DOMPurify take a legacy path that stops sanitizing, which is a second bypass.

To find gadgets faster, the speaker presented a script that instruments a library's JavaScript so that every read of a missing property is logged with a stack trace. This points to the code paths a polluted prototype could influence. He surveyed public research on client-side pollution across many libraries, tag managers and analytics scripts, and closed with a short note that similar bugs appear in server-side JavaScript. The takeaway is to look for both a pollution source and a gadget.

talks.title: OMH 2021: Wyzwania dla bezpieczeństwa sieciowego - Łukasz Bromirski
talks.teaser: Explains how encryption pushes network defenders toward metadata, fingerprinting and behavioural analysis over packet inspection.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how network security has to change as most traffic becomes encrypted, both on the internet and inside corporate networks. The speaker cites public Google data showing about 95 percent of traffic to Google services is encrypted, and notes that over two million certificates are issued each day. A personal home network showed over 98 percent of more than five million exported connections encrypted. Internal traffic in Polish companies, often from in-house software, is far less protected.

Once payloads are hidden, the talk focuses on what stays visible: headers, TLS versions, flow metadata, packet timing and certificate fingerprints. TLS 1.3 adoption was reported at roughly 8 to 9 percent in October, up from under 2 percent in January, while many services and devices still negotiate older versions. Encrypted DNS and browsers choosing their own resolvers are presented as privacy gains that also reduce what defenders can see. The speaker warns that intercepting proxies and DPI boxes have themselves been abused, and that telemetry channels can be turned into command channels.

The closing examples show how timing and fingerprints can separate automated bots from human users, and how a conference network was used to identify devices carrying malware from encrypted samples alone. The takeaways are to combine flow metadata, behavioural analysis and threat intelligence correlation, build fingerprint profiles for your own applications, treat machine-learning security claims with scepticism, and avoid blanket blocking of traffic you cannot read.

talks.title: OMH 2021: Co, w jaki sposób i w jakim celu wpiąć do switcha w serwerowni?
talks.teaser: Walks through a physical intrusion narrated as a text adventure, from a USB stick to a rogue device in a server room.
talks.summary:
The talk is run as an interactive Polish text adventure in which the audience chooses each move of an intruder trying to plug a small device into the server room of a financial company. The story begins with a USB stick that turns out to be a microcontroller, programmed in the Arduino environment to launch a PowerShell payload when plugged in. A cheap clock built on the same chip shows how such hardware can hide in everyday objects. The speaker then shows a simple command-and-control client and a minimal listener, noting that default HTTP settings let a standard user listen on a port without admin rights.

The middle of the story covers forensic traces and extra tools. The registry keeps a history of connected USB devices, and the Run dialog history can reveal commands typed earlier unless the attacker cleared them. A Raspberry Pi Zero-based device is presented as an alternative that appears to the computer as a keyboard and a network card. Card cloning from a keychain and a keypad door lock are shown as ways to move through the building, and a consumer router with an added GSM modem is used to reach the network from inside, with a bridged printer helping to get past network access control based on MAC addresses.

The closing message is that these attacks were based on real work, and that physical access to a reception workstation or an open network port can lead to full compromise. The speaker notes that the device history and command history left on Windows can serve as evidence for investigators.

talks.title: OMH 2021: IT’S A TRAP!
talks.teaser: Explains honeypot goals, where to place decoys in the network, and practical Cowrie and RDP setups that log probes and attacker behavior.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces honeypots as deception layers meant to attract attackers or curious insiders, not to harden systems directly. The speaker ties the idea to widespread exploitation of long-known vulnerabilities and argues that decoys should closely mirror real production services so intruders invest time while defenders gain early warning and richer telemetry on tools, credentials, and scanning behavior.

A large portion compares deployment locations: outside the firewall for internet-facing noise and password-spray insight versus internal or DMZ placement for spotting lateral movement, with clear warnings about firewall load and escalation if a decoy host is compromised. The middle section walks through lightweight examples—a minimal Telnet listener with log review and change alerts—and a Linux Cowrie deployment demonstrated over SSH, including tuning ports, logging sessions, and reviewing captured commands and connection metadata.

The talk closes with field observations from internet-exposed decoys, such as password lists and bot source addresses worth blocking or correlating, plus a Windows-oriented RDP lure project for aggregating attacker IPs. The takeaway is to treat honeypots as a deliberate risk decision: design believable targets, monitor aggressively, and use collected intelligence for detection and response rather than expecting automatic risk reduction.

talks.title: OMH 2021: DNS w technikach ofensywnych
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers use DNS for command and control and data tunnelling, drawn from real campaigns.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how attackers use DNS beyond turning names into addresses. DNS is a hierarchical database that can hold arbitrary data and carry it in both directions, which makes it useful for command-and-control and data exfiltration. The speaker also notes that simple DNS lookups can reveal which applications a company uses, helping attackers choose believable lures.

Several real campaigns are walked through. One ransomware intrusion used four-byte A record answers as tasks over newly registered domains, and blocking only came after the infection window had passed. Another ransomware family moved to DNS command-and-control with TXT records, base64 and hex encoding and long queries. A supply-chain intrusion sent very sparse DNS beacons using a custom base32 alphabet, with answers drawn from public cloud address ranges to look legitimate. Other examples covered a cryptominer that read its domain from a cryptocurrency wallet, and embedded TCP/IP stack flaws where forged DNS responses enabled poisoning and code execution.

The defensive lessons are practical. Quarantining newly registered and newly observed domains helps, but one comparison found an average of 43 hours between a domain's first query and its appearance on vendor lists. Teams should also detect the techniques themselves, such as unusual TXT query volumes and long names, and review which DNS traffic their firewalls allow to pass through.

talks.title: OMH 2021: Diabeł tkwi w nagłówkach - Łukasz Mikuła
talks.teaser: Shows how abused client HTTP headers bypass controls, poison resets, and trigger classic header-driven exploits in hands-on labs.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames HTTP request headers as ordinary untrusted input that backends and proxies may parse, log, or trust. After a short refresher on how browsers send metadata alongside URLs, it argues that penetration testers should probe headers with the same skepticism applied to form fields and cookies, especially in chains involving load balancers and reverse proxies.

Early examples cover spoofing forwarding headers such as X-Forwarded-For to defeat IP-based access rules, and abusing Host or related headers during password-reset flows so recovery links point at an attacker-controlled site while the message still looks legitimate. The speaker then walks through tooling ideas, including Burp extensions with large header wordlists and hunting nonstandard header names in open-source code, before moving to a consolidated GitHub lab meant to be run in isolated virtual machines.

Live demos replay several historical cases: an Http-Proxy header leading to server-side request behavior, Shellshock via CGI environment variables derived from headers, a Ruby on Rails Accept-header arbitrary file read, a brief PHP 8.1 repository backdoor triggered through User-Agent, Java OGNL-style template injection through response-header handling, and Apache request smuggling chained to reach a protected admin area. The closing message is that header testing is rarely central in routine assessments, yet it can surface surprising impact when the underlying application mishandles unusual or duplicated header values.

talks.title: OMH 2021: Online i offline, czyli jak gromadzić dowody po incydencie (...)
talks.teaser: Wojciech Pilszak details OMH 2021: Online i offline, czyli jak gromadzić dowody po incydencie (...).
talks.summary:
This presentation emphasizes the critical importance of combining online and offline investigation methods when gathering evidence after corporate incidents, particularly data theft by departing employees. The speaker, a lawyer specializing in criminal and competition law, argues against the growing trend of limiting investigations solely to digital sources.

The context begins with COVID-19's acceleration of digitalization and remote work, which has led investigative practices to focus increasingly on internet-based activities. However, the speaker warns this is insufficient. Traditional intelligence sources—physical documents, media, specialized literature, and administrative databases—remain essential. A concrete example is Poland's National Court Registry (Krajowy Rejestr Sądowy), where physical courthouse records contain far more detailed information than online versions, including shareholder correspondence and management challenges unavailable digitally.

The central case involved a high-level employee departing with sensitive company data. This represents a common problem in Polish corporate environments: departing senior employees often leave "with the benefits of inventory"—removing client databases, product information, business solutions, and strategic plans. Contributing factors included poorly drafted non-compete clauses difficult to enforce in labor court, inadequate equipment tracking, and insufficient system access controls.

The investigation employed three integrated methods. Standard detective work involved interviews and field observations to document office layouts, access points, and the employee's activities. Forensic IT analysis examined devices, networks, logs, and mobile devices, revealing significant data access activity preceding departure. Active OSINT gathered information through pretext contact with interested parties.

A crucial discovery emerged when comparing online and offline sources: the competing company's court registry records revealed the employee's new employment before this information appeared online—a lag of weeks to months between actual events and digital availability. Physical courthouse visits proved essential, as investigators found evidence that would have been missed relying solely on internet sources.

Through targeted OSINT, investigators confirmed the employee had already provided proprietary information to the competitor. When the client reviewed findings, he inadvertently disclosed data only he should possess, effectively confirming the planned and intentional nature of the departure.

The investigation revealed systemic organizational weaknesses: poor equipment control, unclear IT asset responsibility, and indicators that multiple employees were preparing departures, suggesting cultural issues beyond the single incident.

The speaker emphasizes continuous coordination between investigators and clients—requiring direct phone contact with decision-makers, not email-only communication. Data from all three investigation channels must be analyzed and verified in real-time to avoid wasteful dead-end pursuits.

The final report synthesized evidence from physical fieldwork, digital forensics, and OSINT, providing comprehensive assessment. While the legal team could evaluate whether materials indicated probable criminal activity under unfair competition laws, they presented only data, analysis, and suggestions—never imposing judgment or influencing client decisions on further legal action. In many cases clients pursue court proceedings; others do not.

The conclusion stresses that cyber security professionals must not limit work exclusively to digital sources. Complete investigative pictures require understanding the physical world: even individuals with minimal internet presence have footprints in physical space, financial records, and administrative systems. Holistic approaches combining online and offline methods produce superior results to isolated methodologies.

talks.title: OMH 2021: Modern identity hacking: jak hakerzy odnaleźli się (...)
talks.teaser: Shows how remote access, phishing and MFA token theft let an attacker pivot into a corporate network.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how remote and hybrid work widen the attack surface of an organisation. The speaker, a consulting director and security expert, points to shadow IT, such as personal cloud accounts used to share company files, and cites a 2020 breach dataset in which only 17 percent of data-access breaches involved malware. Attackers often rely on stolen credentials and social engineering instead, phishing remains a common entry point, and financial motives drive most attacks.

The live demonstration follows one path. A booby-trapped attachment opens a shell on a Windows 10 workstation, and a script that runs at restart escalates privileges. From that foothold the speaker connects through a VPN session, adds routes and a SOCKS proxy to reach an internal corporate network, and retrieves credentials saved in a user's client. A second scenario uses a fake Microsoft sign-in page to capture a password and a one-time code, and the captured session tokens stay usable after the victim is redirected to the real site. A final part abuses a certificate written to a user's account attribute to gain access toward a domain controller.

The takeaways are that MFA helps but does not fully protect against token theft. Remote-access systems such as VPNs and ADFS need timely patching, because attackers quickly find unpatched ones. Organisations should apply zero trust, least privilege and just-in-time access, test incident response plans for remote-access scenarios, and run engaging awareness training that teaches staff to recognise suspicious attachments and links.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Mistakes and Trade-offs when optimizing the hot-path (...)
talks.teaser: Shows how to avoid premature optimization by measuring hot paths with JMH and Gatling, then targeting high-traffic code.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the familiar warning that optimizing without traffic or SLA data often adds complexity while leaving overall latency unchanged. A Java accounts example contrasts stream APIs, parallel streams, and fork-join overhead, then uses JMH at roughly 10,000 elements to show that parallel processing can match or trail the sequential version when assumptions about workload size are guesses.

The middle section reframes optimization around how often code runs, not only how slow it looks in isolation. Contrasting high-frequency and rare HTTP endpoints, the speaker multiplies request rate by latency savings to argue for the hot path. Pareto-style imbalance appears again in stress-test sizing for targets such as 10,000 requests per second, using concurrent users derived from per-thread throughput and optional headroom for tail latency.

A small word service illustrates the workflow end to end: Gatling models uneven traffic, metrics timers isolate a multi-second scan phase, and a Guava loading cache cuts validate p99 latency from about five seconds to about 65 milliseconds. The closing lesson is to benchmark with realistic traffic, measure invocations, optimize where multiplied impact is largest, and revisit micro-optimizations only after empirical thresholds justify them.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Virtual Public Speaking - skills that everyone of us needs to (...)
talks.teaser: Explains how to manage nerves, set up camera and lighting, and hold attention when presenting on video calls.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that since meetings moved online during the pandemic, almost everyone who hosts or joins a video call has become a public speaker, because they cannot see who is listening. He organises the session around three areas: the presenter's own comfort and well-being, the hardware setup, and the content itself.

On comfort, he suggests taking a breath before a meeting and naming your current emotional state, while remembering that listeners may be tired, distracted or stressed too. He recommends using deliberate pauses to draw attention and give people time to respond, and imagining a single person on screen to ease the pressure of a large audience. For hardware, he prefers a camera at eye level, even if that means raising a regular laptop on books, avoids a bright window behind the speaker, lights the face from the front, and favours a wired connection with a backup internet provider. For content, he argues that slides should be sparse, with around three points per slide, and that breakout rooms keep longer online sessions from losing listeners.

He closes by restating the three pillars of comfort, hardware and inspiring content, and encourages attendees to practise their virtual talks in front of friends or colleagues.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Production profiling with JDK Flight Recorder & JDK Mission Control
talks.teaser: Shows how to use JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control to profile Java applications in production with low overhead.
talks.summary:
The speaker introduces JDK Flight Recorder (JFR), a recording engine built into the JVM and designed for production use. It captures JVM and application events with very low overhead. JFR has been open source since OpenJDK 11 and was backported to OpenJDK 8 in later updates. Recording templates control which events are captured and how often, and the talk describes the default template as under one percent overhead and the profile template as under two percent.

The command-line demo starts a Spring PetClinic application with a recording enabled, then uses jcmd to manage recordings on the running process. The jfr tool summarises a dump by event type and prints thread park events with their stack traces, which can be exported as JSON. In JDK Mission Control, the automated analysis flags time spent at safepoints and in garbage collection, and an allocation view shows the most heavily allocated classes. A code demo using the Mission Control core library filters monitor-enter events, averages their durations and exports sampled stacks to a flame graph.

The talk also covers custom events added through the Java API, which can carry values such as a trace span ID so they line up with the same timestamps as other JFR data and help correlate long-running spans with JVM behaviour. Disabled events are optimised away by the JIT. The GMC agent, an incubating project, can insert events into existing classes at runtime through instrumentation without recompiling. The talk closes with pointers to the Mission Control mailing list, a Slack channel and a tutorial.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Into the Spring
talks.teaser: Explains how Spring Boot starts an application, from environment setup and listeners to bean creation and context refresh.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a fictional story about a new developer asked to make an auto-configuration apply only when a profile is missing, which turns out to be harder in a multi-tenant design. The speaker then traces how Spring grew from hand-written object creation and factories to dependency injection and a full container, and why startup slows as auto-configurations accumulate.

The core walk-through follows the startup sequence. The run method loads entries from spring.factories, creates application listeners, and merges the environment through environment post-processors. It then builds an application, servlet, reactive or plain context. Bean definitions come from configuration classes and auto-configurations, with conditional annotations deciding what gets registered. Beans are created in phases, and post-processors run as a chain, so code in a post-construct hook can see a context that is not yet finished. To find slow parts, the speaker used Spring Boot's startup tracing, converted the JSON events into a flame graph with a converter he wrote, and recommended async-profiler for finer detail.

The main takeaways are that synchronous listeners can slow startup or stop it when they throw, that annotations behave differently depending on the phase in which they are processed, and that knowing the framework's internals makes slow or broken startups easier to diagnose.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Jak działa Garbage Collector i jak go dobrać do aplikacji?
talks.teaser: Explains how Java garbage collectors reclaim memory, compares the collectors available, and guides choosing one for an app.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by Jacek Bosiacki, explains what a garbage collector does in a Java virtual machine. Objects that no longer have references stay on the heap until the collector finds and frees them, usually by marking live objects and then sweeping or compacting memory. The speaker walks through the generational model, where short-lived objects sit in a young generation with Eden and survivor spaces, while long-lived objects are promoted to the old generation. He explains why collection is split into minor and full passes.

Next, the collectors are compared: Serial, Parallel, CMS, G1, and ZGC, which the speaker presents as arriving with Java 17. For each one he covers how pauses are handled, which threads do the work, and where it fits best, such as older single-threaded machines with little memory for Serial, or very large heaps with strict latency needs for ZGC. He also notes that finalize is deprecated, that try-with-resources and phantom references are safer alternatives, and he advises against calling System.gc() in production.

To illustrate the trade-offs, the speaker ran a benchmark that allocates many strings across heap sizes of 1 GB, 4 GB and 16 GB. With the smallest heap, the application spent most of its time collecting, while larger heaps gave the collectors room to work. The takeaway is to test the collector against the real workload, size the heap with object sizes and region sizes in mind, and enable GC logging to see what the collector actually does.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Moje serce bije w innym takcie niż w scrum booku napisane macie
talks.teaser: Argues that software estimates are inherently random and that agile rituals often drift into harmful, numbers-driven habits.
talks.summary:
This Polish-language talk from JDD 2021 is a critical look at how software teams estimate work and run agile rituals. It opens with a popular monkey-and-ladder story, which the speaker says has no documentation behind it, and uses it as a metaphor for teams that learn to avoid pain without understanding why. The core claim is that estimates are random variables, so treating them as precise promises is a mistake. Software is compared with construction, where repetition is far higher and estimates tend to hold better.

The middle section gives examples of how estimation goes wrong. Berlin Brandenburg airport, first planned to open in 2011, slipped repeatedly and opened only in 2020, with its budget exceeded many times. Closer to home, the speaker describes planning poker debates that waste hours, sprint planning that fills capacity like Tetris, and velocity treated as a target rather than a measurement. He also covers meta-work such as building frameworks and libraries that delays delivery of what users need, and the pressure to trade quality for speed, which he argues costs more within weeks.

The closing takeaways are practical. Estimates are useful mainly for fixed-price bids and large decisions, so small tasks need not be estimated precisely. Scope, time and quality should be balanced deliberately and revisited over the life of a project. Problems and disasters should be communicated openly so that affected people can plan. Finally, the speaker warns against forcing people into metric-driven motivation, which he says distorts work and leads to burnout.

talks.title: JDD 2021: What I wish I knew when I started designing systems years ago
talks.teaser: Explains how to pick what a system should optimize for, weigh monoliths against microservices, and draw module boundaries.
talks.summary:
The speaker looks back on designing a large enterprise system as a student and argues that poor architecture usually traces back to weak management, not careless engineers. No design is good or bad on its own; it only fits when it suits what the system is optimized for. Teams should agree on one to three goals, such as maintainability and extensibility, or flexibility for a startup that expects to pivot.

He compares three styles: the modular monolith, synchronous microservices with independent deployment, and event-based systems. A monolith carries deployment risk and a broken window effect when developers are average, and its technology is hard to change. Microservices bring eventual consistency, devops ownership, shared tooling, observability, and consumer-driven contracts in place of end-to-end tests. He defines a module as a vertical slice built around one process, with a single public API, its own data, and hidden internals, and suggests splitting modules only when the people building the parts need different knowledge.

For data that other modules need, he recommends local read models built from events, so queries require no remote calls. Events are preferred over commands for large multi-team systems, and choreography over orchestration. Finally, applications with different non-functional requirements should be split, as in a vaccination registration system where public sign-ups and nurse access needed different service levels. His takeaway: decide what you optimize for, write it down, and draw boundaries around processes.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Umiejętności miękkie Storming Troopera
talks.teaser: Shows developers how to talk with business stakeholders using personality-pattern ideas and event storming questions.
talks.summary:
This talk from JDD 2021, given in Polish, sets aside technical content and covers general soft skills that help IT people when they work with business. It opens with a light story about a man whose family discourages his car purchase, using it to show that people filter the same situation differently. The speaker then introduces meta-programs, habitual mental patterns such as moving toward goals or away from problems, and focusing on details or the big picture.

The middle applies these patterns to project meetings. Technical teams often answer business requests with objections, which managers may hear as negativity, so the speaker suggests defining a meeting's purpose at strategic, process and tactical levels first. He then walks through event storming: mapping a process on a wall as domain events, with one model for the current state and one for the desired state. Examples include a contract that is drafted and then approved, and a case where a contract template is checked outside the system. Asking what happens next, rather than asking about data structures, helps reveal gaps.

The closing part warns against jumping into design too early, since mixing analysis with solutions overloads a session and leads to tangled architectures. The speaker advises asking business people about behaviour and events, and checking whether an event carries real information. He points to an earlier talk on microservice anti-patterns and concludes that the technique is useful until a team can skip it.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Refactoring Disasters - A Story how I failed
talks.teaser: Shows how a Java PDF library swap from iText 5 to OpenPDF went wrong, and what the speaker learned from the API fallout.
talks.summary:
This talk follows a refactoring of a small Java PDF-generation library that went badly. The project relied on iText 5, which had reached end of life. The newer iText 7 carried licensing terms that did not suit an open-source project, so the speaker chose OpenPDF, a fork of iText 5 released under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, expecting fewer changes to the code.

To protect existing users, the work went onto a separate 2.2 branch. The speaker introduced a PdfRenderer interface with one implementation for iText and one for OpenPDF. The first obstacle was that the PDF reader classes from the two libraries sat in different packages and had different methods, so the old methods were marked deprecated. Overloads that differed only by return type could not coexist, which forced a rename from readDocument to loadDocument. Converting HTML to PDF also needed extra helper libraries and a small helper class. The speaker checked the result with JUnit 5 unit tests and generated a sample document to confirm the output.

The closing advice is to make such changes on a dedicated branch, adapt and run the existing tests, and hide third-party library types behind plain Java interfaces or wrappers. Use semantic versioning so consumers can see that a major version brings API changes. Finally, group breaking changes into infrequent releases so users are not forced to adapt every time.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Practical Domain Driven Design using Clean Architecture patterns & TDD
talks.teaser: Shows how to turn customer requirements into DDD diagrams and hexagonal architecture code using test-driven development.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through a to-do list application built for a fictional startup to show how domain-driven design fits with clean architecture. It begins with the three DDD goals of strategic, tactical and architecture design, then compares layered styles such as hexagonal, onion and entity-control-boundary. The speaker argues that requirements should be worked out with the customer before any code is written. Use case diagrams expose open questions, such as how sharing should work, whether validation must run on both client and server, and why a completed item cannot be edited.

The design is then turned into a model. A rich to-do aggregate exposes behaviour methods, value objects such as title and due date encapsulate their own rules, and events are returned as operation results rather than business exceptions. Ports and adapters keep the domain free of transport and storage details, so use case classes depend only on interfaces. Development follows test-driven development: empty test scenarios for creation, rejection of expired due dates and overly long titles are written first, and only the minimal structures needed to pass them are built. Domain tests need no mocks.

The closing takeaways are to model the domain before coding, which lets other layers be built in parallel, and to apply DDD only where the domain is complex. For simple CRUD applications, the speaker suggests that anemic models and a lighter approach are enough.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Releasing At The Speed of Light
talks.teaser: Shows how an open source Java tool automates releasing binaries to git hosts, package managers and announcement channels.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces JReleaser, an open source tool for releasing Java projects. The speaker starts with the gap between building binaries and getting them into users' hands. A zip file on a web page is not enough when people install software through Homebrew, Scoop, SDKMAN, Snapcraft or Chocolatey, and when releases also need checksums, signatures, release notes and announcements. The tool grew out of GoReleaser for Go and the distribution work done for JBang, combined into one tool that works for any Java project.

The tool reads a model file describing the project and where its releases should go. The demo ran a simple command line application through several steps: a release with a generated changelog on GitHub, then a formatted changelog with category labels, checksums, PGP signatures and a Homebrew formula pushed to a repository. The same setup was then repeated for GitLab and Codeberg by changing only the target. The speaker also covered jlink runtimes, native images, Maven and Gradle plugins, Docker images and GitHub Actions support.

The closing section covered planned work, such as more Git services, cloud storage targets like Amazon S3 and jpackage integration. The main takeaway is that a single declarative model can drive release steps that are often spread across scripts. The speaker encouraged attendees to file issues for any gaps they find in open source tools.

talks.title: JDD 2021: The Killer C’s: Coupling, Cohesion, and Complexity
talks.teaser: Explores how coupling, cohesion and complexity shape software design, and when each helps or harms a system.
talks.summary:
Michael Nygard frames software design around three forces he calls the killer Cs: coupling, cohesion and complexity. He argues that none is purely harmful or helpful. Coupling creates structure and enables change while limiting it, and he illustrates this with mechanical linkages and physics before splitting it into operational, development, semantic, functional and incidental kinds. Using an editor's position interface, he shows how shared names spread change across modules, and how type systems and plain text search change how visible that coupling is.

On cohesion, he traces how one change, such as adding a birthday field, cuts across every layer of a conventional architecture and erodes its boundaries. He presents ports-and-adapters architecture as a way to keep domain concepts in one core, with adapters translating to databases and interfaces. Complexity, he says, grows through dynamic processes: options built with interfaces and factories can limit later change, and slow deployments push teams toward larger, riskier releases in a feedback loop.

He suggests spotting erosion with tools such as design structure matrices and commit analysis across layers, and reducing complexity by drawing larger boundaries first, removing special cases, replacing code with data, using anti-corruption layers and the strangler pattern, and keeping code small. The forces cannot be eliminated, he concludes, but developers have more control over them than they might think.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Query your codebase using CodeQL
talks.teaser: Shows how CodeQL lets developers query a codebase like data and trace tainted input flows to vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
Benjamin Muskalla, a GitHub engineer working on CodeQL's Java support, starts with the wider context: the GitHub Security Lab, supply chain attacks, and GitHub features such as secret scanning, security advisories and dependency updates. He then shows how code scanning is enabled through a generated GitHub Action, and how alerts appear in the security tab with CWE details and commit history. The demo alert is a Java servlet that passed request parameters into command execution without validation.

A research case follows: a GitHub Security Lab researcher found several remote command execution flaws in an Apache open-source project and used CodeQL to trace attack paths before reporting them. Muskalla notes that once one instance of a bug pattern is understood, a query can generalize it, as with a Linux kernel issue where a similar query surfaced about a dozen more. He explains that CodeQL extracts syntax trees, types, and control flow into a database, queried with a declarative language built on from, where and select clauses. VS Code examples then cover basic queries over methods and calls.

The final section covers data flow: sources where outside data enters, sinks where it causes harm, and barriers such as validation that stop flows. Taint tracking follows data through transformations, for example when a string is wrapped in lists and converted to bytes. Built-in remote flow sources, such as those in Apache Commons IO, show where external input enters a system. He closes by pointing to CodeQL learning resources, a workshop on finding vulnerabilities, and the open-source query repository for contributions.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Objective swiss army knife
talks.teaser: Shows Java collection wrappers, visitor pattern, and factory-based decorators for untangling tangled code.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a common developer habit, reusing existing collections everywhere, often leads to duplicated stream code and unclear behaviour. Using a sample Scrum domain with teams and boards, the speaker shows how a typed wrapper around Java collections can hold sorting, lookup and filtering methods in one place. This removes duplicates and makes it clear whether results keep an order or allow repeats. The trade-offs are covered too: wrappers need conversion for external libraries, and a wrapper can end up knowing too much.

For inheritance, the speaker separates designs where the number of subclasses is fixed, so changes mostly add functionality, from open designs such as frameworks, where new subclasses keep appearing. In a goal-tracking example with handwritten and task-based goals, instanceof checks and illegal-argument fallbacks are replaced with the visitor pattern, so the compiler flags any missing implementation. For plugin-style extension points, a single interface that returns every required service lets the IDE guide implementers, instead of them remembering several separate components.

The last section covers untangling concerns in an action service that mixes timing, configuration checks, security and the core calculation. Using a factory, a placeholder action for unavailable actions, and proxies for security, logging and caching, each concern is separated so the core calculation stays easy to test. The speaker admits the factory can become a dumping ground for messy logic. The takeaway is to apply these patterns only when they clearly make the code better.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Games People Play, or How to Understand Hidden Structures (...)
talks.teaser: Introduces transactional analysis as a lens on hidden patterns in workplace communication and recurring psychological games.
talks.summary:
Kamil Rogulski introduces transactional analysis, a theory Eric Berne developed in the 1960s to describe how people communicate. He explains that everyone moves between three ego states, parent, adult and child, and that these states show up in body language, gestures, tone of voice and word choice. He suggests noticing your own state and those of colleagues, for example by reading the mood of a meeting seen through a glass wall.

The middle of the talk covers transactions. A message sent from one ego state tends to draw a reply from a predictable state, often outside conscious awareness. The speaker then describes psychological games: repeated sequences of exchanges that look rational on the surface but carry a hidden purpose. One social example is a party or break-room game where people try to top each other with frightening injury stories. A household example is a game where a spilled cup is blamed on the other person. He links such games to a wider life script formed in childhood, and describes a workplace stereotype of the nerd as someone who mostly sits in the parent and child states.

The talk ends with the main way out of games: answering from the adult state and inviting the other person into an adult-to-adult exchange. The speaker stresses that parent and child states still have their place, using a firefighter evacuating a building as an example. The takeaway is a framework he argues underlies many soft-skills books, along with practice in spotting one's own states.

talks.title: JDD 2021: Clean Valley
talks.teaser: Shows how functional programming in Kotlin, with pure functions and immutable data, helps developers write code with fewer bugs.
talks.summary:
The speaker, presenting in Polish with English slides, argues for functional programming in Kotlin as a way to write code that can go to production on a Friday without fear. He defines pure functions as deterministic, total and free of side effects, using simple examples: an addition is pure, while a function that waits or writes a log line is not. He treats logging as practically harmless. He then covers immutability, showing how data classes remove Java boilerplate and how copy-based updates and persistent collections stay efficient despite looking like copies.

Type inference and expression-style functions are presented as ways to cut noise without losing safety. The main example is an order domain with created, paid and delivered states, where the total of paid and delivered orders is computed with a fold. When a new state is added, the compiler flags the missing branch instead of letting a wrong total reach production. A second example shows a duplicate delivery caused by a later change. Wrapping the side effect in a deferred container, with flatMap, makes it run once at the end. The trade-off is that a forgotten effect can silently never run, but such mistakes are easier to find in testing.

For adoption, he suggests going step by step: banning loops, vars and functions that return nothing through an IDE plugin, and using private constructors so objects can only be created in valid states. He prefers plain Kotlin over more complex type systems because it is easier to persuade teams, and says most people who go far enough are happy with the result.

talks.title: JDD 2021: How to create cache for high volume online data (...)
talks.teaser: Explains a multi-cluster Elasticsearch cache built for banking, covering failover, data sync and production problems.
talks.summary:
Andrzej Augustynowicz presents how his team built a high-volume cache for a banking system on Elasticsearch. He starts with the goals: fast reads, high availability, scalability, reliable data synchronization and migration from older applications. He also explains how the team was formed from outside experts, an internal group and paid vendor support, and how that support relationship developed after a limited first launch.

The architecture uses three independent clusters, two Elasticsearch and one Oracle, each fed by its own data writer so that one cluster can be upgraded at a time. Data packages carry headers with sequence information, and an assurance journal triggers retransmission when packages are missing or broken. Document versions keep older packages from overwriting newer data, and tombstone records mark deletions. The data reader routes queries with session-aware, active-passive or forced strategies and uses health checks to fail over between clusters, falling back to Oracle with reduced search features when needed.

Production testing exposed several issues: sorting on the default id field had to be replaced with a dedicated field, deep pagination beyond 10,000 documents consumed too much memory, a very large index had to be split into time-based indices, and accumulated tombstones called for a vacuuming process. The main takeaway is that index layout and shard design must be tested against real query samples, since no single configuration fits every application.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Cezary Walenciuk - .NET 6, ASP.NET Core i inny styl programowania
talks.teaser: Covers .NET 6 BCL additions, LINQ and JSON updates, minimal ASP.NET Core hosts, and C# 10 style for leaner apps.
talks.summary:
The session opens with .NET 6 runtime speed versus earlier releases and a simple BenchmarkDotNet modulo benchmark, then shifts to concrete library changes. The speaker demos guards and diagnostics such as argument checks, process path helpers, cryptographic random generation, periodic timers, low-level collection utilities, priority queues, date-only and time-only types, bit helpers, capacity tuning, chunking, and LINQ methods keyed by properties, plus indexing ranges, async timeouts, parallel HTTP fetches, and richer System.Text.Json options including ordering, cycle breaking, node APIs, converters, validation hooks, and async streaming serialization.

The middle and closing parts focus on minimal hosting and language ergonomics. File-scoped namespaces, implicit usings, and slimmer Visual Studio templates replace older boilerplate; Program.cs-centric ASP.NET Core samples show map routes, dependency injection, and optional endpoint-definition classes instead of controllers. A short SignalR server and client illustrate streaming with little code.

C# 10 topics include records on structs, improved property paths, string constant placeholders, sealed overrides, and preview static abstract interface members. The speaker argues minimal APIs can start faster than controller stacks when measured carefully, and points listeners to further material on Visual Studio 2022 and related learning resources.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Christos Matskas - Build secure apps with the Microsoft Identity platform
talks.teaser: Shows how to add Microsoft identity platform sign-in to .NET web apps and APIs instead of building authentication from scratch.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the cost of stolen credentials. The speaker cites a projected 6.5 trillion dollars in cybercrime damage for 2021 and argues that attackers increasingly log in with stolen passwords rather than break software, helped by password reuse. The speaker's own attempt to build a login system grew from a three-day task into months of hardening. The talk also recommends passwordless sign-in with an authenticator app or FIDO keys where providers allow it.

The middle section covers the Microsoft identity platform, which serves work accounts in Azure Active Directory, personal Microsoft accounts, and external consumer users through Azure AD B2C, built on open standards such as OpenID Connect. A live .NET 6 web app was set up with the Microsoft Identity Web library, an app registration, a client ID, a tenant ID and a redirect URI, and sign-in worked after a consent prompt. A Blazor WebAssembly front end then called a protected API; a deliberately wrong scope returned a 403 until the permission was corrected. A short Graph Explorer demo showed how to query user data.

The main takeaway is not to build your own identity system when an established provider can do the work. Developers should register redirect URIs exactly, have APIs check that tokens carry the required scopes, and rely on platform features such as multi-factor authentication and conditional access without writing custom code.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Wojciech Ciemski - Dlaczego będziesz musiał zająć się bezpieczeństwem?
talks.teaser: Maps why coding implies protecting data, from team design questions through OWASP lists to CIS hardening for running systems.
talks.summary:
The session opens by reframing the title question for people who build software, especially those still early in programming. It argues that applications exist chiefly to process information entrusted to the organization, so treating security as someone else’s job is unrealistic when design choices determine whether data stays confidential, intact, and appropriately available.

The middle section turns to practical habits before the first lines of code: structured team conversations about encryption, access, logging, password storage, incident handling, documentation, backups, monitoring, and vulnerability scanning. It introduces OWASP Top 10 as a risk-ranked catalog of common web weaknesses, separates weakness, vulnerability, and risk in plain terms, and names additional references such as API and serverless top-ten lists, CWE Top 25, bounty-driven findings, SAMM, and ASVS as ways to grow depth over time.

The closing stretch widens the lens beyond the application layer to DevOps realities—patch levels, server stacks, and operating environments—and recommends CIS Benchmarks as a concrete system-hardening path. It ends on a single practitioner theme: security is a continuous process, not a one-time milestone, and developers should keep learning as business and everyday life keep pushing new demands onto the software they ship.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Oskar Dudycz - Nigdy więcej nie trać danych, czyli Event Sourcing na ratunek!
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for 4Dev Live 2021: Oskar Dudycz - Nigdy więcej nie trać danych, czyli Event Sourcing na ratunek!.
talks.summary: Oskar Dudycz demos event sourcing with a shopping-cart stream: past-tense events, aggregate When handlers in C#, optimistic concurrency on append, and rebuildable read models. He shows EventStoreDB append semantics, JSON upcasts for renamed fields, stream compaction via shorter lifecycles, and basket analytics such as beer-and-apple confidence metrics, arguing event stores preserve audit history relational updates erase.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Damian Antonowicz - .NET MAUI - ewolucja czy rewolucja?
talks.teaser: It walks through .NET MAUI platform support, major features beyond Xamarin.Forms, and how teams can start migrating today.
talks.summary:
.NET MAUI is presented as the successor to Xamarin.Forms: a framework for building native mobile and desktop applications from shared C# code. The talk opens with a short history of Xamarin from 2014 through Microsoft’s acquisition and the gradual retirement of older Xamarin-side services, then situates MAUI at Preview 9 on .NET 6. Target platforms include iOS, Android, macOS via Mac Catalyst, Windows via WinUI 3, Samsung Tizen, and community-supported Linux, with GA pushed to the following year and Xamarin.Forms supported for one year after MAUI ships.

The middle of the session contrasts Xamarin’s multi-project solutions with MAUI’s single-project model, explains handlers as the replacement for custom renderers (faster startup, simpler platform tweaks via property mappers), and covers generic-host app configuration, hot reload, experimental BlazorWebView, control readiness on GitHub, and experimental MAUI Graphics plus vendor UI stacks wired through handlers. Getting started today means Visual Studio 2022 Preview with the right workloads; Windows needs extra steps, and VS Code remains experimental.

For practitioners, MVVM stays central, with experimental Comet illustrating MVU in pure C#. Migration keeps familiar XAML, shifts namespaces, reuses compatible NuGet packages, adopts a MAUI Community Toolkit build, folds Essentials into the framework, and treats single-project layout as optional. Custom renderers can remain via compatibility registration; effects move into unified files with platform conditionals. Upgrade Assistant is preview but aimed at automating much of the move. The closing guidance favors Xamarin.Forms for new work until MAUI’s experimental pieces mature at general availability.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Daniel Lewiński - How to get out of the behavior tree forest?
talks.teaser: Compares game AI techniques from state machines and behavior trees to utility AI, planners, MCTS, and hybrids.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that behavior trees dominate game AI because they are easy to tool and assemble, yet large trees become painful to extend, memory-hungry, and CPU-heavy. A cited Division-scale example illustrates how a single new action can demand days of work, which motivates looking beyond the default hammer.

The speaker walks from simplest to most complex: finite state machines for small automata such as tower-defense turrets; behavior trees and their node types for scripted foes; utility AI with considerations, curves, and aggregators for emergent tactical choices; GOAP and HTN task networks for forward planning and routines; and Monte Carlo tree search for competitive or board-like play. Game references span Halo, Far Cry, The Sims, F.E.A.R., Kingdom Come: Deliverance, Killzone, and Horizon Zero Dawn. Grail work at the studio is used to show utility plus GOAP and MCTS hybrids with valuation heuristics when horizons are cut short.

Neural networks are treated cautiously for in-game decision-making because prototypes change too often, though uses such as Drivatar-style imitation and low-level unit control in strategy titles are noted. The closing guidance maps finite state machines to trivial automata, behavior trees to disposable enemies, utility AI to active agents and bosses, planners to rich environmental interaction, and MCTS to opponents that must try to win.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Konrad Kokosa - Rewolucja w .NET 6 i dalej
talks.teaser: Surveys .NET 6 performance wins, custom interpolated string handlers, source generators, and async file I/O for working developers.
talks.summary:
The session positions .NET 6 as a broad speed-up across the runtime and frameworks, while noting that Stephen Toub’s “what’s new” write-up is enormous and easy to skim past. The speaker contrasts a syntax-focused overview with a practical performance lens: many gains arrive automatically after upgrading, but specialists still benefit from reading the detailed notes.

The core depth is interpolated strings. In older releases, interpolation could box values and allocate temporary arrays; .NET 6 rewrites the default handler to build results incrementally with fewer allocations. The talk walks through custom `InterpolatedStringHandler` types, using structured logging as the motivating case so expensive string work is skipped when log levels filter messages out, including stack-based handlers and compile-time `IsEnabled` checks.

Later segments cover JSON source generators replacing reflection, faster `System.Random` and thread-safe shared instances, thread-pool behavior when pools saturate on awaits, truly asynchronous file APIs (with platform caveats on Linux), profile-guided optimization, and experimental GC regions. The close emphasizes optional, experimental tuning and points listeners to official articles for follow-up reading.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Alexander Egurnov - Testing in Go with Ginkgo and Gomega
talks.teaser: Shows how Ginkgo and Gomega structure Go tests, and which testing mistakes to avoid as a suite grows.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the problem of testing Go services. Writing tests in another language doubles the tooling and skills a team must maintain, and such suites often depend on one person. The speaker compares the standard testing package with testify, which adds assertions, mocks and suites but keeps much boilerplate. Ginkgo is then introduced as a framework that builds a tree of nested specs with setup and teardown hooks, and Gomega as an assertion library that works on its own and accepts custom matchers.

The middle of the talk covers choosing a tool as a test suite grows. The speaker's team uses the standard library and testify for unit and integration tests, and reserves Ginkgo and Gomega for larger, end-to-end style tests. The talk shows focus and pending prefixes, output control, and matchers such as eventually and consistently for asynchronous code. Common mistakes are walked through: float and integer comparisons, passing a result instead of a function to eventually, loop and shared variables captured by closures, panics in goroutines, and goroutines that outlive their test.

The speaker reports more than two years of using these libraries. Tests became easier to read and reuse, but the pitfalls are real and complexity can hurt readability in large suites. Practical advice is to write several kinds of tests, choose tools per job, start with a test that fails before making it pass, and avoid making tests harder than the code they check.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Karol Horosin - CI/CD and tooling for standard Python projects
talks.teaser: Guidance configures GitHub Actions for Python linting, tests, coverage, packaging, published docs, and pipeline notifications.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that new and legacy Python projects often skip a solid delivery workflow until manual checks become painful. Drawing on internal surveys and repeated project setup at Ardigen, the speaker outlines a practical baseline: automate repetitive quality work so developers focus on code rather than command-line cleanup.

The core demo is a small installable wallet package with fixtures and pytest coverage. A compact GitHub Actions workflow runs on pushes to the main branch across a matrix of Python 3.7 through 3.9 on Ubuntu. Steps include dependency install, flake8 (hard failures on syntax and critical issues, warnings on style), pytest with pytest-cov, uploading coverage to Codecov for trend tracking, mypy for static typing, setuptools builds, optional PyPI publish via tokens, Sphinx documentation built and pushed to GitHub Pages, and Slack-style notifications through repository secrets. The speaker also stresses pre-commit so the same checks block bad commits locally, notes GitLab CI parallels, and closes with Docker login, image build, and push as a follow-on pattern plus pointers toward fuzz-based test generation for coverage without exhaustive hand-written cases.

Takeaways for practitioners: copy a boilerplate workflow, run tests on every branch where possible, treat falling coverage as a review signal, and wire notifications so failures surface outside the Actions UI. Publishing and deployment steps can be trimmed or extended—SSH restarts, containers, or cloud deploys—without changing the overall lint-test-analyze-build rhythm.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Miłosz Kusiciel - Python 3.10 to strzał w dziesiątkę. Co nowego w kolejnej odsłonie?
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of 4Dev Live 2021: Miłosz Kusiciel - Python 3.10 to strzał w dziesiątkę. Co nowego w kolejnej odsłonie?.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Prezentacja prowadzona przez Miłosza Kusiciela podczas konferencji 4Developers omawia kluczowe nowości wprowadzone w wydaniu Python 3.10. Prelegent analizuje zmiany składniowe, ułatwienia w debugowaniu oraz ewolucję języka w odniesieniu do wcześniejszych wersji (Python 3.8 i 3.9). Szczególny nacisk położono na wprowadzenie mechanizmu Structural Pattern Matching (`match` i `case`) oraz na kwestię gotowości ekosystemu i bibliotek do wdrożeń produkcyjnych.

### Key Topics
- **Cykl wydawniczy Pythona**: Dążenie do corocznych, przewidywalnych wydań (październikowa premiera 3.10 oraz stan prac nad wersją 3.11 Alpha).
- **Usprawnienia składni menedżerów kontekstu**: Możliwość grupowania wielu wywołań `with` przy użyciu nawiasów.
- **Precyzyjne komunikaty o błędach**: Znaczne ulepszenia parsera w raportowaniu błędów składniowych (`SyntaxError`) oraz podpowiedzi dotyczące literówek w nazwach zmiennych.
- **Uproszczenie typowania unii**: Zastąpienie `Union[int, float]` natywnym operatorem `|` (pipe), działającym także z `isinstance()`.
- **Structural Pattern Matching**: Nowa konstrukcja `match`/`case` jako potężniejsze rozwinięcie tradycyjnych instrukcji switch-case.
- **Pojęcie „soft keywords”**: Kontekstowe słowa kluczowe w Pythonie i ich wpływ na kompatybilność istniejącego kodu.
- **Wsparcie frameworków i ekosystemu**: Stan integracji Pythona 3.10 z Django (od wersji 3.2), FastAPI, Flaskiem oraz dostępność oficjalnych obrazów Dockerowych.

### Technical Details
- **Parenthesized Context Managers**: W Pythonie 3.10 instrukcja `with` pozwala na obejmowanie wielu menedżerów kontekstu nawiasami okrągłymi, ułatwiając wieloliniowe, czytelne formatowanie bez używania ukośników odwróconych.
- **Diagnostyka błędów**: Komunikaty interpretera dokładnie wskazują brakujące dwukropki, niedomknięte nawiasy klamrowe, brakujące przecinki w słownikach czy błędne użycie pojedynczego znaku `=` w warunkach `if`. Dodatkowo wprowadzono sugestie "did you mean" przy literówkach w nazwach zmiennych.
- **Type Hinting**: Wprowadzono syntax `int | float` zamiast konieczności importowania modułu `typing` i stosowania zapisu `Union[int, float]`.
- **Match-Case i dopasowywanie wzorców**: W przeciwieństwie do tradycyjnego `switch` z innych języków (takich jak JavaScript czy Java), mechanizm ten w Pythonie realizuje dekonstrukcję struktur danych (krotek, list, słowników, instancji klas). Symbol `_` pełni funkcję domyślnego dopasowania (wildcard). Klauzule `case` obsługują warunki strażników (`if`), operatory alternatywy `|` oraz dynamiczne wiązanie zmiennych wewnątrz wzorca. Prelegent zaznacza, że konstrukcja `match` nie zapewnia zysku wydajnościowego względem tradycyjnych `if/elif`.
- **Soft Keywords**: `match` i `case` nie są zarezerwowanymi słowami kluczowymi, co zapobiega psuciu istniejącego kodu, w którym te nazwy były wcześniej używane jako identyfikatory zmiennych (np. przy operacjach na wyrażeniach regularnych).

### Takeaways
Python 3.10 przynosi istotne ułatwienia w codziennym pisaniu i debugowaniu kodu, przede wszystkim za sprawą czytelniejszych komunikatów błędów i rozbudowanego pattern matchingu. Mimo że oficjalne obrazy Dockerowe są już dostępne, a frameworki takie jak Django (od 3.2), FastAPI czy Flask wspierają nową wersję, prelegent zaleca ostrożność w migracjach produkcyjnych. Najbezpieczniejszym podejściem jest weryfikacja kompatybilności wszystkich zewnętrznych bibliotek i testowanie nowych funkcjonalności w projektach pobocznych przed wdrożeniem w środowiskach komercyjnych.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Rafał Bigaj - Build Knative controllers in Golang for Tekton tasks with ease
talks.teaser: A walkthrough shows how Knative reconcilers extend Tekton with lightweight custom tasks tied to external batch jobs.
talks.summary:
The session opens with MLOps and why production AI needs monitoring, retraining, and checks for fairness, explainability, and robustness. The speaker illustrates adversarial image perturbations on CIFAR-10 with a ResNet model and IBM’s ART library, showing accuracy fall sharply under small epsilon values, then positions that robustness evaluation as a pipeline step rather than the main engineering goal.

The middle connects Kubeflow Pipelines, Tekton as a Kubernetes-native runtime (instead of Argo in IBM’s setup), and IBM Code Engine for heavy batch jobs. Tekton custom tasks avoid long-lived pods when only an external job’s status must be watched. The talk explains custom resources, reconciliation loops, informers, and why Knative fits Tekton’s ecosystem, using a Tekton CEL extension controller as a compact reconciler example.

The close implements a custom task operator that watches both the local Tekton cluster and Code Engine’s Kubernetes API, keeping the in-cluster footprint tiny while model training and adversarial evaluation run remotely. Demos compile Python Kubeflow DSL to Tekton YAML, run conditional CEL tasks, and complete a full ML pipeline whose evaluation logs report accuracy collapse under adversarial samples—supporting automated reactions such as retraining.

talks.teaser: Traces log search from grep and tail through Splunk and ELK to Loki, comparing the trade-offs of each approach.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that technology swings between centralised and decentralised approaches, and that requirements and pain points shift over time, so each solution trades one set of limitations for another. It then applies that view to log management. Tail and less work for one file, but once several servers or ephemeral containers produce logs, grep across hosts or copying files to one place becomes a fragile workaround.

The speaker walks through the centralised options. Splunk stores events with minimal structure and extracts fields at query time, which keeps ingestion cheap but makes searches slower, and the product can get expensive. The ELK stack parses and types fields at index time and uses an inverted index for full-text lookups, plus a second structure for filtering, sorting and aggregations. That makes queries fast but adds processing, disk and memory overhead. Grafana's Loki indexes only labels, groups log lines into chunks by stream and runs regular expressions over the matching chunks, which lowers storage cost but depends on choosing good labels.

The closing part notes that the products are converging. Elasticsearch is adding runtime fields for query-time extraction and turning off some features by default, while searchable snapshots on object storage cut costs for large volumes. The speaker warns against trusting vendor benchmarks and suggests judging options by the balance of features, speed and cost a team actually needs.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2021 - Ricardo Castro - Need help? Come to the Backstage
talks.teaser: A walkthrough demonstrates installing Backstage locally and using its catalog, TechDocs, and software templates.
talks.summary:
Organizations with sprawling microservices, mixed cloud and on-prem deployments, and many separate tools often waste time hunting for repositories, logs, metrics, CI jobs, and architecture diagrams—especially during incidents. The presentation frames those pain points—fragmented pipelines, weak standardization, and constant context switching—as motivation for a unified developer portal.

Backstage is introduced as Spotify’s open platform for building internal developer platforms, with a high-level architecture covering the core UI, TypeScript or JavaScript plugins (standalone, in-cluster backends, and third-party proxies), and persistence via Knex with SQLite for local work and PostgreSQL for production. The speaker scaffolds an app with the create-app flow, tours the service catalog and ownership metadata driven by catalog-info YAML, wires GitLab integration through app config, enables TechDocs with MkDocs-style docs beside code, and uses a software template plus the scaffolder and Cookiecutter to publish a new Go microservice with CI choices. Kubernetes integration is explicitly deferred.

Practitioners should leave with a concrete mental model of catalog registration, in-repo documentation surfaced on service pages, and template-driven scaffolding they can reproduce locally before extending plugins or deploying with containers and Helm.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2021 - Dave McAllister - The Whats and Whys of Distributed Tracing and...
talks.teaser: Explains how distributed tracing follows requests across microservices and how OpenTelemetry standardizes collecting that data.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the shift away from single servers toward microservices and elastic cloud environments. In those systems failures do not repeat in the same way, and an error reported in one service often originates in another, so teams need to see the path a request takes. The speaker explains that a trace is built from spans, each a unit of work, linked in parent-child relationships along a time series, and shows how tracing data sits alongside RED metrics and logs. A small e-commerce example walks through a front end calling a checkout service and an email service, where a 503 error appears in a different place from its cause.

The middle of the talk covers OpenTelemetry, which grew out of OpenTracing and OpenCensus and is a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project. The speaker describes its parts: APIs, SDKs that define how instrumentation behaves, and a collector that receives, processes and exports telemetry to any destination. Semantic conventions give common attribute names for HTTP, databases and messaging, and resource attributes identify things like Kubernetes pods and cloud functions. The speaker notes that the tracing specification had reached 1.0, metrics was in beta, and logging was still in incubation. A Kubernetes layout with a collector beside each pod is used to show how traces, metrics and logs can be correlated in one place.

The closing part gives practical guidance. Start tracing at service boundaries, calls between services and calls to third-party services and databases, and expect tooling to help with the volume. Auto-instrumentation libraries can be added without changing code, but the speaker warns against running two auto-instrumentation solutions on the same service because the results become unreliable. Correlated telemetry supports evidence-based debugging: begin with a high-level RED metric, drill into traces, then into logs, and act on what the evidence shows.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2021 - Pranjal Deo
talks.teaser: Shows how blameless postmortems turn outages into learning, covering templates, psychological safety and action-item follow-through.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that how a company handles failure shapes its future. After an incident, the on-call engineer first mitigates it and restores service, and the team then needs a formal way to stop the same problem from returning. The speaker defines a postmortem as a written record of an incident: its impact, the actions taken, the root cause, and follow-up actions. The practice is presented as useful well beyond large-scale technical teams, including for personal growth and for leaders explaining unpopular decisions.

The talk walks through a template: an executive summary with dates, duration and estimated user impact; background for newcomers; technical details on impact, root cause and recovery; a review of what went well, what did not, and where the team got lucky; action items with owners, priorities and tracking; and a glossary. Teams should agree on postmortem triggers before incidents happen. The central point is psychological safety. A blameless write-up assumes everyone acted in good faith with the information they had, and it focuses on what went wrong rather than who did wrong. A hypothetical postmortem that blamed one engineer is rewritten using objective facts and metrics, and the speaker notes that blame hides information and makes repeat failures more likely.

To build the culture, the speaker suggests that leaders write postmortems themselves and share them, run role-play exercises based on past incidents, and reward good write-ups and closed action items. Warning signs include lack of time, blameful language and disengagement, and unfinished action items invite repeat outages. The three takeaways are that failure is education, that postmortems should focus on systems rather than people, and that well-written, acted-upon and widely shared postmortems drive positive cultural change.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Kraków 2021 - Peter Varhol
talks.teaser: Argues that data needs DevOps-style pipelines and bias testing, since correlations in analytics and machine learning can mislead.
talks.summary:
Peter Varhol starts by tracing how computing attention moved from hardware to software and now to data, which he argues is the element that matters most today. He presents data ops as a way to apply DevOps-style principles to data: gathering, cleansing, standardizing and delivering information through automated, repeatable pipelines run by cross-functional teams. Real-time delivery replaces monthly reports, and stale or uncleaned data is described as worse than useless.

The middle of the talk turns to machine learning, which learns from data with known results and adjusts its internal parameters. Varhol warns that any dataset is only a sample of reality and can be biased in how it is selected or through how users interact with a system. He cites an Amazon recruiting tool trained on a decade of resumes from a largely male technical workforce, which learned to favour men and was dropped, and Microsoft's Tay chatbot, which absorbed abusive behaviour from users within about a day and was pulled. Software also treats every event as equal, unlike people who recognize when something matters, so human oversight stays important.

He closes by recommending proactive testing: anticipate bias and wrong answers, make sure training data represents the problem domain, and add edge cases that real life may produce but official tests miss. Test results can be used to model how a system behaves across many responses. He ends by stressing that data can support decisions but people remain responsible for them, especially when a response may be needed within seconds.
