talks.teaser: Combine small clues in domain names and certificate data to prioritize suspicious hosts for review.
talks.summary: The speaker describes simple ways to identify potentially malicious domains in streams of newly observed hostnames, using keyword matches, supporting words, name length and punctuation, inexpensive domain endings, certificate details, and hosting clues. Attendees learn how to combine these signals into a scoring flow for prioritizing domains for review, and why the speaker considers these checks sufficient for many common phishing cases without machine learning.

talks.title: CONFidence 2021: Behind the scenes of cyber solutions vendors (Insider info)
talks.teaser: Exposes security vendors that sold products with hardcoded alerts, manual analysis and forged test results.
talks.summary:
Yaniv Miron, a penetration tester and founder of security startups, describes real cases in which cybersecurity vendors sold products that did not work as advertised. In the first, a customer bypassed features at a large vendor, and a code review found an unexplained constant in a key function. The developer who wrote it did not know why it was there, and a colleague suggested simply trying another number. The speaker notes that deals with such products often run to 5 to 6 million dollars per installation.

The next cases follow the same pattern of misleading buyers. A bank CISO judged one product by its attractive interface, but the speaker found its statistics and alerts were hard-coded, so the tool did nothing, and he says investors knew this. Another vendor promised an AI engine that would analyse mirrored network traffic and suggest fixes, but staff sent the packets to the cloud, where one or two people reviewed them by hand. A competitor advertised 24 gigabit per second, a figure that came from total port capacity, while the machine could only process 2 gigabit per second.

The last case came from a former competitor employee, who said a vendor's proof-of-concept trials always succeeded because staff forged attacks and PDF reports. The vendor also insisted on constant remote access during trials. The speaker urges CISOs to challenge their tools with penetration tests and invites hackers to test such products and publish their findings.

talks.title: CONFidence 2021: The unfortunate journey of radio-protocol mistakes
talks.teaser: Shows how radio protocols for ships, industrial remote controls and key fobs can be spoofed, using software-defined radios.
talks.summary:
Radio protocols from the hardware era were built on the assumption that nobody would bother attacking them, and that assumption has aged badly. Software-defined radios now let almost anyone transmit forged signals cheaply. The speaker, presenting for a threat research team, uses several case studies from about five years of work to argue that developers still underestimate this risk.

The first case is AIS, the system large ships use to broadcast their position. Its specification says little about authentication or integrity, so the team built a transmitter in GNU Radio and displayed a fake vessel on nearby receivers. They also forged a proximity alert and a control message that pushed a target transponder onto another frequency, silencing it. Next came industrial radio remote controls. Without any protocol documentation, the researchers tapped the bus between the microcontroller and the radio chip, recovered the modulation, and replayed signals to move a toy crane and then a real crane on site.

Key fobs follow a similar arc: rolling codes replaced simple replay attacks, yet roll-jam techniques and timestamp schemes brought new weaknesses. The talk ends with a radio-based capture-the-signal contest run at conferences since 2018, whose tools are public so others can host their own. The takeaway is that radio device makers should assume attackers will come.

talks.title: CONFidence 2021: The Coming AI Hackers
talks.teaser: Argues that AI systems will find and exploit loopholes in social, economic and political systems at unprecedented speed and scale.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that artificial intelligence will soon hack not just computer systems but social, economic and political ones. It widens the idea of a hack to any clever use of a system's rules that its designers did not intend, citing tax loopholes, a curved hockey stick, mileage runs on frequent flyer programs and the filibuster. Machines already show this behaviour in AI capture-the-flag contests and game-playing systems that find unexpected strategies.

The speaker explains why such hacks may go unnoticed. Modern AI models are hard to explain, so a medical prediction system could reach conclusions that doctors cannot inspect or question. Reward hacking examples from simulations, such as a soccer agent kicking the ball out of bounds or a robot vacuum that learned to reverse because it had no rear sensors, show that systems optimise stated goals rather than intent. The Volkswagen emissions cheat is cited as a human-made case of the same pattern. Speed, scale and scope make AI hacking different in kind, with legal financial loopholes and bot-driven social media debate as examples.

The closing section argues that defence can benefit too. AI tools that find software bugs could let vendors patch code before release, and the same approach could test proposed laws for loopholes. The transition period is dangerous, and the talk concludes that societies need governing structures that can patch rules as quickly as software is patched.

talks.title: CONFidence 2021: Bitcoin is silver, compromise is gold... Sveva Vittoria Scenarelli
talks.teaser: Maps two North Korea-linked groups targeting crypto firms, from phishing lures and infrastructure pivots to Lazarus malware ties.
talks.summary:
The talk follows two intrusion sets that target cryptocurrency and financial companies and that the presenter's team assesses as likely North Korea-based. It opens with the background: Lazarus-linked thefts from exchanges since 2017, and a shift toward phishing aimed at crypto firms. The first group, tracked internally as black alicante and publicly known as dangerous password, sends password-protected archives holding a decoy link file. That file reaches a first-stage server and drops VBScript backdoors, with a fuller backdoor and the MSRAT payload deployed by hand against interesting victims.

The second group, tracked as black dev2 and reported as operation gold hunting, uses remote template injection in Office documents. The documents fetch a template that pulls a DLL out of an embedded image and injects it into a process. The presenter shows how shared document metadata, domain naming, passive DNS, reused certificates and server software versions let analysts pivot to more campaign infrastructure. Document timestamps, plotted in GMT+9, show activity that matches Korean working hours across 44 lure documents.

Shared MSRAT code and overlapping infrastructure lead the presenter to assess the first group as a subset of a Lazarus subgroup, with the second likely the same actor. The presenter stresses that malware alone is not enough for attribution. The practical takeaways are to hunt on initial access artifacts, pivot on infrastructure, and keep older Lazarus signatures, since code reuse keeps linking new samples to past operations.

talks.title: CONFidence 2021: Centrum kontroli odlotów czyli jakoś(ć) zarządzania...
talks.teaser: Outlines incident command, tight communication, and handoffs that replace ad hoc firefighting with repeatable response quality.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a datacenter outage in which one engineer spent six hours alone rewiring a failed router cluster while clients and management interrupted constantly—a story framed as how not to run incident response. It then argues for a shared definition of what counts as an incident, contrasting sensible triggers with environments that log thousands of trivial events per day and close everything automatically.

The core compares informal and highly formal response models, drawing on hierarchical command structures used at large technology firms. It walks through roles such as incident commander and operational officer, the separation of command from hands-on technical work, dedicated internal and external communicators, and practices like central task lists, no duplicate freelancing, escalation when stuck, and controlled use of conference calls during large responses.

Closing topics include structured sync meetings with repeat-back assignments, thorough handoffs between shifts, cycling through observe-orient-decide-act during active work, regulatory notification timelines, and a no-heroes team policy backed by documentation so any responder can step in without relying on a single expert.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Xamarin & Apps with Modern UI
talks.teaser: Bohdan Benetskyi investigates 4Developers 2021: Xamarin & Apps with Modern UI.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at 4Developers 2021, speaker Bohdan—a Microsoft MVP and .NET Foundation speaker—provides a comprehensive guide to building modern user interfaces using Xamarin.Forms. He discusses the current state of Xamarin and its upcoming evolution into .NET MAUI, outlines essential developer tools and community learning resources, and evaluates key NuGet packages and architectural frameworks. The session also walks through practical UI implementations inspired by modern design trends (including Neumorphism and complex animations) and concludes with pragmatic advice on mobile testing strategies.

### Key Topics
- **Xamarin.Forms vs. Xamarin Native and .NET MAUI**: Why developers should focus on Xamarin.Forms over native solutions in 2021, and why it is recommended to start with Xamarin.Forms while waiting for .NET MAUI to stabilize and for NuGet packages to be ported.
- **Tooling and IDEs**: Comparing Windows and macOS setups, highlighting Visual Studio with JetBrains ReSharper and JetBrains Rider, as well as the necessity of macOS environments for iOS builds.
- **Community Resources and Inspiration**: Recommending podcasts, newsletters (Weekly Xamarin), blogs, and YouTube channels such as those run by James Montemagno, Gerald Versluis, Kinfey Lo, and Dweek/Dribbble UI recreators.
- **Essential UI and Helper NuGet Packages**: Evaluating UI suites (Syncfusion, Telerik, DevExpress), core libraries (Xamarin.Essentials, Xamarin Community Toolkit), MVVM frameworks (MvvmCross, Prism, ReactiveUI), and specialized tools like PancakeView, SkiaSharp, MagicGradients, Lottie, and RGPlugins.Popup.
- **Modern UI Implementations**: Techniques for card flip animations, path-based vector shapes and clipping, dark mode support via AppThemeBinding, parallax scrolling, CSS styling vs. XAML StyleClass, and realistic mobile testing philosophies.

### Technical Details
- **MVVM Architecture**: Bohdan recommends established frameworks like MvvmCross or Prism for large enterprise apps, and lighter alternatives like FreshMvvm, MVVMLight, or Caliburn.Micro for smaller apps. Xamarin.Forms Shell is highlighted for unified navigation and routing, though integrating it with external MVVM frameworks can be challenging. For search scenarios needing rx throttling, the lightweight `debounce-windowing` package can replace the entire ReactiveUI dependency.
- **Vector Shapes and Gradients**: Path and Ellipse geometries provide reliable rendering and image clipping across Android and iOS without the sizing artifacts common to older `BoxView` half-radius workarounds. MagicGradients (built on SkiaSharp) parses complex CSS gradients and provides a web-based playground of 700+ designs that can be pasted directly into XAML.
- **Animation Mechanics**: Card flipping can be achieved using sequential rotations (`RotateTo(-90)`, swapping visibility, and rotating to `0`) and coordinating multiple animations using asynchronous tasks or `Task.WhenAll`. Lottie allows importing vector JSON animations with minimal boilerplate.
- **Styling Architecture**: Combining inline CSS or XAML `StyleClass` attributes is recommended over rigid, monolithic static resource styles, allowing granular utility-style composition without creating dozens of rigid named styles.

### Takeaways
Developers should focus on Xamarin.Forms version 5.0.0 for stability today and plan for an easy migration path to .NET MAUI once tooling matures. UI components should leverage community extensions like PancakeView, MagicGradients, and Sharpnado to deliver contemporary looks such as Neumorphism or glassmorphism. Finally, Bohdan cautions against dogmatic 100% test-driven development (TDD) or chasing full coverage in mobile UI code; instead, developers should target regression tests specifically to reproducible bugs in business logic or critical UI paths.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Projektowanie sieciowe aplikacji wielowarstwowych w oparciu o App Service, Grabarz
talks.teaser: Explains how to layer Azure App Service networking for multi-tier apps with access rules, VNet integration, and Private Link.
talks.summary:
The session addresses a common friction point with Azure App Service: deploying there once meant exposing workloads on the public internet, which is unacceptable for many line-of-business systems. After a brief recap of App Service as a managed PaaS and deployment models such as multi-tenant plans versus dedicated compute, the focus shifts to network design for layered applications that may include APIs, databases, or microservices.

The walkthrough progresses from simplest to more advanced controls. Access restrictions gate inbound traffic with IP allow and deny lists, service-type rules, and HTTP header checks, including patterns that force traffic through Front Door or a WAF. VNet integration pulls outbound traffic into a virtual network so the app can reach private databases, on-premises links, and peered networks, with notes on regional integration, dedicated integration subnets, route-all settings, and virtual-network access rules that let a public front end call a backend reachable only from inside the VNet. The speaker also covers service endpoints, the data-exfiltration risk when regional VNet integration is enabled too broadly, Private Link as an admin-controlled private entry path, private DNS for internal names, and NAT Gateway for predictable outbound addresses.

The close compares when an App Service Environment still matters versus Premium v3, and summarizes a practical stack: access restrictions for ingress, VNet integration for private egress, Private Link for private ingress, and optional NAT or firewall tiers for stricter outbound control.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Row, row, row your boat gently with the Flow - Łukasz Wojtach
talks.teaser: Shows how to write a custom buffering operator for Kotlin Flow, handling shared state and concurrency with channels.
talks.summary:
The talk treats Kotlin's Flow as a cold data stream, where nothing runs until a terminal operator such as collect starts it. Using thousands of offer IDs as an example, the speaker contrasts a list, which is fully processed before taking three items, with a flow, where elements pass one at a time and downstream can stop early so only three offers are fetched. He also shows how a map operator differs on a list and on a flow.

The central case is a batching operator. A colleague needs analytics events from an Android app sent in periodic packages, and Kotlin has no built-in buffer operator. The first version groups elements by size with a local accumulator that is emitted as a copy and then cleared. Grouping by time is harder, because a timer and incoming events run concurrently and can race on one mutable list. Options include thread-safe collections, mutexes that are easy to misplace and can deadlock, and confining state to a single thread. He settles on an actor-like design: a producer coroutine feeds a channel, and a consumer drains it on each interval and emits the batch.

The resulting operator is short, is used in production, and inherits backpressure and error handling from the Flow API. The takeaway is that writing a custom operator is less daunting than it seems when no standard one fits, but concurrent operators need deliberate design, and a channel can keep shared state confined.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Architektura aplikacji w React.js Czyli poszukiwania świętego Graala
talks.teaser: Presents practical conventions for organising a React app's files, styles, tests, API calls and authentication.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles React application architecture, a subject broad enough to fill many presentations, so the speaker narrows it to the questions beginners ask most: where files belong, how to organise components, styles, tests and utilities, and how to handle authentication and API calls. He contrasts the vague advice to shuffle files until they feel right with Ruby on Rails' convention-over-configuration approach.

The middle of the talk gives concrete conventions. Small projects can keep everything in one place, while growing ones group files by type and place each component in its own folder, with its styles beside it and test files suffixed .test. Utilities should be split into themed modules rather than one catch-all file, and index barrel files are discouraged. Route-level screens go in a pages folder. Authentication is handled by splitting the app into logged-in and logged-out parts, loading the former lazily. REST calls go behind a facade, with an adapter allowing a fake client in tests. Redux logic stays independent of React and is tested through actions and selectors rather than internals.

The takeaway is a three-step loop: start with the simplest possible convention, keep it consistent while it works, and change it as soon as it stops working. The speaker notes that these ideas suit most React applications, but React Native, server-side rendering or microservices would call for different patterns.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Dobre, Złe oraz Zaskakujące aspekty kompilacji kodu w .NET (C#)
talks.teaser: Walks through .NET C# compiler optimizations, showing which code patterns help performance and which unexpectedly defeat them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how the .NET C# compiler turns high-level code into machine code, and how its optimizations can either help or hurt application performance. The presenter outlines the pipeline a compiler follows: parsing source into a syntax tree, lowering it to an intermediate form, optimizing that form, and emitting native code. A decompiler is used to inspect the output, and small examples are read at the assembly level.

The middle of the talk focuses on branches and exceptions. Changing the order of a return statement or inverting a condition changes which path the compiler treats as the likely one, and adding extra conditions can make the generated code grow. Throwing an exception is treated as an unlikely path, so moving the throw into a separate helper method can keep the normal path simple. Loops over spans are compared with and without bounds checks, and a benchmark is used to show the effect of arranging loop bounds so the compiler can prove access is safe. Other examples cover struct copies and mutations, which can add overhead, and interface calls, which the compiler does not always devirtualize.

The closing advice is to measure rather than assume. Small code changes can switch an optimization off without any visible sign, so the presenter recommends checking the generated code and running benchmarks on the real workload. The presenter then invited audience questions.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: From Microfrontends and back
talks.teaser: Grzegorz Radzio examines 4Developers 2021: From Microfrontends and back.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Greg presents "From Microfrontends and Back: A Journey of a Naive Architect," recounting the architectural decisions made at Kubiro. The presentation analyzes how adopting microfrontends based on industry hype revealed severe trade-offs, leading the team to step back and adopt an alternative architectural approach using an Nx monorepo and Event-Driven Architecture (EDA).

### Key Topics
- **Microfrontends & Purported Benefits**: Understanding microfrontends as hosting multiple independent frontends (often using different frameworks like Angular, React, or Vue) inside a single application. Key promised benefits include independent deployability, polyglot development, modularized and cohesive codebases, faster isolated local development/testing, and autonomous teams.
- **Consequences and Hidden Costs**: In practice, microfrontends introduced complex integration and end-to-end testing challenges, heavy infrastructure overhead across repositories, degraded frontend performance and large bundle sizes from loading multiple frameworks, inconsistent coding styles, difficulties sharing UI libraries and CSS, and fragile inter-module communication (e.g., using `postMessage` or iframes).
- **Root Cause Analysis**: The team realized that their architectural friction was not primarily a tooling limitation, but a team understanding issue regarding how to design well-defined, modular codebases. If a team cannot build a clean modular monolith, microfrontends will not inherently solve their structural problems.
- **Alternative Solution at Kubiro**: Rather than continuing with microfrontends, Kubiro consolidated around a single framework (Angular) within an Nx monorepo, paired with an asynchronous Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) on the frontend.

### Technical Details
- **Nx Monorepo Architecture**: Applications and libraries are split into distinct, isolated units. Apps remain lightweight containers that are buildable, testable, and deployable independently. Libraries are structured into shared libraries (presentational UI components), core libraries (framework-level concerns such as authentication, authorization, and security), feature libraries (smart/container components and domain business logic in clean, framework-agnostic TypeScript), and event libraries.
- **Architectural Guardrails**: The team enforces architectural layering (application, domain, infrastructure, UI) via custom ESLint import rules evaluated during CI, as well as Nx dependency graphs to identify circular dependencies and excessive connection points during weekly architecture reviews.
- **Frontend Event-Driven Architecture (EDA)**: Implemented using RxJS, communication across decoupled modules relies on an asynchronous event bus rather than direct module imports or tightly coupled calls. The EDA architecture consists of four primary components:
  1. **Events**: Plain TypeScript interfaces or JavaScript Data Transfer Objects (DTOs) carrying payloads without embedded business logic.
  2. **Event Bus**: An asynchronous communication channel built with RxJS mechanisms (such as `BehaviorSubject` or `ReplaySubject`).
  3. **Event Dispatchers**: Service classes used by domain components, state managers, or command handlers to publish events onto the bus.
  4. **Event Handlers**: Subscribers that listen for specific event types on the bus and execute relevant handling logic without knowing the event origin.
- **Testing and Consistency**: Teams use consumer-driven contracts to ensure providers and subscribers remain aligned on event payloads. Unit and integration testing leverages Jest rather than Karma to avoid building full browser environments for single-component runs, while ephemeral PR environments facilitate pre-merge testing in trunk-based development.

### Takeaways
Microfrontends shine primarily at large organizational scales (e.g., hundreds of developers across dozens of teams) or when navigating rigid corporate release pipelines. For smaller or medium-sized teams, teams should first master modular monolith principles, enforce boundary rules through tooling like Nx and lint rules, and consider event-driven messaging before incurring the operational and performance overhead of microfrontends.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Sailing Java 16
talks.teaser: Surveys Java 16 changes, from stricter internal access and sealed classes to records and pattern matching, with live code demos.
talks.summary:
The talk gives a quick tour of what changed in Java 16 and opens with the common question of whether teams should upgrade or stay on the latest long-term support release. The speaker's view is that it depends on whether frameworks and libraries support the newer version. Otherwise, moving forward is usually sensible, since long-term support is mostly a business label rather than a sign of technical stability.

The main part covers several features. Strong encapsulation of JDK internals became the default, so the illegal access setting moved from permit to deny and is deprecated for removal. Demos show reflection calls to set accessible failing, and how add-opens flags or debug mode can surface violations, with advice to remove such calls rather than rely on flags. Pattern matching for instanceof binds an alias inside the type test, removing casting boilerplate. Sealed classes let an author decide which types may extend a hierarchy, using a permits list. Value-based classes trigger warnings about identity-sensitive actions such as synchronizing on them, and the speaker showed compiler and runtime output for these.

The closing section covers records as transparent carriers for immutable data, with generated accessors, equals, hash code and toString. Examples include a complex-number record and a collector that uses a local record instead of a hand-written helper class. The speaker notes that records cannot extend classes or hold extra instance fields, and that they are only shallowly immutable.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: CQRS is simpler than you think with C#9 and .NET 5!
talks.teaser: Shows how CQRS can be structured as vertical slices in .NET 5 using C# 9 records, endpoints and handlers.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that CQRS (command query responsibility segregation) can be a simpler alternative to layered architectures in .NET. The speaker starts by defining commands as messages that change state and queries as messages that only return data, and explains why separating them helps optimise behaviour and reduce the cognitive load of finding where a feature lives.

The session is a live coding walkthrough of a small product domain. Records give concise immutable types with init-only properties, while nullable reference types are presented as compile-time checks only, so the speaker pairs them with a private constructor and a factory method that validates basic semantic rules. Endpoints are mapped directly with minimal API calls instead of controllers, and the code is grouped into vertical slices per business operation, each holding its route, contract, data model and handler. Command and query handlers keep business logic away from HTTP and Entity Framework, and a small wrapper lets the endpoint send commands and queries without a mediator library.

The closing argument is that keeping code that changes together in one place reduces coupling between layers and makes features easier to evolve or move out, for example replacing a relational store behind a read-only listing with a search engine. The speaker notes that Swagger was missing from the endpoints at that time and points to sample repositories with more complete code for further reading.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: How to write tests in 2021
talks.teaser: Surveys practical Java and Kotlin testing techniques, from equals contracts to mutation testing and flaky-test detection.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a story about a plane that took off with insufficient thrust because a program underestimated passenger weight by 1,200 kg. The speaker uses it to argue that well-designed tests can catch this kind of production error. The first part covers unit-level correctness: checking equals and hashCode contracts with EqualsVerifier instead of hand-written assertions, controlling time by injecting a clock or using a Java agent such as Time Transformer for code that calls static time methods, and using Awaitility to poll for asynchronous events with timeouts and early aborts.

The middle section focuses on how tests are written and read. Test names should work as specifications, grouped with nesting through Kotest, JUnit 5 display names, or a Gradle plugin that renders the tree. Failing assertions should carry descriptive messages, using AssertJ's withFailMessage or lambda-based messages in JUnit 5, and soft assertions via assertAll or assertSoftly report every failure at once. For legacy code, snapshot tests with ApprovalTests capture current behaviour so refactoring can proceed safely.

The closing part covers test quality beyond coverage. Mutation testing with PITest checks whether tests actually detect changed logic, flaky tests can be caught by re-running tests added in a commit, and ArchUnit enforces architecture rules. Property-based tools such as jqwik or JetCheck can compare a rewritten implementation against the original. The main takeaway is that failing tests should read as useful bug reports and passing tests should read like documentation.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Wszystko co chciałeś wiedzieć o wątkach a bałeś się zapytać
talks.teaser: Walks through how threads, schedulers and thread pools work, using a developer's batch report as the example.
talks.summary:
A developer tasked with an hourly purchase report decides to parallelise the batch job and starts reading how threads work inside the operating system. The talk walks through the process descriptor that holds state, memory, open files and pending signals, and what a context switch must save and restore.

Scheduling is covered next, from a simple run queue to the Completely Fair Scheduler and its policies. Shared counters are compared across synchronized blocks, volatile fields, atomic variables and per-thread cells, and the talk shows how cells on the same cache line can still slow each other down until padded apart.

Thread pools close the talk. A pool sized to the core count suits CPU-bound batch work, while waiting on a remote service at 100 milliseconds per call means one thread serves about ten requests per second. Queue type changes behaviour, and recursive work such as merge sort needs a fork-join pool with work stealing. Fibers that yield instead of blocking are presented as a newer option whose library support is still catching up. The practical takeaway is to match thread count and queue type to the workload, then measure.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Distributed Application Runtime - Łukasz Kałużny
talks.teaser: Explains how Dapr adds a sidecar runtime with reusable building blocks for state, pub/sub, secrets and service calls.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common problem in microservice projects: new services are often created by copying an existing one, infrastructure code drifts between teams, and running services locally or in a cloud sandbox is awkward. Communication tends to stay synchronous even when event-driven messaging would fit better. The speaker presents Dapr, a runtime that started inside Microsoft and now sits under the CNCF, as a layer between application code and the underlying clouds and infrastructure.

Dapr runs as a sidecar process. In Kubernetes it is injected into a pod through an annotation, and locally it can be started next to an app with the Dapr CLI or Docker Compose. Applications call it over HTTP or gRPC. The building blocks cover service invocation, state management, publish and subscribe, bindings, virtual actors, observability, secrets and extensibility. The state example used a MongoDB store configured through a component file, and the same key-value API can target other stores. Pub/sub was shown with Redis as the broker, and secrets were fetched from a store such as HashiCorp Vault. The speaker noted gaps: some resiliency features, such as circuit breakers, are not provided and would need custom code, and the list of supported components is not complete.

For hands-on work, the speaker pointed to a dashboard, a Visual Studio Code extension, and sample applications in the Dapr GitHub organisation. He had not yet used the runtime in production and said he was still testing it. The takeaway is that a shared runtime for infrastructure access may cut repeated plumbing across services, but teams should check maturity and component coverage before depending on it.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Aplikacja od zera C# z CleanArchitecture, CQRS i Event Sourcing
talks.teaser: Walks through building a C# REST API with Clean Architecture, CQRS and event sourcing, from domain model to Swagger testing.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through building a small REST API in C# on .NET 5.0 from scratch, starting with the domain layer rather than database tables. The problem it targets is layered applications whose layers still depend on each other, so the speaker arranges the code in onion-style Clean Architecture, where the core holds interfaces and business logic and infrastructure plugs in from outside. The running example is a developer-application service where a developer can be added, accepted or rejected, and a status that has been set once cannot change.

The libraries used include MediatR for commands and queries, AutoMapper for moving between domain objects and transfer objects, FluentValidation for checks such as a name length limit, and Swagger for a generated test form and documentation. The speaker then moves to event sourcing: each change is stored as an event tied to an aggregate key and a version number, the events are saved to a database and published to RabbitMQ, and a background listener persists them. Version checks reject writes made against stale data, and unique identifiers are generated before saving.

The talk also covers drawbacks: extra complexity, the question of deleting stored history, and eventual consistency, illustrated with a subscription purchase that only appears active after a delay. The main benefit noted is better performance from separating read and write models, which can use different databases. Attendees should take away a structure for splitting responsibilities and a sense of the trade-offs before adopting event sourcing.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Jak pisać czytelne i łatwe do utrzymania oprogramowanie w języku C#
talks.teaser: Shows how refactoring, clear naming, encapsulation and automated tests keep C# code easy to maintain as projects grow.
talks.summary:
Kamil Grzybek opens with a productivity curve: a new project starts fast, but accumulated complexity and tangled code steadily slow the team down. He describes the forces behind this decline, including hard-to-understand code, ripple effects across modules, and the common excuses developers use, such as time pressure, changing requirements, pressure from managers and postponing cleanup until later. He argues that a full rewrite usually recreates the same problems, so the better path is continuous, evolutionary improvement in which maintainability is treated as a key quality attribute.

The middle of the talk turns to concrete practices. Names should carry units and intent, for example a timeout named in seconds rather than a bare number, and magic numbers should be replaced with well-named constants. Code should use the domain's ubiquitous language, comments should be reserved for workarounds and public API documentation, and dead or commented-out code should be removed. For structure he covers extract method, splitting large classes by responsibility, encapsulation at class and module level, and avoiding speculative code. Deduplication should happen only when duplicated code carries the same knowledge. Formatting should be automated with analyzers that run in continuous integration.

The closing part makes the case for automated tests as the safety net that allows safe refactoring and quick feedback. Changes should be made in small steps, and each bug becomes an opportunity to add a test that documents the expected behaviour. The main takeaway for practitioners is to keep improving the code they touch, so that development speed and business value stay stable over time. He ends by recommending further reading for teams that want to adopt this approach.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: API na sterydach
talks.teaser: Grzegorz Kotfis details 4Developers 2021: API na sterydach.
talks.summary:
Grzegorz Korpus presents 'API na sterydach' (API on Steroids) at 4Developers 2021, focusing on three practical API optimization strategies: pagination, sorting, and field selection (delta shaping).

**Pagination Approaches:**
Korpus discusses multiple pagination strategies with their trade-offs. The basic offset/limit approach using SKIP and TAKE is simple but problematic at scale—the database must scan and skip many rows to retrieve results from later pages, causing performance degradation on large datasets. He introduces cursor-based pagination using a marker or key to filter results instead of scanning, eliminating the offset overhead. However, traditional cursor pagination struggles with non-unique values (low-cardinality fields). To address this, Korpus demonstrates SQL window functions like ROW_NUMBER to create synthetic unique markers, enabling reliable cursor navigation. He also covers 'page drifting'—where results shift between requests due to concurrent data modifications—which cursor approaches mitigate. The response can include metadata (page info, total count) via response body or HTTP headers to support client navigation.

**Sorting Implementation:**
Sorting conventions range from predefined field lists to dynamic sorting. Korpus shows hardcoding allowed fields in a switch statement for simplicity, then progresses to the Dynamic LINQ library for programmatic expression building from string parameters. He emphasizes pragmatism: starting with simple, documented approaches may suffice before adopting complex generic mechanisms, keeping code maintainable for the team.

**Field Selection (Delta Shaping):**
Using C# reflection and LINQ expression trees, Korpus demonstrates dynamic projection—letting clients specify which fields to return. The implementation builds LINQ Select expressions at runtime, then uses an ExpandoObject 'shaper' to reduce the response to only requested fields. He addresses practical concerns: default field sets when no selection is provided, case-insensitive field matching, silent omission of non-existent fields, and excluding expensive-to-serialize columns from the database query itself rather than filtering after materialization.

**Core Principles:**
Korpus stresses that APIs should not expose database structure directly. Filtering, sorting, and pagination should occur at the database level to minimize resource consumption and response sizes. He advocates for consistency in naming conventions and parameter formats across all endpoints, proper documentation, and avoiding premature optimization with complex reflection-based mechanisms when simpler approaches suffice.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Practical Contract Testing with Pact in PHP
talks.teaser: Shows how consumer-driven Pact contract tests in PHP check REST API integrations without running both services together.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces contract testing for API integrations between a provider and a consumer. It explains that a contract can take many forms, from API documentation to a Postman collection, and argues that a provider passing its own tests does not show that the consumer uses the API correctly. Pact is presented as a consumer-driven approach in which the consumer's tests generate the contract. Its main parts are a mock server that stands in for the provider, a broker that stores and shares contract files, and a provider verifier that replays the recorded interactions against a real service.

The speaker then builds a short example in PhpStorm. A consumer class that fetches a product list over HTTP is written test first, using a wrapper around the Pact library to describe a GET request to the products path and a JSON API response. Running the test produces a contract file. The verifier is pointed at a Laravel application on the PHP development server; the first attempts fail on the wrong port and then on a 404, and the provider is made to pass with a hard-coded product response. The speaker then notes that the contract is too strict about array contents and replaces those fields with type-based matchers, so a second product no longer breaks verification.

The closing section covers the benefits: each side can be tested in isolation without shared staging environments, contracts and API documentation are generated automatically, results can be wired into pipelines, and contract versions show which application versions remain compatible. Provider states, continuous integration setup and non-HTTP use are named but left for later, since the talk only scratched the surface of the topic.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Looming in the cores
talks.teaser: Explains why unbounded thread creation breaks Java applications and how Project Loom's virtual threads address it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a Fibonacci implementation built on recursion and an executor framework, and shows how a application deployed to a cloud server runs into native thread creation failures. It frames threads two ways: as units of work for developers, and as operating system threads mapped onto hardware execution units. A production case with tens of thousands of threads, which exhausted the machine's resources, shows why the thread count matters.

Hardware trends frame the problem. Clock speeds have levelled off at a few gigahertz, while core counts have grown enormously: the Top 500 entry in 2010 had 1280 cores, and the top machine in 2018 had 2.4 million. Amdahl's law explains why serial work limits speedup, and shared state limits parallelism. Multi-socket servers add memory access costs that depend on which CPU owns the memory, and chiplet designs bring similar effects into single packages, so every system starts to behave like a distributed one.

Blocking code is simple to write but holds threads idle during I/O, while non-blocking APIs use resources better but are harder to write, debug and profile, and callback chains grow hard to follow. Project Loom aims to make threads cheap: virtual threads are lightweight, scheduled by the JVM rather than the operating system, and most blocking calls are being made loom-aware behind a близкий API. The talk stresses that the work is still in progress, that early builds contain bugs, and that it is not ready for production. Framework authors will be the first direct users, and Reactor is expected to build on Loom rather than be replaced by it.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Czy Microfrontends może tworzyć dobraną parę z Angularem lub Reactem?
talks.teaser: Explains when microfrontends fit Angular or React projects and compares two implementation approaches with code examples.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether microfrontends are a universal pattern for Angular or React projects and answers that they are not. Popularity does not decide the fit; the architectural drivers do. Splitting work into teams that own separate business domains can pay off in large applications, while a single shared backlog usually gains little. Communication overhead often matters more than technology, and the main benefits are independent pipelines, limited code access and gradual migration. Mixing frameworks is treated as a risky choice unless those drivers justify it.

Two implementations were shown. The first was a simplified version of a small custom library the speaker built years ago for a banking application. A manifest read at shell startup lists each microapp with its selector, entry point and server location, high-level routing stays in the shell, and components are wrapped as Angular elements for lazy loading. A live demo loaded microapps from separate servers. Its drawback is that every microapp ships its own framework copy, which matters for mobile performance. The second used Webpack Module Federation in an NX workspace with an Angular shell, where shared libraries load once as singletons; the demo covered a remote app and a shared service.

Ultimately, no approach is best in general. Team structure, application size, how close teams sit to each other and the migration plan should guide the choice, ideally made early. Microfrontends can still be introduced later, when a growing project starts to slow down delivery.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Aplikacje Reactowe na serwerze
talks.teaser: Explains React Server Components as a way to cut JavaScript bundle size and client-server request waterfalls, still at RFC stage.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the drawbacks of large single-page React applications. On slow connections the browser must download and run a big JavaScript bundle before the page becomes interactive, and code splitting only postpones that cost. Data loading adds a second problem: when a child component requests its data only after its parent has loaded, the requests form a waterfall. Over-generalised component abstractions also make code harder to maintain.

Server-side rendering sends ready HTML for a fast first paint, yet the full script still has to load and run before the page responds. Static generation suits only some sites. A query language for APIs lets the client fetch just the fields it needs, but rendering costs remain. Next.js is presented as a production-ready option with real server rendering and file-system routing, and a conventional router can still be used with it.

The main part covers React Server Components, a Facebook proposal still at the request-for-comments stage. Server components run only on the server, so their libraries, such as a Markdown renderer or the moment date library, add nothing to the client bundle. They can read files or databases directly, import client components, and pass serialized props over HTTP, while client components load only when rendered. Limits include no state, no lifecycle methods and no browser APIs. The speaker stresses that the design may change, so it is not ready for production, and invites feedback on the RFC.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Test automation in backend projects
talks.teaser: Traces how a TypeScript backend team grew its test automation, and which habits made the tests worth maintaining.
talks.summary:
A backend engineer describes how his team took over a TypeScript backend with roughly 5% test coverage and decided to push coverage as far as it could go. Their rule was that anything pushed to the repository had to be fully covered, and within six months the speaker reported that 52% of the new code and 91% of the code they touched was covered by tests.

High coverage did not guarantee good tests, though. Long, vaguely described test files were hard to review, and reviewers tended to trust them without reading. The team rewrote descriptions in a Gherkin-style given/when/then form with help from a business analyst, moved shared mock data into separate files, and used parameterized examples so one test could cover several user roles. They limited each test to one assertion, verified call arguments and call counts on mocks, and used rejection checks instead of asserts inside catch blocks. For integration tests, they ran a copy of the server, seeded and cleared data per test, and documented why certain lines were excluded from coverage. Fixture generators and timeouts helped check performance on large datasets.

The talk closes with linting and logging as cheap automated checks, and a checklist covering smoke and sanity tests, requirement coverage, varied data, tracked API responses, negative testing, and removing dependencies. The main takeaway is that tests act as living documentation and expose design problems when they are hard to mock.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Konteneryzacja - Czy na pewno jest dla Ciebie?
talks.teaser: Challenges myths about containerization, from stateful apps and resource limits to image security and running costs.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the enthusiasm that often greets containers when a new project begins, when teams expect Kubernetes to solve problems they had in earlier projects. The speaker argues that moving an existing monolith into containers without a plan or refactoring rarely helps. He separates stateful applications, which keep session or basket data, from stateless ones, notes that containers were first designed for stateless workloads, and says an application should be able to run as several instances before it is scaled on Kubernetes.

The middle of the talk takes apart several myths. Memory limits are presented as a safety net for rare emergencies, not a fix for memory leaks, which belong in the code. Containers isolate processes but do not stop SQL injection, XSS or CSRF, so testing and scanning are still needed. Base images pulled from public registries can carry malicious payloads, and a case of images on Docker Hub containing cryptomining scripts is described, reportedly earning around 40,000 dollars. The host machines also need hardening. On cost, the speaker gives rough monthly figures of about 450 dollars for a managed cluster, 50 for a registry and 30 for security scanning, and stresses the staff time needed to run a self-hosted cluster, including the move from Docker to containerd.

The closing advice is to try Docker locally to learn the tooling, but to weigh skills, architecture, security and operating costs before putting containers into production.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Recovery Project Management - zarządzanie projektami w kryzysie
talks.teaser: Presents recovery project management phases to audit causes, decide continuation, negotiate scope, and restart threatened IT delivery.
talks.summary:
The session opens by distinguishing routine project pressure from a genuinely threatened initiative: failure is not merely a blown budget or schedule, but stopping work or delivering something the business never adopts. Risk piles up when teams ignore early warnings, stakeholders disengage, and classic green-amber-red status slides toward red overnight.

The speaker describes the path into crisis through compromise attempts and contract extensions, then contrasts a sudden client rollback after go-live with a doomed effort that showed unrealistic scope-versus-time assumptions from the start. Recovery project management is framed as a deliberate method—not a substitute for risk management—with phases to understand history and stakeholders, audit root causes despite blame and low morale, decide whether continuation is rational, and negotiate compromises that may sacrifice the original time-cost-scope triangle for acceptable business value and quality. A practical example uses must-should-could-won’t prioritization to shrink scope under shareholder deadlines.

Closing guidance covers pausing work, bringing a credible new lead to angry clients, securing organizational backing, restarting with tighter change control and earned-value checks, and capturing lessons so the culture improves instead of burying the story.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Empatyczna komunikacja dla Developerów
talks.teaser: Introduces nonviolent communication for developers, covering listening, needs-based language, and conflict resolution at work.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why organizations increasingly expect empathetic collaboration, citing business research from before and during the pandemic. Workers want to be heard and treated with respect; empathy is framed as supporting trust, responsibility, and innovation—especially relevant for developer teams under deadline pressure.

The core method is Marshall Rosenberg’s nonviolent communication. Four practices are outlined: notice your own feelings and needs without judgment, listen without jumping to advice, state clear requests instead of demands, and avoid blame or verbal violence. Contrasting “jackal” (critical, you-focused) and “giraffe” (observations, feelings, needs) language is illustrated with a late-report scenario and extended to project leads handling delays. The “three minutes” listening habit and video calls with cameras are recommended for remote work.

The closing ties empathy to business outcomes: stronger client and teammate relationships, assertiveness between passivity and aggression, and faster conflict resolution when both sides name needs. Survey figures highlight rising managerial interest in empathy and strong IT-industry appetite for empathetic employers. Common blockers—judging, manipulation, and dodging responsibility—are noted alongside encouragement to study Rosenberg’s materials and rehearse facts, feelings, and requests in everyday disagreements.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Don't shoot yourself in the foot
talks.teaser: Advice from roughly two hundred technical interviews covers preparation, the live conversation, and behavior after the decision.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames technical hiring as something the speaker has seen from the interviewer’s side, drawing on subjective lessons from about two hundred technical interviews. The audience is told to treat the tips as guidance, not absolutes, and to disagree where their experience differs.

The talk is organized into three phases: before, during, and after the interview. Preparation covers checking market value through occasional interviews (for example a few notifications around January or February), thoughtful LinkedIn photos, CVs written so the interviewer can branch into real discussion, and punctuality because late arrival shortens time to demonstrate fit. On the day, candidates should avoid politics, religion, and worldview debates; highlight unpaid or extra-curricular work; practice talking positively about themselves; show up as their best version without excuses or lies; accept not knowing every answer on long question lists; avoid profanity; and never criticize current or past employers or colleagues. Afterward, arguing about rejection is discouraged, while asking about processes, tools, and databases signals genuine interest.

Practitioners should leave with a practical checklist for not undermining themselves in technical recruitment, from first impression through follow-up.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Story of the green chair
talks.teaser: Shows how lost decision context hurts newcomers, and how decision records, glossaries and commit hygiene preserve it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a story about a company where new hires chose their own equipment, and one green chair with a rolling base spread across the office. When a newcomer asked why everyone sat on green chairs, the answer was only that this is how it is done. The speaker argues that such unexplained choices come from a decision lifecycle: each generation of staff knows less about why something was chosen, so the same problem eventually returns and is solved again by people who lack the history.

To break this cycle, the speaker suggests recording architecture decisions in short entries that name the decision maker, the alternatives, the consequences and the trigger that prompted the choice. Postmortems after production incidents should focus on finding solutions rather than blaming people. A shared glossary in the team's own language helps newcomers decode abbreviations and business terms. For onboarding, a whiteboard walkthrough based on the C4 model can start with a high-level view and add detail later. Recorded demos and collected meeting notes give context that would otherwise require many questions.

At the code level, readable test names that describe business behaviour, extracted methods that name each step, and commit messages linked to a tracker task with an explanation of the reason all help later readers find the history. The speaker's aim is that anyone joining a project can understand why its rules exist, rather than simply following them.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Z(gra)ny zespół rozproszony. Uwaga! Testowane na ludziach
talks.teaser: Shows three team games that help distributed developers get to know each other and stay connected while working remotely.
talks.summary:
The speaker describes a development team that works from home, is spread across different locations and projects, and rarely meets in person. Informal bonding such as coffee in the office kitchen disappeared, so the team tried structured games to rebuild connection and shared context.

The first game was a music quiz. Each colleague sent in songs that expressed something about them, the group listened together, and everyone guessed who had proposed each track. The second was a film guessing game: one player shared a single movie frame and the others had to name the title from memory, without looking anything up. The first version of this game, played through a shared chat in spare moments, was rejected, so the team restarted by agreeing on the rules together and then playing during a scheduled meeting. The third was a bingo board of common work situations, built from a brainstorm. Players marked squares that matched their week, which led to stories about recent events and a better understanding of what colleagues were dealing with.

The speaker concludes that the games work because they have clear rules everyone agreed to, and because they make people more interested in each other's work and experiences. Practical advice includes keeping participation voluntary, limiting sessions to about 30 minutes once a week, and treating the activities as a response to individual needs rather than extra work. Gamification elements such as points were also part of the approach.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: 12 lekcji, które pozwoliły mi być ultra produktywnym
talks.teaser: Shares twelve practical lessons on priorities, self-control and focus for a developer who became an entrepreneur.
talks.summary:
The speaker, Michał Guzowski, explains that he spent about ten years as a programmer before moving toward running businesses, which pushed him to rethink how he works. In this twelve-minute talk at 4Developers 2021, he lists twelve lessons he says helped him become highly productive. He starts with the idea that productivity depends less on tools than on knowing your priorities, and that those priorities should follow from your values. He also argues that motivation keeps long hours from becoming exhausting.

He then argues for focusing on what you can control, which is yourself and your attitude, and for separating what you must do from what you choose to do. He warns against solving other people's problems for them, since this can create dependence, and against spending time where you have no real influence, using his former habit of debating politics as an example. He also recommends putting your own needs first, comparing this to the airplane instruction to fit your own oxygen mask before helping others. Instead of dwelling on problems, he advises focusing on solutions, such as arranging mobile internet when a home connection fails before a presentation.

He closes with advice to plan only a day ahead rather than years, to enjoy the process rather than rushing toward a goal, and to seek to understand a situation before judging it. As an illustration, he describes an architect working on his apartment whose delays turned out to reflect serious personal problems. The takeaway for developers and entrepreneurs is to manage attention, priorities and reactions before chasing output.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: How to focus? - Improve your efficiency
talks.teaser: Shows how developers can shield their attention with environment setup, distraction control and a steady daily routine.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how developers can protect their concentration amid notifications, remote work and online distractions. The speaker, who has worked from home, offices and while travelling for years, treats focus as something to arrange deliberately. The session covers preparing the work environment and structuring the day.

On the environment side, the advice includes a paper notepad for stray thoughts, switched-off phone notifications, and mail fetched around noon instead of first thing. On the computer, each of four work applications gets its own workspace, a terminal is summoned with one key, and a single screen is used. Work triggers, such as a dedicated work-only place, a separate work browser profile, and headphones, signal that focus has begun.

For the day, the next one is planned at the end of the current day, the hardest task is tackled first, ideally from around 7 am. Work runs in blocks of two or three hours, each followed by a reset break to tidy up, close tabs, snack and stretch. Similar tasks are grouped to cut down on context switching between tasks, screens and devices. The closing message: look after the environment, remove distractions, plan ahead and keep a routine. Bad days happen, so the speaker suggests allowing a lighter day and starting again the next morning.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Chce zobaczyć swoje logi
talks.teaser: Explains what applications should log, how to pick log levels, and how tools like Loki and Jaeger help trace problems.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that shipping an application is not the end of the work: once users rely on it, the team has to maintain it, and logs become the main record of what the system actually does. The speaker treats a log entry as free text that can hold anything, and warns that this freedom is the problem. He starts with what to record, contrasting a bare error message, such as a failed payment, with a version that adds the order, the cause and a stack trace.

Next comes how to log. The speaker walks through the usual severity levels, from verbose and debug for detailed tracing down to error and critical for failures that need immediate action, and suggests keeping the most detailed levels off in production. He recommends logging the start and end of recurring jobs such as synchronisation, and recording outgoing notifications and incoming events so support can tell which side failed. He favours structured logs that machines can filter, and warns against excessive volume, rising SaaS costs, and storing personal data, tokens or connection strings.

The closing section covers where logs should go. A console is fine locally, but a centralised system is the better target. Tracing with a shared identifier follows a request across services, and the speaker demonstrates this with Loki and Jaeger, filtering by an error code a user reported and following the trace of one operation. The takeaway is to log at the right level, with enough context for someone unfamiliar with the code to investigate later.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Testing in Infrastructure as Code
talks.teaser: Shows how to unit and integration test Terraform and AWS CDK infrastructure code, comparing speed and fragility.
talks.summary:
The talk makes the case for automated tests in infrastructure as code, citing fewer regressions, faster development and better code quality. It borrows the test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and very few UI tests, since higher layers rely on networks, clouds and browsers and become slower and more fragile. The running example is a reusable S3 bucket module that must follow a company naming convention, truncating names longer than 63 characters.

The speaker first tests that module with Terratest in Go, which deploys to a real cloud account and takes over a minute, and can fail when a bucket name is already taken. A custom Groovy and Spock framework that drives the Terraform binary brings a run down to about 50 seconds. He then rewrites the module in AWS CDK, which declares resources in a general-purpose language and deploys through CloudFormation. One integration test is enough there, while the naming logic gets a unit test running in around 100 milliseconds.

The talk places Terraform's limited declarative language against general-purpose options such as CDK, and mentions alternatives such as Pulumi. The speaker notes that calling Terraform or CDK binaries from code is a workaround, and that Pulumi only recently allowed running multiple stacks from code. His prediction is that developer-oriented tools will shape the future, because they allow faster feedback and reusable code. Listeners are encouraged to try CDK and to keep integration tests few.

talks.title: PLNOG Online 2021: Marcin Kuczera - Jak przeskoczyć gigabit w dostępie FTTH nie wydając grubej kasy?
talks.teaser: Explains how to exceed gigabit on FTTH access using 2.5G ports on existing terminals, with a hardware prototype.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why many FTTH subscribers stay at roughly gigabit speeds and how an operator can go past that limit without a costly move to XGS-PON. The speaker, who runs a regional telecom with its own fibre network and tens of thousands of FTTH subscribers, says a gigabit port delivers about 943 Mbit/s at the IP layer. In his view the bottleneck sits in the subscriber terminal rather than the central office, where newer equipment already handles higher rates.

He explains why an XGS-PON upgrade is hard to justify: the installed equipment has not yet paid back its capital cost, and support and warranty add recurring expense. As an alternative he presents 2.5 Gbit/s multi-gigabit Ethernet on the existing access ports, the same family of 2.5G and 5G standards that can run over older copper cabling. He walks through a common single-port terminal chip, then a dual-port chipset design, and a prototype board with a second 2.5G interface. A throughput test through a USB network adapter on a laptop was limited by the adapter itself, so he expects better results with a PCI Express card.

The main problems he reports are the bottleneck moving into aggregation, where buffers can overflow at 2.5G, and software support, since older management systems may not recognise the new port types. Rate limiting is one workaround, and vendor software updates are needed for others. He concludes that this approach can extend the life of gigabit PON at lower cost, keeping the XGS-PON path open, and notes that more routers with 2.5G copper ports are appearing.

talks.title: PLNOG Online 2021:Marcin Ścieślicki-WIFI szybsze od przewodu-marketingowe mrzonki czy rzeczywistość?
talks.teaser: Traces Wi-Fi's evolution from early standards to Wi-Fi 6 and tests whether wireless can really beat wired networks.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether the claim that Wi-Fi is now faster and more stable than a cable is marketing or reality. The speaker traces his own experience from early wireless devices through the 802.11b, 802.11g, 802.11n and 802.11ac generations, the last certified in 2014. For years each generation brought higher theoretical figures, but ordinary users saw little visible change.

The middle of the talk focuses on Wi-Fi 6, the sixth generation. The speaker explains that its reworked modulation lets several clients share one channel at the same time, with small and large transfers handled together, instead of reserving the whole channel for one device. He presents this as useful in dense environments with many devices, such as homes during the pandemic and sports venues. Earlier examples include a 20 km wireless bridge built with antennas designed in Poland.

For practitioners, the speaker stresses careful access point placement, usually on ceilings, and not forgetting the firewall. He recommends centralised cloud management and quality of service policies so that new devices are profiled correctly. He concludes that, in his view, Wi-Fi 6 can now outperform wired networks in practice.

talks.title: PLNOG Online 2021: Krzysztof Załęski - Czy DaaC w sieciach jest możliwy?
talks.teaser: Shows how network operators can treat documentation like code using Git, markup formats, Sphinx, and review-driven publishing workflows.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from a familiar frustration: network projects often ship elaborate technical write-ups that almost nobody reads, while engineers resist writing, duplicate work in silos, and bounce between live configuration and monolithic PDF updates. The speaker reframes documentation as something that must be planned for distinct audiences and purposes, aligning with four complementary forms—guided learning, problem-focused runbooks, dense reference material, and explanatory context for how the environment actually works.

The core argument adapts documentation-as-code from software teams to networking. Plain-text sources live in version control (with Git-style workflows and alternatives such as Gitea), are authored in an IDE with Markdown, AsciiDoc, or reStructuredText, and are rendered through tools like Sphinx into browsable sites or PDFs. Docstrings in Python illustrate how API-level detail can be generated beside narrative docs. The same pipeline can tie merge requests, peer review, automated checks, and publication to configuration changes so documentation stays aligned with what runs in production.

For practitioners, the takeaway is operational: start small with a central repo, define who each document serves, automate generation where tables and repetition dominate, and use reproducible lab environments (for example Vagrant on VirtualBox) to validate configs and preview output. Done consistently, living documentation reduces repeated support noise and keeps network knowledge from drifting behind reality.

talks.title: PLNOG Online 2021: Michał Bentkowski - Świat security w czasach pandemii
talks.teaser: Surveys how attack trends shifted during the pandemic, covering browser zero-days, video conferencing flaws and Exchange exploitation.
talks.summary:
The talk reviews how the COVID-19 pandemic changed attacker activity over the past year. Remote work and more people using personal machines for company tasks widened the attack surface. The speaker starts with browsers, noting that Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild were more frequent in 2020 than in earlier years. He also recalls a case where Google publicly described blocking an attack that critics linked to a Western government operation.

Video conferencing tools form the middle section. Zoom and Microsoft Teams drew many flaws as their use spiked from spring 2020. The speaker notes that the Teams desktop app is built on Electron, so web-style bugs appeared in it. He mentions that Google reportedly barred staff from installing Zoom, and that a yearly contest produced exploits against both products. He then covers Zerologon, which allowed domain controller takeover from the same network, and ProxyLogon, an Exchange flaw exploited before a patch existed. Its disclosure timeline suggests the exploit was obtained through a compromised Microsoft account. Ransomware groups also used a Hyper-V flaw to encrypt virtual machines from the host.

The closing part cites a PwC report showing cybersecurity budgets rose in 2020, some by as much as 25 percent. The speaker advises reviewing what permissions conferencing apps have on user machines and monitoring them closely, since attacks on these tools are expected to keep growing.

talks.title: PLNOG Online 2021: Konrad Tutak - Uwolnij wartość dodaną All-flash w swoim Data Center
talks.teaser: Argues for all-flash data center storage, covering SSD economics, active-active array designs and AI-driven predictive maintenance.
talks.summary:
Konrad Tutak, a product manager responsible for IT solutions at the vendor, opens with the rapid growth of data volumes and the pressure to process that data faster. He links the trend to 5G and autonomous vehicles, citing an estimate of about 64 terabytes of new data generated daily by self-driving cars. In his view, storing data is no longer the hard part; shorter response times and faster results are now the requirement.

The core argument is for all-flash data centers. Compared with spinning disks, SSDs are presented as drawing less power, responding much faster, resisting vibration and failing less often. Although the raw price per terabyte is higher, deduplication and compression are said to stretch one terabyte into four or five of effective space, bringing the cost close to hard disks. The vendor's answer includes sixth-generation Dorado arrays, a switch-based protocol that extends low-latency flash access beyond the array, and an active-active pair of arrays that can be stretched across sites to survive the loss of a whole site. A third data center can receive replicas for disaster recovery.

The closing section turns to AI-driven operations. The array's AI module is described as moving management from reactive to proactive, predicting events, suggesting optimizations and flagging bottlenecks. The simplest example given is replacing a disk before it fails. The takeaway is an all-flash, active-active data center that aims for higher efficiency, shorter response times and lower power use with less hardware.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Jak z dobrego specjalisty NIE zostać beznadziejnym liderem? P Rekowski, K Rakowski
talks.teaser: Maps common traps when strong IT specialists step into leadership and outlines practical habits that preserve careers and team outcomes.
talks.summary:
The session frames a familiar promotion dilemma: a capable programmer, tester, or architect is blocked on the technical ladder and offered a management role, with little preparation and a real risk of years of regret. Cited figures suggest many new leaders are unsure they belong in the role, feel unprepared, and never received formal training. The speaker contrasts technical work—knowing the best way to execute—with leadership, where success depends on enabling others rather than being the smartest person in the room.

Three recurring failure modes anchor the middle of the talk. Micromanagement grows when former specialists still dictate how work is done instead of owning outcomes; soft skills lag because engineering careers rarely reward constant people engagement; and calendars fragment under meetings, messages, and context switching. Remedies include hiring stronger talent, delegating problems back with support rather than absorbing them, using listening-heavy exercises such as question-only meetings, and shielding makers from pointless interruptions. Prioritization tools like urgency-importance sorting help managers delegate or drop work deliberately.

The close argues that management is optional. Specialists who dislike people-heavy, interrupt-driven days can pursue architect tracks or shape their own scope through internal job crafting instead of accepting a leadership title. Supplementary coaching materials and a related podcast are pointed to for deeper self-assessment after the short slot.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Bezpieczeństwo w świecie Javy - Łukasz Mikuła
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed Java debugger, RMI and deserialization features can be abused for remote code execution.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how Java applications can be attacked over the network, focusing on Java-specific features rather than generic web flaws. The speaker defines a hacker as anyone who uses software creatively in ways it was not meant for. The focus is on extra services Java applications often expose beside their web port: the JDWP debugger, RMI registries and JMX management interfaces. Several lack built-in authentication, so anyone who can reach them can interact with them.

The two demos ran against vulnerable test applications. In the first, an nmap scan revealed an exposed JDWP debugger, and a public tool attached to it, set a breakpoint on a commonly called method and forced the application to run an operating system command. In the second, an RMI interface was found by guessing method names, and a method accepting an Object argument was used to send a serialized payload built with a gadget-chain generator. An outdated Apache Commons library on the class path made that payload execute code on the server.

The practical advice is to never run debuggers in production and to bind debugger, RMI and JMX ports to localhost. If JMX is exposed, enable authentication with strong passwords, since it has no brute-force protection. Never deserialize untrusted data; prefer allowlist filters and keep libraries up to date so old gadget libraries are absent.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Narzędzia MLOps do automatyzowania wdrażania rozwiązań ML Konrad Łyda
talks.teaser: Shows how MLOps tools automate ML model training, deployment and monitoring, using a live Airflow and MLflow pipeline demo.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a fictional data scientist, Michał, who is asked by a government client to build a model that spots possums in camera images. His first model reached production with no monitoring, the animals adapted, and every fix meant manual retraining and redeployment. The speaker uses this to introduce MLOps, an extension of DevOps that treats data and models as first-class artifacts next to code. He cites a 2019 report claiming that 87 percent of ML models never reach production.

The talk then walks through the lifecycle as three overlapping phases: design, model development and operations. Model development is split into data engineering, model engineering and code engineering. It describes maturity levels, from a manual process in notebooks, through an automated training pipeline with continuous training, to full CI/CD automation. Tool categories are mapped to each stage, including data versioning, experiment tracking, model registry, orchestration, serving and monitoring, with examples such as DVC, MLflow, Prometheus, Grafana and Git.

The live demo runs an Airflow training pipeline with steps for data loading, validation, preparation, training, evaluation and model validation, logging runs and reports to MLflow. A simple script sends prediction requests to a served model while dashboards track input values and latency. An alert triggers retraining through a small bridge service. The closing takeaway is to choose tools based on team skills, environment and budget, and to document the manual process before automating it. A template repository is offered as a starting point.
