talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Maszyna rozumie tekst - uczenie i wyszukiwanie w mikro i makro skali Ł. Kuczyński
talks.teaser: Covers text preprocessing, vectorization, classical classifiers, transformers, and full-text plus semantic search at scale.
talks.summary:
The talk begins by arguing that machines still struggle with spoken and written language while other engineering feats look routine, using the Turing test and modern chat systems as motivation. It surveys where text analytics appears in products—from support bots and keyboards to marketing recommendations—and notes how companies such as Google and Elastic grew around search and log analysis.

The core walkthrough follows a practical NLP pipeline: corpus splitting, tokenization, stop-word removal, stemming versus lemmatization, part-of-speech tagging, and entity extraction, illustrated with libraries like NLTK and spaCy. Documents become sparse vectors via scikit-learn; TF-IDF weighting and cosine similarity separate themed corpora and power recommendations. A naive Bayes classifier assigns high-confidence labels to held-out sentences, while embeddings and pretrained word vectors support semantic word math. Transformers via Hugging Face demonstrate sentiment, summarization, generation, and masked fill-in tasks.

The conclusion ties machine understanding to retrieval: inverted indexes, Elasticsearch-style engines, database text fields, and semantic search where embeddings cluster related meanings. Practitioners should pair simple vector classifiers with business needs, reserve heavyweight transformer stacks for quality-sensitive tasks, and adopt dedicated search technology when latency and relevance matter beyond SQL convenience.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Testy wydajnościowe - ważne ogniwo w cyklu wytwarzania oprogramowania
talks.teaser: Walks through load, stress and spike tests, test environments, tool choice and the steps from scenarios to reporting.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces performance testing as a non-functional discipline. Instead of checking that a button works, it measures how a system responds under simulated real-world traffic, whether that is a web application, desktop software, a database or the surrounding infrastructure. The main goals are to find bottlenecks early, verify stated requirements and avoid costly production problems, since slow pages drive customers away.

The speaker outlines the common test types. Load tests hold expected traffic for a long period, stress tests push far beyond it, endurance tests look for failures that appear after hours, and spike tests apply sudden jumps in users. Test environments may combine physical machines, virtual machines and a controller with load generators. Tool choice should weigh protocol support, licence cost, vendor support, learning effort and operating system fit. The process runs from defining goals and scenarios, through scripting, user ramp-up and monitoring, to analysing results.

Examples show why results should be compared across several earlier versions: a roughly 20 percent slowdown was invisible when each release was compared only with its predecessor. Other bottlenecks included database connections reserved for queries that did not need them and a misconfigured load balancer. The report should cover the test scope, configuration, references, monitoring and recommendations. The takeaway is to define the goal first and keep tests repeatable and clear to business stakeholders.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Testable architecture: how to build good quality software and build fast K Grzybek
talks.teaser: Learn how testable architecture can make changes easier to verify and maintain.
talks.summary: The speaker presents testability as a way to improve software quality and development speed, drawing on examples where long-running calculations, reliance on a production system, and unclear reports made testing difficult. Attendees learn five testability attributes—control, observability, isolation, understanding, and automation—and how modular design, collaboration from the start of development, and a considered mix of automated tests can support them.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Mutation testing: Too good to be true?
talks.teaser: Explains how mutation testing injects code changes to expose weak tests, and why its tools struggle with real projects.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether mutation testing, which has regained popularity, is ready for everyday use. Piotr Kubowicz explains the idea: a tool makes small changes to production code, such as flipping a conditional boundary, deleting lines or returning dummy values, and then reruns the tests. If the tests still pass after a change that alters behaviour, the mutant survives, which points to a gap in the tests even when coverage reads 100 percent. He walks through how the JVM tool PIT works, from running the tests once for coverage to choosing mutations and running only the tests that cover each changed piece of code.

He then reports practical problems. In his team's projects, which use database-backed tests that are not isolated, mutation analysis ran 10 to 30 times slower than the normal test suite. The default engine wastes effort on data classes and on code that Kotlin's compiler generates, and its reports are hard to read. In a demo of a financial reminder feature with weak tests, the default settings found none of the four planted problems. The alternative engine found only the filtering one, and the all-mutations preset found two. Wrong list values, wrong field assignments and fluent or reactive call chains remained blind spots that only a human reviewer could catch.

He contrasts this with an internal Google system that analyses only changed files and lets reviewers mark suggestions as useful or not, and notes that open-source tools lack that integration and feedback history. Running analysis locally, in CI or as a pull request gate did not work for his team because of false positives. His takeaway is that mutation testing is worth knowing about, and that he now reviews code by mentally mutating it, while human code review remains essential.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Architektura automatycznych testów UI na iOS
talks.teaser: R Herba investigates 4Developers 2021: Architektura automatycznych testów UI na iOS.

talks.title: 4Developers 2021: Rules of Engagement QUESTIONS TO ASK BEFORE YOU START AUTOMATING
talks.teaser: Lists the questions teams should answer about goals, data, ownership and process before automating tests.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that teams should understand their problem before choosing a tool or writing any automated test. Rather than giving answers, the speaker offers a set of questions to work through, since the right responses depend on each team's context. He starts by asking attendees about their automation pain points.

Three cases illustrate the point. In a budget calculation system, a three-month proof of concept produced tests that went stale quickly, because test data could only be created through the UI and the system depended on a third-party source whose data had been corrupted by earlier performance tests. The speaker admits he never asked how test data would be managed. In a shipment tracking project, a suite of 2000 to 3000 tests had more than 70 percent failing in regression, largely because tests were poorly written and unmaintained, and one conditional took a week to fix. Automation there was required by a process guideline rather than tied to a goal. In an online ebook store, the team already had working automation, but releases were limited by testing because automated tests were written after exploratory testing and stories kept changing.

The takeaways are practical. Treat automation as production-grade code with its own planning, documentation and architecture, and treat testability as part of the application's design. Define a measurable goal and check it is achievable, then look at the current bottleneck and whether the delivery process itself works, since automation only speeds up what already exists. Unit tests are usually cheaper and faster than UI tests, so they are a good starting point. Clarify who writes and maintains tests, the test data strategy, the tech stack, and acceptable run time. Answers will change over time, so teams need not answer everything at once.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Jakub Waliszewski - Azure DevOps in a secured World. How to build a safe Pipelines!
talks.teaser: Shows how to lock down Azure DevOps pipelines with permissions, service connections, approvals and data residency choices.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Azure DevOps as one platform that brings developers, testers and engineers together around repositories, artifacts and pipelines. The speaker frames secure delivery as a combination of people, process and tooling, and starts with compliance. Customers may require their data to stay in a particular region, so the location chosen when a project is created determines where its data is kept. The speaker walks through regional options, including Europe, Poland, Australia, the Americas, Canada and the USA, and notes that customer requirements should be checked before setup.

The middle section covers DevSecOps and access control. Service connections should be scoped carefully at organization or project level, and tokens and secrets should not be left in pipeline configuration. Permissions should be limited so most team members can only use or view pipelines rather than change them. Organization administrators can do everything, so that role needs tight restriction. Environment approvals, manual checks and branch policies with required code review can control who is allowed to release, and audit and reporting features help track what changed.

The closing part touches on marketplace extensions, which can add functionality to the platform. The speaker suggests reviewing them before use. The main takeaway is to apply least privilege, separate development from production, and add approvals and monitoring to every pipeline.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Łukasz Panek - Dependency Injection vs Dependency Inversion vs. Inversion of Control
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of 4Dev Live 2021: Łukasz Panek - Dependency Injection vs Dependency Inversion vs. Inversion of Control.
talks.summary: Łukasz Panek notes recruiters confuse SOLID's D with Spring-style dependency injection: most candidates guess injection, fewer explain dependency inversion or inversion of control. The 4Dev Live talk separates the three concepts with DDD and hexagonal architecture examples from years of Java hiring.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Michał Guzowski - Wdrożenia dużych środowisk Low-Code w organizacjach
talks.teaser: Maps how large low-code rollouts succeed through stakeholder alignment, maturity stages, and governance—not only tooling.
talks.summary:
The session frames IT’s staffing gap as something low-code can address by lowering technical barriers while shifting hard work to delivery, communication, and scale. A European transport client with roughly 300 applications and about 1,000 automated flows illustrates why strategy, change management, and guidelines matter once citizen developers join professional builders.

The middle covers spotting problems with business users, classifying work via a solution-assessment matrix (security risk versus technical complexity), and choosing fast-track low-code versus full IT delivery. A developer-services client case replaced costly SaaS with mobile time reporting, geo-fenced check-ins, and management dashboards built in about three months, with savings visible after six months from first contact.

Practitioners should treat mature estates as tens or hundreds of apps: enforce data integrity, avoid privilege escalation across hundreds of connectors, apply DLP and development policies, license deliberately, separate dev/test/prod, and design for end users. IT’s evolving role blends architecture with people and process leadership as low-code spreads.

talks.title: 4Dev Live 2021: Michalina Kotwica - Typed Python ...or what I like to call: Python++
talks.teaser: Shows how Python type annotations, unions, overloads and dataclasses can make large parsers and compilers easier to build.
talks.summary:
The talk presents typed Python as a language that has grown beyond plain dynamic code, which the speaker calls Python++. It traces the history: function signatures and type comments came first with PEP 484, class annotations followed in later releases, and static checkers made the hints useful. The changes arrived in small steps rather than as one plan.

The middle covers the main features. Dataclasses generate the initializer, add comparison and hashing, and offer frozen and slotted variants with no runtime penalty. Unions, a gap in many statically typed languages, gained a compact syntax in Python 3.10 and narrow inside isinstance branches. Type variables with bounds tie a return type to the input, self and cls annotations handle subclass-returning methods, and overloads with literal types describe functions like open whose result depends on a string argument. Stub files let these signatures be added without editing the original module.

The final case is a parser for a graph-based UI document, where the format was described as a hierarchy of classes and unions. One generic function then reported every error with stack traces. The takeaway is that because type information is available at runtime, developers can write their own checks, and teammates can edit a declarative schema more easily than a pile of dictionaries.

talks.title: OMH International 2021: Navigating Microsoft & GitHub Ecosystem For Open (...)- Alex Belotserkovskiy
talks.teaser: Walks through how Microsoft approaches open source across Linux, cloud native, data and AI, and GitHub security tooling.
talks.summary:
Alex Belotserkovskiy, a cloud solution architect who also serves as a Microsoft open source community lead, opens by saying the session is aimed at both developers and infrastructure specialists who use open source. He traces the company's open source history and argues that its growing contribution culture is visible in public GitHub repositories and roadmaps, and notes that much of Microsoft's cloud runs on Linux.

The middle of the talk covers strategic areas. Linux work includes secure hardware enablement and testing large numbers of images at scale. Cloud native projects extend Kubernetes toward the edge, and a set of tools is presented as easier for enterprises to adopt. Data and AI services are described as built on open source components, with managed options such as a distributed PostgreSQL offering. The speaker also covers .NET moving to open source under the .NET Foundation, the release of Visual Studio Code, a Microsoft Java distribution, and Rust work for Windows, and touches on machine learning ethics tooling.

The closing section focuses on supply chain security, which the speaker calls a central concern, and on GitHub features such as Actions and policy checks that help secure build and deployment pipelines. He points listeners to opensource.microsoft.com for projects, internal practices and foundation sponsorship, and ends with the message that open source is about sharing.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Tomasz Zieliński - Jeden plik, wiele znaczeń - eksperymenty z poliglotami
talks.teaser: Explores how one file can be valid in several formats at once, from GIF and JAR hybrids to PDF polyglots.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces polyglot files, which satisfy the rules of several file formats at the same time. The speaker first explains what a file and a format are: a format is an agreement about how bytes are ordered and interpreted, and real-world parsers often tolerate data that breaks the specification. He then shows that a single byte pattern or image can be read as two different formats depending on the interpreter, such as an image that decodes as both an Aztec code and a QR code.

The main part builds hybrids by hand. A GIF and a JAR are concatenated into one file that opens as an image in Windows and as a Java archive, because ZIP readers find the central directory from the end of the file. Other examples include a GIF carrying PHP code in a comment, a Word document combined with an Android APK, and a file that stacks a DOS/Windows executable, a PDF and a ZIP. The talk also covers a magazine whose PDF issues hide PNG images, audio and even a game ROM, and the Mitra generator, which automates many format combinations. Tools such as the file command and binwalk can be made to report many formats in one file.

The closing section draws lessons from the speaker's own offline timetable app, which used a binary format with checksums, a grammar and a validator. His advice is to publish examples of valid and invalid files with edge cases, to plan how obsolete format features will be retired, and to treat long-term backward compatibility as a cost that must be reviewed over time.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Marcin Marciniak
talks.teaser: Explains how to assess risk, plan and test production changes, and handle failed rollouts without repeating past mistakes.
talks.summary: Marcin Marciniak challenges the superstition against Friday production changes with an IT change-management walkthrough: documentation, CAB-style review, risk worksheets scoring impact and probability (domain controller versus ERP patch), human factors like Friday the 13th and long weekends, rollback and discovery-delay windows, phased rollouts, canary traffic, and when to use fast-track versus emergency paths after a failed deploy.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Michał Leszczyński - Miałem WordPressa, ale mi zhakowali
talks.teaser: Walks through analysing and recovering a deliberately compromised WordPress site, from log review to a safe rebuild.
talks.summary:
A security engineer from CERT Polska deliberately sets up a WordPress site, waits for it to be compromised, and then walks through the analysis as an incident responder would. The first sign is a suspicious file modified shortly after the install. The access logs show automated requests to a vulnerable WP File Manager connector, followed by a PHP web shell that runs whatever command is passed in a parameter. The attacker fetches further code from a paste site, uploads a file manager, and disguises responses as a 404 page hiding a password prompt. Enabling full POST logging helps reconstruct what was uploaded.

The talk then looks at why such compromises matter beyond a defaced page. A hacked legitimate site can host phishing pages or act as a proxy for attacks on other WordPress installs. The speaker also tried a social approach, redirecting the attacker's path to an invitation to a chat server, though nobody joined. The attacker later defaced the site and deleted it.

For recovery, the advice is to deploy a fresh WordPress from the vendor, reinstall plugins from their sources or audit them, compare old and new files, scan the database for injected code, and reset user passwords. For prevention, the talk recommends hardening endpoints, adding HTTP basic authentication to wp-admin, tracking file changes with git, and storing backups in a write-only location that is tested by restoring them.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Paula Januszkiewicz - Adventures in Underland: Hacker Tricks to Stay Under the...
talks.teaser: Shows how memory and disk artifacts expose hidden processes, unwritten event logs and recoverable user secrets during investigations.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how investigators can still recover evidence after an intrusion by working through memory and disk artifacts together. The speaker argues that data held in volatile memory often survives when it is missing from disk, so memory should be captured before the disk image. She describes a government incident in which attackers had been inside for months and were only found through log review and a set of indicators that did not match normal activity.

The demonstrations start with hidden processes. A process unlinked from the active process list disappears from a standard process listing but still shows up in a handle-based scan, which is the practical way to catch it. Memory regions marked readable, writable and executable, along with unsigned loaded modules, are presented as signs of injected code. The talk then recovers Windows event log records that never reached disk and carves them from a memory dump with a free repair tool, noting that recovered records can still be incomplete. A simulated NTLM relay is used to deliver a Meterpreter session, and the speaker shows the traces it leaves in memory, in Prefetch files and in the limits of netstat.

The final part covers timestamp tampering and stored credentials. Changed file metadata is shown to be detectable through the NTFS journal when it is enabled and sized adequately. Using a DPAPI domain backup key exported from a domain controller, the speaker decrypts a user's master keys and opens a KeePass database. The takeaway is that anything running in memory is not truly hidden, and that understanding how artifacts are created matters more than any single tool.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Michał Trojnara - Ataki padding oracle na karty elektroniczne
talks.teaser: Shows how padding oracle flaws in CBC-mode smart card encryption let an attacker recover plaintext without the key.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces padding oracle attacks against smart cards and starts from the basics. It explains XOR, why block ciphers split messages into blocks, and why cipher block chaining needs an unpredictable initialisation vector. It then covers block padding under the ISO 7816-4 scheme, where a marker byte 0x80 is followed by zeros.

The core idea is that if a card reveals whether the padding of a decrypted message is valid, through an error code or a measurable timing difference, an attacker who controls the IV can recover the plaintext one byte at a time without knowing the key. The speaker demonstrates the simple case, where the oracle checks the last block, and recovers a message in under 1,000 oracle calls. He then covers a harder case where the padding check runs from the end of the message and the attacker must work on earlier blocks. A further variant uses a fixed zero IV, which roughly doubled the time per attack and pushed the count to about 45,000 calls.

The practical takeaway is that the fix is authenticity, not better padding. Verify a MAC over the ciphertext before decrypting or checking padding, so that tampered messages are rejected without revealing padding status. Keep error responses and timing uniform, generate IVs randomly, and leave cryptographic implementation to specialists rather than writing it by hand.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Paweł Rzepa - Bezpieczeństwo serverless: atak i obrona
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Oh My H@ck 2020 - Paweł Rzepa - Bezpieczeństwo serverless: atak i obrona.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Piotr Filip Sawicki - Jak oswoić audytora?
talks.teaser: Explains how to deal with IT auditors without ego or defensiveness, and how to treat them as a business partner.
talks.summary:
The speaker, an auditor for about 20 years who has also been responsible for security areas himself, argues that audits often go badly because of the audited side's ego rather than the findings. When criticism touches a person's sense of competence, a fight-or-flight reflex takes over and cooperation stops. He walks through four common defensive reactions, shown with short staged examples: playing the innocent victim, pointing to overwork as an excuse, answering criticism with counter-criticism, and attacking the auditor personally.

Next he explains how auditors think. They look for simple technical answers: does a control really reduce the risk, what does it cost, does it create new problems, and does it still work when the one person who runs it is on holiday or sick? Drawing on aviation and healthcare, he says incidents usually come from technology, process and people failing together, and that a just culture punishes only deliberate misconduct. In twenty years, he says, only two people he audited were removed, and both cases involved clear wrongdoing.

He closes with practical advice: treat the auditor as a business partner, check facts with other staff before the audit, and remember that audits are usually scheduled well in advance rather than aimed at you after an incident. Auditors can also back budget requests to management with a company-wide view. A tongue-in-cheek list of tactics for misleading auditors, such as flooding them with documents or planting decoy findings, is presented as something that rarely works on experienced auditors and is not a recommended approach.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Piotr Głaska - DNS ATT&CK 2020 - przegląd najciekawszych technik
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Oh My H@ck 2020 - Piotr Głaska - DNS ATT&CK 2020 - przegląd najciekawszych technik.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Prof. Jerzy Surma - Krótkie wprowadzenie do hakowania Sztucznej Inteligencji
talks.teaser: Introduces attacks on machine learning systems, a taxonomy of them, and ways to build models that resist tampering.
talks.summary:
Prof. Jerzy Surma opens with a short introduction to deliberate interference with machine learning systems, which could disrupt their operation or stop them. He gives examples: a road sign altered so an autonomous car misreads it, and face-recognition glasses that get a wrong person accepted. He separates narrow AI, the only kind in use today, from general AI, and notes that image classification error fell from 15 percent after 2012 to below 1 percent.

The talk then sorts attacks into a taxonomy. Integrity attacks degrade a classifier or force chosen wrong outputs, availability attacks stop or slow a system, and confidentiality attacks gather information. Poisoning injects crafted samples into training data, and a few dozen can be enough to plant a backdoor. Black-box attacks target a finished model. A student project against a Naive Bayes spam filter showed that editing word content and position could send legitimate mail to spam and spam to the inbox, with changes at around the 10 percent level sufficing.

The talk closes by noting active research on robust algorithms as the defensive side, and it points to a recently published Polish book on the subject. The takeaway is that machine learning components are attack surface and need testing against manipulated training data and inputs.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Rafał Jaczyński - V2X. V2H? H2V? WTF?
talks.teaser: Surveys V2X communication roles, cellular latency tests, and rising remote attacks on connected vehicle platforms.
talks.summary:
Connected and autonomous driving pushes a second revolution beside smarter vehicles: roads and fleets that exchange data externally, not only through onboard radar, lidar, and cameras. The presentation outlines V2X-style links to infrastructure, wide-area networks, nearby vehicles, more vulnerable road users, and charging equipment, then contrasts what cabin sensors miss—dense signal heads, weather, blind corners, and occluded merges—with what coordinated messaging is claimed to improve, including safety, convoy efficiency, and urban throughput figures cited from European road statistics and industry examples.

Implementation paths include DSRC versus reusing lower cellular layers, with field tests reporting on the order of 14 millisecond delays on LTE-style links, and a move toward fifth-generation radio with multi-access edge computing so applications sit near base stations rather than distant data centers. The security portion notes sharply rising automotive security incidents, mostly remote and criminal, and describes modern cars as many electronic control units sharing a broadcast bus where admission control, addressing, and reprogramming resistance matter. Aftermarket remote diagnostic dongles, segmented in-vehicle networks, and long-running fleet research illustrate that compromising one model is costly yet high-impact, while standards already define authentication and message security services.

Practitioners should expect risk to concentrate in operator, road-authority, and third-party edge applications, heterogeneous multi-tenant edge sites with weaker physical protection, and privacy tension as highly connected cars generate enormous sensor volumes and pseudonymous certificates still interact with tracking and consent questions left open in law and product design.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Łukasz Mikuła - Deserializacja w Java - czy nadal jest się czego obawiać?
talks.teaser: Shows how Java deserialization flaws are found and exploited through gadget chains, and which defenses still matter.
talks.summary:
Łukasz Mikuła asks whether Java deserialization is still worth worrying about. He starts with how Java serialization works: an object is turned into bytes, sent elsewhere, and rebuilt on the receiving side, which needs matching classes on its classpath. He recalls how public research and a published tool in 2015 made automated exploitation of unsafe deserialization practical.

The middle of the talk covers finding and exploiting the problem. Serialized data often appears as hex or base64 strings with recognisable headers, and a mismatched serialVersionUID or a stack trace can reveal what the endpoint expects. Gadget chains, which are existing classes linked through reflection, are the core of exploitation. The speaker argues that replaying a payload generator in a loop wastes most of its potential. He then demonstrates a DNS callback that needs no extra classpath, and a command-execution payload against a deliberately vulnerable server.

For defence, the speaker favours patching and input filtering, and prefers allowlists to blocklists, since a blocklist tends to miss something eventually. He argues that even a DNS lookup or an opened port is a signal to investigate before a full code execution chain has been found. The takeaway is that unsafe deserialization in Java remains a real risk, and patching is worth doing even when a working exploit is hard to build.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Wojciech Reguła - Od u0 do milionera - atakowanie komunikacji międzyprocesowej...
talks.teaser: Shows how weak client validation in third-party macOS XPC services enables local privilege escalation to root, plus practical fixes.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at XPC, the inter-process communication mechanism macOS apps use to talk to privileged helper services. The speaker explains how XPC connections work, from a listener that publishes a named service to clients that define an interface and call methods on a remote object. Because these helpers often run as root, a flaw in how they accept clients can let a normal local user gain root.

The core of the talk is a set of flaws found across popular third-party macOS software, including antivirus, messaging and firewall products. Cases include helpers that never check the caller, code-signing checks that only compare a bundle identifier or organization name (which a self-signed certificate can satisfy), static checks of on-disk binaries that do not match the running process, and validation based on process IDs, which can be swapped while a request waits in the queue. One helper method let a low-privileged app change file permissions, and another allowed an uninstall with business impact. The speaker also showed injecting an unsigned dynamic library into an app without library validation, including on Catalina.

The closing section reviews fixes: validating clients by audit token, using strict code-signing requirements that pin the developer's team identity, enabling hardened runtime and library validation, and enforcing minimum client versions. The takeaway for developers is that signature checks alone are not enough, and that privileged services must verify the connecting client in a way that cannot be raced or spoofed.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Michał Bentkowski - Ciekawy przypadek Copy'ego-Paste'a - o ryzykach wklejania...
talks.teaser: Shows how copying and pasting between web pages and editors can leak data or enable XSS through browser and editor bugs.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at what can go wrong when content is copied from one web page and pasted into another. It starts with a familiar scenario: a shell command copied from a web page that, once pasted into a terminal, runs an extra destructive command the user never saw. The speaker explains that a copy handler on the page replaced the clipboard contents, and that a trailing newline made the shell execute the injected line immediately. The practical advice is to paste clipboard contents into a plain text editor first and check them.

The second part moves to rich text. Copying formatted content places HTML on the clipboard, and the speaker shows how browser sanitizers and web editors process that HTML. Several sanitizer bugs were found across major browsers, including a Chrome universal cross-site scripting issue that could pull data from a logged-in Gmail session. A comment-closing sequence that parsers handle differently was used against the TinyMCE and CKEditor editors, and a Froala bug came from processing HTML as a plain string. A CSS-only technique was also shown, leaking attribute values one character at a time through chained imports.

The closing takeaway is that pasted HTML should be treated as untrusted input, that editors should parse it with a DOM parser rather than string handling, and that browsers and vendors need to fix these parsing gaps. Many of the issues were fixed before the talk, though the speaker notes that at least one fix arrived without a public changelog entry.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Grzegorz Tworek
talks.teaser: Explains how Windows verifies file signatures through SIP plugins and WinVerifyTrust, and how that can be abused.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how digital signatures on files work inside Windows. The speaker starts with the purpose of signing: showing a file is unchanged and came from a party verified through PKI. Windows has to cover many formats, from executables and installers to text-based PowerShell scripts, and many of them never reserved space for a signature. Some files are therefore signed through separate catalog files instead.

Demos compare tools on a two-byte System32 file that Sigcheck and PowerShell report as validly signed, while Explorer and SignTool's default check find no signature. The gap comes from each tool asking a different question. Verification runs through the WinVerifyTrust API, which hands work to Subject Interface Package (SIP) DLLs registered in the registry, each claiming a file type such as PowerShell, WSH or Appx. The speaker shows how these DLLs are queried, and how a test provider GUID dumps verification data to trustpol.txt, a step that needs administrator rights.

On the abuse side, a custom SIP DLL runs its code whenever a signature check happens, from Explorer, Autoruns or PowerShell, making it a quiet persistence option. Other risks include a SIP that falsely reports files as signed and verification that skips parts of a file. The takeaways: sign your own binaries with a code signing certificate, add RFC 3161 timestamps so signatures outlive certificate expiry, and remember that "signed" can mean different things to different Windows components.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Bartek Jerzman - Podrzucony laptop, czyli jak hakuje się banki w Afryce
talks.teaser: Explains how African criminal groups use planted insider laptops to breach banks, and how analysts trace their infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at attacks on banks carried out by criminal groups from East Africa, which the speaker contrasts with typical phishing-led intrusions. Access begins with a bribed insider who receives a prepared Windows laptop, connects it to the victim's network and hides it there. The group then controls the machine remotely with commercial remote-management tools, moves laterally, and harvests credentials with Python-based keyloggers. Stolen banking credentials are used to change permissions on financial systems so the attackers' accounts can withdraw large sums quickly.

The speaker describes how these groups relate to one another, tracing a Kenyan cartel that later split into smaller crews. A keylogger case study compares samples from different groups that share copied code, similar comments and log-handling habits. Defenders are advised to watch for newly appearing files in unusual locations such as ProgramData, and to write import-based rules, since the scripts ship with their own runtime and string-based rules are fragile.

The second case study follows one group's new Python backdoor, starting from a vendor report that gave only an IP address and port. Historical port data from a search engine, the hosting provider, a screenshot from an exposed remote desktop, and a distinctive HTTP header and error string were used to find related servers. The takeaway for practitioners is that niche open-source tools and unusual server responses can reveal attacker infrastructure before any malware sample is available.

talks.title: Oh My H@ck 2020 - Artur Balsam
talks.teaser: Hackowanie aplikacji na papierze analyzes Oh My H@ck 2020 - Artur Balsam.
talks.summary:
Artur Balsam presents threat modeling as a general tool for finding application security problems at every development stage and level of abstraction, including privacy and business logic. He stresses that it is not a silver bullet and does not replace penetration testing, static analysis or training, but complements them, and that an imperfect model is still worth starting and updating over time.

The practical process starts with a group of four or five people, ideally including developers and QA as well as a moderator who is not only the security person. They sketch a data flow diagram no older than one sprint, split large systems into parts such as single microservices, and set scope by what matters most, like passenger safety on a ski lift or money in a transfer app. The brainstorm then asks what could go wrong, using STRIDE-style categories, and all ideas are written down before anyone judges them.

Four cases from the talk show the payoff. A cow-monitoring app let users set a lifespan that produced an enormous stream of events, overwhelming the messaging layer. Email normalization differed between Gmail and other providers, so two addresses could map to one account. Eventual consistency suited most data but not a points system needing exact balances. An installer app exposed full customer records when only a name was needed. The takeaway: these flaws are cheap to fix when found at design time, and the shared notes become a reusable knowledge base.

talks.title: CONFidence 2020: IoT in the criminal underground (David Sancho)
talks.teaser: Surveys criminal underground forums to show which IoT devices attackers target and how they profit.
talks.summary:
The talk looks past headline-grabbing predictions about smart toasters and talking dolls and asks what criminals actually do with connected devices. The speaker surveys underground forums in Russian, Portuguese, English, Spanish and Arabic. For this survey, IoT means any device without a normal operating system such as Windows, which leaves out phones, servers and desktops. Routers are by far the most attacked devices, with online cameras next.

Where a business model exists, the monetization is concrete. Russian-language sellers offer access to hijacked camera feeds, grouped into themed channels for as little as 50 rubles. Router owners are sold SSH tunnels that turn a compromised home or office router into a VPN exit node, which is hard for ISPs to block. In the Brazilian underground, compromised routers have their DNS changed so that visits to a real bank are redirected to a fake site, and that redirection is sold for about 1,000 R per week, which the speaker put at roughly 250 dollars.

The English, Spanish and Arabic forums show interest in owning routers, printers, industrial refrigeration systems and cameras, including exploit requests, scanning tools and tutorials. The speaker found no clear way to profit from those infections, so the activity looks driven by curiosity rather than money. The bottom line is that routers and other devices will be attacked. Anyone running a sizable fleet should plan protection now, because attacks will keep growing as other criminals learn how to monetize them.

talks.title: CONFidence 2020: How to pwn a Bank using kitchen knives (Maciej Michałowski)
talks.teaser: Walks through physical and social intrusions into banks and plants, from reconnaissance to domain controller access.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a penetration tester who works for banks and industrial and chemical companies, argues that physical access and human trust can open a route into an organisation that network defences do not cover. The talk follows the stages of an engagement: reconnaissance with floor plans, recruitment videos and street-level imagery, then the tools used to get past locks, gates and barriers, and the pretexts used to talk past staff.

Several cases are described separately. In one, the tester scouted a building for days, then followed a group of workers through a controlled entrance and later reached a server room with keys found in a labelled cabinet. In another, a colleague phoned a company while the speaker posed as a senior manager, which got the colleague into a conference room where a Raspberry Pi was connected to the network. A phishing campaign reported a high success rate, with 80 people handing over their details. Inside one target, information shown on locked screens helped identify a staff member with broad administrator rights, which led toward the domain controller. A separate visit to an industrial site ended in a control room that could change process parameters.

The closing message is that careful reconnaissance and preparation matter more than advanced tooling, and that trust extended to unfamiliar people is a common weak point. Defenders are encouraged to review physical controls, staff habits and exit routes alongside network security, and to feed findings back to the security team so procedures can be changed.

talks.title: CONFidence 2020: Jak ominąć analityka (Ireneusz Tarnowski)
talks.teaser: Shows how criminals adapt malware and tradecraft to evade analysts, spanning signed binaries, sandbox checks, and covert channels.
talks.summary:
The session frames an ongoing contest between defenders and financially motivated attackers who shape campaigns around current events and prepare operations with reconnaissance rather than indiscriminate spraying. When standard threat models meet adversaries who study published detections and antivirus logic, familiar controls can miss the point of the attack.

Across the middle, the speaker walks through evasion patterns seen in the wild: abusing code signing and trust lists, waiting out analysts, probing which network paths remain open, and choosing channels that blend into normal traffic. Several cases stress environment awareness—virtual machines, nested guests, disk and firmware fingerprints, and registry tells—so samples refuse to run or hide their real behavior under analysis. File-level tricks, concatenated or padded payloads, and post-install steps that weaken endpoint protection illustrate how small implementation choices become durable bypasses.

The closing argument is that public write-ups feed the next iteration of malware, so blue teams should assume reverse pressure on every rule. Practitioners gain a checklist for comparing samples across analysis generations, watching for the simplest techniques that still work, and turning criminal missteps into durable detection opportunities.

talks.title: CONFidence: 38+2 karty flash z wkładką - dane gratis (Marcin D. Hankiewicz)
talks.teaser: Reveals how much former owners' data can be recovered from second-hand flash memory cards bought on consumer marketplaces.
talks.summary:
The presentation grows out of earlier academic work suggesting that most resold memory cards still hold previous owners' data. The speaker describes buying dozens of used SD and related cards, often from individual sellers, and building a disciplined pipeline: legal review under GDPR, careful logging and photography, forensic disk images, and review with tools such as Autopsy, while avoiding hosts that silently write to inserted media.

On roughly three quarters of the cards, deleted files were easy to bring back because devices usually erase directory entries, not sectors. Phones dominate the recovered material, including years of family photos, geotags, contacts synced from social networks, boarding passes, medical paperwork, scans of IDs, and business documents. One card still held old browser bookmarks with logins and passwords beside newer camera images, enabling reconstruction of hobbies, employers, and travel patterns without advanced exploitation.

Practitioners should treat removable storage as a long-lived witness: factory resets and casual deletes are weak, and cards passed within families or sold online can expose others. The talk urges secure wiping or destruction before resale, awareness that auxiliary storage on Android behaves differently from portable cards, and planning for legal and ethical boundaries when researching found personal data.

talks.title: CONFidence 2020: Złap mnie jeśli potrafisz, czyli z phishingiem zabawa w kotka i myszkę (Adam Lange)
talks.teaser: Walks through how phishing campaigns hide from analysts and scanners, and how defenders can spot the evasion tricks.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how phishing campaigns, often disguised as marketing or streaming-service lures, blend into normal traffic and avoid the analysts and tools studying them. The speaker starts with infrastructure: lookalike domains, subdomains on abused hosting, and legitimate websites that attackers have taken over, which are harder to analyse. A Netflix-themed example traces a message through a redirect to a hijacked site, some of them built on WordPress, serving a Polish-language page.

The middle section covers evasion checks. Kits choose what to show based on the visitor's IP geolocation, language settings, timezone and browser properties, and they filter out visitors from security networks, hosting ranges and bot-protection services. They also detect private browsing, generate page content with JavaScript at runtime, sometimes decrypt it in the browser, and require a random parameter or a per-visit directory name. Visitors who do not match the target get a 404 or 403. The speaker also points to weak admin panel passwords, and to index pages being protected while the resources behind them are not, which allows resource-based fingerprinting.

For practitioners, the takeaway is to revisit suspicious links with different browsers, regions, languages and devices instead of accepting a 404 as proof that nothing is there. Automated and semi-automated collection helps keep up with short-lived campaigns, and treating each rejected visit as a signal rather than a dead end makes the analysis more complete.

talks.title: CONFidence 2020: Mylobot, Detecting the Undetected with Deep Learning (Yael Daihes)
talks.teaser: Shows how a deep learning model spots DGA-generated domains in live DNS traffic and tracks the Mylobot botnet.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Mylobot, a botnet first described in 2018, and at how domain generation algorithms (DGAs) let malware pick rotating command-and-control domains from a shared seed. Defenders have traditionally reverse engineered the malware and reproduced the algorithm, which works only when the seed can be recovered and only for families already known.

The speaker walks through a detection pipeline built on a large volume of live DNS traffic. Simple character-frequency heuristics failed once attackers copied the letter distribution of popular domains, so the team trained an LSTM neural network on about 1.2 million DGA domains and 1.2 million benign ones. The model separated DGA from benign domains well but could not name the family, so generated domains were grouped by the regular expressions they fit, with unmatched groups tracked as unknown families. Running in production, the system reportedly blocks about 2.5 million domains a day, and the speaker says false positives are kept very low.

Applied to Mylobot, the pattern first matched about 1,400 domains and about 8,000 across four variants, with one early variant resolving to a likely sinkhole. A 2020 update showed roughly 200 million DNS requests a day, far more than other botnets in the same data, and infected entities roughly doubling over the past year. The takeaway is that DNS monitoring can catch DGA-based botnets, and that deep learning combined with open threat data is a practical tool for finding them.

talks.title: CONFidence 2020: Lazarus’ Dtrack marathon (Sveva Vittoria Scenarelli, John Southworth)
talks.teaser: Retrospective threat research traces DTrack's evolution, delivery chains, and links among Lazarus-related malware families across campaigns.
talks.summary:
The session opens with background on the North Korea–linked Lazarus intrusion set, its motivations spanning sabotage, espionage, and cybercrime, and naming conventions used in industry and at PwC. A timeline of attributed operations leads into DTrack, a remote access tool used since at least 2014 and known under several vendor labels, including earlier backdoor-like builds and later RAT-style variants with stable capabilities from 2017 onward.

The middle of the talk walks through initialization, string decoding (RC4, XOR, CCS-style obfuscation), dynamic API loading, persistence, anti-analysis checks, and HTTP command-and-control behavior, including use of compromised or internal infrastructure. Campaign geography and sectors are reviewed, with a deep look at a tailored sample linked to Indian nuclear-related incidents: victim fingerprinting via shell commands, staged archives, and exfiltration over internal networks with hard-coded credentials. Track Drop is described as the in-memory loader, including process hollowing, YARA pivoting, and additional payloads such as downloaders, keyloggers, phishing HTML, and the Anonymous downloader tied through encryption and coding habits to Andariel tools such as Rifdoor, Hotcroissant, and Bistromath.

The close emphasizes shared code reuse across Lazarus and Andariel, dual-use tooling for espionage and financial crime, and practical defender guidance: monitor plain HTTP and internal C2, watch for injection and hollowing APIs, net-based lateral movement, code-signing abuse, and user-facing recruitment or banking lures, plus continued signature work and MITRE ATT&CK mapping with shared indicators.

talks.title: CONFidence 2020: Software Zero-Day Discovery: A Journey from Main to Return (Kushal Arvind Shah)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding CONFidence 2020: Software Zero-Day Discovery: A Journey from Main to Return (Kushal Arvind Shah).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, titled "Software Zero-Day Discovery: A Journey from Main to Return," the speaker (introduced in the transcript as Kushal Arvind Shah) discusses methodology, targets, and practical techniques for discovering software zero-day vulnerabilities. The talk outlines how security researchers can identify target software, source test files, build and instrument targets, and use debugging and fuzzing approaches to identify crashes and report security issues.

### Key Topics
- **Target and Application Selection:** The speaker explores how researchers can identify targets by examining platforms, bug bounty lists, and repositories of reported vulnerabilities. Resources such as file extension directories (e.g., file-extensions.org) can be used to uncover less common file formats and the applications that parse them.
- **Sourcing Test Files:** Strategies for collecting sample files, including finding samples via bug trackers, specialized websites, and repositories where sample formats are hosted for testing and fuzzing.
- **Building and Instrumentation:** Approaches to building software, including using address sanitizers (such as ASan) and runtime compiler options to reliably catch memory corruption and runtime errors.
- **Crash Triage and Debugging:** Identifying reproducible crashes, examining call stacks and memory states, inspecting crash logs, and reporting identified vulnerabilities to relevant vendors or project maintainers.

### Technical Details
- **Discovering Vulnerabilities via Public Trackers:** The speaker notes that researchers can inspect existing vulnerability reports and platforms (such as bug tracking platforms, Zero Day Initiative/ZDI advisories, and open-source project trackers) to understand where issues commonly arise and what file types trigger parsing bugs.
- **File Extension and Format Research:** By consulting sites such as `file-extensions.org`, researchers can explore niche file types and map them to open-source or proprietary applications handling complex media, document, or archive formats.
- **Compilation and Sanitization:** When source code is available (in open-source software), the speaker emphasizes compiling targets with sanitizers like AddressSanitizer (ASan) and debugging symbols to catch out-of-bounds reads/writes, use-after-free conditions, and invalid pointer dereferences immediately upon occurrence.
- **Triage Workflow:** The workflow transitions from running or feeding generated inputs into the target, observing crashes, inspecting the program state via debuggers, locating the faulting function or line of code, and preparing reproducible proof-of-concept submissions for maintainers.

### Takeaways
- Systematic target selection—focusing on applications that parse complex or uncommon file formats—is an effective starting point for finding vulnerabilities.
- Utilizing compiler-assisted sanitization (like AddressSanitizer) significantly accelerates detection and triage of memory corruption bugs.
- Tracking existing bug disclosures and public sample corpora provides valuable references and seed files for vulnerability research.
- *Note on Transcript Quality:* Significant portions of the transcript contain corrupted or noisy speech-to-text text, which limits visibility into specific tool command-lines or exact code walkthrough details presented visually during the talk.

talks.title: CONFidence 2020: Mind Games: Using Data to Solve for the Human Element (Masha Sedova)

talks.title: CONFidence 2020: Unveil the devil (Félix Aimé, Ivan Kwiatkowski)
talks.teaser: Examines heuristics that expose off-the-shelf implant C2 on the internet and tie malicious infrastructure into actor clusters.
talks.summary:
The presentation examines how defenders can find and correlate command-and-control infrastructure when cybercrime and APT actors run off-the-shelf implants such as Empire, Metasploit, Cobalt Strike, and related commercial frameworks. These tools are maintained by large communities, cheap to operate, and help malicious activity hide among legitimate red-team use, yet attackers still need domains, IPs, and servers before campaigns go live.

The speakers walk through practical discovery mistakes on deployed C2: default or repository TLS certificates on listeners and admin panels, hard-coded authentication artifacts, developer copy-paste quirks in web pages, HTTP header order that fails to mimic real nginx or IIS fronts, and protocol fingerprints including shared Diffie-Hellman parameters, DNS TXT behavior, and recognizable content in HTTP responses. They extend hunting beyond single hosts by clustering on autonomous systems, DNS and registrar choices, domain patterns, registration and setup timing, and consistent service configuration across batches.

A workflow demonstrated through the INFRAGENE clustering tool replays real cases, including a Rio Crystal–linked Cobalt Strike glue-DNS cluster and an espionage set that staged Metasploit while leaning on red-team-style tradecraft. Automated crown jobs apply heuristic rules against public scan data and feed analysts new servers for tagging and rescanning. The closing note is that WHOIS-centric correlation has weakened under privacy constraints, while certificate and configuration anomalies still surface many APT infrastructure sets, even as some elite actors move toward domain fronting and satellite-linked communication.

talks.title: CONFidence 2020: Pivoting and Exploitation in Docker Environment (Filipi Pires)
talks.teaser: Walks through a web app compromise via zip slip, then pivots through SSH tunnels into a Docker container network.
talks.summary:
The talk covers penetration testing against Docker-based environments, starting with the black, gray and white box models and how red team work differs from a standard pentest. The speaker explains a common methodology and why enumeration comes before exploitation. A recorded demo then runs against a vulnerable web server, where directory fuzzing exposed a secret page with a support chat that hinted at a remote code execution issue.

The upload form accepted archives, and the speaker exploited a zip slip path traversal flaw to place a PHP shell in the web root, gaining code execution as the web server user. A second archive upload dropped an SSH public key for the root account, giving a root shell. From the host, the speaker found several internal network ranges, a notes file referencing a test account, and SSH keys belonging to that account.

Using those credentials, the speaker opened a dynamic SSH port forward through the compromised machine into a Docker container network, then reached a Gogs service running inside that network through a local port. The closing point is that reused passwords, leftover notes and exposed version banners made the chain possible, and that pivoting lets an attacker reach networks that are not directly routable from outside.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Projekt wdrożeniowy realizowany na uczelni (Piotr Boryło)
talks.teaser: A university SDN rollout traces NCBR grant friction, traffic labs, and sFlow control with measured delay and loss improvements.
talks.summary:
The presentation follows a Polish university team that implemented an NCBR Lider-funded project to automate network measurements and optimize software-defined campus infrastructure. The speaker contrasts the original proposal diagram with the delivered architecture: time windows of telemetry feed a prediction module, an optimizer proposes configurations, and a human interface retains final control.

Much of the narrative covers execution realities rather than algorithms alone. Grant rules forced three-year monthly work plans and eight formal change requests to the funder. The group built an internet traffic model from edge-router statistics, published reusable tutorials, and engineered Java generators that replay realistic flows, including nanosecond timing and socket-pooling fixes. Mininet-based simulation demanded time acceleration, Docker-style multi-instance orchestration, Open vSwitch tuning, and abandonment of OpenFlow statistics in favor of a distributed sFlow-integrated controller. Hardware failures, procurement paperwork, team coordination across teaching loads, and a patented first-packet handling scheme appear as recurring themes.

Results shown on physical testbeds report lower delays, fewer links above an 80% utilization threshold, and reduced UDP loss after the system learns across initial windows. The close weighs spin-off commercialization, licensing, and why publicly funded research projects reward disciplined scope and operational pragmatism alongside scientific curiosity.

talks.title: CONFidence 2020: New Era in Telecom Hacking (Ali Abdollahi)
talks.teaser: Shows how mobile operators' radio and signaling protections can be detected and bypassed, with defensive recommendations.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with 2019 telecom abuse news, including SS7 exploitation aimed at SMS-based banking verification, and explains why subscriber identifiers and cell location data are valuable to an attacker. It then maps mobile architecture from 2G and 3G through LTE, with a brief overview of 5G, and frames three attack vectors: the radio access network, the signaling core, and the data network.

On the radio side, a test showed that a network accepted an invalid IMEI value, so IMEI-based device policies can be sidestepped. The talk also shows how a malicious SS7 authentication request sent from a roaming partner returned challenge values and the ciphering key in clear text. Forcing victims down to 2G or 3G with a jammer is covered, along with a VoLTE flaw in which a keystream was reused across calls. In the core network section, home routing is detected by comparing responses to repeated identical queries. Signaling firewall bypasses are shown by removing the application context name from TCAP messages, and by sending a legitimate operation followed by a malicious one that the firewall fails to inspect.

The closing section argues that assessments and penetration tests matter because operators hold millions of subscriber records. It warns against relying on security appliances alone and recommends behavioural analysis plus ongoing monitoring as complementary controls.

talks.title: 4Developers 2020, Jacek Milewski, Arch. App: Login API Security - is that you who attacks my system?
talks.teaser: Shows how credential stuffing and brute-force attacks hit a login API, and how monitoring and blocking helped a team respond.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that teams focus heavily on business logic while the login form, a small and seemingly simple screen, gets little security attention. It opens with public reports about leaked credential databases that are sold cheaply, and notes that many people reuse passwords, so one leaked login can open accounts elsewhere. Adding a second authentication factor is presented as a way to reduce that risk.

The speaker then walks through attacks on their own login API. A first brute-force run came from a single source and visibly cut normal traffic. Later waves spread across many addresses and countries, trying leaked pairs with one attempt per account. Missing logs meant the team could not tell whether account actions came from users or attackers, and success responses returned too much user data. Monitoring invalid logins and unique IP addresses exposed the spikes. A weekly pattern turned out to be a business partner's automated logins. One attack lasted over a day and a half and was handled by allowing only expected countries.

The response combined automated blocking by country and address, account locking after failed attempts, notifying affected users and forcing resets. The main lesson is prevention: strong factors, minimal data in responses, metrics to watch, and a blame-free company culture when incidents happen.

talks.title: 4Developers 2020, Mariusz Gil, PHP: Od modelu do commita - krótka historia pewnego agregatu
talks.teaser: Shows how three library digitization teams discover aggregate boundary mistakes that break loan limits, concurrency, and performance.
talks.summary:
The presentation uses a familiar library run by Ms Jola to spell out business rules: at most five active loans, one extension per loan, no new loans on overdue items, and strict enforcement. Three fictional teams then try to informatize the same desk workflows, and each design exposes different failures.

The first team treats a single loan as the core object and enforces the five-book cap with controller checks and simple flags. That works until concurrent requests hit the database; two threads can both pass validation and leave a reader with six or more loans. The speaker contrasts that low-stakes slip with domains where overdosing breaks hard safety limits.

A second team wraps every loan inside one library-card aggregate so rules live with the data. Invariants hold inside the object, but two sessions editing different loans on the same card still collide on save, and loading entire collections to check a count hurts throughput. The third team splits responsibilities: a slim card aggregate tracks only what is needed for the loan-count rule, while a separate loan aggregate handles lifecycle rules, ordering mutations to avoid extra loans, and injectable policies differentiate staff or university members from ordinary readers without hard-coding user types into the aggregate core.

The close ties the story to Eric Evans’s aggregate principles—real consistency boundaries, small enough roots, identity references instead of wide coupling, and deferring work that need not be instant—and points to PHP sample code on GitHub for readers who want implementations.

talks.title: 4Developers 2020, Grzegorz Piwowarek, Java: Wprowadzenie do ekosystemu Hazelcast
talks.teaser: Walks through the Hazelcast ecosystem in Java, from distributed maps and data structures to stream processing and CP consistency.
talks.summary:
The talk is an introductory tour of the Hazelcast ecosystem for Java developers. The speaker starts from the common view of Hazelcast as a distributed cache and shows that it works as an in-memory platform run by a cluster of machines. A distributed map is presented as one logical structure that is actually split into partitions, with backup copies spread across cluster members so data stays reachable when a node drops out.

The middle of the talk covers the wider toolkit: multimaps, distributed queues and lists, entry processors that run logic on the data where it lives, and aggregators that compute results across the whole cluster. Predicate-based filtering and an SQL-like query layer are shown, along with a local client-side cache for read-heavy workloads. The consistency discussion explains the trade-off between availability and consistency during network partitions, and notes that the CP subsystem needs at least three members to form a quorum. Structures such as a ring buffer, cardinality estimation based on HyperLogLog and a unique ID generator are also mentioned.

The closing section points to stream processing, Spring and Kubernetes integrations, a managed cloud offering and an SQL engine in the 4.1 beta. The practical takeaway is a map of what the platform can do and where to read more about each part, rather than a deep implementation dive.

talks.title: 4Developers 2020, Mateusz Dymiński, Architektury Aplikacji: Architecture Concepts Based on CDC
talks.teaser: Explains change data capture patterns, database setup, and event streaming to decouple legacy applications from modern service designs.
talks.summary:
The session opens by defining change data capture (CDC) as noticing every change on selected database tables and forwarding those changes as events for downstream processing. The presenter contrasts three approaches: database triggers that copy changes into helper tables, timestamp- or polling-based techniques that repeatedly ask what changed, and log-based capture that reads the engine’s transaction log (for example PostgreSQL WAL). Triggers and polling are described as older, heavy on the database, and awkward for deletes; log-based CDC is positioned as transparent to application code once the database is configured.

A live-style walkthrough on PostgreSQL shows raising WAL level, logical decoding slots, and a small listener that emits JSON events for inserts, updates, and deletes, including before/after fields where relevant. The middle section surveys market tooling—especially Debezium with Kafka Connect—including initial snapshots, connectors, and ordering guarantees per partition. Netflix’s DBLog is mentioned as a log-oriented alternative when long-running forward processes block tables.

The closing architecture guidance shows CDC streaming from a legacy monolith database without rewriting the core app, avoiding dual writes by treating the primary database as the single source of truth and replicating via the queue. Patterns include the transactional outbox (business table plus outbox in one transaction, CDC on the outbox) and the strangler fig approach for gradual migration. Practitioners are warned about cascades, duplicate primary keys in certain operations, slot retention, and heavy snapshots—plus an upcoming log-less option aimed at reducing forward-process load.

talks.title: 4Developers 2020, Agnieszka Małaszkiewicz, SS & BR: Occupational Burnout Syndrome (...)
talks.teaser: Gives a short Polish-language overview of occupational burnout syndrome as a workplace wellbeing problem.
talks.summary:
This session from the 4Developers 2020 programme runs about eleven minutes and is delivered in Polish. Its subject, as named in the title, is occupational burnout syndrome, a condition tied to a person's working life. Agnieszka Małaszkiewicz presents it as a short overview within a developer conference, so the focus is on recognising the problem rather than on any specific technique.

Because the talk is brief, it reads as an introduction to the subject rather than an in-depth study. The spoken content that can be followed clearly centres on the topic itself, with little detail beyond the framing of burnout as an occupational issue that affects people working in technology and related roles.

For a practitioner, the main takeaway is a basic awareness that burnout is a workplace concern worth taking seriously alongside technical skills. This short presentation is better suited to awareness than to hands-on methods.

talks.title: 4Developers 2020, Brian Benz, DevOps: Improving applications with DevOps
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in 4Developers 2020, Brian Benz, DevOps: Improving applications with DevOps.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation from 4Developers 2020, Brian Benz discusses how organizations can improve software delivery and operational efficiency through DevOps. Highlighting the balance of people, processes, and products, the talk emphasizes cross-functional collaboration and automated tooling to enable continuous value delivery to end users. Using statistics from the 2019 Accelerate State of DevOps report, Benz illustrates the impact of high-performing DevOps practices on deployment frequency, lead times, failure rates, and incident recovery.

### Key Topics
- **DevOps Core Definition**: Grounded in Donovan Brown's definition—the union of people, process, and products to enable continuous delivery of value to end users.
- **Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)**: Structuring team collaboration across planning, developing, testing, releasing, and monitoring stages with distinct roles for dev and ops teams.
- **DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) Metrics**: Reviewing 2019 Accelerate findings, including 208x more frequent deployments, 106x faster commit-to-delivery time, 7x lower change failure rates, and 2604x faster incident recovery.
- **Tooling Ecosystem**: Examining Azure DevOps components (Boards, Repos, Pipelines, Artifacts, Test Plans) alongside GitHub, GitHub Actions, and third-party integrations like Jenkins.
- **Deployment Strategies & Governance**: Utilizing deployment slots for canary releases, sticky sessions for A/B testing, and automated pre- and post-deployment approval gates.

### Technical Details
Benz demonstrates a live end-to-end continuous integration and deployment workflow for a retail sample site named Tailwind Traders:
- **Source Control and Triggering**: Editing pricing code locally in Visual Studio Code, staging, committing, and syncing changes to GitHub. The push initiates automated workflows.
- **Build Pipeline Execution**: Using an Azure Pipelines YAML file targeting Microsoft-hosted build agents (such as Windows Server 2019 with Visual Studio). The build tasks invoke the NuGet tool installer, fetch Node.js, run Visual Studio build tasks, perform tests, and copy deliverables to an artifact staging directory.
- **Intentional Build Failures**: In a parallel GitHub Actions workflow, Benz demonstrates failing a deployment run deliberately by mismatching Node version requirements (Node 14 vs. Node 10 required by the environment).
- **Deployment Pipeline Architecture**: Staging moves artifacts across a three-stage release pipeline (Staging, Canary deployment slot, and Production). Benz explains how canary deployment slots support traffic splitting for A/B testing. Release progression is safeguarded by pre-deployment conditions, manual approvals, and automated policy gates (e.g., Azure Policy compliance, Azure Functions, or external REST API validation).
- **Preserving Existing Investments**: Highlighting Jenkins integration architectures, where Jenkins handles initial builds and testing (leveraging Azure Container Instances or AWS EC2) before handing off artifacts to Azure DevOps for enterprise governance and release deployment.

### Takeaways
DevOps success relies heavily on cultural alignment, shared responsibilities, and clear role definitions before tooling can be effective. Modern cloud toolchains enable teams to safeguard production through gated releases, deployment slots, and canary rollouts while maintaining high deployment velocity.

talks.title: 4Developers 2020, Monika Bartczak, .NET: Analiza i przetwarzanie dużych zbiorów danych (...)
talks.teaser: Explains fuzzy sets and linguistic summaries for turning large datasets into plain-language insights.
talks.summary:
The presentation addresses how laboratories and businesses face rapidly growing datasets while classical data models and logic struggle with vague, everyday concepts. The speaker contrasts classical set theory with fuzzy sets and fuzzy logic, using examples such as linguistic quantifiers and membership functions, and argues that aggregates are easier for people to use when phrased in natural language instead of long lists of counts.

After introducing NLP, data exploration, and interpretation terms, the talk compares popular natural-language libraries for querying databases and walks through a sample product database queried in conversational form. The core work is linguistic summaries built on fuzzy quantifiers: established single-subject forms, a newer two-subject form from the literature, and the speaker’s extensions for multiple subjects with an explicit truth degree. These are tied to a graph-style client-complaints data model, with worked numeric examples and .NET code that computes whether a summary sentence is sufficiently true.

Practitioners should take away when fuzzy linguistic summaries complement standard NLP tooling, how truth thresholds affect perceived accuracy, and how the approach can support customer-relations decisions such as tracking whether complaints from particular groups receive timely responses.

talks.title: 4Developers 2020, Sławomir Sobótka, Bottega IL: Poznaj swoje granice - o odkrywaniu granic (...)
talks.teaser: Walks through a payment-limit example to show how weak domain analysis leads to tangled modules and how to find real boundaries.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an everyday analogy about a runner whose knee hurts, then turns to software. The running example is a shop rule that checks whether a customer can pay, based on a status, a debit limit and payment history. The speaker first follows a naive approach, with data objects passed to procedures and logic spread across the code. The same rules then appear split into separate modules and services, and each step exposes problems: values copied between parts of the system, status changes that must be kept in sync elsewhere, and inheritance for customer types that becomes unwieldy as new cases arrive.

In the middle section the speaker proposes a different route. Start from behaviour and commands rather than nouns, group the rules that belong together into aggregates, and delegate variant behaviour to strategies. For module boundaries, the talk argues that events should describe meaningful business state changes, that each business question needs a single source of truth, and that each context should keep its own vocabulary so volatile concepts do not leak into payments. Modules should be drawn from analysis of the domain rather than from technical layers.

The closing part repeats the analysis at process, architecture and code levels. The practical takeaway is to invest in understanding the domain and its decisions before splitting a system, because boundaries drawn early are costly to change later. It also suggests checking whether an event reflects a real business change or just an arbitrary field update.
