talks.title: 4Developers Online 2: Krzysztof Wojewodzic, Od pomysłu do pierwszego miliona pobrań
talks.teaser: Covers the mobile app market, validating an app idea, retention and conversion metrics, and planning app projects.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the size and shape of the mobile app market. The speaker cites direct app revenue in the hundreds of billions of dollars a year, growing roughly 15 to 20 percent, and describes Android holding about 70 percent of the European market against under 30 percent for iOS, with iOS near five percent in Poland. Downloads concentrate heavily: the 250 most popular non-game apps account for 97 percent of them, leaving a long tail that earns little. Monetisation through subscriptions, advertising and in-app purchases is also outlined.

The middle section turns to validating an idea and measuring success. The speaker recommends finding a real problem, talking to several companies in the target industry, and designing an app that brings users back. A conversion funnel example runs from 1,000 daily users, 300 interested, 150 adding a product to the cart, and 50 completing a purchase. Retention is measured by stickiness, daily active users divided by monthly active users, and lifetime value is illustrated with a worked calculation of 10 zł per purchase, five purchases a year over two years, giving 100 zł per customer.

The final section covers planning and team roles. The speaker suggests three core documents: a business requirements document, a functional specification and a technical specification. Clear decision-makers, a shared definition of done and up-to-date documentation are presented as essential, and the difference between product manager, project manager, product owner and scrum master is explained. The takeaway is to treat an app as an ongoing product that needs business, functional and technical planning before coding starts.

talks.title: 4Developers Online 2: Dominika Zając, Chrome DevTools - funkcjonalności o których mogłeś nie słyszeć
talks.teaser: Highlights six underused Chrome DevTools features for mock location, throttled networks, performance tracing, and Lighthouse audits.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by noting how many developers still rely on basic console logging even when Chrome DevTools is already at hand. It frames DevTools as powerful but underused, then promises a tour of capabilities that often stay hidden behind extra menus or experimental builds.

Much of the middle is live-style walkthrough material. The Sensors panel fakes geographic positions or location failures for apps that depend on the Geolocation API. Network and Performance tooling replays slow or offline connections, records reload timelines with filmstrip frames, and uses bottom-up views to spot costly style recalculation and long blank screens. Paint flashing in Rendering highlights elements that repaint too often; screenshot commands capture full pages or single nodes. Lighthouse runs category audits for performance, accessibility, progressive web apps, and best practices, with separate mobile and desktop scores plus linked fix guidance.

The close covers Chrome Canary: toggling preferred color schemes without OS settings and emulating common vision impairments to see whether UI remains usable. The speaker urges trying these panels on real sites, saving performance profiles for comparison, and following official docs and release chatter rather than treating DevTools as a DOM inspector only.

talks.title: 4Developers Online: Mariusz Bojkowski, Blazor in practice - Is running C# in a browser (...)
talks.teaser: Explains Blazor Server vs WebAssembly, Razor components, DI, events, binding, and JavaScript interop for interactive .NET UIs.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing Blazor as a way to run C# in the browser, leaning on WebAssembly and a Razor component development model that Microsoft first shipped on ASP.NET Core before pushing full client-side WebAssembly. It contrasts Blazor Server (UI diffs over SignalR, already production-ready) with Blazor WebAssembly (static WASM payloads, hosting options, and newly announced production support), plus optional progressive web app templates for offline use and OS installation.

The middle walks through the default counter demo to show how routable and nested components mix HTML and C#, how parameters and layouts tie into index.html, App, Router, and MainLayout, and how dependency injection and _Imports.razor reduce boilerplate. It then deepens on component parameters, cascading values, child content conventions, click handlers, EventCallback, and @bind for two-way data flow, ending with a focused pattern for JavaScript interop via IJSRuntime and ElementReference when built-in APIs fall short.

Closing notes stress maturity after a volatile preview period: IL trimming and release builds shrink download sizes, Visual Studio debugging for WASM has improved, and practitioners can start from official docs and current Visual Studio tooling. The intended takeaway is a practical mental model for choosing a Blazor hosting mode and composing interactive UIs without leaving the .NET stack.

talks.title: 4Developers Online: Dmitry Soshnikov, Azure Machine Learning: From Zero to Hero
talks.teaser: Shows how Azure Machine Learning tracks experiments, scales training clusters and automates model tuning for Python developers.
talks.summary:
The talk makes the case for training machine learning models on cloud compute, then walks through Azure Machine Learning as a platform sitting between raw virtual machines and prebuilt cognitive services. The workspace is presented as the single home for data storage, compute, notebooks, experiment results and deployed models. A compute cluster that scales down to zero nodes is shown as a way to avoid paying while idle.

Most of the session is a walkthrough on a handwritten digit dataset. A local scikit-learn script is submitted from Visual Studio Code as an experiment, which builds an environment, runs on the cluster and records accuracy and output files. Remote debugging is harder than local, so data should sit in a workspace data store rather than be downloaded on each run. A notebook uploads data via the Python SDK, and a neural network script takes parameters. A HyperDrive sweep launches many child runs with sampling strategies and early termination, and the best model is picked by accuracy.

Other options are covered briefly: a graphical designer for building pipelines, and AutoML, which tries many classification models automatically and reached about 97 percent accuracy on the same digits. The final example trains generative adversarial networks to produce images, logging sample pictures on each iteration and saving models, with one run lasting 11 hours. The speaker closes by suggesting beginners start visually in the portal and VS Code before scripting everything, and points to a blog series and code samples for follow-up.

talks.title: 4Developers Online: Dominik Przywara, Wstęp do OAuth 2.0 i OpenID Connect
talks.teaser: Walks through OAuth 2.0 grant types, access tokens and OpenID Connect, and which legacy flows to avoid.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an early social network that asked users for their mail account password to find friends, and why that approach fails. It then presents OAuth 2.0 as an authorization framework rather than a protocol, separating authentication (who the user is) from authorization (what they may do). Four actors are defined: client, resource owner, resource server and authorization server. The client presents an access token to a resource server, which has to validate it on every request.

The speaker contrasts reference tokens, which the resource server checks by asking the authorization server, with self-contained tokens such as JWTs, which carry a header, a payload and a signature. The signature only protects integrity, and a known weakness appears when a server accepts the unsigned algorithm setting. Grant types are then walked through: the authorization code flow with a PKCE code challenge hashed with SHA-256, client credentials for machine-to-machine traffic, and the device code flow for TVs without keyboards, where the user confirms on another device. Refresh tokens let a client obtain new access tokens without prompting the user again. The implicit and resource owner password flows are described as legacy and discouraged.

OpenID Connect is layered on top, adding an openid scope, an ID token that identifies the user, and a user info endpoint for profile data. The talk closes with practical rules: client secrets belong only in confidential server-side environments, tokens should be short-lived and used once where possible, and developers should avoid building their own flows. Books, documentation and a podcast episode are recommended at the end.

talks.title: 4Developers Online: Rafał Hryniewski, Great Web APIs - learn how to make one in 45 minutes
talks.teaser: Explains REST maturity levels, HTTP status codes and design conventions for building a usable web API.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with web APIs that developers find pleasant to integrate with, and others that make integration painful. The speaker stresses that clear documentation, with every parameter described and a searchable reference, makes a big difference. He argues that a web API should serve its users first, and that many APIs called REST are not truly RESTful, because constraints such as the separation of client and server and the absence of session state are often ignored.

The middle of the talk walks through the Richardson Maturity Model and its four levels. Level zero is a single endpoint that tunnels everything over POST, and level one introduces resources. Level two adds HTTP verbs and meaningful status codes, which the speaker considers good enough for most projects. Level three adds hypermedia links that guide clients to their next actions. He then tours common status codes, such as 201 with a Location header, 202 for operations that run asynchronously with a status link, 409 for conflicts and 429 for rate limiting, and he discusses consistent error responses.

For practical advice, he recommends following common naming conventions, such as plural resource names, rather than inventing new ones. He suggests documenting the API from the start with working samples, validating input, and versioning carefully so that existing clients keep working. He also recommends logging full requests to ease debugging. The closing takeaway is to aim for a consistent, scalable, maintainable design that solves the business problem, rather than chasing a perfect definition of REST.

talks.title: 4Developers 2020, Dawid Mazur, JavaScript: Oddajcie mi moje interfejsy! - dobre praktyki (...)
talks.teaser: Explores applying strategy patterns, dependency inversion, and interface contracts in vanilla JavaScript despite language limits.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from a professional shift toward JavaScript in client work, where the speaker wanted to keep habits from other stacks—SOLID, clear structure, and patterns that previously kept projects maintainable. The central problem is that mainstream examples teach JavaScript as if it were classical object-oriented JavaScript, while classes are largely syntactic sugar and runtime behavior does not enforce the contracts developers expect from books written for other languages.

Using a delivery-strategy example, the talk walks through strategy selection, dependency inversion, and “interfaces” as behavioral contracts rather than language keywords. It covers duck-typing checks, optional TypeScript for compile-time assurance, and the limit that types disappear after transpilation. Further sections use value-object style modeling (money/balance) to show validation, encapsulation, immutability, and why returning new instances beats mutating shared references. Poka-yoke-style API design, emerging private fields, and composition—including dynamic capability via functions—are contrasted with deep inheritance hierarchies.

Practitioners should leave aware that patterns must be adapted, not copied literally; factories and checks can narrow bugs but never fully replace tests; framework-wide prototype patching creates painful migrations; and TypeScript plus discipline trades absolute runtime guarantees for better predictability. The closing stance is engineering judgment: adopt these practices when they reduce risk for the project, not as universal dogma.

talks.title: 4Developers 2020, Dawid Bedła, C++: How software engineering will destroy your project?
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in 4Developers 2020, Dawid Bedła, C++: How software engineering will destroy your project?.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Bezpieczeństwo w abonamencie (Sebastian Strzelak)
talks.teaser: Covers SME attack paths, layered infection controls, field audit cases, and monthly subscription managed security.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames cybersecurity from the viewpoint of a Polish integrator serving small and medium businesses that lack in-house security teams. It opens with scale statistics on phishing volume, data leaks, and business email compromise, then walks through three recurring intrusion patterns: malicious links in the browser, infection via removable media, and email-borne attachments or links, noting that command-and-control traffic often relies on DNS.

Field experience anchors the narrative. A manufacturer lost roughly 50,000 dollars to impersonated supplier email and later resisted further hardening beyond basic firewall and mail tweaks. A public healthcare site already had strong perimeter tools yet still showed after-hours cryptocurrency mining and widespread use of unsanctioned cloud document services. A large food-industry plant suffered ransomware that also encrypted backups on directly attached storage, prompting workshops that led to stronger email, endpoint, and vulnerability oversight.

The speaker argues for staged defenses before, during, and after infection—next-generation firewalls, DNS filtering, email screening, and endpoint protection—while stressing that no single product covers every risk. The closing focus is managed security delivered as a monthly subscription: provider-operated monitoring, updates, and response aimed at SMEs and telecom operators, with example pricing for firewall management, DNS security per user, and endpoint coverage.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Jak zrozumieć bezpiecznika: ATT&CK (Piotr Głaska)
talks.teaser: Maps MITRE ATT&CK for IT collaborators and walks through DNS tactics in phishing, C2, and encoded data theft.
talks.summary:
The session opens by arguing that anyone who works with security teams benefits from learning how defenders name risks and structure incidents. It revisits the pyramid of pain, placing shared tactic-and-technique language at the top as one of the hardest layers for attackers to evade, then introduces MITRE ATT&CK as an open knowledge base of adversary behavior rather than a product checklist.

The middle of the talk tours the enterprise matrix: tactics from initial access through impact, numbered techniques that other tools can reference, and growing variants for cloud, mobile, and pre-attack reconnaissance. Practical uses include purple-team style simulation, structuring internal threat intelligence, comparing vendor coverage, and accepting that no environment will detect every listed technique. ATT&CK is framed chiefly as a common dictionary so network and security groups can coordinate.

The closing segment anchors those ideas in DNS. Examples cover freshly registered domains in phishing, regional SMS payment scams with sloppy localization, homograph domains and redirect tricks that confuse classification, domain generation and dictionary-style algorithms for resilient command and control, DNS-based malware retrieval for isolated networks, and exfiltration of payment-card data in encoded queries observable on passive DNS systems. NS and TXT record abuse for hiding infrastructure addresses rounds out what defenders should monitor.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Roboty, samoloty a w nich AI i cyber - czy to nie za dużo? (Kamil Frankowicz)
talks.teaser: Surveys how machine learning in planes, robots and devices creates new attack surfaces, from adversarial images to stolen models.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how much artificial intelligence already runs in everyday systems, from aircraft and cars to household robots and medical tools. The speaker argues that much of what is marketed as AI rests on basic methods such as classification and regression, and that users and developers rarely consider how these systems can be abused.

Attacks on machine learning come next. A small pixel-level change makes a classifier label a panda as a monkey, while a person still sees a panda. Projected images on a road are described as able to trigger unauthorized actions in a car. Model theft is shown with a handwritten digit recognizer, where a stolen model can leak information about the data it was trained on. Privacy risks around medical records are raised, since sensitive records can be linked back to individuals. Classic software risk is also covered, citing 1600 vulnerabilities found in popular Linux distribution libraries in 2018, 78 percent of vulnerabilities starting in dependencies, and about 70 percent of reported vulnerabilities tied to memory management.

The closing part gives practical takeaways. Training on perturbed data helps against adversarial inputs but costs time and compute, and models on devices should be encrypted and run in isolated processor areas. Teams should keep dependencies updated, run static analysis and move toward memory-safe languages. The speaker notes that models output probabilities rather than certainties, that numerical results can differ between platforms, and that copied code and skipped documentation cause avoidable errors. Hardware and ML security specialists are encouraged to work together.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Cyberbezpieczeństwo systemów Internetu Rzeczy (Jerzy Paczocha)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning PLNOG Live 2020: Cyberbezpieczeństwo systemów Internetu Rzeczy (Jerzy Paczocha).

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Czego świat IT powinien nauczyć się od lotnictwa? (Marcin Marciniak)
talks.teaser: Aviation case studies highlight incident procedures, human-factor risks, and corrective culture gaps common in IT operations.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by asking what IT specialists think the industry should learn from aviation. Colleagues often cite training, knowledge management, threat awareness, accountability, procedures, and post-incident learning, yet rarely mention handling random critical events or leading complex, high-business-risk projects.

The middle of the talk walks through aviation milestones and failures as teaching stories: the B-29 as a demanding innovation, the de Havilland Comet’s fatigue and square-window lessons, how rivals such as the Boeing 747 benefited from earlier painful experience, standardized go-arounds when landings are doubtful, lightning-protection advances including long certification effort, a helicopter bearing procedure that worked as designed, a LOT Boeing 737 gear emergency tied to an unannounced tripped fuse, and the Hudson River ditching where crew cooperation and auxiliary power mattered. Later sections stress risk assessment for every change, limits of full automation, fatigue and cumulative stress scoring, and mental-health risk illustrated by the Germanwings 9525 case.

Practitioners are urged to treat every serious event with documented investigation, corrective action, and proportionate external expertise when needed; to weigh human factors in staffing and on-call design; and to revisit internal “catastrophes” with the same analytical habit aviation uses, expecting outcomes that differ from initial assumptions.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Programy partnerskie i rozwiązania IT dla sektora edukacji (Marcin Ślęczek)
talks.teaser: Surveys partner programs that supply schools with ready-made IT courses, hybrid class tools, and campus lab infrastructure.
talks.summary:
Schools and universities that teach networking and IT face a constant burden: courseware goes stale as technology changes, and building labs plus online delivery stacks pulls instructors away from teaching. The presentation walks through several vendor-linked programs aimed at the Polish education sector and how they fit together operationally.

The first block centers on the Cisco Networking Academy-style partnership: free or low-cost access to structured courses (networking, cybersecurity fundamentals, Windows, IoT, programming), progress tracking, and interactive self-study modules in Polish or English. It also covers ClickMeeting as a ministry-recommended platform for hybrid instruction—teams, boards, breakout-style tooling, encryption, and conference-room integration—plus Nextcloud for on-premises file sharing and calendars where GDPR drives local hosting.

Later segments describe an integrated compute platform for spinning up disposable lab environments (virtual machines, network rules, teardown after class) and software-defined networking controllers for faster service rollout and monitoring. The close emphasizes school-appropriate security: content filtering for minors, protection of personal data, reputation-changing files on the network, and correlating security events across email, endpoints, and firewalls. Practitioners in academic IT operations get a map of which partner paths reduce content prep, which tools support hybrid rooms, and where consolidated threat visibility matters on campus networks.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Zombie routes (Paweł Małachowski)
talks.teaser: Explains BGP zombie routes, real operator incidents, diagnostic web services, and cautious withdrawal and scoping habits.
talks.summary:
The presentation defines zombie BGP routes as entries that stay visible in the global or regional table after a prefix has been withdrawn on the originating side. The speaker outlines conditions that create them, especially when withdrawals propagate unevenly across peers and when more-specific advertisements overlap traffic-engineered paths.

Most of the session walks through operational war stories from Polish and international networks: brief detours through unintended European paths, day-long loops that bounced domestic traffic abroad and back, multi-day intercontinental circles tied to cloud connectivity changes, and a large carrier incident where aggressive filtering broke core BGP stability for hours. In several cases, traceroute showed paths through ASes where the purported peer no longer carried the prefix, yet volume still rode the stale advertisement.

The final portion catalogs external reachability checks, looking glasses, live BGP maps, streaming APIs, and historical replay tools for catching ghosts or unexpected origination. Recommended practice includes staged withdrawals that clear foreign peers before domestic assets, limiting route scope with communities or continent filters, and customer-specific export policy instead of blanket global announcements. The talk closes with warnings that communities and registries vary widely, so operators should monitor reachability and understand intent before re-announcing or withdrawing.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Provisioning Edge za pomocą serwerów konsol i Ansible (Krzysztof Krawczyk)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding PLNOG Live 2020: Provisioning Edge za pomocą serwerów konsol i Ansible (Krzysztof Krawczyk).
talks.summary: Krzysztof Krawczyk shows PLNOG Live attendees how console servers bridge RS-232 console ports, PDUs, and Ansible when IP management fails at the network edge. He contrasts local USB adapters with centralized console access for routers, firewalls, UPS gear, and servers, including hard resets through switched outlets. Ansible playbooks call console TCP ports via JSON token APIs or serial modules to push baseline configs before devices ship from integration centers. Live demos walk HTML5 serial sessions, PDU power cycles, and ad hoc ping/setup playbooks against an ACS 800 console. The talk closes on Vertiv/Emerson scale, 4G fallback on new Ascent models, and carrier customer stories.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Nadaktywność - jak ją okiełznać? (Grażyna Konieczna)
talks.teaser: Defines mental hyperactivity, contrasts thinking styles, and offers ways to channel intensity without burning out.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing mental hyperactivity as a pattern many people—especially in IT—may recognize, citing rough prevalence figures and tying the idea to heightened mental activity and unusually vivid sensory processing. Sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell are walked through with everyday examples, alongside temperament traits such as idealism, justice, empathy, and strong reactions to small social cues.

The middle contrasts people whose minds branch into endless associations with those who filter detail and proceed methodically, then distinguishes hyperactive selective attention from misophonia. A video segment and discussion of follow-on reading stress sensory overload, emotional reactivity, and the cost of dwelling on others’ faults or political “pendulums” that consume energy regardless of stance.

Closing guidance stresses self-knowledge, limiting sensory triggers where possible, choosing sincere projects over fault-finding, and adapting to how most people communicate—including face-saving norms and reciprocity—while using distance, linear consequence analysis, and mind maps to reduce stress. The speaker invites contact and emphasizes that understanding one’s own functioning can improve comfort in relationships and daily life.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Prościej się już nie da utrzymać sieć operatorską (Ł. Bromirski, P. Jabłoński)
talks.teaser: Shows practical segment routing deployment for operator networks, including migration from LDP and a live lab demonstration.
talks.summary:
The session argues that an operator backbone can stay manageable only by deliberately simplifying the control plane. Segment routing is presented as a way to carry transport with a single label stack that stays stable hop by hop, so operators can rely on SR for forwarding while BGP (and sometimes LDP) continues to handle service reachability where needed.

The middle of the talk walks through design trade-offs: traffic engineering without swapping labels at every hop, building disjoint primary and backup paths, steering flows using delay rather than static cost, and avoiding microloops during convergence. A staged migration is described—running SR alongside existing LDP, teaching both label sources, preferring SR via operational commands, and only then turning LDP off where policy allows. Interworking cases cover LDP-to-SR and SR-to-LDP handoffs, redistribution, and when a mapping server injects global segment identifiers so non-SR nodes still participate. Multicast limitations and multi-domain deployment are noted briefly.

The closing live segment uses a multi-router lab to validate hidden SR rollout, issue the prefer-SR command, observe counters move to SR forwarding, and fix a mixed environment where one router lacks SR by advertising a prefix-to-index map. The practical takeaway is that operator SR adoption can be incremental, with service windows and mapping infrastructure filling gaps rather than a single risky cutover.

talks.summary: Michał argues network gear web GUIs remain the weakest admin surface, demos common Polish ISP appliance flaws, and urges operators to treat HTTP management as a primary breach vector alongside SSH.

talks.title: 4Developers 2020, Robert Podsiadły, Testing: Jak my developerzy robimy to na backendzie
talks.teaser: Explores how backend developers approach testing, challenges common myths, and demonstrates practices on a downloadable sample project.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from a veteran programmer’s return to hands-on development after years in management, and from discovering how differently testers and developers frame quality. The speaker argues that tests are primarily the cheapest way to execute arbitrary code with controlled inputs, to document behavior, and to guard refactoring—not a separate art owned only by QA.

Drawing on distributed teams, strict latency event pipelines, and hardware-heavy domains, the talk contrasts mental blockers (clients do not pay for tests, coverage quotas) with practical choices among unit, integration, and end-to-end layers. It rejects equating 100% line coverage with reliability, notes when integration tests should dominate, and covers continuous delivery habits such as smoke checks, canary rollouts, and cautious production experiments outside sensitive systems.

The closing sections walk through a small Spring-based breathalyzer example comparing fast unit tests with fuller integration paths, parameterized data, and mutation testing that flagged four surviving mutants. The takeaway is complementary roles: developers aim to show code works while testers stress it, and both share responsibility for lasting quality.

talks.title: CONFidence Online: Hidden Link Between TrickBot "Anchor" & North Korea "Lazarus” ... (Vitali Kremez)
talks.teaser: Traces TrickBot's Anchor project to a technical link with North Korea's Lazarus group through shared PowerShell tooling.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at TrickBot, a crimeware group that the speaker describes as operating like a company, with separate divisions for bank fraud, ransomware, password theft and cryptocurrency mining. It traces the group's lineage back to the Zeus banking malware and explains how its operators now prefer high-value corporate networks, using Active Directory records to spot promising targets before human operators move in with PowerShell Empire or Cobalt Strike.

The central research concerns Anchor, a TrickBot fork with its own communication scheme. The research team found that a TrickBot Anchor server issued a command to download a PowerShell script called Power Tango, which the speaker says is used only by the Lazarus group. A separate Chilean bank intrusion used the same script, delivered after a developer opened a C# binary sent under the guise of a job application. The speaker also places these findings alongside North Korean activity such as the Bangladesh Bank Swift heist and the APT37 and APT38 split, and notes that US government alerts followed the publication.

The takeaway is that commodity infections should not be dismissed as simple malware, because crimeware groups and state-linked actors can share infrastructure and tooling. Defenders, incident responders and analysts need to understand how these groups operate to attribute threats correctly and to choose effective protections.

talks.title: PLNOG Online: Praktyczny wstęp do uczenia maszynowego oraz sieci neuronowych (Piotr Jabłoński)
talks.teaser: A hands-on tour of supervised learning, model trade-offs, and security-oriented anomaly detection with cloud notebooks.
talks.summary:
The session opens by separating everyday hype around artificial intelligence from areas where statistical learning already beats human judgment, using familiar game-engine examples before widening the definition of AI to sensing, language, images, and robotics. The core is a practical walk through supervised machine learning: regression versus classification, finding rules from labeled data, and why engineers care about generalization rather than perfect curve fitting on training points.

Working mainly in Python notebooks, the presenter trains simple models on synthetic salary and tiny classification sets, compares linear regression with tree ensembles, and shows how too much fitting hurts predictions on new data. He stresses that algorithms are a small slice of real projects—data collection, labeling quality, cleaning outliers, bias in training sets, and per-tenant data silos often dominate outcomes and business case.

The close ties ideas to security operations: vendors using distributed models on telemetry, and a cloud anomaly-detection example that scores user logins and IP patterns for separation usable in access control. A short neural-network segment covers artificial neurons, layers, backpropagation intuition, and interactive boundary-fitting demos, ending with encouragement for security specialists to pair domain knowledge with ML literacy and cross-team communication.

talks.title: PLNOG Online 2: Chmura jest bardzo niebezpieczna... (Michał Furmankiewicz)
talks.teaser: Offers a practitioner walkthrough of Azure security across identity, governance, configuration, networking, and monitoring.
talks.summary:
The session argues that cloud migrations stay risky until teams treat security as a multi-layered practice, not a lift-and-shift of on-prem habits. Public providers differ sharply in architecture and contracts, while much of the threat surface sits in customer-controlled settings. The speaker cites industry estimates that nearly all cloud security failures stem from misconfiguration and poor use of platform controls, and stresses early governance when many subscriptions and partners multiply siloed designs.

Identity anchors the discussion: directory settings, invitations, built-in versus custom roles, and service principals can quietly grant powerful access, illustrated with virtual-machine run-command behavior and cautionary mis-rolled permissions. Service choice and per-service knobs matter as much as architecture—policy enforcement, logging defaults, client-side encryption for storage, and dynamic data masking for databases appear as concrete patterns teams can adopt or avoid.

Networking, centralized monitoring, and Kubernetes add further decision points where defaults often omit logging or advanced features. The talk recommends designing for enterprise scale from the start, consolidating telemetry across subscriptions, and using provider security centers for vulnerability and traffic insight, while noting that hyperscalers increasingly position themselves as embedded security partners.

talks.title: PLNOG Online 2: Jak się nie zgubić w gąszczu mikrousług? Istio i nie tylko. (Bartłomiej Zass)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for PLNOG Online 2: Jak się nie zgubić w gąszczu mikrousług? Istio i nie tylko. (Bartłomiej Zass).

talks.title: PLNOG Online 2: Debata z Rada PLNOG
talks.teaser: Council members debate how lockdown reshaped Polish access networks, cloud plans, peering needs, and operator hiring.
talks.summary:
The session is framed as an online debate in which questions collected from the audience are put to the PLNOG council. It opens on whether the future of consumer and business access is primarily wired or wireless. Participants describe a hybrid model: fiber or cable at fixed locations where possible, cellular and 5G where devices cannot be cabled. Experience during lockdown is used to argue that mobile networks showed capacity and quality gaps when entire households needed stable connectivity for remote work, schooling, and streaming at once.

The conversation turns to how operators and integrators weathered the pandemic commercially. Speakers reject opportunistic “monetizing the crisis” and emphasize supporting customers whose businesses were frozen. Several note that aggressive cloud migration sometimes stalled or reversed as organizations reprioritized hybrid security, tighter access to sites, and consulting around modern access and authentication. On engineering, they cite a sharp rise in traffic with a changed mix—more symmetrical need for upstream bandwidth, more user-to-user patterns, and growing relevance of peering and exchange points for usable remote work.

Later questions cover career moves, founding businesses, and personal projects during isolation. The council portrays specialist hiring as still active in telecom and security-adjacent roles, encourages narrow technical depth, and shares examples from automation, open source, and hardware side work. Practitioners hear a consistent theme: plan for hybrid access, invest in fiber and upload symmetry, rethink peering and QoS under new load, and pair infrastructure choices with deliberate security as cloud strategies mature.

talks.title: JDD Online: Live refactoring towards solid code (Bartłomiej Słota)
talks.teaser: Refactors a legacy Java reservation class live, using isolated tests and IDE automation to improve design safely.
talks.summary:
This live coding session walks through a piece of legacy Java code from a library management application, where a patron reserves a book. The speaker starts by reading the code line by line and grouping steps that belong together. Methods and variables with unclear names, including some in Polish, are renamed so that developers and business stakeholders can follow the logic. The IDE's automated refactorings are used for these changes because they reduce the risk of manual mistakes.

The main obstacle is that the reservation service cannot be tested in isolation: it reads from the database and sends emails. The speaker writes tests that replace those collaborators, beginning with the simplest scenario, such as no book or no patron, and then adding cases step by step until coverage shows what is exercised. Tests are kept focused, so state checks and interaction checks are separated. Later the session moves logic onto the patron object, extracts a method and changes the method signature, and replaces an early exit with a returned result. A cyclic dependency created by the tests is resolved, and loyalty points are split into their own class.

The takeaways are that refactoring must not change observable behavior, that tests are the safety net for each small step, and that the IDE cannot decide where responsibilities belong. Business rules such as a maximum number of reservations should be confirmed with domain experts before they are moved, and a good test should fail for only one reason.

talks.title: JDD Online: A Year With Java 11 in Production! (Andrzej Grzesik)
talks.teaser: Shares lessons from moving a financial company's production Java services from JDK 8 to JDK 11 over a year.
talks.summary:
The talk reports on a year of running Java 11 in production at Revolut, a financial app company, after upgrading its Java services from JDK 8. The speaker explains the reasons for the move, including the end of support for the older release, the need for security fixes and container-friendly improvements, and the appeal of the newer version to developers. The team skipped JDK 9 and 10 because they are short-lived, moved from Oracle's JDK to an OpenJDK build because of licensing concerns with Docker images and production use, and standardised on 11 for both runtime and toolchain.

Much of the migration was about libraries and build tooling. Build tools were used to find module and deprecated API problems, Gradle was upgraded in steps, and several libraries needed specific versions. Flyway was rolled back to an older release after problems, Groovy held back further upgrades, and JAXB had to be added as an explicit dependency. Bouncy Castle was registered differently, embedded PostgreSQL was replaced with Testcontainers, and tests broke when JDK 11 gave microsecond time precision, so the team injected its own time provider. Compiler bugs around generics forced small code changes. At runtime, G1 became the default collector, some containers died because reserved memory grew slightly, and out-of-memory failures surfaced faster.

The main takeaway is to compile against 11 first, update plugins and dependencies, and then run the test suite, since the human side of the change proved harder than the technical one. The speaker closes with plans to test newer features such as Java 14 event streaming and to experiment with GraalVM.

talks.title: JDD Online: An Experiment in Continuous Deployment of JVM applications (Nicolas Frankel)
talks.teaser: Shows how to swap bytecode in a running JVM with no downtime using the Instrumentation and Attach APIs.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how to ship changes to a JVM application without taking it offline. The speaker argues that continuous deployment matters and that common approaches still struggle: blue-green deployments face problems with in-flight sessions and shared database state, and Kubernetes rolling updates do not handle state either. The speaker proposes changing the bytecode of a running JVM instead.

The approach combines two parts of the Java platform. The Instrumentation API can redefine the bytecode of loaded classes, and the Attach API lets an agent be loaded into a JVM that is already running on the same machine, identified by its process ID. The speaker contrasts static agents, set at startup, with dynamic agents attached later. Changed class files are streamed through a stream processing engine, Hazelcast Jet, into an in-memory data grid map. A listener in the running application picks up each change and redefines the class. A live demo was attempted but did not fully work on stage.

The talk closes with limitations. The approach gives no clear record of which version is running, it does not load new classes, and redefinition cannot add, remove or rename fields or methods, or change signatures or the inheritance hierarchy. It therefore suits body-level bug fixes. Suggested improvements include streaming from a CI job, tagging classes with metadata such as git tags, and using a custom class loader so only application classes restart. The practical takeaway is that hot patching can work for narrow fixes but is not a general replacement for deployment.

talks.title: PLNOG Online 2: Application Device Queues (Konrad Czubak, Rafał Słoniewski)
talks.teaser: Covers Intel Application Device Queues for per-application NIC paths that curb tail latency and lift predictability in scaled clusters.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames datacenter networking around three qualities: throughput, latency, and predictability. The speakers argue that as clusters grow, the slowest responders dominate end-to-end completion time, so minimizing tail latency matters as much as raising averages. They illustrate this with everyday analogies and with SLA math showing that each added machine must be more reliable if the fleet should still meet a fixed percentile target.

The core topic is Application Device Queues on Intel adapters. Traffic can be steered from the NIC through dedicated hardware queue groups into applications, with symmetric queues on the return path so request and response stay aligned. The talk ties this to busy-poll style receive paths, noting that shared queues can mix packets across applications and hurt behavior even when the concept looks efficient on paper. Dedicated queues remove that cross-talk when an application opens its gate.

A live segment compares default and queue-tuned setups with several parallel clients, then walks through queue classes, filters, and tooling—including scripts that mirror ingress queue layout on egress. Reported measurements show tighter latency spread under load. The speakers also point to an Intel configuration guide with suggested settings for common applications and invite operators to replicate the experiments.

talks.title: PLNOG Online: Jak zbudować i zarządzać nowoczesną siecią WAN (Jakub Leszewski)
talks.teaser: Demonstrates building and operating a WAN with cloud-based orchestration, from device onboarding to traffic policies.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the problem of building and running a wide area network across many locations, and explains why the team chose to create a new orchestration system from scratch instead of extending older tooling. The platform is cloud-based and aimed at network operators, service providers and their partners. The speaker presents it as a way to cut repetitive manual work and reduce the configuration errors that often lead to outages.

The walkthrough starts with onboarding. A wizard creates a site record, the device is identified by its serial number, and once it comes online it pulls its configuration from the central system. Profiles work as shared templates, so a change to a profile is applied to every device that uses it, while site-specific values are edited on a single screen. Configuration changes pass a verification stage before they are deployed. The speaker also covers automatic tunnel creation between sites, traffic policies for applications, and optimisation categories for Office 365 traffic.

The later part focuses on operations. Monitoring and diagnostics include alerts, per-site views and remote test commands that run on the device and return results to the console. Read-only access can be granted to support staff so they can investigate problems directly. The speaker also mentions an API for integration with other systems and possible future features, such as automatic reactions to threshold breaches and machine-learning-based analytics. The main takeaway is that centralised orchestration can speed up deployment and troubleshooting across a large network.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Jak efektywnie wykorzystywać dyski NVMe. (Tomasz Zawadzki)
talks.teaser: Maps how NVMe polling, per-thread queues, and user-space block APIs in SPDK shrink driver overhead versus the Linux kernel stack.
talks.summary:
The session opens with how storage media evolved from high-latency spinning disks toward NVMe, and why shrinking hardware access time shifted the bottleneck upward into host software. On fast flash, driver latency can account for a large share of end-to-end I/O time, so optimizing the stack above the medium becomes decisive.

The core explains Intel’s Storage Performance Development Kit approach: replace interrupt-driven kernel paths with polling suited to very fast completions, align work with NVMe queue pairs so threads avoid heavy locking, bypass much of the traditional block layer, map device memory for fewer copies, and expose a generic block-device layer so applications can use those gains directly. Compared with the stock Linux kernel path, the project reports substantially lower access times in benchmark-style scenarios.

The closing portion traces SPDK from an internal proof of concept through open-source publication, NVMe-oF targets and initiators, major IOPS milestones, a long-term support release, and a modular architecture (bdev, protocols, Kubernetes-related pieces). Production adopters and an active contributor community are highlighted, with encouragement to try the stack for local, networked, or virtualized NVMe workloads.

talks.title: PLNOG Live 2020: Techniki DevOps w procesie zarządzania dużymi platformami usług (Krystian Baniak)
talks.teaser: Outlines how integrators use DevOps to automate delivery, testing, and lifecycle of large subscribed security service platforms.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames DevOps from the viewpoint of a security solutions integrator who must integrate and operate complex offerings, especially when security is sold as a subscription across many customers and regions. The speaker ties development, configuration architecture, and operations through monitoring and quality practices, arguing that the approach speeds delivery, trims expert headcount, lowers business risk, and improves maintainable documentation.

Practical building blocks include declarative configuration templates, small in-house tools that bridge product gaps, version control, Python and JavaScript utilities, API-driven workflows, and orchestration for production and test. Examples cover stitching vendor functions where no single API exists, microservices spun up in months, and a large 2020 engagement with hundreds of appliances, sixteen regional policy variants, Git-stored deltas, a configuration compiler, staged testing, and automated rollout to field devices—plus lessons on error handling and determinism.

The closing guidance helps practitioners decide when automation pays off: repetitive high-risk changes, tight maintenance windows, and scale that manual work cannot match. Adoption needs engineers who both understand security operations and can build software, vendors with mature open APIs, and upfront investment in the automation apparatus. Benefits include faster analyst workflows, warehouse-ready device provisioning, and repeatable migrations; limits include cost, staffing, and projects where scale does not justify the effort.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Krakow 2020 - Ádám Sándor - How GitOps Changes Everything in CI/CD
talks.teaser: Shows how keeping Kubernetes manifests in git reshapes CI/CD, using an enterprise case and a comparison of sync tools.
talks.summary:
A large German enterprise wanted faster releases, since its cycle took about half a year, and was moving monolithic applications onto an internal OpenShift cloud. Heavy checkpoints and change management risked producing a distributed monolith, so the speaker's team looked for a way to satisfy compliance while still shipping continuously. The approach was GitOps: Kubernetes manifests, including the image version, live in a git repository, and the CI process builds and pushes an image and then updates that repository.

Git then provides a change history, an audit trail, pull request review and access control, and it lets developers and operations work on production changes without tickets. The talk compared ways to sync a cluster from git. A Jenkins pipeline running kubectl apply was the simplest option and the one the team first used. Flux runs as a small agent per namespace, while Argo CD offers a central controller with a UI that can manage many repositories and clusters. Jenkins X bundles the whole flow. Because agents on each cluster pull from git, no central deployment service needs broad access to every environment, which is easier to secure.

The main drawback in the case was the proliferation of git repositories, which made pull requests hard for operations to track. The speaker recommended consolidating repositories or using branches instead. Bitbucket, GitHub and GitLab all support the required review process, and starting with plain pipelines is a sensible first step.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Krakow 2020 - Mikhail Chinkov
talks.teaser: Explains why DevOps stalls when tooling outpaces culture, and how platform teams can share infrastructure expertise.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that adopting cloud services and modern infrastructure tools does not by itself make a company DevOps. The speaker draws on experience from several past companies and points out that many online definitions of DevOps come from vendors with products to sell. The speaker describes DevOps as a company-wide way of working built on five areas: culture, automation, lean thinking, measurement and sharing.

The speaker describes the common failure pattern. When infrastructure knowledge stays inside one team, that team becomes a blocker for the whole engineering organisation, even after adding configuration tools, build pipelines, AWS and Kubernetes. Faster tooling shortened the gap between people and technology but did not shorten the communication gap between developers and operations. In one example, a front-end application deployed once every two weeks; after work on the pipeline it deployed several times a day, yet the team had no measure showing whether the wider development lifecycle had improved. The speaker also outlines maturity stages, from a black box where only a few people can fix problems, through awareness, to contribution, where engineers change infrastructure code on demand in an internal open-source style.

For platform teams, the speaker suggests coaching through workshops and pair programming, showing empathy for developers, writing documentation to answer repeated questions, and using checklists for repeatable operations such as onboarding, backups and cluster upgrades. Roadmaps and stakeholder management matter more than rigid sprint planning when hot fixes keep arriving. The closing takeaway is to tie improvements to both business metrics and platform metrics, treating DevOps as an ongoing journey rather than a one-time transformation.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Krakow 2020 - Jakub Sendor - To boldly go where no one has gone before
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding DevOpsDays Krakow 2020 - Jakub Sendor - To boldly go where no one has gone before.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this DevOpsDays Krakow 2020 presentation, Jakub (Kuba) Sendor examines the evolution of DevSecOps from traditional software development models and outlines actionable steps for organizations transitioning to a secure development culture. Drawing on his experience at SAP and Yelp, Sendor emphasizes that DevSecOps is an organic evolution of agile and DevOps practices. Rather than relying on fear, uncertainty, and doubt (FUD), teams should build security around data, collaboration, and incremental automation across the entire software development lifecycle.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Software Security**: The transition from waterfall models—where security was an afterthought handled late during verification or maintenance—to Microsoft's Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SDL), Agile, DevOps, and ultimately DevSecOps.
- **The DevSecOps Manifesto**: Grounding security practices in data and security science rather than fear, uncertainty, and doubt.
- **The Six Pillars of DevSecOps**: Reviewing the Cloud Security Alliance's six core pillars: Collective Responsibility, Collaboration and Integration, Pragmatic Implementation, Bridging Compliance and Development, Automation, and Measurement/Monitoring.
- **A Four-Step Journey to Adoption**: A pragmatic roadmap focusing on starting small and iterating fast, being inclusive, selecting the right tools, and continuous measurement with course correction.

### Technical Details
- **Historical Approaches & SDLC**: The shift from shipping post-release service packs on floppy disks or CDs toward integrating threat modeling, static code analysis, and fuzz testing during development, followed by incident response.
- **Games & Threat Modeling**: Utilizing gamification and structured exercises to educate teams, including the Elevation of Privilege card game (based on Adam Shostack's threat modeling book), OWASP Cornucopia, and Backdoors & Breaches.
- **Security Culture Initiatives**: Establishing Security Champions to serve as liaisons or bootstrap initial security efforts, and participating in awareness campaigns like Facebook's Hacktober or European Cybersecurity Month.
- **Tooling Implementations**: Bootstrapping Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) and threat detection using open source and commercial tooling. Examples include Elasticsearch paired with Kibana and Yelp's open-source ElastAlert for monitoring anomalous login attempts, Zeek (formerly Bro) for network security monitoring, Splunk for threat hunting, and CrowdStrike.
- **Metrics & KPIs**: Tracking concrete measurements such as deployment frequency, test coverage, tracked/patched vulnerabilities, number of incidents, and mean time to respond (MTTR).

### Takeaways
Sendor stresses that security must be framed as a business enabler rather than an organizational blocker. Organizations do not need radical disruptions to implement DevSecOps; rather, they should start small with foundational resources like the OWASP Top 10, promote cross-team responsibility beyond engineers to finance and product, automate where possible, and regularly use retrospectives and metrics to adapt and improve security posture.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Krakow 2020 - Mofizur Rahman - Managing Kubernetes with Istio
talks.teaser: Shows how a service mesh layered on Kubernetes adds traffic control, observability and security without changing application code.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the move from monoliths to microservices running in containers, and argues that Kubernetes on its own leaves teams to assemble ingress, tracing, metrics, policy and security tools themselves. It presents a service mesh as a way to get these capabilities without each development team building them, and introduces Istio, which places an Envoy sidecar proxy beside each service to intercept and govern service-to-service calls. The architecture is split into a data plane and a control plane, and the speaker notes that the control plane was consolidated into the istiod binary from version 1.5.

The middle of the talk is a demo using a sample travel application with five services, shown in three versions. Traffic is split between versions with weighted routing, a fixed delay is injected into selected services, and HTTP 500 errors are returned to browsers chosen by user agent, which tests how the front end copes with a failing dependency. A 50/50 split between v1 and v3 is then moved fully to v3, a pattern similar to a blue-green rollout. Grafana, Jaeger and Kiali are used to check success rates and the service graph, which exposes a call leaving the cluster through a passthrough route.

The closing part covers mutual TLS and policy that limits which services may talk to which, along with the resource cost of running a mesh. The speaker gave a rough estimate of about half a CPU and 1.5 gigs of RAM at a thousand requests per second. The takeaway is that a service mesh extends what Kubernetes provides and can simplify hard operational tasks, while adopting one remains a trade-off for each team.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Krakow 2020 - Kris Buytaert - From Devoops to Devops, 10 years of learning
talks.teaser: Looks back at a decade of DevOps, arguing that its collaboration roots have been lost to tools, titles and certifications.
talks.summary:
Kris Buytaert traces the origins of the DevOps movement, starting from a 2009 discussion in Antwerp between a small group of engineers who had been speaking at different conferences about the same problems. That conversation led to the first DevOps Days event in Ghent, drawing on open source, agile and cloud-minded practices. He describes how the events spread to dozens of cities, with more than 75 events worldwide by 2019, and how early discussions about infrastructure as code, continuous integration and monitoring have shifted toward tool choices, heavy YAML configuration and container platforms.

He argues that many organisations still struggle with the same basics. Releases are handed over late on a Friday with no dependency or security checks, and approval gates meant to reduce risk are applied manually at the wrong stage instead of being automated. Teams labelled as DevOps often become yet another silo, job titles and certifications have lost their meaning, and tools such as Docker were promoted as fixes for cultural problems. He also points to enterprise transformations that stay on the surface and to frameworks presented as agile that behave like waterfall.

His closing message is that DevOps is about people and collaboration rather than tooling. He asks practitioners to act as both teacher and student, to understand how colleagues on the other side of a handover work, and to speak with people they have never worked with in order to help them improve.

talks.teaser: Ignite-style lightning talks cover password policies, DevOps team roles, service meshes, CI/CD stages, and IoT security flaws.
talks.summary:
The session opened with several short talks on practices that weaken security and team work. One speaker examined password policies, arguing that rules demanding mixed character sets and frequent changes push users toward predictable patterns, such as appending the current month. Strong dice-generated passphrases were also criticised, because many websites reject long, lowercase-only entries. Another speaker described developers who work around locked-down environments when firewalls block too broadly.

Later talks covered team dynamics and infrastructure. A DevOps speaker contrasted three models: the know-it-all engineer, the outsider who sits apart from the team, and the team member who observes, analyses and listens, which the speaker presented as the only path to success. A service mesh talk explained how an open-source mesh with control and data planes can give services cryptographic identities, route a share of traffic to new versions for canary releases, and expose observability without custom code. A CI/CD talk split delivery into stages from development to monitoring, and a satirical talk listed steps for damaging software quality, such as skipping tests and ignoring users.

The session ended with a tour of poorly secured consumer IoT products, including a Bluetooth-controlled toilet and a straightener that could be switched on without authentication. A smart fridge camera was also shown to struggle with poor conditions and Wi-Fi. The shared lesson was to avoid rules users cannot follow, keep engineers collaborating as team members, and require authentication before devices join a network.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 - Adam Kozłowski - Kubernetes buildpacks - from a source code to...
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 - Adam Kozłowski - Kubernetes buildpacks - from a source code to....
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 presentation, Adam Kozłowski, a technical leader at Grape Up and Certified Kubernetes Administrator, discusses using Cloud Native Buildpacks (buildpacks.io) to replicate the developer experience of Cloud Foundry's `cf push` on Kubernetes. Buildpacks transform application source code into runnable OCI-compliant container artifacts at a high level of abstraction, shielding developers from the complexities and security pitfalls of handcrafting Dockerfiles. Kozłowski presents an in-cluster proof of concept that runs the `pack` CLI inside a privileged Docker-in-Docker (dind) pod to package, build, push, and deploy a containerized application directly to Kubernetes.

### Key Topics
- **Cloud Foundry Developer Experience**: The historic appeal of platforms like Cloud Foundry and Heroku lies in developer abstraction, exemplified by Onsi's haiku: *"Here's my source code, run it on the cloud for me, I don't care how."* Developers run simple push commands without needing to manage infrastructure or Dockerfiles.
- **Origins and Evolution of Buildpacks**: Originally created by Heroku, buildpacks were subsequently adapted by Pivotal for Cloud Foundry (CF Linux FS). Pivotal and Heroku later joined forces under the open-source Buildpacks.io initiative to establish a unified specification generating standard OCI-compliant container images compatible with Docker and CRI runtimes.
- **Security and Compliance Challenges in Docker**: While Docker is easy to adopt initially, developers frequently pull unvetted public images without vetting versions, updates, compliance, or base image security. Buildpacks address this by decoupling the build lifecycle and runtime images into maintained, vetted layers.
- **Pros and Cons of Buildpacks.io**: Key benefits include OCI compliance, an easy-to-use `pack` CLI, and out-of-the-box support for languages such as Python, Java, Go, Node.js, PHP, Ruby, and .NET Core. Disadvantages highlighted by Kozłowski include sparse documentation, large base builder image downloads (~2 GB), local Docker daemon prerequisites, and concurrency issues with caching across multiple containers.

### Technical Details
- **Buildpack Lifecycle Phases**: The build process executes through defined stages: analyzing source code, detecting applicable buildpacks, building layers, and exporting artifacts on top of a secure base run image.
- **Cluster-Based Build Pipeline**: To remove the requirement for developers to have Docker installed locally on enterprise workstations, Grape Up built a proof of concept running the `pack` build workflow inside Kubernetes:
  1. A Kubernetes pod runs a Docker-in-Docker (dind) container in privileged mode with dedicated Docker storage.
  2. Source code is archived and transferred into the builder container using `kubectl cp`.
  3. The local Docker daemon inside the pod is started manually.
  4. The `pack build` command executes against a configured builder (e.g., Cloud Foundry's `cflinuxfs3` or Heroku-18).
  5. For Python workloads, the lifecycle detects and applies the Python runtime buildpack and the pip buildpack (resolving dependencies from `requirements.txt`).
  6. Layers (launcher, application code, runtime, dependencies) are assembled into an OCI container image and pushed to a container registry (e.g., Docker Hub or Harbor).
  7. The script deploys the application using `kubectl apply` with a dry-run manifest pattern, exposes it via a ClusterIP service, attaches a Traefik ingress resource, and cleans up the builder pod using an exit trap.

### Takeaways
Cloud Native Buildpacks allow engineering organizations to bring streamlined PaaS developer workflows to Kubernetes environments while centralizing control over base images, dependencies, and container standards. By packaging the `pack` build tool within an in-cluster Docker-in-Docker execution flow, teams can automate artifact generation and workload deployment directly on Kubernetes without enforcing local Docker installations across developer workstations.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 - Ara Pulido
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 - Ara Pulido - Kubernetes at Datadog Scale.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 presentation, speaker Ara Pulido discusses how Datadog manages Kubernetes in production at high scale compared to standard smaller-scale deployments. Prior to joining Datadog, Pulido worked at Bitnami running clusters of 15–25 nodes, whereas Datadog operates dozens of clusters across multiple clouds, each exceeding 1,000 nodes. The talk examines key networking challenges encountered when scaling Kubernetes, focusing on pod networking, service load balancing, and DNS resolution.

### Key Topics
- **Scale Differences in Kubernetes**: While survey data indicated that a majority of users run small clusters (1–10 nodes) and only about 4% run more than 100 nodes, operating massive clusters exposes edge cases and performance bottlenecks not seen in smaller setups.
- **Pod Networking & CNI Plugins**: Comparison between network overlays (e.g., Flannel, Weave Net), BGP-based routing (e.g., Calico), and direct cloud VPC pod routing (e.g., AWS CNI/EKS plugin, Lyft's plugin).
- **Service Networking & kube-proxy**: The limitations of standard `iptables` mode versus IPVS mode for cluster service routing at scale.
- **Cluster DNS Resolution**: Addressing known DNS latency issues and race conditions using local DNS caching mechanisms.

### Technical Details
- **Pod Networking**: The Container Network Interface (CNI) specification governs pod networking rules: every pod gets a unique IP and can route traffic to any other pod. Basic overlay setups like Flannel wrap packets using IP-in-IP, which incurs CPU overhead and increases packet size at scale. Calico distributes routing tables via BGP without a Docker bridge. In cloud environments, Datadog avoids overlay overhead by employing direct pod routing (such as the AWS VPC CNI plugin or Lyft's plugin), assigning every pod an IP directly within the VPC.
- **Service Networking (kube-proxy)**: Default `iptables` mode creates a NAT table that grows linearly with pods and services, requiring a full resync on every update. Datadog uses IPVS mode (GA since Kubernetes 1.11), which provides atomic updates, supports configurable load balancing algorithms (e.g., round-robin, least connection), and maintains stable performance. Calico benchmarks highlighted significant CPU and latency improvements using IPVS starting around 1,000 services. Cilium is also noted as an emerging eBPF-based alternative.
- **DNS Handling**: Kubernetes clusters at scale can suffer from a 5-second DNS delay bug due to race conditions during CoreDNS lookups. Datadog addressed this by deploying a custom DNS cache on every node to resolve queries locally before hitting CoreDNS. Kubernetes later introduced this pattern upstream as `node-local-dns` cache (beta in 1.15).

### Takeaways
- Kubernetes provides significant flexibility for developers, but maintaining it at scale presents notable operational complexity.
- Operations teams must become subject matter experts in their specific CNI plugin, as many scale-related bugs originate in the CNI implementation rather than Kubernetes core.
- The open-source cloud native ecosystem evolves rapidly; features like IPVS service routing and node-local DNS caching quickly transitioned from custom operational fixes to upstream Kubernetes features.
- Underlying networking changes (CNI plugins, kube-proxy modes, DNS caching) can be introduced incrementally across clusters without impacting developer workflow or requiring large application refactors.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 - Daniela Soares Cruzes - Do you even champion?
talks.teaser: Shows how embedded security champions can drive secure development in agile teams without slowing them down.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how software companies can bring security into agile development without undermining the agility itself. The speaker, a research scientist who has worked with Norwegian software companies since 2013, traces the approach to research started in 2015, when firms were strong on agile but unsure how to address security. A survey of developers in Norway found that many were not confident they were coding securely, although some were already following good coding habits without realising it.

The central idea is the security champion: a developer inside each team who takes on part of the security work while the team keeps ownership of its product. The role covers seeking technical and process knowledge, helping adopt security practices, and helping the team manage its own security over time. Champions are recruited either by appointment from service owners or by emergence from keen team members. They are connected through dedicated channels, monthly communities of practice and conference attendance, and they receive coaching, mentoring and recognition. Threat modelling, code review and penetration testing are triggered by the teams, with a yearly threat modelling baseline, and one large company example puts champion time at four to eight hours a week.

The talk closes with the open challenges: ranking security findings against feature work, using a risk register so product owners can accept or fix issues, judging whether the programme pays off, and getting teams to try new tools despite the cost. The practical takeaways are to decide how far teams should self-manage, combine top-down direction with bottom-up ownership, and plan time and budget for the champion role.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 - Patryk Hes
talks.teaser: Examines why replication falls short on integrity and how restore-first planning, sharding, and automation harden large-scale recovery.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by stressing that protecting data at scale is difficult and that integrity is often treated as secondary to availability, even though garbled or missing bits can make services useless despite uptime targets. It frames preservation around durability, integrity, and availability, comparing strict availability SLOs with what similar integrity goals imply for real payloads such as legal records, databases, and media metadata.

The middle challenges the assumption that replication or routine backups alone solve the problem. Corruption and mistaken deletes propagate quickly across replicas that share the same stack and site; geographically concentrated copies face catastrophic loss. The speaker advocates a restore-centric mindset: verifying the right data is backed up, locating it under pressure, testing mounts and merges, estimating duration and extra capacity, and avoiding recovery that harms production traffic. Sharded or replicated layouts can enable per-shard backups, selective object recovery, and careful merging of stale shard snapshots with live peers.

Practitioners are urged to treat the first restore attempt as likely to fail in unexpected ways, automate backup and restore workflows, and exercise those flows continuously as schemas, platforms, and scale change. The close summarizes with plan, practice, automate, and test—so teams avoid panic when critical data must be recovered.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Amazing WebSockets in Netty, Arkadiusz Migała
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a WebSocket server in pure Netty, from the HTTP upgrade handshake to live sports-score subscriptions.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Netty, an event-driven, non-blocking networking framework that sits underneath tools such as Spring WebFlux, Vert.x, Cassandra and Elasticsearch. It covers the core building blocks: event loop groups, channel pipelines with inbound and outbound handlers, channel contexts, promises for asynchronous results, and channel groups for sending one message to many clients. The talk also compares building WebSockets this way with alternatives such as plain Spring, Jakarta EE and Socket.IO.

The main part is a live coding demo, built up in steps. It starts with a basic HTTP handler, then adds a handshake handler that detects an upgrade request and answers with status 101 Switching Protocols. After the handshake, the pipeline swaps in a frame handler that parses subscribe and unsubscribe commands naming a sports team. Subscribers are placed in a channel group per team, and a simulated match endpoint pushes events such as goals, yellow cards and red cards to everyone subscribed to that team. Closing the server shows each connected client receiving a notice that its connection was closed.

The closing takeaways cover WebSocket trade-offs. Connections are full duplex over TCP, which enables real-time updates, but there is no same-origin policy, so tokens should be checked during the handshake. Load balancers need careful setup so a client keeps reaching the same instance, and servers can hit TCP connection limits at scale. Netty suits cases needing low-level control or non-HTTP protocols such as UDP. The speaker advises using the current 4.x line rather than older, unmaintained 3.x releases, and points to Quarkus and Spring WebFlux as higher-level options.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 - Kuba Sendor - Storm Busters
talks.teaser: Shows how to audit an AWS account with open-source tools and build alerting on CloudTrail and GuardDuty events.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at securing AWS accounts, focusing on common misconfigurations in three core services. For Identity and Access Management, it covers weak password policies, missing multi-factor authentication, absent key rotation and inline policies. For EC2 and S3, it flags misconfigured or unencrypted images, secrets kept in plain instance data, disabled bucket versioning, missing encryption and no multi-factor protection on deletion.

Two open-source auditing tools are demonstrated. Cloud Mapper offers infrastructure visualization and a command line with audit, collect and report commands, plus lookups for public resources, admin accounts and unused security groups. Scout Suite, maintained by NCC Group, produces a single-page report that marks good and bad configurations across services and flags public IP addresses. It also tries to detect secrets in EC2 user data, though the candidate it flagged in the demo did not look like a real access key.

CloudTrail is already enabled on every account but keeps only about 90 days of events in the console, so the speaker recommends storing logs in S3 for longer investigations. Those logs can be routed through S3 notifications and SNS into Elasticsearch for dashboards and alerts. GuardDuty analyses VPC flow logs and DNS logs against a learned baseline to spot compromised instances, cryptocurrency miners and unexpected public buckets. A serverless example uses a Lambda function triggered from CloudWatch to snapshot a suspicious instance and replace it with a clean one. The closing advice is that these tools cost little to run, but pipelines and GuardDuty add expense, and automated alerts still need a team to respond.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 - Sebastian Grodzicki - Building Distributed Systems in Distributed Teams
talks.teaser: Shows how a fully remote engineering company at Elastic organises people, meetings, releases and hiring across many time zones.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at building a distributed company rather than distributed software, drawing on the speaker's work as a team lead at Elastic. The company has more than 1,600 people spread across many countries and around 30 languages. It began with founders in different cities, which forced them to write things down, reach consensus and over-communicate. Its offices are mainly for headquarters, sales and marketing, while engineers mostly work from home or from co-working spaces the company pays for.

The speaker describes what holds the team together: a week-long onboarding at headquarters, engineering all-hands gatherings every six months, and smaller team rituals. Working norms are written down as values, including blocking time for family, a week off each quarter for side projects or learning, and a preference for progress over perfection. Process is left to each team, which runs a short daily standup on Slack, a 15-minute weekly planning meeting and occasional retrospectives. Engineering ships on a roughly six-week release train with a feature freeze, keeps no public roadmap and uses semantic versioning.

The talk also covers the downsides. Time zone overlap is hard to find, meetings sometimes end without a decision, and communication breaks down easily across cultures, so teams summarise outcomes in writing. Slack, Zoom with recordings and transcripts, GitHub issues and Google Workspace carry most coordination. Hiring weighs communication skills and is capped at five interviews to shorten time to hire. The takeaway is that distributed work depends on explicit, written communication and clear rules about when people must be available.
