talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 - Ricardo Castro
talks.teaser: Shows how a service mesh moves traffic control, resilience, tracing and security out of microservice code and into sidecars.
talks.summary:
Microservice architectures bring problems a monolith never had, including service discovery, load balancing, fault tolerance, distributed tracing, metrics and security. The talk presents a service mesh as a way to handle these in the network layer instead of inside each application. Every service gets a sidecar proxy that carries its traffic, and a control plane distributes routing rules, certificates and configuration to those proxies. The implementation walked through is built on Envoy, with control-plane components named Pilot, Mixer, Citadel and Galley.

The speaker demonstrates traffic control with canary releases, shifting a percentage of requests to a new version while watching metrics and rolling back if problems appear. Dark launches are shown in two forms: mirroring live traffic to a second environment, and routing only requests that carry a particular header. Retries, timeouts and circuit breaking are declared in configuration rather than coded in each service. Fault injection of HTTP errors and delays is used to check whether timeouts and retries really work. The mesh also blocks outbound traffic by default unless a rule allows it.

For observability, the sidecars generate tracing spans, with sampling recommended over tracing every request, and request metrics flow to Prometheus. A service graph view shows the live topology of the services. Security features covered include mutual TLS, an ingress gateway, service-to-service access control and role-based rules. The practical takeaway is that cross-cutting concerns can move out of application code, but mirroring and fault injection need care, since duplicated requests can cause side effects such as double writes.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2019 - Roman Prykhodchenko - Packaging a Python application after you messed up
talks.teaser: Shows how a team made one Debian package and Docker image share the same artifacts and dependencies for its open-source community.
talks.summary:
Roman Prykhodchenko explains how his team maintained Ralph, an in-house data center infrastructure manager that was later open-sourced. Two separate delivery pipelines produced a Debian package for the community and Docker images for internal use, so the artifacts never matched and community builds often broke. Supporting users was never a company priority, which left the team with little motivation to fix it.

The team redefined a package as a predictable collection of artifacts and state changes applied to a target system. It chose to support only the latest Ubuntu release, built one pipeline for both community and internal use, and used a Spotify-built debhelper extension to bundle Python dependencies that did not match repository versions into a virtual environment. Installing with pip on production was ruled out because the results are unpredictable. The Docker image was built by installing that same Debian package, with a single entry point script, environment variables mapped to configuration, and a separate container for static files.

The closing advice is to support only scenarios the team can test in its own production, ship something usable early and improve it gradually, and avoid irreversible decisions in open-source projects. The approach trades full coverage of user environments for a package the team can keep up with alongside its other priorities.

talks.title: 4Developers Wrocław 2019: Mój pierwszy milion, jak zarabiać na aplikacjach (...), Michał Jankowski
talks.teaser: Outlines market realities, validation methods, monetization models, and promotion habits that shape indie mobile app revenue.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames mobile apps as a large but brutally competitive market, using download and revenue statistics to show that most titles never gain traction while a tiny share of installs can still translate into meaningful money. The speaker contrasts the common “great idea, then code” path with a cycle built on planning, promotion, and monitoring, arguing that development is the easy part and that unpaid promotion time often matters more than feature work.

Much of the middle walks through how to test ideas before coding: paper flows, café tests with strangers, comparing incumbents’ download counts and reviews, and choosing between a breakthrough concept versus improving an existing app by a modest margin. Monetization options—free with ads, paid upfront, hybrids, and in-app purchases—are tied to user expectations on iOS versus Android, along with spreadsheet-style business plans that factor store cuts, taxes, team size, and running costs.

The close stresses operational habits: track crashes and reviews, know when to kill a failing release, protect store ratings, iterate on store listing and keywords, and respond when many users ask for the same feature. The takeaway for practitioners is to treat money and time as scarce resources, validate early, and expect promotion—not new code alone—to drive sustainable income.

talks.title: 4Developers Wrocław 2019: Tajemnicze właściwości GIFów, Karol Wrótniak
talks.teaser: Explores GIF binary layout, timing, and disposal rules that affect how animated images decode reliably on Android.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on a 2012 Android client where leaders’ posts could include animated GIFs, yet platform APIs and common workarounds handled animation poorly, drained batteries, or leaked native memory. That gap led to an open-source Android GIF library mixing Java with performance-critical native code, now widely used on GitHub.

The core of the session walks the GIF 87/89 structure: logical screen descriptor, global and per-frame palettes, indexed raster data, graphic control extensions, disposal methods, transparency as a single palette index, interlacing, loop counts, and legacy fields such as pixel aspect ratio. The speaker contrasts full-frame storage with smaller update rectangles, explains palette sizing trade-offs, and notes how browsers and Android factories disagree on background fill and looping semantics.

Decoder builders hear practical edge cases the specification leaves open: palette indices out of range, frames larger than the canvas, missing disposal or delay values, unknown extension blocks, and zero-sized frames. The talk closes on a design choice between caching every decoded frame versus decoding on the fly to fit tight smartphone memory budgets, plus brief answers on PNG, video, and vector alternatives for animation.

talks.title: 4Developers Wrocław 2019: The Many Faces of Flutter [ENG], Krzysztof Sroka
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning 4Developers Wrocław 2019: The Many Faces of Flutter [ENG], Krzysztof Sroka.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At 4Developers Wrocław 2019, front-end engineer and community organizer Krzysztof Sroka presented on Flutter and the realities of multi-platform development. Having transitioned to full-time Flutter development in early 2019 and organizing the Flutter Europe conference, Sroka examined the history, architecture, compilation model, and platform reach of Google's UI SDK beyond its standard mobile targets.

### Architecture and Compilation
Flutter is structured like an onion across multiple distinct layers:
- **Dart Framework**: The uppermost layer where developers compose UI widgets, manage animations, and interact with foundation libraries.
- **C++ Engine**: Handles frame composition, rendering, and core subsystems beneath the Dart layer.
- **Embedder**: The lowest level interfacing with the host operating system, managing threads, event loops, and render surfaces.

Flutter relies on Dart, combining elements of JavaScript, Java, and Swift. It uses two execution modes: Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation during development to power stateful hot reload, and Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) compilation for release builds, which produces native machine code and strips out debugging checks via tree-shaking.

To communicate with host platforms, Flutter historically used **Platform Channels**, an asynchronous message-passing interface between Dart and native code (Java/Kotlin on Android, Objective-C/Swift on iOS). While suitable for API calls like querying battery level, it is not fast enough to pipe high-framerate full-screen animations. More recently, Flutter introduced the **Foreign Function Interface (FFI)** in developer builds, enabling direct native calls to C/C++ libraries without message serialization overhead.

### Platform Support
- **Mobile**: Android and iOS are fully supported. Community members have experimented with Wear OS, watchOS, and Android TV, but run into limitations such as a lack of circular screen support on wearables (treating them as square viewports) and missing TV-specific integrations.
- **Desktop**: macOS, Windows, and Linux are in varying stages of development. macOS currently offers the most mature tooling (including debug runs and hot reload), whereas Linux relies on a thin OpenGL wrapper and Windows support remains nascent. Desktop targets are in Developer Preview without stable APIs or ABI guarantees, lack brownfield embedding support, and rely on system default fonts unless specific TTF files are bundled.
- **Web**: Originally developed as a fork before merging into mainline Flutter, Flutter Web compiles to a browser layer relying on HTML5 Canvas for non-text rendering, DOM text elements, and JavaScript. At the time of the talk, web lacked hot reload (supporting only hot restart), FFI, plugins, and local file system access, with official debugging limited to Chrome.
- **Google Fuchsia**: Fuchsia is an open-source operating system built by Google on a custom microkernel rather than Linux. Flutter is positioned as Fuchsia's primary UI SDK, indicating that Flutter applications written today may natively target Fuchsia in the future.

### Takeaways
While mobile Flutter support is robust and capable of sustained 60 to 120 FPS rendering, it does not eliminate the need for platform-specific engineers. Business expectations that cross-platform frameworks allow companies to disband dedicated iOS and Android teams are unrealistic because platform integrations, native SDK wrappers, and platform quirks (e.g., iOS certificate management, autofill, map/webview integrations) still require native platform expertise. Across non-mobile platforms, Flutter shows promise but remains largely experimental, with Google prioritizing web over desktop targets.

talks.title: 4Developers Wrocław 2019: Natywne, hybrydowe, a może PWA (...)?, Krzysztof Wojewodzic
talks.teaser: Compares native, hybrid, and PWA mobile stacks with real project examples so teams can pick an approach for performance and delivery.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by asking how teams should choose among native iOS and Android development, JavaScript-based hybrids, compile-to-native frameworks, progressive web apps, and thin native shells that wrap web content. It frames the decision for both project managers and engineers, citing 2019 mobile usage patterns: strong app revenue growth, heavy time in a few dominant apps, and only about ten percent of daily mobile time spent in browsers.

Native code is positioned for peak performance, mature platform libraries, offline rich media, and security-sensitive flows, with examples such as a branded water-promotion app using camera tricks, banking apps, and QR-based fuel payments. Hybrids and cross-platform toolkits are shown through news and insurance projects, including cases where plugin ecosystems forced duplicate platform work. PWAs are contrasted with promotional claims versus limits on offline use, background sync, sensors, and especially Apple support, alongside a lightweight Warsaw civic-reporting product. A dictionary case illustrates store-packaged wrappers used mainly for discoverability and habit, not because the web experience failed.

The close is a capability matrix across performance, complexity, reuse, components, device APIs, and store distribution. The speaker argues that framework choice matters less than solving a clear user job, keeping barriers low, and delivering reliable UX—even when the underlying stack is imperfect.

talks.title: 4Developers Wrocław 2019: Use your IDE like the pros, Wojciech Przechodzeń
talks.teaser: A walkthrough of IntelliJ IDEA navigation, version control, refactoring shortcuts, and live templates for faster daily development.
talks.summary:
The session argues that many developers treat the IDE as a plain text editor because they do not know which built-in capabilities exist. The speaker positions IntelliJ as the demonstration environment and notes that equivalent features usually exist in other IDEs under different names, with handouts covering Java tooling on Windows and Linux.

The first half covers navigation and discovery: Alt-based jumps to menus, tab switching with arrows, integrated Git for commit, diff, push, and branch cleanup, global search for classes, files, and actions (including forgotten shortcuts), recent files, method navigation, bookmarks, expand-selection and multi-cursor editing on large JSON or CSV files, and a live coding segment centered on intentions and refactoring shortcuts such as extract, introduce, move, and pull up or push down.

The closing segment introduces live templates and file templates, including cursor placement variables and expressions such as method name, for repetitive test or boilerplate setups. Takeaways include adopting keyboard shortcuts, using Find Action to rediscover features, and shaping code so generators and refactorings can do repetitive work instead of manual typing.

talks.title: JDD2019: Who ate my RAM?, Jarek Pałka
talks.teaser: Traces a Java application's memory growth from Linux virtual memory down to JVM heap layout and object headers.
talks.summary:
The talk tells the story of a memory problem found on a client's production system in June 2019, where a Java application kept consuming more RAM than expected. The speaker starts with the basics of how an operating system manages memory: each process gets its own virtual address space, mapped to physical memory through page tables, usually in 4 KB pages, and memory is committed lazily when it is requested.

Building on that, the talk covers how the JVM reserves and allocates heap memory, how every object carries a header and is aligned to 8-byte boundaries so its size is not simply the sum of its fields, and how compressed pointers change the layout. The speaker shows how an object layout tool reveals field placement, and how native memory tracking exposes what the JVM reserves beyond the heap. Thread-local allocation buffers, string handling and class metadata are also discussed as sources of overhead.

The incident ended with a case where two JVM processes on the same machine were configured with conflicting memory settings, and the operating system's out-of-memory killer removed one of them. The speaker says the problem was reduced but not fully eliminated. The closing advice is to size JVMs realistically, understand what the operating system and runtime actually do with memory, and be cautious about overcommitting shared hosts.

talks.title: JDD2019: Common mistakes when moving to microservices, Jakub Nabrdalik
talks.teaser: Walks through common mistakes teams make when moving to microservices and public clouds, with practical fixes.
talks.summary:
This talk covers recurring mistakes the speaker has seen while helping organizations move to microservices and public clouds. The problems span architecture, organisation and process. Among them are system designs described only at the infrastructure level with no domain focus, enterprise architects handed responsibility for software architecture, and architecture guilds set up without the practices and culture they need to work.

The middle of the talk moves to testing, deployment and integration choices. Common issues include QA groups who still expect end-to-end tests to be feasible, managers who insist on approving releases, and pipelines that stop developers from adopting devops habits. The speaker also points to developers who rely on REST for everything instead of learning event-based styles, Kafka used as a plain message queue without streaming or read models, and managed cloud offerings assumed to be cheaper and safer than self-hosted open source. Teams created without clear repository ownership and designs that ignore shifting business priorities round out the list.

The talk ends by proposing practical solutions for each of these problems. A practitioner planning a move to services can take away a set of pitfalls to check against their own architecture, team setup and delivery process before the mistakes become expensive to fix.

talks.title: JDD2019: Uncoupling, Michael Nygard
talks.teaser: Maps five coupling types on interfaces and shows how each redesign trades operational resilience for semantic and development drag.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a familiar production pain: a system that felt elegant until a small requirement change broke something far away, pushing teams toward costly rewrites. Coupling is reframed not as something to eliminate but as the joints that hold systems together, using mechanical, biological, and planetary examples to show how removal of one link can collapse stability.

A practical taxonomy follows—operational, development, semantic, functional, and incidental coupling—each illustrated with interface evolution from direct database access through REST to publish-and-subscribe messaging. The same lens applies to a retail case where an SKU identifier accreted meaning until a price-point concept leaked across every downstream feed, multiplying coordinated changes. David Parnas’s module decomposition and a C4-style orchestration sketch show how hiding decisions, reusing fewer interfaces and data types, and adding structure in a different dimension can loosen semantic and development bonds.

Practitioners should treat coupling as explicit degrees of freedom: document what must move together, prefer visible dependencies over tacit ones, and choose change cases before picking patterns. Operational hardening helps runtime failures; semantic and development coupling more often block the changes you have not shipped yet.

talks.title: JDD 2019: 5 reasons why (java) developers don’t buy in the observability hype, Marta Tatiana Musik
talks.teaser: Explores why Java teams resist observability hype and how metrics, tracing, and dashboards behave in microservice production.
talks.summary:
The talk opens on developer skepticism toward observability amid conference rebrands, trend lists, and Java ecosystem tooling such as Micrometer, and frames observability as how reliably metrics, logs, and traces answer what failed, where, and why—not merely another monitoring label.

A Spring Boot hello-world deployment on Google Kubernetes Engine drives the middle: default instrumentation already emits hundreds of metrics and thousands of metric time series across JVM, container, and cluster layers. Customer-scale figures illustrate high cardinality and churn, where pod and container identities multiply series and ephemeral instances complicate storage and search.

The closing sections catalog adoption frustrations—rollup smoothing, biased trace sampling, misleading percentile charts, and overnight alerts on sparse traffic—and treat observability as a shipping requirement comparable to tests. Practitioners are steered toward auto-instrumentation, domain-oriented probe objects, and observability-as-code APIs so dashboards and detectors stay consistent across environments.

talks.title: JDD2019: Being transactional in 2019 - what does this actually mean?, Maciej Próchniak
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD2019: Being transactional in 2019 - what does this actually mean?, Maciej Próchniak.
talks.summary: Maciej Próchniak contrasts Spring @Transactional comfort with darker isolation pitfalls (phantom reads, write skew on family bank balances) and BSON multi-document transactions. He reframes CAP beyond folklore: Brewer’s linearizability versus snapshot isolation, PACELC-style gray guarantees, and why homogeneous distributed databases can use 2PC while heterogeneous microservices need sagas. Kafka exactly-once offsets and Spanner/Calvin/FDB patterns close the arc toward modern transactional logs.

talks.title: JDD2019: Testy wydajnościowe - to proste (*) [PL], Sebastian Korczyk 1
talks.teaser: Explains how to plan, run, and interpret load tests so staging results reflect production behavior.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by asking how many people have done performance testing at work and argues that the job is underrated as a career path. The speaker uses a fictional manager assignment to show the usual chain—architecture, admins, monitoring tools, a load run, fixes, and an Excel report—and states that load tests are “simple” only when a few rules are kept: clear goals, environments that resemble production, confidence that the test measures what was planned, and caution before micro-optimizing a slow system.

Most of the talk is practical planning and execution. It compares test styles such as ramp-up scalability work, endurance runs, typical client usage, and spike scenarios, and ties sizing to real needs rather than overbuilt hardware. It stresses realistic data volumes, funnel-shaped traffic, user think time, virtualization effects, matching software versions, leaving security enabled, isolating test beds, synchronized clocks, appropriate logging, database cache and autocomplete pitfalls, network versus application effects, TCP behavior, and keeping a test diary. When reading results, it warns that means mislead, tail latency and queueing dominate user experience, short monitoring windows hide memory leaks, and weak response validation can fake success.

The close summarizes recurring failure modes—misconfiguration, databases, CPU, memory leaks—and points to profilers, heap tools, and comparison techniques. A short section on microbenchmarks and JMH covers JVM warmup, garbage collection, coordinated omission, and why isolated timings do not predict whole-system behavior. Practitioners should treat performance testing as expensive, evidence-driven work where environment fidelity and honest metrics matter more than a single headline number.

talks.title: JDD2019: Syndrom oszusta, czyli hamulec rozwoju [PL], Anita Przybył
talks.teaser: Omawia syndrom oszusta w środowisku IT: objawy, mechanizm samooceny oraz konkretne kroki łagodzące lęk i perfekcjonizm.
talks.summary:
Prelekcja wprowadza syndrom oszusta jako uporczywe poczucie fałszywej kompetencji, a nie chwilę zwątpienia ani realne udawanie wiedzy. Prelegentka porównuje zdrowy cykl budowania poczucia własnej wartości — sukces wiąże się z własnymi zdolnościami i wiarą w kolejne wyzwania — z cyklem „inwestora”, w którym lęk paraliżuje, dominują perfekcjonizm albo prokrastynacja, a po sukcesie pojawia się ulga zamiast dumy, pochwały są odrzucane, a zasługi przypisywane szczęściu lub nadmiarowi wysiłku.

Omówiono objawy i koszty: skupianie na porażkach, strach przed oceną i „zdemaskowaniem”, wycofywanie z inicjatywy, wysoki koszt emocjonalny wystąpień, ryzyko wypalenia oraz korelacje z lękiem, perfekcjonizmem i negatywną samooceną. Wspomniano skale samooceny (m.in. test z TED oraz skalę Clance), wpływ przekonań z dzieciństwa, błędne porównywanie wiedzy w IT oraz to, jak media pokazują sam szczyt bez drogi do sukcesu.

Na koniec zestawiono praktyczne kierunki: psychoedukację, rozmowę i terapię, spisywanie sukcesów, racjonalną terapię zachowań, mniejsze cele, kryteria „wystarczająco dobre”, słuchanie kompetentnych o ich porażkach, porównywanie się wyłącznie z sobą oraz dzielenie się lukami kompetencyjnymi — z prośbą o wybranie jednego pierwszego kroku.

talks.title: JDD2019: Resilience patterns in practice, Tomasz Skowroński
talks.teaser: Walks through practical resilience library patterns for Java, from time limiters and retries through bulkheads and circuit breakers.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a Dunkirk evacuation clip used as a metaphor for surviving dependency failures in distributed systems. The presenter argues that minor faults can snowball when developers treat error handling as logging or exceptions instead of delivering alternative value to users. On a Java-focused stage, examples use Resilience4j as the maintained successor to Hystrix, emphasizing explicit configuration, functional decoration, and the Vavr Try type for tests.

The core walkthrough covers time limiters, rate limiters (including delayed versus rejected overflow), retries with interval functions and selective predicates, bulkheads via thread pools versus semaphores using a paddle-pool analogy, fallbacks through Vavr and Feign decorators, and circuit breakers with closed, open, and half-open behavior verified through emitted events. The talk also notes JCache integration, composition of retry, circuit breaker, and cache decorators, and mentions gateways, service meshes, and cloud load balancers as higher-level homes for similar patterns.

Closing guidance warns against stacking every pattern or decorating all code blindly; order matters, and metrics help tune production settings. Resilience applies beyond HTTP to any stateful, failure-prone resource such as threads, disks, or networks. The smallest boat used at Dunkirk was about five meters—a reminder that simple mechanisms can still matter at scale.

talks.title: JDD2019: Talk to me nicely - how to communicate your ideas and speed up career [PL], Piotr Stawirej
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning JDD2019: Talk to me nicely - how to communicate your ideas and speed up career [PL], Piotr Stawirej.

talks.title: JDD2019: Purely Dysfunctional Data Structures, Grzegorz Piwowarek
talks.teaser: Shows why naive immutable collections are costly and how persistent data structures reduce copying.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a puzzle: a list-to-list method whose body adds elements, mutates hidden state and changes static fields, showing how unrestricted mutability makes code hard to predict. Restricting an object's states, such as requiring mandatory fields in a constructor, shrinks the room for bugs. The speaker then questions the usual view of Java immutability by pointing to the String class, whose hash field is written after construction. Immutability is treated as an abstraction over a mutable machine: internal mutation is acceptable if it is never exposed, though it can still cause thread-safety problems.

Next, the talk covers why immutable collections that copy everything on each change break expected time complexity. The speaker compares copying, fat nodes and structural sharing, and shows how a sub-list view let a shuffle test pass while a view was quietly altering the original collection. A persistent list gives constant-time prepend, but adding at the other end becomes linear; a queue built from two reversed lists is amortised constant time. A finger-tree queue suffers cache misses in practice, and a persistent hash map built on a trie with a branching factor of 32 keeps lookups within about six or seven levels.

The takeaways are that efficient immutability means minimising copying and maximising sharing, at the price of extra retained memory. Simple solutions often beat complex ones, and immutability is not a silver bullet. For sharing updates between threads, the speaker recommends concurrent collections from java.util.concurrent rather than forcing immutable structures to do that job.

talks.title: JDD2019: Kiedy od softu zależy ludzkie życie - o systemach safety-critical [PL], Maciej Gajdzica
talks.teaser: Shows how safety-critical software is built under strict standards, using deadly failures like Therac-25 and Ariane 5 as lessons.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at safety-critical software, the systems whose failure can kill people or destroy expensive equipment, such as medical devices, cars, trains, aircraft, power plants and space probes. The speaker argues that building them differs from ordinary application work, because teams follow detailed standards that prescribe activities, documents and verification by an independent body.

To show why, the talk walks through two well-known failures. In a radiation therapy machine from the mid-1980s, a configuration flag was cleared too early in a loop, and six patients received overdoses, some fatal. Investigators found a codebase written largely by one person, with no requirements or architecture documents, little testing, and a vendor that blamed operators. In the Ariane 5 rocket, a 64-bit to 16-bit conversion overflowed about 40 seconds after the 1996 launch. The code had been reused from an earlier rocket, and both inertial modules ran the same software, so the flight ended in self-destruction.

The middle and end of the talk cover the tools these standards provide: a V-shaped lifecycle, integrity levels tied to probability targets, a risk matrix, and techniques such as redundancy, voting architectures, diverse implementations and bans on dynamic memory. The speaker also discusses language choice, the cost of about ten times ordinary development, and random faults such as radiation-induced bit flips. The takeaway is that the norms are not only paperwork and can act as an ally for teams that plan their process well.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in JDD2019: The need for speed. What is GraalVM and how can it help you?, Maciej Przepióra.

talks.title: JDD2019: Journey through real time data distribution with Kafka pipelines [PL], Konrad Szatan
talks.teaser: Follows one company's Kafka-based data distribution platform, from SQL Server change capture pitfalls to lessons on running it.
talks.summary:
Konrad Szatan describes more than a year and a half spent building a real-time data distribution platform at his company. The starting problem was one large SQL Server instance that many systems depended on. It was costly to run, it created tight coupling between systems, and it left no clear source of truth for documents and schemas. The team chose Kafka with Kafka Connect to stream changes to other development teams, first running it on virtual machines and later on Kubernetes.

The middle of the talk covers the setbacks. The standard SQL Server connector required an Enterprise or Datacenter licence, so the team wrote its own based on change tracking. That mechanism only reports changed keys, so the connector had to fetch the full rows separately. A MongoDB connector delivered update operations rather than complete documents, which led to an extra patcher component that rebuilt documents for consumers. Other problems included connector tasks that stopped streaming after cluster topology changes, a restart loop that a later connector version fixed, and a forked open-source connector the team had to maintain itself.

The talk closes with what came after. The team added a Git-backed configuration repository managed by a custom Kubernetes operator, and later explored consuming changes through a lower-level API. The speaker's advice is to give developers self-service tools, budget effort for connector stability and maintenance, and be ready to fix open-source components. He estimates the platform saved dozens of teams a great deal of time.

talks.title: JDD2019: Technical interview - stories from the opposite side of desk [PL], Marcin Chrost
talks.teaser: An experienced hiring lead shares practical ways to screen developers, score written tests, and structure live technical interviews.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from the employer side of technical hiring, arguing that while programming knowledge is easy to find online, documented recruitment practice is scarce. Most companies need dependable craftspeople, not Mozart-level virtuosos, and every interview pulls expensive seniors off billable work. The speaker therefore treats recruiters as a first-line filter who can review CVs, repositories, and phone screens to keep unsuitable candidates away.

Screening covers résumé signals such as job hopping versus stagnation, unrealistic client demands, and when to hand interviews to someone who actually knows the stack. The firm favors a roughly hour-long mixed assessment with multiple-choice and open questions, then about an hour of conversation. Poor multiple-choice combined with strong open answers may still advance a candidate; the reverse is a red flag. Live interviews follow a fixed plan: introduction, theoretical checks tied to the test, a practical coding exercise preferably on the candidate’s own IDE, and time for their questions.

Throughout, the speaker stresses honesty over bluffing, enthusiasm and ownership over pure stack listing, lightweight live coding tasks such as string reversal, debugging broken code as a plus, and respecting candidate time including evening slots and quick follow-up when remote work matters. Audience Q&A touches on destroying recruitment data under GDPR, prioritizing tests before presentation, attitude mismatches, and multi-day take-home tasks for internships.

talks.title: JDD2019: Java in Container - Best Practicies for containerized Java Apps, Mateusz Dymiński
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of JDD2019: Java in Container - Best Practicies for containerized Java Apps, Mateusz Dymiński.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at JDD 2019, Mateusz Dymiński outlines practical best practices for containerizing Java applications using Docker. Starting from a basic Spring Boot REST service connected to MySQL, Dymiński demonstrates how standard approaches—such as pulling arbitrary Ubuntu-based Java images and packaging monolithic fat JARs—result in severe pitfalls. These issues include ignored termination signals, massive image sizes (approaching 1 GB), slow build pipelines, resource misallocations, and security liabilities. He then details concrete architectural and configuration patterns to optimize container builds, runtime ergonomics, and operational security.

### Key Topics
- **Signal Handling & Process Execution**: Ensuring SIGTERM and termination signals properly reach JVM processes for graceful shutdowns.
- **Base Image Selection**: Evaluating base Linux distributions (e.g., Ubuntu vs. Alpine) and Java Runtimes (Oracle, OpenJDK, AdoptOpenJDK, Red Hat, Amazon Corretto, Liberica), alongside C library compatibility issues (glibc vs. musl libc).
- **Layering & Multistage Builds**: Deconstructing fat JARs into cached layers and decoupling build environments from runtime images.
- **JVM Container Ergonomics**: Navigating the evolution of JVM awareness regarding Linux cgroups, CPU quotas, and memory limits across Java versions.
- **Container Security & Automation**: Enforcing non-root user execution, read-only filesystems, vulnerability scanning with Clair, and leveraging Google Jib for automated containerization.

### Technical Details
- **Signaling and Entrypoint Formatting**: Using string syntax for Docker `ENTRYPOINT` triggers a shell subshell that swallows Unix signals like `SIGTERM`. Containers must use the JSON array syntax (`["java", "-jar", ...]`) or `exec` in shell wrappers to allow the application to receive `SIGTERM` and perform graceful draining before Docker issues `SIGKILL` after the 10-second timeout.
- **Image Sizing and Portola**: A default Ubuntu base with Java yielded an 881 MB image. Switching to an Alpine-based OpenJDK 8 image reduced the size to 124 MB. However, Alpine relies on `musl libc` rather than `glibc`. While Java 8 supported musl, Java 9 through 11 suffered compatibility issues, which Project Portola worked to solve (reaching near-completion around Java 13).
- **Unpacking Fat JARs & Multistage Builds**: Repacking a 40 MB fat JAR on every code change forces Docker to push the entire layer to registries. By unpacking the JAR into dependencies (`BOOT-INF/lib`) and application code (`BOOT-INF/classes`), unchanged dependencies remain cached, reducing rebuild diffs to kilobytes. Combining this with Docker multistage builds (`FROM ... AS build` and `COPY --from=build`) ensures only source code and POM files are sent to the daemon.
- **JVM Ergonomics Across Versions**: Earlier JVMs (prior to Java 8u121/8u191) calculated thread counts, garbage collection, and heap sizes from host VM resources rather than container cgroups, requiring workaround scripts like Fabric8's `run-java.sh`. Starting in Java 8u191 and Java 10/11+, flags like `UseContainerSupport` and percentage-based heap configurations make JVMs natively adapt to container memory and CPU quotas.
- **Hardening and Jib**: Dymiński recommends adding non-root users (`USER app`), running containers with `--read-only`, and scanning images against CVE databases using CoreOS Clair and Clair scanner. For developers seeking to bypass manual Dockerfile management, Google Jib (via Maven or Gradle plugins) builds optimized, layered images on top of Google's distroless base automatically.

### Takeaways
- Use Java 11 or at least Java 8 update 191+ to ensure native container cgroup awareness.
- Always invoke Java processes using the JSON array entrypoint syntax to enable graceful shutdown via `SIGTERM`.
- Unpack fat JARs across Docker image layers or use multistage builds to drastically cut build times and registry bandwidth.
- Enforce container security best practices: drop root privileges by setting a dedicated application user, use minimal distros, and scan for known CVEs.
- Consider tools like Google Jib to automate best practices and GraalVM native images to achieve ultra-fast startup times without a traditional JRE.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Jak przestać klikać i zacząć pisać! CAŁY Jenkins jako kod [PL], Jędrzej Andrykowski
talks.teaser: Shows how to stand up Jenkins with Docker, plugins, and configuration-as-code so setups stay repeatable, auditable, and out of the GUI.
talks.summary:
The session opens on a familiar tension: teams adopt Jenkins to automate builds and deployments, yet they still configure the controller by clicking through the UI. The speaker walks through a typical manual path in four recurring stages—installation, first-run setup wizard, plugin and global tool configuration, and job creation—and argues that this cycle does not scale when the instance grows, when a second controller is needed, or when production breaks because someone changed settings by hand.

The middle of the talk reframes Jenkins itself as infrastructure to manage like software. After a short tour of generic configuration-as-code ideas (version control, tests, automated application of definitions), the demos center on Docker: running the official image, persisting Jenkins home, baking in plugins, skipping the wizard with environment variables, and driving server settings through the Configuration as Code plugin and related Job DSL and pipeline options. The speaker also warns about the “fear loop” when live servers drift from the repository, and mentions locking down the UI so casual clicks cannot undo codified state.

Practitioners should leave with a concrete file-level picture—Dockerfile, compose, plugins list, CasC YAML, optional DSL or pipeline snippets—and a GitHub example project to reproduce a small Jenkins stack without manual setup. The closing notes acknowledge the upfront time cost of codifying Jenkins, but stress repeatability, audit history, and living documentation as the payoff.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Demystifying Kafka, Nakul Mishra
talks.teaser: Surveys Kafka logs, scaling, replication, exactly-once delivery, Connect, Streams, and ops tips for production clusters.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why traditional message-oriented middleware struggles in distributed environments, citing scalability, throughput, and resiliency pain from forcing broker-centric queues into roles they were not built for. It positions Apache Kafka as an open-source log: topics backed by append-only segment files named by offsets, supporting both point-to-point and publish-subscribe patterns with stronger ordering under parallel consumers than typical exclusive-consumer workarounds.

The middle contrasts Kafka with classic MOM brokers—dumb broker, smart client, log-structured storage, page-cache reliance, and zero-copy transfers that can saturate network interfaces without heavy JVM buffering. It walks through partition scaling and consumer reassignment, idempotent producers and Kafka transactions (with read_committed isolation), in-sync replica replication, and ingestion options via Kafka Connect, stream processing with Kafka Streams, continuous SQL with ksqlDB, and schema registry compatibility rules.

Practitioners are reminded to provision dedicated disk, watch noisy neighbors in cloud deployments, use quotas where needed, add brokers only when partitions move, favor compacted topics for state, keep clusters upgraded, and treat Kafka as an always-on, retention-friendly platform for moving data between teams and legacy systems.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Time-based domain events - how to deal with time, Konrad Jakubiec
talks.teaser: Day-precision Kafka Streams topologies postpone employee benefit effective dates using expiring timeframes and just-in-time domain events.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens in employee rewards and benefits for a large UK retailer, where eligibility rules depend on work-cycle facts and calendar time. A domain expert names an expiring timeframe: after six months of service, a discount becomes effective when an LGBT-related eligibility date is reached. The speaker contrasts that well-named, time-oriented domain language with the rarity of time-based domain events in mainstream DDD literature, citing schedulers and explicit timeframe vocabulary as better than hiding time in implementation details.

A second scenario needs just-in-time handling: when someone marks leave, an active discount must disassociate only once employment actually ends, but legacy systems emit leave events with past or future dates. The proposed pattern is an event shadower on Kafka between contexts—translating through an anti-corruption layer, holding not-yet-effective events in RocksDB-backed state stores, and using processor API punctuation with careful attention to stream time versus wall-clock time. Walkthrough code covers translation, scheduling, range queries keyed by date strings, deduplication cleanup, and extensions for postponed, rescheduled, and canceled leave.

Practitioners hear operational constraints: day-level precision, roughly nine thousand leavers per month among hundreds of thousands of employees, Kafka-only infrastructure, and fault tolerance without duplicate publishes. Takeaways stress reading Kafka internals documentation, measuring RocksDB memory on containers, abstracting time for tests, and comparing alternatives such as suppress windows, Redis TTL semantics, databases with schedulers, or Kubernetes jobs—each with weaker fit or scale trade-offs than partitioned stream processing for this shape of problem.

talks.title: JDD2019: Najlepszym przyjacielem programisty jest jego IDE [PL], Wojciech Przechodzeń
talks.teaser: Demonstrates IntelliJ navigation, search, Git, multi-cursor edits, and live automated refactors for faster coding.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that a modern IDE should free developers from boilerplate so they can focus on harder design problems. The speaker polls the audience on IntelliJ usage, keyboard shortcuts, and Git inside the IDE, then structures roughly forty-five minutes around navigation, finding information, editing text, and automated refactoring—with IntelliJ as the main example, noting that similar tricks exist elsewhere if you learn the right command.

The first half is a coaching-style tour of navigation and discovery: mnemonics with Alt and underlined letters, project-wide and in-editor search, the action search that reveals shortcut bindings, recent files and jump-to-location, error navigation with F2, structure overview, and numeric bookmarks. A segment on text work highlights expand-selection shortcuts and multi-cursor selection for repetitive edits such as extracting email tokens from JSON without a script.

The closing live demo builds a small controller and services almost entirely through intentions and generators—creating types, fields, and methods from red and yellow hints, changing return types, extract-parameter refactors across many call sites, and moving methods to another class or pulling signatures into an interface via the intention menu. Practical takeaways include using a key-promoter plugin, sharing one new shortcut per week in a team, and experimenting with shared shortcut families that repeat across dialogs and panels.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Where did you get this bean?, Dominik Przybysz
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD 2019: Where did you get this bean?, Dominik Przybysz.
talks.summary: Dominik Przybysz debugs mystery Spring beans by inspecting ApplicationContext defaults—environment post-processors, message sources, lifecycle processors—and contrasts XML, Groovy, and annotation configuration eras. He shows how auto-configuration silently registers dozens of public beans engineers can accidentally depend on.

talks.title: JDD2019: Automated tests: You won't find it in a book! [PL], Jacek Milewski
talks.teaser: Presents module-level test design that cuts mock-heavy false positives and scales from in-memory repos to full-stack checks.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by arguing that courses and books still teach automated tests through frameworks first, which nudges teams toward heavy mocking and tests that mirror production code too closely. Using a loan-style rating example tied to user age, he walks through classic red-green unit work, then shows how Mockito-style verification can pass while business rules drift—for example when validation ages change but expectations still assume older thresholds.

He reframes “unit” testing around business modules: a package exposes a small API or facade, internal services stay real inside the module, and tests prove business outcomes instead of every collaborator call. External modules are stubbed at the boundary; databases are approached through test doubles that implement the same repository interface, including throwing on unused methods. After refactoring toward that model, module tests stay green when validation rules tighten. He adds a Spring-based integration layer that boots the app on a test port, hits the REST endpoint, checks the response body, and confirms persistence—without reusing every module-level case.

Practitioners should leave with a layered strategy: module tests for in-module logic, micro tests only where isolation still helps, integration tests for wiring and persistence, and lighter business-flow coverage where needed. He recommends Given-When-Then naming, builders for test data, copying one happy path into integration suites, and watching for falsely green tests caused by API mistakes. He closes by contrasting teams that skip tests—fast early, slower later—with test-heavy teams that pay upfront cost but sustain speed across multi-sprint work.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Project Loom: Fibers and Continuations for the Java Virtual Machine [PL], Tobiasz Kowalski
talks.teaser: It walks through Project Loom on the JVM, comparing blocking code, async styles, and lightweight fibers with live scaling demos.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting everyday blocking Java with callback- or future-driven non-blocking styles. Blocking code stays easy to read and debug, but tying up platform threads limits scale and burns memory when many connections wait on I/O. Async designs raise throughput yet scatter control flow, complicate error handling, and make performance problems harder to diagnose.

The speaker frames OpenJDK Project Loom as a way to keep blocking-style source while mounting huge numbers of lightweight fibers on far fewer carrier threads. He introduces fibers and continuations, shows how blocking in a fiber can park work without freezing the underlying thread, and demos spawning tens of thousands of tasks where ordinary threads quickly hit memory and runtime limits. Comparisons cover ordering, structured concurrency ideas such as deadlines, and how fibers differ from classic async chains.

He also covers practical limits: native code, reflection, synchronized blocks, legacy libraries that pin carriers, and tooling still catching up. A subjective scorecard weighs readability, debugging, performance, and maintenance for greenfield versus legacy adoption. Practitioners should treat Loom as promising for I/O-heavy services once ecosystems adapt, not as a drop-in fix for every pinned-thread dependency.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Vert.x czy można nim zastąpić Spring Cloud-a [PL], Łukasz Guz
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD 2019: Vert.x czy można nim zastąpić Spring Cloud-a [PL], Łukasz Guz.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Wprowadzenie do Kubernetes [PL], Krzysztof Dziankowski
talks.teaser: Introduces Kubernetes core objects, then deploys a sample Java app locally and on a cloud cluster.
talks.summary:
This introductory talk, given in Polish, presents Kubernetes as a platform for managing containerized applications, especially when many microservices run across a cluster of machines. The speaker focuses on four core objects: pods, which hold one or more containers; services, which give a set of pods a stable name and address; and declarative configuration, which describes the desired state the cluster should maintain.

The live demo starts by building a small Java application into a container image and running it with Docker on a local machine. The app reads a file and returns its contents, so the speaker shows how to mount a configuration file into a pod. Objects are then created with kubectl, exposed inside the cluster and through an external load balancer, and scaled to four replicas. On a small local virtual machine the extra replicas run out of memory, which illustrates why resource requests matter. Rolling updates, liveness probes and persistent volume claims are also covered.

To show portability, the same image is pushed to a registry and deployed to a Google Cloud cluster by switching the kubectl context. The talk closes with pointers to the official documentation and an online playground for trying a cluster in the browser.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Nowości w Javie 11, 12, 13 [PL], Adam Kulawik, Rafał Jankowski - część 1
talks.teaser: Covers Java 11–13 release cadence, Oracle licensing, new garbage collectors, and major language and library updates for practitioners.
talks.summary:
The opening segment frames how Java moved from long, delayed major releases to a predictable six-month cadence in March and September, and what that shift means for planning upgrades and compatibility expectations. It then walks through Oracle JDK licensing after Java 8: when commercial use requires a subscription, when development and demos stay free, and practical responses such as auditing deployed versions, adopting OpenJDK builds from vendors like Red Hat, Azul, or Amazon, or paying for long-term support where six-month updates are unrealistic.

The middle of the session is a deep tour of garbage collection changes across versions 11 through 13. It compares classic collectors (serial, parallel, CMS, G1) by pause behavior and workload fit, explains G1 enhancements in Java 12 for honoring pause targets and returning unused heap to the OS, introduces the no-op Epsilon collector for benchmarking and short-lived workloads, and details ZGC’s colored pointers, load barriers, and phased mark/relocation cycles on 64-bit Linux, plus experimental Shenandoah’s concurrent evacuation model.

A second presenter continues with language and API news: local-variable syntax for lambda parameters, expanded String helpers (strip, repeat, lines, isBlank), Optional and collection conveniences, java.time adjustments, Files read/write helpers, the standardized HTTP client, rejected versus delivered features in 12 and 13, switch expressions, and text blocks with indentation rules. The closing message is that many changes modernize everyday coding while larger shifts mirror features from other languages, so teams should weigh migration cost against support and licensing choices.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Fruits of the Loom - Lightweight Concurrency For the Java Platform, Arkadiusz Gasiński
talks.teaser: Covers OpenJDK Loom fibers and continuations, then load-tests Tomcat with threads versus fibers on blocking microservices.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces OpenJDK Project Loom, which began in late 2017 to make concurrent Java programs easier to write and maintain while keeping a familiar blocking style. After a primer on threads, kernel versus user-level mappings, and why Java’s one-to-one threads limit scale and make thread-per-request costly, the speaker contrasts reactive stacks with Loom’s “write sync, run async” approach.

The core additions are continuations as captured execution contexts and fibers as lightweight user-mode threads mapped many-to-many onto a small kernel thread pool, scheduled via executors such as ForkJoinPool. Fibers park on blocking JDK calls like sleep or CompletableFuture.get without pinning the carrier thread when safe. Structured concurrency is tied to fiber scopes that keep child work bounded. Native monitors and JNI on the stack remain known yield limitations.

A demo runs Spring services on Tomcat with a switchable fiber or thread executor. With only two carrier threads, fibers sustain high request rates on I/O-bound upstream calls while plain threads time out at modest load. The takeaway is that fibers mainly help I/O-heavy servers such as servlet containers, not CPU-saturated workloads, and early access builds are already available to experiment.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Shell, tmux, vim - short story about saw sharpening [PL], Michał Borkowski
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning JDD 2019: Shell, tmux, vim - short story about saw sharpening [PL], Michał Borkowski.
talks.summary: Michał Borko uses live audience polls to argue developers need sharp default tools—shell, tmux, vim—before chasing bloated IDEs, comparing minimalist carpentry kits to over-equipped cyclists. The JDD talk frames editor mastery as saw-sharpening that compounds daily productivity.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Jak wytresować Basha [PL], Marcin Stożek
talks.teaser: Shows how to keep large Bash scripts readable, safe and maintainable with practical coding rules and a linter.
talks.summary:
Marcin Stożek talks about a common problem: Bash scripts that grow to thousands of lines, become hard to edit and can behave in unexpected ways. He opens with a real-world example from source code linked to Valve's Steam client, where an unset variable used in a removal command could delete a whole directory. He also describes how a similar mistake cost him a large amount of data, and argues that scripts need safety measures from the start.

The middle of the talk is a set of practical rules. Quote every variable expansion, avoid spaces around assignments, and store script parameters in an array instead of looping with shift. Use find rather than parsing ls output or relying on globs, prefer [[ ]] for tests, and keep variables local inside functions. He suggests treating Bash mainly as a way to run operating system commands, and keeping global variables and parameters to a minimum. He demonstrates set -u to catch undefined variables, set -x to trace execution, and a static analysis linter that flags many of the problems shown.

He closes by stressing that exit codes should be checked explicitly, since a failed command can otherwise let a script carry on, and that a trap can handle cleanup of temporary files. He shows that functions returning strings make code easier to read and reason about, and answers questions from the audience. The takeaway is that Bash can be written in a maintainable way if a few consistent conventions are applied from the beginning.

talks.title: JDD 2019: From Developer to Manager... and Back, Tomasz Borowiec
talks.teaser: Follows a developer's move into a project manager role, the strain it brought, and the decision to return to coding.
talks.summary:
Tomasz Borowiec opens with a belief many developers hold: that they will eventually move into management. He questions that path using a 2018 study of more than 53,000 employees across 214 sales companies, which found that the strongest performers were the most likely to be promoted into management roles. He also looks at the Peter Principle, a 1969 idea that he notes had originally been written as satire and was long repeated without research behind it.

He then describes his own move. A few years after university, he was offered a project manager role at a small company of roughly 30 to 40 people. The job combined delivery, task splitting, team assignment and client contact, and it brought a constant stream of meetings, emails and spreadsheets. He missed the quick wins of seeing tests go green, kept sneaking back into code, and struggled to delegate. Long hours, skipped lunches and weight gain followed, and a partner's blunt advice to do something about it pushed him to act.

He arranged a role swap with a colleague who wanted to try project management, with a month of handover approved by their manager. Back in development, he said his work felt valued again. His takeaways were practical: plan the day with to-do lists and priorities, build a network of trustworthy people, learn to answer hard questions diplomatically, appreciate good managers, test management on a trial basis first, and step back when a path is damaging your life.

talks.title: JDD 2019: No GC coding techniques for low latency Java, Ivan Zvieriev
talks.teaser: Covers low-latency measurement and Java patterns that cut allocation pressure so garbage collection stays off the hot path.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by defining latency as the interval between stimulus and response, stressing that “low latency” must be spelled out in measurable non-functional requirements for each project. He cites high-frequency trading—where a 2014 Canadian exchange reported eleven percent of orders finishing in under one millisecond—alongside online gaming, in-play betting, video chat, and vehicle piloting as domains where tight reaction times matter. Maximum and average latency matter for operations, and both are heavily influenced when the JVM runs garbage collection alongside application work.

He argues Java remains viable for these systems because of libraries, tooling, hiring, and JVM optimizations that narrow the gap to C++, while acknowledging that eliminating allocations is a deliberate trade-off: developers favor mutability, accept harder testing, and may restrict patterns such as heavy functional-style copying. The core of the session walks through coding techniques: singleton (including enum-based forms), flyweight caching, pre-sized collections, third-party primitive collections, StringBuilder instead of string concatenation, enumerated constants versus enums (and the cost of enum values()), guarding debug logging so strings are not built when logging is off, and reusable mutable objects reset between uses.

Audience questions extend into production practice: garbage collection may be tolerated only during warm-up initialization, after which a full collection is treated as an incident; services were single-threaded to avoid synchronization overhead; GraalVM and detailed collector tuning sit outside the talk’s code-focused scope, though GC logging and load tests are used to verify that collectors stay quiet under load.

talks.title: JDD 2019: Java - microservices, Filip Wieladek
talks.teaser: Shows how one company moved from a Python monolith to dozens of Java microservices and built tooling to keep them manageable.
talks.summary:
The speaker from Beekeeper describes moving from a single Python 2.7 codebase to around 40 microservices as the customer base grew. Because the monolith deployed everything together, unrelated changes broke each other and rollbacks wiped out new features. The team wanted independent deployments, the freedom to choose languages per service, and better scaling and failure isolation.

The developer experience work was the core of the talk. Creating a new service had to be easier than editing the monolith, so the team standardised on Dropwizard and a Yeoman generator that cut bootstrapping from 30 minutes or more to about three minutes. Build setup repeated across 20 to 30 repositories moved into an internal Gradle plugin, leaving one line of configuration per project. Each service published a test-support module with WireMock mocks, allowing fast tests without running dependencies. Shared health checks, Kubernetes readiness probes and a common logging and metrics bundle covered production, with Jenkins running pull request builds and scheduled dependency checks.

The takeaway is that microservices carry a large fixed cost in repeated infrastructure that adds no direct customer value. With strong automation and a DevOps culture where teams own their services, the speaker argued the model scales well for larger teams.

talks.title: JDD 2019: 8ms/99th write percentile latency - is it fast? (...), Maciej Lasyk
talks.teaser: Shows how a small team runs Cassandra and other services reliably, using SLOs, error budgets and self-healing practices.
talks.summary:
Maciej Lasyk describes joining a company that grew from about 100 people toward 300 in a few months, where software developers ran everything without an operations team. He found in-house database and monitoring tooling, self-hosted Cassandra and etcd, and a recovery estimate for Cassandra far longer than the business expected. Rather than replace it all, he explained how the setup stayed simple: applications packaged as jars on virtual machines, auto scaling groups with load balancers, few container schedulers, and an in-house tool that ran workloads on spot instances.

The core of the talk is reliability practice. He explains availability in nines, with three nines allowing about 40 minutes of downtime per month and five nines about 24 seconds, and ties each level to cost. He walks through SLAs, SLOs, service level indicators and error budgets, and suggests mapping user journeys so the business can see what customers feel. To build buy-in, he met with one engineer per service, ranked reliability topics such as self-healing and better monitoring, kept a service catalog with severity and self-healing status, and ran blameless post-mortems only for outages that affected customers. He also showed Cassandra latency graphs, with the 95th percentile around two milliseconds, and noted that the service had not paged anyone in the last year and a half.

For automation, his advice is to document manual runbooks, run them repeatedly by hand, and only then attach them to monitoring, using Cassandra node replacement and repair as examples. He suggested reliability workshops built as scenario games and recommended managed services for teams without operations staff. The takeaway for practitioners is to agree on downtime targets with the business, measure what users experience, and earn trust in a procedure before automating it.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2019: No framework frontends in practice - use the platform!, Karol Horosin
talks.teaser: Builds a no-framework frontend with web components, simple routing, and fetch APIs, drawing on a real client project and live coding.
talks.summary:
Karol Horosin opens by contrasting modern JavaScript frameworks with the weight they add: long builds, opaque dependency trees, and sluggish pages on modest devices or slow networks. He argues the platform has caught up—modules, fetch, and web components—while still needing the good parts frameworks popularized: components, structure, and shared standards.

Most of the session is live coding from an empty folder. He walks through npm init, webpack with Babel and an HTML loader, webpack-dev-server with history fallback, then custom elements that extend HTMLElement, register via customElements.define, and nest like familiar SPA shells. He adds a small dictionary-based router with link handlers and popstate, and wires a home view to JSONPlaceholder through fetch, rendering posts with template literals.

He closes without claiming frameworks are obsolete. Large teams may still need conventions; reactivity without libraries means events and attribute observers until platform proposals land. Web components built here can drop into Angular or React, so practitioners can adopt the pattern incrementally rather than rewriting working code. Slides and repository links are pointed to for deeper platform reading.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2019: Webassembly. The end of JavaScript?, Joanna Lamch
talks.teaser: Traces how WebAssembly arrived beside JavaScript in browsers, how it runs, and where it is heading beyond the web.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how browsers moved from static hypertext pages to scripted interactivity. Early pages offered little more than links, and browser makers wanted a scripting language that stayed readable for existing developers, which led to JavaScript. When browser performance wars began around 2008, engines started compiling JavaScript just in time, but the dynamic language still left execution times uneven.

The speaker then explains WebAssembly as a compact binary format that is compiled before it runs, so execution time stays steady and predictable. It uses linear memory and a small set of numeric types, runs in the same sandbox as JavaScript, and is supported by all major browsers. Examples include a long-established desktop CAD application ported to the web, which reached a ready product in about half a year, and a computation-heavy component that reportedly gained 20-30 times in performance after being rewritten. Current limits covered include large file sizes, threads being disabled after the Meltdown fallout, and no direct DOM access, which has to go through JavaScript glue code.

The closing part looks ahead to the WASI system interface for running modules outside the browser, server-side use as a lighter alternative to full virtual machines, and standardisation work on features such as garbage collection. The takeaway is that WebAssembly complements JavaScript for heavy computation rather than replacing it, and that users benefit from faster browser apps without writing WebAssembly themselves.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2019: Electron JS - desktopowe aplikacje pisane w JavaScript, Rafał Jankowski
talks.teaser: Covers Electron history, main and renderer processes, and hands-on steps to build a minimal desktop app with JavaScript.
talks.summary:
The session opens by positioning Electron as a framework for cross-platform desktop programs written with familiar web technologies, then traces its origin from GitHub’s Atom editor through the 2016 Electron release. The speaker contrasts traditional desktop toolkits, rich web apps, and recurring pain points such as inconsistent rendering across browsers, plugin friction, and limited offline use.

The middle section explains architecture at a practical level: Node.js, Chromium, and V8; a single main process that spawns sandboxed renderer processes per window; and why privileged APIs stay in the main process. A minimal project needs package.json, a main entry, and HTML. Live coding adds renderer scripts, toggles nodeIntegration for security, desktop notifications, synchronous and asynchronous IPC over channels, and extra windows opened from the renderer via remote.

Practitioners should treat Electron as Chromium-plus-Node with clear process boundaries, prefer IPC instead of exposing Node in renderers when possible, and plan for native module rebuilds with electron-rebuild. The close points to electron-forge, electron-builder, framework scaffolds, widely used apps such as VS Code, and documentation links for further study.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2019: Honey, I shrunk the node_modules!, Adam Polak
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in 4Developers Katowice 2019: Honey, I shrunk the node_modules!, Adam Polak.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Adam Polak presents practical strategies for reducing the size of Node.js node_modules directories, a persistent problem in JavaScript development. The talk addresses the "bloated node_modules" issue by explaining how npm dependency management works and providing actionable techniques to identify and eliminate unnecessary packages and code.

## How npm Dependency Management Creates the Problem
Polak explains three core principles of npm package installation. First, when a package is installed, not only the requested package but all of its dependencies are downloaded and placed in node_modules with their own nested dependencies. Second, if a package version already exists in node_modules and matches the requirements, it is reused rather than duplicated. Third, when version requirements cannot be satisfied by existing packages, npm creates local duplicate copies within a package's own node_modules directory. This third principle—deduplication failure leading to duplicate installations—is a major driver of bloat. Polak illustrates this with a real project example: updating from Babel 6.x to 7.x caused node_modules to grow from 200MB to 600MB because twelve dependencies required Babel 6.x, forcing npm to maintain both versions locally.

## Identifying the Problem
Polak emphasizes that awareness is the first step. Most developers unknowingly install dozens or hundreds of packages when adding a single library. He criticizes the common practice of copying Stack Overflow solutions that recommend "just use this library" without considering what dependencies come along. He provides the example of installing a small request-making library that brought 46 undocumented dependencies. Using the command `du -sh *` with sorting and filtering, developers can identify which packages consume the most space. Polak demonstrates finding packages over 1GB in real projects and recommends tools like Bundlephobia to analyze package sizes and dependencies before installation.

## Optimization Techniques
Polak details several practical approaches:

1. **Dependency Reduction**: Replace large packages with smaller alternatives when possible. He compares testing frameworks: Mocha (115 dependencies, 12MB) versus lighter options, noting that developers often use only 5-10% of a large package's functionality.

2. **Package Cleanup Tools**: Tools like pruning utilities can remove unnecessary files such as tests, documentation, and alternative build formats. However, Polak notes these are sometimes unreliable—testing showed only 4 out of 10 projects worked correctly after automated pruning.

3. **Production vs. Development Separation**: Using `npm install --production` removes dev dependencies, reducing the example project from 196MB to 144MB (52MB savings).

4. **Custom Cleanup Scripts**: For deeply nested optimizations, developers can create custom scripts to remove specific unnecessary files and configurations from packages before deployment.

5. **Selective Inclusion**: Rather than installing a large package for minimal functionality, copying small code snippets directly (with proper license attribution) can be more efficient.

## Real-World Results
Polak walks through a real project optimization:
- **Starting point**: 297MB (development dependencies)
- **Production build**: 196MB
- **After pruning**: 144MB
- **After custom cleanup**: 106MB

This represents a 53% reduction from the initial size. He notes that the same techniques applied to development builds yield a demo version of 167MB—sometimes lighter than the full production build due to different dependency patterns.

## Security and Control Benefits
Beyond size reduction, Polak argues that understanding and controlling dependencies improves security. Fewer dependencies mean fewer opportunities for malicious code injection. He references a real incident where a package maintainer modified a library after transferring ownership, highlighting why awareness of what is being installed matters. Reducing bloat also improves:
- Build times
- Application startup performance
- Memory usage
- System load for users

## Takeaways
Polak's core message is about conscious dependency management rather than blindly adding packages. Developers should ask whether large packages are truly necessary or if smaller alternatives exist. Understanding node_modules structure, using analysis tools, and regularly auditing dependencies are essential practices. The talk emphasizes that while reusing libraries is valuable, awareness of what is being installed—and why—is equally important for building lighter, faster, and more secure applications.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2019: React on the Hooks, Kaj Białas
talks.teaser: Shows how React hooks replace class components, with side-by-side code and size comparisons for state, custom logic and effects.
talks.summary:
This talk, given at 4Developers Katowice 2019, looks at React hooks and whether they deliver on the claim that they make React code much cleaner. The speaker starts with the history of front-end work, from early jQuery-era widgets to Angular and then React, and explains why React's class components were awkward. Developers needed constructors and method binding, and class property syntax was not supported natively without extra configuration. Splitting code into presentational and container components also made it hard to keep view and logic apart and to reuse stateful logic.

The middle of the talk walks through hook examples. A counter built with the useState hook is compared with the equivalent class component, and the speaker reports about 54 percent less output code. A custom hook that wraps localStorage replaces a higher-order component and gives about 51 percent less code. An effect that subscribes to an event and cleans it up on unmount, with an empty dependency array so it runs only once, is measured at about 46 percent less. The speaker also covers useContext, useReducer, watching specific values through the effect dependency list, and how a Redux selector can be used directly in a function component.

The closing part weighs these results against Facebook's claim of up to 90 percent cleaner code. The speaker concludes that the measured gains are roughly half that, although the code is easier to read and newcomers can follow it more quickly. Hooks are presented as a good fit for small and medium applications, while Redux-style state management is still useful for very large projects where state must be shared across many pages. The takeaway is that hooks are a worthwhile default for new function components.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2019: Nawigacja z Portal API: czy naprawdę tego potrzebujemy?, Marcin Gajda
talks.teaser: Explains the proposed Portals API for seamless page-to-page navigation in browsers, with live demos and open design questions.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Portals, a proposed web platform element that embeds another page much like an iframe but can be activated to take over the browser view. The speaker starts with the long-standing need for pages to show new content without full reloads, then traces how embedded frames handled it and why mobile browsing made smoother transitions more important.

In the middle, the speaker walks through the Portals API in a series of live demos. A portal shows a preview of another page; activating it moves that browsing context into the main window, and the demo showed the page title and state carried over without a reload. A predecessor adoption pattern was shown, where the host page stays alive after activation and can insert a new portal element back in place. A theme shop demo showed that a portal disappears once activated and must be re-inserted to restore the preview. A font-size and night-mode example used message passing to adjust a guest page. Data sent between host and guest is passed as copies rather than shared objects, which the speaker presented as a safety property.

The talk closes with open concerns: the back button behaviour for portals is still unclear, and the speaker noted that pages would need careful testing, especially on mobile, before relying on the feature. The takeaway is that Portals may bring smoother navigation to the web, but developers should track the specification and test navigation and history closely as it matures.
