talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2019: Nginx as reverse proxy for your (micro) services (...), Karol Horosin
talks.teaser: Shows how nginx routes, load-balances and secures several containerised services behind one address, step by step, in Polish.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces nginx as a reverse proxy for placing several services, such as a front end, an API and a mail-related service, behind one address and one domain. The client sees a single entry point, and nginx passes each request to the right backend. The session is practical, and everything is run in Docker containers so the setup can be repeated on any machine.

The live walkthrough starts with serving a static site from a container by mounting a local directory into the nginx image and publishing port 80. Next, the speaker writes a configuration with custom 404 and 500 error pages, keeps internal error pages reachable only from inside, and adds a test location that returns an error on purpose. He then adds a gateway container in front of two instances of the same application, defines an upstream group, and forwards the original host header so the backends see the real request details. The demo moves to HTTPS by redirecting port 80 to 443, loading a self-signed certificate, and protecting one path with basic authentication using a password file.

The closing part lists nginx's strengths: it is lightweight, handles many concurrent connections well, and is widely deployed. The speaker warns that adding modules can mean rebuilding the server, and that changing routes usually means editing the configuration and reloading. Service discovery is mentioned as a harder topic he did not cover in depth. The takeaways are to start from the official documentation, review security settings carefully before production, and use the container-based setup for quick testing.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2019: How Event-driven flow and serverless architecture (...), Paweł Haracz
talks.teaser: Shows how an IoT telemetry platform moved to event-driven serverless components, and the testing and delivery lessons learned.
talks.summary:
The talk, given in Polish, traces how system design moved from one large monolith to smaller services and then to event-driven architecture. In that model a component publishes an event and other systems react to it asynchronously, much like posting a parcel that is picked up and delivered later. The speaker argues this suits systems with many inputs and outputs, since each function can stay small.

The main case is an IoT project for a customer whose roughly 15-year-old devices could only be pointed at a new endpoint. The team built on Microsoft's Dynamics CRM and device-management services, showing data in a portal. An early in-memory design was too slow for near-live views, so the team added aggregation and time-series components and an event pipeline that sends commands back to devices. Growing the system exposed the need for contract, smoke and performance tests, which revealed millions of errors under load.

The speaker is candid about the costs. Serverless functions are quick to wire together but hard to debug and test locally, and queued messages can pile up in test environments. Delivery guarantees have to be chosen and handled deliberately, and per-function cloud pricing and latency deserve attention at scale. The takeaway is to define event contracts and shared standards early, and to plan testing before the system grows.

talks.title: 4Developers Katowice 2019: Next Generation Platform
talks.teaser: Experience report on moving a large travel platform to Kubernetes, covering logging, API gateways, cloud costs and faster delivery.
talks.summary:
Marcin Książek, a product manager on the Next Generation platform, describes how a large travel technology provider serving airlines, hotel networks and travel agencies is moving its estate to the cloud. He starts with scale: about 62 million API calls and 132 thousand flight searches per minute. The company's history runs from mainframes in the 1960s and its first API in 1984 to a Linux migration from 2001 and the Next Generation platform from 2017, a process that has already lasted well over a decade.

The platform uses Kubernetes as an abstraction layer over public and private clouds, so the company does not depend on a single vendor. The talk covers the problems that followed: commercial distributions and cloud components that failed under load, the need to work closely with upstream projects, an API gateway that could not meet high-volume demands and was therefore built in-house, and logging volumes that overwhelmed collection pipelines. Developers who had no resource limits also drove up costs until the first bill arrived, which led to usage reporting and automatic scale-down.

Delivery speed is the other thread. Releases that once took weeks or quarters, bound by audit and change-control processes, are being pushed toward automated pipelines and same-day deployment. Teams are grouped by maturity level, the company built its own orchestration tool after finding open-source options unsuitable, and it used DevOps research metrics such as lead time and deployment frequency. The main takeaway is that tooling is the easier half: legal, security and process work takes as much effort as the coding.

talks.title: 4Developers Kraków 2019: Czy jesteś egoistycznym programistą?
talks.teaser: Walks through incremental Ruby refactors on legacy poker-hand logic, using tests and metrics to cut complexity without big rewrites.
talks.summary:
The session reframes “selfish” programming as making your own life easier by leaving each file cleaner than you found it, using the scout-camp rule instead of blaming technology, clients, or deadlines. Most developers land in years-old codebases where every change feels dangerous, so the speaker argues for small, local improvements rather than fantasies about a full rewrite.

On a non-production Ruby class that evaluates poker hands (roughly two hundred lines with solid tests), she walks through concrete steps: linters, refactoring one hand-ranking method at a time behind tests, moving repeated card data into object state, splitting bloated tests, centralizing rank counts, tightening visibility with private methods, replacing opaque numeric codes with readable symbols, and cautiously using metaprogramming. Metrics such as line counts and Flog complexity drop sharply when the refactor is finished, though she warns that stopping halfway can temporarily make the design worse. She closes with naming, formatting, and duplication examples from agricultural domain code, stressing that micro-level clarity matters more than grand architecture slides.

Practitioners should treat fear of legacy code as a signal to invest in tests and tidy the next touch point, not to freeze or escalate blame.

talks.title: 4Developers Kraków 2019: Błędy, które popełniłem w pracy z legacy code i jak je naprawić,Dawid Mazur
talks.teaser: Delivers war stories from Polish public-sector PHP and homegrown frameworks, plus concrete steps toward tests and incremental refactors.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by reframing legacy code as software that is costly to maintain, not merely old, ugly, or broken. The speaker argues that fleeing such projects wastes a rare chance to grow as an engineer, then walks through three painful mistakes from real work: cataloging bizarre globals and abbreviations instead of changing behavior, betting years on an in-house framework rewrite that still shipped without tests, and becoming the sole on-call expert on a Windows Server 2003 back office with a bus factor of one.

The middle of the talk turns to what to do instead of a full rewrite. Production use is poor test coverage; changes need automated checks. Teams should invest in IDEs, debuggers, and static analysis, stop piling new modules onto rotten cores, and grow cleaner code beside the old system—moving pieces over gradually. A long section explains how to choose test boundaries using simple diagrams, Liskov-style reasoning, and narrow seams, then demonstrates refactor moves such as extract method, extract class, decorators, and test spies on tangled methods thousands of lines long.

The close stresses discipline: refactor only with tests, expect dependency and compliance shocks on decade-old stacks, and read established books on working effectively with legacy code. Incremental improvement beats parallel greenfield efforts that leave two codebases aging together.

talks.title: 4Developers Kraków 2019: How to (git) blame efficiently, Grzegorz Kocjan
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in 4Developers Kraków 2019: How to (git) blame efficiently, Grzegorz Kocjan.
talks.summary: Grzegorz Kocjan argues that agility should live in version control history, not only in process frameworks. Using a museum metaphor for blame messages, he contrasts unreadable default logs with commit notes that explain exceptions, ticket links, and rejected alternatives. Beginner tactics cover renaming fix commits, tagging error types, and splitting formatting from logic in separate commits. Advanced sections promote linear history with interactive rebase, squashing fixups before push, and avoiding merge bubbles that hide concurrent work. He warns that merged formatting edits train readers to skim past risky hunks, and demonstrates bisect, commit --amend, and force-with-lease cautions. The capstone is git reflog as local undo insurance and building a durable knowledge base for engineers who rotate every few years.

talks.title: 4Developers Kraków 2019: Zwinnie czysta architektura, Michał Cisz
talks.teaser: Shows how clean architecture boundaries keep a subscription module agile, testable and independent of frameworks and databases.
talks.summary:
Michał Cisz starts from the idea that architecture is a series of decisions that are costly to reverse. He describes how, under deadline pressure, SOLID code gives way to dead, chaotic or shortsighted architectures, where layers become lasagna and classes become spaghetti, so even small changes get expensive.

To show an alternative, he builds a subscription module for a startup founder's music app with a developer team, starting from domain language gathered from the client and written as behaviour scenarios. The code is organised around a domain core, with use cases at its edge and controllers, presenters, frameworks and databases treated as details. Dependencies point only inward, the folder structure reveals the application's purpose, and a facade with interfaces keeps the module's boundaries explicit. He also explains why boundaries are introduced gradually, splitting components only when needed and adding versioning once they move into separate repositories. The demo showed a purchase going through, a second demo package being refused and an upgrade to a larger package being accepted.

The practical takeaway is that clean architecture can be introduced iteratively within agile timeboxes instead of as up-front design. Keep business rules free of infrastructure, let the domain shape the code, and delay splitting until there is a concrete reason. Slides were shared afterwards.

talks.title: 4Developers Kraków 2019: Jak skutecznie implementować oprogramowanie (...), Rafał Watza
talks.teaser: Shows how dozens of teams build, test and release base station software for cellular networks.
talks.summary:
Rafał Watza, presenting for Ericsson, uses mobile networks as a case study for building complex software that many teams must deliver together. He outlines how cellular technology has evolved across generations, from early voice-only GSM service to 5G, and describes the main parts of a network: the radio side, the core, and the management systems. The main focus is the base station controller, a piece of software that runs on dedicated hardware and must integrate with other nodes made by different vendors.

The talk then follows the delivery process in order: system design, development, testing, release to the customer, and maintenance. Development is split into teams of six to eight people, with more than 2000 people involved overall, all committing code to one shared repository. Testing moves from functional and integration checks to regression tests, a suite of about 1450 tests, and final runs lasting 48 to 72 hours on several test nodes. The speaker stresses that requirements must be measurable, with explicit timing, availability and quality targets, and that defects are far cheaper to fix early. Work is organised in sprints of two to three weeks, with releases on a fixed cycle.

He closes by covering dependencies between teams and products, customer-specific configuration, and security hardening such as disabling insecure services and using longer encryption keys. His takeaway is that network software has to be reliable, secure and responsive together, not just fast. Clear requirements, continuous integration and regression testing are what keep a large, shared codebase working for operators.

talks.title: 4Developers Kraków 2019: Make your applications intelligent (...), Michał Jankowski
talks.teaser: Shows how Azure Cognitive Services add vision, speech, and translation to apps with minimal code, containers, and Custom Vision.
talks.summary:
The session argues that applications gain the most from artificial intelligence when teams start from a business problem, choose a solution, and only then gather data—not the other way around. The presenter outlines reasoning, learning, understanding, and interaction as core AI themes, with customer-facing bots and council service examples for speed gains, alongside cautionary stories about frustrating voice interfaces and workforce impacts.

Most of the time goes to Microsoft Azure Cognitive Services: computer vision for objects, faces, emotions, adult-content scores, handwriting, brands, and landmarks; a mindset shift for face matching via email-linked photo sets rather than phone-camera identification; and live portals plus JSON responses illustrating probabilistic, billable feature calls. A coded demo builds a Star Trek-style translator using speech recognition, translation, and text-to-speech in a handful of lines, including Polish recognition; Docker runs sentiment analysis locally with periodic billing connectivity.

Custom Vision closes the arc with quick training on two dog classes, publishing an endpoint, and caveats about limited training sets, similar breeds, and dataset bias. Pricing tiers, per-feature API charges, and Q&A on model confidence and Microsoft’s use of customer photos round out what practitioners should weigh before shipping intelligent features.

talks.title: 4Developers Kraków 2019: Let's get more functional, Paweł Łukaszuk
talks.teaser: The talk shows how Java teams can adopt functional habits via pure functions, immutability, and small, testable modules at the edges.
talks.summary:
Paweł Łukaszuk frames functional programming as a way to grow as a developer without chasing yet another library, and warns that it is not a silver bullet and cannot carry an entire typical business application on its own. He grounds the ideas in school-style mathematical functions: the same inputs should yield the same outputs, signatures should be honest, and side effects belong at the edges rather than inside core logic.

The middle of the talk works through Java-friendly examples: spotting impure helpers, when throwing exceptions hides behavior versus returning explicit success or failure (including a PESEL validation scenario where bad input was common), optional types and null-handling habits, and separating commands from queries or pure calculation from I/O. He contrasts imperative loops with higher-order collection operations, notes how immutable updates ease reasoning in large pipelines, and mentions trade-offs such as memoization, memory use, and expression-oriented style.

He closes by arguing that many FP discipline rules overlap with general clean-code practice, and urges incremental adoption—extracting small testable functions and using streams or composition where they clarify data processing rather than rewriting whole systems in a dogmatic way.

talks.title: 4Developers Kraków 2019: Domain-Driven Design taktycznie i praktycznie, Kamil Grzybek
talks.teaser: Walks through tactical domain-driven design patterns for rich domain models, aggregates, and persistence in real application code.
talks.summary:
The presentation limits scope to tactical domain-driven design rather than strategic concerns such as bounded contexts or system-wide architecture. It opens by contrasting clean code and clean domain models with anemic data-holder types, then revisits object-oriented basics: abstraction, behavior bundled with state, and encapsulation behind a narrow public API.

Using a familiar order-and-customer example, the speaker explains entities, immutable value objects, and aggregates with a single root that enforces invariants atomically. Commands, domain events, and ubiquitous language tie into a command–aggregate–event flow. Implementation topics include protecting aggregate boundaries, domain services for rules that span aggregates, fail-fast validation versus result objects, eventual consistency, and reducing primitive obsession by modeling concepts such as money or contract lifecycles as types with behavior.

Persistence is discussed through Entity Framework and classic layered architectures (onion, hexagonal, clean) that keep the domain ignorant of infrastructure where possible. The close covers unit-testing aggregates in isolation and points to sample repositories, reference books, and a follow-on session on evolving anemic models into rich ones. A brief Q&A relates long-running processes to event-driven choreography rather than one large transaction.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Artur Piechocki - Obowiązki i dokumentacja w zakresie cyberbezpieczeństwa
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for PLNOG23 - Artur Piechocki - Obowiązki i dokumentacja w zakresie cyberbezpieczeństwa.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Prezentacja Artura Piechockiego na konferencji PLNOG23 poświęcona jest obowiązkom i dokumentacji z zakresu cyberbezpieczeństwa w świetle polskiej Ustawy o Krajowym Systemie Cyberbezpieczeństwa (KSC). Prelegent omawia definicje ustawowe, podmioty objęte regulacją, klasyfikację incydentów, wymogi dotyczące raportowania, a także praktyczne i prawne aspekty outsourcingu cyberbezpieczeństwa (MSP, MSSP, SOC).

### Key Topics
- **Ustawa o KSC i definicje**: Cyberbezpieczeństwo definiowane jako odporność systemów informacyjnych na działania naruszające poufność, integralność, dostępność i autentyczność danych lub usług. Zarządzanie ryzykiem w cyberbezpieczeństwie porównane zostało do podejścia znanego z RODO.
- **Kategorie podmiotów objętych ustawą**: Podmioty publiczne, operatorzy usług kluczowych (OUK – m.in. sektory energii, transportu, bankowości, infrastruktury rynków finansowych, ochrony zdrowia, zaopatrzenia w wodę pitną i dystrybucji) oraz dostawcy usług cyfrowych (platformy handlowe online, usługi przetwarzania w chmurze, wyszukiwarki internetowe spełniające progi zatrudnienia powyżej 50 osób lub obrotu powyżej 10 mln zł).
- **Klasyfikacja incydentów**: Wyróżnienie incydentów poważnych (dotyczących usług kluczowych), istotnych (dotyczących usług cyfrowych), krytycznych (wywołujących znaczną szkodę dla bezpieczeństwa publicznego lub państwa) oraz incydentów w podmiotach publicznych.
- **Obowiązki operatorów usług kluczowych**: Wdrożenie systemu zarządzania bezpieczeństwem, wyznaczenie osoby kontaktowej (zgłoszenie w ciągu 14 dni do właściwego CSIRT), edukacja użytkowników, dokumentacja bezpieczeństwa, obsługa incydentów oraz obowiązkowy audyt bezpieczeństwa (w ciągu roku od doręczenia decyzji, a następnie co 2 lata).
- **Kary i kontrole**: Uprawnienia kontrolne organów właściwych (m.in. prawo wstępu, żądanie wyjaśnień, oględziny sprzętu bez drogi odwoławczej od zaleceń pokontrolnych). Kary finansowe sięgają od 15 tys. zł (brak osoby kontaktowej), 20 tys. zł (niezgłoszenie incydentu poważnego), 150 tys. zł (brak szacowania ryzyka), aż do 1 mln zł przy uporczywych naruszeniach zagrażających bezpieczeństwu państwa. Przewidziano także odpowiedzialność finansową kierownika OUK do 20% miesięcznego wynagrodzenia.

### Technical Details & Outsourcing
- **Terminy raportowania**: Zgłoszenie incydentu do właściwego zespołu CSIRT (np. CSIRT NASK dla przedsiębiorstw) musi nastąpić niezwłocznie, nie później niż w ciągu 24 godzin od momentu wykrycia (w odróżnieniu od 72 godzin w RODO).
- **Centra Operacji Bezpieczeństwa (SOC) i MSSP**: Przedsiębiorstwa mogą realizować wymogi ustawy poprzez outsourcing do wyspecjalizowanych podmiotów MSP/MSSP. Prelegent omawia podział na linie wsparcia SOC (L1 – monitoring i obsługa klienta, L2 – zarządzanie platformą i incydentami, L3 – zaawansowane wsparcie i ekspercka obsługa skomplikowanych incydentów), a także narzędzia klasy SIEM oraz model Security as a Service.
- **Konstrukcja umów outsourcingowych**: Kluczowe elementy kontraktu obejmują dokładne zdefiniowanie przedmiotu wdrożenia (np. która linia SOC), zobowiązanie podwykonawcy do powiadomienia OUK w czasie krótszym niż 24 godziny, określenie odpowiedzialności opartej na starannym działaniu (a nie gwarancji wykrycia 100% incydentów), licencjonowanie procedur i scenariuszy reakcji, SLA definiowane czasem reakcji (a nie czasem usunięcia skutków), limity obsługiwanych incydentów w jednostce czasu oraz posiadanie przez dostawcę polisy ubezpieczeniowej cyber risk i certyfikacji (np. ISO 27001 czy świadectwa bezpieczeństwa przemysłowego).

### Takeaways
Ustawa o KSC nakłada rygorystyczne obowiązki dokumentacyjne, audytowe i raportowe, których niewdrożenie grozi dotkliwymi karami finansowymi dla organizacji i kadry zarządzającej. Dla firm dostarczających usługi IT i cyberbezpieczeństwa stanowi to dużą szansę rynkową w obszarze audytów, wdrożeń oraz usług SOC/MSSP, pod warunkiem precyzyjnego uregulowania kwestii odpowiedzialności, SLA i procedur w umowach.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - T. Janaszka & J. Salamon - Zastosowanie sztucznej inteligencji i uczenia maszynowego...
talks.teaser: Shows how machine learning forecasts link traffic and recommends prefix moves that keep its network balanced.
talks.summary:
The talk, given in Polish, covers how a network team uses machine learning to forecast traffic on its links to international operators. Each link has a capacity limit, and when too much traffic lands on one interface, packets are lost. Engineers had been balancing prefixes by hand and reacting after congestion appeared, so the team wanted a system that anticipates load instead.

The speakers explain their pipeline. Traffic is split into about 86 flows, and each flow is processed as an hourly time series with gaps filled in. For every flow, four forecasting methods run side by side: a library released by Facebook, a classic seasonal statistical model, a neural network model and a simple regression. Their outputs are combined with weights, and models are retrained when their fit, measured with R-squared, drops. Hyperparameters are tuned with a search that reuses results from earlier runs. Around 100 components exchange messages through a broker, and a master node schedules them over a shared distributed file system, so compute is used more evenly and new components can be added.

The forecasts, which look 72 hours ahead, feed a recommendation component that suggests which prefixes to move between interfaces, and an anomaly check flags overloaded links. The talk closes with possible extensions such as long-term capacity planning and closed-loop configuration. A key lesson is that data gaps and planned changes can distort models, so a clear procedure is needed to handle them. The speakers also advise defining anomalies together with operations and keeping engineers in control of recommendations.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Sebastian Pasternacki - Upside Down - przewrotna siła zmiany
talks.teaser: Offers a non-technical look at fear, time management and career change drawn from a veteran network engineer's experience.
talks.summary:
The talk is a non-technical presentation by a network engineer with about twenty years in the IT market. It begins with how his interest in electronics as a child led into networking, then through several employers and a move abroad to a cloud provider. He argues that the infrastructure underneath still matters even as networks become more software-defined, and that people often hold on to habits and decisions for too long.

The middle covers three areas. On skills, he describes his fear of failure and of public speaking, and recommends speaking on stage, even in-house, as a way to build confidence. On time, he describes protecting personal time, such as a quiet Monday morning, sleep and time for sport or meditation, and first setting a short priority list and then automating, eliminating or delegating the rest. On change, he suggests planning the big picture while expecting small deviations, and illustrates the point with overcoming a fear of heights on a walk in the Blue Mountains.

He closes by encouraging listeners to try new places, roles and challenges, to learn something new regularly, and to stop treating perceived barriers as fixed. The takeaway is that most limits are self-imposed and that acting earlier on career changes is usually worth it.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - dr hab Witold Mozgawa
talks.teaser: The lecture explains Poncelet's porism and its link to Benford's law and Fibonacci numbers in a popular math lecture.
talks.summary:
The lecture opens with Poncelet's porism, a geometry result from the early nineteenth century. Two nested circles are given, and a chain of tangent lines is built from a starting point on the outer circle. The speaker shows that when such a chain closes after a finite number of steps, it closes from every starting point. Animations cover triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons and star-shaped polygons, along with a three-circle version of the construction.

The talk then links this to Gelfand's question, an algebraic problem about the leading digits of successive powers of natural numbers, which is presented as analogous in structure. That leads to Benford's law, in which the leading digits of many natural and human-made datasets are not uniformly distributed. Examples include a 1972 check-fraud case where the digit pattern of the amounts exposed fabricated entries, and attempts to spot irregularities in published election and economic figures. The speaker also covers Fibonacci numbers, which appear in petal counts and seed spirals, and whose leading digits follow the same distribution.

The closing section touches on a related problem with elliptical billiards and a queueing question, then returns to the general principle that closure from one starting point implies closure from all of them. The lecture is deliberately non-technical and full of digressions, and it points listeners to two monographs and a film for deeper treatment.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Magdalena Figiel - Portfel kompetencji miękkich inżyniera (nie tylko sieciowego)
talks.teaser: Argues that soft skills like communication, empathy and leadership matter for every engineer, and shows how to build them.
talks.summary:
This talk, given in the non-technical track of a networking conference, argues that soft skills matter for engineers in every field, not only for network specialists. The speaker, a psychologist by training, starts from the familiar stereotype of the engineer 3.0: analytical, procedural, focused on tasks rather than people, and wary of change. She contrasts it with an engineer 4.0 who adapts quickly, is open to new situations and people, and can persuade and influence others. She also points out that automation does not yet match human emotional intelligence or creativity.

She frames soft skills as a mix of character and learned behaviour. They are harder to acquire than technical knowledge, but still learnable. Using a colleague's example, she describes a development plan that combined daily self-observation, a mentor and external events, and notes that a busy workload makes such plans hard to keep up. Her proposed model, a "mental wheelbarrow", rests on three elements: mindfulness, meaning full attention in conversations; empathy, meaning taking the other person's perspective for a while; and recognition with motivation, meaning noticing people's potential and trusting them with delegated work. Together they aim at communication and leadership, and she applies them to recruitment, working with sales or legal teams, and client meetings.

In the question session, an attendee asked how remote engineers can read nonverbal cues. She suggested accepting that body language is lost in chat, using video where possible, and adapting tone of voice on phone calls. She closed by asking the audience to try the approach in their daily work and to share feedback on the session.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - dr inż Michał Wągrowski - Oddziaływanie telefonii komórkowej na ludzi i środowisko
talks.teaser: Explains radio exposure physics, base station limits and health evidence behind the debate on mobile phone effects.
talks.summary:
Michał Wągrowski, who teaches telecommunications at AGH University of Science and Technology in Kraków, opens by noting that public debate about mobile phone radiation flares up whenever new technology arrives, as it does now with 5G. Operators argue that denser networks need looser exposure rules in Poland. He says he will not deliver a verdict, but will map the main areas of impact and show how each can be assessed.

Working upward from physics, he explains that a radio-band photon carries far less energy than visible light or ultraviolet, and that the only well-established biological effect of this non-ionising radiation is heating. He compares base stations with handsets, noting that power falls off steeply with distance, so a phone held to the head can expose its user to more than a nearby macro station. He covers how power control and indoor small cells change exposure, why animal and cell studies do not transfer cleanly to people, and why epidemiological reports on sleep, cancer or hypersensitivity remain weak evidence that often confuses correlation with cause. He also states that Polish limits are far stricter than the EU recommendation.

He closes with environmental costs such as the energy use of millions of base stations, their visual impact and the pressure of frequent device replacement. His takeaway is that the electromagnetic environment cannot be seen, so physics education and reliable scientific sources matter more than media headlines.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Sławomir Pietrzyk & Andrzej Miłkowski - Open RAN
talks.teaser: Explains how open, software-defined radio architecture could make 5G cheaper to deploy and better at handling interference.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by Sławomir Pietrzyk and Andrzej Miłkowski of a Polish company that builds wireless communication systems, argues that 5G should be treated as a new way of building networks rather than another layer of expensive equipment. They open with independent measurements from early 5G deployments in several countries, which show throughput from below 4G up to roughly three times higher, far short of the hundredfold gain once expected. Part of the gap, they note, is that the 4G networks used as the baseline were loaded while the new 5G cells carried little traffic.

They then describe the limits of the current model. A macro base station on a rooftop bundles the full radio stack from one vendor, and neighbouring sites compete for the same channels, causing interference at cell edges. Rollouts take 12 to 18 months, and signal penetration indoors is weak in modern glass buildings. Their alternative is a dense grid of small, low-power radio heads mounted on existing infrastructure such as lamp posts, buildings and bus stops. These connect to an edge server that runs most of the processing close to users, and a controller allocates radio resources across the heads cooperatively. Modelled cost comparisons favoured the small-cell approach, and an early rollout in South America was reported to cut costs by 50 to 70 percent compared with macro sites.

The speakers close by arguing that open interfaces, standardised through the O-RAN Alliance and the Telecom Infra Project, separate hardware from software so that operators, cities and smaller vendors can combine components. Small units also face lighter electromagnetic exposure limits and simpler permitting, which shortens deployment. Their takeaway is that open architecture is needed for 5G to deliver its promised gains, and that the industry has to move away from single-vendor procurement.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Panel dyskusyjny
talks.teaser: A ministerial and industry panel explores Polish 5G policy, spectrum auctions, factory automation, and operator business models.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with Poland’s digital ministry framing telecom rules as serving citizens, including people worried about electromagnetic fields and base stations. Officials describe amended telecom law, upcoming 5G spectrum auctions, coordination across ministries on environmental limits, and EU rollout targets for cities and transport corridors by 2025, plus cross‑border 700 MHz issues involving neighboring states.

Panelists then argue that 5G value is not mainly higher smartphone speeds but industrial and transport use cases—autonomous corridors, factories retooling lines with low latency and guaranteed quality, and hybrid fiber plus mobile coverage. Vendors stress new revenue models for operators, ecosystems pairing enterprises with carriers, software‑defined networks, dense small cells, and edge compute placed close to users. They note standards and standalone 5G mature over years, while today’s deployments often still resemble upgraded 4G.

The close turns to cost pressure, open interfaces, multi‑vendor integration, and examples such as open core trials. Speakers caution against treating 5G as a miracle cure, urge realistic business cases, and briefly contrast lawful intercept interfaces in 5G with older generations and unofficial surveillance tools.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Piotr Bienias - Fortinet SD-WAN czyli bezpieczeństwo i zapewnienie jakości usług w....
talks.teaser: Shows how Fortinet SD-WAN picks the best WAN link per traffic type while keeping firewall security on the same device.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces SD-WAN, a software-defined wide area network that spreads traffic over several WAN links and picks the best link for each flow. The speaker, a systems engineer at Fortinet, explains that the device makes this choice itself, following rules an administrator defines in advance. Link quality is measured with probes that report latency and packet loss, and each rule has target thresholds, for example a strict 50 ms limit for voice traffic. Strategies range from manual link selection and best-quality selection to picking the first link that meets its target.

The middle part covers steering and design options. Traffic can be matched by IP address, application, user group or marking, and well-known cloud services such as Office 365 can be recognised from a maintained list so they break out locally. Branch devices can be provisioned automatically: a unit is registered by serial number and pulls its configuration when it first reaches the internet, and a 3G/LTE extender can serve as a backup link. Central management covers policies, objects and real-time and historical link monitoring.

In the live demo, a client pinged a central network through two tunnels. When the averaged latency on the first link rose toward 100 ms, sessions moved to the second link without packet loss, and traffic was moved back once the first link's quality recovered. The takeaway is that dynamic path selection and a full security stack can run on one platform and be managed from one console.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Marcin Aronowski
talks.teaser: Gives an overview of 5G standards, the three core service pillars, and where real-world deployments stand.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At PLNOG23, Marcin Aronowski delivers an introductory talk examining the realities of 5G standardization, deployment status, and architectural shifts. Drawing from over 15 years of telecommunications experience across network operators and equipment vendors, Aronowski contrasts the theoretical promises defined in high-level standards (such as ITU-R IMT-2020 and 3GPP specifications) against practical operational constraints. He outlines what 5G means today from both end-user and operator perspectives, debunking unrealistic expectations around immediate latency drops and multi-gigabit speeds.

### Key Topics
- **Standardization Evolution & Pillars**: 5G high-level requirements evolved from initial ITU-R 2020 definitions (formalized around 2015) based on three primary pillars: massive machine-type communications (high device density), ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC), and enhanced mobile broadband (higher throughput). 3GPP addressed this incrementally, splitting Release 15 into Non-Standalone (NSA) to quickly leverage existing 4G EPC cores with new 5G New Radio (NR), followed by Standalone (SA) 5G core specifications, while leaving full URLLC enhancements for Releases 16 and 17.
- **Theoretical Targets vs. Real-World Deployments**: While 5G standards outline peak speeds up to 20 Gbps, latency under 1 ms, and densities of one million devices per square kilometer, current live production networks deliver more modest increments—typically 60 Mbps to near 2 Gbps depending on region and spectrum. Latency in current operational networks (such as SK Telecom trials) remains in the 18–19 millisecond range, comparable to optimized 4G LTE.
- **Radio and Spectrum Realities**: Deploying millimeter-wave (mmWave) spectrum (such as 26–28 GHz) allows wider channel bandwidths but introduces severe physical attenuation and limited range (often under 100 meters, unable to penetrate solid walls). Building out nationwide coverage exclusively on mmWave would require impractical base station densities.
- **Core Architectural Transformation**: Transitioning to full 5G requires operators to abandon legacy point-to-point hardware appliances in favor of service-based architectures (SBA), microservices, containers, network slicing, and edge computing to push processing closer to endpoints.

### Technical Details
- **Non-Standalone (NSA) Option 3x**: Most commercial network operators deploy Option 3x, anchoring control in existing 4G Evolved Packet Core (EPC) infrastructure with minor software updates to interface parameters and radio equipment.
- **Network Slicing & Edge Compute**: To physically reach sub-millisecond latencies, data processing cannot remain in centralized operator core networks; it must reside at the network edge. Network slicing enables dedicated radio and core resources per service rather than sharing a single pipe across all traffic types.
- **Open APIs and Microservices**: The 5G core adopts cloud-native microservices architecture and exposed APIs, shifting telecommunications closer to modern IT and developer platforms, though requiring operators to modernize their operational deployment cycles.

### Takeaways
- For end users, current 5G largely represents incremental throughput enhancements rather than a revolutionary leap in latency or novel services.
- True low latency requires edge infrastructure deployment and Standalone (SA) 5G cores, which are still evolving.
- Operators face major organizational and architectural hurdles, transitioning from rigid hardware-centric models to agile, software-defined containerized microservices.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - S. Grabski & M. Baczyński - Dlaczego SD-WAN bez lokalnego wyjścia do Internetu jest...
talks.teaser: Examines local Internet breakout with SD-WAN as cloud apps leave the datacenter, and how to preserve performance without weakening security.
talks.summary:
The session opens with how enterprise networks were built around a few costly, centralized Internet gateways carrying firewalls, antivirus, sandboxing, and SSL inspection. As applications and SaaS such as Office 365 move outside traditional datacenters, user traffic forced through those central breakouts degrades experience, especially for VPN users whose Internet use hairpins through the core.

The speakers argue that bolting equivalent security onto every SD-WAN branch appliance is economically unrealistic and creates a weaker attack surface than a full Internet gateway. They describe shifting to identity-based cloud security: user traffic is steered to a global cloud proxy via tunnels, agents, or SD-WAN API integration that can enable local Internet breakout while policy stays centralized in the cloud.

For practitioners, the takeaway is to plan direct or locally broken-out Internet paths for cloud workloads rather than relying on legacy hub-and-spoke egress, but not to treat the SD-WAN CPE alone as a substitute for a full security stack; orchestrate breakout with consistent cloud-enforced policy instead.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - dr Maciej Wielgus - Biblioteka EHT-imaging, regularized maximum likelihood i pierwszy...
talks.teaser: It traces Event Horizon Telescope petabyte capture, disk-and-plane logistics, and cloud pipelines that yield the first black-hole images.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens at the intersection of relativistic astrophysics and large-scale IT: a global collaboration must coordinate telescopes across continents, keep versioned scientific code coherent, and handle observation volumes that dwarf typical enterprise workloads. The speaker situates the famous M87 ring image in a longer story of rising resolution, theoretical shadows, and very long baseline interferometry that samples Fourier components instead of painting pixels directly.

The middle follows data from the antennas to results. Roughly five petabytes are recorded with atomic timing and custom recording hardware whose throughput grew exponentially. Moving bits from places like the South Pole still favors physical transport over usable wide-area links; correlation and atmospheric calibration then run on dedicated supercomputers and repeated cloud jobs in containers. Quality gates, review loops, and legacy Python stacks mirror production engineering, even though the product is calibrated visibilities rather than a commercial service.

The close focuses on imaging from sparse measurements via regularized maximum-likelihood methods in an open library, blind comparison across four independent teams, and consistency checks against simulations. Practitioners hear honest lessons on reproducibility, brittle tooling, and why sparse Fourier coverage makes prior assumptions decisive—plus how adding data tightens reconstructions.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Marcin Kuczera - Jak zacząć przygodę z serwerami OCP?
talks.teaser: Introduces open server hardware from the Open Compute Project, covering racks, power, cooling and buying a first system.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a telecom specialist, explains how his interest in open hardware grew out of searching for open-source firmware and designs. He argues that Polish companies should look at the Open Compute Project, because openly published specifications let several manufacturers build compatible equipment. That reduces dependence on a single vendor and on its paid support.

The middle of the talk walks through the physical design. He compares the 21-inch open rack with the classic 19-inch cabinet and shows a power shelf with shared busbars and battery backup modules. He explains why several large fans running at lower speed are more efficient than small fast ones, and he outlines liquid cooling options. Facility topics follow, including raised floors, outside-air cooling, humidity limits and load ratings, along with an adapter kit for fitting this gear into existing cabinets. He also shows a server he bought as a demo unit.

He closes by answering practical questions about cost, compatibility and buying used equipment. His takeaway is that anyone planning new servers should consider this hardware as an alternative to mainstream vendors, especially as energy prices rise. Open specifications make replacement parts interchangeable and let operators plan capacity and power around the rack design.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Andrzej Szulc - Zza biurka inżyniera IT - w góry wysokie. Wyprawa na Denali
talks.teaser: Traces a Denali mountaineering expedition from planning and cold-weather gear to teamwork and the climb.
talks.summary:
The talk follows the speaker's route from early hiking in Poland's mountains through the Alps, the Caucasus and Aconcagua to a plan for Denali, one of the harder peaks on the continental highest-summits list. It explains why the count differs depending on how Europe and Australia are defined, and why winter ascents of these peaks were a goal in their own right. Alaska is introduced through its size, its small population and its many glaciers and lakes, before the logistics of the expedition are laid out.

Preparation is described as a sum of small details, and fundraising is named as the hardest stage. Extreme cold, strong wind and heavy snowfall are presented as the first obstacles. Training included running laps around a city stadium and pulling a sled loaded with a tyre. On arrival, the team attended a mandatory briefing run by park rangers, which covered frostbite, fractures and falls into crevasses, and practised crevasse rescue until the response became almost automatic. Camp life meant melting snow for four to five litres of water a day, clearing snow from tents, and moving to higher camps in cooler hours.

At altitude the oxygen level is roughly a third of that at sea level, so climbers stop every 20 to 30 steps to breathe. Summit photos had to be taken quickly because of the cold. The speaker's takeaways were that experience reduces risk, people matter more than equipment, a long route is easier when split into short goals, and attention must stay high on the descent, when most accidents happen.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Attilla de Groot
talks.teaser: Network teams see how GitLab CI, Ansible, and virtual labs run NetQ checks so staging catches BGP and MTU faults before production updates.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why network changes still rely on slow, human-driven processes while servers and containers move faster, and why mistakes on shared infrastructure can have outsized impact even when vendor bugs are expected. It frames continuous integration as the familiar software pattern of automated validation before release, and continuous deployment as a higher bar that many network teams are not ready to trust.

The middle section walks through what automated network testing can cover, from linting infrastructure-as-code through limits of simple health checks, and why correlating state across a fabric matters more than a single BGP session flag. Cumulus VX is described as a Linux-kernel-backed virtual stand-in for real switches so Ansible-driven configs and packet behavior can be exercised without duplicating hardware. Common CI platforms and validation options are compared, with NetQ telemetry, correlation, and API-driven checks as the backbone of the live workflow.

A GitLab pipeline demo pushes an inventory change, rolls Ansible on staging-tagged runners, waits for convergence, and runs NetQ BGP, EVPN, and MTU checks over hundreds of links before auto-promotion. The close covers NetBox as a source of truth, RBAC approvals, branch-based Git flows, and audience questions on staging copies versus production and versioning NetBox for CI.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Michał Małyszko - Zmiany w PLIX (Equinix IX WA) - nowy PLIX
talks.teaser: Covers Equinix PLIX integration, Warsaw IX migration, new nodes, and peering portal changes for Polish network operators.
talks.summary:
The session explains how Poland’s PLIX internet exchange, operated as Equinix IX Warsaw, is aligning with Equinix’s global internet-exchange model after several years under Equinix ownership. The speaker describes a ongoing commercial and technical migration onto the worldwide Equinix platform, including short per-customer service windows while most participants remain passive on their side.

In Warsaw, the exchange runs redundant “colors” in separate fire zones across multiple halls, with hundreds of client ports and a large set of internal cross-connects. The migration team audited physical cabling, corrected records for more than four hundred ports, and kept rollback data so old and new fabrics can run in parallel without overloading temporary links between platforms. Work spans much of the year, adds a fully owned third Warsaw site and a Salomea node aimed toward Poznań, and retires an older Warsaw‑2 style footprint where traffic no longer justifies it.

Operators should expect required moves to new route servers before advanced peering features work uniformly, plus a redesigned portal for peering lists, alarms, and session visibility. The talk urges accurate PeeringDB listings, awareness of MANRS guidance, and growing reliance on RPKI-style origin validation as large content networks filter unsigned prefixes.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Belter & Bęben - Techniki przetwarzania danych na brzegu sieci (Fog/Edge/MEC Computing)
talks.teaser: Explains how moving cloud applications to the network edge cuts latency, and outlines a Polish MEC platform under construction.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces edge, fog and MEC computing as a way to move parts of cloud applications closer to users, such as base stations, network devices or end devices. The speaker first reviews cloud trends, citing strong yearly traffic growth and a shift toward public clouds. The drawbacks of distant cloud data centres follow: extra traffic on operator networks, latency, the risk of unavailability when connectivity fails, and security concerns.

The middle section explains the benefits of edge placement: lower latency for augmented reality and real-time control, less traffic in the core, and longer battery life when heavy processing is offloaded from a phone. The speaker notes that the terms are defined differently by different bodies. The proposed system has an edge server, a platform that exposes operator information such as user location and radio conditions through an API, an orchestrator that chooses where each application runs, and mobility support so applications follow users. Standards work by ETSI began in 2017, while commercial offerings are often closed to third-party developers. Open-source projects are adapting virtual machine and container tooling to this model.

The project is national and covers new server hardware, the platform, an application repository and open northbound interfaces so operators and developers can connect. The speaker expects a first version to run a basic application within about six months and invites developers and operators to collaborate and test prototypes. The takeaway is that operator-hosted edge computing depends on open, standardised interfaces, and much of it is still in development.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Jarosław Zieliński - AI w praktyce - jak zachęciłem sztuczną inteligencję do współpracy
talks.teaser: Walks through AWS managed AI services and demos a forecasting workflow on historical availability data.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the question of how to put artificial intelligence to practical use inside an existing IT environment. The speaker first describes a hybrid setup: an on-premises datacenter connected by a dedicated fiber link to AWS, with regions and availability zones, logging and monitoring attached to each component, and DNS and certificates placed in front of the public-facing application. He then explains that AWS offers AI at three levels: ready-made services for image, document, translation, speech and forecasting tasks, machine learning frameworks for building models, and infrastructure such as GPU servers.

The demonstration covers two cases. The first is a text-to-speech service that reads typed input aloud in several languages, set up with a single API call. The second is a forecasting service fed with six months of historical availability records loaded from a CSV file. The speaker explains that the service can select an algorithm automatically, train a model and produce predictions for the following 31 days, with 10th, 50th and 90th percentile values. One result went above 100 percent because of a problem with February's day count in the data, so that month was left out and the forecast was checked against the average for the period.

The talk closes with a short audience quiz on AWS basics and a question-and-answer session. The main takeaway is that the forecasting workflow needs little specialist knowledge, while programming and infrastructure experience make it easier to follow the model pipeline and to apply it in daily operations.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Grzegorz Siewruk - O tym jak (nie)łatwo dodać Sec do Dev(Sec)Ops w świecie telco?
talks.teaser: Maps telco CI/CD delivery, major supply-chain compromises, and where automated security gates fit beside periodic expert review.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames security integration for telecommunications organizations that ship software through highly automated DevOps pipelines. After tracing how waterfall planning gave way to frequent releases, microservices, and the classic developer–operations split, the speaker walks through a typical path from ticket to production: commit, quality checks, build, unit tests, integration or regression stages, canary rollout, and monitoring. The chain is only as strong as its tests, yet most pipeline tools target developers and rarely embed dedicated security verification at each step.

Automated vulnerability and dynamic scans are necessary but insufficient when attackers focus on application logic flaws and on compromising the delivery path itself. The talk recounts widely reported supply-chain cases such as tampered CCleaner builds affecting millions of users and signed malicious ASUS update packages, then describes an internal incident where forgotten credentials and excessive repository privileges on legacy integration infrastructure enabled attempted malicious code injection—caught because an approver noticed an unexpected change outside planned work.

Practical lessons emphasize meeting developers where they work: actionable findings instead of long PDF reports, team-specific workflows, static analysis before merge, and developer-run smoke tests with realistic authentication on non-production environments. Dynamic scanning struggles at microservice scale without rich test data. The closing proposal adds a centralized pre-production gate that aggregates scan outcomes, configuration benchmarks such as CIS-oriented Kubernetes checks, and policy on critical findings, while reserving deeper manual testing for scheduled intervals rather than every release.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Maciej Lelusz - Disaster Recovery Center w chmurze czy lokalnie?
talks.teaser: Compares cloud and on-premises disaster recovery for a client case, covering recovery objectives, replication and cost.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how a company decides where its disaster recovery environment should live: rented cloud capacity or a colocated site with its own hardware. The speaker, drawing on years of data center design, starts with what an outage costs a business and argues that planning has to begin with an inventory of applications. Each application has an owner who sets how much data loss and how much downtime is tolerable. Two measures frame the discussion: the acceptable amount of lost data and the time needed to bring systems back.

Next come the recovery strategies, ranging from periodic backups copied off site, through a pilot-light setup with a minimal running core, to fully running duplicate environments that switch over within seconds at the highest cost. Replication can be synchronous or asynchronous, and the speaker warns that replication is not a backup, because corrupted or encrypted data gets copied too. The case study walks through sizing a sample environment, connecting the two sites, handling licensing and Windows activation, and comparing costs against buying and colocating hardware, with the cloud option judged reasonable for this client.

The closing part gives practical steps: start with a small set of applications, prove that recovery works through test runs, and keep network and DNS configuration documented so the setup can be rebuilt. The speaker presents cloud services as a strong tool for specific purposes rather than a universal answer.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Marcin Marciniak - What can computer science learn from the railways?
talks.teaser: Draws lessons from Polish railway disasters to improve change management, testing and automated response in IT.
talks.summary:
The talk compares railway safety history with modern IT operations, arguing that many Polish rail accidents came from skipped procedures, unclear signalling and untested changes. The speaker walks through several past incidents, including a 1980 collision in which a driver entered a route despite a red light and no radio stop existed, and a 2009 Białystok disaster tied to overworked staff and circumvented working-time limits. Each case led to concrete fixes such as radio stop systems, brake testing and automatic train control.

From these cases he draws parallels to computing. He recommends clear procedures, access control, and an emergency stop that can isolate a system, such as a virtual machine that suddenly becomes exposed to the internet. Changes should be tested first in an environment identical to production, with defined success criteria and prepared rollback steps, and automated checks should flag misconfigurations before they take effect.

The closing advice is that new tools need staff training, and that subcontractors should follow the same change and test procedures. The practical takeaway is to plan for failure and reversal before a change goes live, since intervention is only realistic at that point.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - T. Charewicz & P. Pieprzycki - Nasza droga w migracji z DC do chmury publicznej
talks.teaser: Walks through a media company's move from its own data centre to public cloud, covering accounts, guardrails and networking.
talks.summary:
The talk tells the story of a media company that ran its own data centre for about a decade, after more than twenty years of hosting its sites, and then moved toward public AWS. The speakers explain the reasons: an existing private cloud, a disaster-recovery copy already held in AWS Ireland, and a plan to sell the server room and focus on publishing. Before building anything, the team negotiated with the provider and ordered physical links to its Kraków site, a process that took several months, and planned how users would sign in through the organisation's identity system.

The middle section covers account design in AWS Organizations. Accounts are grouped into organisational units, and quotas on API calls and resources push large estates toward many accounts. The company split accounts by product and kept separate ones for logs and security monitoring, keeping the management account out of daily work. Service control policies act as the first guardrail, such as limiting activity to EU regions. Control Tower was judged unable to meet their customisation needs at the time, so they built a template-based landing zone defined as code, reusing public modules and patching some of them. Networking used public, private and isolated tiers, and a routing issue across two active links once cut off S3 access even though one link still worked.

The closing part gives practical takeaways: plan the migration and keep the wider organisation informed, treat the landing zone as something to keep evolving rather than a one-off build, define everything as code, and grant actions explicitly in policies instead of relying on broad denials.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Marcin Ślęczek - Automatyka sieci oraz chmur z rozwiązaniami Cisco Systems i Red Hat
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning PLNOG23 - Marcin Ślęczek - Automatyka sieci oraz chmur z rozwiązaniami Cisco Systems i Red Hat.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Tomasz Brol - IoT - Co mogło pójść nie tak?
talks.teaser: Explores how connected household gadgets could shape security and privacy risks over the next decade, with historical examples.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how Internet of Things devices could change security and privacy over the next decade. The speaker starts by defining IoT as physical objects that collect and exchange data over telecom networks, often without any user interaction. He then traces the history of a Coca-Cola vending machine at Carnegie Mellon, which was wired to the network in the early 1980s so people could check whether cold drinks were loaded before walking over. From there he compares predictions from a 2009 broadband panel with today's reality, where fridges report door openings, cameras and toys send data to vendor clouds, and a 2016 worm spread through Linux-based devices such as cameras and routers. He also describes a destructive worm that wiped flash memory on more than ten million devices, a video doorbell whose footage was posted online in a neighbourhood group, and a talking doll that streamed audio from a child's room to a cloud service.

The middle section moves to physical risk. He points to connected medical imaging, where scan data could be altered without anyone noticing because few checks confirm integrity, and to power grid instability if many connected meters were switched at once. He notes that vendors often rush products to market and skip audits and supply chain checks, and that forecasts put the number of connected devices past 90 billion.

He closes with policy ideas, such as requiring vendors to provide security updates for a set period and publishing firmware when a product reaches end of life. He encourages the audience to weigh convenience against these risks before the next wave of gadgets arrives.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Piotr Strzyżewski
talks.teaser: Tracks the shrinking IPv4 pool and the RIPE NCC policy proposals meant to ration what remains.
talks.summary:
The talk is a status update on the IPv4 address pool handled by the RIPE NCC, the regional registry for Europe and the surrounding region. The speaker recalls years of predictions that IPv4 would run out, then shows a chart of the free pool, which fell from just over five million addresses a year earlier to just over one million at the time of the talk. Membership has grown quickly since the final /8 allocation procedure began in September 2012, and the association now counts roughly 25,000 members.

The middle of the talk walks through community policy proposals. Topics include publishing the physical addresses of resource holders, a stricter check on contact email addresses that requires a human reply, and a proposal that would add an IPv4 waiting list and change the default allocation size. Some proposals stalled without consensus. The speaker also explains options for setting aside reserves from the surplus created by membership fees, and notes that new members may have to wait for space.

The speaker then turns to the transfer market, where buyers of address blocks need due diligence, and where company and sole-trader membership, along with poorly documented past transfers, create legal and administrative problems. The practical takeaway is that IPv4 scarcity now shapes both the governance of the registry and what address space costs to obtain, so organisations should plan for waits and for the transfer process.

talks.title: PLNOG23 - Jihad Tohme - How to build and implement an effective ICT infrastructure based on SDx
talks.teaser: Explains how software-defined networking and SD-WAN replace legacy branch and data center designs in enterprise rollouts.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by sorting out the terminology around software-defined infrastructure, from software-defined data centers, storage and compute down to software-defined networking. The speaker frames the goal as reducing manual operator intervention, so that changes which once took weeks of planning and months to apply can be made in hours, with automated failover and policy-based control that hides the physical layer.

The networking section compares legacy three-tier data centers, with blocking spanning tree paths and firewalls at fixed points, to a spine-and-leaf fabric with non-blocking equal-cost multipath and a split between data plane, control plane and application tier. It then moves to SD-WAN, where an overlay network runs over any mix of MPLS, internet or LTE links. In one project, the speaker described moving from MPLS to internet links without reconfiguring the overlay. Application-aware routing selects links based on packet loss, latency and jitter, and bandwidth can be reserved for critical applications. Local internet breakout, a carrier-neutral point for orchestration in multi-cloud designs, and encryption complete the picture.

The speaker outlines a migration path, from a hybrid MPLS plus internet design to a fully internet-based one, and a delivery method running from design workshops through proof of concept, onboarding and handover. Vendor selection used a lab with scored tests. Two large rollouts were described, one of about 1200 branches and another of around 800 sites spread across regions. The main takeaway is that the model shifts focus from IP addresses and devices to applications and user experience, while cutting hardware and connectivity costs.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Przemysław Dziel - Migration of GPON networks to 10G PON
talks.teaser: Explains how GPON access networks can move to 10G PON on the same fiber, coexisting with existing services.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses how fibre access operators can upgrade from GPON to 10G PON without replacing their passive optical infrastructure. The speaker begins with the rising bandwidth demand from video, cloud and file-sharing services, citing forecasts of steep per-subscriber growth, and reviews how access technologies have evolved from DSL-era networks to GPON. The 10G PON standard is presented as the accepted successor, chosen because it reuses the same fibre plant and much of the same equipment.

The middle section focuses on coexistence. Because 10G PON and GPON use different wavelength bands, a filter can be inserted so both systems run on one fibre network under one management system. The speaker compares four ways to install that filter and presents adding a shelf in the cabinet as the most practical. Power budget classes, wavelength plans and cost differences are also covered, with 10G PON optics still many times more expensive than GPON parts. Longer-term options such as 40G PON and a wavelength-based approach are outlined as more disruptive paths.

The closing part reviews vendor readiness, operator trials with large telecom companies, and a commercial four-port 10G PON card planned for 2012. The main takeaway is to choose platforms that support future upgrades, so that fibre investments stay protected over the long term.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Piotr Wojciechowski
talks.teaser: Przypadki z życia multicastów explores PLNOG8 - Piotr Wojciechowski.
talks.summary:
The session looks at multicast traffic in operator networks, where content such as TV streams is delivered from one source to many subscribers. The speaker starts with the basics a diagnostician needs: how receivers join a group, how the source and receivers connect through a distribution tree, and why the RPF check decides whether traffic is accepted on an interface. Tree types, the role of the rendezvous point and the designated router, and the timers that expire when group membership is not refreshed are also introduced.

The middle of the talk walks through reading multicast routing and group state output on a router, following the path hop by hop from the receiver back toward the source. Several failure cases are covered: no receiver registration, an interface that is not active, a broken or asymmetric route that makes the RPF check fail, and duplicated packets during short-lived disruptions or line card overloads. The speaker recommends checking each hop along the path, since a fault can sit on any router.

The closing part summarises a checklist for practitioners: confirm multicast is enabled on every device, verify RPF and routing consistency, check group state on each interface, and make sure receivers have actually registered. The session was presented as a taster for a longer, more advanced multicast discussion.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Piotr Głaska - Rozwiązania sieciowe w Data Center - trendy i rekomendacje
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in PLNOG8 - Piotr Głaska - Rozwiązania sieciowe w Data Center - trendy i rekomendacje.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Paweł Wachelka
talks.teaser: Explains how 802.1X network access control works, from RADIUS authentication flows to port timers and tuning.
talks.summary: Paweł Wachelka walks PLNOG8 through IEEE 802.1X network access control: supplicants on workstations and IoT gear, authenticators on switches and APs, RADIUS backends tied to Active Directory, guest VLAN separation, and scaling port configuration beyond flat ACLs when hundreds of device types join the LAN.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Paweł Białasiewicz - Rozwiązywanie problemów sieciowych za pomocą sniffera
talks.teaser: Shows how packet capture and analysis resolve production network problems, using two real troubleshooting case studies.
talks.summary:
Paweł Białasiewicz presents a session, given in Polish, on using packet analysis to troubleshoot problems in production networks. He focuses on data centre and multi-party environments, where application teams, carriers and external clients often blame each other and console checks give little certainty. The core argument is that a well-placed capture can settle questions quickly and should not be treated as a last resort.

He walks through how to capture traffic. Mirror ports are easy to set up but can alter timestamps, sit low in a device's priority list and drop packets under load. Network taps give an exact copy of the traffic, and intelligent taps can pre-filter high-speed links. Knowing the physical and logical topology is essential to choose the right capture point, and filtering early avoids drowning in data. Flow views and time-delta columns help make analysis faster.

Two cases illustrate the method. In the first, a black-box client application saw a small share of connections take far longer than normal; captures on both sides of the path showed that one field value stalled processing on the application server, which gave the application team enough evidence to act. In the second, slow data transfers between two database servers showed a regular pattern of small batches separated by pauses, which traced back to a recent application change. The speaker closes by recommending a standard incident report template, automating repeat captures, and building experience, since each analysis gets faster.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Panel dyskusyjny - Styczniowe ataki na polskie serwery rządowe. Czy rekomendacje MAC są...
talks.teaser: A panel contrasts January Polish government outages with ministerial portal rules and actionable hardening guidance.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with a concise recap of widespread availability problems that hit Polish public-sector websites around late January, including parliament, ministries, and the prime minister’s portal, amid heavy public interest tied to ACTA-related protests. Participants contrast that wave with a later government report and unsigned ministerial guidelines aimed at protecting information portals in the national administration domain.

Panelists walk through those recommendations and find many items either technically unclear or hard to implement, including ideas around restricting anonymity networks, vague minimum-bandwidth notions, and mixed guidance spanning network and application layers. They argue the January incidents often involved legitimate-looking page loads and browser-driven traffic rather than exotic attack tooling, and that blocking foreign countries would not address traffic that was predominantly domestic in published connection statistics.

The conversation closes on constructive paths: separate policy-level goals from updatable technical specifications, tier sites by criticality, consider centralized hosting and static failover for brochure-like pages, and improve procurement so security requirements survive price-driven tenders. Several panelists commit to community drafting of more actionable public guidance and continued dialogue with administration stakeholders.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Norbert Gulczyński - 100G w sieciach szkieletowych i miejskich
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding PLNOG8 - Norbert Gulczyński - 100G w sieciach szkieletowych i miejskich.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Michał Pyter
talks.teaser: Physical infrastructure examines PLNOG8 - Michał Pyter.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Prezentacja Michała Pytera z firmy APC (obecnie Schneider Electric), wygłoszona na konferencji PLNOG8, koncentruje się na efektywności energetycznej oraz optymalizacji infrastruktury w nowoczesnych serwerowniach i centrach danych. Prelegent wyjaśnia, że sprzęt IT zużywa jedynie ułamek dostarczanej energii na faktyczne operacje obliczeniowe, podczas gdy reszta energii rozprasza się w postaci ciepła i strat na infrastrukturze. Wskaźnik PUE pokazuje, że blisko połowa energii w centrum danych może być tracona poza samymi serwerami, z czego nawet około 40% pochłania klimatyzacja i odprowadzanie ciepła. Głównym celem optymalizacji jest obniżenie kosztów operacyjnych poprzez racjonalne zarządzanie chłodzeniem i zasilaniem gwarantowanym.

### Key Topics
- Efektywność energetyczna i współczynnik PUE w serwerowniach.
- Zarządzanie przepływem powietrza: podział na zimne i ciepłe korytarze oraz izolacja stref.
- Zastosowanie klimatyzacji rzędowej (in-row) i korzyści z podnoszenia dopuszczalnych temperatur pracy.
- Chłodzenie naturalne (free-cooling) z użyciem wody lodowej i zróżnicowanie pracy kompresora w zależności od pór roku.
- Wykorzystanie obiegu zamkniętego (np. system Ecoflair / chłodzenie powietrzem zewnętrznym bez wymiany powietrza serwerowni).
- Architektura i dobór zasilaczy awaryjnych UPS: zasilanie rozproszone, centralne oraz systemy modułowe.

### Technical Details
- **Przepływ powietrza i izolacja:** Kluczową regułą jest niedopuszczenie do sytuacji, w której ciepłe powietrze wydmuchiwane z tyłu jednej szafy trafia na front kolejnej. Brak paneli zaślepiających w pustych miejscach szafy serwerowej powoduje cyrkulację ciepłego powietrza na przód szafy (zjawisko opisane m.in. w APC White Paper nr 44). Uszczelnienie podłogi technicznej i rekonfiguracja szaf mogą pozwolić na wyłączenie nadmiarowych jednostek klimatyzacyjnych.
- **Klimatyzatory rzędowe i gradient temperatur:** Klimatyzacja rzędowa pobiera gorące powietrze bezpośrednio z tyłu szaf. Przykładem jest klimatyzator na wodę lodową (wspomniany AC3, gdzie woda wpływa w temperaturze 6°C, a wypływa przy 15°C). Podniesienie dopuszczalnej temperatury z tyłu szafy z 29°C do 35°C (przy 21°C na froncie) pozwala zwiększyć moc chłodniczą tego samego klimatyzatora z 14 kW do 18 kW bez zwiększania zużycia energii elektrycznej przez samo urządzenie.
- **Free-cooling:** Wykorzystanie chłodzenia naturalnego w okresie jesienno-zimowym pozwala wyłączyć lub ograniczyć pracę kompresora (np. praca na 50% lub całkowite wyłączenie zimą). Dla instalacji 800 kW w warunkach warszawskich oszczędności z wdrożenia obwodu free-coolingowego oszacowano na około 130 tysięcy złotych rocznie.
- **Jakość powietrza:** W systemach wentylacji pośredniej powietrzem zewnętrznym istotne jest unikanie zasysania zanieczyszczeń (np. dymu z palonych liści, co mogłoby wywołać alarm pożarowy). Schneider Electric stosuje systemy o obiegu zamkniętym (np. wspomniany Ecobreeze/Ecostruxure koncept), gdzie powietrze z serwerowni oddaje ciepło na zewnątrz bez wymiany masy powietrza.
- **Systemy UPS:** Nowoczesne UPS-y o podwójnej konwersji osiągają sprawność rzędu 96–97%. Producenci oferują tryby ECO osiągające 99% sprawności, wiążą się one jednak z przełączeniem rzędu 10 milisekund w razie awarii sieci, co bywa nieakceptowalne przy kluczowej infrastrukturze. Częstym błędem jest przewymiarowanie centralnego UPS-a pracującego jedynie przy 20–30% obciążenia, co pogarsza sprawność. Rozwiązaniem są układy równoległe oraz skalowalne UPS-y modułowe (umożliwiające rozbudowę np. do 4 MW).

### Takeaways
Optymalizacja centrum danych powinna rozpoczynać się na etapie projektowym i opierać na dyscyplinie termicznej: bezwzględnym rozdzieleniu strefy zimnej i ciepłej, uszczelnieniu szaf i podłóg oraz odważnym, kontrolowanym podnoszeniu temperatur nawiewu i wywiewu. W zakresie zasilania kluczem jest elastyczne skalowanie mocy UPS (np. modularność) zamiast statycznego przewymiarowywania urządzeń, co zapobiega stratom energii i nieuzasadnionym kosztom inwestycyjnym.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Maciej Eckstein & Dominik Kuc - Radiolinia - Siklu EtherHaul™ 1200L v2 i 1200
talks.teaser: Presents a compact all-in-one radio link for operators, covering throughput options, low licensing costs and built-in switching.
talks.summary:
Maciej Eckstein and Dominik Kuc present the Siklu EtherHaul 1200L v2 and 1200 point-to-point radio links, positioned as products for telecom operators. The unit is fully integrated, with its antenna built into the housing, which measures about 26 cm and weighs around 3 kg. The speakers suggest it for backhaul where fibre is absent or not yet laid, and for customers who need high-capacity connections.

The middle of the talk covers capacity and cost. The link uses a single radio channel with time-division duplexing, and bandwidth can be split symmetrically or in a 75/25 ratio. The speakers compare licensing costs, quoting about 150 zł per year in a large city against about 4,000 zł per year for a conventional microwave link. The lower-capacity model can be upgraded by licence to full gigabit. Hardware includes four ports, two of them combo gigabit Ethernet, a built-in switch, a 20 to 60 V power input and a draw of about 20 W. Traffic management offers eight queues with several scheduling methods, and a configuration rollback restores the last working setup if no key is pressed for 30 seconds. A tester screenshot showed latency staying low under overload.

The closing part addresses weather resilience and reach. Adaptive modulation is said to keep the link up over about 2 km in heavy rain, with a recommended reach of roughly 1.5 to 1.75 km for the integrated antenna. A 60 cm antenna option is available for longer distances, though it is harder to install. The speakers also compare a smaller unit from another vendor that dropped out in heavy rain. They close with support, planning, installation and leasing options, leaving the takeaway that the link suits short to medium distances where installation speed and cost matter most.
