talks.title: PLNOG8 - Jan Zorz - Wizja i kompromisy w przestrzeni mechanizmów przejściowych...
talks.teaser: Compares IPv6 transition mechanisms by progress toward IPv6, state placement and exit strategy for operators.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why IPv6 adoption has been slow, and argues that the core problem is that IPv6 is incompatible with IPv4 on the wire, so a simple switch-over is not possible. The speaker points to small adoption figures in the graphs shown and a shrinking IPv4 pool, and notes that the RIPE pool could run out at any time with no reliable date. The material is a summary of a panel the speaker chaired at an IPv6 summit, with supporting views from other well-known figures in the field.

The middle of the talk sorts transition mechanisms along two axes: whether they make real progress toward IPv6 or only regress to older designs, and whether they keep state in the core or stay stateless. Tunnels such as 6rd and L2TP are described as useful in places but often misused and likely to fade away. Address-sharing approaches such as MAP are contrasted with CGN, and NAT64 is presented as a strategy that mobile operators are already using. The speaker warns that a CGN built without an exit strategy will never be removed, and calls stateless deterministic NAT a regression choice that does not help IPv6 deployment, though it may be acceptable as a short-term fix.

The closing advice is to prefer mechanisms that carry IPv4 inside IPv6, remove IPv4 from the access network, keep state at the edge, and move in dual-stack steps toward an IPv6-only network. Operators should avoid adding complexity they cannot troubleshoot, and should define an exit plan before investing in large boxes. A Q&A exchange with a vendor representative covered the stateful versus stateless trade-off and the practical need to keep services running while transitioning.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Ivan Pepelnjak - Data Center Fabrics - What Really Matters
talks.teaser: Shows how leaf-spine fabrics built from existing switches can offer equidistant, non-blocking bandwidth across a data center.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at what data center networks need to do well as application traffic increasingly moves between servers inside the facility rather than to outside users. The speaker argues that the useful goals are equal bandwidth between endpoints within a bounded domain and lossless transport for storage and backup traffic, and that these can be reached with conventional gear and no new protocols.

The core design is a leaf-spine (three-stage Clos) fabric, where every top-of-rack switch connects to every spine switch. Equal-cost multipath then gives several paths between any two edge switches, with oversubscription acceptable at the edge but not in the core. Layer 3 routing avoids spanning tree, and the speaker works through port-count examples using commodity switches and larger high-end chassis, a five-stage variant for bigger scale, and a vendor fabric that performs a single lookup at ingress. He cautions against stretching one VLAN across a whole data center, citing limits on hosts per VLAN, VMware cluster and vMotion sizes, and the broadcast and MAC-table problems of large layer 2 domains.

The closing discussion covers the risk that a fabric managed as one device makes configuration mistakes easier, and the limits of current zero-touch provisioning. It also covers subscriber access networks, where broad layer 2 domains cause broadcast and security problems. The takeaway for practitioners is to build large networks on layer 3, keep layer 2 domains to roughly a thousand hosts, and add port-level controls and automation as safeguards.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Tomasz Paszkowski - Rozwiązania wirtualnych systemów dyskowych w chmurach obliczeniowych...
talks.teaser: Explains how a distributed open-source storage cluster supplies cloud VM block volumes, covering monitors, replication and placement.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the limits of local disks on cloud virtual machines: data is lost when an instance goes away, so persistent volumes are needed. The speaker surveys the storage options around a cloud platform, including block volumes, an image repository, object storage and static file serving, then focuses on an open-source distributed storage system with no single point of failure and no central lookup database.

The middle section explains the building blocks. Monitor daemons keep the cluster map and placement policy, and a majority of them must be reachable before the cluster serves reads and writes, which is why an odd number is recommended. Each disk runs its own daemon, which isolates failures from the rest of the cluster. Data is placed by a hash-based algorithm, so clients compute where objects live without consulting a central database. Writes can be acknowledged once they reach a journal or only after they reach the disk, and SSD journals speed up the first mode. Two copies are the usual default, and extra copies reduce throughput. Volumes are split into 4 MB objects spread across placement groups.

The closing part covers practical deployment. The speaker suggests at least two disks per server and 10 Gigabit Ethernet with jumbo frames, and notes that network and disk throughput, rather than CPU, usually set the limit. Block devices can be attached through a kernel driver or accessed directly by the virtualization layer, and capacity grows by adding servers. The Q&A touched on stability of the newer features, recovery after a node failure, and how volumes map onto objects.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Wojciech Ehrenfeld
talks.teaser: Chmura- realna szansa na zmianę investigates PLNOG8 - Wojciech Ehrenfeld.
talks.summary:
Wojciech Ehrenfeld opens his PLNOG talk, a deliberately non-technical session, by framing public cloud as an evolution rather than a revolution. He argues that businesses gain the most when they know their own products, processes and service requirements well enough to decide where each one should run. He compares the choice to airline fares: some services need comfort and guaranteed support, while others can tolerate delays for a much lower price.

He then describes how operations work is changing. Virtualisation, automation and closer collaboration between operators and developers replace the familiar cycle of building, running and maintaining systems. Routine tasks such as swapping a disk or configuring a host lose value, while storage keeps getting cheaper and skills shift toward financial management, information security and configuration management. He contrasts an on-site server room, where a small team can fix problems quickly, with a provider outage, where the main options are reading the contract and waiting.

He closes by noting that the cloud will not replace every server room and that hybrid models may suit some workloads. Network engineers and administrators, he suggests, should broaden beyond a single specialisation. Even with a strong contract, the company remains responsible for planning, recovery procedures and a crisis plan. The takeaway is to understand your services and their availability and cost needs before moving anything.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Gaweł Mikołajczyk - Securing the Cloud Infrastructure - from Hypervisor to the Edge
talks.teaser: Walks through securing cloud infrastructure, from virtual switches and segmentation to identity-based access at the network edge.
talks.summary:
This Polish-language session looks at how to secure cloud infrastructure, treating the cloud as virtualized datacenter resources, operator services and security services delivered from the cloud. The speaker argues there is no single definition of the cloud and that security is a process rather than a product. He splits the subject into three areas, starting with the datacenter's server and virtualization layer, then access to cloud services, then security offered as a service.

The central problem he describes is visibility. Traffic between two virtual machines on the same host passes through a virtual switch that network administrators cannot see, so segmentation and inspection have to be built into that layer. He presents a virtual switch with security profiles that bind network configuration to rules, a virtual firewall for east-west filtering, and a larger hardware firewall for high-volume traffic, noting that a virtual firewall consumes host CPU. He also covers identity-based context, where certificate-based authentication and device posture checks feed group tags that hardware switches enforce across the network. A cloud-delivered filtering service that proxies web traffic is shown as another example.

He closes by stressing that server, network and security teams must cooperate, since organizational silos block designs like these. The practical takeaways are that hardware enforcement is more efficient than purely virtual enforcement, that identity context can drive policy, and that vendor reference architecture documents are available for study.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Piotr VaGla Waglowski - Net neutrality i odpowiedzialność za przesyłane treści
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in PLNOG8 - Piotr VaGla Waglowski - Net neutrality i odpowiedzialność za przesyłane treści.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Podczas wystąpienia na konferencji PLNOG8 prelegent omawia zagadnienie neutralności sieci (net neutrality) oraz prawnej odpowiedzialności pośredników i przedsiębiorców telekomunikacyjnych za przesyłane treści. Analiza skupia się na relacjach rynkowych, modelach biznesowych operatorów, orzecznictwie polskich organów regulacyjnych i sądów, a także prawie unijnym regulującym obowiązki dostawców dostępu do sieci i hostingu.

### Key Topics
- **Definicja i rozumienie neutralności sieci**: Postulat równego, niedyskryminacyjnego dostępu użytkowników i abonentów do zasobów i usług internetowych bez nieuzasadnionej degradacji ruchu.
- **Wyzwania techniczne i rynkowe**: Ograniczenia techniczne sieci (np. przeciążenia w sieciach mobilnych na stadionach, specyfika lokalizacji takich jak piwnice czy Bory Tucholskie), konieczność zarządzania ruchem w celu walki ze spamem, złośliwym oprogramowaniem oraz atakami DDoS na strony rządowe.
- **Polskie decyzje regulacyjne i orzecznictwo**: Działania Prezesa Urzędu Komunikacji Elektronicznej (UKE) oraz wyroki Sądu Ochrony Konkurencji i Konsumentów (SOKiK) z lat 2008 i 2010 dotyczące degradacji i dyskryminacyjnego kierowania ruchem w odniesieniu do portali internetowych na rynku dostępu do sieci.
- **Europejskie orzecznictwo i blokowanie treści**: Kwestie nakazów blokowania dostępu do określonych zasobów (m.in. w kontekście prawa autorskiego) oraz unijna zasada braku obowiązku ogólnego nadzoru i prewencyjnego filtrowania całego ruchu na koszt dostawcy.
- **Wyłączenia odpowiedzialności pośrednika**: Ramy prawne wynikające z prawa o świadczeniu usług drogą elektroniczną (oraz unijnej dyrektywy o handlu elektronicznym), w szczególności warunki wyłączenia odpowiedzialności dostawcy telekomunikacyjnego za przesyłane dane.

### Technical Details
- **Art. 12 ustawy o świadczeniu usług drogą elektroniczną (transmisja danych / mere conduit)**: Usługodawca świadczący usługi transmisji lub dostępu do publicznej sieci nie ponosi odpowiedzialności za treści przesyłanych danych wyłącznie wtedy, gdy spełnia łącznie warunki: nie jest inicjatorem (autorem) przekazu, nie wybiera odbiorcy przekazu oraz nie modyfikuje informacji zawartych w przekazie.
- **Zarządzanie pakietami a modyfikacja treści**: Prelegent stawia pytanie problemowe dotyczące praktyk operatorskich: czy ingerencja w pakiety, ich trasy, priorytetyzację lub modyfikacja sposobu komunikacji (np. nakładanie dodatkowych warstw/nagłówków) może zostać zinterpretowana jako wybór odbiorcy lub modyfikacja przekazu, co potencjalnie unieważniałoby ustawowe wyłączenie odpowiedzialności (safe harbor).

### Takeaways
Przedsiębiorcy telekomunikacyjni stają w obliczu napięcia między techniczną i biznesową potrzebą zarządzania ruchem a wymogami prawnymi dotyczącymi neutralności sieci. Ingerowanie w ruch sieciowy lub próby wdrażania modeli różnicujących jakość usług mogą nie tylko naruszać zasady uczciwej konkurencji według regulatorów, ale także rodzić ryzyko prawne: utratę statusu neutralnego pośrednika i narażenie się na bezpośrednią odpowiedzialność cywilną za przesyłane przez użytkowników treści.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Artur Pupin & Cezary Terepka - 10GPON - przyszłość i rzeczywistość
talks.teaser: Maps FTTH growth pressures and shows how unified access platforms and 10G PON address capacity, QoS, and low-cost GPON migration.
talks.summary:
The session opens with vendor and distributor positioning around telecom access equipment, then shifts to the challenges Polish and European fiber operators face as FTTH expands alongside legacy copper. Operators must plan platforms so growth is not blocked by fragmented one-off technology choices, while subscribers treat the access network mainly as bandwidth for services that live on the public internet.

The core proposal is a holistic access strategy built around a single integrated platform that already supports DSL and GPON and can evolve toward 10G PON without replumbing every segment. The speakers stress capacity planning, end-to-end quality of service—including subscriber identification and traffic shaping for external providers—and operational ease through self-service portals, design and operations tooling for passive fiber inventory, and integrated fault management. Customer examples illustrate faster service turn-up and ROI when one platform spans mixed access types.

The closing segment traces PON bandwidth evolution, the move beyond 2.5G GPON, timelines for asymmetric 10G prototypes and commercial rollouts cited in the talk, and migration paths such as adding line cards on existing GPON splits. They outline expected NG-PON2-class targets—higher downstream rates, long reach, very large split counts, and coexistence with mobile backhaul—so practitioners can align procurement with multi-year fiber build plans rather than shortest-term port cost.

talks.title: PLNOG8 - Cloud - panel dyskusyjny
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh cloud adoption in Polish firms, covering SaaS sprawl, legal barriers to hosting data, and the shifting role of IT.
talks.summary:
This Polish-language panel followed up an earlier discussion and asked where cloud now sits in organisations, both in how companies buy services and in how individuals use them. Panelists said many firms run dozens, possibly more than a hundred, external applications with no in-house infrastructure, reaching them mostly through a browser. Business adoption was described as lagging behind personal use, while cloud-based infrastructure increasingly shapes how new applications are built.

The middle of the session focused on barriers to moving data out of on-premises data centres. Speakers pointed to financial supervision rules, unclear legal interpretations and the risk that authorities could access data without the owner knowing. One panelist recalled a case in Ukraine where police seized physical servers hosting several virtualised clients, taking down a radio station's website and a CRM application used by other customers. Providers described building catalogues of services checked for legal, technical and business fit, including control over the regions where data is held. Storage at scale was another example, with one organisation operating well over a million disks, which was cited as a reason to consider outsourcing that work.

The closing part asked whether cloud is a threat or an opportunity for IT departments. Panelists suggested that routine tasks such as mailbox administration or swapping drives will matter less, while teams that can assemble services from providers will gain an advantage. The practical message was that legal questions and decisions about where data physically sits should be answered before any migration.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Wojciech Apel - Telekomunikacja powyżej warstwy 7 na przykładzie projektu 3S
talks.teaser: Shows how a regional fibre network was built and how business and politics shaped it, using the OSI model as a frame.
talks.summary:
The talk uses the seven-layer network model as a frame, starts at the physical layer and then climbs past layer 7 to the business and political layers that shape a network. Speaker Wojciech Apel uses the history of the 3S regional fibre-optic network in Upper Silesia as the case. He opens with an old chart of home bandwidth growth and argues that backbone capacity would have to keep growing exponentially, so optical fibre was the only realistic answer.

The project grew out of a sand-mining company that owned railway lines. The plan was an open regional fibre network for all operators, but the roughly 7 million needed from investors was not raised as the 2002 market slump hit. The team built the network with its own people and money, working through poor weather and mud, choosing between new and used equipment, and using Ethernet for the metro layer. The speaker also describes a former monopoly operator that would not lease its infrastructure, and how the rules around it were repeatedly changed. Later sections cover customers, mostly telecom operators, and a new data centre in Katowice.

The closing part connects security to the upper layers. Effort spent on certificates, secure sessions and robust transmission can be undone by dishonest messaging or poor decisions higher up. The takeaway is that technical choices in telecom depend heavily on business and policy decisions, which engineers should understand.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Tomasz Paszkowski
talks.teaser: Covers how a Polish web portal moved its servers to a new data center, with cost savings, network links and transport.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how a Polish web portal moved its server infrastructure from one data center in Poznań to a new facility in Warsaw. The speaker presents the move as a business decision: operating costs were lower at the new site, with savings of around 30 percent a year. Before choosing a site, the team checked practical limits such as floor load ratings, backup power, nearby water pipes, and the level of support the operator offered, and found that some candidate facilities could not meet their needs.

The migration was staged. Two independent Warsaw uplinks were connected to the new site, and PHP servers were kept close to their databases because packet round-trip time strongly affects page rendering. A cluster of 32 servers was built in the new room, and every operation applied to the old servers was replicated so the data stayed consistent. Traffic was then shifted in steps using a cookie-based split that let the team choose which users were served from which location. Newer hardware, twice as fast as the old generation, allowed 64 servers to replace the previous fleet. Equipment was packed in the original vendor boxes and moved by a professional transport company, with shock-indicator stickers, and the speaker reports that no hardware was lost.

The takeaways are practical: plan rack layout and cabling before moving hardware, keep a dedicated storage room away from server equipment, and treat cooling, temperature setpoints and provider support as part of the decision. The speaker also says Cat 5e cabling has run 1 Gb links for three years without problems, so upgrading was not needed.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Elżbieta Świętek - Praktyczne aspekty modelu przetwarzania w chmurze
talks.teaser: Describes how a datacenter provider builds cloud environments, covering network redundancy, secure remote access and scaling.
talks.summary:
Elżbieta Świętek presents the practical side of cloud computing from the viewpoint of a Polish company that has spent about twenty years in the storage and server integration market. She opens with a short definition of the cloud as a model where customers use services delivered by an external organisation, and outlines the layered view of infrastructure, platform and application services, along with private and public deployment models. Her case for the cloud rests on cost optimisation, a reduced need to hire infrastructure specialists, and energy management.

The middle of the talk turns to what makes a cloud reliable and secure in practice. She covers redundant network design and hardware for high availability, dedicated firewalls and traffic logging, and monitoring that works across servers, switches and routers from different vendors. She describes several ways to give staff and branch offices secure access, including remote access for laptop users and a gateway that routes users to their environment after login. Planning for growth, and treating security as one integrated set of mechanisms across servers, applications and the network, are also highlighted.

The talk closes with the company's new datacenter near Kraków, which started operating in January, and a business continuity offer in which another company can set up a second site or office inside the facility. Her final point is that launching a cloud environment should be handled as a full IT project, with expected resource growth forecast from the start.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Krzysztof Konkowski
talks.teaser: Explores aggregation-network QoS models, hierarchical policies, video monitoring, and proactive service-quality measurement for operators.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens in the world of carrier aggregation networks, where large operators change slowly and legacy QoS setups often linger long after better options exist. The speaker structures the problem around what traffic arrives from access nodes—consumer triple-play, institutional wholesale, and rarer point-to-point business offers—and why that mix determines whether quality can be enforced per subscriber, per service, or only in aggregate.

The middle section compares three recurring service models: one VLAN with class-of-service bits, dedicated VLANs per service type, and strict one-VLAN-per-subscriber designs for internet. That framing leads into consistent DSCP-to-queue mapping on access, internal, and BNG-facing interfaces, hierarchical QoS with parent shapers, WRED to avoid TCP global synchronization, and business cases where many branches feed one handoff. A major thread is video over multicast: modified fast reroute so duplicate paths are always programmed, aiming for roughly 50 millisecond failover, plus video monitoring with media loss, delay, continuity counters, and threshold-driven switch actions.

The close argues that policing and queuing alone are no longer enough when SLAs tighten. Operators should validate policies with video monitoring where relevant, and with standards-based probes such as IPSL and TWAMP for delay, jitter, and loss—preferring application-aware measurement when Y.1731-style Ethernet PM is insufficient, and treating CPU-loaded TWAMP as untrustworthy. The practical takeaway is a consistent end-to-end QoS design tied to how services are actually delivered, backed by measurable proof on the links that matter.

talks.title: PLNOG7
talks.teaser: Operators hear Warsaw exchange expansion, PeeringDB uptake, and European datacenter peering offers in one forum session.
talks.summary:
The session opens with operational updates on a large Polish Ethernet and internet exchange footprint: physical meeting nodes, open peering, and plans to double fabric capacity, add redundant paths to separate routers, and grow ten-gigabit participant ports. The operator describes onboarding major telecom sources, promotional pricing for resellers, and traffic that is expected to climb from roughly thirteen to twenty-five or thirty gigabits as more peers attach.

A follow-on segment reviews growth charts, rising IPv6 peering sessions, prefix counts above fifteen thousand (with hundreds in v6), short average path lengths, and continued scaling on familiar vendor gear. Hurricane Electric then introduces PeeringDB as a community-maintained directory where networks publish sites, peering policy, and prefix data so others can filter and find partners without relying on scattered lists. Adoption gaps among local peers are contrasted with higher participation abroad.

A colocation provider pitches free rack space for several years, green-powered halls, and direct attachment options toward major Dutch exchanges, alongside briefer operator pitches. The chair closes by urging attendees to talk directly with presenters to line up peering, transit, or footprint in cities they care about.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Pierre Francois
talks.teaser: Explains how BGP Add-Paths and prefix-independent convergence let networks keep backup routes and recover faster after failures.
talks.summary:
This is a network engineering session centred on the BGP Add-Paths extension. Add-Paths lets a router advertise more than one path to the same prefix instead of only its single best route. The speaker frames the subject around operators and service providers who run these networks.

Much of the discussion revolves around how many alternative paths to keep and how traffic can be balanced across them. The talk also brings up prefix-independent convergence, meaning how quickly traffic moves to a backup path after a failure without updating every prefix one at a time. Load balancing and the choice of how many paths to advertise recur throughout.

For practitioners, the takeaway is that path advertisement and convergence design determine how a network behaves when a link fails and how evenly load is spread. Operators weighing these options should consider both the number of alternate paths they propagate and how fast recovery needs to be. The session suits engineers already comfortable with routing design.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Obowiązki operatorów internetowych - panel dyskusyjny
talks.teaser: A panel maps Poland's draft Article 175 telecom security duties, monthly reporting, and ISP options to block abuse legally.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with operators noting that administration and industry rarely sit at the same table, and that the goal is a workable common position on incoming obligations rather than each side pulling the blanket its own way. Panelists from large Polish carriers outline daily touchpoints with telecom law, abuse handling, incident response, and regulatory affairs, and stress that compliance is scattered across many statutes—not only the telecommunications act.

The core focus is a proposed Article 175 package on network security. Operators walk through duties such as publishing current threat information, monthly reporting to the infrastructure ministry, prompt notification of serious events, and annual summaries. They contrast vague drafting with Finland’s clearer incident-reporting model, debate whether reporting creates operational value, and welcome language that allows proportionate technical reactions—including blocking or degrading harmful traffic when justified—while pushing back on “censorship” framing. They also examine a shift toward ministerial regulation of security methods, industry-led codes of good practice as an alternative to over-precise rules, and a new state council where industry may hold only three seats.

The close mixes sober cost and staffing reality—especially for small ISPs—with humor about extreme staffing ratios, then urges operators to read consultations, comment through chambers and associations, and supply concrete proposals instead of only criticism. Practitioners should treat the session as a roadmap of what may soon be mandatory, where interpretation risk lies, and how early engagement can shape implementation.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Michał Jura
talks.teaser: Compares full virtualization with kernel-level isolation on Linux for consolidating many hosted services on limited hardware.
talks.summary:
The speaker, an infrastructure manager at a company that runs a large group of websites and applications, explains how the hosting environment grew from 2008 onward, starting with blade servers. Limited hardware and very varied workloads forced the team to squeeze more out of each machine, which led them to look at alternatives to classic virtual machines.

The talk sorts virtualization into emulation, full virtualization and hardware-assisted approaches, and points out the overhead that hypervisors can add. The alternative it focuses on is operating-system-level separation, where isolated contexts share one Linux kernel. The speaker walks through the kernel mechanisms involved: per-context memory and process limits, finer-grained privileges that let unprivileged users perform some administrative tasks, and kernel changes that hide processes between contexts and give each one its own user table and file system view. Network throughput in this model is described as better than in virtual machines, and storage can be shared between contexts by binding directories or with sync tools.

The speaker reports that no security incidents had occurred so far and that a new server with its own context can be set up in about half an hour. Runaway processes and memory leaks were handled with per-context memory limits and monitoring. The closing questions covered the trade-offs of many small virtual machines versus shared contexts, and how memory-heavy services are placed on separate hardware.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Marcin Ułasik - Wdrożenie systemów GPON w różnych scenariuszach biznesowych
talks.teaser: Presents GPON rollout scenarios for operators, from greenfield builds to upgrading existing ethernet networks.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how operators can deploy GPON, a passive optical network, across several business situations. The speaker starts with market pressure: subscribers keep expecting more bandwidth, while many networks still run on 100 Mbps Ethernet. The open question is how to upgrade without overspending on a design that may need replacing soon.

Next he explains the basics. One fiber from the central office is split passively to as many as 128 subscribers, with active equipment only at the ends. The standard gives 2.5 Gbit/s downstream and 1.25 Gbit/s upstream, shared across the split. Reach is quoted at roughly 20 to 60 km depending on optics, and each split reduces optical power, so a power budget must be calculated during design. He then walks through four scenarios: a greenfield build, bringing fiber to a building and reusing its internal copper or coax, adding PON beside an existing Ethernet network for more speed and TV, and an overlay for premium customers or a competitor's area.

He closes by arguing that most operators will eventually adopt this technology, so it is worth learning early and matching the scenario to local needs and the outcome wanted. The vendor's platform, its management system and its design and commissioning support are presented as the practical route, with detailed questions directed to the booth and later technical sessions.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Kamil Ciukszo
talks.teaser: Modele biznesowe na rynku operatorskim investigates PLNOG7 - Kamil Ciukszo.
talks.summary:
This PLNOG7 talk, given by a Cisco Poland representative who said he was not there to sell anything, asks how internet business models for network operators can hold up as traffic grows. It opens with trend data: consumer traffic overtook business traffic, video passed peer-to-peer around 2010, and video was forecast to exceed half of consumer traffic around 2012. Wireless traffic was also expected to surpass wired traffic.

The core section compares four models. In the first, operators keep flat-rate access and add segmented tariffs that charge heavy users more, which the speaker argues would push users toward lighter applications and limit growth. The second makes online content providers pay operators for the traffic they generate, likened to paying for freight, though those providers would resist it and it would need regulatory backing. The third adds premium, higher-quality tiers alongside equal access for other services, and the fourth is cooperation between an online provider and an operator, already used for TV services in Poland. The speaker concludes that no single model will dominate.

For operators, the takeaways are to expect more video, build a network that can carry it, and host services from outside providers that change quickly. Revenue should come from both sides of the value chain, and any differentiation must respect competition and regulation.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Piotr Jabłoński - Jak wygląda mój pakiet?
talks.teaser: Walks through MPLS packet captures from a router lab, showing how label stacks look for different services and how to read them.
talks.summary:
This Polish-language session asks a practical question: what does an MPLS packet look like on the wire? The presenter, who supports telecom operators in Poland and Austria, works through captures taken on a router interface in a lab. The first part breaks down the MPLS shim header, covering the label, the traffic class bits, the bottom-of-stack flag and the TTL field, and shows how TTL copying can be switched off.

The middle of the session compares several service types. Each example shows which labels appear in the stack for a plain transport path, a Layer 3 VPN with its own routing table, and a Layer 2 Ethernet service. The presenter explains how the labels are signalled by LDP, RSVP-TE and BGP, how a label value of 3 signals penultimate-hop popping, and how the control word changes what is carried. Router show commands are used to match prefixes to label values, with hex values converted to decimal.

The session ends with a quiz on which label stacks are not valid, and a discussion of cases where IPv4 and IPv6 traffic cannot be told apart from the labels alone. The practical takeaway is that comparing the label stack against the signalling protocol makes it easier to work out which service a packet belongs to and where a fault may sit.

talks.title: PLNOG7
talks.teaser: Historia polskiego internetu examines PLNOG7.
talks.summary:
A PLNOG7 panel of Polish internet pioneers walks the audience from 1980s academic KASK dial-up networks through the 1990 PSInet founding photo, early commercial providers, and competing social forums before the web era. Panelists trade anecdotes about expensive phone tariffs, FidoNet versus Usenet culture clashes, modem racks at university machine halls, and the August 1991 Copenhagen link that finally gave Polish academia routed IP.

Stories cover zero-złoty promotional dial-ups that taught customers the internet existed, frame-relay backbones that almost replaced the public internet, Allegro’s accidental birth on a shared hosting shelf, and operator billing fights when engineers answered after-hours customer calls while clocked on another client. A 1998 prosecution for unauthorized remote login illustrates how criminal law lagged technical reality.

The session is nostalgic operator folklore rather than a configuration guide, aimed at PLNOG attendees who lived through deregulation, TP beginnings, and the shift from X.25-era thinking to always-on broadband.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Ferenc Csorba - What’s new at the RIPE NCC?
talks.teaser: Surveys the RIPE NCC's registry role, IPv4 exhaustion rules, IPv6 policy changes and the RIPE Stat and Atlas services.
talks.summary:
Csorba begins with the registry system, showing how IANA supplies regional registries such as the RIPE NCC, which serve members and end users. Policy is set by the open community at RIPE meetings, not by staff.

The main focus is IPv4 exhaustion: IANA's pool is empty and the RIPE NCC is working from its last /8, about 16 million addresses. Requests now cover only three months of need, and LIRs can transfer empty blocks of at least a /21. Under the final /8, each LIR gets one /22, but only if it already holds IPv6. Independent resources reach end users through a sponsoring LIR or direct assignment, which carries a 50 euro fee.

On IPv6, the RIPE ripeness rating gives members up to four stars, and 55% of members in the region lacked an IPv6 allocation, against 47% in Poland. Allocations are now easier than IPv4, and a pending policy would drop the multihoming requirement for IPv6 provider-independent space. He closed with RIPE Stat, a single page of resource data, and RIPE Atlas, a network of about 1,000 USB probes that volunteers can host.

talks.title: PLNOG7 - Bartłomiej Anszperger - MPLS - trochę głębiej
talks.teaser: Questions whether MPLS is the only sensible way to build networks, weighing its label-switching benefits and drawbacks.
talks.summary:
This Polish-language session, given by a presenter from Cisco's advanced services group, takes an opinionated look at MPLS. The speaker asks why networks are built almost exclusively on this technology and invites the audience to challenge his view. He explains the core idea: a short label is attached to each packet so routers can forward it along a predetermined path without examining the full header. The architecture is split into a control plane, which gathers routing and label information, and a forwarding plane, which switches traffic using those labels.

The talk also recalls earlier history, including the backbone problem that label switching was meant to address. The speaker weighs benefits such as one mechanism carrying many service types, traffic steering across alternative paths, sharing resources between virtual networks, and predefined backup paths that switch traffic quickly after a failure instead of waiting for routing to reconverge. Drawbacks include label overhead that uses up bits and the need for hardware to look beyond the top of the stack. The audience is invited to debate whether labels are still faster and whether optical switching will displace them.

The speaker closes by noting that router port costs and optical equipment economics will shape the outcome, with a hybrid mix seen as the likely direction. Link and path protection were left for a follow-up session because time ran out, so the talk ends with the questions open rather than a verdict.

talks.title: CONFidence 2019: "Vulnerabilities for Sale - The Good, the Bad and the Ugly"
talks.teaser: Udo Schneider examines CONFidence 2019: "Vulnerabilities for Sale - The Good, the Bad and the Ugly".

talks.title: CONFidence 2019: "Let’s play a game - challenges..."
talks.teaser: Explains how to assess production network risk passively and demonstrates attacking a PLC controlling traffic lights.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a problem many security teams now face: management hands them industrial and production systems they know little about, and they must judge the risk. The speakers argue that a security officer who accepts a risk without checking it carries the consequences, so the first step is to inventory what is on the network and which known vulnerabilities apply. They describe the stakes of an attack on production, from stopped lines and lost revenue to safety failures. Examples include a 2008 case in Australia where control of water sluices was taken over, and a pharmaceutical line whose production was altered while operators were misled.

The middle of the talk covers scanning. Active scanning can crash fragile industrial devices, which often run on old hardware for 15 to 20 years or longer, so the approach favours passive monitoring of copied network traffic. That reveals device types and firmware versions, which are then matched against vulnerability databases, and active checks are prepared only for specific components. The speakers also cite an active scan on the Large Hadron Collider's control network that disabled controllers across a 27 kilometre link, forcing staff to restart them by hand. A second presenter then picks up the practical side of where and how to scan.

The takeaway is to document the risk, present it to production teams with evidence, and where permitted, demonstrate an exploit so the exposure is clear to decision makers. The talk closes with a hands-on demo in which attendees can take control of a pair of PLCs running a road intersection, to see how such controllers interact.

talks.teaser: Philip Tsukerman analyzes CONFidence 2019: "Sneaking Past Device Guard".

talks.title: CONFidence 2019: "Sandbox dla PowerShell'a - zrób to sam!"
talks.teaser: See how modifying the PowerShell interpreter can reveal script activity and help build a tailored analysis sandbox.
talks.summary: The speaker demonstrates ways to inspect PowerShell scripts, then shows how modifying and rebuilding the interpreter can support a custom analysis sandbox. Attendees learn how to change debugging behavior, examine command activity and variables, and prevent selected script actions while testing samples. The talk also discusses the programming work involved and how scripts may detect that they are running in a sandbox.

talks.title: CONFidence 2019: "Using stylometry and learning..."
talks.teaser: Shows how stylometric features and similarity measures can link an anonymous bomb-threat message to known writing samples.
talks.summary:
Forensic analysts from a Polish digital forensics firm explain how stylometry, the study of writing style, can help narrow down the author of an anonymous message. The talk opens with the wave of fake bomb threats in Poland in early 2019, which targeted supermarkets, government offices and schools, including during the spring matura exams, and explains why tracing an anonymous sender is often easier than proving authorship in court.

The middle part covers the method. Candidate documents are collected, converted to one text format, and cleaned of stray characters and formatting. Features are then measured, such as average sentence length, average word length, punctuation counts, common words and character trigrams. Several similarity measures compare each candidate with the anonymous note, and the results are shown as a heatmap. A colleague then runs the pipeline live on a small set of about eleven documents, and the closest match is highlighted. The talk also warns that comparing unrelated features, or texts in different languages, produces meaningless scores.

The closing takeaway is that stylometry works best with several features rather than a single metric, and that its results are investigative leads rather than proof. Practitioners should expect preprocessing to take much of the effort, check that the compared features are meaningful, and explain their methods clearly if the results are to be used in court.

talks.title: CONFidence 2019: "Powershell kung-fu"
talks.teaser: Shows how a hired attacker uses PowerShell to phish passwords, bypass Windows Defender and tunnel data out over DNS.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a fictional engagement in which a hired attacker is asked to steal employee passwords from a company. The presenter starts with reconnaissance, noting that the target runs Windows and uses GitHub and Outlook, and then plans a phishing campaign that delivers a document with a malicious macro. Asking the user directly for their password is presented as the simplest and most effective route, with PowerShell chosen as the execution tool because it is available on almost every Windows system.

The middle section covers evasion and data theft. Windows Defender blocks a downloaded script and a macro, and simple renaming or obfuscation of suspicious keywords gets past it. With outbound web traffic blocked, data is moved out through DNS queries split into chunks. Further demonstrations include a keylogger that writes to a file, clipboard scanning that replaces copied bank account numbers, a shortcut that launches scripts around execution policy, compiling a script into an executable, and running C# code from PowerShell without a compiler. The talk also shows PowerShell discovering SQL Server instances and using a database feature to run operating system commands, and storing payload values in the registry for persistence.

The closing part turns to defence. Script block logging and cloud-based antivirus telemetry are discussed as controls that make these techniques harder, along with the risk that an attacker downgrades to the older PowerShell version 2 to avoid logging. The practical takeaway is that built-in Windows scripting can carry an entire intrusion, so defenders should log PowerShell activity, restrict legacy versions and watch for unusual DNS and clipboard behaviour.

talks.title: CONFidence 2019:"Breaking Extreme Networks WingOS: How to own millions of..."
talks.teaser: Reverses an embedded access point operating system to find a hidden root shell and over-the-air memory corruption exploits.
talks.summary:
The talk examines an embedded Linux operating system with proprietary components, used in wireless access points and controllers. The speaker notes that little public material exists on its internals, and that these devices appear in aircraft, transit systems, campuses, hotels and other sites, so the attack surface includes physical access, Wi-Fi and the internal network. The research began with a restricted command-line interface that exposed a service command leading to a root shell. Reverse engineering showed that the password was derived at runtime from a file, an RC4 decryption routine and the device's MAC address, and that the password changed after each successful use. Creating a persistence file then removed the prompt.

With root access, the speaker looked at listening services and found a pre-authentication stack overflow in a UDP service. A later firmware fix added a size check that terminated the process, and repeating that trigger caused the watchdog to reboot the whole device, a global denial of service. The speaker then turned to a proprietary layer 2/3 protocol named MiNT, implemented as its own socket family in the kernel. A device running the same operating system could act as a MiNT client to reach neighbouring devices. Several pre-authentication heap overflows were found, one gated by an authorised address list that an unauthenticated function could populate.

Exploiting the MIPS target required flushing the data cache so that shellcode would be executed from memory, which was done through a return-oriented chain that called sleep. Standard shellcode also had to be adapted to the MIPS o32 system call numbers. A demonstration showed a root reverse shell obtained over the air through the target's Wi-Fi network. The vendor first doubted that over-the-air exploitation was possible, later patched most critical issues, and the speaker concluded that controllers are high-value targets because one compromise could reach many access points.

talks.teaser: Szymon Kozak examines CONFidence 2019: "SIEM według potrzeb: Elasticsearch, Energy Logserver, Wazuh...".

talks.title: CONFidence 2019: "Utilizing YARA to Find Evolving Malware"
talks.teaser: Shows how to write YARA rules from compiled code so they keep matching as malware changes its strings.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why YARA rules built only from strings often stop working once malware authors move strings into arrays or encode them, and how to write rules that last across generations. It recommends testing every rule against a layered set of samples: a small clean set, a larger clean set, known malicious files grouped by family, and random files. Managing these collections in a YARA-oriented tool such as Clara is presented as a practical way to keep the testing organised. It also separates loose hunting rules, which accept more noise to catch new variants, from tight detection rules aimed at specific variants.

The core of the talk is building rules from compiled code rather than text. Using a sample compiled for the demonstration, the speaker shows how a string rebuilt as a stack-initialised array breaks a plain-text rule, while the surrounding instructions stay largely the same. Volatile parts such as register choices, stack offsets and relative call targets are wildcarded, constants are kept as anchors, and differing opcode lengths are handled with skip ranges. Overly broad wildcards are shown to cause false positives, and testing against clean files is presented as the way to catch them.

The case study targets APT15 and its Mirage tooling, using a function that decrypts the C2 configuration. A rule built from that code, with the configuration length and addresses wildcarded, matched Mirage samples dating from 2012 through 2017, and it also matched a different APT15 malware sample. Practitioners without large budgets can apply the same approach by running such rules as VirusTotal retrohunts and watching the false-positive results. The takeaway is to prefer shared code over strings, since code is harder to change than text.

talks.title: Just DevOps 2019 - Mariusz Gil - Service mesh with Istio [PL]
talks.teaser: Walks through Istio as a service mesh layer, covering traffic routing, resilience, telemetry and typical microservice use cases.
talks.summary:
The talk gives an overview of service meshes and Istio, starting from the problems that come with microservice architectures. As services multiply, teams struggle to decide where business boundaries should lie, how data stays consistent when several services must change together, and how communication should behave when services scale independently and fail in different ways.

The speaker explains how Istio moves networking concerns out of application code. Each service instance gets a proxy placed beside it, traffic passes through these proxies, and a control plane configures them. Typical use cases include splitting traffic by percentage, such as sending a small share of requests to a new version, routing by headers, and mirroring traffic to a new version to test it under production load. Timeouts, retries and circuit breaking can cut off a failing service and return a fallback response. Telemetry gathered by the proxies can feed metrics systems, build a visual map of how services connect, and support tracing of a request across services.

The closing part stresses that this extra layer adds operational complexity and that several of these features are still maturing. Teams should compare alternative tools, understand the setup before adopting it, and assess their own organisational maturity first. The speaker suggests reviewing the configuration files of a demo application to see how deep the setup goes.

talks.title: Just DevOps 2019 - Marcin Stożek -- Kubernetes logging techniques with a touch of LogSense
talks.teaser: Compares ways to get application logs out of Kubernetes, from direct shipping to node agents, and shows log analysis with LogSense.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how applications running in Kubernetes can get their logs to a place where operators can read and search them. The speaker argues for writing logs to standard output rather than local files, since the platform then controls where logs go and administrators do not have to configure each application separately. He also points out that plain text log lines are hard to query or chart once volume grows, especially when they are not structured.

Four approaches are compared. Sending logs straight from the application to a remote backend is simple, but it ties every service to logging libraries and their versions, and logs can be lost if the remote endpoint is unavailable. A sidecar container can read a log file written by the app through a shared volume and forward it, though it can fill the disk if it falls behind. A node-level agent running on every machine collects container output automatically, and the speaker favours it at scale. Throttling can limit how many messages a noisy application sends, which helps when one error repeats many times.

The demo shows LogSense ingesting these logs, adding Kubernetes metadata such as labels and container names, and letting the viewer filter by fields. It can also turn a value pulled from unstructured log text into a graph and detect when that value changes sharply, sending an alert by email. The takeaway is to prefer standard output with a node agent, avoid direct shipping where possible, and make logs structured so they can be analysed.

talks.title: Just DevOps 2019 - Matthew Renze - DevSci: Data Science for Developers
talks.teaser: Covers what data science means for developers, the standard workflow, and using pipeline metrics to guide product choices.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting everyday decision-making with the volume of available data, arguing that many organizations still decide by anecdote rather than evidence. It defines data science as the blend of computing, statistics, and domain knowledge, outlines typical team roles, and walks through skills, languages, databases, Spark-style platforms, and the iterative process from question through collection, cleaning, modeling, evaluation, and deployment.

The middle section illustrates industry shifts in finance, baseball scouting, and insurance, then turns to software: embedding analytics and machine learning in products, and applying hypothesis-driven experiments such as feature preference surveys, pair-programming trials, A/B tests, and feature toggles.

The closing focus is the DevOps pipeline as a source of measurable insight—code quality, source-control history, and production telemetry—to prioritize features, improve quality, and spot anomalies. Practitioners leave with a conceptual map of tools and practices, plus encouragement to treat experiments as backlog items when the information gained outweighs the cost.

talks.title: PLNOG 6 - Łukasz Bromirski, Rafał Szarecki - Przełączniki i Routery - co jest ważne i dlaczego?
talks.teaser: Compares switch and router designs, covering fabric blocking, packets-per-second limits and forwarding lookups.
talks.summary:
Łukasz Bromirski and Rafał Szarecki present a joint session that sets out shared terms for comparing switches and routers before moving into design details. They start with port speeds and duplex modes, and warn that headline throughput figures are often inflated by multiplying numbers. They then explain what a switch fabric does, and why a non-blocking design depends on the combined bandwidth of the ports staying within the fabric's capacity.

The middle section focuses on forwarding. Packets per second is presented as a stronger indicator than raw bandwidth, because small packets stress the decision logic while large packets stress the links. Routers decide based on destination IP addresses, which requires far more involved table lookups than MAC-based switching. The talk also covers the memory access budget per packet, internal cell-based switching, and how certain packet sizes can cause throughput to drop.

Toward the end the speakers discuss predictability. They describe keeping control, management and forwarding functions isolated with guaranteed resources, and the trade-offs between centralised hardware platforms and modular chassis. The practical takeaway is to judge a switch or router by its internal architecture and per-packet limits, not only by its headline numbers.

talks.title: PLNOG 6 - Piotr Wojciechowski - IPv6 - dwa kliknięcia i działa
talks.teaser: Walks operators through a fast IPv6 rollout and the security and privacy issues it brings for networks and users.
talks.summary:
This PLNOG talk looks at how an internet operator can bring IPv6 to its subscribers quickly, under the heading "two clicks and it works." It starts from the pressure on IPv4 addresses and the fact that many routers, customer devices and operating systems do not yet handle the new protocol well, so the rollout has to be planned around what each device supports.

The middle part compares ways to deliver IPv6 to customers, including dual-stack setups and a method that does not require IPv6 support on the customer side. The speaker describes a controller-based deployment prepared for the conference, where configuring the routers reportedly took about 20 minutes. Security points include the weak spots of the older protocol design against spoofed router and address messages, customer firewalls that are often off by default, and privacy concerns, since a stable address can follow a device across networks. That is why temporary addresses that change periodically were introduced.

The closing part stresses that administrators need retraining for new attack types and monitoring tools, and that customer education matters as much as the technology. Operators should weigh cost, scalability and the extra support load before choosing a deployment model.

talks.title: PLNOG 6 - Łukasz Bromirski - Protokoły warstwy 2
talks.teaser: A survey covers Ethernet layer-two for operators: spanning tree, ring resiliency, provider bridging, and link OAM.
talks.summary:
The session belongs to a PLNOG educational track on how network layers are built, with this installment devoted to layer two as operators actually run it. Ethernet is treated as the default cheap transport, while the industry moves again toward richer switched services, standard client-to-backbone models, and higher-speed aggregation where a single large flow can waste much of a line card.

Most of the time covers classic spanning tree and its successors. The speaker explains why tree-based layer two is painful at scale: long convergence, topology-change storms, and weak fault localization when many switches fail together. Rapid spanning tree and MSTP are compared for convergence in seconds, backward compatibility, and design pitfalls such as oversized MST regions or mixed legacy gear. Ring designs and protocols such as ERP, REP, and ITU-T G.8032 are surveyed, including sparse public documentation and nested ring complexity, with a recurring note that layer three often handles resilience more cleanly.

The closing segments address operator Ethernet extensions—provider bridges, Q-in-Q style tagging, and related bridge types—and connectivity fault management under 802.1ag and Y.1731 for continuity check, loopback, and link trace without climbing to layer three. Emerging multipath ideas around 802.1aq and related work are sketched as alternatives to classic STP blocking. The takeaway is blunt: a large provider network cannot live on layer two alone without accepting many partial standards, uneven vendor support, and heavy operations pain, though OAM and newer bridging work narrow some gaps.

talks.title: Just DevOps 2019 - Jakub Hajek - Container orchestration with Docker Swarm
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Just DevOps 2019 - Jakub Hajek - Container orchestration with Docker Swarm.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from Just DevOps 2019, Jakub Hajek discusses container orchestration using Docker Swarm as a practical, lightweight alternative to complex platforms like Kubernetes. Drawing from his background running projects and leading a DevOps/admin team at Sole Metal / Elastometal, Hajek argues that many teams rush into Kubernetes due to industry hype rather than actual architectural needs. Docker Swarm provides a low barrier to entry, out-of-the-box cluster management, and stable orchestration that fits many production workloads without unnecessary operational overhead.

### Key Topics
- **Rationale for Docker Swarm**: Avoiding overengineering and excessive complexity; understanding core business needs and achieving faster delivery without the steep learning curves of Kubernetes or service meshes.
- **Swarm Architecture & Consensus**: Node roles (Managers vs. Workers), Raft consensus algorithm for maintaining state, quorum requirements, and leader election.
- **Declarative Services & Scheduling**: Defining desired states (replicas vs. global mode), placement constraints, placement preferences across availability zones/datacenters, and automatic reconciliation.
- **Zero-Downtime Updates & Healthchecks**: Rolling updates with configurable parallelism, delay, healthchecks, and automatic rollbacks on failure.
- **Networking, Discovery & Security**: Ingress routing mesh, internal service discovery via built-in DNS, encrypted overlay networks (IPsec), and native secrets/configs management.
- **Edge Ingress with Traefik & Consul**: Dynamic routing, automatic SSL/TLS certificate generation and renewal via Let's Encrypt, and horizontally scaling ingress with Consul as a distributed key-value store.

### Technical Details
- **Cluster Initialization & Management**: Initializing a single-node or multi-node cluster requires just `docker swarm init`, followed by `docker swarm join` using generated authentication tokens over mutually authenticated TLS (gRPC/HTTP2).
- **Consensus & State**: The Raft database is stored on manager nodes at `/var/lib/docker/swarm/raft`. The leader coordinates log replication, while manager nodes maintain quorum and handle scheduling. Workers merely execute tasks and report statuses.
- **Declarative Service Definition**: Services can run as replicated (0 to N tasks/containers) or `global` (exactly one container per node, useful for monitoring agents like cAdvisor or node exporters). Scheduling can be influenced by labels, resource constraints (CPU/RAM), or placement preferences across availability zones.
- **Rolling Updates**: Configured via update parameters such as parallelism (e.g., updating 1 container at a time) and delay (e.g., 10s intervals), relying on healthchecks (HTTP response status 200 via curl or wget) to halt and roll back if tasks fail.
- **Secrets and Configs**: `docker secret` stores sensitive data encrypted in Raft, mounted decrypted in-memory under `/run/secrets/<name>` for explicitly permitted services. `docker config` provides a non-encrypted equivalent, requiring versioning conventions (e.g., appending version numbers) when configurations change.
- **Traefik and Consul Stack Demo**: Demonstrated on AWS `t2.micro` instances provisioned via Docker Machine across three VMs. Traefik listens on `/var/run/docker.sock` to detect Swarm service events automatically and dynamically update routes defined by Docker service labels. Consul acts as the shared key-value store for Let's Encrypt certificates, enabling multiple Traefik replicas to synchronize certificates without collision.

### Takeaways
- Master Docker fundamentals (image optimization, 12-factor principles, environment configuration) before advancing to complex orchestrators.
- Docker Swarm provides production-grade clustering, built-in ingress routing mesh, service discovery, secrets, and zero-downtime rolling updates out of the box with minimal maintenance.
- Swarm serves as an ideal baseline for projects requiring stability and simple operational overhead, with the option to migrate to Kubernetes later if complex features become strictly necessary.

talks.title: CONFidence 2019: "Cyber Policja- co to i z czym to się je?" - Łukasz Pietrzyk
talks.teaser: Introduces the work of Polish police cybercrime units, their tools and tasks, and real cases from online fraud to weapons sales.
talks.summary:
The talk gives an overview of how Polish police work on cybercrime, covering the offences the units pursue. The speaker lists computer fraud, child sexual abuse material, weapons trafficking, stalking, hacking, document forgery and the so-called grandparent phone scam. He links this to the rapid growth of internet use in Poland since the late 1990s, which widened the space for offenders. Routine work is described as long hours of data analysis drawn from partners, police databases and extractions from seized phones and tablets, and officers also run awareness sessions in schools and universities.

Several cases illustrate the work. In one romance scam, a Facebook contact posing as a woman in trouble gradually persuaded a man to send money over several weeks. In another case, a victim transferred large savings to an alleged foreign officer until bank staff intervened and police were called. In a separate case, police traced an online shop selling firearms and an anti-aircraft gun through payment records, followed the seller for months and later detained him. In a child abuse case, an offender who kept returning under new accounts was identified and a large collection of material was found at his home.

The speaker stresses that international cooperation is the main obstacle, because requests pass slowly through courts and prosecutors abroad, and short telecom data retention periods in some countries can erase evidence before it arrives. He closes by emphasising prevention, since many victims are caught by trust and lack of knowledge, and by encouraging people to report incidents early.

talks.title: CONFidence 2019: "Latest Android threats and their techniques"
talks.teaser: Surveys Android malware found on Google Play, from fake apps and adware to clippers and banking trojans, with prevention tips.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys malicious Android apps that appeared on Google Play, grouped by what they were built to do. It starts with fake apps that copied the listings of Instagram and a cryptocurrency wallet, one of which had better ratings than the genuine app, and with fake antivirus apps that flagged themselves as risky. Adware families come next, including a newer family whose developer chooses the payload after install, followed by ad fraud apps that click ads in the background and consume mobile data.

The middle section covers credential theft. An Instagram stealer sent stolen logins to a service that sold likes and follows, a fake earning app collected PayPal logins, and other apps phished Facebook accounts. Cryptocurrency scams took three forms: fake exchanges and wallets that kept the user's funds, a clipper that swapped copied wallet addresses, and miners. A spyware app exposed open servers and an unsecured Firebase console. The largest part covers the Anubis banking trojan, which abuses accessibility services, blocks its own removal, overlays banking apps with fake login screens, and spreads by text message to the victim's contacts.

The talk closes with practical advice: check reviews, developer details and install counts with caution, since fake reviews can mislead. Reach a service's app through its official website rather than search results. Do not grant accessibility permissions to apps you do not know, and do not assume a security app is trustworthy without checking it.

talks.title: CONFidence 2019: "Vulnerabilities from a grave. Forever dead or maybe alive..."
talks.teaser: Shows how decade-old flaws and encodings still enable keystroke injection, filter bypasses, privilege escalation and code execution.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits vulnerabilities that were disclosed years ago but remain widely exploitable. It opens with wireless presenter dongles, where unencrypted radio traffic from a Logitech receiver can be abused to inject arbitrary keystrokes from a distance. A live demo opens the calculator on a Windows machine. The speaker notes that several models and vendors remain affected and that some devices have not been patched.

The middle section covers web and server issues. HTTP pipelining combined with HTTP/0.9 requests can slip past a filter that inspects only the first request, and absolute URLs can route around access rules that match on host names. An IBM037 character encoding and folded headers can confuse inspection devices. LD_PRELOAD is shown being used to run code under a setuid binary to gain root, and a CGI script on the GoAhead IoT web server is abused to obtain a shell. A PHP phar file, uploaded under an ordinary image extension, is triggered through an XML external entity when a file-existence check parses its metadata, leading to remote code execution.

The final part covers credentials and archives. NTLM hashes are shown to be crackable at very high GPU speeds. ZipCrypto archives fall to a known-plaintext attack or fast brute force, so the advice is to avoid ZipCrypto and use AES. Path traversal and symlink flaws in zip extraction are demonstrated against a document management application, where a crafted archive places a JSP web shell for command execution. The takeaway is to validate archive contents on extraction and retire legacy cryptography.

talks.summary:
## Overview
Timur Doumler discusses the many ways to initialize variables in modern C++, a topic he notes is remarkably complex for such a basic operation. He covers initialization in C++17 and previews changes in C++20, providing recommendations for practical usage.

## Key Topics Covered

**Default Initialization:** Not initializing a variable at all. This results in undefined behavior for local variables and uninitialized class members. Doumler emphasizes always using default member initializers in class definitions to avoid this pitfall.

**Copy Initialization:** Using the equals sign (e.g., `int i = 2`). Also occurs when passing by value or returning by value. Performs implicit type conversion if needed.

**Aggregate Initialization:** Uses brace syntax for arrays and simple struct types. Allows omitting initializers, which get zero-initialized. Features "brace elision" for nested aggregates.

**Direct Initialization:** Uses parentheses syntax (e.g., `widget w(1)`). Uses normal overload resolution rather than conversion sequences. Differs from copy initialization, particularly with explicit constructors.

**Value Initialization:** Empty parentheses (e.g., `int i()`). Calls the default constructor if user-provided; otherwise zero-initializes. Includes subtle distinction between user-provided and user-defined constructors that affects behavior.

**List Initialization (C++11):** Uses braces for "uniform initialization." Creates initializer_list objects, which are problematic in several ways: difficult to reason about constructor selection, doesn't work well in templated code, incompatible with macros, and problematic interactions with move-only types.

## Technical Details

Doumler explains specific pitfalls with list initialization, including:
- Vector initialization with `vector<int> v{3}` versus `vector<int> v(3)` producing different results
- String initialization `string s{48, 'a'}` producing unexpected output due to character conversion
- Undefined behavior with nested braces like `vector<string> v{{"a"}}`
- Narrowing conversion prevention with braces

He discusses the "most vexing parse" problem where `widget w()` declares a function rather than calling a constructor.

## C++20 Features Preview

**Designated Initializers:** Members can be initialized by name using dot notation (e.g., `.member = value`), similar to C99 feature.

**Direct Initialization of Aggregates:** C++20 allows using parentheses syntax for aggregate types, avoiding many list initialization problems and enabling use in templated code and macros.

## Recommendations

Doumler's personal style recommendations:
- Always use default member initializers in classes (first recommendation)
- Use `auto` for variables in function scope to prevent uninitialized variables
- Use copy initialization syntax for simple values
- Use braces only when necessary (containers, aggregates, temporaries)
- Use parentheses for constructor calls with direct initialization for clarity and predictable overload resolution
- Avoid braces for constructor calls due to complexity and template incompatibility

## Takeaways

C++ initialization is significantly more complicated than in other languages, with multiple syntax options producing different behaviors. The language gained greater flexibility but also greater complexity since C++11. Users should understand which initialization method calls which constructor and the implications for their code. C++20 aims to unify some of this complexity by making parentheses work for aggregates, reducing reliance on the problematic list initialization syntax.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Serverless w Chmurze (...), Michał Furmankiewicz, Przemysław Malak
talks.teaser: Shows how serverless functions are built, versioned, monitored and scaled in the cloud, including their practical limits.
talks.summary:
The session explores serverless computing, where a cloud provider runs small functions on demand and the developer manages only the code. The speakers concentrate on how functions are built and structured, along with their known and less known limits, rather than on the wider set of managed services. They start with a local setup in Visual Studio Code, creating a Python function from a template with a trigger and running it on a laptop before deploying. They then connect a database table, a queue and a permission role, and remove a policy on purpose to show how the resulting error appears.

Telemetry shows each call, its duration, its dependencies and any captured exceptions. Versioning was shown through published versions and aliases, where traffic can be split, for example sending 10 percent of calls to a new version while the rest stays on the first. In a queue test, 300,000 messages drove the number of concurrent function instances to over 800, and the speakers judged the test runs cheap compared with keeping virtual machines running. A scaling test with 100 threads and 10,000 calls showed delays in creating new instances, and the default limit of 1,000 concurrent executions per account was reached without an increase during the test.

The closing takeaways are that functions suit event processing and consumption-based billing, while dedicated plans give control over instance count and size. Compiled code reduced call times and memory use in their comparisons, and language and operating system support differs between plans. An API gateway with a rate-limit policy, such as a 30-second wait between calls, helps protect a publicly exposed function from abuse.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Najbardziej popularne wzorce architektoniczne w chmurze, Łukasz Kałużny
talks.teaser: Surveys popular cloud architecture patterns, such as queues, circuit breakers and sharding, and when each one makes sense.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that moving to the cloud does not remove reliability problems by itself. Regional outages, management API failures and network latency still happen, and managed services have limits that marketing materials often skip. The speaker warns that chaining services lowers overall availability, since the availability of each component multiplies, so each new building block needs a deliberate reason to exist.

Next come common patterns. A publisher and subscriber setup with queues lets slow work run later, and the talk covers delivery guarantees: at most once, at least once and exactly once. Since duplicates are possible, consumers should handle messages idempotently, and a 202 Accepted response signals that a request has been queued. For resilience, retries cover transient faults, and a circuit breaker moves between closed, open and half-open states to stop calls to a failing service. Kubernetes health checks decide when containers receive traffic or are restarted. For scaling, horizontal partitioning and sharding route data by lookup, range or hash, with rebalancing as the hard part, and queue length can drive auto-scaling. A facade such as an API gateway can centralise authentication, throttling and versioning.

The closing advice is to keep designs simple and to step back when a system grows complicated. Prefer ready-made libraries and managed features over writing your own circuit breaker, since a hand-written version in a client project needed an application restart to recover. Patterns should only be adopted when the scale of the application justifies them.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019:Serverless approach in Azure - another buzzword or 'Holy Grail'(...)? Paweł Fiderek
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of 4Developers 2019:Serverless approach in Azure - another buzzword or 'Holy Grail'(...)? Paweł Fiderek.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from 4Developers 2019, Paweł Fiderek explores whether the serverless architecture pattern is merely an overhyped buzzword or a true "Holy Grail" for developers. Using Gartner's hype cycle as an analytical framework, the speaker reviews the historical evolution of hosting and cloud infrastructure, explains key concepts behind Backend as a Service (BaaS) and Function as a Service (FaaS), and demonstrates how to build an event-driven serverless workflow in Microsoft Azure.

### Key Topics
- **Hype Cycles and Technology Adoption**: The speaker applies the hype cycle model (technology trigger, peak of inflated expectations, trough of disillusionment, slope of enlightenment, and plateau of productivity) to explain how serverless moved past initial inflated hype into a pragmatic, selective architecture pattern.
- **Evolution of Hosting Models**: The transition of modern application deployment from on-premises hardware and shared hosting to virtualization, Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), Software as a Service (SaaS), BaaS, and FaaS.
- **Shift from Infrastructure to Innovation**: Referencing Mark Russinovich, the presentation highlights how moving higher up the abstraction stack allows organizations and developers to focus on business logic and customer experience rather than server patching, runtime configuration, and operating systems.
- **Core Azure Serverless Components**: An introduction to Azure's key building blocks for event-driven systems, including Azure Functions, Azure Logic Apps, Azure Event Grid, Azure Service Bus, and Azure Cosmos DB.

### Technical Details
The speaker conducts a hands-on live demonstration implementing an automated employee onboarding notification system using Azure services:
- **Azure Functions**: An HTTP-triggered Azure Function configured with anonymous authentication. When invoked with an HTTP POST containing employee details (first name, last name, department), the function generates an email address and unique identifier.
- **Azure Cosmos DB**: Used as the persistence layer. A globally distributed multi-model document database where the Azure Function writes the newly generated employee document using native input/output bindings. The speaker notes its multi-model capabilities (key-value, column, graph via Gremlin) and automatic replication across data centers.
- **Azure Service Bus**: Configured with a simple queue (`employee-info`). The Azure Function outputs a message onto this queue to signal that a new employee record was created.
- **Azure Logic Apps**: Orchestrates the downstream workflow by listening to the Service Bus queue. Because queue messages arrive base64-encoded, Logic Apps decodes the payload, parses the JSON structure without a pre-defined schema, checks conditional logic (whether social sharing is flagged as true), and utilizes built-in social connectors to publish announcements directly to LinkedIn and Twitter.

### Takeaways
Serverless is neither an empty buzzword nor an all-encompassing "Holy Grail." It represents a middle ground that provides immense developer productivity and operational offloading for specific workloads, provided teams evaluate pricing models (such as Consumption vs. App Service plans) and operational constraints.
