talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Client had a dream, czyli od zera do rozwiązania chmurowego, Tomasz Marciniak
talks.teaser: Traces how a team turns a naive client cloud brief into Kafka-linked microservices, managed services, and hexagonal structure.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a client who wants a Google Cloud solution for a seemingly simple idea: pull structured order data from incoming mail, analyze it, and prepare downstream paperwork. What looks small on paper becomes a multi-part pipeline as each shop needs its own extraction logic, mail layouts shift, and ancillary capabilities such as market price lookup and service-provider submission grow in scope.

The speaker walks through delivery reality when the product owner lacks technical depth and formal specifications are missing. The team still has to unblock developers quickly, respect regulatory constraints such as keeping certain tooling in multiple regions, and choose scale-friendly boundaries. The described system uses four cooperating microservices connected by Kafka topics, consumer groups to spread heavy batch work, and deliberate naming so each service owns one database. Infrastructure choices favor managed cloud offerings where possible, Docker-based local workflows, contract testing, and observability hooks for versions.

Later segments compare choreography versus orchestration pitfalls, queue-based fire-and-forget integration, database isolation patterns, and when serverless at the edge fits cost and latency. The close advocates hexagonal architecture with ports and adapters so domain logic stays independent of Kafka, databases, and HTTP, plus behavior-driven tests that narrate the flow in business language practitioners can reuse when scoping similar cloud migrations.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Od pomysłu do milion pobrań - jak odnieść sukces w mobile? dr Krzysztof Wojewodzic
talks.teaser: A product-focused walkthrough explains monetization, user retention, and app-store positioning for apps targeting millions of downloads.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by noting he is not a hands-on technologist but a business advisor who has sold software companies and helped products pass a million downloads, including an education app that ranked first in six countries. He frames the session around why mobile still matters amid billions of smartphones and heavy time spent in apps, using Polish market examples such as OLX, Allegro, Rossmann, and fuel-retail clients to show how penetration and offline touchpoints shape adoption.

The middle of the talk walks through monetization patterns seen in platforms like ride-hailing and antivirus products, stresses aligning the app with the sponsor’s real business (not a coupon page that could be a website), and discusses differentiation, measurement, and habits that bring users back. He warns against shallow corporate gamification and in-app social networks, favoring convenience and clear user benefit instead. Personas and field research with real users—such as school energy-saving concepts—illustrate how assumptions from the office fail without validation.

He closes with app-store discovery: keyword positioning beyond the brand name, strong visuals and descriptions, ongoing features (voice, biometrics), team standards as scale grows, and financial discipline when chasing mass reach, citing large local marketing spend and the need for support and risk control as complexity rises.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Android Developer Toolbox in 2019, Bartosz Kraszewski
talks.teaser: Walks through the Android libraries and architecture choices a developer can use, from Kotlin features to offline data.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys the tools and libraries the speaker reaches for when starting an Android project. It opens with the size of the mobile market, citing roughly two billion active users and a large number of job offers in Europe, and notes that mobile work suits small teams and remote arrangements. The speaker then explains that the Android API carries historical baggage, which is why support libraries and Kotlin matter for day-to-day work.

The middle of the talk covers architecture and specific libraries. The speaker argues for a layered design in which views only display data and a model layer makes the decisions. Observable fields and two-way binding keep the interface in sync with that model. Kotlin features such as data classes and extension functions are presented as ways to cut boilerplate. Reactive streams are shown for combining asynchronous sources, and an offline-first approach uses a local database through a repository so the app still works without a connection. A list-binding library removes adapter code, and further tools cover image loading, permission requests, a panel for inspecting the local database, a memory-leak watcher and crash reporting.

The closing section looks at background work scheduled by the system, so tasks such as synchronisation run when the battery and network allow. The speaker points to a weekly Android newsletter, community blogs and forums, and a starter project on GitHub. The advice is to follow new trends in small steps rather than adopting every new framework at once.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Standardising Linear Algebra for C++23 [ENG], Guy Davidson
talks.teaser: Proposes a standardized C++ linear algebra vocabulary for C++23, spanning matrices, promotion rules, and customizable matrix engines.
talks.summary:
Guy Davidson outlines work to add linear algebra vocabulary types to the C++ standard library, motivated by games, graphics, simulation, and machine learning. He frames linear algebra as representing linear equations and matrices, walks through vectors, matrix arithmetic, inverses, and geometric transforms, and contrasts his long experience building small fixed-size game libraries with general-purpose needs such as complex, dynamic, and sparse matrices.

The middle surveys existing ecosystems: BLAS and its level-one through level-three APIs, Eigen’s scope and member-function-heavy design, expression templates for fused evaluation, and gaps around std::complex promotion and mixed scalar types. He argues for element promotion traits, parameterized storage via fixed-size and dynamic matrix engines, support for non-owned data akin to mdspan, and operator traits that separate API from algorithm so implementers can swap naive multiplication for Strassen or other approaches without changing client code.

The close assembles column and row vectors, matrices, flags for density and shape, free-function operators, and a worked multiply example resolving template parameters through engine and multiplication traits. He notes deliberate exclusions such as cross products and Hadamard products from the linear-algebra proposal scope, ties the effort to ongoing paper work ahead of a Cologne presentation, and invites questions on the evolving API.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Implementing Physical Units Library for C++ [ENG], Mateusz Pusz
talks.teaser: Compares Boost.Units and nlunits with a C++20 strong-typing approach aimed at clearer compile-time unit safety.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why mismatched physical units destroy missions and endanger pilots, citing the Mars Climate Orbiter mix-up between customary and SI assumptions and life-critical glide-range calculations in open-source flight software written mostly with raw doubles. The speaker argues that fundamental types force painful, error-prone unit conversions and that the standard library still lacks full dimensional analysis beyond chrono.

The middle reviews Boost.Units and nlunits on a minimal average-speed example: header sprawl, manual return-type deduction, weak compile-time diagnostics, macro-based interfaces, and painful extension when vendors add base dimensions. A personal work-in-progress library targets zero runtime cost, standard-library-only dependencies, no macros, and clearer errors using C++20 concepts, strong types, type identity upcasting, class types as non-type template parameters to avoid dimension ID collisions, and class template argument deduction for quantities.

The close is a call for contributors toward something eventually suitable for the standard library, with open design questions documented publicly. Practitioners should treat unit safety as a typing problem, scrutinize error messages and extensibility before adopting a units framework, and watch C++20 features as enablers for safer physical code.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Using Exceptions in C++: a practical guide [ENG], Zbigniew Skowron
talks.teaser: Explains how C++ exceptions replace error-code boilerplate with RAII, rich diagnostics, and practical rules for safety and threading.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting integer error codes with exceptions: codes give little context, lose detail as they pass through libraries, and bury real program logic under duplicated cleanup checks. In C++, deterministic destructors let success paths stay readable while resources release automatically when failures occur.

The middle walks through practical rules: treat throw like return but never throw from destructors except in controlled patterns; pack errors with rich data (including Boost.Exception); catch only at boundaries such as main, UI, or APIs; use scope guards and scope_success for ad hoc cleanup; and treat exceptions as rare control flow so happy-path assembly stays lean while throws pay for stack unwinding. Thread cancellation via Boost interruption, propagating failures with exception_ptr and std::future, containing throws in C callbacks, and selective serialization for remote errors extend the same model.

Practitioners should reserve destructors for cleanup—not contract logic like implicit flush—and aim for strong or basic failure safety so invariants hold after errors. The speaker closes by noting that exception-safety discipline applies to error codes too, and points to longer CPPCon material for a deeper treatment.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Move Semantics for Trvial Classes [ENG], Nico Josuttis
talks.teaser: Explains when C++ move semantics, perfect forwarding and return-by-value help a simple class, and where they backfire.
talks.summary:
Nico Josuttis walks through how a simple Customer class with first and last name strings should take its constructor arguments under modern C++. He starts with the traditional approach of passing const references and counts the string allocations caused by literal conversions and temporaries. Adding move-based overloads reduces copies but multiplies the overload set, and default arguments can make the calls ambiguous.

Passing by value and moving into the members needs far fewer allocations, and perfect forwarding with a template covers every case, though it can hijack the copy constructor for non-const arguments unless a convertibility constraint is added. The talk also covers setters, where by-value parameters can shrink a string's capacity, so the traditional const-reference form is kept. For getters, returning by value is much slower in loops over many objects, and returning a const reference is faster, but a range-based for loop over a member of a temporary dangles. An overload for temporaries that moves the member out offers a safe, fast compromise.

The takeaways are to keep constructors and accessors simple by default, reach for move semantics and forwarding mainly in foundation libraries where every allocation matters, and never bind a reference to a member of a temporary. He also notes that string_view does not help when the result must become a std::string anyway, and he argues that C++ needs modern style guides aimed at different levels of programmers.

talks.title: 4Developers2019:Wzorce i podejścia architektoniczne wspierające refaktoryzację(...),Szymon Szylhabel
talks.teaser: Shows how to structure a monolith into modules so it can later be split into microservices.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a new system should usually start as a well-structured monolith rather than as microservices, and that early structure decides how easily it can be split later. The speaker, who has a decade of experience with distributed systems, measures modularity by the effort needed to pull one part out of the application. He criticises layered architecture, where technical layers cut across business features, and proposes vertical modules, each with its own API and clear business context.

The demo app, a tool for fighting smog, lets users register, set alerts for a postal code and get notified when pollution crosses a threshold. Modules talk through a command-style mediator instead of direct calls, so the transport can change later. Each module owns its database schema and migrations, so tables are not shared. Cross-module business processes run as sagas driven by a state machine, and reporting uses read models updated from events, since querying across modules is slow and breaks boundaries.

The talk is candid about trade-offs. A monolith is quicker to start, but a shared process forces common dependency versions and coordinated releases once several teams work on it. Microservices allow independent deployment yet make pipelines and development harder from day one. The takeaway is to build clear module boundaries inside a monolith now, so a later move to microservices replaces the communication layer instead of rewriting the system.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Distributed journey, Piotr Gankiewicz
talks.teaser: Traces e-commerce microservices adoption through gateways, discovery, messaging, sagas, observability, deployment, and meshes.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a fictional e-commerce split into microservices from two viewpoints: engineers building backend services and frontend teams consuming them. Early pain appears when clients must call many heterogeneous APIs with different protocols and auth schemes, which motivates an API gateway to unify cross-cutting routing, load balancing, retries, and circuit breaking, using options such as Kong, Ambassador, Tyk, or Ocelot.

Scaling instances exposes service-location problems in dynamic environments like Kubernetes, leading through Consul-based registration, Fabio or Traefik-style routing, HashiCorp Vault for secrets, and message brokers for asynchronous commands versus synchronous queries. The speaker stresses correlation IDs, status feedback via polling or push, separating business from infrastructure failures and dead-letter handling, event-driven local read models to cut synchronous aggregation, and saga-style compensation when distributed workflows miss handlers.

Closing topics cover centralized structured logging, Jaeger distributed tracing, Prometheus and Grafana metrics, CI/CD artifacts and containers via Portainer or Rancher, and optional Istio or Consul Connect sidecars for TLS, policy, and rate limiting—ending with the reminder that each addition must match the problem rather than hype alone.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: EventStorming Lessons Learned-kilkadziesiąt tysięcy post-itów później, Mariusz Gil
talks.teaser: Shares practical lessons from running EventStorming workshops, from choosing participants to keeping sessions productive.
talks.summary:
The talk shares lessons from running EventStorming workshops, a method where developers and business people map a domain together, often with sticky notes. The speaker recalls a project for a London client where a two to three hour session gave him and a colleague enough understanding to start implementation and to spot further risks.

The middle of the talk focuses on what goes wrong. Business and technical people often use different vocabularies, so sessions should include everyone who shapes the project, including decision makers. In one case, a network switch overload raised during a session revealed that infrastructure had been left out of a project already backed by multi-million contracts, and the room fell silent. Another example describes a session that ended with the team discouraged rather than motivated, which the speaker links to a focus on finding faults instead of improvements. He also walks through a loan repayment scenario with four possible outcomes, and says that roughly half of what matters in such sessions concerns interactions between people rather than the model itself.

To close, the speaker recommends stating the session's purpose first, using hotspots to surface risks, and cutting the resulting model into slices that can each be delivered with clear acceptance criteria. The main takeaway is that the goal is a shared understanding among developers and the business, illustrated by a team whose large process map helped it present its project to the wider organisation.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Refactoring live session toward tactical Domain-Driven Design, Michał Michaluk
talks.teaser: A live session refactors legacy Java toward tactical DDD, using repositories, anti-corruption layers, and modular boundaries.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames consulting work around a familiar gap between ideal modular architectures and the operational mess of distributed services, then commits to live refactoring on a B2B Java codebase rather than slides alone. He warns the session will be uneven because compile fixes and small mistakes happen in real time, yet argues each step is transferable to production systems teams already maintain.

Refactoring begins in deliberately painful code, not easy wins. Legacy entity lists and mixed persistence shapes are wrapped behind module-specific types, with repeated extract-object and extract-method moves to isolate emotion-laden data access from domain behavior. Finder-style helpers shrink as domain objects gain methods, and compilation errors drive incremental abstractions instead of big-bang rewrites.

The arc completes with repository construction, an application service for the classic fetch-then-act flow, and an anti-corruption layer plus adapter that translate foreign structures into a local model without leaking them inward. Calculation code is untangled by separating policy choice from variant math using small strategy-like types. The closing message is practical: cap outside complexity, test the new domain shell aggressively, leave the untested legacy path alone, and end with a module boundary thin enough that moving to remote services is mostly a data-access swap.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: How does architect know? Łukasz Szydło
talks.teaser: Shows how architects pick patterns using change vectors, decision records, and quality attributes at block and component levels.
talks.summary:
The session asks where architects—and programmers acting as architects—get the confidence to choose design patterns without over- or under-building. Using document-numbering and validation examples, it contrasts tangled conditional code with heavy pattern use, then introduces change vectors as the likely directions a feature might evolve. Two planned changes illustrate how one structure absorbs a small extension while another forces a painful rewrite.

The speaker warns that at an early product stage, defending every vector is often unnecessary, yet teams must still communicate why a simpler design was chosen so later maintainers avoid “master builder” blame. He recommends architecture decision records with a structured context: requirement stability, business importance, time pressure, which change vectors are supported or rejected, and what kind of complexity dominates. At component level he layers business, project, and quality concerns, splits quality attributes across implementation, delivery, runtime use, and operations, and shows how deployment-frequency evidence can justify test and pipeline work to management.

Components are classified as state-changing workflows, read-only reporting, or pipeline processing, each linked to familiar architectural styles, while rejecting one-style-everywhere dogma. System design should pursue autonomous modules rather than superficial package boundaries. The talk closes by separating strategic context from tactical patterns and pointing to further reading and the “droga nowoczesnego architekta” initiative.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Event Storming - jak skracać dystans pomiędzy IT a biznesem, Sławek Sobótka
talks.teaser: Event Storming uses wall charts and past-tense domain events to align technical and business views of processes before design or code.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by arguing that mental models shape outcomes in physics, driving, chess, and software. Formal methods such as DDD and BDD help only when the underlying business knowledge is sound; otherwise teams model confusion. The speaker introduces Event Storming as a way to externalize knowledge on colored sticky notes, run sessions at big-picture, process, and design levels, and shift how IT and business people see the same work.

The core walkthrough defines events as meaningful past-tense state changes, distinguishes commands and policies, and stresses soft skills: parking ideas, golden bridges for dominator personalities, and working backward from outcomes like payment. Examples move from toy blocks to a car-dashboard factory order flow, then to untangling mixed concerns on screens such as price versus availability. Bounded contexts and subdomain discovery follow, with rules for a single source of truth and propagating availability changes only through the owning context.

Practitioners should treat the sticky-note wall as analysis, not mere formatting: notice what changes, ask why, and deepen domain understanding over time rather than shipping noun-first data models. A large auction-site anecdote illustrates how event-centric language can later justify safer modular refactors.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: DevOps: (r)ewolucja w rozwoju ludzi (...), Rafał Barszczewski, Grzegorz Kozub
talks.teaser: Explains what DevOps means for teams, careers and architecture, and the four metrics used to measure delivery performance.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that DevOps is more than pipelines, scripts and containers. The speakers present it as a change in how products are built, how teams work and how developers, architects and engineers grow. They draw on a multi-year research study of about 2,000 companies and tens of thousands of workers, which found that teams using these practices deploy dozens of times more often, cut lead time from commit to production from months to minutes, and are twice as likely to meet business goals.

The middle of the talk covers culture, product work and technical practice. Culture is described through a generative model, where information flows freely and problems are raised openly, and the speakers suggest that adopting continuous delivery and lean-style product development tends to shift culture over time. Teams should test many ideas with real users through quick prototypes before building, since one cited estimate says 60 to 90 percent of delivered features did not earn their expected returns. Technical practices are grouped into flow, feedback and continual learning: small batches, separating deployment from release with feature flags and canary releases, automated testing, evolving architecture with fitness functions and microservices, monitoring and alerting, telemetry, pair programming and experiments.

The closing part encourages developers to build broad knowledge across several areas and to own a product from discovery through running it in production. Attendees are urged to track four metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, time to restore service and change failure rate. They are advised to choose the practices that fit their own context rather than adopting everything at once.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Kiedy od softu zależy ludzkie życie - o systemach safety-critical, Maciej Gajdzica
talks.teaser: Shows how safety-critical software is built, using Therac-25 and Ariane 5 failures to explain standards and redundancy.
talks.summary:
Maciej Gajdzica opens by asking what changes when software can injure people or destroy expensive equipment. He points out that software now runs in cars, aircraft, trains, medical devices and nuclear plants, and that most developers never work under such constraints. Drawing on his own embedded and medical projects, plus material on how NASA builds software, he frames the talk around the methods used to make these systems reliable.

He then walks through two failures. The Therac-25 radiotherapy machine delivered doses far above the prescribed level in several fatal accidents. The cause was a shared flag cleared inside a loop, so a high-power beam could fire before the filter was in place. The investigation also found a one-person codebase, no reviews, little architecture documentation and weak system testing. In the Ariane 5 first flight in 1996, the rocket was lost after a floating-point value was converted to a 16-bit integer without protection. The backup navigation unit ran the same software, so it failed the same way, and reused code had never been checked for the new flight parameters.

The middle and end of the talk cover the norms that govern this work: safety integrity levels that map hazards to acceptable failure rates, a V-shaped lifecycle, and recommendation tables for coding and testing techniques. Examples include avoiding dynamic memory, restricting pointers, redundant channels with voting, and protection against radiation-induced memory faults. He warns that off-the-shelf libraries arrive with unknown histories, and that safety-critical work can cost up to ten times more. He closes by arguing that many norm requirements, such as tests, documentation and deliberate design before coding, are things good teams should do anyway.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Secure Domain, Dominik Przybysz
talks.teaser: Explains how to shield the core of an application with clear naming, strong types and validation at its edges.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how to protect the most important part of an application, its domain, by placing it at the centre of a hexagonal, ports-and-adapters architecture. Frameworks, external libraries and data-access details stay in adapters outside the core, so the domain code that earns money for the business is isolated from outside concerns and from foreign data types.

The middle section covers naming and typing. Vague names such as manager or generic suffixes hide what a class really does, and abbreviations that the business does not use should be avoided. Raw strings, numbers and booleans are replaced with dedicated types for things like money, units, consent and identifiers, so the compiler rejects mixed-up arguments and invalid values. Lists are wrapped so that only meaningful operations are exposed, object creation goes through constructors or factories that validate input, and state is shared through read-only snapshots rather than internal fields.

The closing part argues that validation belongs at the boundary, with explicit errors or results instead of annotations or null-tolerant shortcuts. Status changes such as marking an order as paid should happen through a clear domain command rather than a loose setter. The takeaway for a practitioner is to keep an explicit list of accepted and rejected input, and to model values precisely enough that many defensive checks and tests become unnecessary.

talks.title: 4Developers 2019: Mikroserwisy - technologiczne piekło, Radosław Maziarka
talks.teaser: Argues that microservices often create a distributed monolith and suggests starting with a modular, business-aligned design.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why microservices so often disappoint in practice. The speaker describes a common path in which a monolith is simply cut into pieces, producing a distributed monolith with shared databases, business operations spread across several services, unclear data ownership and changes that require coordinating many teams. He proposes four checks for a healthy split: a business transaction should stay within one service, each service should own its data, services should deploy independently, and each should have an assigned team. He then lists the costs that come with distribution, including monitoring, securing service-to-service calls, versioning APIs, service discovery, error handling and debugging across processes.

The middle of the talk argues that many of these problems come from adopting technology for its own appeal rather than for business value. As an alternative, he recommends starting with a modular monolith organized around business capabilities. Domain-driven design tools such as bounded contexts, context maps and Event Storming workshops help locate those boundaries. A cinema seat booking case is used as an example: after the process was separated along business lines, the speaker reports a roughly twentyfold reduction in processing time.

The closing part suggests extracting a module into its own service only when a real need appears, such as scaling one area or frequent changes to one model. Teams should keep internal boundaries strict, so that outsiders interact only through defined interfaces. The main takeaway is that the move to microservices should be a business decision, not a technical fashion.

talks.title: 4Developers2019: Everything as Code(...)środowiska Cloud Native oparte na kontenerach,Tomasz Cholewa
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of 4Developers2019: Everything as Code(...)środowiska Cloud Native oparte na kontenerach,Tomasz Cholewa.
talks.summary:
### Overview
W prezentacji Tomasz Cholewa omawia koncepcję „Everything as Code” w kontekście budowy i utrzymania środowisk Cloud Native opartych na kontenerach i platformie Kubernetes. Prelegent, odwołując się do analogii z bolidami Formuły 1 oraz supersamochodami takimi jak LaFerrari, zwraca uwagę na konieczność unikania ręcznych wdrożeń („klikania”) i przejścia na pełną automatyzację środowisk za pomocą kodu. Prezentowane podejście opiera się na doświadczeniach zdobytych przez prelegenta m.in. jako architekt w firmie Mindbox przy wdrożeniach dla największego operatora telekomunikacyjnego w Polsce.

### Key Topics
- **Infrastruktura jako kod (IaC):** Wyeliminowanie ręcznych modyfikacji, SSH oraz klikania w konsolach dostawców chmurowych na rzecz powtarzalnych i testowalnych definicji kodu.
- **Demokratyzacja dzięki Kubernetes:** Niezależność od dostawcy chmury lub środowiska on-premise (np. VMware) – Kubernetes zapewnia spójną warstwę abstrakcji umożliwiającą szybkie dostarczanie środowisk niezależnie od bazowej platformy.
- **Zarządzanie konfiguracją jako kodem:** Traktowanie konfiguracji jako kluczowego elementu (porównywanego do mieszanek opon w F1) oraz organizowanie jej w hierarchiczne struktury za pomocą narzędzi takich jak Kustomize czy Helm.
- **Podział ról i separacja repozytoriów:** Rozdzielenie repozytoriów z kodem aplikacji od repozytoriów konfiguracyjnych i infrastrukturalnych, co umożliwia deweloperom skupienie się na logice biznesowej, a architektom i inżynierom platformy na bezpieczeństwie, limitach zasobów i sieci.
- **Automatyzacja CI/CD i środowiska ephemeral (preview):** Zastosowanie pipeline'ów Jenkinsa do zarządzania środowiskami stałymi oraz tworzenia dynamicznych środowisk poglądowych na żądanie dla Pull Requestów.

### Technical Details
- **Warstwa infrastruktury:** Do provisioning infrastruktury bazowej prelegent jednoznacznie rekomenduje narzędzie Terraform (wskazując m.in. na rezygnację Oracle z własnych narzędzi na rzecz providera Terraform oraz wsparcie w Azure i VMware). Odradza stosowanie Ansible na najniższej warstwie.
- **Warstwa platformy i instalacji:** Do wdrażania OpenShift (określanego jako „Kubernetes na sterydach”) wykorzystywane są playbooki Ansible, a sam proces instalacji weryfikowany jest w pipeline z użyciem narzędzi testowych, takich jak BATS, Testinfra czy Goss.
- **Struktura konfiguracji aplikacji:** Konfiguracje w postaci ConfigMap, Secrets, reguł sieciowych czy limitów CPU/RAM są wersjonowane w Git i organizowane hierarchicznie (wykorzystując Kustomize wprowadzone w Kubernetes 1.14) w modelu wielu repozytoriów (multi-repo) z bazowymi szablonami na samej górze piramidy.
- **Konfiguracja i orkiestracja Jenkinsa:**
  - Jenkins traktowany jest w całości jako kod dzięki wtyczce Jenkins Configuration as Code (JCasC).
  - Wykorzystanie OpenShifta pozwala na integrację natywnych obiektów Kubernetes (ConfigMap, Secret) jako poświadczeń i zmiennych Jenkinsa.
  - Agenci (slave'y) Jenkinsa są w pełni efemeryczni – podnoszą się dynamicznie jako pody tylko na czas trwania buildu.
  - Zamiast rozbudowanych Dockerfile prelegent rekomenduje technologię Source-to-Image (S2I) w celu unifikacji bazowych obrazów kontenerowych dla technologii takich jak Java/Spring, Node.js czy Python.
  - Pipeline'y CI/CD definiowane są jako współdzielone biblioteki (Jenkins Shared Libraries).

### Takeaways
- Klikanie w interfejsach chmurowych sprawdza się wyłącznie na etapie początkowym; w środowiskach złożonych i o dużej skali zarządzanie kodem skraca czas dostarczania środowisk do pojedynczych godzin lub minut.
- Kod infrastruktury należy traktować jak zwykły kod aplikacji: pokrywać go automatycznymi testami (BATS, Goss itp.), aby przełamać strach przed wprowadzaniem zmian i degradacją środowisk (tzw. driftem konfiguracyjnym).
- Kubernetes pozwala na tworzenie nowoczesnych, wysoce zautomatyzowanych środowisk również w infrastrukturze lokalnej (on-premise), nie ograniczając innowacji do chmury publicznej.
- Kluczem do skalowalności organizacji jest podział odpowiedzialności: deweloperzy rozwijają kod aplikacji, natomiast architekci platformy dbają o szablony, bezpieczeństwo oraz izolację parametrów środowiskowych.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Jakub Leszewski - Citrix SD-WAN - niezawodny, efektywny i bezpieczny dostęp...
talks.teaser: Shows how Citrix SD-WAN bonds branch links, steers traffic by path quality, and secures cloud access for reliable connectivity.
talks.summary:
The talk, given in Polish, presents Citrix SD-WAN as a way to keep wide-area connections between company sites reliable, efficient and secure. It opens with everyday problems such as application availability, slow or unreliable links between branch offices and headquarters, and the fact that no single link offers guaranteed uptime. The system groups several physical links, such as broadband and cellular, into one virtual connection and sends each flow over whichever path performs best at that moment.

Path quality is measured per packet, tracking latency, jitter and loss, so a degraded path can be marked as bad within milliseconds and traffic moved elsewhere. Traffic classes can be prioritised, with voice and video getting preference, and critical packets can be duplicated across two links to reduce loss during a failure. Links with limited data plans can be reserved as backup and used only when primary links are down. For cloud services, the speaker described sending Microsoft Office 365 traffic straight to the internet rather than through the central site, with local DNS support, and recognising applications through signatures for about 4,500 applications.

Deployment is possible as a physical appliance or as a virtual instance in Azure or Google Cloud, and a single management system handles configuration, monitoring and historical reporting across branch, central and cloud components. A Danish fisheries agency was presented as a case, where ships without a fixed cable needed reliable connectivity at sea. The main takeaway is that one platform can steer traffic by application and path quality rather than relying on a single link.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Marcin Kuczera - Open Compute Project by John Laban
talks.teaser: Explains the Open Compute Project and how open data center hardware designs cut cost and complexity for telecom operators.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a board member of a small telecom operator in Silesia, explains how he came to open technology. While looking for an open-source way to get his FTTH network devices to work together, he found the Open Compute Project. He likens open sharing of designs to a buyers' club, arguing that publishing designs lets many parties improve them faster. He points to large companies such as Facebook, which needed a leaner approach at data-center scale.

Most of the talk walks through design choices the project has reworked. Standard 19-inch racks give way to a wider format. Servers drop rear cabling, redundant power supplies and extra ports in favour of a single shared connection at the front. Components are replaced without tools, using levers and colour-coded points. Cooling relies on airflow at higher inlet temperatures instead of conventional air conditioning, and centralized UPS systems are replaced by smaller distributed power. He also notes that slowing fans reduces energy use, and that a wider chassis allows better heat sinks.

He closes by noting that the hardware designs, including schematics and bills of materials, are publicly available, and that some telecom operators are only starting to adopt such equipment, for example in container-based sites. For practitioners, the takeaway is that open designs can reduce vendor lock-in and cost, though moving away from established equipment takes time.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Krzysztof Załęski
talks.teaser: Praktyczne zastosowania narzędzi (Net)DevOps investigates PLNOG22 - Krzysztof Załęski.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a story from the speaker's early career, when adding a 129th instance to a backbone whose devices supported only 128 triggered a loop and took the network down for about an hour. He argues that network engineers still configure gear by hand at the console, with little standardisation, undocumented drift and repeated mistakes, while software teams version, test and review every change before release.

The middle section introduces a toolchain for adopting automation step by step. Git holds configurations under version control, with changes made on a branch and approved before they reach production. Vagrant lets engineers rebuild a matching test lab on a laptop from a short text file, and Ansible applies declarative, repeatable changes over SSH without an agent. Jenkins then runs tests as a pipeline, and a central source of truth describes the network independently of vendor, so configurations can be generated from it.

The closing advice is to start small: pull read-only show output from production, then change low-risk settings such as NTP or syslog. Keep the last approved configuration as a rollback point, check the network after each change, and maintain out-of-band management access. The speaker concludes that automation should be built on understanding rather than copied snippets, and that network staff will increasingly need these skills as networks move into containers and cloud.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Krzysztof Rydz & Dominik Sabat - O tym, co CERT Polska wie o Twojej sieci
talks.teaser: Shows what CERT Polska observes about Polish networks through honeypots, botnet tracking, and DDoS amplification data.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Prezentacja przedstawicieli CERT Polska (NASK) na konferencji PLNOG22 poświęcona jest działaniom zespołu na rzecz poprawy bezpieczeństwa polskiego internetu oraz wiedzy, jaką CERT Polska gromadzi na temat zagrożeń występujących w sieciach operatorów. Prelegenci opisali ramy prawne wynikające z Krajowego Systemu Cyberbezpieczeństwa, w ramach których CERT Polska odpowiada za ochronę sektora prywatnego, obywateli, jednostek samorządowych i szpitali (ok. 30 mln użytkowników i 2,5 tys. systemów autonomicznych AS). Przedstawiono również skalę obsługiwanych incydentów oraz zaprezentowano autorską, bezpłatną platformę n6 służącą do agregacji i wymiany informacji o zagrożeniach z właścicielami sieci.

### Key Topics
- **Działalność CERT Polska**: Obsługa zgłoszeń (prawie 20 tys. zgłoszeń i 3 tys. obsłużonych incydentów w poprzednim roku), przejmowanie złośliwych domen w rejestrze .pl, współtworzenie serwisu No More Ransom, działalność edukacyjna i wydawanie biuletynu OUCH!.
- **Krajowe i międzynarodowe źródła danych**: Udział w projektach prowadzonych przez NASK, w tym utrzymanie sieci honeypotów (około 20 węzłów w 50 krajach, blisko 1000 sensorów) oraz monitorowanie ciemnej przestrzeni adresowej (darknet / network telescope z pokryciem ponad 100 tys. prefiksów /24) wychwytującej m.in. skanowania, błędne konfiguracje i pakiety z ataków SYN flood.
- **Kategorie rejestrowanych zagrożeń**: Infekcje złośliwym oprogramowaniem (botnety), serwery dowodzenia (C&C), dystrybucja malware, phishing, podatne lub źle skonfigurowane usługi oraz usługi wykorzystywane do ataków DDoS z amplifikacją.
- **Zagrożenia w polskich sieciach w 2018 roku**: Statystyki dotyczące infekcji (m.in. botnety Andromeda, Mirai), spadek aktywności trojanów bankowych, serwisy hostingowe i platformy współdzielenia plików (np. Chomikuj) wykorzystywane do dystrybucji złośliwego oprogramowania.
- **Podatności i amplifikacja DDoS**: Pomiary usług podatnych na wykorzystanie we wzmacnianiu ataków DDoS (NTP, DNS, SNMP, Portmapper, SSDP, CharGEN) oraz publicznie dostępnych w Polsce protokołów i paneli (SMB, NetBIOS, Telnet, RDP, sterowniki przemysłowe).

### Technical Details
Prelegenci szczegółowo omówili wektory ataków DDoS z odbiciem i wzmocnieniem (amplifikacją), w których spoofowany adres IP ofiary jest wykorzystywany w zapytaniach UDP (np. DNS oferujący wzmocnienie do ok. 179x, SNMP do 5-6x). Omówiono rozkłady widoczności tych usług w polskich sieciach telekomunikacyjnych oraz spadki w wyniku interwencji u operatorów (np. redukcje widoczności SNMP w sieci Multimedia czy Portmappera w UPC). 

Kluczowym elementem technicznym prezentacji była platforma **n6**. System ten integruje 104 strumienie danych pochodzące z honeypotów, sinkholingu domen .pl, systemów darknet, spampotów, własnej piaskownicy (sandbox) do długoterminowej analizy złośliwego oprogramowania oraz źródeł zewnętrznych (CSIRT-y narodowe, firmy antywirusowe, źródła publiczne). Dane w n6 są deduplikowane (agregacja powtarzających się połączeń w zliczane zdarzenia), parsowane, wzbogacane (rozwiązywanie domen, dopisywanie numerów AS) i normalizowane do prostego, jednolitego modelu opartego na czasie, miejscu (IP/URL) i typie zagrożenia. Platforma n6 została udostępniona na zasadach open-source na serwisie GitHub.

### Takeaways
- Każdy właściciel sieci posiadający co najmniej prefiks /29 lub domeny może bezpłatnie dołączyć do systemu n6 (poprzez kontakt mailowy na cert@cert.pl), aby otrzymywać powiadomienia o zagrożeniach w swoich zasobach.
- Dostęp do informacji z n6 realizowany jest za pośrednictwem dedykowanego interfejsu webowego oraz API REST (zwracającego dane m.in. w formatach JSON i CSV), co umożliwia bezpośrednią integrację z systemami SIEM operatora.
- Operatorzy i administratorzy powinni aktywnie blokować lub ograniczać publiczną dostępność protokołów podatnych na amplifikację oraz usług administracyjnych i przemysłowych nieprzeznaczonych do wystawiania w publicznym internecie.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Dorota Szczepan Jakubowska - Co zrobić w sytuacji kryzysowej?
talks.teaser: Explains why people freeze, blame or deny during cyberattacks, and how leaders can restore calm and control.
talks.summary:
A psychologist who works with IT and crisis teams, rather than as an IT specialist, looks at why cyber incidents leave people disoriented. She argues that when we meet something we do not understand, we force it into categories we already know, and the body and emotions react before any real understanding arrives. The hardest opponent, in her framing, is the one that leaves you confused.

The central example is a regional government office where servers were infected. A manager told staff to switch off their computers, and they left the building as if it were a holiday, showing no sign of concern. The IT staff were busy with other work and did not realise the scale of the problem until a crisis-management official stepped in. She describes common reactions seen in such cases: denial, passivity, anger aimed at the wrong people, guilt, paralysis and learned helplessness. She also outlines a sequence of stages, from fear and denial through anger and blame to sadness, before relief and action return. Her bank work showed that staff often hid facts or failed to report incidents.

Her practical advice starts with the body: slow breathing and calm posture come first, then letting people talk and listening to them. Ask simple questions about what they see and whether colleagues see the same thing. Use plain language and everyday metaphors, such as comparing a computer to a book with chapters. Never blame users, and ask whether they have handled something similar before. For organisations, she recommends rehearsing incident handling, posting short, colour-printed instructions with reporting contacts, and building a culture of non-blame where people can admit what they do not know.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Piotr Wydrych - BGP w świecie SDN
talks.teaser: SDN w świecie BGP explores PLNOG22 - Piotr Wydrych - BGP w świecie SDN.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at PLNOG22, Piotr Wydrych discusses the architectural evolution of large content distribution network clusters, specifically moving away from traditional expensive core routers and transitioning from OpenFlow-based Software Defined Networking (SDN) to using BGP as the control and programming protocol. While SDN controllers and BGP were traditionally seen as disjoint networking paradigms, the team unified them by using centralized software controllers that communicate forwarding rules to merchant silicon switches via BGP.

### Key Topics
- **Scaling Challenges in Modern Clusters:** Modern internet traffic is heavily concentrated in major metropolitan areas with high-bandwidth interconnects and exchange points. Traditional designs relying on massive, single-chassis routers face prohibitive costs and scaling limits when handling multi-terabit traffic loads.
- **Limitations of OpenFlow in Production:** The initial SDN deployment attempted to use OpenFlow across commodity hardware. However, vendor-specific OpenFlow implementations, inconsistent rule installation confirmations, slow state dumps during reconnections, and lack of active vendor support made it impractical for robust, large-scale production use.
- **BGP as a Transport Protocol for SDN:** The architecture was redesigned by swapping the execution layer from OpenFlow to BGP. Because BGP is mature, widely supported across switch hardware, and features deterministic session teardown and state synchronization, it serves effectively as a transport protocol to inject forwarding rules computed by the SDN controller directly into switch silicon.
- **Handling Switch FIB Constraints:** Inexpensive commodity switches lack the memory capacity to hold the full Internet routing table (hundreds of thousands of prefixes). The SDN controller dynamically computes and injects only the most popular and relevant prefixes (e.g., 60,000 out of hundreds of thousands) based on traffic patterns and local CDN demands, leaving default routes or alternate paths for the remainder.

### Technical Details
- **Pre-computed Forwarding vs. Reactive Controller Hits:** Unlike early academic OpenFlow designs where unknown packets triggered controller round-trips, the centralized controller pre-calculates routing tables and pushes them in advance. Unknown or unrouted packets are simply dropped silently in silicon, preventing switch CPU exhaustion.
- **Redundancy and Path Determinism:** Controllers run redundantly in pairs. Because standard BGP path selection ties can lead to non-deterministic path choices across multiple controllers (especially with BGP Add-Path extensions), additional software criteria are applied to ensure consistent FIB state and prevent routing loops.
- **Traffic Engineering and Load Balancing:** The central controller monitors port utilization across outgoing links (e.g., transit and peering) and samples prefix traffic. If a link approaches high utilization (e.g., >90%), the software can dynamically shift specific prefix subsets to alternate transits or peering links to balance load before packet loss occurs.

### Takeaways
- OpenFlow's real-world vendor fragmentation and operational complexities led to its retirement in this environment.
- BGP can serve reliably as a programmable transport protocol between external SDN controllers and switch hardware, leveraging decades of battle-tested hardware implementation.
- Successful network modernization can be achieved incrementally, progressing from small pilot clusters to fully software-controlled multi-terabit production networks.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Leszek Miś - Symulacje zdarzeń i anomalii sieciowych jako proaktywne źródło wiedzy...
talks.teaser: Simulates attacker behaviour and network anomalies to reveal unidentified attack vectors and test SOC and SIEM detection.
talks.summary:
Leszek Miś opens by explaining why he wants to model attacker behaviour on a network. His stated aims are to understand the real security posture, validate SOC and SIEM tooling, improve incident response and find attack vectors that have not been identified before. The focus is on activity after an attacker is already inside the network, rather than on initial exploitation, and he argues that such simulations should run continuously instead of as one-off projects.

The middle of the talk walks through concrete examples. Traffic is analysed by behaviour rather than signatures, using client fingerprints for TLS and SSH to spot a new client appearing on a host, along with certificate age and issuer checks and DNS record types and volumes. Domain registration dates can flag domains that are new to the environment. One demo hides data in DNS TXT records, reassembles it from a zone transfer and runs it in memory without touching disk. Other cases cover writable directory attributes that can carry data, eBPF-based profiling of critical services, and memory analysis with Volatility to find hidden Windows processes.

He closes by arguing that vendor claims should be validated rather than trusted, and that network data should be combined with logs, memory and the source code of critical services. He also points to a platform his team is building to automate this kind of validation. The practical message is to test detections with realistic attacker actions and keep that process running.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Jerzy Domżał - Czy stać nas na dyskryminację teleinformatyki?
talks.teaser: Explains why Polish patent rules make protecting software-related inventions hard, using a personal case and European comparisons.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether Poland can afford to weaken intellectual property protection for IT and telecommunications. The speaker outlines three ways to protect work: copyright for code, trade secrets for know-how, and patents for inventions. Patentability rests on novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability, yet Polish law contains no formal definition of an invention.

The main focus is computer-implemented inventions. Polish law excludes computer programs as such, while the European approach accepts algorithms that have a technical effect. The speaker recounts a university team's application around 2010 that was refused until a 2015 amendment added technical-effect wording. Later the team obtained a patent in Taiwan, while a US application met resistance. Figures presented show foreign applicants receive far more European patents validated in Poland than domestic ones, and Polish firms file few patents at all.

The closing argument is that without protection, small firms and researchers risk losing their work to others who patent it abroad. The speaker points to uneven court rulings, to funding schemes that reward patent filings, and to a pending overhaul of Polish patent law. The takeaway is that Polish companies should invest in protection that fits their work rather than leave the field to foreign applicants.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Dawid Dudek - XGS-PON czy to już szczyt potrzeb dla użytkowników indywidualnych?
talks.teaser: Follows an operator's XGS-PON fiber rollout, covering traffic growth, equipment choices and multi-gigabit speed testing.
talks.summary:
Dawid Dudek asks whether XGS-PON already goes beyond what home users need. He starts with internet growth: a little over half of humanity was online, adoption was far lower in less developed countries, and video services such as Netflix and YouTube dominate traffic. Using forecasts and graphs from his own network monitoring, he shows a peak of 120 gigabits per second on a link that serves content providers and notes that new releases or major operating system updates push it higher.

He then explains how the operator tries to ease this load. Content caches placed at local points of presence keep popular traffic closer to users and reduce traffic between operators. He describes the PON architecture, with fiber, splitters and customer terminals, and how XGS-PON runs symmetric 10 gigabit service on a separate wavelength so it can coexist with existing GPON through a multiplexer. The first production launch took place at a gaming arena in Poznań. Lab tests used a Nokia platform and several laptops. A single browser session reached only about 24 to 28 gigabits per second, so three to five browsers were needed to fill a 10 gigabit link, which he attributed to operating system resource allocation. Chrome performed worst in these tests and Edge best.

He concludes that 10 gigabits is a practical step rather than an endpoint. Cost, not technology, currently limits higher speeds, and services, applications and end devices must catch up before users can really use multi-gigabit access. Operators should expand capacity gradually, staying a step ahead of demand.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - DEBATA OKSFORDZKA - Chmura jest skuteczniejsza niż własna serwerownia
talks.teaser: A structured debate compares cloud platforms and private datacenters on cost, security, compliance, and operational effectiveness.
talks.summary:
The session is an Oxford-style debate on whether cloud computing is more effective than running a private server room. The proposition side defines cloud around on-demand elasticity, usage-based billing, a broad catalog of services, and global reach, and cites survey figures on large-enterprise adoption of major platforms. They argue that cloud frees IT to focus on business outcomes, surfaces costs more clearly, provisions capacity faster than long hardware lead times, and can meet compliance through provider certifications combined with customer responsibility for workloads.

The opposition holds that staying on familiar on-premises kit is often the quickest path to “effective” operations for finance, staff, and known applications. They stress multi-year transformation cost, training risk, vendor policy changes, the blast radius of hyperscale outages, legal and sector rules that favor local control, unpredictable monthly cloud bills, and limits on mirroring entrenched security stacks in multitenant SaaS. Both sides trade questions on shared responsibility, audit rights, hybrid colocation, elastic traffic peaks, and whether portability tools truly remove lock-in.

Closing speakers synthesize the clash as a question of fit, not fashion: migration and operating-model change are expensive and risky, yet cloud can win when elasticity, service breadth, or scarce operations talent matter. The practical takeaway is to decide from business constraints, regulatory context, and honest cost of change—not from adoption statistics alone.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Bartosz Partyka - Reliable DNS Cluster
talks.teaser: Case Study explores PLNOG22 - Bartosz Partyka - Reliable DNS Cluster.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Bartosz Partyka, a network/systems engineer at an Internet service provider, presents the architectural evolution and implementation of a highly available and reliable recursive DNS cluster. Serving over 260,000 retail and 100,000 business customers with symmetric FTTH and other access technologies, the operator faced peak traffic of approximately 200,000 queries per second (QPS). The presentation walks through moving away from fragile single-server and centralized models to a multi-node Anycast deployment backed by Linux Virtual Server (IPVS) and automated health checking.

### Key Topics
- **Client Behavior and DNS Failure Impact**: Operating systems handle DNS resolution failures differently. While Android caches aggressively, Windows waits 1 second before retrying, then escalates up to 4 seconds before querying secondary resolvers simultaneously. Default Linux resolver configurations wait up to 5 seconds. In the context of 10G connections, these resolver timeouts drastically harm perceived customer quality of experience (QoE).
- **Anycast Routing Architecture**: Transitioning from centralized resolvers to multiple geographically distributed nodes using BGP Anycast allows queries to automatically route to the topologically nearest resolver node, mitigating latency and offering baseline redundancy without needing hardware appliances.
- **Load Balancing and IPVS**: Within each Anycast point of presence (PoP), the team implemented Linux Virtual Server (IPVS) using Direct Routing (DR) mode. This avoids returning outbound traffic through the load balancer, modifying only destination MAC addresses so DNS response packets egress directly back to the client, conserving compute power.
- **Health Checking and Automation**: IPVS lacks application-level intelligence, so Keepalived was implemented to actively probe DNS endpoints every second. If an instance fails, Keepalived dynamically updates IPVS tables. A supervisor process monitors active backend counts; if all DNS resolvers in a PoP fail, BGP Anycast announcements from that site are withdrawn to seamlessly divert queries to another node, incorporating delayed re-advertisement to avoid route flapping.

### Technical Details
- **DNS Engine Selection**: The team chose PowerDNS (pdns) as the resolver engine due to its comprehensive metrics/statistics and Lua scripting capabilities. Lists of blocked domains are managed efficiently without disrupting resolver performance.
- **Central Management & Dynamic Cross-Node Balancing**: A central management server monitors real-time load across nodes. By establishing cross-node Layer 2 tunnels between load balancers and backend resolvers in different sites, the orchestrator can dynamically offload queries from saturated nodes to idle nodes without breaking BGP routes.
- **Security and Compliance Filtering**: The cluster integrates daily updates to block malware and satisfy legal requirements (such as the Polish register of banned gambling domains, sinkholing clients to ministerial advisory pages). On peak days, the system blocks up to nearly one million domain queries.
- **Real-World Monitoring with Probes**: Beyond aggregating metrics in Zabbix and analyzing week-over-week trends, hardware probes deployed on DOCSIS, GPON, and core links simulate real user web browsing, television, and resolution requests. Measured response times average around 2–3 ms on GPON and 13 ms on DOCSIS, outperforming external public resolvers (such as 1.1.1.1).

### Takeaways
- Software-defined architectures using standard open-source tools (Linux IPVS in Direct Routing mode, Keepalived, BGP Anycast, and PowerDNS) can reliably handle high-throughput recursive DNS (200k+ QPS) at low cost.
- Avoiding return-path routing on load balancers drastically preserves system capacity.
- Automated route withdrawal, hysteresis to prevent flapping, and synthetic end-user probing are essential to guarantee continuous service availability and high customer quality of experience.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Jarosław Grabowski - The Age of Enlightenment is Coming, or Telemetry in Networks
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding PLNOG22 - Jarosław Grabowski - The Age of Enlightenment is Coming, or Telemetry in Networks.
talks.summary:
### Overview
During the PLNOG22 conference, Jarosław Grabowski presented a session on network telemetry as an evolution beyond traditional network monitoring mechanisms like SNMP. The talk focuses on the operational shortcomings of SNMP, architectural models for streaming telemetry from network devices, and practical ways network engineers can build and experiment with telemetry labs at minimal cost using virtual machines and open-source software.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of SNMP**: SNMP requires specific, manual polling of hierarchical OID trees. In large environments with hundreds of devices and thousands of ports, pulling data periodically creates high query overhead, provides only fragmented snapshots in time, and frequently misses transient state changes that happen between polling intervals.
- **Push vs. Pull Model**: Telemetry places the transmission mechanism directly on the network device, streaming structured state information outward to one or more collectors in near real-time.
- **Operating System Architecture**: Operating systems traditionally split telemetry into internal helper processes that poll other processes, which can degrade stability and recreate polling bottlenecks internally. In contrast, Arista's architecture centralizes state in an internal database (SysDB). Operational processes are stateless consumers; when any state changes, the central process automatically streams updates internally to subscribed agents and externally to collectors.
- **Unified Software Images**: Arista utilizes a single binary operating system image across more than 200 hardware models and multiple ASIC families. This approach standardizes telemetry feeds, CLI, and APIs, avoiding behavior discrepancies caused by maintaining separate code branches.

### Technical Details
- **Data Volume and Performance**: Even in a stable state, a single device typically generates 100 to 200 events per second, resulting in roughly 1 GB of telemetry data per device per day. Efficient encapsulation and compression are necessary to manage transport and storage.
- **Lab Environment & Demo**: The speaker demonstrated telemetry streaming using GNS3 on a home server running virtualized Arista switches and Arista CloudVision. In the live demo, modifying an interface description (`hello plnog`) propagated instantly to CloudVision without manual polling. For open-source setups, engineers can combine Arista virtual machines with time-series databases and tools like Prometheus, Grafana, or Kibana.
- **In-band Telemetry and Analytics**: Ongoing developments include In-band Telemetry (INT), where metadata is injected into packet headers, updated across network hops, and stripped upon network exit. Because the resulting dataset constitutes a big data challenge, automated analytic background processes ("turbines") continuously parse the database to detect anomalies and flag unexpected network behavior.

### Takeaways
Streaming telemetry provides a real-time, high-fidelity view of network states that eliminates the visibility gaps inherent in periodic SNMP polling. Network engineers can test and validate end-to-end telemetry pipelines locally using virtual machines, GNS3, and open-source stacks like Prometheus and Grafana before implementing large-scale historical retention and automated anomaly detection.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Artur Gmaj & Robert Ślaski - Czym dziś routujemy w sieciach operatorskich
talks.teaser: Surveys the router platforms used in operator networks, weighing hardware architecture, scale limits and operating systems.
talks.summary:
The talk asks which routers operator networks rely on today. It starts with the history of routing, recalling early router-like devices from the late 1960s and 1990s, and then widens the idea of an operator beyond internet providers to include city, industrial and regional network operators and providers of tailored services.

The middle section compares platforms by what should drive the choice: throughput, features, price, and the balance between hardware ASICs and programmable CPUs. One case shows the limits of capacity. A router rated for two million prefixes was deployed for a customer whose routing table grew to about 1.9 million prefixes. After roughly a dozen hours, its CPU utilization sat near 99.5 percent, and the device was being replaced. The speakers also cover memory sizing for full routing tables, the shift of network operating systems toward Linux-based platforms, and physical limits such as chassis depth in data-center cabinets, interface density, and the power draw of high-speed ports.

The talk closes by walking through example platforms, from small fixed boxes to large modular chassis, grouped by scale and feature set. The main takeaway is that the right router depends on the functions required and the expected growth, and that an operator should know exactly what it needs to configure before choosing hardware.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Piotr Wojciechowski - I tak to ty zbudujesz automatyzację
talks.teaser: Shows how to join several infrastructure automation systems, avoid common pitfalls, and why knowledge transfer matters.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common enterprise situation: infrastructure comes from many vendors, each offering its own automation with impressive demos, and the organisation is left to connect the pieces itself, including links to internal systems. The speaker argues that automation is a continuous process involving the whole IT team, not a product bought from a box, and that the goal is to connect systems through APIs instead of building isolated islands tied to one vendor.

In the middle, the speaker walks through pitfalls seen in practice: adapting business processes to a product rather than the reverse, treating a vendor offer as a remedy for everything, and keeping business goals apart from the daily engineering work. He recommends building standard service templates, testing what was deployed, documenting changes, and keeping configurations simple enough for a newcomer to understand.

The talk closes with a case from a company that moved manual, mail-based approvals and document handling into automated workflows. Staff time was freed for work that earned money, and the change was made in small steps. The takeaway is to start with a few systems where savings are clear, avoid reinventing existing tools, and spread knowledge across the team.

talks.title: PLNOG22 - Marcin Marciniak - From Pole to Pole - Communication Before the Internet Era
talks.teaser: Traces pre-internet communication in Poland, from telegraphs and manual exchanges to maritime radio and microwave links.
talks.summary:
Marcin Marciniak opens with a thought experiment: a world without social networks, television, radio or the internet, where messages travel by post, telegraph and telephone. He then traces the telegraph, from hand-keyed lines and paper tape to the automatic telegram networks used in Poland, which were only retired in the 1990s. Telephony follows, with manual switchboards staffed mostly by women, the move to automatic exchanges, and the signalling that let an exchange route a call.

The middle of the talk covers maritime radio. Coast stations such as those at Szczecin and Gdynia relayed telegrams to ships, broadcast lists of waiting messages at scheduled times, and followed strict procedures, including silence periods reserved for distress calls. The speaker shows example forms and recordings and describes the transmitter hardware used in Poland. Longer-distance links come next: tropospheric scatter stations, military microwave networks from the Cold War era, and a Soviet system that carried telephone and television to remote northern regions.

To close, the speaker notes how little of the old equipment survives. He points to microwave links that are still used today, mainly by financial firms, because radio through the air is faster than light in optical fibre. The takeaway is how much earlier infrastructure shaped the reach and reliability of today's networks.

talks.title: JDD 2018: Optimal control, no! Than what? (...) by Tomasz sikora
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning JDD 2018: Optimal control, no! Than what? (...) by Tomasz sikora.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Tomasz Sikora discusses the evolution from computational exactness to practical optimization, using Go and AlphaGo as a pivotal example of when exact computation must yield to approximate methods. He argues that many real-world business problems cannot be solved with pure brute force, and presents a spectrum of optimization algorithms suited for different scenarios.

## Key Problems and Context
The speaker identifies a recurring business challenge: given a table with many attributes (columns) and potentially billions of rows, find the minimum or maximum value across a dataset as efficiently as possible. Traditional database indexing may not work if calculations involve third-party API calls or complex logic. He emphasizes that before adopting deep reinforcement learning or complex frameworks, practitioners should explore simpler metaheuristic methods.

## Optimization Algorithms Presented

**Simulated Annealing**: Inspired by metallurgy, this approach performs random search through a parameter space while gradually reducing randomness (lowering temperature). Tested on a highly multimodal benchmark function in 2D, 5D, and 30D spaces, it checked ~360,000 points in 30-dimensional space to approximate the global minimum efficiently in real-time.

**Differential Evolution**: A population-based method using genetic operators (crossover, mutation). Unlike genetic algorithms, it simplifies implementation by avoiding explicit operator design. On the same test function, it checked ~300,000 points in 3D space with proper parameter tuning (300 genes, population of 100). Supports multi-threading for parallel execution.

**Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)**: Simulates social cooperation among agents (particles) exploring the search space. Introduced approximately 22 years prior to the talk. With 25 particles, it found good approximations using 250,000 checks in 2D. Scaling to 30 dimensions with 50 particles and reduced iterations required only 5,000 tries, demonstrating efficiency in higher-dimensional spaces.

## Reinforcement Learning and Deep Learning
The speaker briefly covers reinforcement learning, where agents take actions, observe state changes, and receive rewards or punishments. He presents DeepMind's Atari game solver (solving 260 games) as an example of end-to-end learning using convolutional neural networks. The Atari example involves 84×84 pixel inputs with 256 colors and movement tracking—a massive search space (10^8,68,000 possibilities). However, he cautions that deep reinforcement learning should not be the default choice for business problems.

## Key Takeaways
1. **Abandon perfectionism**: The goal is a "good enough" solution, not global optimality, especially given computational constraints.
2. **Start simple**: Before investing in heavy frameworks or AWS infrastructure, test lightweight implementations (often 4–5 classes on GitHub).
3. **Unit test with benchmarks**: Use continuous benchmark functions to validate algorithm selection for specific business problems.
4. **Match method to problem**: Simulated annealing, differential evolution, PSO, and ABC each have strengths depending on dimensionality and function characteristics.
5. **Java limitations**: Java is not ideal for deep learning; consider Python microservices called via REST instead.
6. **Accept risk**: Local minima are an inherent risk, but interactive refinement with business stakeholders can help define acceptable solutions.

## Q&A Highlights
Audience questions addressed real-world applicability (table with 20 columns, 1 million rows), the requirement for continuous/differentiable functions (gradient methods require this; metaheuristics do not), and how to detect sufficient training convergence. Sikora emphasizes that discrete-space and non-differentiable problems favor metaheuristic (Monte Carlo-based) methods, and that visualization and dimensionality analysis guide algorithm selection.

talks.title: 4Developers Wrocław 2018: Graylog: one tool to log 'em all, Piotr Przybył
talks.teaser: Shows Graylog ingesting syslog and app logs, normalizing fields with extractors, and aligning timestamps across routers and instances.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that treating logs as local console or `/var/log` tail output is outdated when events happen across servers, routers, and applications. Using metaphors for observability and remote syslog (RFC-based UDP delivery), it positions Graylog as a central place to collect, search, and analyze messages from many technologies.

The walkthrough covers quick deployment from the official appliance, default web login, and wiring sources: Linux rsyslog to port 514, Java applications via Logback and a GELF appender, and router remote logging (with pfSense-style firewall logs as a working example during live issues on the presenter’s laptop). Processing features include streams, regex extractors that normalize awkward source fields, and pipeline rules that repair timestamps when senders omit time zones—so messages do not vanish from “last five minutes” searches. A simulated multi-instance web service illustrates correlating HTTP errors across instances using structured fields.

Practitioners should expect real-world friction (firewalls, bridges, clock skew) and use wider time ranges when debugging. The closing notes mention dashboards, REST automation, Elasticsearch scaling for volume, plugins, and licensing as open source—enough to pilot Graylog on Monday in a small office.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2018 - Jarosław Stakuń
talks.teaser: Explore ten predictions for developer tooling, from collaborative web IDEs to security data embedded in the development workflow.
talks.summary: The speaker describes how container-based and distributed application architectures are changing development work, then shares ten predictions for developer tooling. These include cloud-hosted web IDEs, collaborative code editing, support for multiple languages and runtimes, more automation, and development tools that surface security and dependency information. The talk also presents Eclipse Che and related tools as examples of this shift.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2018 - Łukasz Przybył - The Panda Experiment
talks.teaser: Shows how a travel company turned embedded DevOps engineers into a floating team of infrastructure consultants and measured the change.
talks.summary:
The talk describes how a mid-sized German travel company moved from a model where developers filed tickets to a separate operations team, to one where operations engineers sat inside each development team. That placement created new silos within teams, uneven support, and painful handovers whenever someone went on holiday. The answer was a floating group of infrastructure consultants, each linked to two or three contact teams but able to help anyone.

Instead of a long manual, the group worked from five simple tenets covering equal treatment of requests, knowledge sharing, openness to discussion, challenging requests to find the real need, and getting developers involved in infrastructure. A three-month pilot with a few teams tracked developer happiness, workload distribution and resolution time. After two months a survey showed 82% of participants preferred the new setup and none gave negative feedback, so the model was rolled out to all teams. Daily work moved to a shared Jira backlog and Kanban board, with stand-ups twice a week and small requests handled on the spot.

Problems remained: some engineers slipped back into ticket-driven habits, pairing with developers lagged, and moving build servers to the cloud raised cost questions. Knowledge gaps were exposed by a monthly check asking people how confident they would be taking over another team tomorrow, which prompted targeted sharing sessions. The speaker closed with plans for self-service tooling that turns requests into reviewed pull requests, and for hiring more engineers from development backgrounds.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2018 - Thiago de Faria
talks.teaser: Explains how to move data science models into production with DevOps practices, plus a short MLflow tracking and serving demo.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a familiar handover problem: a data scientist builds a model on a laptop, presents it, and then passes it to an operations team that has to run it. The speaker argues this gap is as much cultural as technical, and that machine learning needs continuous integration, delivery and evaluation of models, with data pipelines treated as a software engineering problem. He contrasts traditional rule-based software, which is easy to test and debug, with models that learn from data and must be retrained as a whole to fix a single edge case.

The middle section covers three kinds of model risk: bias in the training data, drift as the world changes, and fragility when upstream data or schemas change. Practical problems include versioning code and data, measuring a model's effect through proxies because users rarely report wrong predictions, and getting data scientists to share work and join the on-call rotation. Ways to run these workloads were also covered, including Spark on Kubernetes, Docker containers on Hadoop 3.1, and Kubeflow.

The closing demo used MLflow to log experiment runs with their parameters and metrics, compare them, package a model, and serve it as a REST API that returns a prediction. The takeaway is that bridging data science and operations needs collaboration and shared responsibility, and that tooling for data versioning and model evaluation is still immature.
