talks.teaser: Demonstrates Test Kitchen, ServerSpec, and InSpec for test-driven Puppet, Terraform, and Packer on mutable and immutable stacks.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames infrastructure reliability around mutable versus immutable patterns. Mutable setups that apply configuration in place invite drift and fragile transitions; replacing whole instances after building and testing images reduces that risk. He assumes mature infrastructure-as-code with version control and strong teams.

The first case study covers a large OpenStack and Puppet estate at Good Data: thousands of VMs, a dense dependency graph, and brittle manual dry-run plus smoke tests. The team adopted Chef Test Kitchen with Docker system containers, the Puppet provisioner, custom fact overrides, a shim called shemagh to mock packages and commands, and ServerSpec for expectations. He walks through red-green-refactor TDD for infra, CI/CD stages from lint through Kitchen to staging and production, and reusing the same ServerSpec checks in post-deploy monitoring to catch drift.

A second story at Quantum Black (McKinsey) applies the same ideas to immutable AWS flows: Packer image builds, Kitchen-Terraform with InSpec and Terratest-style checks, propagating Terraform outputs into tests, and promoting a single tested artifact through the pipeline. He stresses blocking heavy integration on fast static checks, testing what you actually deploy, and build-once-promote-many for images.

talks.title: 4Developers 2018: DDD Q&A - czyli co gryzie programistów i programistki? (Sławomir Sobótka)
talks.teaser: Surfaces DDD guidance on aggregates, APIs, CRUD, modularization, and business dialogue tied to process and rules.
talks.summary:
The session follows an earlier introduction to domain-driven design and focuses on what teams face once they are seriously applying the approach. The speaker groups recurring dilemmas into five themes—aggregate boundaries, module APIs, living with CRUD, modularization, and earning real conversations with the business—and argues that workable answers usually depend on business process and rules, not a single technical recipe.

Aggregate design is developed through a reservation-and-product example: modeling behavior versus static structures, avoiding one huge order class with statuses that throw exceptions everywhere, and deciding when an offer is a snapshot versus a true aggregate. Four consistency patterns show when nothing needs aggregating, when the reservation or product owns rules, or when only one aggregate may commit per transaction—with event-driven follow-up where domains differ. API design contrasts document-and-command flows (bureaucratic “applications” and hypermedia-style next steps) with naive resource CRUD; read models and CQRS are positioned for screens that are not the domain core. A cautionary integration story highlights version-churning low-level events across hundreds of services versus publishing stable business facts.

For organizational alignment, the speaker recommends event storming in the past tense, separating events from rules, and reading stakeholders’ metaphors. Practitioners should treat tactical patterns as tools to surface business questions, keep logic at the aggregate that owns the truth, and treat modular boundaries as a strategic exercise that resists copy-paste DTO coupling.

talks.teaser: Shows Java programmers how monads tame side effects using Vavr, map, flatMap, and compiler-checked error handling.
talks.summary:
The session opens by reassuring a tired conference audience that monads need not be frightening or purely theoretical. The speaker argues that annotation-driven frameworks such as Spring encourage risky runtime magic, illustrated with @Transactional failures: private methods after refactors, calls across threads, self-invocation without proxies, custom aspect jars missing from production, and a real banking case where transactions silently stopped for months while tests stayed green.

The core lesson reframes monads as a type plus an explicit effect. Starting from nested null checks on user, group, and admin lookups, the talk moves through Optional with map and flatMap, Vavr’s immutable collections, Either for typed failures instead of exceptions, Try for legacy throws, and briefly Future, Reader, and stacked effects including the limits of composing Try with Future.

Practitioners should leave treating monads as everyday tools: keep effects in types, prefer map and flatMap over get, and let the compiler block incomplete handling. Functional style here means side effects stay visible and refactorings stay safer than imperative code that hides failure modes until production.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2018: Andy Davies - FEATURE TOGGLES: THE GOOD, THE BAD, AND THE UGLY
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Atmosphere 2018: Andy Davies - FEATURE TOGGLES: THE GOOD, THE BAD, AND THE UGLY.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Andy Davies explores the operational realities, benefits, and severe pitfalls of using feature toggles in software engineering. Drawing from catastrophic real-world failures, successful enterprise turnarounds, and personal development experiences, the presentation illustrates how improper toggle management can destroy a business, whereas disciplined implementation accelerates continuous delivery and reduces technical debt.

### Key Topics
- **Catastrophic Failures and Anti-Patterns**: The presentation begins with the collapse of Knight Capital, an American high-frequency trading firm. During a deployment across eight servers, one server failed to receive the update. Knight Capital reused an existing feature toggle named for an obsolete feature ("Power Peg") to activate new functionality ("SMASH"). When enabled, the un-updated server triggered defective eight-year-old dead code that could no longer count executed orders, firing orders indefinitely. A panicked rollback to the old code exacerbated the problem across all eight servers, ultimately costing $450 million in 45 minutes and bankrupting the firm.
- **Toggle Lifecycles and Types**: Davies categorizes toggles into distinct operational roles:
  - *Release Toggles*: Facilitate continuous delivery and phased rollouts.
  - *Experiment Toggles*: Short-lived toggles tied to metrics and A/B testing (e.g., button colors).
  - *Operations Toggles*: The only category that should live long-term, used for system degradation or load shedding (such as disabling heavy background tasks during database spikes).
  - *Permission Toggles*: Strongly discouraged as an anti-pattern; user permissions belong in dedicated authentication and authorization systems (such as IdentityServer or Keycloak).
- **Binding Phases**: Toggle states can be bound at compile time, startup, periodic polling intervals, or per-activity checking. Davies warns against compile-time flags due to deployment delays when emergency changes are needed. Periodic background polling with an in-memory store is recommended for dynamic flags to avoid per-request network latency.

### Technical Details & Architecture
- **Hewlett-Packard Transformation**: HP’s printer firmware team (FutureSmart) struggled with a monolithic codebase of 10 million lines across 800 developers, releasing only twice per year with an eight-week build/test feedback cycle due to excessive branching and compile-time `#ifdef` toggles. Merging consumed 25% of developer time. By migrating to trunk-based development and startup feature flags loaded via model-specific configuration files, HP reduced feedback cycles to two days on actual printer hardware and achieved continuous deployment readiness.
- **Architectural Isolation via Branch by Abstraction**: Rather than scattering conditional toggle checks throughout the codebase, teams should use design patterns like branch by abstraction, dependency injection, factories, or decorators. For front-end code (such as React), components can be wrapped to isolate conditional rendering to a single location.
- **Case Study (Phased Email Service Rollout)**: At a previous company, an unstable SOAP-to-Exchange service was rewritten using RabbitMQ and decorator-pattern workers behind an `IEmailConnector` interface. A feature toggle routed through Active Directory groups enabled a gradual, team-by-team rollout over 6–8 weeks. Early beta testers uncovered order sequencing bottlenecks, leading to the creation of separate direct and bulk queues before full adoption. Once 100% traffic was stabilized, the toggle and old code were deleted.

### Takeaways
Davies outlines five core rules for managing feature toggles:
1. **Never reuse a feature toggle**: Always introduce a distinct toggle for new functionality.
2. **Enforce short lifespans**: Treat toggles as temporary scaffolding and delete them alongside old code immediately after rollout (operations toggles being the rare exception).
3. **Name toggles explicitly**: Avoid obscure ticket numbers or vague labels; names must communicate exact intent.
4. **Maintain sound architecture**: Feature toggles are not an excuse for messy code; encapsulate toggle checks in single integration points.
5. **Monitor toggle usage**: Track how frequently toggles are queried and evaluate rollout metrics to know precisely when code is safe to clean up.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2018: Jukka Forsgren
talks.teaser: Shows how Spinnaker runs multi-cloud delivery pipelines, from image baking to deployment, with lessons from a real rollout.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a cloud architect, describes a customer whose custom Lambda-based deployment system for AWS auto scaling groups was built by an engineer who had since left, which prompted a search for an open source replacement. Manual release processes that depend on emails and calendar bookings are presented as slow, while automated pipelines allow frequent releases backed by automated tests.

Spinnaker, which Netflix started and open sourced in 2015, is shown running as a set of microservices, usually on Kubernetes, in a demo instance. Pipelines begin with triggers such as cron, Git, Jenkins, Travis, Docker registries and webhooks, then pass through a Packer-based bake stage, deploy stages targeting configured cloud accounts, and strategies such as red/black, with rolling red/black still experimental. The speaker recommends templated pipelines applied from Git through a CLI, and shows a custom strategy used for smoke tests plus a stage that runs a Docker container on Kubernetes.

The closing part covers installation options (Halyard, a Docker container, and a Helm chart for quick tests), a comparison of the Kubernetes v1 provider with the unfinished v2 provider, and lessons learned. Attendees should adopt an open source mindset, budget months rather than weeks, expect fiddly configuration, and check the Armory documentation. For a simple Kubernetes-only setup, the speaker suggests that a Jenkins pipeline pushing images may suffice.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2018: Oleksii Kliukin - POSTGRESQL HIGH AVAILABILITY ON KUBERNETES WITH PATRONI
talks.teaser: Shows how Patroni-managed PostgreSQL clusters get automatic failover and run on Kubernetes, with a live demo of the setup.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a database engineer at a German retailer, explains why the company runs PostgreSQL for critical payment data and how its setup moved from physical data centers to AWS and then to Kubernetes. The early environments lacked automatic failover, so the team wrote Patroni, an open source failover manager. Patroni keeps cluster state in a distributed key-value store and relies on atomic lock operations so that only one primary exists at any time.

On Kubernetes, the team first looked at StatefulSets, which were slow to reattach volumes, and then at Helm, which still required manual steps. They built a custom operator that turns a short cluster manifest into StatefulSets, services, secrets and disruption budgets. The operator creates users and databases, performs rolling restarts by failing over before restarting a node, and corrects drift from the declared state. To avoid running a separate etcd cluster, they stored leader and member information in Kubernetes annotations and endpoints. The talk also covers a custom PAM module that lets staff log in with short-lived tokens instead of stored passwords.

A live demo created a test cluster from a manifest, showed the primary and replica pods bootstrapping, and checked that the primary was not in recovery. The main takeaway is that databases on Kubernetes are workable when failover, configuration and credentials are automated. The speaker also stresses that Patroni does not replace monitoring or routine maintenance such as vacuuming.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2018: Tetiana Khotiaintseva
talks.teaser: A live service map built from traces and host data gives Allegro engineers quick intuition during outages and post-mortems.
talks.summary:
Allegro runs more than five hundred microservices and adds more daily, so hand-drawn topology and stale institutional knowledge no longer match reality. Standard dashboards excel at reactive investigation after alerts, but the monitoring team needs a quick, holistic read of whether the platform is healthy right now—a need Netflix framed as intuition engineering.

The presentation walks through Netflix’s open-source Visceral UI and a failover demo, then Allegro’s Phobos: same front-end stack, but grouped by business areas and tied to business-process impact rather than regional traffic volume. Phobos merges host runners that snapshot TCP connections on Mesos nodes with Zipkin trace hierarchies, streams both through Kafka into Spark jobs, stores connection maps in Cassandra, and serves graph JSON via a Python backend. Custom renderers support drilling into areas and individual hosts; notices refresh every thirty seconds while topology refreshes every minute, with partial fetches to keep the view responsive.

Primary uses include scoping live outages, replaying history for post-mortems, and teaching how requests flow. The speaker notes incomplete Zipkin instrumentation across heterogeneous languages, roughly one-minute end-to-end delay, and a planned move from Cassandra to a graph database. Phobos remains internal, though some collectors might be separable for open source.

talks.title: 4Developers 2018: RxJS: Everything is a stream (Tomasz Ducin)
talks.teaser: Clarifies RxJS through streams, inversion of control, multicast subjects, and alternatives to hot-versus-cold labels.
talks.summary:
The session argues that teams often compare JavaScript stacks without understanding the patterns underneath, and uses RxJS to make those patterns concrete. It extends the idea that everything can be treated as a stream, then contrasts reactive streams with arrays, generators, and promises, emphasizing time, laziness, pull versus push, backpressure, and the need for an active subscriber.

A live audience exercise models the observer pattern and Hollywood-style inversion of control, linking the same ideas to Redux, declarative UI work, and combineLatest-style currency examples that avoid manual synchronization. The talk then reframes familiar hot versus cold labels as unicast versus multicast behavior, explains subjects as proxies for many subscribers, and walks through publish, refCount, connect, and share alongside behavior, replay, and async subject metaphors.

It closes with a decision ladder for asynchronous JavaScript: callbacks and promises for one-shot work, generators and async/await where pull fits, and streams when many dependent values change over time and events form a graph that reactive composition can keep aligned.

talks.title: 4Developers 2018: TensorFlow - od zera do jeden (Mateusz Budzar)
talks.teaser: Builds a TensorFlow neural classifier step by step in Jupyter, from data prep through training and evaluation on a tabular dataset.
talks.summary:
The session opens as a hands-on introduction meant to pair short theory with practice: what programming, machine learning, and deep learning mean in plain terms, and why TensorFlow is described as Google’s open library for implementing learning systems. The running example uses a CSV of blood-test style measurements to predict whether someone averages at least ten alcoholic drinks per day, framed as a binary “likes” versus “does not like” classification problem.

After setting up Anaconda and Jupyter Notebook, the presenter loads the dataset with pandas, selects five feature columns, simplifies the label, and splits records into training and test sets. Data is scaled with a min-max scaler fit on training data only. The talk explains a single neuron as weighted inputs plus bias and activation, then why one neuron may fail on non-linearly separable data—illustrated with TensorFlow Playground and a brief MNIST training animation before returning to code.

A Keras-style `DNNClassifier` with hidden units is defined in TensorFlow Estimators, features are wired in, and the model is trained with batches and steps, then evaluated on held-out data with accuracy reported around ninety-four percent. The close recaps the pipeline—load, clean, split, scale, train, test—and invites questions on scaling choices, saving graphs, model size on mobile versus backend inference, and TensorFlow Lite.

talks.title: 4Developers 2018: The turbulent road to byte (Piotr Balcer)
talks.teaser: Shows how byte-addressable persistent memory changes storage design, and how pointers and atomic transactions are handled in C++.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the problem: storage has always been block based, reached through layers of file systems, the kernel and database software. Byte-addressable persistent memory, which sits in memory slots yet keeps its contents across reboots, lets an application reach data directly and avoid many of those layers. The speaker, who works on a data center memory group, places this hardware between DRAM and NVMe SSDs and notes that current 3D XPoint drives still expose block interfaces.

The middle covers why ordinary programming breaks down. Pointers from mapped files are not fixed between runs, so the approach uses offsets relative to the mapped pool, a pool identifier and a root object. Writes are atomic only at 8 bytes and caches must be flushed, so larger updates need transactions. The first C runtime, built on setjmp and longjmp, was error-prone, so the C++ version offers persistent smart pointers and closure-based transactions. An attempt to reuse standard containers failed because their allocator pointer types and internal details could not be intercepted for rollback, so the team forked an LLVM C++ library and plans its own containers.

The closing part looks at ongoing standardization work, including a proposed low-level persistent map and transactional memory extensions that could intercept loads and stores automatically. The speaker's takeaway is that developers need to build higher-level interfaces on top of the 8-byte guarantee, and invites the audience to get involved.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2018: Mirosław Nagaś - HOW (NOT) TO MIGRATE TO A NEW APPLICATION PLATFORM
talks.teaser: The session explains how over-scoping and months of PoC work left a platform migration with no production clusters or migrated services.
talks.summary:
The presenter walks through Base’s attempt to leave a homegrown application platform that had carried production since 2012—dozens of nodes, thousands of workers, and roughly 150 microservices—and replace it with a “Nextgen” stack. Leadership planned about ten months of work for four people, but shifting organizational priorities meant the effort lasted only five to six months with a smaller team and ended without a production cluster or any production service migrated.

Most of that time went into roadmaps, tooling research, and proofs of concept: cluster provisioning, cross-platform routing, Linkerd deployment modes, configuration and secrets management, Helm-based deployments, and even commercial-support discussions—while coding spikes produced plugins such as a Helm secrets integration and later test harnesses. The speaker ties the stall to Brooks’s second-system effect: soliciting wide stakeholder wish lists and trying to ship a feature-complete platform for years ahead instead of incremental value. They also describe how a Nomad evaluation meant to fit two sprints dragged on, daily infrastructure churn broke sandbox and staging, and stability reviews exposed poor change visibility until scenario-based tests and a failure-as-a-service tool improved feedback.

The closing lesson is that migrating even one service spans clustering, routing, packaging, observability, security, and reliability concerns, and that stabilizing non-production environments and automated validation matter as much as choosing Kubernetes or Nomad. An update notes eventual success: services on Nomad with about 25% of production traffic shifted there.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2018: Milos Malik
talks.teaser: Walks through troubleshooting SELinux denials, from confirming the cause in audit logs to fixing labels and policy rules.
talks.summary:
This talk is a practical walkthrough of troubleshooting SELinux for users and administrators whose applications fail or misbehave under enforcing mode. The speaker presents SELinux as a complex system and cites bug statistics since 2012, showing that policy bugs far outnumber user-space bugs, with roughly a tenfold difference in one comparison. The stated aim is to help attendees cope with common policy problems and keep SELinux enforcing rather than permissive or disabled.

The workflow moves through five phases. Identification checks whether SELinux is really behind a failure by searching the audit log for denial messages, which can appear before the audit daemon starts and need a different lookup. Analysis then reads a denial's source and target labels, the permission and the command involved, and uses tools such as restorecon to compare file labels with policy, se search to find allow rules, and audit2allow to turn denials into rules or a policy module.

Conservative fixes come first. semanage can add a non-default port to a service's label, so a daemon moved off its usual port can start, and restorecon repairs files whose labels drifted while SELinux was disabled. Radical fixes change or write policy modules, with sepolicy generate as a starting point. The speaker warns that denials involving executable memory or writes to kernel module objects deserve scrutiny, since the kernel is trusted. The talk closes with a troubleshooting flowchart and a request for feedback on where it falls short.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2018: Marcin Stożek - PROGRAMMABLE API GATEWAY WITH A TOUCH OF MOONLIGHT
talks.teaser: Shows how to change requests and responses on the fly at an nginx gateway using OpenResty and Lua.
talks.summary:
Marcin Stożek, from a small Kraków startup, describes a case where he had to add behaviour to an application he received from an outside party and could not easily change. Early ideas such as a CGI layer or a separate Java service felt heavy for such a small job. A colleague pointed him to OpenResty, which bundles Lua scripting into nginx. The talk gives a short background on Lua, a compact language from Brazil that is easy to read and runs fast under LuaJIT.

The demos run on Docker Compose. A simple handler returns a greeting, then a correlation ID is added to forwarded requests and removed from responses, and a response body is rewritten on the fly, which suits legacy applications. Routing decisions are read from Redis based on the user agent, with notes on sharing database connections per worker and the thread-safety that requires. Image thumbnails are generated on demand behind a signed URL. A web application firewall style check blocks a request carrying a script alert, and a honeypot idea diverts suspicious requests to a logging server. Finally, Kong, built on OpenResty, gets a service, a route, key authentication and a correlation ID plugin added at runtime.

Benchmarks showed that Docker's network proxy slowed requests and that generating random IDs added measurable cost. The takeaway is that Lua inside nginx lets teams change traffic without touching the application, though it does not carry over to Apache. In questions, an attendee described automatic Let's Encrypt certificate creation through an OpenResty module.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2018: J. Szatyłowicz & M. Biela - 24/7 ONLINE SERVCIES ON AWS EC2 SPOT INSTANCES
talks.teaser: Explains how spot instances cut EC2 costs and how paired auto scaling groups kept production services up through interruptions.
talks.summary:
The talk covers Amazon EC2 spot instances, which AWS offers at a steep discount to on-demand prices in return for the right to reclaim them with about two minutes' notice. The speakers explain how spot prices behaved over the previous year, with large spikes at first and later a flatter pricing model and per-second billing. They describe three ways to learn about an interruption: the instance metadata endpoint, the spot request status API and CLI, and CloudWatch events. They then compare the request types, including standard spot requests, fixed-duration spot blocks and spot fleets, and explain why they chose Auto Scaling groups, since fleets could not scale their on-demand portion.

Their in-house tool, Spotty, runs a paired spot and on-demand Auto Scaling group for each service and keeps no database, using AWS tags as state. When spot capacity is about to disappear, it raises the on-demand desired count first and lowers the spot count once the warning passes. They also describe problems they hit. Zone imbalance appeared when a whole zone lost spot capacity, and they fixed it by splitting groups per availability zone. They also ran into API call limits and instance quotas, and they found that switching to a new instance family could fail because capacity arrived late.

The speakers report that spot instances made up more than half of their largest product's capacity and that overall EC2 billing fell by roughly 25 percent. Their practical advice is to keep on-demand capacity as a safety net, request quota increases early, avoid abrupt instance family changes, and drain stateful services when a termination notice arrives. They said they planned to open source the tool.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Bezpieczeństwo przy tysiącach wdrożeń (Wojciech Lesicki, Paweł Czubachowski)
talks.teaser: Shows how automated security scanners and pipeline checks keep thousands of monthly microservice deployments under control.
talks.summary:
Allegro's application security team describes how its deployment volume has grown to thousands of releases a month across more than 500 microservices, which makes manual testing of every release impossible. They also explain why DevOps and security teams weigh risk differently.

The core of the talk is an automated security pipeline. A build triggers a service that selects which scanners apply to a repository and publishes events to a messaging bus, where worker services wrap static analysis tools. A verification service filters out findings already marked as false positives before a report returns to the developer through the build pipeline. Most static scans finish in about three minutes, and the longest, on a large monolith, takes around ten minutes. In one sample, about 70 valid findings came with roughly 55 false positives. Dynamic scanners run daily against a test environment and take hours, but had produced no false positives so far.

The team also built a library scanner after a vulnerable framework was disclosed, letting them find affected projects in minutes instead of hours. They also run penetration tests and red team exercises, consult developers early in design, hold internal CTFs and reward staff who report bugs, and rotate people between teams for one to three months. Their takeaway: automation removes basic mistakes so specialists can focus on serious threats, and security must supply developers with both tools and knowledge.

talks.title: Bitspiartion 2018: Marcin Kwieciński, Jak ogarnąć chaos (nie tylko) w sprzedaży?
talks.teaser: Shows how to plan time, set priorities and avoid overwork while still reaching ambitious sales goals.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a metaphor: everyone receives the same daily budget of 86,400 seconds, which cannot be saved and is lost if unused. The speaker argues that few people manage this resource deliberately, and that doing so can give a competitive edge. Productivity is framed as producing the results you want without burning out, with the focus on personal habits rather than team or company processes.

The middle section sets out a sequence of initiative, design, planning and execution. Initiative means separating what you can influence from what only concerns you. Design is a picture of where you want to be in two or three years, and planning turns that into yearly goals and weekly steps. Practical tips include assuming tasks will take about twice as long as estimated, planning no more than about 60 percent of your time, and blocking calendar slots for work you know will come up. A weekly review spreads 15 tokens across priorities, each worth an hour, and the speaker suggests protecting focus because regaining it after an interruption can take around 15 minutes. He also covers delegating routine paperwork to a lower-cost or virtual assistant, and choosing mentors by asking them specific questions. The Milgram experiment illustrates how easily people hand over decisions to an authority.

The closing advice is to pick one to three ideas and apply them within the current month, since not everything can be adopted at once. The takeaways are selectivity, intentionality and cleverness, along with the reminder that each listener owns their own time.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Practical intelligence-driven defense (Igor Ivanov, Daniil Yugoslavskiy)
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn to extend MITRE ATT&CK into complete detection use cases and prove coverage with automated adversary simulations.
talks.summary:
The speakers open by positioning intelligence-driven defense as an extension of classical security, anchored on the cyber kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK. They argue the public ATT&CK matrix is too high level to drive detections directly, so their organization built an extended use-case framework in a Confluence knowledge base. Each use case ties a technique to triggering conditions, required data sources, logging policies, alerts, correlation logic, and analytics.

They walk through DNS exfiltration as a concrete example: which logs to collect, how to enable DNS query logging, high-level detection logic that works across SIEM products, and commands that trigger the alert for testing. The second half covers continuous validation by wrapping one-liner technique tests and full attack chains in DevOps-style automation, choosing UberMeta for cross-platform playbooks. They map the documented Phineas Fisher attack against Hacking Team to ATT&CK and run a Jeunesse Fisher scenario, comparing simulated red activity in Kibana to expected technique coverage.

Audience takeaways include treating completeness as the quality bar—logging, data, and detection stay linked so customers know what to deploy—and using threat reports or breach write-ups as simulation profiles to measure whether alerts actually fire. Q&A clarifies the framework content is proprietary while methodology is shared, mitigation and automated blocking sit in the same model but were out of scope for this session, and machine learning is deferred in favor of solid fundamentals and in-house verification of intelligence.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Darknet (Piotr Bazydło)
talks.teaser: Shows how unused IP address space captures scans and backscatter, letting analysts fingerprint botnets and DDoS campaigns.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a darknet, meaning blocks of IP addresses that should be unused and so should see no traffic. The speaker explains the sources of what still arrives there: misconfigured devices, hosts scanning for open ports or vulnerable devices, backscatter from spoofed denial-of-service attacks, and UDP exploitation attempts. Because the sensor only sinkholes traffic and never answers, it sees one side of each exchange. Volume is large, with roughly 25 billion packets a month across more than 100,000 addresses, so the data has to be grouped into events and classified before it is useful.

The middle of the talk walks through cases. A rise in scans on port 8080 matched a signature tied to Mirai-derived code and, once a public alert described a new Satori variant exploiting routers, was linked to that botnet, with about 35,000 infected addresses counted over a few days, many in Asia. A burst of memcached scanning grew around the GitHub attack, and source port choices and payload details were used to group scanners into likely actors. Backscatter from a flood against Telegram in Russia showed SYN/ACK replies and later traffic that may have been mitigation, and ICMP errors exposed the original spoofed packets.

The speaker then covers packet generation algorithm (PGA) signatures, where header fields such as IP ID, sequence number and source port follow patterns that point to a specific tool. A small experiment compared random generation with a botnet's signature and showed the signature approach to be faster. The takeaways are that darknet data can help forecast campaigns and track botnets over time, and that it is most useful when correlated with honeypots and sandboxes. The speaker invited collaboration on mapping PGA signatures to tools and malware.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Security Awareness for VIPs. Piece of cake or a tough nut to crack? (Piotr Peszko)
talks.teaser: Shows how to tailor security awareness training for executives and VIPs using behavior models and one-on-one sessions.
talks.summary:
Piotr Peszko, who works on security awareness at ABB, argues that teaching executives and other VIPs is harder than teaching general staff. Standard compliance training, measured by completion certificates, tells an organisation little about whether people act securely, and senior leaders are busy and rarely care about certificates. The talk therefore shifts the focus from completion to behaviour.

To frame behaviour change, the talk borrows from BJ Fogg's model, in which a behaviour happens when a trigger meets enough motivation and ability. Reporting a phishing email is the running example: make the report a single click, and repeat simulations so people build a routine. For designing materials, the speaker suggests the CCAF loop from Michael Allen (context, challenge, action, feedback). For VIPs, the team first approaches their assistants, observes how they work with their own tools and routines, identifies needs, and then runs one-on-one sessions of roughly 45 minutes to an hour using real cases, real devices and examples from personal life such as home security.

Early results included requests from other teams for similar sessions, and the speaker gave the target pool as about nine and a half thousand employees. Measurement covers delivery, consumption and behaviour, including the ratio of phishing links clicked to emails reported. In the Q&A, the speaker argued against quizzes as proof of learning and against public scoreboards, and suggested that a backdoor route through assistants often works better than an official rollout.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Detecting Phishing from pDNS (Irena Damsky)
talks.teaser: Shows how passive DNS records and simple domain features can flag phishing domains before users reach them.
talks.summary:
The talk explains phishing and the domain name system, then introduces passive DNS, a historical record of name lookups captured by network sensors. Because only lookups that really happened appear, a domain's first sighting shows when someone first visited it, not when it was registered. Collection options include sensors above recursive resolvers, scraping zone files, buying vendor datasets, or building a private store of domain-to-IP records from port 53 logs.

Its central part is a set of symptoms for scoring suspicious domains, starting from a brand keyword. One day of data for names beginning with Microsoft returned about 7,500 domains, many of which Microsoft does not own. Warning signs included many subdomain labels, repeated labels, cheap new top-level domains, hyphens in second-level domains, and URL paths rewritten as dotted names. Typosquatting variants and mixed scripts within one name also raised scores. Lookup services that prepend a queried name to their own domain should be whitelisted. Shared IPs, networks and dedicated name servers can reveal clusters worth blocking.

The speaker closed with follow-up ideas: scraping pages behind flagged domains for trackers, attributing campaigns, and spotting a shared substring that suggests one phishing kit. Machine learning could extend the approach beyond known brands, but simple scoring on data an organization already holds works well. Scores should be reviewed before blocking anything.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2018: Bartosz Majewski, Budowanie sprzedaży w małych i średnich firmach B2B
talks.teaser: Delivers trench B2B sales lessons on first-call structure, funnel analytics, lead quality, rep onboarding, and cash-focused growth for SMBs.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that most small and medium B2B firms mishandle the first sales conversation, then walks through a simple meeting flow: introduction, a question phase meant to close three kinds of information asymmetry, restating the prospect’s problem for confirmation, a deliberately short solution pitch, and explicit next steps including follow-up timing.

A large middle section treats measurement as management. It covers stage-to-stage conversion, time in each stage, and segmented loss reasons; stresses weekly or monthly review cycles; and separates quantity metrics from lead-quality signals visible before and after the first call, including practical budget questions. It also addresses intellectual honesty about forecasts, onboarding new reps through intensive role-play modeled on tough clients, exit interviews when customers leave, and hard people decisions in a values-and-performance matrix.

Later topics include raising prices without punishing early believers, deferring automation until roughly a hundred leads per month, minimum deal size before in-person meetings, founder transition from top closer to manager, concentration risk among top accounts, personal financial discipline for founders, and treating cash and upfront payment as the main buffer in downturns. It closes by urging practitioners to copy tactics only from businesses with similar deal size and margin, not from distant success stories.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Busting Advanced BotNet’s (Senad Aruc)
talks.teaser: Shows how researchers infiltrated botnet control panels to reveal campaign setup, stolen data, and banking fraud tactics.
talks.summary:
Senad Aruc describes how his research team broke into the control panels of several well-known botnets to see what operators did after infection, rather than analysing the malware alone. The first case is an early ransomware operation from 2014. Its panel held per-country campaign configurations, harvested email lists, SMTP details, payment settings tied to Bitcoin addresses, and chat logs in which victims who had paid reported never receiving decryption keys.

The middle of the talk covers banking and device botnets. One kit was a builder for man-in-the-middle browser injections, with victims routed by geolocation and features that hid transfers from the user. Another automated money drops that split stolen funds between operators and mule accounts. A Shellshock-based campaign against QNAP NAS devices patched the flaw to lock out rivals, installed a CGI backdoor, added DDoS tooling, and kept scanning for more hosts, with around 25,000 seen at one time. A final all-in-one kit paired an Android app that forwarded SMS second-factor codes with bank-specific injected text.

The end of the talk turns to how the team found and disrupted these operations. Weak points included misconfigured web servers, vulnerable panels, and leftover backup archives, which made directory enumeration useful. Takedown requests to hosting providers and fake card data pushed into drop zones were other tactics, though removing a panel can make operators harder to track afterwards. The talk points to a full research set covering more than twenty-five botnets.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Hunting for the secrets in a cloud forest (Paweł Rzepa)
talks.teaser: Explores how cloud access keys and public storage buckets leak, and how entropy-based scanning can catch them.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how cloud access keys leak and why they are harder to contain than ordinary passwords. The speaker argues the cause is usually customer configuration. Keys tend to be hard-coded, are rarely rotated, and are difficult to protect with multi-factor authentication for programmatic access. Public storage buckets also remain common, and a legacy "any authenticated AWS user" group stayed assignable through the command line after it was removed from the console.

To measure exposure, the speaker built a bucket scanner and collected bucket names from certificate transparency logs and archive snapshots. Of almost 25,000 valid buckets, more than 5,000 allowed public reads and 6% allowed writes. Backups inside them held scripts, passwords, private keys and whole databases. Other routes included keys handed to browsers by a web application, server-side request forgery reaching the instance metadata service, and secrets pasted into forums or public repositories. One case involved a job candidate's public repository that exposed keys, which led to a bill of almost $100,000 from cryptocurrency mining.

For detection, the speaker noted that access keys have a fixed length and draw random base64 characters, which gives them high Shannon entropy. AWS secret keys measured above 4.3 in the speaker's tests. The speaker presented Dumpster Diver, an MIT-licensed tool that scans files, archives and git history for such strings, with adjustable lengths and rule-based searches. The closing countermeasures were to enforce access control, encrypt data at rest, restrict access to a VPN, require MFA, scan data before publishing, and test your own environment.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Google's journey with CSP (Lukas Weichselbaum, Michele Spagnuolo)
talks.teaser: Covers rolling out nonce-based Content Security Policy at Google, plus newer web hardening headers and browser isolation settings.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how Google has used Content Security Policy as a defense-in-depth layer for web applications. The speakers frame it as a safety net for cross-site scripting bugs that slip past secure coding, not a replacement for it. They explain why allowlist-based policies are easy to bypass, pointing to a crawl of publicly visible policies where their tool defeated more than 94% automatically. That pushed the team toward nonce-based policies combined with strict-dynamic, which keeps existing dynamically created scripts working. They also cover the trade-offs of each variant, remaining DOM XSS and unsafe-eval gaps, and why CSP is weak against data exfiltration.

The second part covers other mitigations. Subresource Integrity pins third-party scripts to a hash so a compromised CDN cannot inject code. SameSite cookies stop cross-site requests from carrying session cookies, with Strict and Lax modes trading off differently. Chromium's site isolation and read blocking reduce the risk of Spectre-style memory leaks through cross-origin resources. Suborigins and origin policy are presented as proposals, and a prototype extension shows how much refactoring a sub-origin split would require.

For practitioners, the takeaway is to focus on preventing script execution first, use nonces with strict-dynamic where the stack allows it, and use the policy evaluator and violation-report tooling to roll out gradually.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: The new era of Digital Investigations: past, present and future (Selene Giupponi)
talks.teaser: Explores merging digital forensics with cyber threat intelligence for dynamic investigations across mobile, SCADA, and IoT cases.
talks.summary:
The presentation contrasts today’s digital investigations with roughly fifteen years of prior forensic practice, emphasizing that the last two years brought a sharper shift toward methodologies that are both static and dynamic. Digital forensics and cyber threat intelligence are often run as wholly separate functions, yet the speaker describes an integrated approach now used on cyber espionage, attacks, insider threats, and newer domains such as drones, automotive systems, GPS, and IoT.

Standard forensic phases from identification through presentation are mapped alongside intelligence planning, collection, exploitation, analysis, and dissemination. Integration is framed as starting at collection: drives and networks on one side, and external intelligence from the dark web, network intelligence, or botnets on the other. Proactive intelligence is paired with post-mortem and live analysis so teams can confirm malware families, infection context, and exposure. Reporting tiers, IOC and tactical feeds, static and dynamic code review, and enrichment pipelines feed a platform that ties human, cyber, and signal intelligence—not only IOCs and TTPs.

A recent mobile-and-network case and a SCADA power-plant scenario illustrate the merged workflow. Modbus TCP traffic (often unencrypted on ports such as 502) is correlated with mobile filesystem analysis on custom SCADA handsets, including OTA compromise via SMS on reprogrammed secure devices. Threat intelligence surfaces external exfiltration while forensics shows internal compromise from the phone into corporate infrastructure. Practitioners should expect forensic teams to generate intelligence and intelligence teams to lean on forensic depth, especially where SCADA, mobile, and stealth tailored malware intersect.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Intel ME: Security keys Genealogy, Obfuscation (Dmitry Sklyarov, Maxim Goryachy)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in CONFidence 2018: Intel ME: Security keys Genealogy, Obfuscation (Dmitry Sklyarov, Maxim Goryachy).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this CONFidence 2018 presentation, researchers Dmitry Sklyarov and Maxim Goryachy (sharing research conducted alongside Mark Ermolov) present an in-depth analysis of the security architecture, hardware crypto engines, and key derivation genealogy within Intel Management Engine (ME) 11. Running on a separate microprocessor inside the chipset with access to system memory and peripherals, Intel ME operates autonomously even when the main CPU is powered down. Because Intel provides minimal public documentation, the researchers leveraged ROM dumps obtained via a previous buffer overflow exploit, JTAG debugging, and reverse engineering to map out ME's cryptographic internals.

### Key Topics
- **Dedicated Security Hardware**: Examination of the internal ME architecture, including its isolated ~2 MB RAM, Huffman decompressor embedded in the flash controller, hardware SHA/HMAC, AES, RSA, and RC4 engines, and Secure Key Storage (SKS).
- **Secure Key Storage (SKS) Policies**: Hardware key storage enforcing restricted policies where cryptographic results can be re-routed directly back into key slots rather than plain memory, preventing key leakage even under compromised software execution.
- **Security Fuses as Root of Trust**: Hardware fuses burned during manufacturing provide per-platform root secrets that are isolated early during the ROM execution stage.
- **Key Genealogy and SVN Rollback Protection**: Key generation pathways for file system protection, fTPM, and runtime operations driven by HMAC derivations tied to Security Version Numbers (SVN) and hardcoded strings.
- **ROM Boot Flow and the IDLM Mechanism**: Execution checks across firmware partitions (FTPR, FTUP, DLMP) and the special role of the IDLM module.

### Technical Details
ME relies on a multi-stage boot sequence starting from non-modifiable ROM into user-level execution, led by the Bring-Up (BUP) module and Virtual File System (VFS). Cryptographic derivation roots in fuses that are available to ROM only for a brief window before access is permanently locked:
- **Hardware Engines & Key Storage**: The flash controller incorporates a hardware Huffman decompressor (for which the researchers reverse-engineered decompression tables) paired with HMAC verification. SKS holds 128-bit and 256-bit keys across designated slots (such as slot 12 and slot 21) and supports policies preventing intermediate or unwrapped keys from ever appearing in plaintext memory.
- **Key Derivation Scheme**: ME utilizes a master wrapping HMAC key derived from fuses. Through AES decryption and HMAC hashing with static ASCII strings (such as `CC Wrapping Key` and `CC Internal Root Key`) combined with an SVN byte, it produces wrapping keys. To support anti-rollback without losing user data, ME derives two sets of file system keys—current SVN and previous SVN—so data can be read under older revisions and re-encrypted.
- **Hibernate & Boot Partition (IVBP)**: The IVBP partition stores kernel structures for warm starts, encrypted with an AES key and verified by HMAC using unique boot seeds combined with the wrapping key and SVN.
- **The IDLM Module**: During ROM initialization, the boot code checks partitions including `DLMP` for a module named `IDLM`. If found at index 0, this module executes *before* fuses are locked and wiped from memory, presenting an architectural capability for early code execution before fuse-locking occurs, provided the partition signature check passes.

### Takeaways
The researchers characterize Intel ME's key management architecture as exceptionally rigorous and "paranoid," noting that keys exist in plaintext for mere moments—if at all—before being pushed into secure storage or wrapped. While an exploit allowed arbitrary code execution and selective key recovery on a specific platform at a fixed SVN, the architecture prevents attackers from extending recovered secrets to future SVNs or other machines without obtaining private Intel RSA signing keys or low-level fuse values.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Who and why should fear hardware trojans? (Adam Kostrzewa)
talks.teaser: Explains how hardware trojans can hide in a CPU, where they enter chip production, and why detecting them is so hard.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether integrated circuits can be trusted when many organisations cannot build their own silicon and must rely on large manufacturers. It defines a hardware trojan as hidden logic that adds, removes or changes a chip's function, and contrasts it with software malware: a trojan cannot be patched after deployment and does not spread from chip to chip. The speaker traces interest in the topic from a 2005 defence report and notes a sharp rise in publications since then.

The main demonstration runs on an emulated SPARC processor. A small hardware description change adds a payload that switches the processor into supervisor mode, triggered by a signed divide instruction that is normally available in user mode. The demo shows the arithmetic result unchanged, a privileged register readable after the trigger, and a null-pointer fault ending in a crash, which raises the question of how such a crash could be told apart from ordinary errors in logs. The talk then walks through where a trojan can enter the design flow: logic design, synthesis and mask production, each often handled by a different party.

Defensive options are weighed. Comparing a suspect chip against a known-good layout requires decapsulating and imaging it, which is costly and destructive, and optical inspection can miss dopant-level changes. Functional testing may catch some trojans, but rare trigger conditions can evade it. The speaker suggests building in-house hardware skills and testing products, and notes that market restrictions on certain vendors are one response already seen in several countries.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Remote detection of low and medium interaction honeypots (Julio C. Fort)
talks.teaser: Shows how SSH handshake probes expose Kippo and Cowrie honeypots before login, and maps them across the internet.
talks.summary:
Julio C. Fort opens with the basics of honeypots, decoy systems that imitate real services so researchers can catch malware and study attacker behaviour. He separates low, medium and high interaction designs, explaining that low-interaction traps are too easy to spot and high-interaction ones are real machines that are costly to maintain. The talk focuses on medium-interaction honeypots, and he reviews earlier detection work, most of which relied on virtual machine checks or only worked after an attacker had already logged in.

The case study targets Kippo and Cowrie, popular SSH honeypots built on Python Twisted. Instead of authenticating, the approach compares how they react before login to unusual version banners, a doubled banner, stray carriage returns and fuzzed key exchange, against how OpenSSH responds. The honeypots return different errors or crash where OpenSSH answers cleanly. A scoring script built on these checks flagged a honeypot on one test port while a real OpenSSH server on another was not flagged in a live demo. Some misconfigured OpenSSH versions produced false positives.

For internet-wide scanning, he modified masscan's banner parsing so the full pre-login response was kept. The scan took about 20 hours on a cheap cloud VPS and produced roughly 900 MB of logs, though repeated abuse complaints led the provider to shut the host down after a month. Among the results were banners naming a GCHQ honeypot. The takeaway is that medium-interaction honeypots are fairly easy to fingerprint, published probes are likely to be patched, and researchers relying on them for threat intelligence should be cautious.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Pentesting Voice Biometrics Solutions (Jakub Kałużny)
talks.teaser: Shows how voice biometric logins can be bypassed through audio manipulation, threshold probing and replay-detection evasion.
talks.summary:
The talk covers a black-box penetration test of a voice biometric login, offered both in a mobile app and on an IVR phone line. The speaker explains enrollment, where a user repeats a phrase three times, and argues that published false acceptance and rejection rates look weak: vendor tests use small participant pools, so an attacker can match some customer's voice by chance.

The main attack targeted replay detection. Using a cheap microphone at five meters in a cafe, the speaker captured a voice, isolated the vocal with noise reduction and filters, then altered pitch, pauses and background noise. With replay detection off on test accounts, about 250 variations were built and the strongest kept. Other weaknesses included weak enrollments, voices reused across accounts, thresholds that shifted after repeated attempts, and noise profiles that triggered replay flags. Playback was automated through a VoIP client with audio routing, DTMF tones and response-length analysis.

The closing advice is to test business assumptions, use many accounts, and separate voice-authenticated sessions for fraud detection. The speaker concludes that voice biometrics is a reasonable idea, but its error rates are not yet good enough for every deployment, and that AI may be needed to design tests against AI-based defenses.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Linux Kernel Runtime Guard (LKRG) under the hood (Adam "pi3" Zabrocki)
talks.teaser: Explains how the Linux Kernel Runtime Guard detects kernel exploitation and checks kernel integrity while the system runs.
talks.summary:
Linux Kernel Runtime Guard (LKRG) is an open-source module that protects a running Linux kernel from exploitation and from unauthorized changes to its code and data. The talk starts with a threat model that sorts attacks into three groups: boot chain tampering, kernel software flaws, and persistent memory changes made through malicious DMA-capable devices. The current main branch targets the last two, through its exploit detection and runtime code integrity features.

The exploit detection feature keeps its own record of each task's credential and seccomp state and validates it at intercepted system calls and on return to user mode, killing a process whose state has been corrupted. The integrity feature hashes kernel text, read-only data, per-CPU data and loaded modules, and cross-checks the module list against kernel objects to catch hidden modules. The speaker covered known limitations, including race conditions and the possibility of attacking LKRG's own data, and ran a demo in which an exploit for a UDP fragmentation offload bug was stopped while the module was active. Reported overhead was about 2.5% with all random validation events enabled and under 1% without them.

The talk closed with why LKRG does not yet run at hypervisor level, citing uneven hypervisor support across Linux environments and the difficulty of rebooting long-running servers, and with planned extensions such as capability and container escape detection. Practitioners would take away that LKRG is a practical hardening layer whose strength depends on how costly a bypass is for an attacker.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Military style tactics in the fight against Cybercrime (TJ Campana)
talks.teaser: Shows how a global bank builds a fusion-style security operations center that combines network, fraud and physical threat views.
talks.summary:
The speaker spent twelve years at Microsoft, where he helped build teams that went on the offence against systemic threats, before moving to HSBC to lead a security operations effort. The talk looks at why a large financial institution needs a military-style, multi-dimensional approach rather than relying on network defence alone. Attackers look for the weakest point, whether that is a customer site, a third party or a newly deployed application.

Customers are targeted too, through banking trojans and malware campaigns aimed at payment systems, so defenders must work beyond the technical team. The speaker describes working with colleagues in fraud and physical security, who see the threat landscape differently. A fusion centre merges internal telemetry with external crime statistics, giving situational awareness across domains so the organisation can act earlier. He notes that the operations centre processes roughly 10 to 15 billion events a day, with volume expected to quadruple this year, so instrumentation and data processing matter as much as the tools themselves.

Building that capability means staffing threat hunters, escalation engineers and watch commanders in every location where the bank operates, rather than outsourcing. The Krakow team is being built with software developers, IT administrators and analysts, and the bank works with the Polish CERT and universities in Krakow and Warsaw to prepare graduates. The main takeaway is that people with the right mindset, combined with well-instrumented data, matter most. The talk closes with an invitation to questions.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Everything’s Connected aka Threat Intelligence 102 (Marcin Siedlarz)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of CONFidence 2018: Everything’s Connected aka Threat Intelligence 102 (Marcin Siedlarz).
talks.summary: Marcin Siedlarz walks through FireEye adversary pursuit practices that treat indicators, hosts, files, and infrastructure as nodes linked by labeled edges in a hypergraph. He contrasts tactical IOC piles with strategic questions about motivation, targeting, and infrastructure reuse, then builds a spearphishing case study where behaviors such as phishing, macro dropper families, Mimikatz staging, and password-hash exfiltration receive typed aspects. Separate trees capture capabilities, host commands, malware obfuscation, and CVE or family signatures so analysts inherit context automatically. He explains UNK buckets for weak overlaps and later merging APT20 with a dormant UNC set when passworded RAR exfil patterns and gif filenames aligned. Passive DNS and certificate pivots rediscovered Helsing APT hosts from a bespoke OpenSSL client hello. Closing advice: dedicate intel staff, enable Snort and Yara pushes, avoid news-aggregator feeds, and hunt inside your own IR telemetry.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Outsmarting smart contracts (Damian Rusinek)
talks.teaser: Delivers walkthroughs of Ethereum smart contract failure modes and a demonstrated exchange withdrawal exploit.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on the tension between blockchain’s reputation for cryptographic strength and recurring headlines about stolen or frozen cryptocurrency. It positions Ethereum smart contracts as programs whose bytecode and state live on an immutable public ledger, then walks through how transactions invoke contract functions via selectors and parameters.

Security discussion centers on concrete failure modes: default-public functions behind the Parity wallet incident, plaintext secrets defeated by public storage and transaction history, integer overflows in token transfers, library initialization that froze vast ether holdings, gas limits abused to lock auction bidding, and reentrancy against withdraw patterns. The speaker also targets integration bugs, describing a short-address padding issue on exchange withdrawal flows and a withdrawal that inflated roughly 120 Golem tokens from a deposited fraction on an unverified platform.

Closing material covers responsible disclosure when owners are unknown, including a client-side tool that encrypts advisory text to a contract owner’s key and leaves it recoverable from chain data even when execution fails. Practitioners are urged to treat on-chain data as public, enforce visibility and safe math, test platform limits, audit dependencies, scan with common analyzers, and test dapps and exchanges as whole systems.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: A 2018 practical guide to hacking RFID/NFC (Sławomir Jasek)
talks.teaser: Shows how common RFID and NFC access cards are cloned and cracked using cheap tools and known attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk sets out to dispel the idea that cloning RFID and NFC cards needs elite skills or expensive equipment. It explains the difference between low-frequency and high-frequency cards and how simple phone apps can help identify them. The speaker then covers the simplest access control systems, which trust a UID that anyone nearby can read. Such UIDs can be copied onto writable or magic tags, or emulated with inexpensive reader modules, Proxmark devices, or a rooted Android phone.

Next comes MIFARE Classic, which is common in transit cards, student IDs and payments. Many cards keep default or weak keys, so a dictionary attack can recover them quickly, and a nested attack can recover the remaining keys once one key is known. The talk also covers hardened MIFARE variants and a 2015 attack, and notes that a secure chip still fails when the reader checks only the UID. A hotel card example shows data obfuscated per card, which the speaker reversed by XORing repeated bytes. The speaker withheld the method used to create a hotel master card because the vendor has not patched it.

The closing section previews mobile access control, where a phone stores a reader-specific key and a user-specific UID that a user with a rooted phone can edit. The speaker argues that these attacks have become cheaper and the risk has grown. Systems should avoid relying on secrecy, use per-installation keys and mutually authenticated end-to-end encryption, and move away from MIFARE Classic.

talks.title: CONFidence 2018: Surfin on you CAN-bus (Thomas Fischer)
talks.teaser: Covers in-vehicle CAN messaging, side-panel connectors, and practical hooks for USB-linked automotive network tooling.
talks.summary:
The session contrasts familiar IT-style networking with in-car designs that are message-first: many ECUs exchange framed traffic over CAN rather than behaving like a typical corporate LAN. The speaker points to physical access paths such as a Direct Connect-style port on the vehicle side and ties that to hobby and workshop setups where adapters bridge CAN to familiar interfaces.

Examples sprinkled through the talk include powertrain and body electronics (airbag, climate, transmission-related traffic), mentions of FlexRay alongside CAN-style controllers, and project-style work such as engine-bay connected computers and bolt-on kits with Bluetooth or WiFi. A mapping-oriented view of the bus surfaces the scale of the problem—on the order of thousands of distinct messages—while demos lean on commercial or beta interface hardware rather than implying unrestricted ownership of every vehicle.

Practitioners should leave with a clearer picture of why automotive buses demand different tooling, what connector and adapter choices enable bench or in-vehicle testing, and why electric and highly networked models widen the monitoring surface compared with older platforms.

talks.title: 4Developers 2018: Structured logging (Bartek Szurgot)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for 4Developers 2018: Structured logging (Bartek Szurgot).
talks.summary:
## Overview
Bartek Szurgot presents a critique of current logging practices and proposes a structured logging approach that prioritizes machine readability and type safety over traditional human-readable text logs. Rather than introducing another logging library, Szurgot argues that the fundamental approach to logging must change, particularly at scale where logs can exceed hundreds of gigabytes per second.

## Core Problem
Szurgot illustrates common logging failures through a personal anecdote involving hexadecimal representation in embedded systems logs. Without enforced formatting standards, the same value appears inconsistently across logs—uppercase vs lowercase hex, with or without leading zeros, with or without 0x prefixes, or even as signed integers. When logs number in the millions, inconsistent representation makes pattern matching and automated analysis nearly impossible. The speaker notes that current logging approaches (stream operators and printf-style formatting) perpetuate these problems and make automated parsing at scale impractical.

## Proposed Solution: Structured Logging
The core idea is to treat logs as data structures rather than text files. Instead of converting fully-typed values to English text and then attempting to parse that text programmatically, structured logging preserves type information and creates machine-parsable output (typically JSON). This enables automated analysis, filtering, statistics generation, and rule-based alerting without regex-based fragile parsing.

Key requirements for the proposed system include:
- Uniform representation across all logs
- Machine readability as primary goal
- Support for user-defined types
- Ease of use comparable to traditional loggers
- No internal hidden state
- Compile-time checking of format correctness
- Support for translation and localization

## Technical Architecture
The implementation centers on a recursive field_info data structure using variant types. Each field has a tag (key) and a value that can be simple (boolean, integer, string) or complex (vectors of field_info, enabling tree structures). This design preserves the hierarchical nature of logged data.

For basic logging, the API is straightforward: pass strongly-typed parameters directly without format strings. The compiler knows parameter types, enabling consistent representation through argument-dependent lookup. For optional human-readable output and translation support, a formatted variant uses compile-time format validation. The format string specifies parameter order (using dollar-index notation like $0, $1), allowing translation without changing parameter order.

The format validation happens at compile-time through constexpr functions that parse format strings and verify parameter counts match. If validation fails—mismatched counts, missing parameter indices—the compiler rejects the code immediately rather than allowing runtime errors in error-handling code paths (a critical weakness of traditional logging).

Szurgot demonstrates the field tagging pattern: simple helper functions convert user structures to field_info while applying semantic tags (e.g., tagging a string as "name" rather than generic string). This composition pattern allows complex nested structures to be logged naturally without boilerplate.

## Real-World Impact
When implemented, structured logging enables new capabilities:
- Automated anomaly detection (e.g., detecting performance degradation by analyzing processing-time fields)
- Automatic scaling decisions in cloud environments
- Support for automatic remediation (alerting support teams)
- Ability to change log format retroactively through translation tables
- Space optimization in embedded systems through string-to-number mapping

## Design Tradeoffs
While structured logging processes more data per log entry (thus not the absolute fastest), it remains practical (hundreds to thousands of logs per second on desktop hardware) while providing actionable information. The alternative—high-volume but unstructured logs—becomes useless at scale since neither humans nor machines can process it effectively.

The proposed API design allows wrapper functions to provide domain-specific defaults, addressing different logging needs across organizations without forcing unnecessary fields. This flexibility supports various architectural requirements (distributed systems, single-machine services, etc.).

## Implementation and Availability
Szurgot maintains an open-source C++14 implementation in the basic utilities and tools library (bat namespace, BSD license), which includes additional features beyond the talk (log rotation, Elasticsearch integration, Kibana support) and Docker SDK availability.

talks.title: 4Developers 2018: Java 9 - beyond Jigsaw (Piotr Stawirej)
talks.teaser: Covers Java 9 modularity beyond Jigsaw: module graphs, services, encapsulation, reflection opens, and slim custom runtimes via jlink.
talks.summary:
The session opens by comparing shifts in programming paradigms to natural adaptation, then asks whether Java can keep pace as platforms evolve. Modularization arrives with Java 8 through Project Jigsaw, and the speaker outlines goals: smaller deployable footprints, resolving duplicate library versions on the classpath, stronger encapsulation, performance, and structures that mirror sound design patterns.

Using a progressive planet-themed example, the talk walks through module-info.java, exports, requires, requires transitive, qualified exports, the service loader with provides and uses, factory methods for hiding ServiceLoader from clients, and filtering implementations with annotations. It also covers optional modules via requires static, runtime resolution limits, how public no longer implies globally visible access, and opens for frameworks that depend on reflection and dependency injection.

The closing sections show Maven plugins for modular builds, jlink custom runtime images shrinking a demo to about 12 megabytes versus hundreds for a full JDK install, module path resolution at startup, limits of the @Version annotation versus Maven for versioning, contrasts with OSGi, and cautions that IDE quick fixes can create unintended module coupling.

talks.title: 4Developers 2018: The A-Team - czyli jak dobierać ludzi (Michał Szczepanik)
talks.teaser: Maps TV-style squad chemistry onto real hiring: team phases, role mixes, passion, and communication fit for new and existing dev teams.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a familiar frustration: teams stocked with strong individuals often fail to collaborate, while tight-knit groups can deliver under pressure with little oversight. The speaker frames this using the forming, storming, norming, and performing model, noting that performing teams are rare and that managers cannot shortcut storming by forcing artificial conflict.

He argues for deliberate diversity in skills and working styles, citing a blogger’s taxonomy of builders, stability-focused developers, and experimenters, and adds archetypes such as pioneers on unfamiliar stacks, mentors who guard quality, and detail obsessives. Hiring into a stable team differs from staffing a greenfield group: fit with how the team already communicates and works often beats a candidate who matches the job description on paper. A successful hire integrates quickly; still being labeled the newcomer after months signals misfit. Each addition can reset the team back through earlier development phases.

Closing guidance stresses intrinsic motivation and passion for the work, aligned goals so people finish the project together rather than in parallel silos, and practical communication constraints such as overlapping hours for remote members. The aim is a self-directed unit that reaches high performance with minimal pushing.

talks.title: 4Developers 2018: Wypalenie zawodowe dla programistów (Grzegorz Godlewski)
talks.teaser: Explains how developer burnout builds up, its symptoms, and practical ways to limit workload and protect well-being.
talks.summary:
This Polish-language talk looks at burnout among programmers. The speaker starts by noting that psychologists are unsure whether burnout counts as a disease or a syndrome, and argues that the stress concept was poorly translated into Polish. In his reading, the better term is excessive load. He compares a developer to overloaded hardware: a machine that runs hot can be cleaned or given better cooling, but if nobody reacts early it wears out, and a human brain cannot be swapped out like a graphics card.

The middle of the talk covers how burnout appears and develops. It builds gradually, moving from eager early commitment to fading recognition, changing attitudes and finally an inability to work. Symptoms include fatigue that brings no satisfaction, insomnia, lapses in memory and attention, and a shift from low motivation to a strong urge to avoid the work. The speaker recalls a network administrator who spent weeks configuring servers with long hours and had a heart attack at 30. Other causes discussed are a growing backlog of unfinished projects, irritation spreading through a team, and workload measured by task counts and the cost of switching between projects.

The closing section offers remedies. Listeners are advised to find where their load comes from, keep working hours at a sustainable level, and learn to say no and negotiate. Non-financial rewards deserve to be raised as well as salary. When a colleague harms a project, escalating to management may be needed. For severe burnout, the speaker suggests leaving a job sooner rather than later and taking time off between projects. The talk ends with audience questions.

talks.title: 4Developers 2018: Warsztat dla liderów technicznych (Agnieszka Biernacka)
talks.teaser: Shows technical leads how respect, competence and autonomy motivate teams, and how shared code quality can be governed collectively.
talks.summary:
This hands-on workshop for technical leads argues that motivation cannot be installed in people, but its growth can be supported. The speaker starts with respect and relationships, noting that a leader people trust gets far more willing cooperation than one who manipulates. Next comes competence: challenges should sit between too hard and too easy, and teams need training, mentoring and time to learn. Autonomy closes this part, built on explicit, transparent decision rules and a visible route by which junior members earn the right to decide alone.

The middle section treats shared code as a commons and applies Elinor Ostrom's research on managing shared resources. Her design principles are walked through as a guide for teams: build a group identity, state the team's goal as delivering a high-quality business solution, share the costs and benefits of quality work fairly, let the people affected make the decisions, monitor agreed behaviour through peers, use graduated sanctions, and resolve conflicts quickly by debating options rather than people. Participants worked in pairs on exercises about what drives their own teams.

The closing point is that these practices only last when management supports them, for example by defining when a team may decide on its own. Participants leave with a concrete plan for their own team: clarify the goal, learn what each person values, and agree transparent rules together.

talks.title: PLNOG20 - Marcin Kuczera
talks.teaser: Shows how microbursts overflow shared switch buffers and drop IPTV packets, and how priority queuing fixes it.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who works at a Polish regional ISP with over 700 km of fibre in the former Rybnik coal district, opens with the problem. The company sells internet, IPTV and telephony. Brief interruptions often go unnoticed on internet access, but even small glitches in IPTV bring a flood of customer complaints. He asks the audience what QoS means to them and points out that many operators treat it only as rate limiting.

The core point is that a switch's shared buffer can be filled by microbursts lasting only fractions of a second, and per-minute statistics never show them. In one case, a switch had four 1 Gbps ports. One carried IPTV, while the other three carried up to 400 Mbps each, and the switch dropped IPTV packets because it could not drain the buffer fast enough. The remedy is to split the buffer into priority queues so IPTV is served ahead of bursty internet traffic. He covers 802.1p priority bits for tagged traffic, DSCP for routed traffic, reserving priority 7 for control traffic, and clearing incoming priority markings on untrusted ports. Mapping must be repeated at every hop, including the OLT and routers.

His takeaway is to check per-port drop counters, because drops can appear at 30 to 40 percent utilisation. Prioritisation should be applied at the points where wide links feed narrower ones. He also describes tests that saturate a link while watching IPTV. After prioritisation, he says, many complaints tend to disappear.
