talks.title: PLNOG20 - Arne Heitmann
talks.teaser: Shows why flash and NVMe push storage onto Ethernet fabrics, and what a storage-optimized switch adds.
talks.summary:
Arne Heitmann, presenting for a networking vendor, argues that storage is moving away from Fibre Channel toward scale-out Ethernet fabrics. He points to flash media as the driver: a 10 Gb link that once suited spinning disks is saturated by two SATA SSDs, and a single SAS SSD can fill one. As NVMe arrives, storage has to sit closer to front-end servers, which calls for faster networks and a dedicated Ethernet storage switch rather than a shared general network.

The example product is the SN2010, described as an 18-port 25G switch in half a rack unit. The features listed include lossless converged Ethernet for RDMA, which bypasses the kernel to free CPU cycles, buffering for microbursts without packet loss, low latency, support for running applications in containers, and a management tool that integrates with VMware and OpenStack. The speaker stresses an open choice of operating system and a standards-based design, so customers are not locked into one vendor. A storage-oriented quality of service setup, the speaker says, can be applied in a single line on a suitable switch.

The closing advice is to draw a blueprint of the storage environment before redesigning it, starting small and adding racks as the environment grows. The speaker claims the design scales to several thousand ports. The takeaway is that, with a storage-optimized switch, Ethernet storage becomes a resilient, fully redundant fabric. Slides and a test report were offered after the session.

talks.title: 4Developers Gdańsk 2017: Should we Go? (Patryk Małek)
talks.teaser: A practical tour of Go's toolchain, concurrency model, and production wins at companies shipping containers and cloud services.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by asking whether teams should adopt Go, framing it as a statically typed language Google began in 2007 to escape complexity in mainstream stacks while staying fast to compile and easy to read at scale. The speaker walks through the bundled toolchain—build, run, test, formatting, vet, coverage, and profiling—and shows how strict defaults such as rejecting unused variables and enforcing gofmt reduce debate and keep diffs mechanical.

The core of the session covers runtime design: implicit interface satisfaction, composition via embedding, lightweight goroutines scheduled across OS threads and processors, WaitGroups for joining work, and channels as the idiomatic way to synchronize. Examples include ping-pong over channels, select with timeouts, built-in deadlock detection, cross-compilation with GOOS and GOARCH, escape analysis flags, and a rough Apache Bench comparison of a minimal Go HTTP server against Boost.Beast in C++.

Closing arguments point to large-scale rewrites and ecosystems—Google's dl.google.com download infrastructure, Docker, Kubernetes, etcd, and widely used DNS layers—suggesting practitioners weigh Go when networking, concurrency, and operational simplicity matter, and noting that errors return as values rather than exceptions.

talks.title: 4Developers Gdańsk 2017: Striving for ultimate Low Latency (Mateusz Pusz)
talks.teaser: Explains how C++ low-latency code avoids allocations, virtual calls and smart pointers on the hot path.
talks.summary:
Mateusz Pusz opens by separating latency, the time an action takes from start to finish, from throughput, the amount of work completed over time, and notes that the two often trade off against each other. He uses electronic trading as the main example of why low latency matters, and also mentions voice over IP and online gaming. He walks through a trading pipeline and isolates the short fast path where orders are sent, since only that code needs aggressive tuning. A 2012 trading incident, in which a software deployment mismatch caused heavy losses within 45 minutes, shows why error handling and correctness matter as much as speed.

The middle section covers the hardware and operating system side. Threads busy-spin instead of sleeping, are pinned to dedicated cores, and avoid kernel transitions and context switches. The main concern is worst-case execution time rather than averages, so any source of jitter is a problem. The speaker then lists C++ features to avoid on that path. In his compiled comparison, a shared_ptr needed about ten times as much assembly as a unique_ptr when no sharing was required, because of atomic reference counting and type erasure. Virtual functions, polymorphism, multiple inheritance and RTTI each add indirection that blocks inlining and instruction cache prefetching, and CRTP is offered as a static alternative. Exceptions add little measurable cost on most compilers, though error paths still need to be handled. For dynamic memory, he suggests custom allocators, small buffer optimization and fixed-size in-place strings.

The closing advice is to keep one busy thread per physical core, pass data through fixed-size lock-free queues, precompute what can be computed at compile time, and always measure release builds. He recommends profilers such as perf and VTune, flame graphs, reading assembly, and hardware-level timing of the whole system.

talks.title: 4Developers Gdańsk 2017: Two strings to your bow (Mariusz Łapiński)
talks.teaser: Benchmarks C++ string concatenation across compilers against Java and C#, and walks through building a custom string builder.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how strings are built and joined in C++, using repeated benchmarks of assembling a sentence from separate words. The speaker first runs the same task in Java and C#, where a reused string builder reaches about 300 nanoseconds, then shows that naive C++ appending can run noticeably slower, with results depending on the compiler used. String literal handling and string_view constructors also change the outcome across compilers.

The middle section examines what std::string does internally, including small string optimisation and capacity growth, and how compilers treat length calls on literals. The speaker then builds his own string builder variants: one with an in-place buffer, one with heap-allocated storage, and one made of chunks that grow without copying existing data. Tuning such as reserving space, reusing objects, compile-time evaluation, prefetching and branch hints helped in some cases and hurt in others.

The closing advice is to measure before optimising, since performance gains can quietly erode as a codebase changes. Reserving capacity and reducing dynamic allocation were the most reliable wins, and keeping small data on the stack often helped. The speaker recommends owning strings with std::string, using string_view for read-only views, and keeping the compiler updated, since newer versions improved some results. He also warns that forcing optimizer hints without measuring can break code that was already well optimised.

talks.summary: Neil C Smith demos Praxis LIVE and related “write now, run anytime” tooling that lets Java and visual-media developers hot-reload pipelines for VJ performances and interactive installs. He argues immediate feedback loops beat batch compile-run cycles when experimenting with audio-visual graphs.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Event Processing in Action (Sebastian Malaca)
talks.teaser: Explores event-driven architecture using CI/CD examples, from event types through producer-consumer design.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing clean code as a business enabler, then argues that event processing mirrors how organizations already think about triggers and reactions in the real world. Continuous integration serves as the main domain: builds start and finish, pipelines turn red or green, and notifications follow failures on pull requests or master branches.

The middle section builds a vocabulary for practitioners. Business events stay stable across implementations while system events reflect technology choices. Events can report state changes, mere occurrences, or conditions such as five greens followed by a failure. Interactions may be scheduled, request-response, or fully event-driven, where publishers do not know who will react. Complex events add enrichment and aggregation; uncertain and absent events call for analysis or escalation when expected signals never arrive. Design rules include immutable past-tense naming, fat event payloads, and separating recognition from side effects.

The close maps producers, channels, processors, and consumers, with patterns for deduplicating reactions, extracting predicates into their own components, and choosing whether to emit events when nothing meaningful changed. Separation of concerns, easy wiring changes, and component tests are presented as maintainability wins, with pointers to further books on event processing and microservices.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Graylog: one tool to log 'em all (Piotr Przybył)
talks.teaser: Shows how Graylog gathers syslog, Java application and router logs into one searchable place, with fixes for common gotchas.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that tailing local log files with tail and grep does not scale once many machines are involved. It introduces Graylog as a centralised log management system that collects, processes and searches logs from syslog, applications, web servers, databases and firewalls. Metadata is kept in MongoDB, while the log messages themselves are stored in Elasticsearch. The speaker starts with a quick appliance-image install in VirtualBox, then forwards syslog messages from a Linux host over UDP and inspects the fields Graylog extracts from each message.

The middle section covers practical gotchas. Streams split incoming messages by source, for example by the IP address of a pfSense router, and an extractor based on a regular expression removes a trailing colon from the source field. The router's syslog messages carried no timezone, so Graylog treated them as arriving in the future; a pipeline rule fixes the timestamp by parsing it in the local zone. A small Java program using SLF4J with a Gelf appender sends its logs to Graylog without recompilation, and the speaker searches by user name across several instances receiving requests in round-robin. Alerts can trigger an email or an HTTP action when a threshold is crossed within a set time.

The closing part covers the REST API that the web client uses, and scaling advice: give the Graylog and Elasticsearch nodes enough RAM and SSD storage, and cluster them when one node is no longer enough. Retention is limited because Elasticsearch is costly to keep large volumes in, so older data is archived. Compared with Logstash and Kibana, Graylog is licensed under GPL v3 and ships its own user interface. The takeaway for practitioners is a single place to collect, search and alert on logs from many sources, including devices that are no longer running.

talks.title: JDD 2017: A Hitchhiker's Guide to the Functional Exception Handling in Java (Grzegorz Piwowarek)
talks.teaser: Maps Java exception pain points to functional Try, Either, and Optional patterns using the Vavr library for everyday code.
talks.summary:
The session opens by cataloging why checked and unchecked exceptions complicate Java maintenance: hidden control flow, swallowed failures in async code, misuse for ordinary business cases, and the cost of stack trace capture in hot paths. It contrasts Go’s explicit error returns with Java’s throw model and argues for leaning on static types for faster feedback than slow test suites alone.

The core walkthrough introduces Vavr-style Try as a success-or-failure wrapper with map, filter, recover, and flatMap to compose I/O without nested try types. Either is presented as an unbiased pair type suited to error values or alternate branches such as DNS delegation, with left and right projections. Optional is recommended instead of throwing for absent values, citing widespread NoSuchElementException use on public code hosts.

The close favors pragmatism: these types are not silver bullets, Vavr is gaining adoption over older utility libraries, and community pressure via the JCP can bring pattern matching ideas into the language. Questions revisit whether Try still materializes exceptions, propagation clutter with checked exceptions, and where to find tutorials plus blog examples.

talks.title: JDD 2017: 9 Lifes of JAVA 9 (Tomasz Borek)
talks.teaser: A historical tour of Java platform releases culminates in JDK 9 modularity, jshell, G1, and cloud-oriented deployment changes.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames JDK 9 as the latest "life" in a long platform story, from early JVM goals—portability, built-in threading, applets and sandboxing—through J2EE divergence, Tiger’s generics and memory model fixes, and the long delay that left lambdas for Java 8 while Java 7 shipped Project Coin and invokedynamic groundwork.

Most depth sits on Java 9 itself: Project Jigsaw and the module system targeting jar hell, bloated classpaths, and monolithic JDK installs, including smaller custom runtime images and stronger encapsulation of long-abused internal APIs. The speaker walks through jshell as an interactive face for the platform, G1 becoming the default collector with region and humongous-object tradeoffs, HTML5 Javadoc and UTF-8 property files, industry-backed Flow for reactive streams, TLS and cryptography hardening, serialization filters, and a sweep of JVM and library conveniences such as the release compiler flag and multi-release JARs.

The close ties these changes to microservices, IoT scarcity, and DevOps shipping, notes faster quarterly and LTS release plans, and the migration of enterprise Java toward Eclipse while Oracle pushes the SE platform for cloud operators. The practical plea is to trial JDK 9 beyond trivial API sugar—especially modules and slimmer runtimes—and to follow dedicated deep dives on jigsaw, Flow, and upcoming releases.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Refactoring in Business World... for Developers? (Włodek Krakowski)
talks.teaser: Code-reading sessions, trust, and autonomy show how delivery teams sustain refactoring under business shipping pressure.
talks.summary:
The presenter contrasts IDE refactoring mechanics with a wider view of code improvement inside organizations that must ship business value. He frames production against production capability: customers pay for working functionality, while maintainable code determines whether the team can keep delivering. Over roughly seventeen years he moved from junior developer toward team leadership, and from complaining about quality fights toward coaching, working in both strict hierarchies and cultures built on delegated responsibility.

In hierarchical, micromanaged settings, refactoring rarely survives planning and backlog prioritization, so teams often perform hidden refactoring or skip it entirely. After trainer experience and a return to product delivery, he tried formal solo refactoring demos before the team; high preparation demands and perfectionism killed that habit. A colleague’s code-reading format—one person reads aloud while others question and refactor together—revived sustained improvement with readability as the shared goal. He ties this to trust, constructive disagreement, explicit standards, and Patrick Lencioni’s team dysfunctions, citing empowerment, experimentation, and developer-owned timing at Akado Technologies.

He closes with a layered refactoring pyramid, appropriate test scope for each change size, clear autonomy boundaries, and Kanban used by the team rather than as management control. Business stakeholders may ask why delays happen, but technical staff should decide when structural cleanup is warranted.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Napraw swój zespół (Anita Przybył)
talks.teaser: Maps five classic team dysfunctions to developer work and outlines daily habits that rebuild trust, debate, and shared results.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting deep technical expertise with weak practical knowledge of how groups actually cooperate. It argues that many organizations lose to rivals despite better specialists and tools, because human dynamics cap what delivery can achieve. Effective collaboration is framed as a real workstream, not optional team-building games.

The core walks through a pyramid of five interlocking dysfunctions: absent trust, fear of conflict, weak commitment, shirking accountability, and indifference to collective outcomes. Each layer is illustrated with audience checks—whether leaders admit mistakes, whether meetings feel dull, whether silent members get heard—and with tactics such as explicit meeting agreements, written decisions at the end of discussions, short weekly priority rounds, structured peer feedback, and visible scoreboards tied to goals. Stories range from a U.S. Navy ship turnaround under a new captain to sports examples where individual glory undermines the squad.

The close stresses sizing teams small, privileging shared objectives over private preferences, and reinforcing results through communication cadence and mixed incentives. A cited large-company study is used to highlight communication skill and emotional intelligence as the strongest correlates of team performance, leaving practitioners with repeatable habits rather than one-off exercises.

talks.title: Tips on Quality Assurance process in Machine Learning projects (Viktor Zhurbenko)
talks.teaser: Explains how to assess data and build simple prototype models to catch quality problems in machine learning projects early.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Viktor Zhurbenko discusses practical Quality Assurance (QA) practices tailored specifically for machine learning (ML) projects. Rather than framing QA around traditional software testing mechanisms such as unit, integration, or system tests, he defines QA in ML as a continuous set of practices to assess and improve the state of the product throughout its entire lifecycle. In traditional software projects, data is used to test the software, whereas in machine learning, software tests are executed to evaluate and validate the data. Drawing on his experience building natural language processing (NLP) applications—specifically systems that extract structured reservation data from emails for calendar integration—the speaker outlines actionable techniques for data assessment, feature engineering, missing data handling, and production maintenance.

### Key Topics
- **Role of the Expert vs. Automated Feature Assessment**: Evaluating whether data features are sufficient or overwhelming. While human domain experts are crucial in areas like medicine or industrial equipment monitoring, automated feature selection algorithms (e.g., using Scikit-learn to eliminate features with low variance) can serve as built-in experts to reduce parameter counts and accelerate training.
- **Data Visualization in NLP**: The importance of plotting and color-coding tokens in text to discover and engineer compound features (e.g., spotting that a person and location token together represent an airport name).
- **Handling Missing Samples**: Addressing missing data using imputation techniques, such as average imputation or multiple imputation (training small predictive models to infer missing feature values).
- **Bias, Variance, and Transfer Learning**: Balancing bias and variance when training models on limited data, and leveraging transfer learning by chaining a generic model with a task-specific model.
- **Production Degradation and Mutation Testing**: Managing the inevitable degradation of models in production when live data formats mutate.
- **Pragmatic Prototyping**: Prioritizing fast experimentation, simple models, and tooling flexibility over rigid upfront software architecture.

### Technical Details
- **Feature Reduction**: In a diagnostic scenario predicting flu based on symptoms (fever, ache, chills, and two blood pressure parameters), blood pressure features exhibited very low variance and had no predictive value. Using Scikit-learn's built-in feature selection to remove low-variance parameters reduced five features to three while maintaining the same hypothesis evaluation accuracy and speeding up training.
- **Feature Discovery via Experts**: Speaking directly with domain experts helps uncover missing features without premature code changes (e.g., iteratively determining that identifying a crocodile requires adding a 'teeth' parameter alongside 'green', 'long', and 'in water').
- **Missing Data Imputation**: When samples have missing numerical values, average imputation calculates the mean to fill gaps. Alternatively, multiple imputation uses auxiliary machine learning models trained on available attributes to predict missing values.
- **Transfer Learning Pipeline**: When samples are too scarce for complex models, transfer learning can be applied (noted by the speaker as applicable in roughly 5% of real-world cases). In sentiment analysis, an initial generic model learns sentence structure and identifies co-occurring words (e.g., coupling 'great' and 'loved'), while a second, simpler model classifies the sentiment polarity of those coupled words.
- **Data Mutation in Production**: Live production inputs inevitably change (e.g., email providers changing structure or users sending images instead of plain text), breaking model assumptions. Teams must monitor production data, collect new features and samples, manually inspect them, and retrain models regularly.

### Takeaways
- **Data-First QA**: ML testing is primarily about testing, assessing, and refining the underlying data and features rather than just testing code.
- **Always Visualize**: Irrespective of data type—including text tokens—visualizing data reveals structural relationships and informs feature engineering.
- **Fight Fire with Fire**: Use small, simple helper models to clean, impute, and assess data before committing to complex production architectures.
- **Prototype Over Rigid Architecture**: Avoid spending excessive early effort on rigid frameworks or corporate architecture; pick familiar tools, prototype rapidly, and prove model feasibility first.
- **Plan for Long-Term Maintenance**: Deploying an ML model is only the beginning; data mutates over time, requiring ongoing monitoring, manual evaluation, and model retraining.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Think in Cloud, Develop in Cloud (Paweł Janusz)
talks.teaser: Walks through AWS cloud service models and core services, then builds and deploys a small Java Lambda behind API Gateway.
talks.summary:
The talk sets out cloud service models, from renting virtual machines to running small functions, and notes that using a managed platform ties a team more tightly to one vendor. It then explains regions and availability zones, why spreading workloads across locations matters for latency and resilience, and surveys AWS offerings in compute, networking, storage, databases, messaging, monitoring and security.

The middle narrows to a few services. API Gateway serves as a single entry point for REST APIs, while Lambda runs small functions billed by memory and runtime and can be triggered from storage events, database changes or queues. DynamoDB is presented as a serverless NoSQL database whose cost follows throughput, S3 as backup-friendly file storage, and SQS as a queue service. A live demo built a Java request handler, uploaded it as a function, tested it with a sample JSON payload, then exposed it through a POST method that was deployed and called from Postman.

In the questions, the speaker mentioned that the first invocation runs slower until the environment warms up, that a free tier required a payment card and would begin billing after a year, and that code can be deployed from a command-line client instead of the browser. The closing advice is to consider serverless for customer-facing workloads, since you pay only when it is used, while weighing the vendor dependence it creates.

talks.title: JDD 2017: EventSourcing i CQRS. Wprowadzenie, którego brakowało (Sławomir Jachowicz)
talks.teaser: Introduces Event Sourcing and CQRS via an e-commerce walkthrough using the Axon Framework.
talks.summary:
The session targets developers who have heard of Event Sourcing and CQRS but lack a clear mental model. The speaker frames both as design patterns applied to specific problems, not as whole-system architecture styles, and walks through a fictional e-commerce platform: creating and confirming orders, managing line items, sending mail on confirmation, and crediting promotional points, plus the non-functional goal of adapting to new business rules.

Using the open-source Axon Framework on that example, the talk follows the write path from user intent through commands, a command bus, and command handlers into a domain aggregate that emits events. Events land in an event store—the append-only journal that is the system’s source of truth—and propagate via an event bus to handlers that refresh optimized read models on the query side. The narrative covers command/query separation, aggregate reconstruction by replaying events, snapshots for heavy lifetimes, polyglot persistence, eventual consistency between write and read stores, and scaling reads and writes independently.

Later flows add and remove products, confirm an order, trigger email only for live events (not replays), and route bonus accrual through another aggregate. The speaker explains error correction as compensating events rather than edits, schema changes through upcasting, and contrasts rich historical event data with CRUD when product owners ask for retroactive behavior. The closing message is to choose patterns deliberately when starting new work and to use Axon as a practical next step.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Benefits of columnar data layout (Marcin Stanisławski)
talks.teaser: Explains why columnar data layout speeds up analytic queries, covering Dremel-style encoding, Parquet and Arrow.
talks.summary:
The talk traces columnar storage from row-oriented databases and the 1985 decomposition storage model, through MonetDB and C-Store, to Google's Dremel paper. It explains how nested records are flattened into column trees, with each stored value carrying a definition level and a repetition level so that nulls and repeated fields can be rebuilt from the schema.

The speaker then moves to the Apache Parquet file format built on these ideas. Because values for one column sit together, encodings such as bit packing and delta encoding compress them well, and nulls can be left out of storage. Predicate pushdown lets readers skip blocks, and bloom filters were described as work in progress. The main costs are reassembling full rows when an application needs them and extra CPU work on writes, so columnar layouts suit analytic reads over wide tables rather than write-heavy, mission-critical storage.

The final part introduces Apache Arrow, an in-memory columnar format that allows zero-copy sharing between languages and processes. The speaker contrasts its buffer layout with FlatBuffers, which lets a reader pull one field without deserializing a whole record. The takeaway is that data layout matters, that alignment and SIMD help modern CPUs, and that open-source components can be combined like building blocks.

talks.title: JDD 2017: From Java bytecode to instant class diagrams with Class Visualizer (Jonatan Kaźmierczak
talks.teaser: Shows how Class Visualizer turns compiled Java bytecode into navigable class diagrams for large codebases.
talks.summary:
Jonatan Kaźmierczak presents Class Visualizer, a tool he built to turn compiled Java code into interactive class diagrams. He starts with a common problem: large Java codebases have thousands of classes and little or outdated documentation. He lists four wishes for such a tool: diagrams generated automatically, correct, accurate, complete and readable.

He explains the design choices behind it. For a cross-platform desktop app he chose Swing over JavaFX and SWT, and bytecode rather than source as input, since the compiler already validates it and the Java reflection API is enough to read it without third-party libraries. In a live demo he loads the Spring PetClinic sample with 2053 Maven libraries, and its 229 classes load in about one second. He then loads the Java standard library, 12,862 classes in about 7.666 seconds, and inspects Unsafe (136 members, used by 181 classes), the Throwable hierarchy and Object, which has nearly 15,000 children. He also recalls a 48,000-class project that crashed other tools.

In the Q&A he said that when several versions of a library are loaded, the tool sorts classes so the newest version is usually taken first, though not in every case. Fat jars and archives are supported, and a request for package-level dependency views was declined because other tools already cover it well. His focus, he says, is fast navigation between classes.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Case study of a good enough architecture (Jakub Kubryński)
talks.teaser: A startup case study shows how good-enough architecture, microservices, and monitoring enable daily deploys without chasing perfection.
talks.summary:
The talk begins by arguing that perfect architecture is unreachable, and that pragmatic designs should optimize for fast feedback and cost-effectiveness. Lessons come from consulting in large European enterprises versus running a smaller company, where spending choices and outcomes stay visible.

The middle section ties continuous delivery to that feedback loop, separating technical deployment from business-facing release decisions. Expensive full regression is traded for unit tests, critical-path checks, and rapid production fixes—often within about thirty minutes. Microservices shorten build and deploy cycles but compound uptime risk across many services; shared canonical models fail when teams evolve fields independently, so consumer-driven contracts align producers and consumers without relying on full end-to-end staging.

The closing themes cover backward-compatible versioning, canary rollouts, APM-style monitoring over brittle performance suites, safe-to-fail patterns with feature switches, broad automation including infrastructure as code, convention over configuration, and backups limited to code and data. The intended takeaway is an architecture that tolerates small defects while staying shippable and observable.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Turbo Charge CPU Utilization in Fork/Join Using the ManagedBlocker (Dr Heinz Kabutz)
talks.teaser: A hands-on walkthrough parallelizes large Fibonacci work with fork/join, BigInteger tweaks, caching, and ManagedBlocker for fuller CPU use.
talks.summary:
The session opens by comparing idle versus busy CPU graphs on a multi-core laptop, arguing that better algorithms must come before threading. Using Fibonacci as a stress test, it contrasts naive recursion, iterative approaches, and Dijkstra’s fast doubling method implemented with BigInteger, then measures single-threaded cost versus parallel expectations.

The middle implements recursive decomposition with Java’s fork/join pool, counts excessive forks, and explains why speedups stall when late recursive steps dominate. The speaker patches multiplication paths inside BigInteger via boot classpath, parallelizes squaring and Toom-Cook style multiplies, and adds a concurrent cache with reserved placeholders so duplicate subproblems are computed once under contention.

The close introduces ManagedBlocker so waiting threads let the pool grow and preserve desired parallelism, with brief comparison to CompletableFuture homework. Takeaways: fix algorithmic complexity first, expect duplicate work in divide-and-conquer, design cooperative caching for races, and tune pool behavior when threads block on shared results.

talks.title: JDD 2017: How functional programming change my Java code (Bartek Kuczyński)
talks.teaser: Explores how immutability, side-effect separation, and clearer specs can reshape production Java without pure functional style.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting familiar object-oriented habits in Java—DRY, KISS, YAGNI, SOLID, and design patterns—with the limits those patterns expose when the language cannot express concepts such as a true singleton as cleanly as Scala’s `object` keyword. He argues that bolting map, filter, and reduce onto arbitrary classes is not functional programming; the shift is about recognizing side effects, separating pure logic from I/O, and not forcing category-theory constructions or pure FP style into Java when the syntax fights back.

Through anecdotes about recursion, trampolines, pattern-matching libraries, and mixing object-oriented domain models with functional tricks, he warns against imitating Haskell in production Java and recommends JVM languages with native FP support when purity matters. The practical middle of the talk applies functional ideas inside Java: immutable values, isolating side effects, splitting “what” from “how,” and refactoring bloated specifications with business analysts by standardizing verbs, actors, and adjectives so documentation and code shrink together.

He closes with tradeoffs—slower naive functional paths that profiling can fix, harder onboarding, and selling the approach to teams—and a client story where a roughly thousand-page spec was reduced to about one hundred fifty pages and delivery finished about two years ahead of schedule. Practitioners are urged to adopt ideas, not magic, and to reach for deeper FP learning only when it serves the business problem.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Me, My Organization and My-croservices (Krzysztof Mejka)
talks.teaser: Three anonymized cases contrast botched microservices adoptions with platform teams, training, and organizational learning.
talks.summary:
The presenter argues that microservices describe whole-system architecture, not merely small applications: services should deploy, run, and store data independently, tolerate instance failures without stopping the platform, and usually appear in numbers large enough to earn the label. He cautions against hype-driven development, silver bullets, and repeating old habits while expecting better outcomes.

Three anonymized case studies anchor the talk. One company let developers spin up separate apps for new features without ownership of the full system, kept core business data in the original monolith database, and discovered too late that it needed DevOps, monitoring, and shared infrastructure such as an API gateway and centralized logging. A second needed a public API but chose microservices amid industry buzz, shared a relational model through jars, used Elasticsearch as primary storage, and pushed every developer into hands-on AWS work—winning a fast indexing demo but landing on slow batch jobs, tightly coupled releases, and destructive full-stack redeploys. A third treated the shift as organizational learning: training, independent feature teams, technical product owners, a platform DevOps group, Cloud Foundry on AWS, and a security-enforcing API proxy supported polyglot services and easier replacement of poorly bounded components, though the gateway remained a single failure point.

He closes by recommending honest postmortems on why legacy systems failed, long-lived teams aligned to services, a master plan with accountable technical leadership, dedicated DevOps skills with hosting abstraction, and cultural room to fail and learn—rather than assuming architecture labels fix entrenched problems.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Legacy, for lack of a better word, is good (Uberto Barbini)
talks.teaser: Presents phased legacy renewal via acceptance tests, vertical modules, and facades rather than risky full rewrites.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting greenfield enthusiasm with brownfield reality: obsolete stacks, scaling pain, buried requirements, and the temptation to declare big-bang rewrites. Drawing on maintenance metaphors and typical failure modes—scope creep, drained teams, half-finished replacements, and adapter-thin “new” systems—the talk reframes legacy software as code that already works and funds the business.

The core proposal is a phased “safe route” rather than a rewrite cliff. Milestones might peel services from a monolith or expose a REST layer while backends move incrementally. The outlined “chemical factory” path starts with reproducible environments, broad acceptance tests that treat production behavior as a black box, and vertical domain modules instead of horizontal layers. Rejuvenation may fix bugs while refactoring; alchemical nicknames label concrete moves such as facades to sever dependencies and a coagula-style pass that gathers methods as static functions to reveal ownership before splitting classes.

A financial pricing example walks through introducing a data-context module that hides connections and options, then simplifying callers. A smaller label-printing sample shows disentangling cycles between client, address, and printer types. The close urges kaizen-style upkeep, deliberate retirement planning, and real architecture ownership so systems do not slide into unmaintainable legacy by default.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Brace yourself! Storm is coming! (Łukasz Gebel, Michał Koziorowski)
talks.teaser: Attendees learn Apache Storm basics, tuple flow through spouts and bolts, and how to run a word-count topology locally or on a cluster.
talks.summary:
The presenters introduce Apache Storm as an open-source framework for distributed, real-time processing of data streams, tracing its origins at Twitter and typical production uses cited for Yahoo, Spotify, and Infochimps-style clickstream analytics.

They walk through core building blocks: serializable tuples, spouts that ingest from queues or APIs, bolts that transform or aggregate, and topologies as directed acyclic graphs. Processing guarantees range from best-effort through at-least-once acknowledgment trees to the stateful Trident exactly-once model, which they only flag for follow-up reading. Cluster roles include ZooKeeper coordination, Nimbus deployment, supervisors hosting workers, executors, and tasks.

A Java word-count topology demonstrates reliable spouts, split and count bolts, tick tuples for periodic logging, shuffling versus fields grouping, local debugging, and a minimal single-machine cluster with Storm UI and log viewer metrics. Closing notes cover resource-aware placement on heterogeneous cloud hardware and managed Storm clusters on Azure HDInsight, with encouragement to experiment when large volumes must be processed quickly.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Keep IT clean: mid-sized building blocks and hexagonal architecture (Jakub Nabrdalik)
talks.teaser: Explains mid-sized Java modules via package scope, facades, and hexagonal architecture so teams run sub-second behavioral tests.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens from Allegro’s large Java and microservice estate and cites Pieter Hintjens on complexity as a people problem rather than a tooling problem. He describes a blind spot between a few hundred and a few thousand lines of code, where layered packages such as model, repository, service, and web force most classes to be public. Contrasts with JDK libraries, Guava’s package-scoped types, GitHub keyword statistics, and languages where public is the default leave package visibility marginal in everyday Java.

The talk promotes mid-sized modules built from packages: one primary public facade per feature area, public DTOs and exceptions where data crosses boundaries, and package scope for controllers, validators, and internal domain code. Allegro article and category examples show CQRS-style query objects, infrastructure behind interfaces plus Spring configuration beans, and facades assembled without registering every class in the IoC container. He links this to ports and adapters so module tests inject only external I/O and run in milliseconds, while full Spring integration startups steal attention during test-driven work.

A film-rental planning exercise turns requirements into module boundaries, Spock specifications, and an in-memory repository before adding HTTP and persistence. He closes by treating public as a published API, testing modules only through that surface, limiting slow integration tests to positive wiring paths, and noting that well-faceted packages are straightforward to peel into separate microservices.

talks.title: JDD 2017: Modern DevOps with Kubernetes (Michał Wroński)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD 2017: Modern DevOps with Kubernetes (Michał Wroński).
talks.summary:
## Overview
Michał Wroński presents a hands-on exploration of Kubernetes as a modern DevOps solution, emphasizing that Kubernetes is a container orchestration engine designed to manage microservices at scale. The talk centers on three foundational principles for microservices: robust logging, monitoring, and health checks—without which infrastructure management becomes blind. Kubernetes enables automation, continuous delivery, and proper code isolation across services, making it invaluable for teams managing 10+ microservices.

## Key Architectural Concepts
Kubernetes clusters consist of master nodes (the "brain" managing scheduling and desired state) and worker/agent nodes (where services are deployed). Access requires a secured context that proxies traffic properly. The fundamental deployment unit is a pod—a container or group of containers treated atomically, sharing network namespace, IP, ports, and volumes. Pods are ephemeral and managed by higher-level constructs; they should not be created manually in production.

## Core Technical Features
**Deployments** provide declarative state management, specifying desired replicas, resource limits, and probe configurations. **Liveness probes** report whether deployment was successful, while **readiness probes** implement circuit-breaker logic—removing overloaded instances from load balancers during traffic spikes. **Replica Sets** (or replica controllers) maintain desired pod counts and enable rapid traffic switching during updates. **Services** provide load balancing and logical grouping of pods; they also enable service discovery via built-in DNS, allowing services to reference each other by name within the cluster. **ConfigMaps** and **Secrets** store key-value configuration separately from deployments, ensuring consistency across environments. **Daemon Sets** deploy a single pod instance on every node, useful for monitoring and logging agents. **StatefulSets** maintain startup order and state for services with dependencies. **Ingress** provides a single external entry point with routing rules, reducing security exposure from multiple service endpoints.

## Rolling Updates and Rollback
Rolling updates occur without downtime or with minimal downtime. Kubernetes maintains old replica set versions in history, allowing rapid rollback via simple commands. Update strategy can be configured—for example, reducing instances by 50% during deployment on large services. The underlying mechanism is fast (milliseconds to nanoseconds) because it simply switches traffic between replica sets.

## Scaling and Monitoring
Manual scaling uses simple commands to adjust replica counts. **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)** reads metrics from Heapster, a central metrics aggregator that collects data from cAdvisor on each node. Monitoring integrations like Datadog use daemon sets to forward metrics and logs from nodes to aggregation services.

## Cloud Deployment Options
**GCP** is the easiest entry point—Google invented Kubernetes, offers free master nodes, automatic scaling, and transparent cluster updates out-of-the-box. **Azure** provides Kubernetes via Container Service with single-command deployment, though auto-scaling support was still developing. **AWS** requires the Kops tool (more complex setup) but offers auto-scaling and version management. **Local development** uses Minikube instead of Vagrant or Docker Compose.

## When to Use Kubernetes
Kubernetes is ideal for 10+ microservices, high resource utilization without idle time, and multi-team infrastructure sharing. For 2–5 microservices, manual scripts may suffice. Kubernetes enables multi-environment setups on single clusters via namespaces with resource quotas (e.g., development limited to 5% of cluster power, QA to 20%). **ECS vs. Kubernetes**: ECS handles only scaling; Kubernetes provides comprehensive orchestration including configuration management and service discovery. Kubernetes is cloud-agnostic, enabling migration and generic architectures.

## Key Benefits and Drawbacks
**Advantages**: Eliminates shell scripts and configuration tools (Puppet, Chef); provides standardization through declarative manifests; ensures idempotent operations; transparent updates; built-in service discovery; integrated configuration management; supports local development. **Drawbacks**: Complexity increases with cluster size; Ingress creates additional hop in traffic path; requires understanding of multiple abstractions (pods, deployments, services, etc.).

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2017 - Bastian Widmer - Is #NoOps The New Evil? Or Is It Just „I Don’t Care“-Ops?
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning DevOpsDays Warsaw 2017 - Bastian Widmer - Is #NoOps The New Evil? Or Is It Just „I Don’t Care“-Ops?.
talks.summary:
# Overview
Bastian Widmer, a system engineer at Amazo (a Swiss company), explores the concept of NoOps—not as the elimination of operations, but as the natural evolution of DevOps through aggressive automation and self-service infrastructure. The talk challenges misconceptions about NoOps while demonstrating how his company has implemented it in practice.

# Key Topics
Widmer defines NoOps as an operational paradigm and service design approach where infrastructure is so well-defined and standardized that developers can deploy and manage services without needing to contact operations teams. He contrasts this with DevOps, positioning DevOps as the culture and collaboration aspect while NoOps represents the focus on automation. The core misconception he addresses is that NoOps means eliminating operations staff—in reality, it redistributes their focus toward infrastructure improvement rather than repetitive manual tasks.

# Technical Implementation
Widmer's company demonstrates NoOps principles through several concrete practices:
- Automated environment creation: developers create a git branch and receive a Slack notification within 30 seconds confirming the environment is deployed, with no operational effort required
- Infrastructure as code: treating infrastructure configurations as versioned, tested code rather than precious "snowflake" servers
- Self-service tooling: developers modify nginx configurations and Docker containers locally, with automated checks preventing catastrophic failures
- Externalized services: outsourcing email delivery (SendGrid) and other non-core operations, with one contact required per year for scaling needs
- Blameless post-mortems: when an employee accidentally deleted customer files, the team focused on process improvements rather than blame, restoring everything within an hour

The team runs containers in production, uses a fully open-source stack, and conducts annual security audits by giving customers root access to their repository for self-directed penetration testing.

# Cultural Shifts
A critical insight is that modern software developers must increasingly understand operational concerns—distributed systems, queuing mechanisms, performance characteristics—to be effective. Rather than viewing this as burden-shifting, Widmer frames it as empowerment: giving developers access to configuration files and deployment tools enables faster iteration while safeguards (automated checks, staged rollouts) prevent disasters. His developers were "very welcoming" to this increased autonomy.

The team practices direct customer communication through Slack rather than ticketing systems, improving documentation when patterns of repeated questions emerge. This philosophy extends to support: if customers can self-serve, the operations team scales better and can focus on infrastructure resilience.

# Takeaways
NoOps is not about job elimination—cloud computing, containerization, and service automation have increased rather than decreased operational workload over the past 10+ years. Instead, NoOps represents a redesign of what operations teams focus on. Operations teams still exist; they work on building systems robust enough that developers need minimal intervention. The phone call analogy encapsulates the principle: you don't call your service provider to make each call; the system simply works through self-service standards. Widmer suggests renaming NoOps to "RelaxOps" to better capture that it's about building systems that take care of themselves while operations teams handle exceptions and continuous improvement.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2017 - Kamil Szczygieł - Infrastructure As Code
talks.teaser: Lessons Learned analyzes DevOpsDays Warsaw 2017 - Kamil Szczygieł - Infrastructure As Code.
talks.summary:
Kamil Szczygieł traces infrastructure automation from 2000s bare-metal runbooks through VMware hypervisors, today’s Kubernetes hype, and the infrastructure-as-code discipline. He contrasts mysterious snowflake servers, hero hotfixes, and siloed dev–ops hate with versioned Terraform, immutable AMIs, and CI pipelines that plan, apply, test, and promote across environments.

Pitfalls include culture without trust, using Terraform provisioners as config management, mixing Chef and Ansible arbitrarily, picking tools for popularity, and assuming k8s for two containers. He advocates Terragrunt-style skeleton modules, separate state per component, coordinated immutable replacements, and reviewing IaC like application code.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2017 - Tomasz Pająk - What Can Possibly Go Wrong With Your DevOps Transformation?
talks.teaser: Explains how leadership, org structure and feedback loops make or break a DevOps transformation, with real examples.
talks.summary:
The session starts from a working definition of DevOps as a technology change that also depends on process and culture, measured by speed of delivery and stability. The speaker ties these measures to State of DevOps figures for high-performing organisations, citing lead time, deployment frequency, failure rate and time to recover. The argument then draws on analogies from car manufacturing, house building and batch sizes to show how local optimisation, context switching and large batches slow delivery down.

The middle of the talk separates complicated problems, which analysis can solve, from complex ones, which call for experiments and short feedback loops. A release pipeline example shows a stage that let only about 10 percent of runs through. The team traced the failures to the move to multi-node environments, built multi-node test setups with Docker Compose, and automated deployment steps, which shortened rollout durations over time. The speaker also describes how traditional silo organisations differ from matrix setups and from platform teams serving product teams.

The closing example is a post-mortem of a payment outage in which a failed settlement job left a message queue full and transactions stalled, and a fix went out without the others being told. The lesson drawn is to monitor thread pool consumption as an earlier weak signal, and to build enough trust that people can admit mistakes. The practical takeaways are to reduce handoffs, shorten feedback loops, and treat culture as the foundation for any tooling change.

talks.teaser: Puść ansibla gitem przez dżenkinsa investigates PLNOG19 - Krzysztof Załęski.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a network architect at a Cisco partner integrator, argues that network configuration is still mostly manual and rarely tested before or after rollout. Application teams already use CI/CD pipelines and unit tests, while networking teams often hope a change works. He proposes treating network devices like servers: describe the intended state in declarative YAML files and apply it with Ansible, which connects over SSH or APIs without an agent and is idempotent, so reapplying an unchanged configuration makes no changes.

The live demo keeps the device configuration in GitLab, where a commit triggers a Jenkins pipeline. The first deployment, which configured OSPF on two Nexus-class routers, failed. The Ansible unit test showed that the OSPF neighbor did not come up, and checking the parameters revealed an MTU mismatch (1400 on one side against 1500 expected). After the value was corrected in the repository and redeployed, the pipeline passed and the session came up.

The speaker says a full network cannot be modeled in a lab, so tests can only check basic functions before production. He concludes that automation does not remove the need to understand the protocols being automated. Learning structured data formats, APIs and tools such as Ansible pays off whatever automation stack is chosen.

talks.title: PLNOG19 - Vincent Vais - The road to a interconnected distributed eco-system
talks.teaser: Outlines how a distributed European exchange fabric supports multi-cloud direct connects, peering, transit, and peer-to-peer services.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames interconnection for both buyers and sellers of network and content services, using NL-ix as a case study. Founded in 2002 as a Netherlands internet exchange competing with metro-limited alternatives, the operator grew across the Benelux and into more than fifteen countries, twenty-five cities, and 105 carrier-neutral data centers, with hundreds of peers on a single distributed VLAN and peak traffic on the order of 1.7–1.8 terabits.

The speaker walks through an “application journey” from on-premises basements through carrier and carrier-neutral colocation, hyper-connected campuses, and the enterprise shift toward OPEX and public clouds around 2015–2016. Multi-cloud and geo-dispersed offices add complexity: enterprises may need the same reach in Paris, London, and Warsaw to several providers, with latency and compliance driving direct connects rather than tunneling solely over the public internet. Close to fifty named cloud and SaaS destinations can be reached via established transports, peering (including Office 365–related paths), or transit, often kept on the operator’s private backbone where possible.

A closing taxonomy contrasts incumbent exchanges, cloud-enabled but walled data centers, national carriers, interconnect platforms, integrators, and application providers without their own interconnection strategy. Practitioners should treat interconnection as an ecosystem fabric—VLANs and partnerships for DDoS scrubbing, content, and cloud on-ramps—not a single-site peering decision.

talks.title: CONFidence 2017: Człowiek w systemie bezpieczeństwa (Paulina Piasecka, Krzysztof Liedel)
talks.teaser: Explains how Poland built its national cybersecurity doctrine around the state, companies and citizens, using Estonia and Georgia as cases.
talks.summary:
The two speakers, who previously worked in a national security office in Poland, describe how the country began building a strategic approach to cybersecurity around 2011. At that time Polish law had no definition of cyberspace, and an attempt to add one through a presidential-powers statute sparked a public controversy. They argue that any definition should cover the human relationships between people, not only the networks and information they handle.

The talk then turns to the doctrine, which rests on three pillars: the public sector, the private sector and the individual citizen. The speakers compare Estonia, which set up a volunteer cyber defence league after the 2007 attacks, with Georgia, where drones bought from Israel were later taken over by Russia, showing the risk of relying on imported equipment. They also discuss the difficulty of building offensive capabilities, the gaps in international law for hybrid conflicts, and why coordination should rest on mechanisms rather than a single named coordinator.

In closing, the speakers present the National Cybersecurity Centre as a space where business, banks and public bodies exchange information and build trust. Questions from the audience covered whether companies could be allowed to test systems and how intrusions should be reported. The practical takeaway is that national cyber resilience depends on cooperation among all three groups, and that legal and organisational details matter as much as the technology.

talks.title: CONFidence 2017: Post-its, post-its, post-its everywhere (Jos Weyers)
talks.teaser: Shows how photos, press coverage, and video leak key bitting so locks stop acting like secrets.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a physical key as a password: once the bitting is visible, copying or milling a working duplicate is often practical. The speaker, a sports lock picker affiliated with TOOOL and Dutch hackerspaces, opens with sport-picking ethics—only locks you own or have permission to test—and walks through decades of real failures.

Cases span mail-in key cloning, telephoto decoding of keys on a terrace table, shared TSA luggage keys reproduced from news photos, NYC subway master keys published after scare stories, fire-department and elevator master keys in the press, and a prank where a rival space’s mailbox key photo became a laser-cut duplicate. A frame-by-frame video of a Belgian Speetgaz meter key yields a guessed code that works on a purchased unit. Low-budget casting from dental impression compound and high-end slug millers illustrate duplication when blanks are restricted.

The close ties these leaks to modern cameras, CCTV, social posts aggregated by sites like pleasebreak.in, and products that ask users to photograph keys for “security” accessories. Takeaway: treat keys like credentials—shield them in use, never publish them, and assume compromise after brief exposure.

talks.title: CONFidence 2017: Cyberprzestępczość - wyzwaniem w pracy Policji (Jan Klima)
talks.teaser: Maps cybercrime growth in Poland and how police units close cases from phishing to transnational fraud rings.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with an Interpol-aligned definition of cybercrime and Polish statistics showing sharp rises in computer-related offenses while conventional crime fell, including regional patterns around Kraków. The speaker describes an industrial underground that commissions vulnerability research, sells exploit kits, rents botnets, and outsources targeted crimes, illustrating botnet rental consoles and familiar human-factor risks.

Most of the session walks through investigations the cybercrime unit closed despite operational secrecy limits. Examples include a law-firm campaign that exfiltrated documents before ransomware-style extortion, identity-theft job scams and a fake branded e-shop that moved hundreds of thousands of złoty, a long-running SMS Premium scheme netting millions, and a cross-border laundering case tied to Nigerian-style fraud, a Europol joint investigation team, dozens of arrests abroad, and large proven losses plus stolen payment-card data.

The close highlights persistent public unawareness, highly effective social engineering, gaps in Polish rules for digital evidence and live forensic collection, slow cross-border data access, and anonymity tools criminals use. Practitioners gain a law-enforcement view of scale, prosecution constraints such as complaint-driven procedures, and why reporting and education remain decisive.

talks.title: CONFidence 2017: Hacking embedded with OpenWrt (Vladimir `vovcia’ Mitiouchev)
talks.teaser: Shows how to reach an embedded router's serial console, boot loader and flash, then rebuild and modify OpenWrt firmware.
talks.summary:
The talk covers hacking embedded devices, mostly home routers, with techniques that the speaker says apply to most IoT hardware. It starts with serial basics: RS-232 signal levels that can reach around 15 volts and would damage a 3.3 volt board, RS-422 and RS-485 for longer or multipoint links, and UART as the chip behind the serial link. It then explains CMOS and TTL voltage levels, when a logic level converter is needed, and how serial adapters compare, from FTDI-based devices to cheap clones and a Raspberry Pi or ESP8266 used as a bridge.

Next the speaker shows how to find a console: locate ground with a multimeter, identify the transmit pin by watching voltage change during boot or by checking the processor datasheet, then guess the baud rate, starting with common values. The boot log reveals a U-Boot bootloader, its environment variables and flash partitions. Using OpenWrt as the example system, the speaker walks through the build steps, including selecting the target profile and image type, and warns that images larger than flash or RAM will fail to build.

To load an image, the speaker transfers it over serial with Kermit and U-Boot's loadb command, noting that slow serial links can take twenty minutes or more, and mentions TFTP as a faster option where a network is available. Firmware can then be analysed with binwalk, extracted with sasquatch or firmware-mod-kit, and edited, for example to change a default password, before repacking and flashing. For locked bootloaders, direct SPI flash access or JTAG are presented as riskier alternatives. The main takeaway is that the boot loader is often the easiest way into cheap devices, and that a bad write can brick the hardware.

talks.title: CONFidence 2017: Hacker Inside Dude (Paweł Maziarz, Karol Celiński)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in CONFidence 2017: Hacker Inside Dude (Paweł Maziarz, Karol Celiński).
talks.summary: Paweł Maziarz and Karol Celiński demo human-interface-device attacks such as USB Rubber Ducky implants used on years of penetration tests, explaining why HID keystroke injection still beats phishing for internal pivoting.

talks.title: CONFidence 2017: Threat Management in Mozilla (Michał Purzyński)
talks.teaser: Mozilla's security team walks through a fictional administrator compromise and the detection stack used to investigate and contain it.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a security operations center scenario: an alert flags an administrator account that appears to log in from San Francisco and Moscow within hours, triggering questions about impossible travel and compromised credentials. The narrative follows an investigation that is described as having never actually occurred, yet is used to show how Mozilla would respond at scale across thousands of people and servers.

The middle of the talk reconstructs lateral movement starting from a public-facing foothold, abuse of jump hosts and SSH, suspected second-factor compromise, credential hunting in memory, and reach into sensitive roles including cases where multi-factor requirements had exceptions. The speaker emphasizes hunting tactics, techniques, and procedures rather than relying on easy-to-change indicators such as IP addresses, and describes correlating sessions, certificates, exfiltration paths, and reverse tunnels while trying to contain an agile adversary.

The closing sections pivot to Mozilla’s ongoing threat-management platform: large-scale packet capture and network sensors, custom Bro-style scripting, application and host monitoring plugins, Elasticsearch-backed analytics, automated alerting into the SOC workflow, and privacy-conscious design tradeoffs. A short demo illustrates interactive compliance checks on systems. The takeaway is that dense telemetry plus codified detection and tight exception discipline turns the security stack into something attackers must fight through during investigation, not a silent ally.

talks.title: CONFidence 2017: Hacking Card Emulation (Sławomir Jasek)
talks.teaser: Explores how host card emulation stores payment keys on Android and demonstrates practical cloning attacks against mobile banking apps.
talks.summary:
Mobile wallets increasingly rely on host card emulation instead of onboard secure elements, so contactless payment credentials and cryptographic keys live in normal application storage. The presenter frames the work as stress-testing the only safeguards that matter once commercial and legal barriers fail to stop motivated attackers.

The attack narrative rules out naive phone theft and NFC number skimming because tokenization and EMV session keys block reuse. Root-capable malware is the realistic path: privileged access enables backup or extraction of the wallet’s private data, restoration onto an attacker device, and—when issuers bind keys to hardware identifiers—cloning or spoofing those traits with frameworks that intercept system properties. Demonstrations include contactless payments from copied data, impersonating the genuine handset to the wallet server, and capturing push-delivered key replenishment so limited-use keys can be renewed. Several apps allow patching consumer-device verification so high-value charges avoid terminal PIN entry.

Across nine banking applications and seven common HCE library stacks, cloning succeeded with effort scaling from simple file copy to root hiding against native integrity checks. Practitioners should assume cloning cannot be eliminated outright; risk drops when apps check more device signals, resist tampering, integrate stronger attestation, and avoid being the weakest option in a crowded market.

talks.title: CONFidence 2017: Escaping the (sand)box (Robert Swiecki)
talks.teaser: Surveys Linux sandboxing mechanisms, from chroot and ptrace to seccomp-bpf and namespaces, and where each one breaks down.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the practical need to run untrusted code: image and video converters, PDF parsers, hiring platforms that compile candidate submissions, shared CTF servers, and malware analysis. The speaker argues that compiler hardening and sanitizers do not make a sandbox. Even a well-built sandbox can fall below the process level, for example through a CPU virtualization flaw that let an unprivileged guest reach ring zero on the host.

The middle of the talk goes through the Linux mechanisms in turn. chroot was never meant as a security boundary and can be escaped by design. Capabilities are numerous and hard to reason about, and several are effectively root-equivalent. Software CPU emulators are slow and bug-prone. ptrace-based tracers suffer from signal-handling races, time-of-check-to-time-of-use problems on syscall arguments held in user memory, and confusion between 32-bit and 64-bit syscall tables. Strict seccomp is too restrictive to be useful, seccomp-bpf is practical but cannot inspect user memory, and namespaces combined with raw sockets once enabled privilege escalation. Native Client is presented as an effective software jail that is costly to build and limited to whitelisted instructions.

The closing takeaway is that layered designs work better than any single mechanism. A seccomp-bpf policy paired with a broker process, namespaces, resource limits and a hypervisor can form a reasonable sandbox, but its author needs a deep understanding of kernel corner cases.

talks.title: CONFidence 2017: Odpowiedź organów ścigania na przestępczość... (Dominik Rozdziałowski)
talks.teaser: Maps how Polish police and prosecutors built cybercrime units, case trends, and industry liaison for high-tech offenses.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that while traditional crime figures fell sharply in Poland, cyber-related offenses and case volumes rose through the mid-2010s, even as dedicated staff remained a tiny fraction of overall criminal police. Polish law lacks a formal definition of cybercrime, so investigators rely mainly on Interpol-style categories and specific articles in the penal code, spanning online child abuse, stalking, identity abuse, and computer-related fraud and intrusions.

The speaker traces a path from a small translation-and-basics support cell around 2007 to provincial cyber sections and, in late 2016, a national coordination bureau at police headquarters with operational, research-support, and recognition divisions. He shares workload metrics, forensic activity, arrest logistics, encryption as an investigative obstacle, uneven cross-border help, and faster cooperation with some non-EU partners than with certain EU states. The unit distinguishes cybercrime enforcement from corporate cyber security, offers malware and device analysis to trusted firms, and discusses weak sentences in high-impact cases such as large data leaks.

Practitioners hear how to reach the cyber duty desk without flooding it with noise, why the unit avoids publicizing operations, and how police may alert banks to freeze suspect transfers while evidence is gathered. Planned penal-code changes and cyber-security legislation are noted as ongoing levers, alongside the need for responsible industry reporting.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Etienne Caron, Mixed Reality for Social Good
talks.teaser: Shows how volunteers can build a mixed reality project with Lego, Raspberry Pi, AR markers and Unity for hospital kids.
talks.summary:
The talk presents mixed reality, which blends virtual and augmented reality, as a community effort rather than a solo build. It argues that volunteer groups can use affordable tools to bring VR experiences to children in hospitals, and it questions who actually gains when headsets and high-end computers remain expensive.

The demo project has four parts: a Lego model mirrored by a virtual one, a Raspberry Pi running Android Things that blinks an LED and drives a conveyor belt motor through a motor driver chip, an AR window that aligns virtual Lego blocks onto the physical model using a visual marker, and a Unity VR scene on Google Daydream. A real-time database keeps the components in sync. The speaker explains that Project Tango hardware was too costly, so a web AR library was used instead, and marker size affected alignment.

The Unity section covers the Google VR SDK, a controller emulator for faster testing, teleportation to reduce nausea, and a simple door animation triggered by colored keys. The closing message is that non-programmers can contribute art, models and electronics, and that shared mixed reality setups let an outside helper guide a headset user. Examples from the community include a Cardboard sea-floor experience for children with limited movement.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Cyril Mottier, Seamless Linking to Your App
talks.teaser: Explains how Android intent filters, verified app links, and Smart Lock unify web and native apps into one product experience.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames mobile apps, websites, and related clients as one product and argues that opaque handoffs between them hurt users. On Android he walks through declarative intent filters in the manifest: scheme, host, and path rules, when to enable filters only after login, and parsing incoming URLs in activities, using Trainline-style multi-country domains and legacy hostnames as a real-world pattern.

He then covers verified app links: `android:autoVerify`, HTTPS-only checks at install time against `/.well-known/assetlinks.json`, JSON content types and HTTP 200 responses without redirects, and tooling to validate statements. Chrome related-app banners via `manifest.json` promote installs when engagement heuristics allow; Smart Lock for Passwords plus an added `get_login_creds` relation in asset links, with manifest metadata pointing back to the same file, auto-fills credentials across web and app in both directions.

The close briefly notes app indexing, Firebase dynamic links for post-install context, and Android Instant Apps as a future ideal. Practitioners are urged to own their domains’ links, verify association, and treat the small manifest and server changes as high-impact glue rather than optional polish.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Ashley Benigno, Humans at the heart of digital
talks.teaser: Maps the shift toward living services and offers experience-led, nimble design practices for human-centered digital work.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by arguing that imagined technology from science fiction has largely arrived—drones, connected cars, voice assistants, and rapid product cycles—and that customers now judge every industry against the best digital experiences anywhere, not only direct competitors. The speaker frames a third wave of digital built on “living services,” where everyday objects gain connectivity and expectations flow fluidly across sectors.

The middle of the talk stresses that transformation remains a human problem despite slick keynote demos. Examples from consultancy work illustrate the point: retail and telco apps that grew adoption by clarifying bills and journeys, festival engagement for a mobile operator, frontline tools for a large telco, and pediatric communication aids for Harvard Medical School. The speaker advocates experience-led design—contextual IoT alerts, loyalty that favors customers, employee “tours of duty,” and “minimal lovable products” beyond bare feasibility—as well as nimble prototyping, risk-taking for learning, and blending physical and digital assets in ecosystems.

The close and Q&A reinforce a discover–envision–design process grounded in ethnographic research, journey mapping, and cross-functional workshops. Practitioners are urged to digitize routine work, give staff better tools, prototype faster than long planning cycles, and keep people—consumers, employees, or patients—at the center of every service decision.

talks.title: MCE 2017, Alexander Steinhart: Let’s get hooked on autonomy. Digital Technologies for Team Human.
talks.teaser: Argues that technology should empower people rather than addict them, and sketches design approaches that support that goal.
talks.summary: Alexander Steinhart argues smartphones exploit evolutionary cravings for information and social reward, producing distraction worse than teens rate privacy concerns. Drawing on psychology and prior Offtime studies, he contrasts attention-harvesting UX with positive-tech alternatives—calm technology, time-well-spent design, digital charters, slow media, and KPIs that measure user intent rather than engagement—and calls on builders to empower autonomy instead of addictive feeds.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Sophia Voychehovski, Object-Oriented UX
talks.teaser: Shows how object-oriented UX design keeps interfaces consistent across screens by modeling the objects users actually care about.
talks.summary:
Sophia Voychehovski draws on her time as a lead UX designer at CNN, where a 2012 election-results redesign had to be built responsively on a tight deadline. Given only days of notice, she cut the template set from nine to about four and reduced the number of modules, arguing that fewer moving parts make a system easier to build, test and use.

The core of the talk is object-oriented UX, which she distinguishes from modular design. Instead of starting from a component library, designers identify the real-world things users care about and let interface representations follow from them. She shows "shapeshifter" modules, where one thing looks and behaves differently across views, such as a listing in map view versus grid view on Craigslist or a file in Google Docs versus Google Drive. She also shows "masked" modules, such as a single healthcare card style reused for a calculator, a whitepaper, two kinds of video, a blog post and a demo form. Kickstarter is held up as an example of "integrity" modules that stay the same across contexts.

She argues that global navigation should be a backup plan, with contextual links from metadata and nested objects doing most of the navigation. The session closes with an object-mapping exercise: extracting objects from business goals, separating core content from metadata, building a matrix of nested relationships, and turning the result into modules, detail pages and list pages. The practical takeaway is to keep representations consistent by default and vary them by context only when user research supports the change.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Svetlana Isakova, Coroutines in Kotlin
talks.teaser: Presents Kotlin coroutines for non-blocking UI work, comparing suspend functions with threads, callbacks, and async/await.
talks.summary:
The session opens by asking who already uses Kotlin and who has tried coroutines, then frames coroutines as the headline feature in Kotlin 1.1. The speaker motivates them with a simple image-load example: long work on a UI thread blocks the app, while callbacks work but push code into nested handlers. Coroutines offer sequential, imperative code that can wait without holding a thread, using suspend points similar in spirit to C# async/await but implemented via library functions and compiler support rather than built-in keywords.

The middle of the talk contrasts naive one-thread-per-task designs and Java executor pools with suspendable computations. A coroutine is described as work that can pause and resume on shared threads, preserving locals through compiler-generated state machines that keep memory overhead low. Examples cover async, launch, await, parallel image loads, overlay on click with UI-thread continuation, try/catch around await, custom suspend functions, and cancellation behavior when library calls cooperate.

The close covers Java interop through wrapping futures, testing with runBlocking, brief mention of yield-based sequences, and the kotlinx.coroutines ecosystem including channels. Q&A notes experimental status in 1.1, a small Android UI context dependency, and pointers to Roman Elizarov’s guide for deeper material. Practitioners should leave understanding when to suspend instead of block and where to read next for production use.
