talks.title: MCE 2017: Sally Shephard, Helping users create good habits
talks.teaser: Explains how to build user habits in apps using triggers, simple actions, rewards and investment, and how to test them.
talks.summary:
Presented by an iOS developer who usually works on accessibility, this talk explains how apps can build habits that keep users returning. It starts from the point that downloads do not equal active users, and that many top-grossing free apps depend on repeat use. A habit is described as a behavior repeated over time, combining a trigger, motivation and an action. A four-step model follows: trigger, action, reward and investment. Triggers move from external prompts such as notifications toward internal ones, and actions should be reduced to the fewest possible steps.

The middle section looks at streaks and rewards. Hard streaks that reset at midnight can drive users away after one missed day, while softer designs, such as a month-long bonus calendar, tolerate gaps. Time zone handling also broke one singing app's streak, and points with no clear meaning quickly lose their pull. The speaker walks through a vocal training app to show how repetitive reminders, exercises that grew too long, and levels with no visible progress each weakened the loop over months.

For testing, the speaker recommends analytics that log failure points as well as successes, and a habit time machine that revisits triggers, actions, rewards and investment at set intervals, with empathy for what users feel after a missed day. Action failures often come from time, money, physical effort, social pressure or non-routine demands. The talk closes by noting that the line between habit and addiction is blurry, and that designers should help users reach their goals rather than simply extract spending.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Olivier Jeannel, Beyond Design: Inclusion
talks.teaser: Shows how live call transcription on Android helps deaf users place everyday calls and how inclusive design reshapes the phone.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why voice calls still matter for urgent, emotional contact even when chat apps dominate, and why roughly one in a hundred people cannot rely on ordinary telephony. The presenter describes building an Android calling app that streams the other party’s speech into readable text, driven by a simple goal: staying in touch with family across distance while working inside the telecom industry.

The middle follows product and design choices: favoring Android’s reach and Google’s speech stack, reworking navigation around accessibility guidelines, and partnering with designers who questioned assumptions through interviews and rapid prototypes. User tests exposed confusion about whether the tool was messaging, Skype, or a paid service, which pushed humbler iteration, stronger visual identity, and attention to privacy fears when voice data is processed.

Practitioners hear that speech recognition lag and noisy environments remain partly outside app control, so UX must surface context visually without overwhelming users. The close ties inclusion to mainstream gains—larger text, flashes, captions—and argues that challenging legacy phone habits, not only adding features, is what makes assistive calling stick.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Michael May, Romain Piel: Cats and Dogs (working together as an iOS and Android team)
talks.teaser: Explains how iOS and Android engineers can collaborate through joint kickoffs, pairing and shared Swift and Kotlin code.
talks.summary:
The speakers, both mobile developers, describe how the iOS and Android engineers at Songkick came to work as one team. Features started with whole-team kickoffs that included QA, product and design, so platform differences did not split the work. Developers paired across platforms, tested each other's builds before release, and presented showcases as a team. A weekly mobile breakfast shared knowledge on topics from new languages to platform releases.

They describe mobile engineers as T-shaped, with deep knowledge in one platform and broader skills across the product. Cross-platform tools such as React Native offer little to engineers already expert in one native platform, because they bring new languages, tooling and quirks. The speakers noted that Swift and Kotlin look alike, and that iOS auto layout and Android constraint layout rest on the same underlying technology. To test this, they paired on a conference schedule app, writing the iOS version in Swift and the Android version in Kotlin. They then added a server layer using the backend-for-frontend pattern, which returns screen-specific JSON, with both languages used on the server. Models could be shared between the server and the Android app.

Their advice was to hold kickoffs as a whole team, pair often, share work through talks and showcases, test each other's apps, learn a second platform's language, and consider backend-for-frontend so developers can work across layers. In the Q&A, one speaker described pitching this to a CTO as a way to reduce work, with pull requests that kept backend control in place.

talks.title: MCE 2017: M.Grzechociński, J.Karaśkiewicz: Save users’ data! Tips for reducing the APK size.
talks.teaser: Shows how an Android app team cut its APK from 62 MB to about 16.5 MB using image, icon and resource shrinking techniques.
talks.summary: The speakers address Android APK size, using a banking app with about 200 screens, more than a million active users and support back to API level 14. Their app had grown to 62 megabytes, so they first learned the difference between raw, download, install and update sizes, and used an APK size estimator to predict the figures a user sees. Their analysis of the built-in optimizer showed that it only helps in narrow cases: it handles grayscale and alpha detection and reduces palettes when an image has 256 colours or fewer, which saved about 5 percent for them. Larger gains came from their own work on images. They converted opaque PNGs to lossy palette PNGs, then recompressed them, and moved some photos to JPEG, choosing quality by a perceptual similarity score. They dropped medium-density resources and kept only the highest density for less-used screens, and converted about 900 PNG icons into vector drawables, which fell to roughly 310 files. Enabling resource shrinking removed unused resources, and keeping only the two languages the app supports removed more. Their final build came to about 16.5 megabytes, a 73 percent reduction. The speakers closed by suggesting that teams start with the APK analyzer, check download and install size, and weigh the cost of splitting APKs before adopting it.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Magdalena Paluch, Designing AI Personality
talks.teaser: Shows how to give an AI assistant a personality through purpose, values, voice and backstory, using a hands-on writing exercise.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a designer who has worked on automotive and advanced product strategy projects, argues that AI carries a negative image and that designers and engineers can help give it a more positive one. She notes that design work is shifting toward writers, psychologists and character designers, and that cultural context changes how people view machines.

The core of the talk is a framework for building a system's personality, borrowed from how novelists create characters. Designers start with purpose, then pick an archetype such as a caregiver, define the relationship, values, physical movement, voice and language, and finally a backstory and name. The speaker also lists politeness principles attributed to Alan Cooper and says well-designed systems should recognise their own limits and ask for help.

Attendees wrote short love letters to everyday services such as an ATM or a coffee machine, then worked in groups to turn one into a full persona. Volunteers presented a rescued delivery robot named Puggly, a cleaning service named Pat and an airline check-in assistant named Jack. The speaker advised running the exercise with multidisciplinary teams, converging from playful ideas to a focused personality, and studying extreme users in the field.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Hilary Kenna, Designing the Future Reading Experience (RX)
talks.teaser: Explores how digital habits reshape focus and how designers can blend print depth with screen discovery.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by asking how audiences read on phones and social feeds today, arguing that constant connectivity trains superficial skimming and weakens focus, retention, and critical thinking. She contrasts slow, contemplative print habits with fast, productive screen use, drawing on audience research from redesigning a major Irish newspaper—where data scientists challenged intuitive layout choices yet helped grow readership by roughly two million—and on reader segments she labels snackers versus gorgers.

She organizes future reading design around four themes: data-informed personalization, broader typographic formats beyond responsive layouts, discovery in crowded information ecosystems, and emerging devices beyond traditional screens. Through principles pairing the codex with the smartphone, experiments such as one-word spritz reading, and a Faber iPad edition of The Waste Land that keeps the poem central while adding navigation, annotation, and performance media, she shows how interactivity can support rather than replace deep text engagement. She also warns that stacked digital interfaces hinder the cognitive “spread” print affords, and that licensed e-libraries and obsolete digital editions erode preservation of noteworthy interactive books.

Practitioners should treat reading modes explicitly—research versus contemplation—and offer engagement choices from text-only focus to enriched audio. She closes by urging a deliberate mash-up: accept fast, distributed consumption while clawing back space for slow, thoughtful reading across wearables, spatial media, and tactile prototypes still on the horizon.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Fernando Cejas, Hidden mysteries behind big mobile codebases
talks.teaser: Enforced architecture, layered tests, CI, and team pairing keep large Android and iOS codebases readable and shippable as they scale.
talks.summary:
Fernando Cejas frames how a solo pet project grows into a mobile program serving more than 100,000 installs on both platforms, using SoundCloud as the working example. He opens with a release mishap that pointed production traffic at a tiny development API tier, illustrating how mistakes amplify once an app scales.

The core of the talk is a set of recurring pressures on big mobile codebases: sheer size, entangled complexity, flaky UI and acceptance tests, inconsistent patterns such as AsyncTask or many ways to perform the same request, and accumulating technical debt. He advocates picking an architecture and enforcing it (their internal “spoker” variant near clean architecture), evolving through small refactors—including an RxJava 1 to RxJava 2 migration in end-to-end slices—and keeping pull requests near a 500-line review limit. Testing is treated as non-negotiable, with on the order of 6,000 unit tests, about 1,000 integration tests, and about 500 acceptance tests, plus a rotating “sheriff” role to chase flaky tests. A technical-debt radar maps pain versus estimated fix time to prioritize work like dependency injection startup cost or modularizing the data layer.

He closes on sharing code across listener and creator apps via Android kit, Skippy, and Cycle; full CI with no manual QA; release trains every 15 days; and team structure spanning tech lead, core, feature, and testing engineering teams, with heavy pairing for onboarding. The takeaway for practitioners is to treat readability, consistency, tests, automation, and teamwork as the levers that keep large mobile codebases from stalling as headcount and features grow.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Erik Abbing, Flaminia Del Conte: Humanising tech to...
talks.teaser: A service-design duo delivers a three-stream framework and case studies on putting human needs before technology push.
talks.summary:
Two presenters from a multi-office service design firm reframe “positive technology” as human technology: tools that stay in the background while people reach their goals. They argue developers and designers often fall in love with capability for its own sake, while meaningful work starts from impact on lives across healthcare, government, and everyday devices.

They introduce a braided framework integrating a business stream (cost savings and new revenue), a human stream (functional, emotional, and social outcomes, illustrated with ride-hailing-style journeys), and an organization stream (buy-in, shared vision, staff capability). A playful Philips pediatric MRI prep experience contrasts with “solutions waiting for a problem” such as gimmicky gadgets. Three applied stories follow: NHS outreach in Tower Hamlets via channels people already use, Zodiac Aerospace’s passenger-centered innovation lab versus materials-only roadmaps, and TransLink’s research on bank-card transit payment across risk-averse and tech-eager personas, including aligning banks and operators.

They close with a human technology manifesto: every design choice affects customers and employees, sustainability matters for business and society, and proficiency with tech does not guarantee value for those who must use it. Audience questions cover selling organizational co-creation, treating five-year Excel business cases as design artifacts, and staying agile when leadership vetoes agreed directions.

talks.title: MCE 2017: Dale Knauss, Introduction to Virtual Reality Development with Unity
talks.teaser: Maps Unity VR development from editor basics through scripting, starter libraries, and habits that keep projects shippable.
talks.summary:
The session opens by gauging how much of the audience has tried consumer headsets or built VR content, then frames the speaker’s move from web and mobile work into leading VR and AR product builds. VR is portrayed as familiar in some engineering ways yet far more collaborative and specialized, with teams leaning on full engines rather than small libraries and often choosing between Unity and Unreal for cross-platform client work.

The core walkthrough is a compressed Unity orientation: editor panels, scene hierarchy discipline, game objects and components, inspector-driven tweaks for non-programmers, C# scripting patterns, enabling VR targets, and follow-on study areas such as graphics basics, shaders at a high level, linear algebra, and time spent inside headsets. Practical starting advice covers small prototypes, placeholder geometry, open-source helpers like VRTK, free or store assets, and active communities for questions.

The close packages seven working habits—sensory richness, in-editor tooling for the team, early performance tuning for nausea-safe frame rates, fearless prototyping balanced against optimization, frequent headset checks, outreach to practitioners, and building what feels exciting—with audience questions on designers committing via Git, painful scene merges and prefab workflows, VR as a forward-looking business bet, locomotion and comfort research, and picking HTC Vive or Daydream to experiment. The same skill stack is noted as relevant to augmented reality platforms Unity already supports.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: The Babel Fish Data: A Case Study (Norbert Wójtowicz)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding 4Developers 2017: The Babel Fish Data: A Case Study (Norbert Wójtowicz).
talks.summary:
## Overview
Norbert Wójtowicz presents a thesis that data, rather than objects, should be the foundational principle of software systems. He uses the Babel Fish metaphor from Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy to illustrate how data enables different systems written in different languages to communicate. He then draws a historical parallel to scurvy—a disease eradicated in the 18th century but tragically reintroduced in the 19th century through misguided practices—to argue that programming has similarly lost the benefits of data-oriented development.

## The Core Problem
The speaker argues that in the 1960s-70s, programming languages discovered functional programming, logic programming, relational databases, and garbage collection—essentially all the foundations of modern computing. However, the 1980s-90s saw the adoption of object-oriented programming (Java, C++), which reintroduced complexity and fragility. Modern software struggles with late deployments, bugs, and crashes despite having washing hands (TDD, agile, scrum). The solution is recognizing that data is the vitamin C of programming.

## Fundamental Data Structures
All systems can be built from three essential data structures:
1. **Streams**: Ordered sequences that introduce temporal order
2. **Trees**: Hierarchical structures underlying all UIs, whether mobile, web, or desktop
3. **Meshes**: Interconnected graphs representing business domain relationships

The speaker illustrates with Spotify's example: three core objects (listeners, artists, songs) with everything else being relationships between them. As features accumulate, the mesh becomes denser. Collection types needed are lists (order), maps (key-value association), and sets (mathematical operations), with important distinctions between homogeneous and heterogeneous collections.

## Clojure Spec Details
The talk focuses extensively on Clojure Spec, a specification library enabling:
- **Validation**: Predicates that return true/false for data, with detailed error explanations showing exact failure points
- **Composition**: Building complex specifications from simple ones using logical operators (and, or)
- **Conforming**: Not just validating but transforming data through specification layers
- **Generation**: Automatically creating valid test data matching specifications
- **Function specifications**: Adding constraints to function arguments, returns, and relationships between them
- **Instrumentation**: Runtime assertion checking in development/staging environments
- **Test automation**: The test.check library generates hundreds of thousands of tests automatically

## Property-Based Testing Patterns
Drawing from QuickCheck (developed by John Hughes), the speaker outlines testing patterns:
1. Idempotency: Repeated operations yield the same result
2. Invertibility: Operation plus its inverse returns the original value
3. Model-based testing: Verify against a simpler reference implementation
4. Business axioms: Invariants that must always hold (e.g., Facebook friendships are bidirectional)
5. Distributed system testing: Generate random event timelines, distribute across multiple clients, verify eventual consistency

Computers can generate millions of test cases revealing edge cases humans never anticipate. Shrinking automatically reduces failing cases to minimal reproducible examples.

## Front-End Architecture Application
The speaker demonstrates applying these principles to front-end systems using data log as the query language. Components comprise: queries (graph queries for data), renders (pure functions returning UI trees), mutations (pure data streams), and reconciliation (pure functions transforming mutations into state snapshots). Testing occurs purely in code without running a browser, using specifications to verify layer integration. CSS testing is achieved by generating millions of data variations and rendering them.

## Takeaways
Programming should be data-centric, with data treated as immutable, semantic (clear meaning), and recursive (composable). Adopting data-oriented principles, specifications, and property-based testing yields better composability, superior testing, and simpler systems.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: Introduction to RxJS (Krzysztof Furmann)
talks.teaser: Live coding and marble diagrams introduce observables, operator chains, and flattening patterns for asynchronous front-end work.
talks.summary:
The session opens from a practical angle: rebuilding an application in Angular 2 meant leaning on RxJS for HTTP, user events, and state shaped as streams rather than one-off promises. The speaker contrasts callback sequencing, promise chaining for single outcomes, and observables as ongoing sequences listeners can join over time.

Most of the middle is hands-on. Demos cover lazy versus eager execution, cold observables that restart on each subscription, and hot sharing via publish and replay. Marble diagrams explain concat, reduce versus scan, and higher-order streams. Switching between inner observables is shown with clocks and clicks, then compared briefly to merge-all and concat-all.

A small text-history demo ties operators together: input events, drag selection, combineLatest, skip, and switch. The close points to ReactiveX documentation and well-known community teachers, with a warning that RxJS 5 naming differs from older tutorials. Attendees leave with a mental model for reading docs and choosing flattening operators in real UI code.

talks.title: CONFidence 2017: Interview with Gaweł Mikołajczyk (Cisco)
talks.teaser: A Kraków stage interview spans enterprise SOC work, fresh ransomware waves, and how newcomers can build skills for security careers.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens at CONFidence in Kraków with someone who wears several hats: technology partner to the conference, program council member, and day-to-day lead of Cisco security operations centers in Kraków and Tokyo. He describes rising complexity for large customers who expect help analyzing threats, spotting compromises, curbing malware—especially ransomware—and delivering both future mitigations and hands-on incident response when systems are actually breached.

He ties that mission to a presentation refreshed almost at the last minute around a global Windows-targeting campaign that preyed on long-unpatched machines, spread like a network worm, and encrypted files for bitcoin ransom. For enterprise SOCs he stresses a harder everyday problem than headline malware: separating noise from confirmed IT compromise, because suspicious IPs or reputation hits do not equal successful attacks. The Kraków SOC’s first anniversary framed recent weeks’ cases, though far more material existed than fit the session.

Closing segments pivot to students flooding the conference. He argues fundamentals—operating systems, programming, networking, curiosity about cyber security—plus reading network traffic where attacks surface, open paths to internships and analyst roles locally, and notes veteran specialists still find depth in the same teams.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: Unleashing Your Super-dev-powers (Karol Sójko)
talks.teaser: Shares personal productivity experiments for developers, from calendar time-boxing and Pomodoro to team goal mapping and gamification.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who leads a remote team of developers on productivity and growth, frames self-improvement as part of a developer's craft. Over about two years the speaker tested many methods, starting with a getting-things-done workflow and a search for the perfect to-do app. The lesson was that a tool suits a person's workflow rather than being universally best, and that an empty inbox is not a goal in itself.

Time-boxing every task on a calendar made the speaker busy but not more productive, so the calendar was gradually stripped back once routines formed. Pomodoro worked for demanding focus work but was too tiring to use daily. Journaling in a team chat channel brought transparency, and simple automation reduced the effort of keeping it. Mind maps of each developer's growth goals were reviewed weekly, while a Slack bot announced achievements and a points-based house tournament added energy. Starting each day with demanding work and ending with a short report rounded out the routine.

The closing section argued that methods should be treated as experiments, and that a two-week break from them showed what really helped. A yearly theme, shared publicly so others could offer help, was the final idea. The takeaways were to keep things simple, build trust, automate, find an accountability partner, experiment, take breaks, and make goals public. In the Q&A, the speaker noted that a shared journal can be read whenever suits, so it does not demand anyone's time.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: Architecture antipatterns and how to beat them 1/2 (Łukasz Szydło)
talks.teaser: A narrative diagnosis names mono-models, anemic domains, and read-write coupling in deep systems and outlines bounded contexts with CQRS.
talks.summary:
The session frames large, domain-rich applications as “deep” systems where UI screens cannot specify real behavior, unlike shallow CRUD apps. Through a fictional developer maintaining an ambitious e-commerce platform, common structural failures are cast as diagnosable diseases developers must treat.

The first illness is a single overloaded domain model: bloated entities, getters and setters, poor scalability, and stunted growth. The speaker ties it to vague ubiquitous language and shows how separating bounded contexts—shopper, customer, payer, delivery subject—replaces one “user” god-object with precise types sharing only identity. Anemic models are illustrated with a crocodile feeding metaphor: pulling data out instead of asking objects to behave. A second mono-model splits reads and writes; the talk contrasts safety, idempotency, multiple representations, and the typical 80/20 read-heavy usage pattern, introducing CQRS as separate command and query models without mandating exotic infrastructure.

The first half closes on “chronic transaction” antipattern symptoms: Spring `@Transactional` service boundaries that roll back order placement when email fails, blocking microservice extraction. The audience votes for a break before continuing with further diseases in part two.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: Architecture antipatterns and how to beat them 2/2 (Łukasz Szydło)
talks.teaser: Part two counters oversized flows, layered test debt, and ORM amnesia via eventual consistency, hexagonal ports, and recorded facts.
talks.summary:
The second installment continues a medical metaphor for software architecture, following a fictional developer named Gwidon through a system where everything is wired into oversized ACID-style flows. Chronic transaction disease is unpacked with a pre-computer shop scenario: orders are copied, retried, and sometimes compensated for rather than forced into millisecond database transactions. The prescribed shift is eventual consistency, one aggregate per technical transaction, repository-level atomicity for the entity and its outbound fact, and domain events that let downstream services catch up later.

A testing antipattern is framed with axioms that separate crashing Type A failures from silent Type B logic mistakes, plus prevention versus fast-deploy “treatment.” The speaker argues layered stacks pile dependencies on business code, then walks through inverting dependencies with ports and adapters so domain logic stays testable like a PC with peripherals. Uniform “monotony” across modules, one-size technology choices, and skyscraper thinking are contrasted with a city metaphor where each module picks an architecture that fits its job.

Closing material covers amnesia from ORM snapshot persistence that erases meaningful user actions, contrasting shopping-cart rows that look identical after different behaviors. Recording business facts as first-class events is offered as the cure, with a nod to a separate CQRS talk for mechanics. The closing advice is to let the business domain shape each building block instead of imposing generic patterns.

The presentation opens with Edwin Land as a metaphor for seeing familiar technology with fresh depth, then introduces badass.js as a mental framework for mastering JavaScript rather than another npm package. The speaker traces a personal arc from treating JS as a toy in 2006 to treating it as a primary craft, rejecting simplistic “follow your passion” narratives in favor of Cal Newport’s argument that sustained skill precedes passion.

The core weaves Carol Dweck’s growth versus fixed mindset, Daniel Kahneman’s fast and slow thinking, and a kanban-style limit on concurrent learning topics. A concrete deliberate-practice story describes reimplementing Promises against the official tests over two difficult days. The Dreyfus skill model and a London team anecdote stress pairing with slightly stronger peers for perceptual learning and steady feedback.

Later sections use the classic monkey parable to argue for reading primary sources, walking through test-driven implementation of abstract equality from the ECMAScript spec and when double equals is defensible. Deliberate reimplementation of everyday libraries, Deep Work versus shallow interruptions, and a closing note on dopamine myths reinforce one practical message: depth in the language itself repays more than chasing frameworks.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: It's all about the state, czyli co skrywa async/await w C#? (Dariusz Pawlukiewicz)
talks.teaser: Explores how C# async/await compiles into state machines and IL, with a live rebuild and deadlock pitfalls.
talks.summary:
The session opens by revisiting how synchronous and asynchronous methods interleave when a caller uses await, and why the Task type models a pending operation. It then sketches the .NET compile pipeline from C# through Intermediate Language to JIT, stressing that async and await are not IL instructions but syntactic sugar the compiler must expand.

The core argument is that each async method becomes its own IAsyncStateMachine-style struct, with one state per await plus an initial segment, orchestrated by an async method builder. Through a step-by-step demo, the speaker reimplements a simple GetTextAsync method by hand: MoveNext switches on state, TaskAwaiter handles completion without blocking threads, and the builder schedules continuations when work is still pending. A debugger walkthrough and ildasm comparison show how closely this mirrors real compiler output, including when the machine moves from stack to heap.

The close ties theory to production pitfalls: blocking on tasks via GetResult or .Result on a UI thread can deadlock when SynchronizationContext tries to resume on a blocked thread. ConfigureAwait(false) is recommended for library code. Practitioners should treat async/await as convenient surface syntax over a state machine they can reason about when things stall or misbehave.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: Browsers behind your back (Phil Nash)
talks.teaser: Shows how service workers, IndexedDB, and the Background Sync API let web apps queue POST requests offline and deliver them after reconnect.
talks.summary:
The presentation contrasts fire-and-forget messaging in native apps with the fragile web experience when users submit forms or POST data while offline. Most progressive web app work until then focused on caching pages via service workers; sending likes, cart updates, or messages still failed without connectivity.

Using a small SMS demo backed by a communications API, the speaker registers a service worker, intercepts form submission, persists outbound messages in IndexedDB (via promise-friendly helpers rather than raw callbacks or localStorage), and registers a background sync tagged event. When the browser regains network access, the sync handler keeps the worker alive, reads the outbox, posts each item with fetch, and removes successfully sent rows. Browser support at the time is largely Chromium-family, with notes on Samsung Internet, Firefox, Edge, and gaps on iOS Safari.

The talk closes by sketching newer background capabilities—background fetch for large media and periodic sync for scheduled updates—and walks through a live offline send that fails on a mistyped URL before succeeding. Practitioners should treat these APIs as progressive enhancement: unchanged behavior where unsupported, reliable deferred submission where available.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: 5 architectures of asynchronous JavaScript (Tomasz Ducin)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of 4Developers 2017: 5 architectures of asynchronous JavaScript (Tomasz Ducin).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at 4Developers 2017, Tomasz Ducin addresses a widespread issue among JavaScript developers: a lack of understanding regarding asynchronous execution order and mechanics, which frequently leads to brute-force workarounds and overcomplicated code. Ducin clarifies JavaScript's core concurrency model—a single-threaded, cooperative concurrency system governed by an event loop, message queues, and run-to-completion semantics. The talk walks through five major architectures for managing asynchronous operations: Callbacks, Event-Driven Architecture, Promises, Coroutines/Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP) / Async-Await, and Reactive Streams (RxJS).

### Key Topics
- **Concurrency Models and JavaScript Mechanics**: Comparing single-threaded synchronous (blocking, linear), multi-threaded (parallel execution with shared memory requiring semaphores/deadlock handling), and event-driven asynchronous execution. Ducin explains cooperative concurrency versus pre-emptive concurrency, highlighting that JavaScript tasks run to completion and cannot be interrupted by the scheduler.
- **Event Loop and Message Queues**: How asynchronous actions (timers, HTTP requests, UI events) push messages and callbacks onto a first-in, first-out queue, which the event loop processes sequentially. Ducin notes that `setTimeout` and `setInterval` guarantee only a minimum delay, not an exact execution time.
- **Callbacks and the Event-Driven Approach**: Inspecting synchronous callbacks (`map`, `filter`, IIFEs) versus asynchronous callbacks (`setTimeout`), as well as browser and custom DOM/framework events. The discussion touches on the callback hell / pyramid of doom issue and architectural challenges with multi-directional event flows.
- **Promises and Combinators**: Using ES6 Promise objects to handle single deferred computations cleanly in chains. The speaker contrasts sequential versus parallel flows and details combinators including `Promise.all`, `Promise.race`, and Bluebird additions like `Promise.any` and `Promise.some`.
- **Generators, Coroutines, and Async/Await**: Combining ES6 generators (`function*`, `yield`, `next()`) with promises to build coroutines, paving the way for the native ES8 `async`/`await` syntax. Ducin also demonstrates Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP) via libraries like `js-csp`.
- **Reactive Streams (RxJS)**: Explaining observables and reactive streams as a combination of the Observer pattern, the Iterator protocol, and functional programming, contrasting their multi-value, lazy, and cancellable nature with promises.

### Technical Details
- **Run-to-Completion**: If a computationally heavy task processes thousands of DOM nodes or heavy data in a single turn, the browser UI freezes because tasks cannot be pre-empted; resolving this requires slicing work into chunks using `setTimeout` or `setInterval`.
- **Promise Mechanics and Aggregates**:
  - A promise can only transition from `pending` to `fulfilled` or `rejected` once; subsequent attempts to settle are ignored.
  - `Promise.all` fails immediately if any single promise rejects.
  - `Promise.race` settles as soon as the first promise settles (resolve or reject).
  - `Promise.any` requires at least one promise to resolve, rejecting only if all fail; `Promise.some(n)` generalizes this to $n$ resolutions.
- **Coroutines & CSP (`js-csp`)**: Coroutines run within a single thread. In CSP, processes communicate via channels using `yield put` (which blocks the process if no receiver is listening) and `yield take` (which blocks until a value is placed in the channel), passing execution back and forth.
- **Observables vs. Promises**: Citing André Staltz (author of Cycle.js), Ducin notes that promises are single-value, always asynchronous, eager, and uncancellable, whereas observables handle multiple values, can be synchronous or asynchronous, are lazy (execution starts only upon subscription), and can be cancelled or completed.

### Takeaways
A deep grasp of JavaScript fundamentals—specifically function scope, context, closures, and the single-threaded event loop—is required before architecting complex applications. Developers should avoid assumptions about external network request timing to prevent race conditions. While callbacks and events suit simple interactions, modern patterns like `async`/`await` offer synchronous readability for single-value operations, CSP enables coordinated sequential tasks, and reactive streams (RxJS) provide powerful control over multi-event asynchronous pipelines across time.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: Functional JavaScript for everyone (Bartłomiej Witczak)
talks.teaser: Introduces functional JavaScript habits—pure functions, currying, and composition—for developers who want clearer, testable code.
talks.summary:
The session opens by reassuring a mixed Polish-and-English audience that deep JavaScript fluency is not required, then grounds functional style in everyday functions: higher-order functions, functions as first-class values, and why impure code that touches globals or databases is hard to test compared with explicit inputs and outputs.

The middle walks through practical patterns with live examples. Immutable data structures make outputs predictable; currying reorders HTTP client parameters so a shared auth token is applied once; map, filter, and reduce replace hand-written loops so transformation logic stays in one place. Function composition chains small parsers and render steps for JSON album data. A burrito metaphor wraps values so map applies inside a container, leading to optional-style Maybe handling that avoids scattered null checks before rendering.

The close stacks these ideas on a larger pipeline using flatMap and argument order familiar from lodash-style APIs, then stresses that functional style is not a silver bullet—worth trying in selected places rather than everywhere. Practitioners leave with mental models for purity, immutability, and reusable small functions they can trial in existing JavaScript projects.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: Reaktywny PHP (Arkadiusz Kondas)
talks.teaser: Introduces ReactPHP event loops, streams, and promises for non-blocking PHP with concurrency comparable to Node.js.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with a familiar pain point: sequential PHP that fetches multiple URLs spends most of its time idle while waiting on the network. The speaker contrasts thread-per-connection servers such as Apache with multiplexed designs like nginx and relates that model to Node.js and the C10k idea that software, not hardware, often becomes the bottleneck.

The middle of the session maps PHP options into thread-heavy extensions versus multiplexing-oriented stacks, then centers on ReactPHP. Its layout spans an event loop built on stream select (with optional ev and libevent extensions), EventEmitter, readable and writable streams—including piping—socket components, promises, timers, and child processes so CPU-heavy work does not stall the loop. Examples include a small chat server, an async HTTP client with non-blocking DNS, a pure-PHP Redis server benchmarked near 60,000 requests per second against roughly 160,000–170,000 on native Redis on one core, and a browser multiplayer demo using Ratchet.

The close covers PHP Process Manager for long-lived workers that avoid repeated Symfony bootstrap cost, with gains on the order of 120 versus 1,600 requests per second in shown charts but warnings about globals, leaks, and debugging. The speaker stresses that ReactPHP only helps when code is written asynchronously, notes AMPHP as an alternative, and says production use was still experimental for them at the time.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: Jak zrobić bota w 45 minut (Adam Marczak)
talks.teaser: Walks through Azure Bot Service, Bot Framework, and LUIS to show how a simple intent-driven bot is built, tested, and published.
talks.summary:
The session opens by separating chatbots from full artificial intelligence, plain text shells, and standalone natural-language processors. Bots are framed as conversational interfaces on top of existing applications: users reach them through familiar channels such as chat and mail, while hosting stays lightweight and consumption-based on Azure.

The middle of the talk maps three Microsoft pieces—Azure Bot Service, Bot Framework (SDK, emulator, developer portal, connectors), and LUIS for language understanding. The speaker compares built-in templates (basic echo, form flows, proactive messaging, language understanding, QnA-style bots), explains intents and entities with examples like greetings and weather queries, and describes how connectors reach Skype, Messenger, Teams, Slack, SMS, and other channels. Planned live demo issues force a slide-driven walkthrough: provision Bot Service (noting preview caveats), register LUIS, add and train a “contact” intent, link Cognitive Services billing keys, publish, and wire intent handlers in code.

Closing guidance stresses narrow, process-oriented bot scope, dialog prompts and rich cards to guide users, Bot Emulator and ngrok for local testing, and QnA Maker for FAQ-style workloads. Practitioners leave with a end-to-end mental model from Azure provisioning through LUIS training to channel-ready deployment.

talks.title: 4Developers 2017: Budowanie aplikacji PHP bez użycia frameworków (Michał Łukaszewski)
talks.teaser: A case for building tailored PHP applications by choosing frameworks, micro-frameworks, or custom stacks based on real business needs.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by questioning fashionable PHP framework adoption without losing sight of what frameworks do well. The speaker argues that heavy stacks ship large codebases developers may not understand, pile on transitive Composer dependencies with real outage and security exposure (including widely cited supply-chain incidents), demand enormous documentation surface, slow adoption of newer PHP features, and encourage “framework programmer” thinking where forums replace problem design.

The middle shifts toward a constructive model: every web app needs routing or dispatch, response rendering, and business logic, optionally layered with persistence, validation, and caching used deliberately rather than by default. Architecture should stay flexible—multiple data stores or alternate backends should not force fighting Doctrine or Symfony conventions—and optional component models illustrate swapping implementations without dragging an entire platform along.

The close rejects a blanket ban on frameworks. Full stacks, micro-frameworks, and domain-specific platforms remain valid when requirements justify them; bare custom PHP can fit trivial flows. Practitioners should treat technology choice as a business decision, pick tools consciously per project, and preserve readable architecture so newcomers are not stranded on undocumented internal frameworks. Audience pushback on Symfony scale at large sites and onboarding cost of homegrown stacks extends that economic trade-off discussion.

talks.title: PLNOG 18 - Sebastian Pasternacki
talks.teaser: Bezpieczeństwo sieci operatorskich oraz enterprise... investigates PLNOG 18 - Sebastian Pasternacki.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how spreading encryption, mainly TLS, changes what network operators and enterprise security teams can see and do. The speaker says encrypted traffic now makes up a large share of web traffic, with figures of roughly 70 to 80 percent for major services. He argues that browser vendors and large platforms push HTTPS and newer protocols such as HTTP/2, which effectively require TLS. Reasons for encrypting range from integrity and privacy to protection after a breach.

The middle section covers what breaks for defenders. Interception with a locally trusted certificate authority works in browsers, where users can be warned or blocked, but applications that use certificate pinning, such as Dropbox in the speaker's example, refuse to connect. QUIC runs over UDP and is harder to inspect, and the server name in the handshake can be spoofed, so filtering by name is unreliable. Blocking unreadable flows is a common default, yet the speaker notes it cuts off visibility and control.

The closing section offers alternatives to decryption: DNS visibility, with examples of resolver data used to spot command-and-control domains with short lifetimes; telemetry from switches, firewalls and endpoints; and anomaly detection trained on known bad and known good traffic. In a lab test, flow metadata alone flagged 99.76% of traffic linked to malware without any decryption. The speaker introduced the open-source Joy tool for flow analysis and urged practitioners to learn these protocols now, since no method gives complete coverage.

talks.title: PLNOG18 - Jarosław Ulczok - Podsłuchać światłowód? Przezentacja LIVE
talks.teaser: Reviews fiber-optic tapping techniques, debunks common myths, and compares encryption options for protecting transit data.
talks.summary:
The session opens by challenging the belief that optical links cannot be monitored, tying the topic to earlier conference material on encryption as a remedy when the physical path is untrusted. Common myths are addressed: fiber is not a perfect light conduit, splices and commercial splitters can be installed without long outages, and injection into the core is feasible in principle.

Several interception approaches are walked through in order of practicality. Macro- and micro-bending leak measurable power but often show up as attenuation anomalies; fused and polished splitters (including high-loss-ratio taps) and twinkle-style couplers are widely available test gear repurposed for listening. Evanescent-wave coupling can add extremely small loss that may fall inside measurement error on long spans. A reported incident involving engineers in a high-rise and a tap reachable from a parking-level duct illustrates how passive taps can run for years before discovery.

Defensive options include hardened cable designs, modal power monitoring, reflectometry, and line-speed encryption. The speaker argues that encrypting transit removes dependence on controlling every manhole and cabinet, while noting trade-offs among IPsec, MACsec, and dedicated Layer-2 encryptors in throughput, latency, key handling, and certification. A recorded lab demo shows cleaved fiber, a tap, and recovery of streaming traffic; encrypted payloads still pass but appear as unusable alternate frames. Traffic shaping on encrypted channels can still leak metadata, motivating padding-style mitigations.

talks.title: PLNOG18 - Marcin Kowalski - Żegnaj chmuro witaj blacho
talks.teaser: Argues that dedicated hardware often beats public cloud on cost and predictability, tracing virtualization's history along the way.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the history of virtualization, beginning with early mainframes where many users shared one large machine and the virtualization was done in hardware. The speaker notes that software virtualization was once very expensive, while today the hypervisor takes roughly 2-3% of CPU power, which he considers negligible. He argues that many of today's ideas, such as the hard disk, are decades old and have changed little at their core.

He then criticises current IT hype: the internet of things, containers used to speed up deployments at the cost of losing control, and software-defined everything, which he says still needs administrators. The main focus is the cloud. He cites an Amazon outage, the second in about a year and a half, and argues that the cloud rarely saves money. He describes a client who would pay 1000 zł for a server that costs about 2800 zł in the same configuration on Amazon, and says IT costs can end up roughly doubled.

He concludes that the cloud suits rapidly changing workloads, such as marketing campaigns that cause traffic spikes, while stable environments are better served by private clouds or bare-metal servers. He gives an estimated 4% yearly chance of a hardware failure on a dedicated server, argues that physical hardware is more predictable and flexible on monthly contracts, and urges organisations to choose the right solution rather than the one that is marketed best.

talks.summary:
The talk is given by a Polish network operator engineer who starts from a question put to an equipment vendor: why can't GPON optical network terminals (ONTs) from different manufacturers simply work together? He explains the difference between an ONU and an ONT, points to the G.984 and G.988 standards, which leave implementation options open, and notes that customer terminals are one of the largest costs when building fibre access networks.

He then describes examining ONTs from Chinese and other suppliers. A few large factories make most of them, and many vendors rebrand the same hardware. Units built on common chipsets share bootloaders, so a clone with the same board ID can run a vendor's official firmware after its serial and model values are changed. One case involved Ericsson-branded terminals based on a Marvell chip. After the chip was discontinued and the business passed to Calix, those terminals could no longer be bought. He showed how vendor-specific managed entities and OLT vendor detection through OMCI cause small differences that break operation, so software has to branch by the OLT vendor it meets.

He also discussed protocol analyzers, which he judged too expensive, and chose a simpler route: a single-port Ethernet ONT with a low target price and cheap packaging, with custom software written with a contracted engineer. He closes by urging operators to ask vendors for proof of certification before buying, since vendors' reluctance to share firmware pushes operators toward reverse engineering.

talks.title: PLNOG18 - Łukasz Bromirski - CEF, NetFlow, NetFPGA, Superman, Eureka, fd.io, DPDK ...
talks.teaser: Traces how packet forwarding evolved from ARPANET routers through Cisco CEF and NetFlow to software data planes like VPP.
talks.summary:
The talk, given in Polish, follows how network traffic forwarding has changed from the early ARPANET era to current routers and software data planes. The speaker argues that many networking ideas return in new forms, and that vendor and market pressures shaped technical choices as much as engineering did.

Along the way he covers process switching, fast switching and Cisco's CEF, and explains how the flow-based idea behind NetFlow grew out of an earlier flow switching feature. He describes the move from central-processor forwarding to line cards and dedicated ASICs, the late 1990s race between vendors over throughput and routing protocols, and the early programmable network processors. He also places OpenFlow and the push to separate control and forwarding planes into the wider software-defined networking trend.

The later part looks at x86 forwarding and the open-source FD.io VPP project, which runs on DPDK and processes packets in vectors to reduce cache misses. The speaker compares its throughput with a traditional Open vSwitch setup and then turns to operational trends: virtualised network functions and upgrade handling, fewer control protocols through segment routing, and richer telemetry export from data centre fabrics. He closes by saying that predictions about the next few years may age quickly.

talks.title: PLNOG18 - Rafał Budweil - Triggo - polska innowacja e-mobilnosci miejskiej
talks.teaser: Presents Triggo, a narrow Polish urban vehicle mixing motorcycle and car advantages, with its engineering and business plans.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Triggo, a Polish urban vehicle its designers describe as a blend of a motorcycle and a car. The speaker explains the gap: motorcycles skip traffic and park easily, but they need helmets, special licences and weather gear, and cannot carry passengers or goods comfortably. Triggo adds a cabin, seat belts and year-round use. It has a road mode capped at about 90 km/h and a narrow manoeuvring mode, about 92 cm wide and limited to 25 km/h.

The engineering centres on drive-by-wire steering, with no mechanical link to the front wheels. The team chose it to tame the vehicle's strong oversteer and to keep the design simpler, lighter and ready for autonomy. Homologation under the EU L-category rules is far simpler than for cars, and two rear motors are capped at 15 kW. Parking is easy because the vehicle fits one bay, and battery swaps at fuel stations, taking five to seven minutes, are planned instead of many charging points. Carsharing operators are the main market, with sales bundled with support.

The closing section covered funding: patents granted in several countries, a research grant, a planned financing round, and a search for managers and sponsors. In questions, the speaker said control and monitoring are a key concern, though he had no detailed security answer yet. Winter tyres, operator crash handling and battery choice were also raised.

talks.title: PLNOG18: Wspominamy początki Internetu
talks.teaser: Participants swap early Polish dial-up memories, IRC, slow pages, and the habits of life before always-on broadband.
talks.summary:
At PLNOG 18, a group looks back at how the Polish internet felt in its early years. They trade prompts about the first sites people opened, early mailboxes with tiny quotas, and whether early chat felt human or automated. Dial-up through Telekomunikacja Polska at home, 56k links, IRC, and metered evening connections thread through many stories.

Several voices recall internet cafés, fifteen-minute access packs, and watching the clock until cheaper night rates. Others describe agonizingly slow image loads and the boredom of waiting for pages to finish. One anecdote covers dialing in just before 22:00 to save money, only to learn that billing rules still produced a large parental bill.

The segment closes on shared cultural touchstones: modem handshakes, frustration when lines failed, and humor about how much of youth revolved around being online. The through-line is oral history and community memory rather than technical instruction.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Deliver Fast with Confidence (Joseph W. Yoder)
talks.teaser: Shows how teams keep fast delivery sustainable by managing technical debt, refactoring and continuous improvement.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why teams that start out fast often slow down as their software grows. A focus on features can hide architectural quality, and messy code spreads as new work piles on top of it. Because values drive practice, the speaker argues that adopting a method such as Scrum or TDD by rote will not keep a team agile or sustainable.

Practical responses include refactoring as work proceeds, using safe moves such as renaming and extracting methods, and never leaving code worse than before. Consulting cases show the same pattern: a company whose retrospectives led to no action, and a large Java system spread across many teams that needed new ways to add features without adding mess. One team in Brazil began each day with about thirty to sixty minutes of cleanup, guided by overnight code analysis reports. The speaker also argues for slack time, so that savings from removing waste go into experiments and quality rather than only more features.

The closing advice is to make technical debt visible on the backlog, set triggers based on code quality metrics, and use checklists at natural pause points. The core takeaways are small, frequent releases, clean code kept as the work goes, and regular time for continuous improvement, with the goal of sustaining development rather than speed alone.

talks.title: JDD 2016: REPL driven development (Daniel Lebrero)
talks.teaser: Shows how a Clojure REPL attached to a running Java service gives instant feedback without rebuilding or redeploying.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that developers lose focus when every change requires a build, package and deploy cycle. The speaker, a Java back-end developer, points out that even starting an empty Tomcat application took about thirty seconds. His proposal is to run a Read-Eval-Print Loop inside the running application and connect to it from the IDE over a socket. Code sent from the editor is evaluated in the live process, and the results come straight back. The demo uses Clojure, and the speaker says no prior Clojure experience is needed.

The demo builds a small REST service step by step. The speaker first queries database metadata to find the tables, then inspects a stored procedure and calls it directly from the running application. Because that code already runs in the live service, it can be reused as production code, copied into a test, and used for test-driven development. The REPL can also re-run only the tests affected by a changed file. The endpoint is then wired up, checked through the IDE, and tested with an HTTP call, and the speaker shows that state such as a counter can be kept across reloads or reset on demand.

The speaker concludes that a REPL helps developers explore real third-party systems, mix data from databases and HTTP services, and use any JVM library, which means fewer surprises at startup. He mentions that the same technique has been used to inspect or patch running systems, including a spacecraft, but says it should not be a routine practice in production. In the questions, he explains that each language has different limits: scripting languages usually run whole files, while on the JVM the long-running process is what makes the workflow different.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Demystifying G1GC (Arkadiusz Głowacki)
talks.teaser: Explains G1 garbage collection for large JVM heaps: regions, concurrent marking, pause targets, flags to avoid, and reading GC logs.
talks.summary:
The session opens by asking why Java needs another garbage collector when Serial, Parallel, and CMS already exist. Each older algorithm was built for much smaller machines; CMS helps concurrency but fragments the old generation until a full compaction can pause responsive apps for seconds or minutes on multi-gigabyte heaps. G1 was aimed at heaps above about six gigabytes, promises easier tuning through heap size and a pause-time goal, and was expected to replace CMS while becoming the JDK 9 default.

The middle walks through G1’s region-based layout, young and mixed evacuations, concurrent marking starting around forty-five percent heap use, and the garbage-first idea of reclaiming regions that are mostly dead. Remember sets track cross-region references with post-write barriers and varying granularity. The speaker contrasts lower throughput with steadier pauses for UI and server workloads, notes that full GC is rare unless misconfigured, and describes young, marking, remark, and cleanup phases in plain terms.

The closing focuses on operations: enabling meaningful GC logs, using tools such as GCeasy, and reading pause lines plus worker phases. Pitfalls include tiny minimum heap sizes that explode region counts, humongous old-gen allocations from large string concatenation that triggered an out-of-memory crash, legacy young/old sizing flags that break pause goals and cause evacuation failures, and tuning concurrent worker counts or marking thresholds. JDK 8 update 20 string deduplication on G1 and heap inspections for duplicate strings round out practical takeaways.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Writing your own RDD for fun and profit (Paweł Szulc)
talks.teaser: Explains how Apache Spark wires RDD partitions, dependencies, and compute so practitioners can author custom cluster datasets.
talks.summary:
The session targets developers who already use Apache Spark and warns newcomers that it dives past a short RDD recap into implementation details. It revisits resilient distributed datasets, lazy transformations versus triggering actions, partitions as the unit of parallelism, and why group-by forces a shuffle that splits work into stages.

The core explains what every RDD must provide: partition layout, a parent link, and a compute method that yields partition iterators. Hadoop RDD reuses HDFS splits; map-style RDDs inherit a parent’s partitions. Wide versus narrow dependencies determine when shuffling is required. Actions funnel through SparkContext runJob, with collect and count as concrete examples, and optional data-locality hints plus partitioners to limit redundant shuffles after key changes.

A prepared demo walks through a trivial random RDD and a censorship RDD with a custom collect action, showing how mutating data in compute can break downstream filters. The closing argument is that reading the Spark source with this mental model speeds debugging when jobs, stages, or cluster behavior look wrong in production.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Machine Learning dla programistów (Dominika Puzio)
talks.teaser: A developer-oriented session covers machine learning fundamentals, ID3 decision trees, and deploying Iris classifiers with H2O on TAP.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by explaining why machine learning dominates current technology discourse, pointing to plummeting storage and data-center costs, cheaper compute, and headline events such as TensorFlow’s release, Deep Dream images, AlphaGo beating a Go world champion, and Microsoft’s Tay bot melting down on Twitter within hours.

From a programmer’s perspective, the speaker defines machine learning as learning from examples instead of hand-coding every rule, describes how models predict or classify new data, and separates machine learning from data science’s domain expertise. The classic Iris dataset motivates classification; model forms include polynomials, decision trees, and neural networks. A street-survey commute example drives a step-by-step ID3 build using entropy and information gain, with numeric attributes handled similarly via C4.5-style threshold search.

The talk closes by stressing that sensible projects still need humans to pick features, algorithms, and parameters, then demos H2O on the TAP platform: upload Iris CSV data, train gradient boosting, inspect generated Java, publish a scoring engine, and classify a sample flower via a REST score endpoint. Audience questions touch on offline-only model updates in H2O and scaling scoring services through Cloud Foundry.
