talks.title: JDD 2016: Prezentacje i wystąpienia (Sławomir Sobótka)
talks.teaser: Shows how IT professionals can prepare engaging talks, tame early-stage nerves, and deliver with clearer structure and calmer delivery.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens from a programmer’s perspective on why conference and internal talks trigger dread, procrastination, and openings that apologize before anything useful begins. He contrasts self-centered intros with inclusive framing that makes the audience the protagonist, and notes that technical crowds usually want the speaker to succeed, unlike some high-pressure business settings.

Preparation is organized around realistic goals—inspire rather than fully teach—and a story built backward from the closing takeaway, linked by rhetorical questions and content patterns suited to technical listeners. He outlines concept introduction through analogy before formal detail, pacing for short attention windows, and blending principles with hands-on points. On stage, practical body work matters: arriving early, diaphragm breathing, and brief vocal warmups to reduce stress and improve presence.

Delivery advice covers matching style to the room, speaking in short downward chunks when fluency fails, and avoiding risky live coding unless rehearsed to the point of autopilot. The close stresses humility about perfection, choosing goals within personal control, seeking honest feedback afterward, and treating each talk as material to refine rather than a test of cosmic importance.

talks.title: JDD 2016: A Practical Introduction to Akka Streams (Jacek Kunicki)
talks.teaser: Hands-on coding delivers reusable Akka Stream flows for gzipped file import, ID-based averages, and Cassandra persistence.
talks.summary:
The session blends lecture with hands-on coding for developers who can follow along via a tagged GitHub repository or watch without a prepared environment. It opens by contrasting distributed stream engines with Akka Streams on a single node, explaining sources, flows, sinks, lazy graph composition, back pressure, and materialization through an actor-based materializer.

The exercise imports gzipped, semicolon-separated files where consecutive lines share an ID. Participants build flows step by step: frame byte streams into lines, parse valid or invalid readings asynchronously, group pairs to compute averages (using minus one when both values are invalid), and write results to Cassandra with tuned parallelism for files, CPU work, and concurrent inserts. Composition wires single-file and whole-directory imports; a resuming supervision strategy logs errors without aborting the entire run. A short demo confirms rows land in Cassandra within seconds.

With time remaining, the speaker sketches Akka Streams TestKit probes to assert average computation, then notes richer graph DSL features such as broadcast, merge, and Stateful flows. A closing Q&A argues Akka Streams fits when distributed Spark-style processing is unnecessary, and mentions Monix and Java APIs as alternatives. Practitioners should leave with reusable flow patterns, sensible execution contexts, and error-handling habits for production-style file ingestion.

talks.title: JDD 2016: DB for next project? Why, Postgres, of course (Tomasz Borek)
talks.teaser: Practitioners get a Postgres-over-rivals case and tours of logging, in-database scripting, document types, and planner behavior.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by positioning himself as an architect rather than a classic DBA, then frames a light-hearted “database wars” tour meant to help teams pick a datastore for a new project. He traces Postgres lineage from Ingres through Berkeley’s faculty project and notes how that lineage influenced Sybase, Informix, Illustra, and the early Microsoft SQL Server deal with Sybase. He highlights yearly releases, broad vendor support, and deployments at large web and science organizations.

The core of the talk contrasts strict versus forgiving databases using a VARCHAR overflow example, favoring Postgres error detail over silent truncation. He walks through reporting and logging: default stderr, PG_LOG location, SHOW and GUC settings, logging collector, CSV and syslog integration, log_statement versus syntax errors, and log_line_prefix. Further sections cover procedural languages in the server, JSON, XML, Hstore, foreign data wrappers, window functions, CTEs, indexing including PostGIS-style cases, client-server and per-connection process architecture, WAL and replication basics, data directory layout, parser-planner-executor flow, and reading EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE costs versus real timings. MVCC, autovacuum, and process isolation explain concurrency without dirty reads.

He closes with a candid strengths-and-weaknesses list: rich ANSI-oriented SQL, extensibility, and observability versus no optimizer hints, a learning curve on types, and mixed reports on replication difficulty. The implied takeaway for practitioners is to treat Postgres as a mature default when you want strictness, observability, and SQL depth, but to benchmark replication and operations before committing.

talks.title: JDD 2016: DROP DATABASE - przypowieść galaktyczna (Jarosław Ratajski)
talks.teaser: A galactic pizza parable contrasts in-memory Java with database-centric stacks through benchmarks, outages, and persistence patterns.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames the talk with a multiverse joke, then introduces Galak Pizza: a scale fantasy where a thrifty magnate must route one rocket across ten thousand pizza-loving planets while sustaining ten thousand orders and status checks per second. Two parallel teams implement the same domain—orders, planets, variants, and a pizza-boy dispatch queue—in “normal” Java versus a Java-plus-database style stack.

In the in-memory branch the model centers on immutable orders, per-planet lists in a hash map, a priority queue for busiest planets, and fixes for mutability and concurrency via wrappers and serialized command lambdas written to disk. A sibling implementation leans on MySQL, Hibernate, extra tables for counts, and transactional retry patterns. JMH-style simulation with multiple client and monitoring threads reports on the order of hundreds to roughly one thousand pizza orders per second in RAM versus hundreds per second on SQL, with stark gaps in cheap read-side monitoring.

Production vignettes cover power loss, laptop hibernation, and the folly of hard-deleting orders when stakeholders want history. The closing thesis ties cheap RAM and multicore hardware to cargo-cult persistence: event-flavored logging, snapshots, simpler testing without database fixtures, and a nudge to prototype in-memory command persistence on small systems before reaching for enterprise frameworks.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Testowanie wydajności kodu za pomocą narzędzia JMH (Wojciech Oczkowski)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD 2016: Testowanie wydajności kodu za pomocą narzędzia JMH (Wojciech Oczkowski).

talks.title: JDD 2016: Architecting your codebase (Kamil Szymański)
talks.teaser: Shows how reorganising a Spring pet clinic app into separate contexts makes its code easier to navigate and change.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through restructuring a Java Spring sample application, the pet clinic, so that a newcomer can work out what it does and where things belong. The speaker starts by removing superclasses that create inheritance without a real is-a relationship, such as a shared person base for owners and veterinarians, and a named-entity superclass that constrained how pets could be named. A base entity holding technical identity moves into infrastructure, and a helper class used only by the web layer moves into the controller that uses it.

Next, the code is split into visit, veterinarian and client contexts, each in its own package with its own service and repository. Moving classes breaks the application context until component scanning and JPA repository configuration are corrected. Removing public access to each context's persistent state keeps it behind its service. Splitting the tests exposes two smells: a test needs services from two contexts, which points to a bidirectional link between pets and visits, and it checks the order of specialties when order should not matter. The speaker argues specialties should be value objects rather than identified entities.

The closing takeaways are four rules: remove accidental complexity, apply single responsibility at the context level, encapsulate state, and aim for high cohesion and low coupling. The speaker admits that swapping repository implementations becomes harder, but argues that changing requirements is more likely, so a change such as booking visits touches one package instead of half the codebase.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Backend less Development revisited (Tomasz Ducin)
talks.teaser: Shows how front-end teams work without live backends via API contracts, JSON Schema, and dynamic browser mocks for faster delivery.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting classic server-rendered pages with single-page applications that load once and then talk to the server through small REST-style requests returning JSON. The speaker argues that tight coupling still hurts organizations when backends fail for days while front-end work stalls, and when API shape changes ship without telling client teams.

The core idea is backend-less development during the build phase: front and back teams agree on a written contract first, then front-end work can proceed without waiting on services or core systems. The talk walks through where to mock—the server API, browser AJAX layer, or framework HTTP helpers—and why mocks should behave dynamically across GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE rather than replaying one static file. JSON Schema supports validation and fake data generation; Swagger, API Blueprint, and similar toolchains turn contracts into documentation, mocks, and backend conformance checks in continuous integration.

Examples cover Sinon fake servers intercepting XMLHttpRequest, AngularJS-style HTTP backends with callback handlers that update in-memory collections, and bundling mock data plus logic behind a build flag for development and UI-focused end-to-end tests. The closing message is that prioritizing clear contracts and independent clients benefits front-end, back-end, and business timelines alike.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Javaslang - Functional Java Done Right (Grzegorz Piwowarek)
talks.teaser: Surveys Javaslang as functional Java beyond Java 8 lambdas, covering control types, persistent collections, and pattern matching.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting the enthusiasm around Java 8’s lambda expressions, streams, and optionals with the limits practitioners soon hit: few functional control structures, painful checked exceptions in lambdas, mutable collections, and APIs that still encourage hidden state and side effects. He illustrates how ordinary methods can depend on global state, mutations, and exceptions that never appear in their signatures, then frames functional style around immutability, referential transparency, and composing small pure building blocks.

The core of the session introduces Javaslang as a library that fills those gaps with immutable values, extended function arities, checked functional interfaces, lifting partial functions to optionals, currying, memoization, tuples, and types such as Try, Lazy, Either, Future, and Validation. He compares Java 8 streams with Javaslang sequences, highlights a richer collection API informed by Scala, and demonstrates pattern matching workarounds for Java, plus related modules beyond the core library.

Practitioners should leave with a clearer picture of what “functional Java” means beyond syntax sugar, when immutability and explicit effects reduce debugging pain, and how Javaslang can interoperate with existing Java code through iterables while offering tools the standard library lacks.

talks.title: JDD 2016: How deep are your tests (Thomas Sundberg)
talks.teaser: Contrasts deep end-to-end checks with fast, focused unit tests and shows how mocks and stubs limit combinatorial test growth.
talks.summary:
Software delivery depends on confidence that releases work for real users, not only for a QA department standing in as a proxy. The speaker argues that “done” means working software in production and that teams should ship often in small batches to learn what users actually need.

The talk surveys UI, endpoint, integrated, unit, and end-to-end testing with a car-assembly analogy, then reframes the familiar testing pyramid as a cone that separates depth (layers touched) from width (business paths covered). End-to-end flows can protect revenue-critical behavior, illustrated by a broken purchase path that stayed down for days, but they are usually slow, fragile, and weak at pinpointing failures. Integrated tests that bundle many objects multiply execution paths explosively; the speaker urges fewer assumptions, citing Occam’s razor and single-assumption unit tests that run quickly and in parallel.

A worked example around VAT reporting mocks a rule engine, stubs expected due dates for a company registration number, then implements the real engine using the same values so fakes and code stay aligned—likened to balanced bookkeeping. The closing advice is a small set of deep “does it start and wire up” checks plus many shallow unit tests for speed, precision, and release confidence, with outside-in acceptance tests and established test-driven design books as follow-on reading.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Golo, the tiny language that gives super powers (Philippe Charrière)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for JDD 2016: Golo, the tiny language that gives super powers (Philippe Charrière).

talks.title: JDD 2016: Code for life - inspiring the next generation of developers (Celine Boudier)
talks.teaser: A charity-backed platform shows how free school games move children from Blockly to Python while supporting overloaded teachers.
talks.summary:
Most software developers wish they had learned programming before university, yet many children still meet computing only as consumers of games and apps. The speaker argues that coding builds logical thinking and confidence in a digital world, not only as a path into tech jobs. She traces her own late start on a programmable calculator and work on educational robotics before leading Code for Life at Ocado Technology.

Code for Life is a volunteer-driven, open-source education initiative backed by the Ocado corporate charity model. Its flagship Rapid Router game targets primary ages roughly five to eleven with free browser levels themed around delivery vans, progressing from drag-and-drop Blockly to Python while introducing loops and debugging through playful failure. Teachers receive lesson plans, unplugged activities, solution guides, and dashboards because many lack computing training and face overwhelming online resource noise.

Upcoming work includes a multiplayer sandbox for secondary students, an offline Unity iOS variant for iPad-heavy classrooms, Crowdin translations including Polish partnerships, and GitHub-based coordination mixing full-time staff with Wednesday volunteer sessions. User personas from teacher interviews drive portal redesign. The stack spans Django, Skulpt in-browser Python, Google Cloud, and CircleCI, and the project invites contributions from developers and educators.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Meet the assertable Chaos Monkeys (Bartosz Majsak)
talks.teaser: Shows how Arquillian and Docker make integration tests repeatable and faster, and how injected network faults test resilience.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that unit tests alone miss failures in how components work together, and that higher-level tests often feel too hard to set up, too slow and not repeatable. The speaker presents Arquillian, an open-source testing middleware that handles the environment plumbing so that integration and black-box tests read much like ordinary unit tests. Examples show a test running inside a container and a test that exercises a deployed REST service from outside, using REST Assured.

Next, the talk moves to Arquillian Cube, which brings Docker into the test lifecycle. It pulls images, starts and cleans up containers, and can orchestrate them with Docker Compose. A Node.js service is tested from a Dockerfile generated at runtime. For speed, the speaker runs builds against several application server and database versions in parallel, each in its own isolated Docker network, which gives feedback for all of them in about three and a half minutes instead of running them one after another. For resilience, a Toxiproxy-based extension adds latency and takes a dependent service down, and a live demo shows a circuit breaker opening as the service degrades.

The takeaway is to keep unit tests as the base, use a small number of high-level tests for key user journeys rather than repeating unit-level checks, and use chaos-style tests to see how an application behaves under unexpected conditions before it reaches production.

talks.title: JDD 2016: A needle in a logstack (Tomasz Gągor, Paweł Torbus)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD 2016: A needle in a logstack (Tomasz Gągor, Paweł Torbus).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from JDD 2016, Tomasz Gągor (system administrator at Interia) and Paweł Torbus (system architect) present practical lessons from implementing and maintaining the ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) across their infrastructure. They walk through the real-world operational challenges encountered with each component, tuning recommendations, and concrete use cases where log analysis and visualization in Kibana uncovered production bugs, performance degradations, and configuration oversights.

### Key Topics
- **Architecture of the ELK Stack:** Deploying Logstash (log preprocessor running on JRuby), Elasticsearch (distributed storage, indexing, and search engine based on Lucene), and Kibana (visualization front end), along with ecosystem tools like Filebeat, Logstash Forwarder, Shield (access protection), and Watcher (alerting).
- **Log Ingestion & Logstash Pitfalls:** Handling multi-line logs (e.g., XML, Java stack traces), thread bottlenecks, event timestamp extraction, avoiding variable collisions in Logstash (e.g., overriding the `message` field), and moving from syslog UDP to reliable shippers like Logstash Forwarder and Filebeat.
- **Elasticsearch Cluster Operation & Tuning:** Shard and replica allocation, handling disk space and node restarts, switching from auto-discovery (broadcast) to unicast discovery to avoid switch packet drops, disabling shard reallocation during maintenance, JVM heap limits (under 32 GB), and tuning the field data cache.
- **Production Troubleshooting with Kibana:** Visualizing web front-end status codes, Varnish cache hit rates, REST API function performance, external integration bottlenecks (Apple iTunes proxy sniffing), unexpected cron job resource contention, and massive log volume spikes.

### Technical Details
- **Logstash Ingestion & Parsing:** Logstash uses three internal queues: input, filter, and output. When processing multi-line logs such as Java stack traces or XML, multithreaded filtering cannot easily scale across lines, forcing single-thread processing or horizontal scaling via multiple Logstash instances. In contrast, Filebeat can perform multi-line handling on the source server and forward single grouped events. The speakers also stressed the importance of parsing native event timestamps from access logs (otherwise Elasticsearch records the log ingestion time) and converting numeric variables using Grok and `int` casts so Elasticsearch can perform aggregations, averages, and min/max statistics.
- **Log Forwarding:** Relying on syslog over UDP caused dropped logs during traffic peaks and server failures. Interia moved to Logstash Forwarder (written in Go), which supports compression, encryption, backpressure/waiting, and automatic detection of new files. However, an unclosed file handle issue in Logstash Forwarder required configuring timeouts (e.g., 10 minutes of inactivity) to prevent disk space exhaustion from unlinked open log files.
- **Elasticsearch Sizing and Maintenance:** Elasticsearch nodes should not exceed 32 GB of JVM heap memory to preserve compressed object pointers (avoiding switching to slower 64-bit pointers) and leave the remaining system memory (at least 50%) for OS filesystem caches. Disabling swap is mandatory. Interia configured nodes with a maximum of 200–250 GB of data per node to avoid multi-day shard synchronization times upon restarts. When updating nodes sequentially, administrators must disable shard allocation before restart to prevent the cluster from prematurely rebalancing shards across remaining nodes.
- **Investigating Outages via Kibana:** In one case, a cluster experienced a surge from typical daily volumes of 15 GB (around 300,000 events per 10 minutes) up to 96 GB, peaking at over 30 million events per 10 minutes. Kibana visualizations isolated the spike to a single testing server looping over missing files and outputting endless Java stack traces. In another instance, Kibana graphs revealed an unexplained daily latency spike between 10:00 AM and 11:00 AM caused by a typo in a Tomcat cron task scheduled during peak daytime hours rather than at night.

### Takeaways
- Never rely on default ingestion or cluster settings: enforce strict field types, configure unclosed file handle timeouts on log shippers, and explicitly disable shard allocation during node rolling restarts.
- Limit Elasticsearch heap to under 32 GB and avoid large disks per node to ensure shard resynchronization remains manageable.
- Centralized log visualization makes it possible to detect intermittent cross-service latency, misconfigured background jobs, and application regressions that are impossible to spot using conventional command-line tools like grep across multiple web servers.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Clojure by neophyte (Paweł Kapała)
talks.teaser: Introduces Clojure on the JVM through immutable data structures, REPL examples, and a fairy-tale scenario coded as pure functions.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting bloated enterprise abstractions with clear data flow, describing long debugging hunts when mutable, threaded code hides what values move where. Clojure is offered as a mostly functional JVM language that needs only an older JVM and one JAR, reuses Java libraries, and has an active community.

After REPL basics—nil, booleans, numbers, ratios, keywords, lists, vectors, maps, immutability, symbols, and function definition—the talk builds a fairy tale live: King Crackers, a castle, stored rams, knights, a hungry dragon, attacks, a cobbler’s sulfur-and-tar ram trap, lazy infinite water from the Vistula, and threading macros that finish the beast. Each step prints the data underneath the abstractions.

The narrative is framed as a small domain-specific language with few built-ins. Learning paths include functional programming books, beginner sites, 4clojure-style exercises, and mentors on chat. Questions cover Haskell versus Clojure on the JVM, quote syntax to skip list evaluation, and real production use through ClojureScript on backend and frontend.

talks.title: JDD 2016: 6 tips for your JavaEE project be less depressing (Jakub Marchwicki)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for JDD 2016: 6 tips for your JavaEE project be less depressing (Jakub Marchwicki).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at JDD 2016, Jakub Marchwicki addresses the common frustration and negative perception surrounding enterprise Java EE projects. Often inherited as legacy systems in rigid environments like banking and insurance, Java EE is frequently criticized for being bloated, outdated, or overly restrictive. Marchwicki argues that much of this dissatisfaction stems from corporate cargo-cult practices, poor architectural choices, and developers lacking familiarity with modern platform capabilities. Rather than hastily rewriting working applications in alternative stacks like Spring, Marchwicki outlines five practical technical tips to modernize and streamline Java EE development.

### Key Topics
The talk centers on five practical strategies to make Java EE projects cleaner, more productive, and less painful:
1. **Understanding the Modern Stack**: Dispelling misconceptions about Java EE limitations, such as threading restrictions, by highlighting built-in concurrency and asynchronous features.
2. **Treating Standards as Guidance**: Recognizing that perfect vendor portability across application servers is largely a myth in real-world applications, and embracing specific application server features rather than writing awkward workarounds.
3. **Reducing Boilerplate with Extensions**: Utilizing CDI (Contexts and Dependency Injection) extensions, particularly Apache DeltaSpike and DeltaSpike Data, to eliminate repetitive database and repository code.
4. **Going Beyond JPA**: Bypassing heavy ORM frameworks when complex SQL is required by integrating lightweight persistence libraries like JDBI and jOOQ using CDI producer methods.
5. **Decoupling Front-End Development**: Allowing front-end engineers to use modern tooling (Node.js, npm, Bower) while packaging static UI assets into JAR files via Maven and Servlet 3.0 `META-INF/resources`.

### Technical Details
- **Concurrency & Events**: While spawning unmanaged threads directly is prohibited because the application server cannot monitor or throttle resources, modern Java EE provides `@Asynchronous` and `ManagedExecutorService` (introduced in Java EE 6/7) to safely manage asynchronous tasks. CDI events also enable reactive, decoupled internal communication.
- **Application Server Realities**: Cross-server portability often breaks due to varying interpretations of specifications (e.g., differences in CDI implementations between Weld and OpenWebBeans, or bean resolution between Apache TomEE and WildFly/JBoss). Acknowledging the application server as the concrete framework allows developers to use underlying libraries directly, such as the latest Hibernate or EclipseLink implementations.
- **CDI Producers & Apache DeltaSpike**: DeltaSpike Data provides Spring Data–like repository patterns using simple interfaces and query annotations, avoiding repetitive JPA code. Furthermore, CDI `@Produces` methods enable developers to easily inject non-standard objects, custom data mappers, or specialized configurations directly into the dependency injection context.
- **Alternative Persistence (JDBI & jOOQ)**: For complex queries involving groupings, concatenations, or vendor-specific SQL, standard JPA native queries add unnecessary overhead. By using CDI producers to expose JDBC connections, teams can cleanly inject JDBI DAOs or jOOQ typed domain-specific languages (DSL) directly into enterprise beans.
- **Modern Front-End Integration**: To avoid the rigid styling and steep learning curves associated with JSF (JavaServer Faces), teams can isolate the front end. Using Maven plugins to execute Node/npm builds, front-end assets can be compiled into `target/app` and packaged into a JAR's `META-INF/resources`. Under the Servlet 3.0 specification, any files placed in `META-INF/resources` inside `WEB-INF/lib` JARs (the mechanism behind WebJars) are automatically served as static web assets.

### Takeaways
Developers can significantly improve their Java EE development experience without rewriting their systems. By learning recent platform enhancements, embracing their target application server rather than chasing theoretical portability, using CDI producers with modern libraries like jOOQ and DeltaSpike, and packaging separate npm-driven front-ends into Servlet 3.0 resources, teams can build maintainable and productive enterprise applications.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2016 - Stefan Thies - Monitoring and Log Management for Docker Swarm and...
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for DevOpsDays Warsaw 2016 - Stefan Thies - Monitoring and Log Management for Docker Swarm and....
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this DevOpsDays Warsaw 2016 presentation, Stefan Thies from Sematext examines the complexities of centralized logging and performance monitoring across containerized environments, focusing specifically on Docker Swarm and Kubernetes. Thies outlines the full lifecycle of log management and metric collection, highlights differences in orchestration abstractions, discusses the advantages of interacting directly with the Docker API, and reviews lessons learned from the community-driven Swarm 3k test project.

### Key Topics
- **Centralized Log Management Architecture**: Managing logs involves reconfiguring applications to emit logs to stdout/stderr rather than static files, employing log shippers (such as Fluentd, rsyslog, or Logstash) for log collection and parsing into structured JSON, and storing/indexing logs in systems like Elasticsearch alongside alerting mechanisms (e.g., PagerDuty).
- **Performance Monitoring & Time-Series Data**: Monitoring containerized systems requires exposing metrics (sometimes necessitating specific web server or app configurations), shipping them to time-series databases (e.g., Prometheus, InfluxDB, Elasticsearch), aggregating data over varying intervals, and visualizing metrics in dashboards like Kibana.
- **Kubernetes vs. Docker Swarm Concepts**: Kubernetes uses atomic deployment units called pods—keeping tightly coupled containers (like Elasticsearch and Kibana) together on a single host—alongside replication controllers, services, DaemonSets, Heapster, and built-in autoscalers. Docker Swarm provides familiar Docker commands, overlay networks, and scales services or containers across multiple hosts.
- **Docker Logging Drivers vs. API-Driven Agents**: While Docker logging drivers (JSON-file, journald, syslog, Fluentd, Splunk) ship logs via TCP/UDP, issues like unbuffered UDP packet loss or container startup failures during syslog TCP outages can disrupt operations. In contrast, an agent communicating directly with the Docker API can read local stdout/stderr streams, capture rich metadata and labels, buffer data during network outages, and route logs intelligently.
- **Application Metric Discovery**: General container metrics provide resource usage, but application-specific endpoints (such as Elasticsearch or Nginx statistics) require dynamic discovery (e.g., via etcd registrations or reading container labels and network bindings via the Docker API) to automate agent configuration.
- **Large-Scale Testing (Swarm 3k)**: Experiences and telemetry from deploying monitoring agents across thousands of Docker Swarm nodes in a real-world community test.

### Technical Details
- **Container Metrics & Sizing**: The Docker API exposes over 70 distinct metrics per container, including memory fail counters, out-of-memory events, and CPU throttling. Monitoring these metrics enables proper configuration of CPU limits (quotas) and Java heap memory limits to prevent out-of-memory errors.
- **Docker Events**: Utilizing Docker API events allows operators to trace lifecycle actions, including image pulls, container start/stop events, volume mounting, and task statuses.
- **Agent Deployment**: While early Swarm setups required custom shell scripts and loops to launch monitoring agents per node, modern orchestration features—such as Swarm global services and Kubernetes DaemonSets—simplify deploying monitoring agents universally.
- **Swarm 3k Benchmark Results**: In the Swarm 3k community experiment, monitoring agents were deployed across 4,700 nodes. During the run, 28 GB of metrics were collected, scaling up to 60,000 containers (short of the 250,000 container target due to disruptions when one of the three Swarm manager nodes encountered issues and restarted). Visualizing 4,700 ungrouped hosts proved challenging, emphasizing the need for label-based grouping and filtering in dashboards.

### Takeaways
- Standard container metrics are easy to capture, but gathering application-level metrics still involves considerable configuration and discovery effort.
- Relying on the Docker API enables smart agents to gather logs, metrics, labels, and Docker events together, while offering disk buffering when remote destinations become unreachable.
- Effective multi-node monitoring at scale requires consistent tagging, labeling, and automated agent deployment via DaemonSets or global services.

talks.title: JDD 2016: How to bake reactive behavior into your Java EE applications (Ondrej Mihályi)
talks.teaser: Shows how Java EE 7, CompletableFuture, and Payara Micro add reactive responsiveness to existing enterprise apps without a full rewrite.
talks.summary:
The session targets developers who already run Java EE and want responsive behavior without rebuilding everything from scratch. It opens by framing reactive systems through the Reactive Manifesto: responsiveness, elasticity, resilience, and message-driven design, then contrasts blocking request handling with threads that wait on slow databases and remote calls versus asynchronous callbacks that free worker threads.

On Java EE 7, the speaker walks through asynchronous options in JAX-RS client APIs, CompletableFuture chaining to reduce callback nesting, and Concurrency Utilities executors plus ContextService so callbacks preserve managed EE context. A Cargo Tracker extension illustrates the pattern: route planning moves to a REST microservice, the main app calls it asynchronously, streams partial results over WebSockets, and uses Payara Micro CDI outbound events so each discovered route fires an event to the browser while computation continues.

Payara Micro is presented as a lightweight Java EE runtime with embedded clustering and Hazelcast for elastic scale and distributed events. The close warns that async code is harder to debug and may silently skip work on failure, so reactive refactors should stay scoped to hot paths. A closing question on retries and circuit breakers is answered with CDI interceptors and ad hoc patterns rather than built-in Netflix-style breakers in the EE stack.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Microservices Architecture’s Influence on Team Organization (Michał Wdaniec)
talks.teaser: Explains how a telecom software company's move to microservices reshaped its product teams, handoffs and ownership.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who works at a company in Kraków building operations support software for telecom operators, explains how adopting a microservices architecture reshaped the company's team organization. The product helps operators plan, configure and verify their networks. Two cases illustrate the work: a merged German firm that wanted to cut rented transceiver stations, and a fiber network design project in Brazil.

Before the change, the system was closer to a monolith with services around it, and teams were organized by projects for single clients. A formal production process with many handoffs slowed delivery and bred conflict. The company moved to product teams that held product owners, analysts, developers and quality assurance, and the architecture and organization shifted together, in line with Conway's law. Operations deployed standardized, stateless, scalable packages and reported problems back to teams, while a separate UI team supplied a contract-based front-end framework.

The speaker warned that microservices bring hard problems: no distributed transactions, weaker data consistency, heavy communication overhead, and difficult request tracing across many hops. Splitting services too finely was an early mistake, and he suggested that organizations below about 30 developers may be better served by a monolith. Teams were encouraged to avoid hard dependencies on each other's libraries, do cross-team code reviews, and rotate developers between teams. The aim was for teams to build, test and run their own services quickly.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Blazing Fast Feedback Loops in the Java Universe (Michał Kordas)
talks.teaser: Explains how Java teams shorten CI feedback with Jenkins health checks, compiler warnings as errors, and parallelized tests.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens from the idea that development work needs fast, verifiable feedback rather than assumptions, and narrows a broader manifesto to technical excellence on a Java-centric stack. He describes a small team maintaining dozens of JVM repositories with Maven or Gradle, Jenkins, and GitHub, and treats recurring pain—broken environments, opaque stack traces, stale dependencies, late code-review nitpicks—as signals to automate earlier checks.

The middle of the talk walks through concrete patterns: periodic Jenkins health builds after outages, catching exceptions only to add context before rethrowing, Stack Overflow self-answers and wiki updates, treating compiler warnings as build failures, dependency update reports, Groovy commit-message validation, wall-mounted build monitors, and GitHub status APIs with branch builds that merge master before testing. He covers FIRST-style unit tests, parallel surefire and module builds, Gradle performance tweaks, shared Checkstyle/PMD/FindBugs configuration via internal plugins, IDE inspections, SpotBugs, fail-at-end reporting, build matrices for varied environments, incremental Pitest mutation coverage, Mondex for fragile JDK API assumptions, dedicated Jenkins executors for quick GitHub notifications, and multi-stage pipelines from compile through system tests to promotion.

The close ties feedback loops to code-review hygiene, visible open pull requests, contributing guides, and lightweight retrospectives, urging teams to keep shrinking latency wherever quality breaks down.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Myślenie prowokatywne w świecie IT (Joanna Czarnecka, Norbert Grzybek)
talks.teaser: Shows IT specialists a provocative thinking approach for working with business colleagues through hands-on exercises.
talks.summary:
This JDD 2016 session, given by Joanna Czarnecka and Norbert Grzybek, looks at provocative thinking as a way for IT specialists to communicate with colleagues from outside their field, such as business people and clients. The speakers opened by asking the room about everyday friction with the business side, where a common theme was IT saying something cannot be done while the business keeps asking for it anyway.

The core of the talk was a pair exercise. In the first round, one participant guided a partner, whose eyes were covered, toward a chosen spot while avoiding places the partner wanted to skip. In the second round, the leader deliberately made the path harder. Afterwards the audience described passivity, resistance and irritation in the first round, and more engagement and playfulness in the second. The speakers linked this to how people react when they are pushed and when they are obstructed, and to the way a business request can stand in for a different goal.

The closing part covered a follow-up exercise in which one partner asked the other only one question, what the problem is for them, and the speakers argued that this reframing gets people thinking rather than defending positions. They named three conditions for this approach: a goodwill environment, seriousness about work without taking oneself too seriously, and challenges tackled together rather than against each other. Practitioners should take away the habit of asking what a problem means for the other person and leaving room for shared ideas.

talks.title: JDD 2016: JIT me baby one more time (Jarek Pałka)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning JDD 2016: JIT me baby one more time (Jarek Pałka).

talks.title: JDD 2016: JPA
talks.teaser: Beyond copy-paste (Jakub Kubryński) explores JDD 2016: JPA.
talks.summary:
This session is a condensed extract from a longer JPA training for Java back-end developers who apply fixes from search results without understanding their effects. Using small code examples, the speaker walks through common Hibernate traps: annotations without attributes do nothing, an explicit save inside a transactional method is redundant, and mixing field and method annotations changes access for the whole class. A reserved word as an entity name breaks inserts, and renaming an entity changes how queries must refer to it.

Mapping and performance issues follow. A one-to-one relation without an owning side creates two foreign keys that block deletion, while a one-to-many relation without a join column silently adds a linking table. Bag collections force a full rebuild on every change, which an order column on a list avoids. The N+1 select problem is shown alongside batch size and join fetch. Optimistic locking with version columns is covered, including the catch that REST clients must send the version back. Equals and hashCode based on a database-generated ID break before persistence, and a UUID is offered as a workaround despite its storage cost.

The closing part covers caching and queries. The first-level cache is always on, while a clustered second-level cache such as Hazelcast is needed across multiple application instances. Batch inserts need periodic flushing and clearing. The speaker warns that HQL injection still happens when parameters are concatenated instead of bound. The final advice is to read Hibernate's logs and step into framework code when behavior looks wrong.

talks.title: JDD 2016: Concurrency options on the JVM (Christin Gorman)
talks.teaser: Explains why blocking threads limit JVM concurrency and compares thread pools, event loops and Quasar fibers.
talks.summary:
Christin Gorman argues that concurrency is often presented as far harder than it needs to be, and that developers should understand what their frameworks do underneath. The talk separates true parallel execution from concurrency, where tasks take turns and waiting is the central problem. On the JVM, concurrency maps onto operating system threads, which handle blocking calls well but do not scale: in the demo, around 3,000 threads on default memory settings ran out of memory, and a blocked thread pool left the server idle while queued tasks waited.

The speaker then walks through alternatives. Akka spreads work across actors on separate thread pools so that long-running and short-lived tasks do not starve each other. A single-threaded event loop, the model used by Node.js and a JVM framework of the same style, handled 10,000 sleep calls of 1000 milliseconds each in just over one second, but any slow callback stalls the whole application, and callback-based code is hard to write and unit test. Quasar fibers keep a blocking-style API while running on lightweight fibers, and a million sleeps took 8 seconds in the demo. The speaker had not used it in production and reported odd errors when pushing its limits.

The closing story comes from seismic control software, where a asynchronous JMS messaging layer made failures harder to see than synchronous calls, because a rejected message could simply sit on a queue. The takeaway is to adopt asynchronous designs only when the scale demands it, and to make sure timeouts and exceptions are surfaced rather than hidden.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2016 - Tomasz Torcz - The Song of JBoss and Chef
talks.teaser: Explains how a bank automated JBoss application server clusters with Chef, and the parsing pain that came with it.
talks.summary:
A bank's DevOps team set out to manage JBoss application servers with Chef. Their clusters ran in domain mode, with load balancers, virtual hosts and domain controllers, while most tutorials cover a single standalone instance. JBoss can be configured through a web console, a command-line interface or XML files, and the XML files clashed with Chef templates because JBoss rewrites them at runtime. The team chose the CLI and translated vendor installation instructions, written for the web console, into JSON data bags mapped to CLI commands.

Parsing the CLI output was the hardest part. The output was almost a Ruby hash, but quirks such as undefined standing for an empty set and stray hexadecimal fragments forced a series of workarounds before a usable parser existed. Once the current configuration could be dumped at the start of a run, Chef execution sped up, since each CLI invocation took 23 seconds and roughly 50 invocations ran per round. Scaling out doubled the number of hosts in about an hour, with much of that time spent waiting for the security team to open firewall ports.

The cookbooks were divided between the DevOps team and the application and middleware teams, but the DevOps team wrote most of the code and the specialist teams rarely carried it on. Keeping configuration in data bags made clusters easy to compare and let settings be tested and then copied to production. The main takeaways were the value of treating configuration as code and the cost of undocumented output formats and unclear shared ownership.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2016 - Tomek Pająk - DevOps Transformation Tailored to Organizational Culture
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of DevOpsDays Warsaw 2016 - Tomek Pająk - DevOps Transformation Tailored to Organizational Culture.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this DevOpsDays Warsaw 2016 presentation, Tomek Pająk explores why organizational culture is a decisive factor in successful DevOps transformations. Referencing research on organizational initiatives such as Total Quality Management, business process reengineering, and downsizing, Pająk notes a 75% failure rate, largely attributed to ignoring organizational culture. Because DevOps requires breaking down silos, adopting continuous integration, continuous delivery, and shared goals between development and operations, neglecting culture risks reverting organizations back to square one.

### Key Topics
- **Organizational Culture Models:** Pająk introduces the Cameron and Quinn competing values framework, which categorizes culture into four quadrants across two axes (flexibility vs. stability, and internal vs. external focus): Hierarchy (coordinators, process efficiency), Clan (mentors, team cohesion), Adhocracy (visionaries, agility, experimentation), and Market (results-driven, aggressive market competition).
- **Culture Assessment in Practice:** Using the six-dimension Cameron and Quinn survey (evaluating dominant characteristics, leadership, management of employees, organizational glue, strategic emphasis, and success criteria), Pająk evaluated teams at his fintech employer (SEQR in Poland). The assessment highlighted distinct cultural perceptions between the Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) team and its leadership, as well as divergence between software engineers and management seeking a more market-driven mindset.
- **The Cynefin Framework & Continuous Delivery:** Pająk applies Dave Snowden's Cynefin framework (Obvious, Complicated, Complex, Chaotic) to continuous delivery. He notes that continuous delivery pipelines are rarely identical between companies and cannot be solved purely through expert analysis (the complicated domain); rather, they reside in the complex domain, necessitating emergent experimentation and adaptive probing.

### Technical Details & Case Study
- **Testing Host Card Emulation (HCE):** Pająk shares an example from SEQR's mobile contactless payment deployment. To ensure real-time production monitoring before customers encountered failures across multiple third-party systems, the engineering team avoided prolonged theoretical debates and built an experimental test setup: a physical robot integrated with Bamboo and Appium that interacted directly with payment terminals using a mobile device.
- **Cultural Profile for DevOps:** Pająk illustrates that DevOps relies on continuous delivery maturity models spanning architecture, build, deployment, test verification, and information reporting. Experimenting with architectures and pipelines demands an Adhocracy culture, while aligning output with customer value demands Market culture. Autonomous, decentralized teams require Clan culture to establish trust, which requires leaders to disempower themselves and distribute authority.
- **Mechanisms for Cultural Influence:** Drawing on Edgar Schein's model, Pająk explains that transformation succeeds when survival anxiety exceeds learning anxiety. Rather than artificially inflating survival anxiety through threats or extrinsic motivators, leaders should reduce learning anxiety by fostering safe-to-fail environments. Additional influence tactics include managing natural constraints rather than artificial rules, socializing new hires with cultural champions, and actively reinforcing weak signals of autonomy and market focus.

### Takeaways
- **Culture Eats Strategy:** Implementing automation and tooling without cultural adaptation almost invariably leads to regression.
- **Evolution Over Target State Design:** Cultural change in complex adaptive systems should be treated as an evolutionary journey guided by direction and context rather than an idealized, rigid future design.
- **Challenges for Hierarchical Organizations:** Hierarchical cultures face the steepest barrier to DevOps adoption, as coordinators focused on procedural adherence must shift toward embracing calculated risk, autonomy, and experimentation.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2016 - Diogo Oliveira - The OutSystems R&D Continuous Delivery Journey
talks.teaser: Traces how an R&D team cut a 26-hour test run to about one hour through automation and staged pipelines.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how OutSystems, a low-code application platform with a large .NET and Java codebase, worked toward continuous delivery in its R&D group. Around 2014 the team had grown from 18 to 41 engineers, kept about 30 active SVN branches that took weeks to merge back, and ran roughly 10,000 tests across many stack combinations in a full pass that took 26 hours. Test machines were built by hand from a 49-page manual, which meant about three weeks of waiting plus three days of configuration per environment.

The fixes came in stages. Environment provisioning was scripted with Chef and then moved to AWS, bringing machine setup down to about an hour. A grassroots prototype, built in a single week, ran incremental builds, assigned failures to likely committers, and showed build status on office TVs. The team then moved the back end to the open-source GoCD tool, split tests into three stages that ran in about 10 minutes, half an hour and under an hour, reran suspected flaky tests, and capped quarantined tests at seven.

Today about 8,000 tests run in roughly one hour for two stacks, with around 2,000 legacy tests in an old internal DSL being rewritten as ordinary code. Open problems include a monolithic product architecture, unclear code ownership, and the need to change culture while still shipping releases. The practical takeaway is that faster feedback depended on automation, visibility and the right tests, and that the team still aims to remove developers from the release decision.

talks.title: PLNOG17 - Leonir Hoxha - Next Generation Network Architecture
talks.teaser: Segment Routing examines PLNOG17 - Leonir Hoxha - Next Generation Network Architecture.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Leonir Hoxha presents a comprehensive introduction to Segment Routing (SR) and its application in next-generation service provider network infrastructure. SR was developed to address operator requests for simpler, more efficient, and SDN-ready network architectures. Though still in IETF draft stages (starting in 2013, now with 10+ drafts), SR already has numerous implementations and satisfied customers reporting high satisfaction.

## Technical Foundation
Segment Routing is a source routing technology that fundamentally changes how networks forward traffic. Unlike traditional MPLS approaches, SR stores routing state in the packet header rather than across network infrastructure. The control plane uses standard IGP protocols (IS-IS, OSPF) with SR extensions, while the data plane remains unchanged—still using MPLS label forwarding, now called Segment IDs. Two forwarding variants exist: SR-MPLS (covered in this talk) and SRv6.

SR operates with three basic label operations: Push (add a segment), Continue (swap to the next segment), and Pop/Next (remove the label). The technology introduces two segment types: Global Segments, understood by all network devices via the Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB—typically labels 16,000 to 24,000), and Local Segments, significant only to the generating device for outgoing interfaces. Critical segments include Node Segments (Prefix Segments) identifying specific devices via loopback interfaces, and Adjacency Segments enabling explicit path selection through direct links.

## Key Use Cases
**Topology Independent LFA (TI-LFA)**: Achieves 100% failure coverage by pre-calculating backup paths for each prefix segment. When links fail, devices automatically push backup segments onto packets for rerouting without complex state management or additional configuration beyond enabling LFA in the IGP.

**Disjoint Path Routing**: Uses Anycast Segment IDs to establish geographically diverse paths. Assigning identical Anycast IDs to devices across separate planes (e.g., routes through different countries) enables traffic engineering to avoid shared failure points.

**Centralized SDN Traffic Engineering**: Leverages BGP Link State (BGP-LS) and Path Computation Elements (PCE) giving SDN controllers complete network visibility. Applications request specific paths—low-latency or bandwidth-constrained routes—via controller APIs, which automatically program the network without manual configuration.

## Operational Benefits
Key advantages include low OPEX and CAPEX due to simplified architecture; ECMP-aware automatic load balancing across equal-cost paths; micro-loop avoidance during convergence; smooth incremental deployment allowing coexistence with traditional LDP networks via mapping servers; and full SDN integration for dynamic orchestration. Minimal configuration—essentially two commands to enable SR within IGP processes—is required. Explicit traffic engineering eliminates RSVP-TE midpoint state management, centralizing state only at network edges or SDN controllers.

## Current State
Though not yet official standard, SR has progressed from initial draft (2013) through multiple implementation stages. Vendors including Cisco offer production deployments. Customer deployments highlight reduced operational burden and future-proof automation-ready infrastructure.

talks.title: PLNOG17 - Shabbir Ahmad - Dell EMC’s SDN strategy based on Open Networking
talks.teaser: Explains Dell EMC's open networking approach to SDN, separating switch hardware from network operating systems for data centers.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Dell's software-defined networking strategy, presented as open networking, within the context of the merged Dell Technologies group and its position in analyst rankings. The speaker contrasts traditional networking, where each chassis bundled proprietary hardware, operating system and protocols, with an approach that runs separate network operating systems on merchant-silicon switch hardware. The shift is compared to the earlier move from mainframes and Unix platforms to standard x86 servers.

Several product lines were covered as examples of this model. A data center leaf-and-spine fabric can be run as a controller-based design from Big Switch or as a controllerless design from Pluribus, while IP Infusion software can add MPLS and WAN functions to the same switches. A Big Switch monitoring fabric was described as a packet broker for tapping traffic, and it can be placed inline rather than only out of band. NSX was positioned for micro-segmentation and overlay networking in virtualized environments. The speaker also explained why a single-tier leaf-spine design replaces a large modular chassis, with the control role moved into spine switches.

In the closing question, the speaker explained that one physical infrastructure can host different operating systems for different purposes, but each function needs its own dedicated spine switches because control decisions are split between solutions. The main takeaway is that hardware and software can be chosen separately, so a team can change network function without replacing switches, provided the design is built to match the requirements.

talks.title: PLNOG17 - Elisa Jasinska - Network Automation - Design your Systems
talks.teaser: A practitioner maps six reusable system categories for building maintainable, microservice-style network automation.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting straightforward configuration automation with harder goals such as automated troubleshooting, failure analysis, and routing changes, which depend on reliable data sources and explicit, repeatable rule sets. Operational procedures and vendor differences matter as much as scripts: engineers should prioritize the workflows that consume the most time and fold pre-checks, post-checks, and maintenance habits into the design rather than bolting tools onto ad hoc habits.

The core framework groups every automated network task into six roles: a single authoritative source for inventory and configuration data, templating that stays independent of device push mechanisms, device access for uploads and upgrades, collection spanning logs, backups, custom reachability tests, and metrics with backends suitable for programmatic decisions, monitoring built from written alert criteria and corrective actions, and orchestration that chains review, deploy, convergence waits, and health checks. Shared pieces such as one alerting path and one configuration-delivery path should serve provisioning, customer rollout, and reroute scenarios alike. Large multi-component stacks are framed as loosely coupled services with clear interfaces, extendable piece by piece.

Practitioners are urged to avoid duplicated router lists across Cacti, Grafana, and logging tools, to plan long-term upkeep of collectors alongside the live network, and to treat orchestration as the layer that only works once the underlying data, templates, and monitoring exist. A brief Q&A covers SSH keys, generated operator accounts on devices, centralized Ansible execution hosts, and vault-style secret handling versus operational pragmatism on customer private keys.

talks.title: PLNOG17 - Alexis Dacquay
talks.teaser: Explains how merchant silicon brings dense 100 gig switching to service providers and why streamed telemetry beats polling.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why networking hardware has lagged behind CPUs and storage in density, and how merchant silicon from large chip vendors is changing that. Built for maximum density and performance, these chips offer 100 gig ports at a much lower price than traditional platforms. The talk argues that such switches can take on roles once reserved for expensive wide area gear, such as aggregation, peering and packet brokering. Software customization lets one platform hold a full internet routing table in hardware, while convergence speed still matters. Hardware encryption paired with wavelength division multiplexing is presented as a way to link sites up to 3,000 or 5,000 kilometres apart without a separate encryption box.

The second half turns to visibility. Traditional SNMP polling and syslog are coarse and delayed, so short-lived congestion can pass between polls unseen. The alternative is streaming telemetry, where each switch keeps a local state database and pushes updates when something changes, such as a MAC address, a routing entry or a BGP neighbour. A full switch state stream was described as roughly 100 to 200 megabytes per day, depending on activity. A demonstration portal showed MAC table changes and BGP learned-path counts over time, so engineers can compare device states at any past moment.

For practitioners, the takeaway is to weigh programmability and software features alongside raw specifications, and to consider merchant silicon where cost per port matters. The talk also argues for replacing polling with event-driven streaming, which scales monitoring and leaves historical data for troubleshooting, trend analysis and anomaly detection.

talks.title: PLNOG17 - Alexander Nardella - Mellanox Ethernet Switching Solutions for Data Centers
talks.teaser: Vendor overview of Mellanox Ethernet switches, adapters and cables for spine-leaf data center networks.
talks.summary:
Alexander Nardella, presenting for Mellanox, gives an overview of the company's Ethernet products for data centers. He explains that the Ethernet business is relatively new and that Mellanox designs and manufactures its own chips, with a portfolio that spans network adapters, optics, cables and switches. The session also introduces the company's own operating system, a free automation and monitoring tool, and its in-house support team.

The middle of the talk focuses on speeds and design. The speaker walks through 25, 50 and 100G port standards and how higher-speed ports can be split into lower-speed ones. He argues that the switches run without oversubscription and do not drop packets. He then makes the case for moving from modular chassis to spine-leaf designs, noting that 80% of data center communication happens east-west between servers. The Spectrum switch family, built on a Mellanox-designed ASIC with 6.4 terabit throughput, is presented alongside operating system choices of Mellanox OS or Cumulus.

The closing part reviews the adapter and cable lines and recent product launches, and points to switches suited to storage and cloud deployments. The main takeaway for a buyer is that hardware, software and optics can be chosen independently, with the speaker stressing investment protection for future bandwidth upgrades.
