talks.title: Obsługa 100M pps na platformie PC Paweł Małachowski i Przemysław Frasunek
talks.teaser: Shows how commodity PCs with DPDK can process around 100 million packets per second for DDoS filtering.
talks.summary:
The speakers, from a Polish company that runs a large CDN, explain why they built an anti-DDoS service on ordinary PC hardware instead of buying expensive appliances. Their first attempt used a generic operating system and a 10G card, and sending topped out at about 7 million packets per second, while receiving performed much worse. Moving to the open-source DPDK framework, which takes network cards away from the kernel and gives user-space applications direct access to frames, let a single PC with three cores handle full 10G line rate of 14 million minimum-size packets per second.

The middle of the talk covers why general-purpose systems struggle at this load. At 10G with minimum-size frames the per-packet time budget is roughly 1300 nanoseconds, and it shrinks sharply at 40G and 100G. The speakers walked through PCIe bandwidth limits, multi-queue NICs that spread traffic with RSS, and Intel CPU features such as DDIO and AVX2 that help when data stays in cache. They compared several user-space data plane options and chose DPDK for its maturity and supporting libraries. Practical lessons included processing packets in batches, using hugepages, avoiding runtime allocation and locks, inlining hot code, pinning cores and profiling with perf.

They concluded that commodity PCs can reach very high packet rates when the software is carefully engineered, and argued that building the system in-house cost less than a single commercial appliance. The resulting service is offered to customers as DDoS protection, and the speakers stressed that results depend heavily on tuning, testing and hardware choice.

talks.title: Publiczny IX jest czubkiem internetowej góry lodowej Zasada 9;1 PNI Martin Atkinson
talks.teaser: Explains why private peering carries most internet traffic and how colocation supports blended peering strategies.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames internet interconnection around an iceberg model: public internet exchange peering is visible and important, but roughly nine tenths of traffic is exchanged over private network interconnect between large content owners and networks. The speaker traces Equinix’s history from a single peering fabric with colocation in 1998 to a global footprint, and discusses the acquisition of BLIX in Warsaw as an extension of that model while preserving operational independence and neutrality.

Transit pricing is portrayed as under sustained competitive pressure, with dense metro campuses sometimes enabling large reductions compared with median market quotes. That pressure draws more enterprises, cloud providers, and content networks into colocation, while mature operators blend transit, public peering, and private cross-connect sessions sized from ten-gigabit toward hundred-gigabit links. The talk contrasts colocation-centric peering campuses with more distributed European exchange layouts and argues that private peering beside peers lowers cost and improves performance as volumes grow.

Practitioners are urged to plan for private peering to scale faster than public exchange traffic for large players, to treat leading local exchanges such as BLIX as the public layer while using nearby colocation for PNI, and to favor campus peering over expensive metro stitching. Closing figures cite BLIX membership near two hundred seventy-nine and peak traffic just under five hundred gigabits per second, with global Equinix presence presented as an enabler for Polish networks seeking wider reach.

talks.title: Bitspiration For Charity 2015: Interview with Bershan Shaw
talks.teaser: A motivational coach offers advice to startup founders and women in tech, and describes her online support community.
talks.summary:
This short interview was recorded at the Bitspiration for Charity event in Krakow with motivational speaker and life coach Bershan Shaw. She explains that she was brought in to help startups and businesses make their work more purposeful, and to encourage women who hold back from the startup field because they fear failing. Her online platform, which she likens to a support-focused social network, lets people talk privately or publicly about health, family, relationship, money and career problems through blogs, podcasts and live chat.

Her main advice for founders is to keep going, since she argues that people often stop short of the finish line just before the hardest part, and that failure should be treated as a lesson rather than an ending. For women, she urges them to drop the belief that they are not good enough or strong enough, and to spend time with people who inspire and uplift them instead of negative voices.

The closing questions cover her plans while staying in Krakow, which include visiting the castle, the city market and local food and culture. The clip is aimed at motivation and confidence rather than specific business methods or technical detail.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2015 - Caoimhin Graham
talks.teaser: Explains technical debt as a tactical trade-off, how to spot it early, and how to prioritise and repay it in a team.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames technical debt as the tactical compromises teams make while chasing a strategic vision, using a Jenga tower to show how building features before a stable foundation leaves a shaky structure. Martin Fowler's quadrant sorts debt into reckless or prudent and deliberate or inadvertent, with examples such as adopting a new technology in production before anyone understood it. Security shortcuts are treated as negligence rather than debt, and bad code is kept separate from debt.

Debt is not inherently bad when it is known and tracked, since it lets an organisation pivot to market demands; ignorance is the real danger. A broken window theory analogy shows how neglected problems invite worse ones, until debt spirals into a vicious cycle of pressure and shortcuts. Twitter's move from a large Ruby on Rails monolith to services is cited as an example of tackling debt before it became too costly to repay.

To find debt, the speaker suggests watching trends over time, such as falling team velocity, painful releases and tightly coupled code, rather than single data points. Each item should be logged with a short description and an estimate of its impact on people and future changes. Repayment can be built into everyday work, for example by setting aside part of each sprint, through refactoring, rewriting, or an over-minimum-viable-product, or by accepting the interest on code rarely touched.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Logowanie zdarzeń w architekturze opartej na mikroserwisach (P. Grajewski, Ł. Kamiński)
talks.teaser: Explains centralized event logging and metrics collection for microservice ecosystems using ELK, InfluxDB, and Grafana.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a familiar pain in microservice landscapes: many services and hosts generate floods of logs, so tracing a slow page or failure back to one component by SSH and grepping local files stops scaling. Observability data splits into asynchronous events (log lines) and synchronous metrics (numeric samples over time), and the talk walks through each stack with live demos.

For events, the presenters describe the ELK pattern—Logstash agents shipping data to Elasticsearch and Kibana for search and dashboards. They start from tailing rotated log files, show how unstructured access logs force grok parsing, and argue for JSON logs so fields stay queryable. Kibana Discover, Lucene-style filters, bar charts by HTTP status and application, and shared dashboards illustrate day-to-day triage. Scaling adds per-node Logstash Forwarder, a Redis queue before Elasticsearch indexing, stdout logging aligned with twelve-factor practice, and optional Docker log paths.

The metrics half contrasts time-series storage with log search, layers measurements from CPU and memory up through business KPIs, and recommends collecting broadly for later diagnosis. InfluxDB retention buckets, tag-based queries, and Grafana panels—including a Spring Boot app that exports heap metrics—mirror the ELK workflow. Closing advice stresses that these toolchains are inexpensive to adopt, that most teams already log but under-instrument metrics, and that structured export early pays off when incidents span many services.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2015 - Yegor Bugayenko
talks.teaser: Argues that continuous integration breaks down under blame and ignored red builds, and proposes pre-flight builds guarding master.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that continuous integration, as most teams run it, stops working in practice. A build server checks each commit to master and shows green or red, but the speaker says a broken master is rarely fixed right away. He describes two outcomes seen across several teams: red builds get ignored, or a stop-the-line rule is enforced, which leads to finger-pointing, fear of breaking the build, long-lived branches and discarded code.

The proposed fix is pre-flight builds. Direct pushes to master are blocked, so every change must go through a bot that merges a pull request with master, runs the full build and tests, and merges only if they pass. The speaker presented Ruler, an open-source hosted service that does this for GitHub pull requests, and said more than 200 open source projects have used it. Reported results from the speaker's own projects include about 95% of builds staying green, developers no longer fearing breakage, failures treated as a gap in the gate rather than a person's fault, and smaller, quicker branches.

In the question round, the speaker separated this approach from Jenkins jobs with voting, such as Gerrit setups. Those work only when master is protected and nobody can push to it directly, since a red build found after a merge comes too late. Code review stays a separate step before the pre-flight build, covering architecture and design, while the build checks whether the code and its tests hold. Audience members also framed the problem as cultural, and the speaker agreed it has an organisational side but said a technical gate was the only thing that had worked for them.

talks.title: DevOpsDays Warsaw 2015 - Łukasz Szczęsny - JaaC
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in DevOpsDays Warsaw 2015 - Łukasz Szczęsny - JaaC - Jenkins as a Code.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At DevOpsDays Warsaw 2015, Łukasz Szczęsny, a system engineer at 4finance IT and co-organizer of the Warsaw Linux User Group, presented "Jenkins as a Code" (JaaC). The talk addresses the operational challenges of managing Jenkins at scale, including manual UI configurations, brittle upgrades, unversioned job changes, orphaned plugins, and plain-text credentials. Szczęsny details how his team transitioned hundreds of manually clicked Jenkins jobs into fully automated, version-controlled infrastructure and pipeline definitions using Ansible and the Jenkins Job DSL plugin.

### Key Topics
- **Pitfalls of Manual Jenkins Management**: Relying on manual UI configuration leads to un-auditable changes, breaking updates, plain-text credentials stored in SCM XML files, and fear of upgrading legacy instances.
- **Infrastructure Automation**: Automating Jenkins master installation, plugin installations, tool provisioning (JDK, Maven, Gradle), and slave node lifecycle management.
- **Jobs as Code (JaaC)**: Comparing approaches for version-controlling jobs—such as Jenkins CLI with raw XML, Jenkins Job Builder (from OpenStack), Workflow plugin, and Jenkins Job DSL plugin.
- **Case Study at 4finance IT**: Implementing an Ansible-driven provisioning workflow and a Gradle-based Jenkins Job DSL repository with tests to automate roughly 1,000 jobs.
- **Jenkins 2.0 Roadmap**: Upcoming improvements discussed by Kosuke Kawaguchi and the community, including decoupling Groovy from core, JavaScript modularization, a UX overhaul, Jenkinsfile integration, and open-sourcing the Stage View plugin.

### Technical Details
- **Provisioning & Infrastructure**: Szczęsny uses Ansible for master configuration and tool setup. Slave management uses AWS CloudFormation with Auto Scaling groups and Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) equipped with the Jenkins Swarm plugin, allowing new EC2 instances to auto-connect to the master. Docker plugins and Groovy console SSH scripts are also noted as alternatives.
- **Job DSL Implementation**: Jobs are maintained in a Gradle project stored in Git/Stash. The Gradle setup allows developers to write Groovy DSL code in their IDE, compile, and run tests verifying generated XML before changes are applied. 
- **Enforcing Read-Only Jenkins**: The team locked down Jenkins UI modifications. All changes must be proposed via pull requests. A single initial "seed job" runs automatically every five minutes to scan the DSL repository and create, update, or prune Jenkins jobs.
- **Disaster Recovery**: Szczęsny highlights an incident where a misplaced exclamation mark in a Groovy console script deleted almost every job; because everything was defined in code, the entire pipeline suite was recreated within five minutes.
- **Interoperability with Workflow**: In the Q&A, Szczęsny clarified that Job DSL does not compete directly with the Jenkins Workflow (Pipeline) plugin. Instead, Job DSL can be used to generate the initial Workflow seed jobs programmatically.

### Takeaways
Automating Jenkins setup and treating jobs as code eliminates human error, provides an audit trail via Git pull requests, resolves credential management issues, and makes Jenkins instances reproducible and disaster-resilient. Combining configuration management (Ansible) with Job DSL and automated seed jobs allows engineering teams to scale to thousands of jobs without relying on fragile, manual UI interactions.

talks.title: JDD2015 - -XX:+UseG1GC (Jakub Kubrynski)
talks.teaser: Covers G1 on large Java heaps, mixed and full collections, and JVM flags that curb long stop-the-world pauses.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why garbage collection matters for production Java: memory is finite, collectors pause application threads, and on multi‑gigabyte heaps those pauses can reach seconds or tens of seconds—unacceptable for interactive web workloads. The speaker sketches reference counting and why cycle islands rule it out for Java, then mark‑sweep and mark‑compact tradeoffs, the generational hypothesis, and card tables for tracking references from old to young space.

The core of the talk is G1: the heap is carved into many small regions (on the order of one megabyte each), with remembered sets per region, refinement threads, collection sets, and humongous objects for allocations larger than half a region. Young collections remain stop‑the‑world and parallel; a concurrent marking cycle piggybacks on young GC, after which mixed collections reclaim part of the old generation incrementally—often spread across several cycles—while full GC remains a slow, serial fallback that can run for minutes on large heaps.

Practical guidance covers starting concurrent marking earlier via initiating heap occupancy, adding concurrent marking threads, reserving heap for copying, enabling parallel reference processing, and enlarging regions to avoid humongous allocations. The speaker warns to watch for concurrent mode failure, promotion failure, and evacuation failure in verbose GC logs, and to visualize runs with tools such as GC log viewers or Mission Control. Parallel GC still wins raw throughput for batch-style work; CMS is treated as legacy; experimental low‑pause collectors are mentioned briefly. The talk closes with production experience using G1 on eight‑ to twelve‑gigabyte heaps and notes the move toward making G1 the default collector in newer JDK releases.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Sustaining Architecture When Dealing with Data Variability... (Joe Yoder)
talks.teaser: Shows how to keep a software architecture clean when client requirements and data formats keep changing.
talks.summary:
The talk explores keeping a software system sustainable when parts of it must change often, such as product types, service plans, insurance rules or game contests. The core idea is to separate fast-changing parts from a stable core, so variation can be added without tangling the core. The speaker links this to the big ball of mud problem and to buildings that layer components changing at different rates, noting that schemas and platforms usually change more slowly than code and data.

A front-door layer of adapters, facades and translation keeps client-specific quirks out of protected components. Metadata describes variation so it can be read at runtime, and dynamic hook points let new business rules plug in through a common interface. Templates, generators and small DSLs streamline work that keeps repeating. The main example is an order-import system receiving orders in mainframe, CSV, spreadsheet and delimited formats. Its hundreds of one-off importers became a maintenance burden, so the redesigned version used generic gathering, transformation, validation and metadata mappings, letting a new client come on in hours or days, with custom code only for unusual rules.

The closing advice is to act at a more responsible moment rather than at the last one, and to keep refactoring as the system is learned. Continuous inspection and architecture conformance checks can catch misuse early. A good sign is that developers are not afraid to touch any part of the system. The speaker warns against over-designing highly flexible meta-architectures, which can add confusion, maintenance cost and performance problems.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Migrating to continuous delivery in the world of financial trading (David Genn)
talks.teaser: Explores how a regulated retail trading firm adopted continuous delivery over three years despite audit, uptime, and legacy constraints.
talks.summary:
Retail brokerage IG runs web and mobile trading platforms for roughly 120,000 active clients and about four million trades per month. The speaker frames continuous delivery through lean ideas—flow efficiency versus resource efficiency—and argues that measuring cycle time from idea to production matters more than sprint velocity or keeping every role fully utilized.

FinTech constraints shape the rollout: strict uptime for money-moving systems, regulators and auditors who want a clear record of what changed, legacy platforms from the early 2000s, cross-team dependencies, and primarily on-premises data centers rather than a cloud-native footprint. The API team’s approach rests on four principles: treat every merge to master as a production candidate, rely on strong automated tests, automate release steps, and separate deployment from release. Technically that means feature branches merged to master, Bamboo pipelines that build tagged release candidates into Nexus, blue-green Tomcat clusters with manual promotion gates, smaller services carved from monoliths, and feature flags managed with Zookeeper. culturally, teams self-organize around when code ships, QA often triggers production releases, and audit trails benefit from smaller, traceable changes.

Q&A covers stateless apps and cache warmup when switching clusters, feature-flag discipline and canaries, two-week feature branches as a norm, load testing as a manual pipeline add-on, and database change pain—with schema isolation, Flyway, and most schema work still needing downtime. The journey is ongoing as the firm grows development sites in London, Bangalore, and Kraków.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Yes We Scan! Software Analysis Using jQAssistant (Dirk Mahler)
talks.teaser: Introduces jQAssistant for scanning codebases into a graph store and applying rules on structure, dependencies, and complexity.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why teams struggle when production behavior diverges from what source code seems to say, and when applications hide inside opaque libraries and frameworks. The speaker argues that developers need repeatable scans that reveal real structures—not just what an IDE shows at the surface—so migration, maintenance, and governance decisions rest on evidence.

The core walkthrough centers on jQAssistant as a plugin-oriented analysis framework: download a distribution, point scanners at repositories (often Java-centric artifacts such as classes, manifests, and scripts), load results into a graph database, and explore them through a browser or command line. Custom plugins can enrich the model. Examples include mapping packages and classes, tracing dependencies and content relationships, spotting duplicate or mismatched types, and computing complexity or hotspot metrics across large class counts. A brownfield-style scenario illustrates reading legacy structure before refactoring.

The closing emphasis is extensibility—teams can define their own labels, relations, and rules—and the value of keeping disparate facts (exceptions, packages, services, patch cycles) in one correlatable graph. Practitioners should leave with a concrete workflow for turning repository scans into queryable architectural insight they can extend over time.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Kubernetes - Beyond the basics (Paul Bakker)
talks.teaser: Covers the steps needed to move Kubernetes from basic containers to automated, zero-downtime production deployments.
talks.summary:
Paul Bakker argues that containers become most useful once they run in production, and that Kubernetes on its own is only a building block that needs extra work before it is production-ready. He starts with the core concepts: the master that hosts the API server, the nodes where pods run, replication controllers that keep a set number of replicas alive, and services that give changing pod addresses a stable endpoint.

From there he builds up the surrounding pieces step by step. Deployments are driven through the Kubernetes REST API rather than manual commands, and an HAProxy load balancer is kept in sync with running pods using etcd and confd. A virtual network layer such as flannel makes pod addresses reachable from machines outside the cluster. A custom deployer component watches the cluster, waits for healthy pods, and then switches traffic to a new version, giving blue-green deployments. A live demo runs a Bamboo build that rolls out a new release, and load tests with Gatling reported no dropped connections.

The closing part covers what the application itself must provide: health check endpoints, a stateless design without HTTP sessions, centralized logging to trace problems across many pods, and configuration passed through environment variables or etcd. The main takeaway is that Kubernetes needs tooling and application changes around it before it suits production work.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Forgetting Java: Why Java Should Die in Flames (Piotr Limanowski)
talks.teaser: Argues that Java's tooling and build habits hold developers back, comparing them with Ruby and Elixir approaches.
talks.summary:
Piotr Limanowski opens by asking whether Java is dead, and answers that it is alive but stagnating. He points to how rarely the language changes, to COBOL shops that keep migrating to Java, and to a community habit of settling on old choices instead of looking at what other ecosystems do.

The middle of the talk is a tour of developer tooling. He contrasts the shell, REPL-driven workflows and prompt customisation with the Java experience, then compares Maven's and Gradle's sprawling XML and DSL files with Rake, Mix and Bundler. He also covers version managers that make trying a new Java release easy, the argument for packaging applications self-contained rather than deploying them to application servers, and the stability patterns from Michael Nygaard's book, such as bulkheads and circuit breakers. Logging configuration and the value of understanding design patterns, rather than applying them by rote, come up as well.

He closes with a short live demo of a Phoenix web application on Elixir, built on actors and supervisors, and urges developers to question inherited practices, update their tools and keep enjoying their work. In the questions, he argues that Gradle exposes too many options for newcomers, so the problem lies partly in the tool design rather than only in how people use it.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Where refactoring meets Big $$$ (Michal Gruca)
talks.teaser: Outlines refactoring styles and ways teams justify rework to leadership using metrics, trust, and real case studies.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by aligning the room on Martin Fowler’s definition of refactoring—changing code without altering observable behavior—and argues that refactoring without tests is only hopeful editing. The speaker sorts work into everyday IDE-backed cleanups, risky “big bang” rewrites, and gradual “sprouting” (strangler-style) growth of new code that slowly replaces legacy pieces, with warnings about microservice extraction leaving orphaned old modules.

Midway, the focus shifts to winning permission from people who control budgets. Business audiences respond to numbers, so the talk recommends Sonar and simpler repo or profiler measures, plus input from support and QA on where pain concentrates. Velocity, defect hotspots, infrastructure cost, and Boy Scout–style process tweaks are framed as money saved, not technologist whims. Trust can start with unpaid weekend fixes whose before-and-after metrics make the next sprint negotiation easier.

Career stories illustrate each pattern: a nested-map structure tamed with IDE-only “refactoring golf,” a recruitment platform where a模型 change exploded estimates and forced a frank rewrite conversation, and a monolith where modules were peeled out behind APIs and Liquibase plus Maven improved releases. The closing takeaway rejects dedicated refactoring teams as unsustainable; everyone should improve code through shared hooks and rotation instead.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Jak rozmawiać z obcymi formami inteligencji - poradnik dla craftsmanów (Slawomir Sobotka)
talks.teaser: Surfaces developer-business misfires with brain models, nonviolent communication, and metaprogram tools for craftsmen.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a familiar IT scene: a junior apologizes that they do not understand someone's code, and a senior snaps back. The speaker walks through a layered model of perception, emotion, identity, and defensive behavior, using that exchange to show how much of a conversation sits below the words people hear.

He contrasts task-focused flow with social cognition, describes the first fractions of a second when the limbic system can dominate, and notes that naming an emotion in a few abstract words can help restore rational prefrontal processing. Drawing on years of technical training work, he argues that stronger frameworks alone do not fix teamwork or business contact, and introduces nonviolent communication built on separating universal needs from strategies. He outlines metaprograms such as away-from versus toward, general versus specific, necessity versus possibility, and sameness versus difference, plus time representations that explain deadline clashes between programmers and business stakeholders.

Practitioners are urged to tailor messages to the listener's filters, offer options instead of closing them, agree on signals when deep technical focus must not be interrupted, and use plain metaphors rather than dumping internal detail. The close describes five stages of growing awareness so reactions in reviews or meetings can be recognized and gradually reshaped.

talks.title: JDD2015 - What is Code? (Jakub Marchwicki)
talks.teaser: Argues that requirements, runbooks, and QA artifacts deserve the same Git workflow developers expect from application code.
talks.summary:
Enterprise projects often treat “code” as only what developers commit, while requirements spill across Excel, Enterprise Architect, Word, and Confluence without blame, diffs, or a single owner. Marchwicki argues that developers end up as the main documentation audience, yet the workflow fights how they already work in Git, which produces hundred-page specs with opaque version jumps and no traceability.

His response is “design as code.” REST boundaries stay in Swagger annotations reviewed in pull requests; longer process and design narrative moves into AsciiDoc (with optional PlantUML) beside the repository. Operations material—Jenkins jobs, Docker images, Packer templates, and Flyway SQL migrations—belongs in source control too, so provisioning and schema history are diffable instead of tribal knowledge spread across servers.

Test automation, readable QA scripts, and test data can follow the same pattern. The talk surveys concrete tools, then stresses that adopting them means rethinking roles: architecture as decision records, operations as codified delivery, and testers as analysts who collaborate inside the repo—not reorganizing people last while tools stay in silos.

talks.title: JDD2015 - JDK not so hidden treasures (Andrzej Grzesik)
talks.teaser: A walkthrough of bundled JDK command-line utilities for GC logging, process inspection, heap dumps, and thread diagnostics on Linux servers.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by arguing that Java’s deep stack of abstractions rewards curiosity, and that most teams only touch java and javac while roughly forty other binaries live under JAVA_HOME. The single takeaway urged up front is to enable garbage-collection logging on development and production JVMs, using release-appropriate flags, so stalls and out-of-memory failures can be tied to pause length, reclaimed memory, and cases where the collector spends too long reclaiming.

The core of the session is command-line diagnosis on headless production Linux or Unix hosts. Tools demonstrated include JPS with -lvm to list processes and VM flags; jar to list archive contents; javap to inspect bytecode and constant folding; jinfo for live flags and system properties; jmap and jhat for heap dumps and OQL queries over a minimal HTTP UI; Jstack for all-thread stacks, with warnings that output is sequential rather than a true snapshot; and jstat for repeated VM metrics, with pointers to OpenJDK sources and external articles on custom formats. JCMD is presented as a Java 7+ umbrella that exposes the same channels, and JVisualVM—with the Visual GC plugin—reuses the same profiling and OQL machinery graphically.

Practical guidance closes the loop: prefer offline heap analysis when heaps are large, name threads to correlate long transactions, remember kill -3 versus Jstack and stdout redirection pitfalls, and treat per-release flag lists as moving targets rather than memorizing one universal flag set.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Thorny Path to Data Mining Projects (Alexey Zinovyev)
talks.teaser: Delivers a roadmap for Java developers joining data mining projects via Hadoop, Spark, algorithms, and Java ML libraries.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames a keynote for programmers in Poland, linking graph theory, traffic prediction, and his own path as a Java developer using Hadoop and Spark. He jokes about local culture, contrasts glamorized data scientists with production reality, and separates management reporting and OLAP cubes from true pattern discovery. Simple examples cover weather prediction limits and image classification before he argues that Java engineers are needed to pull data from many sources, fix missing values, drop bad signals, and join large tables with production-grade memory control.

He surveys typical business questions—credit risk, card fraud, sales forecasts, music and video recommendations—and common sources from social networks and banking to warehouses, CSV, email archives, and academic formats. The walkthrough covers association rules, clustering without labels, regression, classification, Kaggle-style supervised learning, decision trees on Titanic-style features, and k-nearest neighbors. Language and library comparisons span Octave, R, Python with pandas and scikit-learn, versus Java APIs, Weka, SPMF, JDM, and javax.data.mining gaps. On big data he describes Hive and Pig for features, why graph iteration fits poorly in classic MapReduce, Spark as in-memory MapReduce with cited ten- to twenty-fold speedups in his work, Mahout, and MLlib for classification, clustering, and regression at scale—with a warning that MLlib prototypes pay a shuffle cost when parallelism is unnecessary.

He tells beginners not to sink weeks into MapReduce job boilerplate upfront, to befriend DevOps for cluster and JVM tuning, to learn algorithms enough to translate shared Python into Java, and to prefer Java parallel stacks over abandoning the language for the mining project.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Ratpack: the core of your microservices (Andrey Adamovich)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for JDD2015 - Ratpack: the core of your microservices (Andrey Adamovich).

talks.title: JDD2015 - Reactive database mapping with Scala and Slick (Jacek Kunicki)
talks.teaser: Walks through mapping Scala case classes to database tables with Slick, from schema and queries to joins and typed SQL.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Slick, a Scala library that acts as a functional relational mapping layer over JDBC rather than an object-graph ORM. The speaker explains that queries are built lazily, in the style of Scala collections, and only reach the database when a run call is made. Slick's database operations return futures, and results can also be consumed as a stream that follows the Reactive Streams API.

The live coding part starts from a simple conference domain of rooms, speakers, talks and votes, modelled as immutable case classes. Each one is mapped to a table in a schema trait, with primary and foreign keys, a many-to-many link table, an optional auto-generated vote ID and a custom conversion between Java time values and SQL timestamps. The schema is created only when it is absent, sample data is inserted in a transaction, and votes are updated, deleted and re-read, with generated keys returned on insert.

The final section covers joins written as for-comprehensions, including a version that returns case class instances directly. It then shows a grouped count of positive votes per talk, a plain SQL query with a custom row reader, and typed SQL checked at compile time, which needs database access during compilation. The takeaway is that Slick keeps database round trips explicit and leaves the shape of each query under the developer's control.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Efficient HTTP applications on the JVM with Ratpack (Alvaro Sanchez-Mariscal)
talks.teaser: A walkthrough of Ratpack on the JVM shows handler chains, registry injection, modules, and non-blocking HTTP for high-throughput services.
talks.summary:
The session introduces Ratpack as a lightweight, Java 8–oriented stack for building non-blocking HTTP applications on the JVM, usable from Java or Groovy. The speaker contrasts it with heavier servlet-based frameworks and Spring Boot on startup time and developer workflow, including Gradle-based projects, the dedicated Ratpack configuration directory, and continuous reload during development.

Live demos progress from a minimal Groovy script and a Gradle layout through the handler chain model: global handlers, path and HTTP method routing, path tokens, and handler classes. The talk covers request context, continuing or terminating the chain, per-request registry scoping, dependency lookup, functional tests that bind a random port and HTTP client, Guice integration, official modules such as Jackson and H2, renderers, and promise-based composition with ordered execution and separate pools for blocking work.

Practitioners gain a concrete picture of when Ratpack fits microservices or high-throughput services, how routing and injection are structured without the servlet API, and how asynchronous pipelines stay predictable compared with typical promise-heavy stacks.

talks.title: JDD2015 - Twenty-one Years of Design Patterns (Ralph Johnson)
talks.teaser: Reviews twenty-one years of Design Patterns: vocabulary impact, catalog errors, core patterns, and cautions for adopting them.
talks.summary:
Ralph Johnson opens with how the 1994 Design Patterns catalog was built by four experienced framework developers, distributed via FTP and an active mailing list before wide release, and how the book’s naming shaped later communities—including Java APIs aligned to pattern names.

He argues the book’s structural versus behavioral split is weak, proposes a “core” set practitioners should learn first, and walks through Composite and Observer in detail. For Composite, he explains leaf-versus-composite child management and why mainstream libraries diverged from the book’s recommended error-on-leaf approach. For Observer, he contrasts textbook subject–observer coupling with Java listeners, event hierarchies, push versus pull, and data binding patterns the catalog never captured. He also discusses value objects, null objects, dependency injection as a post-book pattern, peripheral patterns such as Visitor, and frequent misuse of Singleton and Mediator.

He closes with critiques the original edition omitted: apply patterns lazily through refactoring, never treat pattern count as design quality, and treat patterns as gateways to principles rather than goals. He notes second-edition planning, John Vlissides’s death, and uses Q&A to discuss Visitor overuse and teaching patterns through examples where they are tempting but wrong.

talks.title: PLNOG15 -The Exascale Future of Today (Rob Bird)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for PLNOG15 -The Exascale Future of Today (Rob Bird).
talks.summary:
### Overview
Robert Bird, head of Big Data Architecture and Big Data Research at Akamai Technologies, examines the state and challenges of exascale computing (processing quintillions of operations, bytes, or bits per second). Drawing from Akamai's operational reality—delivering 30% to 50% of global web traffic, peaking at 40 Tbps across roughly 250,000 servers, and managing about 5 petabytes of logs per day—Bird assesses why the anticipated arrival of exascale computing has stalled since predictions in 2007. The presentation breaks down exascale feasibility across three primary pillars: compute architectures, networking, and storage, while emphasizing the convergence between traditional supercomputing, cloud architectures, and peer-to-peer (P2P) systems.

### Key Topics
- **Defining Exascale:** Exascale refers to quintillion-scale operations (exaflops), data storage (exabytes), or transmission rates. While storage has already entered the exascale tier, compute is hovering near petascale thresholds, and true exascale networking remains largely theoretical.
- **Real-World Drivers:** Projects driving exascale demand include high-energy physics (the Large Hadron Collider, which could produce 36 exabytes per day but limits retention to 30 petabytes per year due to transmission constraints), astrophysics (the Square Kilometre Array), 8K video streaming, intelligence cartography, and large consumer web platforms like Akamai, Google, Facebook, and Netflix.
- **The Networking Bottleneck:** Transmitting an exabyte over a 100 Gbps link would require roughly 1,000 days (or 2.5 days across Akamai’s entire global bisection bandwidth), highlighting data movement as the single most prohibitive factor in exascale progression.
- **Storage, Multi-Tenancy, and Data Locality:** Effective big data storage requires moving past simple bulk storage (e.g., standard HDFS) toward anticipatory caching, multi-tiered data placement, and database architectures capable of handling heterogeneous queries.

### Technical Details
- **Compute and Efficiency Limits:** Achieving an exaflop using smartphone-class hardware (e.g., ARM Cortex-A9 in iPhone 6) would take one billion units consuming roughly 7 gigawatts. Leading supercomputers, such as Tianhe-2 (achieving roughly 35 to 55 petaflops peak at 18 to 30+ megawatts), demonstrate extreme power requirements. In contrast, purpose-built networks like Bitcoin reach 5.4 exahashes/sec via ASICs, and the human brain operates at an estimated exaflop-equivalent pattern recognition capability on just 20 watts at 10 Hz.
- **Interconnects and Signaling:** High-performance computing utilizes custom fabrics (e.g., Cray Titan, IBM Blue Gene) and InfiniBand, which reaches near 1 Tbps aggregate bandwidth and is evolving into routable datacenter environments. Optical signaling approaches theoretical limits around 1.2 petabits/sec; an experimental 255 Tbps fiber link demonstrated in the Netherlands only spanned approximately two feet.
- **Storage Formatting and Query Processing:** Big data architectures face significant trade-offs between write efficiency and read optimization. Once multi-exabyte stores are committed in specific formats (row vs. column vs. pre-aggregated cubes), transforming them is computationally prohibitive. Distributed database systems like Google Spanner face graph-based Hamiltonian path optimizations for query planning across mobile users, pointing toward Michael Stonebraker's concept of "polystores"—multi-engine platforms capable of concurrently evaluating relational, graph, full-text, and array data.

### Takeaways
- Moore's Law scaling based on raw clock speed and transistor doubling has plateaued, shifting the design focus toward non-von Neumann models, neuromorphic computing, FPGAs integrated into server chips, and specialized accelerators (GPUs/ASICs).
- Exascale datacenters will require radical physical design shifts, including floor-based passive immersion cooling handling 200 kW to 1 MW per rack.
- Progress depends on cross-pollination: supercomputing contributes insights into power management, interconnect hierarchies, and MPI-style parallelization, while cloud computing provides lessons in commodity resilience, planetary caching hierarchies, and software-defined architectures.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Bitspiration 2015- Europe's West Coast for Awesome Startups (Sigrid Johannisse).
talks.summary:
### Overview
At Bitspiration 2015 in Poland, Sigrid Johannisse, Director of StartupDelta, presented on building and scaling startup ecosystems in Europe, using the Netherlands' national initiative StartupDelta as a blueprint. Working alongside Special Envoy Neelie Kroes, StartupDelta aims to merge regional tech hubs into a unified, interconnected ecosystem to position the Netherlands—and Europe as a whole—as a competitive alternative to Silicon Valley for scaling technology businesses.

### Key Topics
- **StartupDelta's National Ecosystem Model**: Rather than promoting isolated regional hubs, StartupDelta integrates clusters across Amsterdam, Rotterdam, technical universities, and eastern regions into a single coordinated network accessible within 90 minutes.
- **Cross-Sectoral Innovation**: Combining the Netherlands' strengths in core technologies (nanoelectronics, photonics, and quantum computing) with traditional industry leadership in agriculture and food to spur cross-disciplinary IT innovation.
- **Policy and Systemic Reforms**: Adapting national regulations, fiscal incentives, and intellectual property frameworks originally designed for large corporations to better serve startups.
- **Internationalization and Talent Mobility**: Establishing global mentoring networks in hubs like New York, Boston, San Francisco, and Tel Aviv; setting up hub-to-hub exchange programs (such as an MoU with Toronto); and proposing an EU-wide startup visa during the upcoming Dutch EU presidency.
- **Support Mechanisms**: Operating the "Orange Carpet" service to help foreign startups land, find housing, navigate the Chamber of Commerce, access capital, and test the European market.

### Technical Details & Infrastructure
Johannisse highlighted structural and infrastructure advantages underpinning the Dutch ecosystem:
- **Connectivity**: Cited by UPS as the world's most connected economy, offering rapid 24-hour physical transit access across Europe alongside top-tier broadband infrastructure.
- **Advanced Tech Clusters**: Research and commercial leadership in nanoelectronics, photonics, and quantum computing housed across Dutch technical universities.
- **Corporate Density & Unicorns**: Home to domestic multinationals and tech companies including Shell, Unilever, Philips, ASML (commanding 80% of the semiconductor lithography/chip machine market), TomTom, Adyen, and Booking.com, as well as European hubs for Tesla, Sonos, LinkedIn, and Netflix.

### Takeaways & Q&A
During the Q&A session, Johannisse outlined three observed categories of startup founders: globally minded proactive teams that scale rapidly; early-stage founders seeking mentorship and market fit; and newer entrants attracted by entrepreneurship culture. Addressing international expansion, Johannisse emphasized the "Orange Carpet" initiative, which assists smaller foreign companies (e.g., 30-person US teams) in entering and validating their products across the 500-million-consumer European market without prohibitive upfront capital investments.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- How to properly subbmit your idea to 500Startup Accelerator (Marvin Liao)
talks.teaser: Outlines how founders should pitch accelerators on story, market size, traction, team fit, and execution.
talks.summary:
A 500 Startups investment partner describes how applying to programs such as 500 Startups, Y Combinator, TechStars, and AngelPad mirrors raising seed investment. He stresses clarity of the idea, storytelling that convinces investors before product exists, sharp articulation of the customer pain, and evidence that the market is large enough for venture economics—not every business needs VC.

He walks through differentiation versus real competition, concise Q&A, hustle and urgency, customer segmentation, and why execution and traction matter more than hiding ideas. Mobile apps need meaningful download numbers; B2B needs paying customers, acquisition strategy, and unit economics. Balanced teams, cultural fit with the program, and a compelling long-term vision round out the pitch framework, along with picking accelerators deliberately rather than spraying applications.

Questions cover recruiting Eastern European founders, balancing networking with building product, technology-only focus, non-US markets, and how the San Francisco batch evolved toward companies that already launched, with revenue in some cases, because the program emphasizes distribution and sales.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- What startups should learn from Usain Bolt (Peter Torstensen)
talks.teaser: Compares elite sports development with startup building, stressing serial founders, assumption testing, and low-cost market experiments.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames entrepreneurship through sports: regional talent pipelines, individual excellence, and structured development systems. FC Barcelona’s youth academy is contrasted with big-transfer club models, arguing that scouting young talent and training systematically beats buying expensive players when mobility and methodology align. Parallel trends in startups include global mobility, cheaper paths to product-market fit, diverse funding, emerging methodologies such as lean startup, and access to accumulated knowledge online.

Success is modeled like athletics: innate ability, deliberate practice, quality of practice, and a demanding peer environment. Analysis of roughly 60,000 startups over twenty years shows first ventures near a fifty-fifty survival picture by year three, dip on later early attempts, then rise sharply by the fourth and fifth companies across survival, growth, and founder income. Startups are defined as searches for a scalable business model, not execution of a known one. Founders iterate hypotheses through experiments, seek hard evidence, and balance iteration speed, input quality, and converting feedback into action.

Accelerators are positioned as trainers for that loop, lowering experiment cost and focusing on assumptions, prioritization, experiment design, and honest interpretation of customer meetings. Learning must happen by doing, over long horizons akin to ten thousand hours in sport. Q&A covers Jedi-style mentorship and investing in serial entrepreneurs rather than single ventures.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- FireChat WIth Sarah Drinkwater (Paul Papadimitriou, Sarah Drinkwater)
talks.teaser: Shows how Google's London campus supports early-stage founders and what is planned for a new Warsaw site.
talks.summary:
Sarah Drinkwater, who leads Google's campus in London, explains what the space offers early-stage founders. It combines a co-working area run with partners, a cafe open to members, a device lab, a jobs board and a programme of events that anyone can host if the event is free and aimed at startups. She describes how the London site was shaped by founder feedback asking for community and co-working, and how partners such as local co-working operators and accelerators run parts of it.

The talk then turns to the planned Warsaw campus, which she expects to open by the end of the year once a partner and a manager are in place. She gives London's dense startup scene, Poland's technical talent and Polish founders getting international press as reasons for choosing the city, and says the campus is meant to serve the wider region. Google, she explains, treats the campuses as a long-term investment in entrepreneurship rather than a route to Google Ventures funding, and the London campus does not yet make money.

In audience questions she outlines Warsaw outreach, including working with existing meetups in Warsaw, Krakow and other Polish cities, free weekly mentoring sessions and a campus exchange for later-stage companies. She also says the London campus does not screen applicants, so anyone with an idea can become a member. The takeaway is that a campus is only as useful as the community that uses it.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- The “Series A” Crystal Ball (David Putts)
talks.teaser: Advice on Series A readiness, unit economics, team credibility, and pitfalls Polish startups face when targeting U.S. investors.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames Series A as a moving target: rounds that once looked like roughly two million dollars now often sit in the four-to-six million dollar range, while angels and more than two hundred micro VCs fund deals near the old Series A size and flood Silicon Valley with companies competing for the same institutional capital. Drawing on raising about thirty-five million dollars for a prior venture and later exits, plus work as an investor with a U.S. fund expanding toward Poland, he urges founders to imagine where they want to be in three or four years and what they could regret today.

He walks through a practical checklist—the “five Ts” spanning team, target market, technology, attraction, and unit economics—and stresses that U.S. investors writing multi-million-dollar checks expect a credible CEO and advisory halo, not only strong technologists. Traction mistakes include building a product on modest seed money without proving per-customer economics; he illustrates simple lifetime value versus acquisition cost math as the lever for scaling raises. Poland’s domestic scale is compared to a single U.S. state, so international revenue and sometimes a U.K. or other interim funding path matter before the big U.S. round.

Closing guidance covers prototyping and customer testing before large raises, trusted mentors beyond accelerators, investor chemistry, recovering from operational stumbles, shipping something buyers want, avoiding spend-before-pivot traps, and refusing early capital that grabs outsized control. A brief Q&A notes reasons to invest in Poland, including deeper technology and capital efficiency when funding is sized to reach “orbit.”

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- Diversity in Tech (Paulina Mazurek, Ela Madej)
talks.teaser: Explores gender diversity in tech through Polish startup data, interview bias, workplace culture, and early education for girls.
talks.summary:
The session is a wide-ranging panel on gender diversity in technology, anchored in the speakers’ experience as entrepreneurs, investors, and leaders at large Polish tech employers. They agree the problem is real even when individual careers feel sheltered: women report friction advancing without being treated as “the girl,” while headcount statistics can mask how few women hold developer roles versus product or scrum positions. They contrast Poland’s relatively visible women in startups with gaps in programs that actually help, and note rising urgency abroad as research ties late hiring of women to lasting cultural damage.

Discussion moves to causes and remedies that teams can act on. Interview loops stacked back-to-back favor men unless processes are adjusted; offices signal “boys’ club” culture through naming, decor, and jokes; even diversity-minded companies can stumble with pink lounges that reinforce stereotypes. Both speakers stress awareness, open feedback, bias training, and checking whether female colleagues would feel comfortable in the space. They touch hiring advantages for women engineers, investor filters when women undersell themselves, and richer minority meetup ecosystems in places like New York.

The closing segment focuses on education and pipelines: early praise that emphasizes looks over ability, declining women in engineering over decades, Google’s Mind the Gap outreach before girls drop math and science, and storytelling that links technology to purpose rather than abstract competition. Audience questions cover attracting women via capital and parents, teaching girls to code young, and role models for female founders. Takeaways emphasize fixing culture and education early, not treating diversity as a cosmetic late-stage hire.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- Girls Code Fun (Karolina Cikowska, Zuzanna Kobrzynski)
talks.teaser: A Warsaw nonprofit shows student Scratch games and explains why girls-only classes aim to keep young women in technology.
talks.summary:
The speakers introduce Girls Code Fun, a foundation they run in Warsaw to teach programming to girls. They are not professional developers; one studied psychology in the United States and Poland. She describes losing momentum in advanced-placement physics after feeling unwelcome as one of two girls in a large class, and recounts a close friend who left mechanical engineering for mathematics after similar isolation from peers and faculty.

After a short video of semester projects, children aged nine and eleven demonstrate Scratch games they built, including collection and maze-style mechanics. The cofounders report launching the organization in January, running about five courses, and graduating roughly fifty girls, with female mentors who study or have studied programming. They discuss expanding to preschoolers with screen-free logical exercises, Scratch Jr. for ages five to seven in mixed groups, and follow-on Scratch courses.

During questions they explain that girls-only sessions for ages eight and up use the same curriculum as mixed classes; the separation is meant to keep girls visible in the classroom and to signal to parents that coding is for daughters, not only sons. They cite early ages—around eight—as when girls often step back from STEM interest, and they ask the audience to spread word about enrollment and support.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- Silicon Valley beyond Tech. What else can you build (Tytus Cytowski )
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Bitspiration 2015- Silicon Valley beyond Tech. What else can you build (Tytus Cytowski ).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Bitspiration 2015 presentation, attorney and investor Tytus Cytowski presents an argument that Silicon Valley and San Francisco should not be seen exclusively as the domain of software engineers and technical founders. Drawing an analogy between contemporary Silicon Valley and Renaissance Florence—a capital of ideas, smart people, and capital—Cytowski urges non-technical European entrepreneurs to move to California. He emphasizes that major technology firms and venture capital ecosystems are in search of liberal arts perspectives, humanities backgrounds, and innovative ideas to disrupt massive, traditional non-technical sectors.

### Key Topics
Cytowski outlines several key trends driving the demand for non-technical talent and traditional industry disruption:
- **The Need for Non-Tech Talent:** Citing Oliver Samwer and Steve Jobs, Cytowski stresses that technical skills alone are insufficient to build large-scale consumer and internet businesses. Significant capital is trapped in non-technical assets and traditional business sectors awaiting transformation.
- **Disrupted Non-Tech Sectors:** The talk focuses on four specific non-technical industries ripe for innovation: education, fashion, food, and art.
- **Geography and Market Roles:** Cytowski contrasts the US East Coast and West Coast, arguing that Silicon Valley is optimal for pilot testing, early feedback, and product development, whereas the East Coast serves as a platform for broad distribution and marketing.

### Technical Details & Industry Examples
Cytowski examines four sectors undergoing technology-led evolution:
- **Education:** Traditional educational companies and universities are stagnating due to a lack of data, poor UX, and inadequate transparency. Contemporary ed-tech requires real-time interaction, project-based learning, mobile accessibility, and strong social experiences. Examples cited include Stanford, Google-funded Singularity University, GSV Capital (investors in General Assembly and Coursera), Lynda (acquired by LinkedIn for $1.5 billion), Khan Academy, Udacity, Udemy, and Platzi.
- **Fashion:** Despite Silicon Valley's informal reputation, high-margin fashion businesses are adopting personalization, mobile interfaces, and supply-chain efficiencies. Noted entities include Forerunner VC (investing in Warby Parker, Everlane, Bonobos), Stella & Dot, Chubbies, Pinterest as a distribution channel, and incumbent brands like Gap and Levi's struggling with digital transitions.
- **Food:** Shifting lifestyles and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors are transforming the food sector through kitchen appliances, delivery networks, and data aggregation. Examples highlighted include grocery delivery platform Instacart (reporting 20% weekly growth), Postmates (reporting 10x annual growth), Yelp, Fooducate, and sensor companies like 6SensorLabs (gluten detection) and Mark One.
- **Art:** Highlighting art's role in inspiring technology trends, Cytowski points to Instagram as a bridge between artists and collectors. Silicon Valley tech leaders (Marc Andreessen, Marissa Mayer, Larry Page's wife, Mark Zuckerberg via Facebook's artist-in-residence program) actively invest in art, while platforms like Vango build marketplaces connecting collectors with artists.

### Takeaways & Advice for Founders
During the presentation and subsequent Q&A, Cytowski provided tactical advice for European and Polish founders:
- **Relocation Mentality:** Success depends on showing up, proactive networking, and adopting a pay-it-forward mindset rather than fixating on the monetary costs of expansion.
- **Validation Process:** Founders seeking to establish a presence should first undertake a 'soft approach'—visiting Silicon Valley for feedback and mentorship rather than immediate aggressive fundraising, returning home to iterate on product revisions, and using those mentors for later VC introductions.
- **Market Entry Routes:** European companies can enter the US market through three primary paths: prolonged Series A preparation (typically 12–18 months), US accelerators (such as Y Combinator, 500 Startups, Techstars, or Dreamit), or early product-market validation and traction via crowdfunding campaigns like Kickstarter. Dev shops and software houses must specialize heavily (e.g., medical, IoT, or bio-health SaaS) to overcome global outsourcing competition.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- The Startup Slog (Beth Kolko)
talks.teaser: A founder recounts unglamorous lessons from years building affordable medical hardware for regulated global health markets.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the speaker’s path from literature and engineering academia—portable ultrasound research that could not move through university commercialization or incumbent device makers—into founding Shift Labs to close the gap between strong ideas and real-world impact. The middle is a candid tour of the slog: raising the first dollar took about three years while shipping hardware first; co-founders departed; fundraising brought rude rejections, shifting term sheets, and gendered harassment; sales meant vulnerable customer conversations and long cold outreach; FDA and CE paths were opaque despite bench testing rather than clinical trials; prototyping relied on beg-borrow networks, field trips, and intentional failures abroad; manufacturing survival came from in-house builds of hundreds of units and negotiating components instead of fully outsourcing relationships.

The talk closes on mission and product: avoiding U.S. hospital economics, targeting the much larger global care market, and shipping simple reconfigurations of existing tech rather than flashy R&D. The DripAssist drip-set flow meter replaces manual drop counting for most hand-run infusions worldwide. A veterinary distributor pivot funded early units; an Ebola-era hackathon prototype led to a same-day USAID application and later WHO-facing validation. Practitioners hear that regulated hardware rewards persistence, transparency about regulatory paperwork, distributor pattern-matching, daily incremental progress, and business models that make low-margin lifesaving devices viable.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015-Equity vs Debt in early stage investing
talks.teaser: A panel contrasts debt and equity for seed-stage startups and illustrates blended financing with Polish fund and agency loan examples.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with straightforward trade-offs: debt keeps founders from diluting ownership and can close faster, but repayments and interest strain cash flow and the balance sheet. Equity brings non-repayable capital and can strengthen the balance sheet for later borrowing, yet rounds take longer and carry heavy indirect costs such as diligence, legal work, and travel.

For companies without revenue, the panelists argue equity is usually the realistic path, while debt appears mainly where public or EU-backed programs exist or where projections show enough free cash flow to service the loan. One investor describes a flight-simulator startup that paired fund equity with a multi-year innovation loan from Poland’s enterprise development agency to fund prototyping and trade shows. Another case shows a manufacturing firm where the bank matched new equity with an equivalent loan once fixed assets were in place, doubling total capital for expansion.

They stress reading cash flow forecasts, industry type, and available collateral before choosing debt, and often recommend mixing equity with debt rather than either alone. The closing summary walks from friends-and-family seed money through angels, incubators, and VC toward exits or an IPO, and cautions that over-reliance on subsidies can distract from market-focused value.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- How Not to Get Fucked When Negotiating Your First Financing (Augie Rakow)
talks.teaser: The session equips startup founders to negotiate first financing by prioritizing money, control, and who elects the board.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by noting that even repeat founders face a structural disadvantage against investors who negotiate financings constantly and see long-term consequences of terms. Rather than memorizing dozens of clause types, the talk collapses everything into two buckets: money and control. Founders should lead the business conversation themselves, deferring unfamiliar legalese until rapport exists, and treat “standard” language as a warning sign.

On control, the emphasis is who elects board members, not merely who sits on the board. A three-person board with two founder-elected seats and one investor-elected seat preserves leverage better than schemes with an “independent” director (often tied to the investor’s network) or a CEO seat that founders do not control if leadership changes. The speaker describes expanding to three founder-elected seats after the Series A closes, before a Series B, so later rounds do not erode control.

On money, valuation is explained with a simple pre-money and post-money example, then the argument that private startup valuations are not directly negotiable like public markets. Founders should instead negotiate how much capital they raise and what percentage they sell, protecting equity across future rounds so incentives stay aligned.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- Technotopia (John Biggs)
talks.teaser: A journalist reframes dystopian fears through historical parallels and emerging medical, robotic, and AI innovations.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting his usual startup-focused material with a futurist talk tied to a book on techno-optimism. He polls the room on whether the next decades look inevitably bleak, then illustrates that anxiety with images of e-waste labor abroad, ship breaking, and compulsive screen use, while insisting the outcome is not fixed.

He argues that societies often mistake present crises for permanent collapse, using 1890s urban manure as a problem that cars erased overnight and citing William Gibson’s idea that people repurpose technology in unforeseen ways. He walks through early but real advances—electrical tongue stimulation restoring spatial sense for a blind wearer, mind-linked prosthetic arms, fecal microbiome transplants affecting weight and Crohn’s symptoms, Canadian legal-research automation, Uber’s pull on Carnegie Mellon roboticists, self-driving taxis, and a quadcopter steered by simulated bee cognition. Charts on conflict, emissions, and life expectancy support a cautious optimism despite environmental and social risks.

The close chains medieval meat-turning dogs and pendulum regulators to elaborate mechanical watches, treating comfort and curiosity as drivers of breakthroughs. He urges builders in the audience to keep shipping work that improves the future and asks contacts for other futurists contributing to the book.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- The Skype of Payments (Andrzej Horoszczak, Maciej Łuczak)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Bitspiration 2015- The Skype of Payments (Andrzej Horoszczak, Maciej Łuczak).
talks.summary:
### Overview
At Bitspiration 2015, the presenters introduced Billon, describing it as a peer-to-peer digital mobile cash platform and 'PayPal without the bank account.' Designed to operate across PCs, servers, tablets, smartphones, and POS devices, the system enables users to transact electronically without needing a traditional bank account or upfront contract. Billon works with financial institutions such as Plus Bank, eCard, and Citibank—having won the Citibank Mobile Challenge—by drastically cutting operational overhead and facilitating instant digital cash transfers directly between users.

### Key Topics
- **Unbanked and Underbanked Populations:** The speaker noted that approximately 2.5 billion people globally and nearly one-third of the population in Poland lack bank accounts, largely due to high bank maintenance costs (30–50 euros per dormant account annually) where 70% of accounts do not generate profit.
- **Direct Peer-to-Peer Settlement:** Rather than relying on traditional multi-party clearing networks and bank transfer rails, Billon executes direct peer-to-peer transfers of digital fiat currency without external intermediaries.
- **Regulatory Compliance:** Operates legally within European financial frameworks under the E-Money Directive, utilizing deferred KYC (Know Your Customer) and AML (Anti-Money Laundering) procedures for lower-tier activity.
- **Real-World Deployments:** Demonstrated case studies including market research agency IQS replacing cash and bank payouts for 100,000 questionnaire rewards per year, and live stream testing with Polish content creator 'Izak,' who collected over 2,500 PLN across 11,000 transactions within 12 hours from followers aged 13 to 34.

### Technical Details
- **Data and Content Encryption:** Traditional security models often encrypt only data access via passwords. Billon employs an advanced cryptosystem that directly encrypts the content of the data itself. Through this method, real money is represented and stored as secure electronic files across host devices.
- **Direct Device-to-Device Movement:** Transactions transfer the encrypted electronic cash files directly between user hardware (demonstrated over Wi-Fi between laptops) rather than executing ledger updates across intermediate banking databases.
- **Merchant Integration & Micro-transactions:** Features an open API supporting micropayments. Demonstrated use cases include paywall micro-charges (e.g., paying 20 cents for an article), embedding buy/pay links inside marketing emails or social media posts, and automatic data delivery alongside payment approvals.
- **Cash Mechanics & Irreversibility:** Because the system functions as digital cash, transactions settle instantly. Misdirected transfers cannot be arbitrarily reversed by an intermediary; users must request returns from recipients, though the user interface incorporates multi-step confirmation prompts to verify receiver login names.

### Takeaways
Billon provides banks and merchants with a low-cost, digital alternative to physical cash and cumbersome bank account infrastructures, reportedly reducing bank operating costs by up to 90%. By enabling software-based electronic money files that transfer instantly peer-to-peer without requiring bank accounts, it broadens participation in the digital economy and makes frictionless online micropayments viable.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- Trapdoor in the sun… waiting for start-ups in the investment process
talks.teaser: Walks through investment-stage pitfalls for Polish startups, from protecting pitched ideas to due diligence and earn-out deals.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how young Polish companies raise money and which investment mistakes to avoid. Drawing on years of legal work with firms in Krakow, the speaker urges founders to focus on a business that earns money and to know what the funding is for before approaching investors. Options range from seed funds and business angels at an early stage to private equity and venture capital later, with bonds as another route. Two local examples follow: a translation office that aimed for a NewConnect listing within five years and reached it, and a biotech company that listed on NewConnect and later moved to the main market.

The investment process has several pressure points. Polish law does not protect a bare idea, so founders should protect what they disclose through an NDA, public proof of their work, or a notary deposit. Due diligence is another critical stage: one company claimed valuable IP, but copyright had not been transferred in writing with the fields of use, and the investor withdrew. Agreements should also set dividend rights clearly, since an investor joining mid-year could otherwise claim profits from the previous year.

On deal structure, upfront payment can be paired with an earn-out tied to yearly KPIs, as in a marketing automation company where an investor took a 20 percent stake and extra payments depended on targets. The talk advises expanding abroad only once a product is ready to sell, and warns that foreign advisers can be four times more expensive. The takeaway is to seek legal advice before problems surface.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- Startup community around you (Jason Saltzman)
talks.teaser: A panel compares Poland's maturing startup scene with New York co-working culture and how local hubs vet members and spark collaboration.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a New York co-working founder describing Alley NYC's role helping early-stage companies and why he shifted the planned NYC ecosystem talk toward what is happening in Poland. Three Polish hub operators join him: a Gdańsk business incubator with acceleration and event programs, Warsaw's Reaktor co-working space, and a Kraków community-focused space aimed at helping startups raise funding.

Discussion covers how Polish entrepreneurship differs by city, the shift from clone-the-local-market plays toward global B2B products, and why founders still hesitate to leave private offices for open spaces. Panelists stress shared meals, informal networking, peer support through hard times, and access to each other's extended networks as core benefits. They contrast vetting styles—from customer referrals and commune-style acceptance to open membership with natural turnover—and describe waitlists, graduation after about three years, and simple online applications followed by short in-person conversations.

The New York operator closes on curating culture over décor, daily programming, diversity of members, day passes, and relationship-building rituals like lunches and happy hours. Audience questions touch on visiting the NYC space and how one founder bootstrapped community through influencers and personal relationships before the hub outgrew a single personality.

talks.title: PLNOG15 - Simplifying network deployment using Autonomic networking and Plug-and-play (Bjarnason)
talks.teaser: Shows how autonomic networking and plug-and-play can bring up network devices with little manual setup.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the cost of deploying network hardware. The speaker says setup can take up to about thirty percent of a budget and around thirty days before a device earns money, and that pre-configuration alone averages about seven hundred dollars per device. Roughly one device in ten arrives or fails in a way that needs a site visit. The proposed fix is autonomic networking, an idea from IBM in 2001, in which devices configure, protect and heal themselves once they are trusted.

The middle section explains the mechanics. A registrar checks each new device's product ID and serial number against an allow list and issues a domain certificate if it passes. Neighbouring devices then form encrypted tunnels over IPv6 link-local addresses, build a management network with the RPL routing protocol, and learn available services such as AAA automatically, so no usernames or server addresses need to be pre-configured. Where layer 2 reachability is missing, a Plug-and-Play server reached through DHCP options, DNS names or a vendor call-home can bootstrap the device, with a phone-based serial method offered as a fallback. The speaker reports CPU overhead of about three percent for the management network.

The closing part turns to security. Hardware tampering in transit and rogue cloned devices motivate a tamper-resistant chip that stores the serial number and a public key, enabling trusted boot and attestation before a device joins the network. The speaker said the work is being standardised through IETF drafts, released as open source, and that a prototype was expected to be shown at Cisco Live Berlin.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- Digital Health - More than just a hype?! (Min-Sung Sean Kim)
talks.teaser: An investor maps digital health trends, patient empowerment, and where venture capital sees prevention, diagnosis, and telemedicine growing.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that digital health is accelerating because medical knowledge and decision-making are shifting from clinicians alone toward informed patients, with smartphones and online communities as the main levers. The speaker describes a European venture fund that invests hundreds of thousands to several million euros per deal, has reviewed on the order of sixteen hundred startups, and reaches general practitioners and hospitals partly through a strategic tie-in with a large medical software vendor.

Using spending and prevention statistics, patient stories, and portfolio examples, the talk tours categories such as posture and mindfulness tools, pattern-based screening games, voice-linked mood and disease signals, diabetes companion apps, glucose-monitoring hardware ambitions, and Finnish telemedicine. A hands-on exercise with neighbors’ phones underscores how much personal and health data lives on those devices, alongside figures on search interest, venture funding, projected savings, and notable public listings.

The close acknowledges regulation, privacy, data protection, and closed electronic health record vendors, plus physician fatigue from too many apps. Integrations that pipe patient-generated data into doctors’ systems are offered as a practical path, and audience questions address rolling features through existing practice software, pharmaceutical business models tied to adherence, market differences the fund knows less about, German privacy hesitation, and scaling software before optional hardware.

talks.teaser: Explains how talent, culture, capital, and regulation underpin UK startup success and ongoing founder-government dialogue.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the speaker’s role at Coadec, described as the policy voice of UK startups, and the recent UK startup manifesto. The UK is portrayed as thriving: a large share of new European unicorns are British, with well-known fintech and consumer technology firms cited as examples.

The core structure follows talent, culture, capital, and regulatory environment, with repeated emphasis that political leadership cuts across all four. Examples include university and bootcamp talent pipelines, computing on the school curriculum, London’s developer density, regional clusters, rising venture and crowdfunding investment, SEIS and EIS tax incentives, and regulator engagement such as the FCA innovation hub and sharing-economy reviews. Events like Pitch at the Palace and trade missions illustrate how startups have moved into establishment venues.

The close notes limits: European scale still lags US giants, gender diversity in tech remains weak, and immigration or EU exit rhetoric worries the ecosystem. The speaker remains broadly optimistic while urging ongoing policy attention.
