talks.teaser: Outlines why Israel's startup scene grew, covering R&D spending, human capital, government support and venture capital.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a quick quiz on Israel's startup density and then surveys what the speaker sees as the ingredients behind the country's innovation record. Research spending is high, with the speaker citing close to five percent of GDP going to R&D and roughly 25 billion US dollars in tech exports each year. Human capital is central: a large engineering workforce, a wave of skilled immigrants from the former Soviet Union in the 1990s, and compulsory military service that the speaker linked to leadership and technical skills.

Government ministries coordinated support for R&D, technology transfer and trade, and laws and bilateral agreements were used to attract multinationals that set up R&D centres. The speaker described the venture capital sector as roughly thirty years old, with more than 5,000 startups, mostly in Tel Aviv, and said Israel ranks second in venture investment per capita after Silicon Valley. Around 60 Israeli companies are listed on NASDAQ, second only to China outside the US.

The closing section covered exits, with 99 companies exiting in 2014 for almost 7 billion US dollars. The speaker noted that competition for capital is now global, which makes it harder for local investors to stand out. The talk ended with a recommendation to read the book Startup Nation as a further guide to the factors discussed.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- Startup Germany, Startup Ecosystem in Germany (Markus Schranner)
talks.teaser: Explains how Germany's startup scene grew around Berlin and what funding and education gaps Startup Germany targets.
talks.summary:
The speaker, chairman of Startup Germany, opens by describing how attitudes toward internet companies in Germany have changed over the past few years. He points to Berlin as the country's leading startup hub, citing 2014 figures of about 1.1 billion euros in investment and two IPOs. He also estimates that around 39 percent of German startups are based in Berlin, with Munich, Cologne and Hamburg as the other main hotspots. He notes that most founders hold university degrees and that most startups are launched by teams rather than individuals.

He then turns to the obstacles. Germany has a large amount of money sitting in bank accounts, but older business owners are cautious and reluctant to invest in young companies, and the wider public still has little understanding of venture funding. He argues that a culture that values safe jobs discourages people from starting companies, and that high unemployment leaves many people without the skills to found one. He also describes how founders outside Berlin often struggle to find investors who see a market large enough for their ideas.

To respond, Startup Germany focuses on three areas: inspiration, education and support. The organisation runs workshops and online courses, funded by private and public sponsors, and organises Startup Weekend events in Germany since 2010. The speaker's main takeaway is an innovation circle in which successful founders later become mentors and investors for the next generation, spreading activity beyond a single hotspot.

talks.title: PLNOG15 - Automation of deployment and management of network devices (Oscar Jagodziński)
talks.teaser: A walkthrough shows how Ansible, Ralph CMDB, and a web portal automate deploying and managing thousands of multi-vendor switches.
talks.summary:
The speaker contrasts manual switch-and-router work—with console sessions, copied configs, and duplicate entries in authorization, logging, and monitoring—with the pace of virtual-machine provisioning in the data center. Copy-paste deployment scales poorly, hides bugs, and lacks formal review; operators wanted consistency via templates, safe self-service for simple port and VLAN tasks, and one-place pushes for changes across hundreds of devices.

The described stack centers on Ansible and Python over SSH, plus custom modules for resets, console-server provisioning, TACACS registration, and change logging. Ralph acts as an open-source CMDB for rack placement and IP data; a database caches live device state so portals stay fast. Facts, Jinja templates with conditionals and loops, and Git-stored playbooks mirror developer review workflows. A demo updates syslog and related settings on four multi-vendor switches through a web UI keyed on hostname and model.

New gear deploys from a short form—hostname, selected actions, run—including console-based bootstrap when management links are absent. Developers self-serve port changes with validation that blocks mistakes such as dual VLANs on access ports, while tickets capture before-and-after values. The speaker closes with possible next steps: full config in version control and richer parameter databases where hardware allows.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- "BUILDING STARTUP ECOSYSTEM" (G.Levin, W. Szadziński)
talks.teaser: A panel compares European startup hubs on founder-led communities, capital, unicorns, and practical roles for government.
talks.summary:
The session opens by asking whether entrepreneur leadership, long-term commitment, inclusiveness, and community activities—ideas linked to Brad Feld’s Boulder thesis—are the right foundation for startup ecosystems across Germany, Estonia, the UK, Israel, and Poland. Panelists contend that founders who have built companies must lead mentoring and connectivity, while governments can assist but cannot substitute for people who understand failure pressure. Several speakers emphasize linking entrepreneurs to capital, corporates, and peers, and caution that distant executives or generic advisors often miss what early-stage founders need.

Discussion moves to retaining companies in European hubs instead of losing them to Silicon Valley, with examples such as a London dating startup struggling to raise before relocating, Estonia’s outward scaling model, and Poland’s universities, NCBR capital on the order of 1 billion, and technology-transfer gaps. On money, the group argues capital exists globally but quality investors, portfolios, and experienced backers matter more than chasing funding first; UK measures mentioned include tax reliefs and a high-growth London Stock Exchange segment with eased listing rules.

The closing thread examines unicorns as signaling rather than daily goals, referencing Soundcloud in Berlin, Skype in Estonia, TransferWise founders’ frustration with sell-out questions, and preference for milestones like roughly 100 million dollar outcomes. A final audience question on local government draws answers that cities and mayors can champion clusters, yet durable communities start with founder-driven meetups and traction that institutions follow later.

talks.title: PLNOG15 - From FTTH to BTTH - Fiber Broadband Through the Home (Stijn Coppieters)
talks.teaser: Explains how operators extend FTTH bandwidth throughout the home with layered Wi-Fi, wired links, and multi-technology in-home connectivity.
talks.summary:
The presentation contrasts fiber-to-the-home uptake in Europe with continued triple-play packaging, and argues the market is shifting toward “infinite play,” where gigabit-class access must reach every device and room—not only the demarcation point in a meter cupboard or basement. Consumer expectations include reliable coverage, sufficient speed without new cabling, zero-touch setup, and operator-assured quality of service, while homes keep adding tablets, phones, and IoT gear on unpredictable wireless paths.

A scalable in-home connectivity layer is framed as the missing link between the ONT and applications. Wi-Fi standards from 802.11n through 802.11ac and ax are walked through with a “myth bust” on headline throughput versus real per-device rates, channel crowding, and range across rooms; beamforming and multi-user MIMO are described as partial improvements. Wired and hybrid options—Cat6, PLC, MoCA, HPNA, and trial plastic optical fiber—are compared on symmetry, reliability, and cost, leading to the conclusion that no single technology satisfies every demand.

For telecom operators, declining classic triple-play revenue motivates selling tangible value: extended wired and wireless infrastructure, home management apps, and add-ons such as security, data protection, and cloud gaming once bandwidth can be guaranteed in the home. The speaker closes by positioning their company’s gateways, extenders, and management portfolio within that end-to-end vision from FTTH to broadband through the home.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- Founder and President of European Young Innnovators Forum (Kumardev Chatterjee)
talks.teaser: Maps Horizon 2020 SME Instrument phases, eligibility, and how European startups tap equity-free EU grant funding.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the European Young Innovators Forum as a continent-wide network that links young entrepreneurs to EU decision-makers, mentors, and partners, and briefly describes outreach hubs and related programs. The main focus shifts to public innovation spending under Horizon 2020, especially the SME Instrument reserved for innovative products and processes rather than ordinary small businesses.

The presenter explains SME definition, prototype requirements, and three progressive funding phases: a six-month feasibility phase with a 50,000 euro lump sum, a two-year innovation phase from 500,000 up to 2.5 million euros in non-dilutive grants with large upfront payments, and a commercialization stage that expects private investment. He covers application expectations such as business plans and market rationale, sample budgets and deadlines, and reported results through 2015 including 1,110 supported startups, 336 million euros disbursed, and Phase 1 and Phase 2 winners in multiple countries.

The talk closes by urging founders to treat EU grants as one part of a funding mix. Audience questions address early-stage valuation effects of large grants, why some member states show stronger success rates, whether national origin affects awards, practical paths for small firms to begin, and whether founders should prepare Commission applications alone or with experienced help.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- From kickstarter to shipment ? IOt in real life (Kamil Adamczyk)
talks.teaser: Covers the wearable market, a light-therapy sleep mask, and the design and component delays behind its late shipment.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the growth of the wearable market, pointing to a sleep tracker that raised large Kickstarter and later funding rounds, and a fitness wearable that recently went public. The speaker argues that most wearables gather data without telling users what to change, and that results differ widely between devices. Sleep staging is also subjective: manual scoring by physicians can disagree by as much as sixty percent, so the team trained its analysis on averaged expert output instead of a single reader.

The device is a sleep mask that records brain activity through three electrodes on the forehead and analyses sleep stages automatically. It then sends light pulses through closed eyelids to influence melatonin release, a method based on research from Stanford Medical School last year. The speaker lists uses such as adjusting to jet lag, falling asleep faster, waking more easily and feeling more alert in the morning. Clinical trials were starting with a sleep foundation doctor and a clinic at Henry Ford Hospital in Detroit.

The project ran more than a year behind schedule. Electrodes must stay in contact with the skin for accurate data, and comfort decides whether people keep wearing the mask, so a nearly finished design was reworked after trial feedback. Component lead times, paid upfront, added further delay, and deliveries were planned for September. In questions, the speaker contrasted the approach with competing constant-light products, arguing that light timed to the most sensitive part of the night shifts the body clock more effectively. The main lesson is that first-time hardware makers should plan for comfort and long lead times.

talks.title: PLNOG15
talks.teaser: Explains how Group Encrypted Transport VPN uses key servers and group members to secure any-to-any traffic without tunnels.
talks.summary:
Two Cisco engineers present Group Encrypted Transport VPN, a tunnel-less design that encrypts any-to-any traffic across a private IP network such as MPLS. Key servers hold the policy, authenticate boundary devices called group members, and generate the keys. Members use a key encryption key to protect control traffic and a traffic encryption key to protect data, while header preservation keeps the original IP header so the provider's routing and QoS still work. Because no per-pair tunnels are built, the design avoids the N-squared tunnel growth of a full mesh.

The talk then covers GDOI, the original group key management protocol, which reuses IKEv1 phase one over UDP 848. Registration is a pull initiated by members, while rekeying is a push from the key server, sent either by multicast, which requires a multicast-enabled network, or by unicast with acknowledgements from each member. Redundant cooperative key servers elect a primary that keeps the others synchronised. The newer IKEv2-based method reduces registration from ten messages to four, moves fragmentation to the IKE layer, adds Suite B algorithms, and can read pre-shared keys from a RADIUS server. A migration path runs both protocols side by side, with a new gkm keyword replacing gdoi in the CLI.

The session closes with the product history: first released in 2006, group capacity was limited by the 64 KB key payload, which was optimised to reach 8,000 group members. The presenters described plans to scale further with IKEv2 fragmentation, and scheduled rekeying so key changes can happen off-peak.

The presentation opens by arguing that describing virtual reality in words is awkward, then puts an audience member in a headset for a brief demo intended to show instant transport to another place in Poland. The speaker contrasts traditional rectangular “window” media with VR’s aim to place the viewer inside a world, using a light analogy about perception and dimensions before calling VR a way to overcome limits of place, time, and cost.

Most of the middle is a business case. Cited forecasts describe the combined VR and augmented-reality market surging over the next several years, with entertainment—games, film, and theme-park-style experiences—as today’s main driver. The speaker frames use cases broadly: education, tourism, automotive, commerce, and medical training such as observing surgery safely. A recurring theme is that headsets may scale quickly while quality content remains the bottleneck, with game-engine production and premium 360 video called expensive compared to emerging camera ecosystems.

The close pitches next-generation VR media and a project positioned as an easier path to 360-degree video for YouTube, Facebook, and VR apps. In questions, the speaker says the gear may be rented or bought, with a goal of semi-professional 360 capture near DSLR pricing versus roughly ten thousand euros for some existing rigs, with availability targeted toward the beginning of the following year.

talks.summary: Natalia Burina tells Bitspiration how Parable, an Instagram-like app for short thoughts, evolved through user-driven design. She expected artists but attracted tweens and international teens, prompting quick safety-reporting features. Burina walks the creation, discover, and engagement pillars, hook-model retention loops, brand color choices, usability A/B tests, polish metrics that lifted comments, and device-by-device iOS QA that helped earn an Apple feature. She cites Ira Glass on the taste-versus-craft gap, Product Hunt discovery, and feedback channels from in-app rating prompts to social polls.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- Innovation in the Global Silicon Valley (Luben Pampoulov)
talks.teaser: Maps how venture capital, talent and ecosystems shape billion-dollar startups, with founders' rejection stories along the way.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a co-founder and partner at an investment firm focused on mid- and late-stage companies, opens with startup statistics: about 400,000 new US businesses a year, and eight in ten failing within 18 months. He argues that setbacks are normal and illustrates this with founders who were rejected, fired or went broke before succeeding, including Abraham Lincoln, Thomas Edison, Walt Disney and Steve Jobs. He also recounts how Christopher Columbus was turned down by several backers before one agreed to fund his voyage.

The middle section covers venture capital and markets. He compares long-term venture returns with private equity and the S&P 500, notes that IPOs have become far rarer and that companies now stay private longer, and describes so-called uber-corns, private firms valued above ten billion dollars. He presents an ecosystem that needs human capital, investment capital and entrepreneurs, pointing to Stanford, Berkeley and early Silicon Valley investors, and says places such as the Nordic countries, London, Paris and Warsaw are trying to replicate that model. He also notes how attitudes to risk shift from one city to another.

He closes with a formula for lasting change: a clear long-term mission, incentives tied to milestones, and inspiration. In the question session he argues that many failed bets are an expected part of early-stage investing, where investors back many companies expecting only a few to succeed. He sees Paris and Poland as places with talented people and growing enthusiasm for startups, though they are short on local investor capital.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- Golden Tips for Startup Marketing and Sales (Navid Nathoo)
talks.teaser: Fifteen marketing and five sales lessons from building an enterprise B2B startup, drawn from costly founder mistakes.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by framing the session for founders selling into enterprise B2B, citing roughly 1.2 million dollars worth of mistakes learned while building and selling AirPost, a cloud-oriented product aimed at curbing employee data use in tools such as Dropbox, Evernote, Salesforce, and Box. He stresses prerequisites before any go-to-market push: knowing customers’ top priorities, who pays, whether an MVP exists, and securing at least one paying reference customer.

The core of the talk separates marketing from sales. Marketing means qualified leads, built by teaching prospects about the problem, talking to paying users for messaging, focusing on one segment, matching channels to how buyers research (webinars, white papers, case studies), thought leadership, usage-based positioning, and measuring conversion—not raw lead volume. He warns against broad segmentation, competitor mimicry, paid ads as a default, marketing weak products, and overspending without fit.

Sales comes after marketing generates leads. Founders should close deals themselves before hiring; add sales staff only when the calendar is saturated, ideally two reps for comparison. A full feedback loop should tie campaigns, messages, channels, qualification, cycle length, and revenue. In questions, he names bulk purchased lead lists and weak email copy as a major waste, and recommends advisory-style outreach to decision makers with the right message and timing to shorten enterprise cycles.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- What Silicon Valley Investors Look For in Companies (Peter Szymanski)
talks.teaser: Explains what Silicon Valley investors look for in a startup, from pitch decks and traction to team and market.
talks.summary:
The talk, given at a Polish event, lays out the expectations American venture backers hold for early-stage companies. The speaker, who helps entrepreneurs raise funds, starts with pitch decks: investors spend about three minutes and 44 seconds on one, a typical deck runs about 19 slides, and team content appears in every deck. Vision and mission should come first, and funding rounds usually take far longer than founders expect.

The middle of the talk turns to markets and traction. The speaker argues that a weak market can sink a strong team, citing disk-drive makers overtaken by cloud storage and horse-and-carriage builders displaced by cars. Investors look for steady growth, with 30 percent per period as a rule of thumb, and they track retention and churn closely. Competitive position, a revenue model that charges users and a proven management team also matter. Founders are advised to check an investor's portfolio and speak with its management teams, since internal conflict is common in startups.

The closing section covers global trends that let companies outside Silicon Valley compete, including cheaper smartphones, bandwidth and computing, rising mobile usage in Poland, and an on-demand freelance economy that is drawing regulators. The speaker urges founders to find squandered resources to fix and to design products that give instant gratification. In the questions, the speaker suggests investors can still back companies whose technical teams stay abroad when a US sales presence exists. Founders should arrive with solid metrics.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- (Greg Pietruszynski) "Go Global" strategy from the day 1
talks.teaser: Maps a B2B founder path from Warsaw to global customers using content, influencers, Twitter outreach, cold email, and accelerators.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames global company building as two timed milestones: landing international paying customers, then attracting international investors. He argues B2B ventures need a market large enough to support roughly hundred-million-dollar annual revenue if a billion-dollar outcome is plausible, and that the strongest early validation is sales—his team sold lead-generation outcomes before shipping automation software.

Polish traction alone failed to impress foreign investors, so the talk emphasizes credibility tactics abroad: a small blog, blunt outreach to marketing influencers, guest posts on established sites, and creative Twitter networking (including engaging people an expert followed). Early wins produced case studies, outbound Twitter conversations, and high-volume cold mail with persistence. Delivery quality turned buyers into referrers.

With revenue and many customers, they joined an accelerator—chiefly 500 Startups—for Silicon Valley relationships and US investor legitimacy despite being Poland-based. A closing Q&A covers building targeted prospect lists via public data and crawlers, and iterating subject lines and copy rather than perfecting the first message.

talks.teaser: The session walks through turning a nightly bike-light annoyance into a hardware product, from soldered prototypes to industrial design.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by contrasting how software ideas move from concept to MVP with architecture, UX, and quick prototyping against hardware, where electrical, mechanical, and industrial design dominate and failure modes multiply. He describes riding a small scooter in Los Angeles without lights, borrowing cheap handlebar LEDs, and growing tired of turning each light on and off separately in the dark.

To validate synchronized control, he hand-soldered garage-door-style transmitters and receivers into the lights so one button toggled both. A cyclist friend with four separate lights asked for the same fix, and a shop test with a messy first unit led to a request for five hundred units. The middle of the talk covers IoT power asymmetry when two small batteries must keep a receiver listening, iterative industrial design through remote designers, low- versus high-end 3D prints, and a one-handed magnetic mount prototype. Branding for “Blink” ties Bluetooth linking to an ambigram logo negotiated via a small Kickstarter revenue share instead of a large commercial fee.

He closes by arguing software-minded founders can reuse MVP thinking if they unlearn pure UI focus, outsource specialists affordably, prototype physically, and use crowdfunding creatively to fund design talent. Audience questions touch on limited time on the side project, factory scaling, mold costs, and the lack of hardware beta channels comparable to mobile app test distribution.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- (Mike Rosenthal) OK Go and the 21st Century Music Industry
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Bitspiration 2015- (Mike Rosenthal) OK Go and the 21st Century Music Industry.
talks.summary:
NOTE: This is NOT a cybersecurity conference talk. This is a music industry strategy presentation about OK Go's business model transformation.

Mike Rosenthal, who worked with American rock band OK Go for six years, discusses the band's evolution from Capitol Records artist (signed 2001, first album 2002) to independent success amid the 21st-century music industry collapse. Digitization of content and distribution eliminated the scarcity and manufacturing costs that justified record label infrastructure, while simultaneously creating an 'attention crisis' for advertisers.

OK Go's Strategic Innovation: The band realized they possessed content millions wanted to see, while brands desperately needed audience access. They pioneered a new value exchange where the band creates and distributes premium music videos with complete creative control, and brands fund productions through sponsorships (State Farm Insurance, Chevy, Honda) to reach engaged viewers. This model funded multiple album cycles without traditional album sales.

Key Inflection Point: The band's second-album music video was rejected by Capitol Records executives as 'the dumbest thing we've ever seen,' but became one of the most-viewed videos of its era and won a Grammy when released independently online. After three years of touring, they realized Capitol could not convert viral success into physical sales. Released from their contract in 2009, they implemented their sponsorship model.

Modern Revenue Streams: Rosenthal identifies digital streaming (currently minimal but growing via Spotify, Apple Music), touring and VIP experiences, merchandise, crowdfunding (Kickstarter), and brand partnerships. Even niche bands can leverage sponsorships, which Rosenthal identifies as a high-growth industry area.

Core Principle: Artists must control their direct fan relationship and build the largest possible fan base, as this relationship is now the modern equivalent of owning distribution infrastructure. Transparency with fans about sponsorships is essential to maintain authenticity.

talks.title: Bitspirations 2015- Alternative Ways of Reaching the Audience: TV, ADS, GAMES
talks.teaser: Shows how TV placements, commercials and game soundtracks can build a musician's audience, drawing on real placement stories.
talks.summary:
This panel looked at older media routes for getting music heard, such as TV, advertising and video games, as a counterpart to the social media tactics covered earlier in the day. A composer and producer described a song she wrote that was picked for a magazine commercial, which brought messages from friends and sparked interest in her work. A representative from a production music company explained how ready-made tracks from libraries get placed in film, TV and ads, and how emerging artists can take part without signing with a major label.

Concrete cases followed. One Scandinavian artist's songs were featured in a Polish TV series, and the company then pitched an interview with the broadcaster and a live show in Warsaw, which drew attention back home in Scandinavia. A publisher described signing a Polish band with growing buzz and then placing its songs in commercials. A band's track used in a video game soundtrack from a Polish studio also led to more gigs. In another example, an instrumental piece played in a scene from a popular TV series was shared on the show's fan page, which had more than 600,000 followers, and drew more than 200,000 hits within two days.

The panelists' advice was to send links rather than large attachments, stay persistent, and consult music consultants who work with TV productions. They stressed that a placement is a starting point, so artists should move listeners from social platforms to streaming, downloads, merchandise and concerts. One artist also called for managers who could handle social media so musicians can focus on making music.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015- (Thamina Watson) "U.S Visa Options for Startup Founders"
talks.teaser: Maps U.S. visa categories for foreign founders, from short business visits through work and investment visas to green-card routes.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the reality that the United States still lacks a dedicated startup visa, and that founders must navigate a patchwork of existing categories instead. For short trips such as investor meetings, a B-1/B-2 visitor visa hinges on proving non-immigrant intent and strong ties to a home country—especially relevant where ESTA waiver access does not apply.

The core of the session walks through employment and investment routes: L-1 intracompany transfer for managers and founders with at least a year abroad in the qualifying entity; E-1/E-2 treaty trader and investor visas with substantial investment, source-of-funds documentation, and majority ownership concerns; the H-1B lottery with degree, prevailing wage, employer control, and difficult self-employed startup paths; and the O-1 for founders with documented extraordinary achievement. J-1 and H-3 appear as shorter training or accelerator bridges toward other statuses.

On the permanent side, the talk explains PERM labor certification limits for self-owned roles, entrepreneur national interest waiver, EB-1 paths linked to O-1 and L-1, and EB-5 investment thresholds. It closes with Obama-era executive actions: entrepreneurial parole as a hoped-for alternative, H-4 work authorization for certain spouses, and earlier filing of green-card paperwork with interim work permits. Practitioners should treat visa choice as a sequence—eligibility, documentation, and long-term residency goals—not a single application.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015 - Nothing comes sailing by itself (M. Kusznierewicz, P. Papadimitriou)
talks.teaser: An Olympic sailor recounts launching a connected photo-frame venture, winning a carrier partnership, and leading a dispersed product team.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with a sailing career spanning multiple Olympic Games, emphasizing written lessons, long-term goals, and systematic preparation after painful near-misses. The speaker then pivots to a personal problem: sharing smartphone photos with relatives who lack modern computers or phones, which sparked the idea for a free networked picture frame instead of costly subscription hardware.

He explains how a dinner with an orthopedic doctor led to introductions with Polish hardware veterans, a two-day founding retreat, and partnership with GoClever for roughly nine million zlotys of prototype and production funding. The team deliberately manufactured buzz at a GoClever press event, drawing national media and an inbound approach from T-Mobile’s agency, which led to an NDA, joint development, retail distribution, and a Lewandowski advertising campaign. Usage figures cited include more than sixteen thousand connected devices and over four hundred seventy-three thousand pictures transferred since launch, with transfer-only hosting and no long-term storage on their servers.

Closing themes cover single accountable leadership, motivating remote teammates through transparency, annual product iteration toward video and larger screens, and possible smart-home or telemedicine directions while seeking partners with sector expertise. The personal credo is to define explicit goals, plan the route, and work only with people who know their own destination.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - MIMOSAWRITERROUTER - Abusing EPC on Cisco Router. (Joaquim Espinhara, Rafael Silva)
talks.teaser: Abuses Cisco embedded packet capture to export router traffic remotely and automate intelligence gathering across many devices.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that Cisco’s Embedded Packet Capture (EPC) feature—meant for legitimate network troubleshooting—can be turned into a practical post-exploitation channel when an attacker already holds privileged access to a router. The speakers stress that their work is not a zero-day against Cisco IOS; instead it automates configuration of capture buffers, capture points, and remote export of pcaps so penetration testers and threat-intelligence teams can harvest traffic at scale without building a separate tap infrastructure.

They introduce the MIMOSA framework as a command-line orchestration layer backed by MongoDB, showing how linear versus circular buffers affect performance and data loss during long captures. Demos walk through exporting captures via protocols such as FTP and HTTPS to a collector, then mining the results with tools like Bro, VirusTotal lookups on DNS, and dashboards fed from Elasticsearch. Customer case studies include cleartext credentials, HTTP traffic useful for application testing, botnet and Shellshock activity, banking malware hosted on client networks, and file extraction from captured traffic.

Practitioners should treat EPC remote export as a durable sniffing primitive: ACLs may block it, but anyone with enable on the box can typically re-enable the feature. Defenders need strong router credentials, monitoring of EPC configuration changes, and awareness that a single compromised gateway can yield terabytes of internal traffic over time. The speakers release MIMOSA as open source and outline future support for additional vendors, brute-force helpers, and richer analytics views.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - Defensive Time-Out
talks.teaser: Explores how time, clocks and NTP shape defensive security, from physics definitions to Kerberos and leap-second failures.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames defensive work as a repeating loop, using metaphors from basketball, Groundhog Day and film to argue that defenders get stuck in routine and abstraction. The talk then asks what time means for security, covering timestamps, uptime, boot time and password expiry, along with physics views of time from Newton to relativity.

The middle section turns to practical timekeeping. Clocks are traced from sundials to atomic standards, and UTC's leap seconds are explained. Network Time Protocol is presented as the main way distributed systems keep time, with its history back to David Mills's work in 1985 and a 2036 rollover problem. Concrete failures include Windows NTP not synchronising beyond a configured time gap and Kerberos breaking when clock skew passes five minutes by default. A 13-hour cloud outage tied to a leap-second problem, described in a post-mortem, illustrates a single point of failure, and timing side-channel attacks are covered with their code-level fixes.

The closing part argues that time should be treated as a risk to assess. Listeners are urged to check whether their organisation uses NTP for encryption or authentication, and to build deep knowledge in their own specialty while admitting what they do not know.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - when something overflowing... (Peter Hlavaty)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in CONFidence2015 - when something overflowing... (Peter Hlavaty).
talks.summary:
## Overview
Peter Hlavaty presents kernel exploitation techniques through analysis of a real Android vulnerability discovered in Trinity/Fazer devices. The vulnerability exists in a spice function related to pipe buffer handling and was originally known from 2012 but remained applicable to current market phones. Triggering required two simple steps: resizing pipe buffer sizes and calling the spice function with manipulated parameters that caused out-of-bounds access when setting buffer indices.

## Key Topics
**Vulnerability Mechanics**: The pipe buffer overflow manifests differently depending on buffer size. Small sizes trigger stack allocation and fast path execution, while large sizes cause kernel malloc allocation from the heap. Each path presents different exploitation constraints and opportunities.

**Stack vs. Heap Exploitation**: Stack-based overflow is simpler because the kernel contains no stack canaries, allowing direct return pointer corruption. However, each Android ROM has different memory layouts due to compilation differences, requiring custom exploitation for each variant. Heap-based overflow is more complex but more reliable, involving careful manipulation of slab allocations and kernel object placement.

**KASLR and Pointer Constraints**: The vulnerability cannot overflow with arbitrary data—only with kernel pointers and page sizes in fixed patterns. This constraint requires identifying specific kernel data structures to target. The speaker discovered that overflow from multiple buffers simultaneously adds complexity, as corrupted memory affects unrelated kernel objects.

**Memory Spraying Techniques**: The speaker introduces post-bank techniques using pipe splicing for efficient kernel memory spraying. Rather than traditional approaches, they exploit the pipe splice function to write data repeatedly into pipes, controlling where kernel memory allocations land. This involves creating about 5-12 pipes, writing data repeatedly for several seconds, and filling kernel address space with controlled patterns—a lightweight yet effective approach compared to traditional pool spraying on 64-bit systems.

**Slab Allocation Strategy**: Exploiting involves creating many kernel objects of identical size to populate specific slab caches, freeing selected objects, and triggering overflow when new allocations land in freed spaces. The challenge is that kernel caches are organized by size and object type, requiring careful coordination to place exploitable structures adjacent to the overflow target.

## Technical Details
The exploit requires handling multiple complex stages: initial vulnerability trigger, reliable memory layout control through spraying, target structure placement, and controlled overflow execution. On 64-bit platforms with execution prevention enabled, the speaker notes that finding suitable targets (like TTY buffer structures with function pointers) requires extensive analysis. One limitation encountered was magic value checks in some structures—overwriting these triggers panic, making the target unsuitable unless the magic value can be preserved within the overflow constraints.

## Takeaways
Modern kernel exploitation is primarily an engineering discipline requiring deep OS internals knowledge, multi-stage attack chains, and platform-specific adaptation. Proactive vulnerability patching is essential for companies, as successful kernel exploits typically achieve full system compromise. The speaker's team emphasizes responsible disclosure, knowledge sharing through security conferences and CTF competitions, and supporting the research community. They argue that understanding these techniques is crucial for defensive security and that security research, while challenging, is vital for protecting systems against both known and future vulnerabilities.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - Bypassing malware detection mechanisms (Jakub Kaluzny, Mateusz Olejarka)
talks.teaser: Explains how browser-based anti-malware scripts in online banking can be evaded through weak obfuscation and exposed signatures.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at anti-malware solutions that banks run inside the browser to spot banking trojans on customers' machines. The presenters, both penetration testers who mostly assess financial web and mobile applications, explain how this malware alters banking pages through web injects, and why the detection scripts that sit alongside them are worth testing. They compared network traffic from a clean machine with one infected by the malware, then read the JavaScript that the server delivered.

On an infected machine, the detection script made an extra HTTP request that a clean machine did not, so blocking or altering that single request was enough to hide the infection. Some vendors sent a red-light alert that included the user's login, time and behaviour, and the presenters could change that report so that an infected user appeared clean while a different user was flagged. In one case, logging in fast enough meant the script had not loaded yet, so no alert was raised. Signatures were checked either on the server, using regular expressions against rendered HTML, or on the client, by looking for named functions and strings. The result array could also be forged. Obfuscation was often weak, with hex or base64 strings that were easy to spot.

The presenters advised buyers to ask how detection works, request a live demo on their own infrastructure, and test for false positives against a clean web application. They stressed that detection is only one layer, that the speed of deploying new signatures matters most, and that in-house understanding helps teams verify vendor claims. They said all vulnerable vendors were reported through responsible disclosure.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - SCADA and mobile (Alexander Bolshev, Ivan Iushkevich)
talks.teaser: See how mobile app flaws could expose industrial systems and mislead the people monitoring them.
talks.summary: The speakers describe three types of mobile applications used with industrial control systems: local control-room tools, clients that read data from middle or upper system layers, and remote clients that monitor or control processes. They explain their review and testing methods, including checklist-based analysis, reverse engineering, and fuzzing, then discuss weaknesses they found across about 20 Android applications. Examples show how altered traffic or project files could mislead operators or disrupt monitoring; attendees learn why mobile access can create risks for industrial processes.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - Security challenges in an ever-changing world (Zoltan Bakos)
talks.teaser: Explains a transparent proxy appliance that records and replays privileged sessions, and why trust must be set carefully.
talks.summary:
The speaker, from a Hungarian log management vendor, starts from the problem that a fence around important servers no longer works. Computers now sit in the cloud, and third-party administrators connect to them, so keeping infrastructure secure is an ongoing task. Threats range from a bored script user to outsourced staff and paid attackers, and the administrator is the one held responsible when something goes wrong.

The core of the talk is a privileged activity monitoring appliance that works as a transparent proxy between client and server. It takes the connection, records it, and forwards it re-encrypted in both directions. In a live demo, an RDP session was opened to a normal Windows server through the appliance, some text was typed, and the session was then found by searching the recordings for a keyword and replayed in a browser. The speaker also said the appliance can protect SSH connections and that the device itself is hardened against attack.

The closing argument is about trust. Staff and the vendor get a measured level of trust, outsiders get healthy mistrust backed by contracts, and full auditing and recording let administrators loosen technical control while keeping visibility, much like a flight data recorder. The takeaways were to stay a step ahead of attackers, surround yourself with reliable people, question vendors about whether they understand your needs, and choose tools that support a secure infrastructure.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - Polska cyber armia ochotnikow (Gatis GRAUDIŅŠ)
talks.teaser: Explains Latvia's volunteer cyber defense unit, its recruitment, training, and backup role when civilian CERT capacity runs out.
talks.summary:
The presenter introduces himself as commander of Latvia's Cyber Defense Unit within the National Guard, a militarized volunteer reserve distinct from ordinary reserve forces that are only called in emergencies. He contrasts cyber crises with physical disasters: a country cannot simply "close" and redirect citizens elsewhere, so the state needs a skilled reserve when CERT LV, the army, and other agencies exhaust their people and expertise.

The talk traces how Estonia's 2007 DDoS events and Georgia in 2008 motivated years of political work, formal approval in 2013, and full establishment by early 2014. The unit stays small on paper but draws far more applicants than its initial 98 slots. Recruitment uses public contact channels, declared-capability questionnaires, internal exercises, and mandatory national, EU, and NATO security clearances. Personnel form a mixed pool of deep experts, capable sysadmins, and eager learners; tasks are assembled from a capability catalog rather than fixed sections. Training stresses broad baseline skills plus depth in one or two areas, heavy participation in alliance exercises, peer lectures inside the unit, and sanitized real incidents passed from CERT LV for collective analysis.

Audience questions probe centralized logging, bug bounties, wartime activation, citizenship, clearance rejections, whether volunteers weaken private-sector incentives, and offensive versus defensive mandates. Answers stress invitation-only support for critical infrastructure after CERT LV is overwhelmed, legislative limits on scope, growing non-technical roles, two-digit incident engagements last year, classified wartime details, and partnerships with Estonia, Michigan National Guard components, and regional allies—including outreach to Polish talent at the conference.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - High Availability of Onet Sites and Services (Rafal Chyzy)
talks.teaser: Explains how a major Polish media group classifies services, runs redundant data centers, and tests quarterly failover to AWS.
talks.summary:
A chief security officer describes how Group Onet, a large Polish electronic media business, keeps news, mail, video, and advertising platforms available despite cyber attacks, DDoS pressure, and strict domestic privacy rules. He outlines operational scale—billions of monthly page views, very high mail throughput, large parallel video capacity, petabyte-scale processing, and two Kraków data centers with substantial IT power—and explains why availability, integrity, and confidentiality must be prioritized differently across free and paid offerings.

The organization labels sites and services with airline-inspired availability tiers and separate integrity or confidentiality grades, then adds business-continuity classes that reflect cost and recovery expectations. Risk review ranked IT failure as the most likely severe driver, followed by people and external supply dependencies such as power, fuel, and connectivity. Mitigations include active-active style separation across primary and secondary facilities, a private cloud migration path, continuous replication, and AWS as a standby venue that already carries a small share of production traffic while scaling under full quarterly exercises.

Practitioners hear how crisis mode is governed, how SMS, backup corporate mail, Skype coordination, and an external status portal keep communications alive when primary systems fail, and how segregation of duties limits insider abuse. The speaker stresses real testing over paper drills, notes multi-year rollout effort and hourly-scale cloud cutover targets, and closes by urging personal continuity planning for staff and families.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - The Top 10 Web Hacks of 2014 (Matt Johansen, Johnathan Kuskos)
talks.teaser: Walks through the ten most-voted web hacking techniques of 2014, from covert timing channels to Heartbleed.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how the annual list of top web hacks is assembled. Community members submit new web attack research, the community votes a shortlist of about fifteen, and a panel of application security experts sets the final top ten and their order. Past lists were dominated by encryption attacks, and Heartbleed took the top spot for 2014.

The lower entries include a covert timing channel built on HTTP cache headers, a denial of service that appeared to come from Facebook, a chain of three remote code execution CVEs in an Apache framework caused by incomplete fixes, and a Google two-factor bypass in which attackers had phone carriers forward SMS codes. The deep dive starts with Misfortune Cookie, where malformed cookies sent to an old RomPager router firmware bypassed authentication. Rosetta Flash converts binary SWF files into alphanumeric content to abuse JSONP endpoints, POODLE uses an SSLv3 downgrade to recover data one byte at a time, and Shellshock reaches bash through a single request to CGI scripts.

Heartbleed, the last entry, lets an attacker read up to 64 kilobytes of server memory per malformed heartbeat request, potentially exposing keys and session data. The takeaways are that encryption research remains highly regarded, that creative reuse of long-lived bugs matters, and that web security still drives most major breach headlines. Practitioners should disable SSLv3 on clients and servers, avoid JSONP on sensitive domains, and make sure incomplete patches are caught.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - pgp you said? a crypto rant with aluc. (Aluc Dracul)
talks.teaser: Surveys broken public-key deployments, Internet-wide key collection, and fragile CA and anonymity trust assumptions.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames public-key cryptography as the everyday answer to mass surveillance, then walks through Diffie–Hellman and RSA at a level meant for listeners who already know the basics. Attack options are grouped into brute force, analytics, social engineering, and implementation mistakes; factoring and published cost estimates show why short RSA moduli are risky, while proper key sizes mainly push attackers toward the other classes.

The middle of the session is hands-on analytics: harvesting certificates and SSH keys with tools such as ZMap, operating a PGP keyserver, and mining Bitcoin data for weak material. Findings include repeated keys, shared prime factors recovered quickly with GCD, DSA signatures broken when nonces repeat, and weak entropy on embedded gear—illustrated with Fritz!Box routers booting at identical Unix times. Industrial firewalls and copied default keys appear as recurring weak points.

The closing shift is trust: browsers trusting hundreds of certificate authorities, Apache deployments stripping certificate passwords, Tor’s exposure to timing correlation, and the gap between hoping protocols work and verifying counterparts first. The speaker argues implementation leaks and misplaced trust undermine encryption even when algorithms look sound, and points to forthcoming verify-before-trust work without fully detailing it.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - DTrace + OS X = Fun (Andrzej Dyjak)
talks.teaser: Walks through DTrace dynamic instrumentation on OS X, covering its D language, one-liners, and scripts for vulnerability analysis.
talks.summary:
DTrace is a dynamic instrumentation framework that started on Solaris in 2005 and later reached BSD systems and OS X. Its design goals were system stability and no measurable overhead for applications that are not being traced. To meet those goals, the D language leaves out loops and conditionals. The speaker explains the structure of a D script: a provider, probes such as pid and fbt, a predicate that acts as the only if-statement, and actions. He also covers the C-like syntax, variable scoping, built-in variables for processes and threads, and the difference between copyin and copyout.

The demonstrations move from one-liners to full scripts. Examples count the system calls a process makes, measure how many bytes a read call requests, and trace posix_spawn instead of execve, because Apple's own code paths can hide behaviour that the latter would miss. Larger scripts track file descriptors and memory-mapped input, and the speaker found that memory which is mapped but not yet touched cannot be dumped when mmap returns. Another script logs memory allocation calls in a format that can be piped into a visualizer. He also outlines an idea for measuring how reliable a heap exploit is by probing allocation functions, and a heat tracing approach that records which functions run for a given input.

The talk closes with safety notes. Copyin is safe, but copyout and actions such as system, stop, and panic are destructive, require an explicit pragma, and need root. The speaker mentions earlier work, a 2008 Black Hat framework and a 2013 Infiltrate talk, and notes that SystemTap offers similar capabilities on Linux. In Q&A he said that processes which deny debugger attachment may not be traceable through the pid provider, and that he planned to verify this.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - Who put the backdoor in my modem? (Ewerson (Crash) Guimaraes)
talks.teaser: Investigates a Brazilian ISP modem whose configuration hides plain-text backdoors and weak vendor accountability.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a personal investigation into a GVG home modem used in Brazil, where industry news already documents backdoors in consumer routers and similar CPE. Rather than treating hidden access as novel, the speaker focuses on what changes when the backdoor is embarrassingly obvious: exporting the device configuration reveals plaintext backdoor and priority flags per account, and flipping those fields after re-importing the file grants privileged use without cryptography or encoding standing in the way.

The middle of the talk maps an opaque supply chain—Anatel certification, firms such as Observer Telecom and Xingzhuang, firmware strings mentioning TP-Link, Haier Tech on the board, and Wi‑Fi passwords derived from MAC addresses and serial numbers. Logging in through the backdoor exposes telnet, expanded administrative commands, cleartext user lists, and further secrets in memory dumps. Internet-wide exposure search finds thousands of similar units online; the speaker demonstrates reaching a stranger’s device and changing its settings remotely.

The closing message is operational: audit your own CPE, try to learn who actually built and supports it, patch or disable the backdoor via configuration when possible, prefer open firmware where supported, and accept that attribution across vendors, integrators, and overseas partners may stay unanswered. The burned test unit underscores how untrustworthy such hardware can be for everyday traffic.

talks.title: CONFidence2015 - The Modern Wired Terrorist Mind: Spy versus Bot versus Spy (Richard Thieme)
talks.teaser: Examines how fiction, propaganda and influence operations shape the global information battlefield security practitioners must navigate.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames post–World War II security as a Möbius strip: espionage, disinformation, and commerce interleave until inside and outside, truth and cover, are hard to separate. Drawing on decades advising intelligence and law-enforcement communities, the speaker argues that in the national security environment, fiction and entertainment often carry what direct disclosure cannot, and cites examples from his own stories that later echoed public surveillance debates.

The core develops through geopolitical and corporate power shifting beyond classic nation-states, porous identities online, and four modes of attack bridging physical and digital realms. Russian and ISIS messaging, NATO monitor burnout, paid persona blogging, corporate “attack” decoy sites, and an anecdote that vigilante takedowns of extremist sites may be thwarted to preserve monitoring—all illustrate that perception management, not raw hacking alone, sustains advanced persistent campaigns. Historical threads tie Cold War brainwashing panics, interrogation policy blowback, and CIA-planted press narratives to modern reflexive control and ridicule as denial weapons.

Practitioners are urged to treat the social mind as the decisive terrain: question premises, follow incentives, and resist assimilating the propaganda they study. Operational security begins with honest definitions of identity, threat, and success—not vendor promises of perfect defense.

talks.title: CONFidence2015
talks.teaser: Shows how PHP stream wrappers and unsafe include paths leak source and enable remote code execution in CTF and production audits.
talks.summary:
The presentation starts from a simple premise—opening a file should be a thin call to the operating system—and contrasts that with PHP’s stream wrappers, which can fetch HTTP resources, treat zlib and ZIP entries as ordinary files, and pipe reads through arbitrary filters on what still looks like a single open call.

The security story centers on include and require, which load a path and execute its contents as PHP. When attackers influence that path, wrappers become weapons. A Coldgate qualifier challenge used php://filter with base64 encoding to include index.php without executing it, recovering full application source. In a customer image-hosting audit, a boolean logic bug in scheme/host checks plus phar:// parsing let an attacker normalize a crafted path and read index.php as plain data despite “valid” URL rules. Another Coldgate step chained JPEG-plus-ZIP polyglots with a zip wrapper include to run uploaded shell code after source disclosure.

The closing argument treats include as evaluation, not mere loading: block user-controlled paths entirely rather than relying on brittle deny lists or options like allow_url_fopen as an afterthought.

talks.title: CONFidence2015
talks.teaser: Walks through the worst CTF challenges the speaker's team met since 2013, and how the team scored each one.
talks.summary:
This lighthearted talk walks through the worst capture-the-flag challenges the speaker's team has encountered since 2013. Each challenge receives a penalty score, with points deducted for tedious work, missing clarifications, unsolvable problems and solutions that felt trivial. The opening examples cover QR codes that were cut into pieces, photocopied and had to be repainted by hand, a process that could take hours.

The middle of the talk covers several cases in turn. A 2015 geolocation challenge gave nine photos that had to be matched to Street View locations, but street names at road crossings depended on the direction a player approached from, and key information was only given later in the IRC channel. A hex-to-decimal password puzzle was solved with a one-liner, and a graph theory task turned out to be an open research problem. A 2013 exploitation challenge required proxies in seven countries, including the Netherlands Antilles, and was really a networking task involving a Windows Vista machine posing as Internet Explorer 7 and an obscure file-protocol behaviour.

The closing part takes audience questions, including a photo-based puzzle from another contest where the answer was a city in Utah. The practical takeaways are to test that challenges are solvable, write complete descriptions, avoid tasks that are only tedious manual work, and make sure the skill being tested is the one the challenge claims to test.

talks.teaser: N.A.P.A.L.M. support (Elisa Jasinska) investigates PLNOG15.
talks.summary:
The speakers, who work in network automation, presented NAPALM, an open-source Python library that gives one API for configuring devices from several router vendors. Its operations follow a Juniper-style workflow: load a configuration, replace or merge it, compare it against the device, then commit or discard. For vendors without a native candidate-configuration model, the library provides that behaviour itself. A second set of getters returns structured data in the same layout for every supported vendor, and Ansible modules ship with the package.

The live demo ran on three virtual routers. The IOS XR virtual machine was dropped because it kept crashing, so the demo used two Juniper devices. Using Ansible, the presenter kept vendor-neutral variables in files, applied per-vendor templates to generate configurations, and deployed them in stages: management bootstrap, DNS and NTP servers, interface addressing, and OSPF. Each deployment produced a diff file, and re-running an unchanged configuration made no changes on the device.

The main takeaway is to separate vendor-agnostic data from vendor-specific templates, so a change to one variable file, such as a DNS server, can roll out across the whole fleet. Configurations generated offline can also rebuild a replaced router from its management address. The speakers pointed to the project's code repository, its example files from an earlier, larger demo, and a mailing list for questions and problems.

talks.title: 4Developers 2015: 10 przykazań bezpiecznego kodowania (W. Dworakowski)
talks.teaser: Walks developers through ten proactive controls against common web flaws, from SQL injection to access control.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a familiar problem: security is often tested at the end of a project, when fixes are costly or leave systems patched rather than sound. Many developers receive no formal secure-coding training, and security requirements are rarely stated in concrete terms. The session introduces the OWASP Top 10 Proactive Controls, a developer-oriented list of the most important defensive measures, and stresses that it is a baseline rather than a full security strategy.

For SQL injection, parameterized queries are presented as the most reliable defence, and a demo shows boolean-only queries extracting a whole database. An Oracle dynamic block bypassed one API's protection, and escaping is called the weakest fallback. For cross-site scripting, output encoding must match the context: HTML, attribute, JavaScript or URL. A demo shows a script planted in a transfer description taking over an operator's browser on an internal banking network. Validation should use allowlists, and access control should be enforced server-side with default deny and policies kept outside the code. A login example showed a key-generation function reachable before the second factor was checked.

The closing advice is to educate developers, reuse vetted libraries and build security into architecture early. Attendees were pointed to cheat sheets, encoder libraries and a weekly free consultation slot.

talks.title: Bitspiartion 2015 - NCBR & VPP: Panel Discussion
talks.teaser: Polish officials and a funded startup explain public financing stages for high-risk technology ventures.
talks.summary:
The panel opened with a representative of a Polish government agency that funds high-risk technology startups. He outlined a staged path: a first proof-of-principle phase to test whether an idea is feasible, then a proof-of-concept phase that should yield a working laboratory prototype. Under the Bridge Alpha program, the agency covers about 80 percent of the cost of each of these early stages, with private players providing the rest. Later development can draw on grants covering roughly 50 to 60 percent of a project.

Selection is delegated to private management teams rather than run by the agency itself. The Start Ventures Poland fund described reviewing over 600 applications, around 30 percent from Poland and 70 percent from abroad, and picking 35 or 36 for proof-of-principle work. A founder of Virtual Power Plant then described its energy-efficiency business, which claims about 25 percent energy savings for large facilities such as swimming pools, and said the funding helped it reach first clients.

In the audience question round, expectations were given: roughly 20 to 25 ideas through the first phase, five to seven ready for venture capital, and about 50 to 70 well-prepared startups across the current contracts. Panelists said direct Horizon 2020 money is very hard for Polish SMEs without venture backing or a program like Bridge Alpha. The takeaway for founders is that public money, advice and network support come together, and early private co-investment matters.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2015 - Ela Madej & Seth Bannon: Why starting a company is like eating glass?
talks.teaser: Surfaces the emotional cost of founding companies and practical habits—sleep, rest, movement, and meditation—to sustain leaders.
talks.summary:
Two founders open by contrasting polished startup success stories with private crises: layoffs, resignations, cash crises, and the “WFIO” moments Ben Horowitz describes as common even on winning paths. They tie Elon Musk’s “eating glass” metaphor to Y Combinator pressure, product pivots, immigration stress, and the loneliness of leading teams through hiring, firing, and constant unknowns.

The middle turns clinical: chronic anxiety symptoms, depression as a measurable brain state, rising founder suicide risk, and Brad Feld’s example of breaking silence in the community. They introduce cortisol as the stress driver, then walk through studies linking sleep, vacation, dance, massage, exercise, and mindfulness meditation to lower stress and sharper thinking.

They close with self-management discipline—calendar-blocking for recovery—and a “four P’s” frame: builders’ focus, passion, purpose, and perspective, including when to quit or climb a different mountain. Q&A covers investor coaching obligations, burnout recovery stories, honest peer networks versus party small talk, and checking on friends’ sleep and mental health.

talks.title: Wykorzystanie podejścia Domain-Driven Design w systemach legacy
talks.teaser: Outlines four walled integration patterns that let teams graft domain-driven design onto legacy systems without a full rewrite.
talks.summary:
The speaker begins with a show of hands about code age and prior exposure to domain-driven design, then argues that useful DDD in legacy estates starts with changing how developers think—not with full rewrites. He names three recurring obstacles: developers who prefer frameworks over the business domain, anemic layering and getters-and-setters habits, continuous patching of old code, and pattern catalogs applied without grasping bounded contexts.

He repeats that no whole system will be well designed end to end; strategic DDD should target the small slice where the client actually makes money. Clear boundaries must precede any tactic. The centerpiece is four ways to “build a wall” between new and legacy parts, illustrated with a deliberately silly project-renaming core: bubble context with a repository anti-corruption layer on one database; asynchronous synchronization to a separate store; upstream legacy exposed through domain services and transformers; and event streams with queues, eventual consistency, and long-running sagas instead of naive distributed transactions.

Walking through aggregates, value objects, and repositories co-located with the model, he compares investment, isolation, and risk for each step. Takeaways are to scope DDD narrowly, accept imperfect periphery, reuse valuable legacy logic where it fits, and align motivated people—rather than forcing the entire organization or codebase to change at once.

talks.title: Programowanie synchroniczne i asynchroniczne - dwa światy które można połączyć - Łukasz Nawojczyk
talks.teaser: Compares Java's futures, callbacks, promises and reactive streams for asynchronous code, and shows how to test each one.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at asynchronous programming in Java from the point of view of a back-end developer. It starts with the C10K problem, where one machine has to serve ten thousand simultaneous connections, and with the early thread-based model, which was hard to write, debug, test and document. The speaker then walks through what Java added over time: Future and ExecutorService, which can block on get but cannot signal completion, and listener-based APIs such as Guava's ListenableFuture and an Elasticsearch client that report results through callbacks.

The middle section covers the callback pyramid that appears when tasks depend on one another. Promises are presented next, from jQuery and the Promise/A+ standard to Java ports such as JDeferred, followed by CompletableFuture as a single-object alternative. Reactive libraries are shown for handling streams of values with subscriptions, error strategies and operators. The speaker also covers a ring-buffer event dispatcher, the Akka actor model, and Vert.x, with a small HTTP server example and a note that a non-blocking handler delays the events queued behind it.

For testing, the speaker uses Awaitility to wait for asynchronous results in unit tests, while noting that its polling approach suits tests rather than production code. The closing advice is to make network, disk and external API calls the places for asynchronous work, avoid tying up threads, prefer frameworks that scale horizontally, and plan for failure from the start.

talks.teaser: See how Hystrix handles slow or failing dependencies and makes their behavior visible through live metrics.
talks.summary: The speaker explains how Hystrix wraps potentially unsafe operations such as network and database calls with timeouts, thread pools, and circuit breakers. Through a simulated service, the talk shows how fail-fast behavior responds to slow or failing dependencies, and how Hystrix streams and dashboards expose command and thread pool metrics. Attendees also learn how statistics can be aggregated or stored and how batching concurrent requests can reduce calls to a backend at the cost of added latency.

talks.title: It's not always the application fault
talks.teaser: Shows why infrastructure limits application performance, with practical advice on monitoring, backups and virtualized hosts.
talks.summary:
Tomasz Borek opens with the idea that developers often see their application as a high-performance racing car, while the infrastructure it runs on may be a budget setup built for something slower. He argues that user experience depends on both halves, so application and infrastructure should be treated as one system, with DevOps involved from the design stage. His suggested approach starts with how the application is used: traffic spikes, new customers, and business transactions. If problems persist, the investigation moves down the stack, from application code to the runtime, operating system and hardware.

He then covers monitoring and recovery. Monitoring tools can themselves consume large amounts of CPU and storage, so their overhead should be measured. He stresses that a backup is not real until it has been restored and tested, and introduces RTO and RPO as shared terms for recovery time and acceptable data loss. On hardware, he cautions that vendor switch and firewall figures often assume ideal traffic, and that stacking every layer behind the same firewall defeats defense in depth. In virtualized environments, a host can show modest user load while system load stays high because of context switching and automatic resource rebalancing.

The closing advice is practical. Give developers read-only access to logs and environments, share a repository for build and deploy scripts, and agree service levels with platform teams. Averages hide slow requests, so he recommends measuring percentiles instead. The takeaways are to test infrastructure regularly, monitor the application the way users experience it, and let developers and operators learn each other's side.

talks.title: Enabling Continuous Delivery
talks.teaser: Shows how feature toggles, smaller applications and fast tests let a team deploy to production many times a day.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who spent four years as a consultant on a large real estate portal, describes how a monolithic application that once shipped every quarter came to deploy several times a day. He separates releasing a feature, which means exposing it to users, from deploying code, which means putting a new build into production. Feature toggles let product owners switch features on or off, so the team can deploy unfinished work safely and turn off anything that misbehaves without redeploying.

The talk then covers the steps that made this possible. Application size is judged by how long its tests take, with unit tests under ten minutes and integration tests under fifteen as rough baselines. Where tests are fine but the codebase is still too large, the team split it into micro applications sharing one single sign-on service, rather than going straight to microservices. Branching by abstraction replaces long-lived branches, and testing concentrates on the core domain logic, since integration-layer mistakes can be fixed quickly after a deploy. Configurable builds, automated checks, metrics and easy server provisioning completed the setup.

The closing part covers the trade-offs. Developers initially resisted putting conditionals in code, but within a few months most of them defended the approach. Toggles need cleanup: product owners decide which ones stay, and a recurring technical story removes the rest. The team did not test every combination of toggles, accepting brief user interface glitches in exchange for faster delivery.

talks.title: DevOps sum is greater than its parts
talks.teaser: Traces how a media company's teams leave waterfall silos for DevOps, covering culture, small batches and automated deployments.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how a Polish media group's development and operations unit moved from a waterfall, silo-based model to DevOps. Early on, heavy project management, functional silos and a 24/7 support line meant projects finished on time but quality was low and delivery was slow. To show why batch size matters, the speaker used an envelope-stuffing exercise, arguing that small batches give faster feedback and fewer handover problems.

DevOps was described as cross-functional, self-organized teams working in short cycles, with culture ranked above tools. Practices included blameless postmortems, product teams that own a feature from front to back, and treating servers as cattle rather than pets. Infrastructure is automated, with an Amazon environment used for disaster recovery, and about 200 production deployments happen each day. A cross-organization team chose Jira, Bamboo, SonarQube and Selenium and promoted percentage-based rollouts.

Monitoring was treated as a shared responsibility, with product alarms shown in team rooms and a 24/7 monitoring-as-a-service team handling escalations and feedback on alarms. The closing advice was to start with one team or product, build a visible success story, and recruit internal ambassadors before scaling. Audience questions covered how administrators can grow into DevOps roles and how helpdesk feedback reaches product teams.
