talks.title: PLNOG14: Zarządzalne sieci WiFi - tradycyjne vs. Edge-Core Cloud (T. Sadowski)
talks.teaser: Compares traditional controller-based WiFi management with a cloud-managed Edge-Core approach for access points.
talks.summary:
The talk compares two ways of running a managed WiFi network: a traditional on-premises traffic controller and a cloud-managed system from Edge-Core. The speaker, a product specialist at a hardware manufacturer, presents the company's portfolio, which covers controllers, indoor and outdoor wireless access points, and network switches. With a controller, an administrator manages all access points from one place, changes settings across them at once, and relies on automatic channel selection and coordinated transmit power.

The controller topology is shown with redundancy in mind: if one access point fails, the others can take over its role and its users. The speaker also describes how the management interface can detect a foreign access point and disable it, which helps with rogue devices nearby.

In the cloud model, the management panel is reached through a web or mobile application, so the customer needs little local equipment and the access points connect to a service rather than to an on-site server. The panel can show access points on a map, display currently connected users, and separate users into different wireless networks. The speaker presents this as a more cost-effective option for some customers than a traffic controller. The talk closes with network switches that can run third-party network operating systems such as Cumulus, which the speaker mentions as a common open option for building switching infrastructure.

talks.title: PLNOG14: Darmowe narzędzia wspomagające proces zabezpieczania Twojej firmy (B. Łącki)
talks.teaser: Surveys free security tools for company defenders, covering antivirus, hardening, encryption, scanning and password auditing.
talks.summary:
This talk is a tour of free security tools a company can use to protect itself. The speaker, a penetration tester who finds weaknesses for clients so they can be fixed, frames security around confidentiality, integrity and availability, and notes that attackers go after the weakest link. Paid editions with nicer interfaces or reports are only mentioned in passing.

On the defensive side, antivirus choice should rely on independent comparison rankings, since a product near the top handles mass attacks. Microsoft's free utilities cover asset inventory, extra protections for older Windows systems, and monitoring of changes such as new firewall rules. Other tools audit server and workstation settings, map open ports, analyse packets, and tunnel traffic over SSH. Data protection gets attention too: secure deletion before devices are serviced, encryption for laptops and USB drives, and encrypted attachments whose password travels separately.

The offensive part covers self-testing: a Linux distribution bundled with testing tools, password audits against weak or default credentials, an exploitation framework with beginner-friendly front ends, a social engineering toolkit, wireless cracking suites, web proxies and automated scanners whose findings need manual checking. Application allowlisting that blocks disguised executables is recommended too. The speaker closes by saying no control is unbreakable, so layered defences should make attacks too costly.

talks.title: PLNOG14: (Nie)bezpieczeństwo w sieciach bezprzewodowych (S. Pasternacki)
talks.teaser: Explains how rogue access points and deauthentication attacks break Wi-Fi trust, and which built-in and wireless defenses stop them.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that wireless networks have no physical boundary, so a Wi-Fi network can be reached from outside a building and is often the weakest route into an otherwise wired network. The speaker says that in his consulting experience, most organisations that claimed to have no wireless turned out to have at least one access point installed by an employee, often with a weak password or none at all.

The middle of the talk walks through an attack chain. First the attacker surveys nearby networks and clients, then deauthentication frames push a device off its network. A rogue access point using the same name and a stronger signal lures the device back, where a fake DHCP service hands out addresses and a fake login page collects credentials. The demo was a recorded video from an earlier Cisco presentation, since a live demo was not possible. The speaker also warns that clicking through certificate warnings is one of the biggest mistakes users make. Other threats covered include bridging two networks together, interference from Bluetooth or microwave ovens, and directional antennas used from a distance.

For defense, he recommends WPA2 with AES, certificate-based 802.1X authentication, and management frame protection. Wireless controllers and intrusion prevention systems can detect rogue access points, correlate them with switch ports, and contain them. Identity-based policies, location tracking and, at high-risk sites, shielding also help. He closes by urging administrators to use the controls they already have, since these are not hard to deploy.

talks.title: PLNOG14: Najnowszy raport bezpieczeństwa firmy Radware (M. Karczewski)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of PLNOG14: Najnowszy raport bezpieczeństwa firmy Radware (M. Karczewski).
talks.summary: A Radware presenter walks PLNOG14 through the latest security report: longer multi-day DDoS campaigns, education and healthcare rising as targets, volumetric versus application-layer attack mix, and growth in HTTPS and UDP reflection floods. He positions hybrid scrubbing plus on-prem DefensePro and web application firewall signaling, with Q&A on false positives and behavioral detection.

talks.title: PLNOG14: System ochrony przed atakami DDoS - dla kogo? (M. Janik)
talks.teaser: Compares DDoS defense options for companies and operators, from on-demand scrubbing and BGP tricks to Flowspec and inline cleaning.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether an organisation can get by without a DDoS protection system. The speaker, who works on IP products at Huawei Enterprise, sorts attacks into volumetric, application-layer and infrastructure-layer types. He explains which victims each one tends to hit, including content portals, financial institutions, government websites and operators with end users.

He then walks through the defence options in turn. A subscription scrubbing service is effective but expensive, and an on-demand service only works if routing has been arranged in advance, since BGP announcements take time to propagate. Blackholing cuts off a targeted prefix, but the attack still succeeds because the service disappears. Spreading BGP sessions and withholding announcements suits content providers rather than operators. BGP Flowspec is widely supported but static, and it relies on flow data such as NetFlow, which is also the usual detection method for operators. The speaker describes a detector and cleaner architecture, with traffic redirected by policy routing, BGP or Layer 2, and says inline cleaning is the only way to cover infrastructure-layer attacks, provided upstream links are larger than the attack.

The closing part covers vendor hardware capacity, including a 200 Gbit chassis, planned throughput increases and a reference deployment at Alibaba. It also describes a Dutch shared, non-profit scrubbing center that spreads cost across many small providers, and proposes a similar model for smaller Polish ISPs and portals. The takeaway is to know how a service will behave during an attack, test devices before buying, and prepare for an attack before it arrives.

talks.title: PLNOG14: CSP Infrastructure Performance and Security Assessment (R. Wiszniewski, D. Zmysłowski)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of PLNOG14: CSP Infrastructure Performance and Security Assessment (R. Wiszniewski, D. Zmysłowski).

talks.title: PLNOG14: DNS jako broń w walce ze złośliwym oprogramowaniem (P. Jaroszewski)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding PLNOG14: DNS jako broń w walce ze złośliwym oprogramowaniem (P. Jaroszewski).
talks.summary: A NASK CERT Polska engineer explains why domain names outlive bulletproof IPs in botnet infrastructure, then presents DNS as an operator weapon against malware: passive monitoring, customer notification, and low-cost hygiene services. The talk complements DDoS-on-DNS sessions by focusing on the DNS protocol as telemetry, not amplification attacks, and invites ISP cooperation with CERT data.

talks.title: PLNOG14: Vectra i Infoblox Advanced DNS Protection (A. Obszyński, T. Parol)
talks.teaser: A Polish cable operator describes deploying a DNS protection appliance after DNS outages and shows its results.
talks.summary:
Vectra, a Polish cable operator, describes why it added DNS protection to its network. A pilot with two appliances was already running when a series of attacks in August left its DNS servers answering very slowly. The operator then bought the Infoblox platform, which was installed in November.

The speakers walk through the rollout. The installation was tested in two cities before going nationwide on 11 November, and the team had to fix a misplaced cable and a spanning-tree problem along the way. The appliance includes a dedicated network card that inspects DNS traffic and can block, redirect or pass each query. Reporting shows the sources and targets of an attack, and about 6,000,000 events were blocked in the first month.

According to the talk, DNS stayed available through later attacks and subscribers noticed little impact. Future ideas include moving the cache onto the same platform, notifying infected customers through a redirect portal, and offering a DNS firewall as an add-on service. The session closed with questions on whether load balancers add latency, which the presenters argued they do.

talks.title: PLNOG14: Ceph in practice (P. Stefański)
talks.teaser: Shares practical lessons from running Ceph distributed storage, covering placement groups, journals, disks and rebalancing pitfalls.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Ceph, an open-source distributed storage system that began as an academic project and was later developed by a commercial company. The speaker explains its design goals: running on commodity servers, disks and switches, tolerating failures and healing itself. Ceph can serve as cloud block storage, as S3- or Swift-compatible object storage, and through file interfaces that are still maturing.

The middle of the talk covers operational lessons. Monitors coordinate the cluster while clients reach the OSD daemons directly, so monitors do not need to scale out with the data. Each OSD should sit on one raw disk rather than a RAID volume, and XFS is recommended over ext4 and btrfs, which the speaker found immature. A separate journal device helps, but if it fails the OSD has to be recreated, and constant journal writes can wear out cheap SSDs. The default placement group count is too low, so the speaker suggests planning for hundreds of placement groups per OSD, ideally a power of two. Uneven data distribution is common, and map changes or forced rebalancing move large amounts of data, which can hurt clients on busy production clusters.

The closing part compares triple replication with erasure coding, which gives redundancy at roughly 50 percent overhead but writes more slowly. Object checksums were announced as coming. For upgrades, the speaker advises waiting a month or more after a release before adopting it, and recommends automating deployment with existing tools. The talk ends with a short question round about SSD choices and cluster size.

talks.title: PLNOG14: Jak projektować konwergente, wydajne i najszybsze sieci w Data Center (K. Jantas)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of PLNOG14: Jak projektować konwergente, wydajne i najszybsze sieci w Data Center (K. Jantas).

talks.title: PLNOG14: Active Networks - dlaczego skończyły jako SDN (M. Szczęsny)
talks.teaser: A tour from 1990s DARPA active networks and PLAN through ABONE to how that design lineage surfaces in current SDN arguments.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames today’s software-defined networking buzz against a personal path from graph theory and early-2000s DARPA reading lists toward active networks. It recounts mid-1990s goals—autonomic nodes, downloadable modules, and packets treated as programs—and the split between integrated “every packet is code” designs and more pragmatic discrete models such as scout-style routing probes.

Major U.S. research lines (MIT ANS, Pennsylvania’s Switch and PLAN, BBN’s Smart Packet) are outlined alongside testbeds like ABONE, including a Polish operator node that still appears in later academic work. PLAN modules written in a functional style illustrate intelligent ping and routing behavior carried inside packets. The speaker then compares that heritage to OpenFlow-style SDN, questioning cross-vendor control planes and recalling stalled operator platforms such as IMS and RCS next to consumer messaging apps.

Closing threads include an “app store for routers” metaphor on top of commodity switches, skepticism that provisioning extra optical capacity is a breakthrough, and three takeaways: active networks as an SDN precursor, the need for a unifying industry champion, and continued defense-funded roots behind the idea. A brief question discusses whether carrier forums can deliver reusable network applications like mobile app stores.

talks.title: PLNOG14: Overlay Networking (A. Gmaj)
talks.teaser: Connects datacenter overlay design to VLAN limits, MAC growth, tunneling choices, and operator-style underlay abstractions.
talks.summary:
The session picks up themes from an earlier talk on datacenter evolution: server virtualization is mature, but many networks are still planned for physical hosts. That mismatch drives VLAN ceilings near 4096 identifiers, growing MAC tables when many VMs share hardware, pressure to isolate tenants, and the need to add services without rewiring the whole facility each time.

The presenter argues for an overlay on a stable physical underlay. Logical topology can change while the physical fabric stays flexible. The stack spans bare metal, hypervisors, virtual switches, appliances, and software-defined services that must interoperate across vendors and generations. Physical switches need enough header visibility to steer overlay traffic; overlay methods such as VXLAN, GRE, MPLS, and Geneve are compared on how they tag and deliver frames to the right VM.

Control and orchestration tie overlays to automation so new virtual workloads can gain tunnels without hand-editing every device. The same model supports service chaining so traffic can pass through firewalls or other virtual network functions in a defined order. The close is a compressed roadmap for practitioners modernizing provider or enterprise datacenter networks.

talks.title: PLNOG14: Sieć w Openstack w Grupie Allegro (M. Dopierała, Sz. Kowalski)
talks.teaser: Follows an operator's OpenStack networking redesign, from legacy setups to Neutron, Open vSwitch and SDN.
talks.summary:
Two network administrators from Allegro describe the private cloud their group has run on OpenStack since around 2011, starting with the Essex release. Production now runs on Havana, with about 1,800 virtual machines on roughly 600 hypervisors, around 3,000 virtual machines across all installations, about 28,000 virtual cores, 75 TB of RAM and 140 TB of block storage. The early network relied on nova-network with Linux bridges and iptables, floating IPs translated through NAT, and a custom driver that pushed rules to hardware firewalls in one data center.

Moving to Neutron in Havana brought Open vSwitch, chosen over the Linux bridge for its room to grow. Tunnel-based overlays performed poorly in their tests. Routing all traffic through a few dedicated network nodes would have been a bottleneck at their scale, so they sent traffic directly through network devices and kept DHCP and metadata agents on dedicated nodes with a stretched layer 2 network and manual active-passive failover. Problems along the way included Open vSwitch restarts under load, which an upgrade resolved, virtual machines reported as active before their security group rules existed, and orphaned ports left behind after instances were deleted. Scripts were needed to clean these up.

The stretched layer 2 network and the growing number of per-project networks pushed them toward a newer SDN controller with distributed routing, MPLS tunnels and hardware gateways. In their tests it reached about 80 percent of a 10 Gbit link. The main gains were the removal of layer 2 across the data center and network creation through a single API call instead of configuration on eleven devices. Deployment was automated through Puppet manifests.

talks.title: PLNOG14: Sesja Peer & Beer
talks.teaser: Presenters brief operators on exchange scale, colocation promotions, and nonprofit stewardship of Polish peering platforms.
talks.summary:
The session opens as a fast Peer and Beer format: each speaker gets only three slides before a joint question block, so updates stay short instead of turning into long single-topic lectures.

The first briefing summarizes a major European internet exchange footprint—hundreds of member networks across dozens of countries, steady growth in client ports and backbone capacity, and lower cross-connect pricing plus bundled gigabit ports under a flat membership fee. A second operator-oriented segment covers colocation and connectivity themes: large CDN and cloud footprints on site, a growing catalog of television distribution channels, longstanding discount programs, rising evening traffic on the order of hundreds of gigabytes, and newly offered high-speed ports.

The closing segment announces that a nonprofit association has taken formal responsibility for two Polish internet exchange nodes and their traffic exchanges in Katowice and Warsaw. Technical separation and diverse paths remain, especially west-fed capacity in Katowice, while participants can still redundant-connect through both cities under one contract. Scale figures cite substantial international operator capacity, intercity transmission, and thousands of ten-gigabit ports, with pricing described as falling for members.

talks.title: PLNOG14: Historia epickiej wyprawy - od ARPANETu do Internetu (Ł. Trąbiński, R. Woźny)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding PLNOG14: Historia epickiej wyprawy - od ARPANETu do Internetu (Ł. Trąbiński, R. Woźny).
talks.summary: PLNOG14 hosts deliver a tongue-in-cheek saga from Sputnik shock through ARPANET IMP routers, TCP/IP, Vint Cerf, Jon Postel’s DNS and routing mailouts, NSFNet, Mosaic, gopher versus the free WWW, BGP, and privatized backbones—interleaved with Woodstock analogies and live audience quizzes on satellite years and Sex Pistols gigs. The arc stresses how a handful of engineers once ran global routing compared with today’s mass online audience.

talks.title: PLNOG14: Network and application performance monitoring (B.Cronin)
talks.teaser: Shows packet-based monitoring of multi-tier Oracle and VoIP services, tracing problems through dependencies like LDAP, DNS and SIP.
talks.summary:
The talk shows how a packet-based network performance monitoring platform can be used to watch multi-tier Oracle applications and voice over IP. The speaker argues that a poor user experience rarely comes from one protocol or one server. A web front end may depend on load balancers, a database, LDAP authentication, DNS and SMTP, so problems have to be traced across those dependencies. The approach captures packets at probes placed throughout the infrastructure, applies deep packet inspection, and keeps session records that link client communities to servers.

For an Oracle case, the dashboard maps client communities, front-end servers and back-end databases, highlighting retransmissions, timeouts and latency. Drilling into one session showed a user who was not authenticating through LDAP, so the fault sat in the directory rather than the database. Other errors listed included insufficient tablespace space. For voice, the tool correlates SIP call signalling with the RTP streams, so an operator can start from a telephone number. It also reassembles audio to check loudness, echo and background noise, rather than relying only on mean opinion score.

The closing message is to monitor the group of applications and infrastructure that together deliver a service, and to separate application performance from network health, traffic and capacity. Keeping the packets available lets teams move from a summary view down to a single session.

talks.title: PLNOG14: Evolved Programmable Network (K. Konkowski)
talks.teaser: Explains a service provider reference architecture that splits MPLS networks into segments and unifies subscriber services.
talks.summary:
A Cisco routing consultant presents the operator reference architecture known as Evolved Programmable Network, currently at version 4.0. The goal is for a subscriber to get the same subscribed service whether they connect over fixed broadband, mobile or microwave links. The architecture has three parts: a transport network, integrated and virtualised services, and unified control of subscriber services.

The main problem is that a single large MPLS domain grows heavy as device counts rise. Prefix tables can exceed 20,000 entries, which small access devices cannot hold, and traffic engineering for fast convergence adds operating cost. The design splits the network into isolated segments joined by hierarchical labels, so intermediate nodes only need to know where traffic exits their segment. Access devices learn only the prefixes they need, and border routers use next-hop-self. Route reflectors run as virtual functions in the data centre, with one inline exception in the access-to-aggregation path. For ring-based access, G.8032 gives convergence under 50 milliseconds without complex traffic engineering. The talk also covers virtual CPE, unified policy and billing that share one subscriber repository, and business services such as time-based bandwidth.

The speaker closes by pointing listeners to documentation available to partners after login. A roughly 40-page system concept document links to design and implementation guides that include tested configurations for transport, mobile and multicast. Practitioners can use these to see how the components fit together before deploying them.

talks.title: PLNOG14
talks.teaser: A lawyer discusses how businesses can balance legal compliance with commercial goals in fast-moving internet technology.
talks.summary:
This short interview from PLNOG 14 in Warsaw features a lawyer whose firm focuses on new technologies. Her practice mainly serves investment funds backing startups in gaming and mobile apps, and she also advises several telecom operators, both large and small, that want to offer services. She explains that the conference stood out to her for its scale and positive energy, and she mentions that the event has also been held in Kraków, where her firm is based.

The core of the discussion is the gap between technology and law. In her view, reality moves well ahead of regulation, Polish law often follows European and American standards, and enforcement lags even further behind. The main challenge for entrepreneurs is that they want to act lawfully while also running a sound business, and finding a path that satisfies both sometimes requires unconventional solutions. She describes the practical, step-by-step legal problems that her clients and acquaintances run into online, which was the focus of her own session.

She notes that audience questions and follow-up conversations were more numerous than in the previous year, which she takes as a sign the topic resonated. She closes by promoting an upcoming June conference in Warsaw aimed at startups and funds, where she plans to cover investment agreements and the intellectual property pitfalls that startups face.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Building a brand not just a product (N. Coronges)
talks.teaser: He describes how integrated hardware, software, and services let global sports and music brands engage customers beyond gadgets alone.
talks.summary:
The presenter reframes a planned corporate-startup talk around a single idea: for connected products, the brand, product, and service are one experience. He sketches R/GA’s path from film-effects hardware through digital and mobile work, then walks through Nike’s partnership with Apple on Nike Plus—APIs linking sensors, iTunes, and the web, later phones and apps, with scale figures cited for users, miles, and countries—and how that engagement helped Nike reclaim running share. FuelBand extends the same motivational logic with a universal “fuel” metric; he notes hardware can fade while metrics persist, including Nike Fuel appearing in Apple’s HealthKit.

He contrasts genuine motivation-oriented products with parody wearable ideas, arguing brand means emotional belief, not gadgets alone. Beats Music illustrates human, emotional service layered on hardware. He closes with R/GA Ventures and a Techstars-powered connected-devices accelerator: portfolio verticals, client mentors, service hours for startups, and brief profiles of cohort companies such as Hammerhead, Keen, Owlet, Grove Labs, and enert, plus funding amounts mentioned for several.

Practitioners hear that lasting value comes from services and identity customers want daily, that big brands win through ecosystem partnerships, and that early hardware startups benefit when design, engineering, and marketing ship as one branded system rather than a device alone.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Case Study - Infoblox Advanced DNS Protection (A. Obszyński)
talks.teaser: Outlines DNS flood risks and how purpose-built appliances filter attacks while preserving legitimate resolver traffic.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing DNS as a lightweight UDP service that underpins nearly every online experience, which makes outage or slowdown feel like a full application failure even when other controls are solid. It walks through why attackers favor DNS floods and misuse, including inexpensive rented attack services and malware that relies on DNS for command and control or tunneling past generic security gear.

The middle section contrasts broad network anti-DDoS tools with appliances built only for DNS. It describes hardware-oriented designs that answer from silicon, sustain very high query rates under attack, and add capabilities such as passive monitoring, clustered failover with VRRP, mitigation of queries for non-existent names, reputation-based blocking, and checks that delegations still match what the organization believes it published.

Customer anecdotes—mostly anonymized—illustrate triggers such as public-sector availability pressure, banking reputational risk, operator tests interrupted by live floods, and campus outages before exams. The speaker argues that simply buying bigger servers does not scale against growing botnets. The closing material points practitioners toward DNS risk questionnaires, published good practices, wider DNSSEC adoption abroad, and benchmark clips comparing common servers under stress.

talks.title: PLNOG 12: Przyszłość zabezpieczenia sieci szerokopasmowych w Europie ( N. Babaali)
talks.teaser: Maps global and European fiber penetration, Poland's weak metrics, and the investment case for future-proof FTTH rollout.
talks.summary:
A representative of FTTH Council Europe addresses operators at a Polish network forum in English, framing fiber-to-the-home as the only future-proof access technology and describing how the council collects market data, case studies, and financing guidance for stakeholders across the continent.

The presentation walks through worldwide subscriber totals and penetration rankings, then narrows to Europe and Poland. Poland remains below one percent household penetration with weak take-up, while eastern European states and the Nordics show stronger adoption; large EU markets often favor VDSL or cable instead. Regional aggregates distinguish broader Europe, EU without CIS countries, and EU28, highlighting faster growth in subscribers than homes passed. The speaker explains FTTH versus fiber-to-the-building counting rules, typical take-up lags, continued growth since 2007, and an analyst threshold of twenty percent penetration as “fiber maturity,” with projections for when various countries might reach it.

Closing sections rebuff common excuses for delay, cite an estimated EU-wide deployment cost near 202 billion euros against longer-term operator economics, and argue for public investment in future-proof infrastructure. Practitioners hear that demand and service innovation follow capacity, early fiber leaders gained service-industry advantages, and delayed rollout risks competitive disadvantage relative to the cost of building now.

talks.title: PLNOG 12: Wprowadzenie do Software Defined Data Centre (S. Flack)
talks.teaser: Compares legacy pod layouts with leaf-spine fabrics, merchant silicon, and eBGP for scalable enterprise design.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by walking through familiar enterprise data center pods: load balancers, firewalls, distribution switches, and top-of-rack attachment, with BGP toward the internet and spanning tree inside large layer-two domains. The speaker argues that this model is stable but complex, oversubscribed, hard to troubleshoot without ping and trace, and unable to scale beyond a few dozen racks.

Cloud operators are described as optimizing for simple architecture, high performance, low cost per bit, near-unlimited scale, and automation. The middle of the talk compares ring, tree, mesh, butterfly, and related topologies, then focuses on leaf-spine (Clos) as the practical non-blocking choice. Merchant silicon timelines illustrate port density growth; formulas relate switch counts to top-of-rack ports for two-tier and three-tier fabrics. eBGP with private AS numbers per leaf is favored over OSPF or IS-IS for churn and policy control, with BGP fast failover, BFD, and ECMP for bandwidth use and maintenance draining.

Practitioners are left with pay-as-you-grow sizing examples, notes on VXLAN and NVGRE for layer-two adjacency across layer three, cabling aggregation, path monitoring on layer-three links, and automation-friendly regular designs without heavy QoS.

talks.title: PLNOG 12: Krótka historia chmury CC1 (M. Nabożny)
talks.teaser: Explains how a Kraków physics institute built the open-source CC1 private IaaS cloud after moving on from OpenNebula.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with familiar cloud models—software, platform, and infrastructure services—and contrasts public providers with private clouds that keep data and compute on an organization’s own hardware. The speaker argues that choice should follow real needs: burst capacity for promotions, heavy simulation for research, or sensitivity rules that rule out sending banking workloads to shared public environments.

The core story is CC1, developed at the Institute of Nuclear Physics in Kraków after EU funding roughly four years earlier, when local physicists lacked suitable cloud access. Management began with OpenNebula and custom code, then shifted to in-house CC1 software that provisions virtual machines as IaaS. The stack is largely Python, licensed under Apache 2, and today drives more than nine hundred CPU cores and on the order of one and a half terabytes of RAM, pooling idle lab workstations that once sat near twenty percent utilization.

Operationally, users reach resources through a web console (with a compatibility interface mentioned alongside it), while modular “blocks” allow simple single-site layouts or redundancy spread across server rooms. The team built dedicated testing tools because validating a dispersed fleet of over a hundred machines exceeded ordinary application QA. They also note tension when tenants hold root on VMs, complicate isolation, and ship version 2.0 with 2.1 in progress, inviting feedback from new adopters.

talks.title: PLNOG 12: Ruchome piaski internetu ( A. Wolski)
talks.teaser: Maps shifting global internet pillars—names, DNSSEC, IPv6 scarcity, and RPKI—and what operators must watch, allocate, and secure today.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames the internet’s slow, global evolution from a regional registry trainer’s view, contrasting operator-focused conference themes with worldwide trends in naming, addressing, and routing. It opens with scale pressures—billions of users and devices against exhausted IPv4—and groups the landscape into domain-name issues, numeric addressing, and routing, while noting that RIPE’s community-driven model mainly exports what members ask for.

On names, it walks through global, country, and infrastructure domains, internationalized labels, and the new gTLD program: high cost, complex applications, brand protection disputes, single-label TLD hazards (search suffixes, internal host collisions), and SSL certificate challenges that helped pause some bids. Operators are urged to track weekly additions because clients will hit unfamiliar suffixes. DNSSEC is explained as signed responses that curb cache poisoning when resolvers validate, plus optional uses such as SSHFP and DANE for certificates; much of the signed root and TLD space is already in place.

IPv6 is treated through registry statistics and a four-star deployment scorecard (allocation, DNS, prefix announcement, route objects), with Poland compared to neighbors and Romania called out. Closing on routing security, BGP’s trust weaknesses motivate RPKI: ROAs tied to regional registry data, automatic distribution, and router states (valid, invalid, unknown) that can inform filtering, though adoption remains sparse and cautious.

talks.title: PLNOG 12: Wymagania formalno-prawne do świadczenia usług IPTV (B. Łagowski, M. Wilczyński)
talks.teaser: Walks through the Polish legal requirements for launching an IPTV service, from telecom registration to consumer contracts.
talks.summary:
The talk, given in Polish, is aimed at operators who want to start a television service. It opens with the presenting company's planned IPTV offer, which has three parts: sublicences for broadcaster content, direct content access delivered over IP, and a platform where an operator manages channels, packages, pricing and the EPG and can add its own channel. Access is planned for set-top boxes, Android and Chromecast, with catch-up and premiere episodes included.

The legal part, presented by two lawyers, starts with telecom law. A provider must first be entered in the register of telecommunications entrepreneurs kept by UKE. The speaker said the office has 7 days to act and that silence after 14 days counts as acceptance. A distinction is drawn between an operator and a service provider, with operators carrying broader duties. Distributing a programme over a teleinformatic system uses a simplified notification to the KRRiT register, which takes about 30 days and costs 104 zł per programme. Other areas covered were broadcasting law, personal data registration, intellectual property, and collective management organisations, where rates are no longer approved and it is disputed who should pay. Fines can reach 3 percent of the penalised company's revenue.

The closing point was consumer contracts. Abusive clauses can lead to large numbers of lawsuits, so the presenters urged careful contract drafting from the start and offered a sample agreement at their stand. The main takeaway is that the legal groundwork should be finished before launch.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning PLNOG 12: Nowa generacja ruchu aplikacyjnego (K. Baniak, G. Kornacki).

talks.title: PLNOG 12: Umowy w telekomunikacji- jak uniknąć problemów. Studium przypadków (A. Piechocki)
talks.teaser: Walks through telecom contract drafting, consumer-protection clauses and regulator fines that can catch operators out.
talks.summary:
This lecture, given at a Polish telecommunications event, is a legal talk aimed at operators in a regulated market. The speaker, a legal counsel, presents the telecom regulator's powers and the consumer courts as the main sources of risk. He explains that a natural person who trades online repeatedly may be treated as an entrepreneur, while recent court practice has become more willing to treat such people as consumers.

Much of the talk covers abusive contract clauses under the Civil Code. A clause is unlawful when it goes against good practice and seriously harms a consumer, unless the main obligations are stated unambiguously or the term was individually negotiated. A clause sending disputes to a court based at the entrepreneur's seat is treated as always prohibited. Under telecom law, a contract may be concluded only in writing or electronically, while amendments can be made by phone at the customer's request. The speaker also covers the consumer's withdrawal period for distance contracts, the ban on upfront payments, liability caps tied to discounts, and the subscriber's right to terminate when terms change.

The closing section outlines penalties: a 3 percent fine for companies that breach the act, personal fines for managers of up to 300 percent of their remuneration, and a fine of 10 percent of revenue for harming collective consumer interests. The practical takeaway is to check contract wording, price lists and complaint procedures before rolling out changes.

talks.title: PLNOG 12: Jak w 45 minut zbudować kompletną infrastrukturę ISP- migracja od IPv4 do IPv6 (K. Mazepa)
talks.teaser: Outlines how carriers detect volumetric floods, steer dirty traffic to scrubbing centers, and return clean flows without routing loops.
talks.summary:
The presentation targets telecom operators and their customers who face large-scale volumetric attacks that overwhelm customer firewalls and links. The speaker distinguishes application-layer attacks, which stay closer to the victim, from volumetric floods that upstream providers are positioned to blunt, and notes that mitigation is usually a paid, cooperative service rather than something the operator does alone for free.

Several common mitigation patterns are compared on practicality and side effects. DNS redirection can soak abuse aimed at hostnames but fails when attackers target IP addresses directly. Cloud-style BGP diversion with longer prefixes can pull attack traffic toward a scrubber yet often sweeps legitimate traffic along at typical aggregation lengths. Classic and remote-triggered blackholing stop the flood but also cut off reachability, which means the attack still wins operationally. Building an in-network scrubbing center trades cost and complexity for finer prefix control and better separation of dirty versus clean traffic.

Architectural choice matters as much as the widget. A central scrubbing hub simplifies operations but can become a bandwidth bottleneck; distributed edge scrubbers reduce transit of dirty traffic but multiply facilities at peering and billing points. Detection leans on NetFlow export into collector platforms that signal attacks and trigger more-specific BGP announcements. The closing walkthroughs stress offramp and onramp design: GRE tunnels or VRF injection to re-admit cleaned traffic, and on Cisco IOS-XR, access-list-based forwarding that activates only when a synthetic prefix appears—keeping the rest of the network untouched until an attack starts.

talks.title: PLNOG 2014: Nie ma żadnych czarnych dziur (R. Woźny)
talks.teaser: Describes layer-two black holing on Poland’s TPX peering platform to drop unwanted attack traffic before it reaches customer prefixes.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames a talk titled as if about “black holes,” then shifts to operational work at TPX, a Polish internet exchange where operators peer and exchange traffic, often with better locality and cost than transit paths. Operators see DDoS and noisy traffic—NTP floods, DNS attacks—and customers ask for ways to block harmful flows without taking entire networks offline.

The core design adapts BGP black holing to a layer-two exchange. Under attack, a participant can announce a prefix with a nexthop pointing at a dedicated black-hole router. TPX still validates that the prefix belongs to the announcing operator so one party cannot black-hole someone else’s space. Because the platform switches at Ethernet rather than routing at the edge, unwanted flows targeting the black-hole MAC are stripped on ingress ACLs; only ARP needed to resolve that hop is allowed, while TCP, ICMP, and other traffic toward the sink is discarded before it crosses the fabric.

Walkthroughs contrast normal peering through the exchange with an assault on a sample web host and selective announcement of a black-holed prefix toward specific peers. Practitioners learn trade-offs: flooding the sink router is undesirable, so edge filtering matters; operators can choose a /32 or broader blocks such as /24 when upstreams resist tiny prefixes; and route-server communities can limit which peers receive the black-hole route.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: The Friction Between Users & Advertising (J.Krawczyk)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Bitspiration 2014: The Friction Between Users & Advertising (J.Krawczyk).

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Bringing Context Home (B. Plontsch)
talks.teaser: Outlines personal iBeacon home apps, beacon deployment models, room-level use cases, and iOS UI for context-aware microlocation.
talks.summary:
The session positions context awareness as a way to narrow the gap between everyday physical spaces and digital tools, focusing on home rather than heavy automation. The presenter outlines two iOS products built on iBeacons: Travel Radar, which pairs a beacon with luggage to show distance and notify on movement or in-range changes, and Launch Here, which surfaces microlocation-based app shortcuts on the lock screen for spots such as a sofa or refrigerator.

A large portion maps how people obtain beacon infrastructure—retail and venues where owners deploy hardware, personal setups where the user must buy and place devices, and bundled beacons inside appliances with companion apps. The speaker walks room-by-room and object-by-object to link intents with existing apps, using navigation, grocery lists, music, and room-local temperature control to show how focus and UI should shift as someone moves. For iOS specifically, the talk stresses keeping users unaware of beacon jargon, avoiding manual UUID-style linking, handling location authorization and repeated iOS 8 consent prompts, leaning on background scanning and local notifications (including quick actions), and offering an in-app off switch.

Closing points encourage rethinking where an app is used, optionally combining HomeKit or Handoff with beacons, embedding radios in physical products to revive neglected companion apps, and addressing personal beacon buyers even when the market still skews toward retail.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: The rise of Beacons and fall of friction (J. Krzych)
talks.teaser: Links coin-sized beacons to nearby object context and distance on phones, cutting friction in retail, airports, and mobility.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with human context: eye-tracking studies of athletes and children, and how people cannot walk safely for more than a few seconds with eyes closed. Smartphones in pockets are similarly blind indoors—GPS fails and landmark schemes like QR codes and NFC never achieved mass adoption because the steps were too awkward.

The middle contrasts heavy visual recognition, including short-battery augmented-reality phones, with coin-sized battery beacons that radiate identity and distance so a phone can focus on one nearby object, echoing how a child picks a single toy. Painted futures include IKEA-style browsing without pencil lists, one-tap payment flows comparable to ride-hailing apps, inventory-light showrooms, and OS features that surface the right app from lock screens based on place. Live demo ties a bag beacon to on-screen motion via accelerometer data.

Closing Q&A stresses selective interaction when many beacons coexist, misconceptions such as useless in-plane luggage alerts, complementary hospital uses with head-worn displays, commoditized beacon hardware versus securing and fleet-managing deployments, and a Heathrow airline pilot that routes passengers by terminal context. Practitioners hear that physical retail still dominates transactions and that experimenting with contextual stacks now matters as penetration rises.

talks.title: PLNOG13: IPv6 implementation in mobile network-stage II (T. Kossut)
talks.teaser: Outlines Poland's IPv6-only mobile rollout: no DNS64, F5 iRules, NAT64, CLAT, roaming APNs, and vendor device requirements.
talks.summary:
Orange Poland’s mobile network pursued an IPv6-only subscriber architecture about a year before this session, starting with a Sony Xperia handset. The design deliberately turns off DNS64 because some applications—notably Origin for titles such as Battlefield 4—fail server authentication when literal IPv4 addresses and domain names are handled inconsistently. Instead, the operator uses F5 iRules at the DNS layer, deploys NAT64 (after testing Jool and an open-source option), and embeds CLAT in terminals so generic devices still reach IPv4-only services such as FTP, RTSP, and PPTP.

NAT64 hashing had to move beyond interface identifier–only schemes so large fleets of identical devices do not collapse to one translated address. Roaming relies on a secondary APN sharing the home name but using a different PDP type; it works on many visited networks, though some foreign SGSNs reject traffic in ways that are hard to observe from the home core. Device readiness consumed roughly two years: Android vendors and Windows Phone 8.1 reached production CLAT support, while Apple still offered dual-stack patterns akin to U.S. carriers. The team published mandatory terminal requirements covering tethering, router advertisements, local DHCPv6 for DNS on Windows, and LTE “ASM info” flags to avoid opening unused IPv4 default bearers.

Adoption climbed from about 1% to 12% of subscribers in six months, with a 20% year-end target; roughly 60% of an IPv6 session’s traffic is native IPv6, while Polish content sites still drive much IPv4 demand. The operator positions itself as the only large Polish network running 464XLAT with DNS64 disabled, and sketches future “CLAT to zero” work using DHCPv6 prefix delegation.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Wywiad z Emilem Gągałą

talks.title: PLNOG13: Wywiad z Grzegorzem Janoszką
talks.teaser: A Booking.com peering architect compares PLNOG to global forums and reflects on conference networking value.
talks.summary:
The recording is a hallway-style interview from PLNOG in Kraków with a Booking.com engineer who describes himself as an internet peering architect. He explains that his day-to-day work sits on the connectivity and peering layer that underpins the company’s online business, rather than on marketing video production, and that living inside a very large organization with relatively modest traffic creates recurring misunderstandings with vendors and partners about scale, budgets, and expectations.

He says recent operator forums helped him trade ideas with people from many backgrounds, and that a peering-focused presentation he gave roughly a week earlier at a European Union forum in Split opened the door to speaking in Kraków. When asked how PLNOG compares with RIPE, Tweak.pl, regional NOG groups, and gatherings such as NANOG, he emphasizes PLNOG’s unusually large crowd, international mix, youthful energy, humor, and polished logistics. He rates Polish speakers alongside international presenters, praises slide quality, and argues that sponsor-heavy marketing slots common abroad are kept to a minimum here while technical depth stays high.

He recommends the event to newcomers because parallel tracks and beginner-oriented spaces make entry easier, even though no single attendee can cover everything. He also treats informal networking and business matchmaking in the corridors as a major reason to attend. He closes by sketching near-term travel to operator meetings in London, Japan, and further European venues.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Kickstarter - neuro:on sleep well (K. Adamczyk)
talks.teaser: Explains how a wearables startup used Kickstarter prep, trust-building, and first-day momentum to reach global backers and fund research.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes founding a company after university neuroscience research ran out of funding, with a goal of staying independent while continuing brain-wave related work. The team chose crowdfunding, built an MVP, targeted a global audience rather than Poland alone, and ran a campaign that raised on the order of four hundred thousand dollars.

The middle of the talk compares platforms and constraints: Kickstarter versus Indiegogo, rules that block some medical or safety products, and the option to run crowdfunding on your own site when a platform rejects a project. He stresses reading platform guidelines, planning months ahead for U.S. entity setup and approval, and understanding that platform fees plus payment costs mean backers’ totals are not what lands in the bank.

Crowdfunding is framed as trust, not retail. Pre-campaign outreach, short campaign videos, roughly thirty- to forty-day timelines, stretch goals, and updates are presented as levers for a strong first day on Kickstarter’s homepage. Practitioners hear concrete lessons on backer geography, pre-orders with discounts, and keeping dialogue with backers who often know the product deeply.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Startup Valuation Controversy (T. Cytowski)
talks.teaser: Links sky-high startup valuations to VC incentives, lean metrics, geography, and early pricing as experiment runway.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by noting frequent disputes over how much young companies are worth, despite having no corporate finance training as a practicing lawyer working with venture capital and founders. He cites headline deals—Instagram, Snapchat, Nest, Oculus, WhatsApp—and Polish examples such as Estimote and Intel Clinic to argue that pre-revenue or story-driven companies still command large sums, and shares AngelList-style averages by accelerator pedigree, role, sector, and city from Poland through Silicon Valley.

He ties elevated prices to low interest rates and yield-seeking capital, the digital transformation of traditional industries, and the limits of market, asset, and income approaches when software lacks profits or physical collateral. Investors, he argues, prize long-horizon growth verticals, conversion, retention, engagement, scalability, and virality; Paul Graham’s view that early valuation is mainly a staging metric fits financing experiments rather than bank-like ROI. Portfolio math—most bets failing while one must return enough for the fund—explains black-swan hunting, ownership-driven pricing, dilution across rounds, and his closing claim that founder–investor alignment can inflate numbers.

Q&A covers downsides of high valuations versus control and dilution, liquidation preferences from simple non-participating terms to later participating structures, practical early-range reasoning including time sheets, services-for-equity bands, and structuring legal work via nominal purchase rights rather than fixed percentages.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Why People Hate Analyzing Data? (A. Kurasinski)
talks.teaser: Examines resistance to data analysis amid ubiquitous data capture, using audience polls and network-science localization predictions.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by framing how much data people create and leak without noticing, from social networks and phones to smart TVs, wearables, and games. He argues that analyzing data feels optional or frightening even though modern life constantly transmits information.

He cites Albert-László Barabási’s work with a mobile operator, predicting where people would be over the next days from one to three days of location history at about ninety-four percent accuracy. He then runs three live audience polls: most attendees use some analytics tool, fewer know a basic metric such as bounce rate, and only a small fraction have configured goals—patterns he says repeat at many conferences. He contrasts free, powerful tooling with interfaces that resemble airliner cockpits and with habits like lottery play that abandon clear odds.

He closes by urging listeners not to fear the unknown, to start thinking about their data, and to analyze what they can so they better understand their businesses and themselves.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Talent Acquisition - Success of Failure? All Depends on Your People (D.Bizer)
talks.teaser: Five recurring startup hiring failures are unpacked with culture examples, bar-setting, and lessons on candidate experience.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that startup hiring often fails in predictable ways, and reframes the session around five reasons teams underperform at recruiting. Each point ties to observations from years of working with young companies: unclear company identity, weak role definition, rushed decisions after fundraising, compromised hiring bars, and recruiting treated as a side task among busier priorities.

The middle of the talk uses stories to make those ideas concrete. Messaging and values should shape how candidates understand the firm, not only investor pitches. Perks can impress visitors without reflecting daily culture; small office details may tell a truer story. The speaker contrasts slow, mistake-prone rushing with the need to accelerate when a strong candidate is hooked, describes long candidate experiences at a former Austin employer (including tailoring visits to personal interests), and discusses explaining technical tests and longer on-site evaluations.

The close stresses that great companies concentrate intensely on people, with investors reportedly seeing better scaling where that focus holds. Hiring is hard and draining, yet persistence matters. Practitioners should clarify what they want each hire to achieve within a year, keep a short list of target people, stick to standards, and give recruiting enough attention to move strong candidates through without losing momentum.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Creating a Culture That Provokes Failure And Boosts Improvement (B. Dressler)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Bitspiration 2014: Creating a Culture That Provokes Failure And Boosts Improvement (B. Dressler).

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: When Idea Meets Money: How To Survive In a World of Numbers (T. Drosio)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Bitspiration 2014: When Idea Meets Money: How To Survive In a World of Numbers (T. Drosio).
talks.summary: Thomas Drosso recounts how Zortrax, a Polish 3D printer maker, paired product hype with staged financing from Kickstarter, domestic corporate bonds sold in hours, and later larger bond tranches to fund R&D scale-up. He argues finance teams belong beside CEOs and investors, not in a separate Hogwarts caricature, and that founders must read statements even when numbers feel tedious. Lessons include documenting equity splits early, avoiding paying vendors with equity, outsourcing inventory risk, and building cushions for surprise costs. He pushes simple forecasting tools: explicit budgets, revenue targets, complete cost lists, break-even math, and contingency reserves he nicknames a pillow. Drosso warns that only a fraction of European startups survive a year, often because cash ran out without financial strategy, and urges pairing product roadmaps with finance roadmaps before chasing IPO dreams.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Lean Investments in an Oil Fueled Economy (E. Sand)
talks.teaser: Outlines lean investment practices for Norwegian tech startups facing oil-economy constraints and a thin angel-investor base.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with Norway’s resource-heavy economy, where oil and fish absorb much innovation energy while tech founders lack mentors and capital compared with larger markets. The speaker describes an investor-side organization that backs portfolio companies with a SWAT-style team, lean board practices, and committed capital outside a traditional fund structure, where backers may decline individual deals.

Lean investing is framed as betting after problem–solution and product–market fit, often skipping earlier rounds through bootstrapping, then adding capital incrementally at the scaling moment. Pre-deal work includes investor dinner clubs, automated inbound deal funnels, and active venture scouting at conferences and demo days. Transactions emphasize speed: predefined deal frameworks, light diligence, early go-or-no-go interest, and structures tying equity to forward customer or revenue targets with buyback options.

After funding, the focus shifts to US mentors and accelerators, demanding engaged investors, transparent online collaboration, simple KPI dashboards, and a “law of three” for objectives, experiments, and metrics. A hardware audio startup example shows how repeated small checks unlocked loans, grants, and European distribution POs. Crowdfunding complements the model; the closing message urges entrepreneurs to seek small, active investors who enjoy participating, not passive stock watching.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Home intelligence - Reimagine The World Around You (R. Han)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Bitspiration 2014: Home intelligence - Reimagine The World Around You (R. Han).

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Learn Faster, Understand Better, Decide Quicker (A. Patryas)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Bitspiration 2014: Learn Faster, Understand Better, Decide Quicker (A. Patryas).

talks.title: JDD14: Real Big Data (S. MacGregor)
talks.teaser: Surveys Akamai's big-data stack from collection through SQL monitoring, security analytics, and multi-petabyte log archives.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames big data as applications that keep outpacing the platforms built to serve them, using Akamai's own footprint as the anchor example. Roughly 150,000 collector nodes worldwide feed billions of jobs daily; volume reaches multi-petabyte queries for reputation work, velocity around 50 million transactions per second, and wide variety across logs, metadata, and unstructured feeds.

It contrasts batch map-reduce style jobs on static stores with online processing at producers, then walks core primitives: collection over many protocols, parsing into key-value pipelines, time and hash partitioning, statistical filtering such as top-k sketches and Bloom filters, throttling to protect the mesh, merge-sort aggregation with large volume reduction, and completeness tracking plus integrity checks before billing. Concrete systems include petabyte-scale billing pipelines, the SQL-facing Query monitoring tree, columnar media analytics, a thousand-node security stack feeding reputation and threat products, and a 45-day log archive indexing hundreds of petabytes with probabilistic client-IP sketches and high query latency.

The close maps common goals to the Apache Hadoop ecosystem—HDFS, Hive, HBase, Spark, Kafka, and related tooling—and sketches forward work: 100× scale, wide-area Hadoop, automated DDoS mitigation, low-latency collection at enormous cardinality, and DevOps-grade realtime control. The implicit takeaway is that most value still lies in new Java-driven applications atop mature primitives, not in replaying the same infrastructure story.

talks.title: PLNOG13: SDN or Open Contrail Network Virtualization (N. van der Smagt)
talks.teaser: Covers open-source OpenContrail datacenter overlays, multi-tenancy, service chaining, and OpenStack integration.
talks.summary:
The presentation contrasts heavily marketed proprietary SDN approaches with a simpler goal: scalable, automated datacenter networks that stay programmable and avoid vendor lock-in. It walks through classic tiered datacenter designs, the pain of complex Layer 2 control planes, growing east-west traffic, and why multi-tenancy is awkward when VLAN and routing separation must be bolted onto aggregation and core layers.

OpenContrail is introduced as Apache-licensed network virtualization software that builds a Layer 3–centric overlay on ordinary switches, using tunnels such as MPLS over GRE or UDP (and optional Layer 2 modes) while the control plane exposes NETCONF-based open interfaces plus analytics. Multi-tenancy is described in MPLS VPN terms—separate forwarding tables per customer with firewalls, load balancers, and other services attached via policy rather than dedicated hardware per tenant. A live-style OpenStack example shows virtual networks, gateways for Internet or external reach, and service insertion including firewall VMs chained between front-end and back-end networks.

Later sections cover physical-datacenter MPLS VPN integration where hardware allows, high-availability scale-out, orchestration with OpenStack and CloudStack, and using the same overlay for fine-grained security policy between many small networks instead of monolithic perimeter firewalls. The closing argument is operational: commodity switching, centralized policy, elastic service instances, and full source access so teams can adapt the stack to their own datacenter.

talks.title: PLNOG13: User Defined Network (J. Wosz)
talks.teaser: Shows how a telecom operator can sell on-demand virtual firewalls to business customers using software-defined networking.
talks.summary:
The speaker, from an integrator team, opens with the pressures telecom operators face: services losing appeal, competitors reacting quickly, and the need to scale a new offer without buying large hardware. The talk asks what an operator would need to deliver network functions on demand, such as data centre servers, a network controller and a virtual router, and proposes a portal where customers order services with a few clicks.

The middle of the talk walks through a proof-of-concept lab. A virtual next-generation firewall is ordered from the portal and takes roughly 90 seconds to start. Routing protocols link the controller, the virtual router and the physical router, so traffic from a business customer's site is steered through the firewall instance. Usage reporting shows per-user activity such as web categories, and the speaker notes that some parts still need manual setup, including default-route handling and some limits on linking out of the box.

The closing takeaway is commercial as much as technical. The integration works by exchanging prefixes over BGP, and the speaker argues operators must first check whether a service will sell. A small initial batch of instances and a targeted campaign can test demand before larger investment.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Peering Session (LINX, TPIX, PLIX)
talks.teaser: Three internet exchanges review membership growth, platform monitoring, and new peering locations plus service options.
talks.summary:
The session chains three short operator briefings introduced as a peering block for LINX, TPIX, and PLIX. The LINX segment notes a quiet build period focused on running the network rather than major expansion, then walks through scale figures: roughly twenty years on the market, nearly 550 members across dozens of countries, growing application volume, on the order of 1,350 customer-facing ports split between 10G and gigabit capacity, aggregate connected bandwidth near 2.1 Tbit/s, and hundreds of BGP prefixes on the platform. Traffic charts show seasonal dips but long-term growth, and the speaker describes publishing availability statistics only after validating an in-house method that places inexpensive dual-gigabit probe hosts on every edge switch, exchanging continuous UDP tests so probes spread across bonded 10G paths and surface loss in a day-wide matrix. They cite roughly 99.999% availability on the sixth decimal field, a U.S. links segment without outages, a new London-area POP with a U.S. partner and possible 100G, and regional footprints in Manchester, Scotland, and Wales with some fiber delays.

The TPIX portion stresses hardware upgrades toward 100 gigabit readiness and a virtual cross-connect style service for private multipoint exchange among operators beyond classic public peering. It reminds attendees of 10 gigabit options in Warsaw locations, “lite” 10G pricing when committed traffic stays modest, service bundles from prior meetings, interconnection to other European exchanges, and discounted paths toward TPNet where Orange access allows.

The PLIX update covers a neutral colocation and peering business after a corporate rename, roughly 360 Gbit/s backbone traffic with gradual improvement, replacing core switches with Black Diamond X8 gear and refreshed branding, unchanged port promotions, hundreds of colocated switches and added datacenter space, a new Wars access point tied to acquiring Varion Telecom, expanded colocation near former Netia territory with multiple carriers present, and new staff joining from that integration.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Network Function Virtualization - operatorskie sieci przyszłości (D. Koralewski)
talks.teaser: Details NFV on shared servers, SDN differences, orchestration stacks, and a four-stage maturity ladder to dynamic chains.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by defining network function virtualization as a way to deliver networking capabilities through virtual machines on a common server platform, rather than scaling stacks of dedicated appliances for each function. Virtual firewalls, routers, and similar services can share infrastructure, grow with demand, and shift resources when traffic spikes, such as during major sporting events.

The middle section contrasts NFV with SDN, describes ETSI-driven standardization among operators, and walks through a reference stack: bare metal, hypervisors, virtual network functions, controllers, and orchestration layers including an NFV Director-style operational plane. A four-stage maturity ladder runs from appliances on dedicated hardware through virtualized VNFs, automated scaling, and—not yet widely seen—end-to-end dynamic control across the service chain. Examples cite operator initiatives around cost control, traffic engineering, proactive maintenance shifts, geographic load distribution, and blends of virtual routers with physical switching for CDN and enterprise footprints.

Practitioners should treat NFV as a cross-functional program, not a pure technology swap: strategy, processes, and product boundaries matter as much as virtualization. Offered planning workshops stress aligning business goals with technical steps. Closing discussion notes that generic servers suit many early operator workloads, while high-throughput cases can pair virtualization with SDN steering into specialized or high-performance hardware when scale demands it.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Wirtualizacja CPE w środowisku SDN / NFV (A. Kruszyński)
talks.teaser: Explains how operators virtualize customer premises equipment using SDN and NFV to deliver scalable home and SME services from the cloud.
talks.summary:
The presentation outlines virtualizing customer-premises equipment within software-defined and network-functions-virtualization architectures aimed at broadband and mobile operators. It situates the design among controllers, transport networks, and data centers, contrasting OpenFlow-centric device management with approaches that integrate legacy protocols alongside open-source platforms such as OpenDaylight and Ericsson’s service controller for subscriber access.

Operators face pressure to move beyond bit transport, yet rolling out new services on traditional CPE remains slow and costly because homes host many device generations and upgrades hurt availability. The proposed model keeps the home unit as a simple relay while security, parental controls, storage, and similar capabilities run in the operator cloud, configured in real time through a customer portal and centralized orchestration.

Benefits include faster service activation, fewer truck rolls, richer offers for consumers and SMEs, and partner-delivered add-ons that increase stickiness. Closing discussion acknowledges live operator projects, elastic data-center scaling, and audience concerns about demand forecasting and privacy when household traffic is processed off-premises.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Wywiad z Marcinem Stadnikiem
talks.teaser: A CDN vendor representative outlines content-delivery priorities, PLNOG sponsorship motives, and Kraków hiring growth.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens at PLNOG in Kraków with Marcin Stadnik from Akamai describing the company as a global CDN platform focused on getting rich web content to end users on many device types. He stresses that as media grows heavier, the time required for delivery becomes a central problem their customers need solved.

He explains why Akamai became a platinum conference partner: opening a Kraków office about three years ago aimed at hiring experienced engineers, expanding that site, and building partner and customer relationships in Poland. He compares PLNOG with other events such as Confidence and a planned autumn NASK Secure appearance, highlighting PLNOG’s mix of deeply technical attendees whose knowledge extends beyond pure networking as especially valuable for a deeply technical vendor.

On recruiting, he says hallway conversations skew toward network engineers and other technical roles, with some business contacts. The Kraków site employs roughly two hundred people today, with more growth expected the following year. He frames the main challenges as scaling the firm and strengthening presence across central and eastern Europe, treating Poland as a developing market reached through hiring, partners, and end customers rather than a pure sales pitch from his own role.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Wywiad z Mateuszem Konkolem
talks.teaser: An integrator executive outlines telecom integration, cloud trends, and the value of an industry-neutral operator conference.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens in Kraków during the thirteenth edition of a Polish operator networking conference. Mateusz Konkol from Infradata explains that the company began as an integrator focused on telecommunications operators, where the network is the core business platform rather than a supporting tool. The firm has since expanded into finance and the public sector while staying focused on large network builds and telecom-oriented security around network access and resources. He also describes growth toward cloud computing, virtualization, and SDN, including tools that bridge telecom layers with application stacks and move network functions onto servers.

He summarizes recent conference presentations: lessons from deploying a nationwide video transport network for a cable operator, with tight timelines, in-service migration of television from an old network, and more than sixty sites nationwide; forward-looking sessions on SDN and Contrail-based virtualization; and ways operators can offset falling transmission prices through node-based services such as parental control, DDoS protection, and content injection.

On partnership with the event, he stresses keeping quality high, preserving a vendor-neutral industry forum, and using the format chiefly to meet peers and exchange experience across vendors, integrators, and customers. He notes growing participation from niche suppliers and hopes future editions regain more decision-maker and policy-oriented panels alongside the technical program.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Wywiad z Rafałem Szewczykiem
talks.teaser: An industry partner describes DDI and network management work plus security growth and conference sponsorship rationale.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens at PLNOG in Kraków with questions about what Infoblox does. The guest describes the company as working in two intertwined areas: DDI services—DNS, DHCP, and IP address management—and broader network management, with a growing security portfolio that recent campaigns emphasize.

On sponsorship, he explains that Infoblox has been the main partner of the event for multiple consecutive years through cooperation with Pro Idea. Investment is driven mainly by brand visibility and customer awareness of products, not a one-off appearance. Compared with other conferences such as Cisco-oriented events, PLNOG is strongly focused on the service-provider sector while also moving into enterprise; that alignment fits offerings tied to carrier markets. He notes that current and potential customers visit the booth and can exchange experiences freely, including about Infoblox and other partners, which he treats as the conference’s core value.

Looking ahead, goals include deepening security solutions for service providers while pushing further into finance, the public sector, and general enterprise. Existing strength among service providers is positioned as a reference for convincing other sectors to adopt the same tools.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Wywiad z Sylwestrem Chojnackim
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning PLNOG13: Wywiad z Sylwestrem Chojnackim.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Wywiad z Wojciechem Ehrenfeldem
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of PLNOG13: Wywiad z Wojciechem Ehrenfeldem.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Podczas konferencji PLNOG13 przeprowadzono wywiad z Wojciechem Ehrenfeldem, związanym z branżą IT i portalem Onet od 15 lat. Rozmowa skupia się na jego doświadczeniu w budowaniu oraz zarządzaniu infrastrukturą jednego z największych polskich portali internetowych, wyzwaniach operacyjnych związanych z ruchem sieciowym, a także trendach technologicznych, takich jak migracja infrastruktury i przyszłość komputerów stacjonarnych.

### Key Topics
- **Doświadczenie i rola w Onecie**: Praca w portalu przez 15 lat, przejście od zarządzania całą infrastrukturą i budowy platform do obecnej roli odpowiedzialnej za budowanie i dostarczanie rozwiązań dla partnerów zewnętrznych oraz klientów.
- **Wyzwania utrzymania serwisu**: Wpływ skali ruchu i incydentów na życie zawodowe i prywatne. Zmiana priorytetów działów utrzymania: od samego działania serwisu do zapewnienia najwyższej jakości treści i zaangażowania użytkowników w obliczu rosnącej konkurencji.
- **Przyszłość urządzeń stacjonarnych (desktop)**: Refleksja na temat tego, czy era komputerów stacjonarnych się kończy. Ehrenfeld ocenia, że standardowe komputery nie znikną, zachowując swoją rolę w 8-godzinnym dniu pracy, choć rano i wieczorem są coraz częściej wypierane przez inne urządzenia.
- **Transformacja infrastruktury (Cloud i usługi)**: Przejście od marketingu dostawców do realnej zmiany sposobu świadczenia usług. Infrastruktura staje się powszechnym dobrem, porównywalnym z prądem czy dostępem do internetu, co skutkuje realizacją zadań w dużych projektach zamiast małych lokalnych wdrożeniach.
- **Plany konferencyjne**: Udział w wydarzeniach branżowych w Warszawie (na początku października) oraz planowane uczestnictwo w kolejnej edycji konferencji infrastrukturalnej w kwietniu.

### Technical Details
- **Skala i operacje**: Obsługa bardzo dużego ruchu na portalu Onet wymagała szybkiej reakcji na awarie i incydenty, również poza standardowymi godzinami pracy. Kluczowym wskaźnikiem jest zapewnienie odpowiedniej jakości dostarczania treści w warunkach wielokanałowej konkurencji (telewizja, inne platformy internetowe).
- **Trendy rynkowe**: Na rynkach rozwiniętych (amerykański, angielski, irlandzki) infrastruktura IT podlega komiodytyzacji i standaryzacji (utility model), przesuwając ciężar z lokalnych serwerowni w stronę scentralizowanych modeli chmurowych/usługowych.

### Takeaways
- Złożona infrastruktura wielkich portali wymaga dbałości nie tylko o dostępność (uptime), ale przede wszystkim o jakość doświadczenia użytkownika (user engagement).
- Komputery klasy desktop nie znikną całkowicie z rynku pracy, ponieważ pozostają najwygodniejszym narzędziem operacyjnym w standardowych godzinach pracy biurowej.
- Infrastruktura teleinformatyczna przechodzi głęboką transformację, stając się usługą powszechną (utility), co sprzyja konsolidacji w dużych platformach kosztem małych, lokalnych projektów.
