talks.title: JDD2014: JEE'ish development without hassle (J. Marchwicki)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning JDD2014: JEE'ish development without hassle (J. Marchwicki).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at JDD 2014, Łukasz Marchwicki explores alternative, lightweight architectural approaches to Java Enterprise (JEE/Spring) web development. He addresses common industry tendencies where development teams repeatedly rely on heavyweight monolithic stacks and complex frameworks like Spring or full JEE application servers for basic web applications and database access. Marchwicki argues that while full-stack frameworks offer rapid initial development via convention and annotations, they often obscure the underlying mechanics, leading to fragile code, difficult debugging, and suboptimal performance. By deconstructing a standard ToDo application into lightweight, lower-level components, he demonstrates how using focused micro-frameworks and libraries can reduce cognitive overhead, speed up testing, and deepen developers' technical comprehension.

### Key Topics
- **Corporate Mindsets and Architectural Inertia**: Teams often adhere rigidly to historical practices, complex XML configurations, and monolithic frameworks simply out of habit or organizational policy, even when building simple CRUD services.
- **The Hidden Cost of High-Level Abstractions**: Heavy dependency injection, magic annotations, and ORM mapping (like Hibernate) hide HTTP processing, servlet mechanics, and SQL queries. When exceptions or performance bottlenecks arise, developers without foundational understanding struggle to diagnose issues.
- **Separation of Concerns and Tool Selection**: Selecting targeted, purpose-built libraries instead of monolithic frameworks allows developers to tailor solutions to specific needs, such as using lightweight SQL mappers for reporting while keeping domain logic distinct.
- **Sharpening the Saw (Technical Growth)**: Getting closer to "the metal"—writing explicit SQL or defining basic HTTP handlers—serves as an educational tool that helps engineers understand how enterprise platforms actually operate underneath.

### Technical Details
To demonstrate alternatives to heavyweight stacks, Marchwicki contrasts standard Spring and JEE solutions against multiple lightweight combinations using a sample ToDo backend connected to MySQL:
- **Dropwizard**: Combines proven ecosystem libraries (such as Jersey and embedded Jetty) with minimal glue code, avoiding extensive boilerplate while retaining clean separation and fast boot times.
- **Sql2o & DBI / JDBI**: Lightweight database libraries that bypass full ORM complexity. Instead of abstracting away SQL into entities, they map native SQL query results directly onto plain objects. Sql2o provides high performance and low overhead, which is particularly beneficial for in-memory or fast integration testing.
- **MyBatis**: Offers declarative SQL-to-object mapping with support for transactions without imposing full ORM assumptions, making it well-suited for complex queries, reports, and mixed-access patterns.
- **Spark Framework & JOOQ**: Demonstrates micro-framework routing similar to Ruby's Sinatra, coupled with JOOQ’s typesafe query DSL, allowing programmatic construction of SQL without full framework weight.
- **Webbit**: An event-driven, single-threaded HTTP/WebSocket server that starts in milliseconds, giving complete control over request handling and HTTP headers, which significantly accelerates integration test execution compared to deploying to traditional application servers.

### Takeaways
- **Match Tools to the Problem**: Not every enterprise problem requires an all-encompassing framework; simple microservices and targeted endpoints can be implemented faster and cleaner with focused tools.
- **Understand the Fundamentals**: Stepping outside high-level abstractions enables engineers to better understand HTTP protocols, connection lifecycles, and relational database mechanics.
- **Optimize Testing and Feedback Loops**: Lightweight servers and direct database utilities allow rapid, standalone test setups that avoid lengthy application server deployment times.
- **Cultivate Engineering Mindsets**: Mentoring new developers through hands-on interaction with lower-level layers fosters deeper problem-solving skills rather than reliance on framework-specific tutorials and Stack Overflow debugging.

talks.title: JDD2014: Uwierzytelnianie i zarządzanie sesją w Java EE (P. Bucki)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD2014: Uwierzytelnianie i zarządzanie sesją w Java EE (P. Bucki).
talks.summary:
### Overview
Podczas konferencji JDD 2014 Piotr Bucki (ówczesny CTO w j-labs) przedstawił zagadnienia związane z uwierzytelnianiem i zarządzaniem sesją w aplikacjach webowych, ze szczególnym uwzględnieniem środowiska Java Enterprise Edition (Java EE). Tematyka prelekcji nawiązuje do kategorii podatności Broken Authentication and Session Management sklasyfikowanej na drugim miejscu zestawienia OWASP Top 10.

### Key Topics
- **Fundamenty uwierzytelniania i sesji**: Trzy czynniki uwierzytelniania (co wiesz, co masz, kim jesteś), bezstanowość protokołu HTTP oraz implementacja sesji po stronie serwera aplikacyjnego (często w Javie identyfikowana przez ciasteczko JSESSIONID).
- **Wektory ataków**: Ataki typu brute-force (słownikowe, hybrydowe na hasła i klucze sesji), podsłuchiwanie sesji (session sniffing), ataki replay, session fixation (utrwalenie sesji) oraz kradzież sesji (np. przez Cross-Site Scripting lub fizyczny dostęp).
- **Bezpieczeństwo haseł**: Zasady konstruowania polityki haseł, bezpieczne przechowywanie w bazie danych (skróty, sól per użytkownik, sekrety globalne) oraz prawidłowa implementacja procedury odzyskiwania hasła.
- **Zarządzanie sesją i ciasteczkami**: Ochrona identyfikatorów sesji, unieważnianie sesji, wymagane atrybuty ciasteczek (Secure, HttpOnly, ograniczenia domeny i ścieżki) oraz wymóg ponownego uwierzytelniania przy operacjach krytycznych.
- **Frameworki i ochrona infrastrukturalna**: Rozwiązania wbudowane w Java EE, Spring Security oraz Apache Shiro, a także rola systemów IDS, IPS i WAF.

### Technical Details
- **Session Fixation**: Atak polega na podesłaniu ofierze linku z ustalonym identyfikatorem sesji. Jeśli serwer zaakceptuje nieznany klucz sesji i nie zregeneruje identyfikatora po poprawnym uwierzytelnieniu użytkownika, atakujący przejmuje dostęp do konta.
- **Przechowywanie haseł i kodowanie**: OWASP rekomenduje stosowanie soli per użytkownik wraz z funkcjami skrótu. Prelegent zwrócił uwagę na kwestie kodowania znaków w Javie (np. wywołania `getBytes()` na hasłach z polskimi znakami), co w procesie aktualizacji aplikacji może prowadzić do problemów z logowaniem.
- **Obsługa błędów i brute-force**: Odpowiedzi serwera nie powinny zdradzać, czy błędny był login, czy hasło. Szczegółowe komunikaty powinny trafiać wyłącznie do logów serwerowych. Wśród metod mitygacji brute-force wymieniono: wprowadzanie sztucznych opóźnień odpowiedzi, blokowanie kont po nieudanych próbach, czasowe ograniczanie po adresach IP oraz nietypowe loginy.
- **Konfiguracja ciasteczek sesyjnych**: Ciasteczka sesyjne powinny mieć ustawiony atrybut `HttpOnly` (uniemożliwiający odczyt z poziomu JavaScriptu) oraz flagę `Secure` (dla połączeń szyfrowanych). Powinny być powiązane ze ścisłą domeną/ścieżką i wygasać wraz z zamknięciem przeglądarki.
- **Walidacja po stronie serwera**: Prelegent przestrzegł przed weryfikacją stanu zalogowania wyłącznie po stronie klienta (np. flaga w kodzie JavaScript przesyłana na serwer), co umożliwia ominięcie zabezpieczeń.

### Takeaways
- Nie należy implementować własnych mechanizmów kryptograficznych i sesyjnych od zera; należy korzystać ze sprawdzonych frameworków (Java EE, Spring Security, Apache Shiro).
- Konieczne jest regularne weryfikowanie używanych bibliotek, frameworków i serwerów aplikacyjnych pod kątem znanych podatności i instalowanie poprawek.
- Istotne jest całościowe podejście do bezpieczeństwa: bezpieczne przechowywanie haseł nie ochroni systemu przed innymi podatnościami, takimi jak XSS czy błędy w sterownikach JDBC.
- Należy bezwzględnie weryfikować uprawnienia na serwerze, stosować Code Review oraz zadbać o rzetelne logowanie zdarzeń aplikacji.

talks.title: JDD2014: QA to AQ: Shifting from Quality Assurance to Agile Quality (J. Yoder)
talks.teaser: The session shows how agile teams embed quality early instead of deferring security, performance, and usability to release time.
talks.summary:
Organizations that adopt Scrum, TDD, and short sprints often validate user stories and functional behavior while pushing security, performance, scalability, and usability to the last possible moment. The presenter argues that misunderstands agile values: change and working software matter, but the responsible time to address system qualities is usually much earlier, before architectural rework dominates the schedule.

The middle of the talk contrasts quality control gatekeepers with quality woven through the whole team, drawing on manufacturing analogies, startup constraints, and a Caterpillar financial modeling project where late security requirements forced painful refactoring. Practical patterns include breaking cultural walls between QA and developers, embedding QA in cross-functional teams, putting qualities on the backlog, running quality-focused sprints, and using lightweight stimulus–artifact–response scenarios with targets, acceptable ranges, and dashboards.

Practitioners are urged to be agile rather than ritualistically “do agile,” mixing fast delivery with deliberate slow thinking in planning and pairing. Usability and complex fraud-recovery stories may need manual or near-production setups; simpler metrics can often be automated. Combining several quality techniques beats relying on one silver bullet. The closing message is that everyone on the team owns quality from the start, prioritizing the qualities that matter most under real time and resource limits.

talks.title: JDD2014: Strategiczna refaktoryzacja (M. Bartyzel, M. Sieraczkiewicz)
talks.teaser: Coaches explain daily versus strategic refactoring, legacy context, metrics, and patterns that contain decay while evolving large systems.
talks.summary:
The presenters, who coach development teams at BNS IT, argue that large-scale refactoring is primarily an organizational undertaking, not a purely technical one. They separate quick, local “daily” refactors from “strategic” efforts that need planning, backlog space, testing, and sustained team agreement over weeks or months.

They warn against treating legacy code as proof that earlier authors were incompetent, and instead urge reconstructing why decisions made sense at the time. Discovery work includes talking with sponsors and developers, challenging stated wishes against real constraints, using root-cause thinking when architecture symptoms mask process problems, and aligning on a shared view of system building blocks. Code structure, commit patterns, quadrant-style hotspot analysis, and tools such as Structure101-style views help prioritize where change might pay off.

A second theme is stopping further decay before heroic rewrites: basic structural order, cautious use of heavy architecture models in mixed teams, and recognizing when technical mess is reinforced by organizational habits—including workarounds everyone knows are wrong. They describe interface partitioning on enormous classes, shifting team language before removing hacks, branch by abstraction, strangler-style ports, anti-corruption layers, and bubble contexts for incrementally isolating new models. They close by stressing a deliberate team process for proposing, estimating, and approving architectural change rather than ad hoc refactors.

talks.title: JDD2014: Pragmatic Pair Programming (K. Szabelski)
talks.teaser: Shows how pair programming works in practice, including mentoring and quick-help variants, and the pitfalls that make teams drop it.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that Agile teams often focus on process frameworks such as Scrum, while Extreme Programming supplies the engineering practices needed to build software that can absorb change. Pair programming is one of the least popular of those practices, often joked about, yet the speaker, an internal technical advisor, has used it for months. He frames the goal of a development team as delivering working software the client needs on time, and says pairing supports that goal by raising code quality, building team skills and breaking down project silos.

He separates three forms of pairing. Classic driver and navigator pairing suits complex problems with many edge cases. Mentoring through pairing means the mentee types and the mentor only prompts with questions, which he finds an effective and motivating way to teach a newcomer. The third form is a brief quick-help session, where a colleague looks at the code much like a rubber duck would. He notes that published research on pairing gives inconsistent results, so teams should test the practice themselves. He also warns about pairing on tasks that are mostly reading documentation, about navigators who only check syntax, and about mentors who grab the keyboard.

Common obstacles include invading personal space, heavily customised setups, unfamiliar keyboard layouts and people who do not believe in the practice. His remedies are to plan sessions in advance, agree on a keyboard-switching rhythm such as every 5 to 10 minutes, set clear break and end times, and provide a neutral workspace with enough room for two people. He suggests that sessions beyond about four hours become exhausting.

talks.title: JDD2014: Conversation Patterns for Software Professionals (M. Bartyzel)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD2014: Conversation Patterns for Software Professionals (M. Bartyzel).

talks.title: JDD2014: The Responsible Developer (T. Sundberg)
talks.teaser: Argues that a responsible developer favours small steps, shared learning, clean tests and frequent deployment over heroics.
talks.summary:
The talk asks what makes a developer responsible and starts by ruling out the superhero or the firefighter who sets the fires they later put out. Instead, the speaker describes an ordinary programmer with a passion for the craft who wants to do good work. Responsibility is framed mostly as a mindset: accepting change, dividing problems into small parts, and communicating with teammates and customers in the customer's own terms. The agile manifesto and the simple design rules serve as reference points.

Much of the middle covers practices. Simple code is preferred over clever code, and pair programming and mentoring are presented as the best ways to learn and share code ownership, with the rubber duck idea shown as a way to understand a problem by explaining it. Test-driven development and readable tests act as a safety net for refactoring, which should happen in small steps without asking permission. Building in vertical slices with walking skeletons, and a Unix pipeline example, illustrate how to grow a system incrementally.

The closing part argues for delivering value often through small, frequent releases. Continuous integration, keeping the build green, feature switches that hide unfinished work, and automated deployment are presented as the enablers. Deploying late on a Friday is discouraged. The talk ends with honest estimates, a software craftsmanship manifesto, and concrete actions: try test-driven development and pair programming, and share a pet project on GitHub.

talks.title: JDD2014: Crazy Fast Builds or When 10 Seconds Starts to Make You Nervous (D. Bodart)
talks.teaser: Shows how slow Java and Scala builds were cut from minutes to seconds by restructuring tests, libraries and tooling.
talks.summary:
The talk, presented by D. Bodart, argues that build times tend to creep upward as projects mature and that a slow build should not be accepted as normal. Because a build is a developer's main feedback loop, every extra minute slows each change. The speaker shares an experience report from several Java projects and libraries, including one where a 45-minute build was cut to three minutes by extracting parts into separate libraries, and another that dropped from 30 minutes to two.

Many of the techniques target tests. Moving slow tests into a separate build is criticised as a way of ignoring the problem. Sorting tests and sharding them across 16 cores, each with its own database, took one team's build from about 1.5 hours to 20 minutes. Contract tests against interfaces, with in-memory implementations used in most tests, and removing repeated login steps from acceptance tests also cut run time. Lazy initialisation in Spring reduced one test's setup from 14 seconds to one second, and embedded Jetty on dynamic ports let web tests start in milliseconds. For build tools, a Scala project's clean build of 56 seconds fell to 6.9 seconds after a rewrite in Java.

The talk closes by suggesting that teams treat folder layouts and artifact formats as contracts, serve artifacts from static file hosting such as S3 behind CloudFront, and weigh faster hardware against developer time. The speaker stresses that every change must be measured on the project at hand, since his figures may not carry over to other codebases or machines.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Openstack, Ceph, SDN (A.Heczko)
talks.teaser: Explains how OpenStack, Ceph, and software-defined networking fit together when building operator-scale private clouds.
talks.summary:
The session speaks to network operators and others with mixed cloud experience. It contrasts public, private, and hybrid models, then makes the case for OpenStack in production—particularly high availability and pairing with Ceph as hypervisor-attached storage that can scale toward very large data sets without proprietary SAN-centric designs.

The core maps familiar OpenStack pieces: Keystone for identity and the service catalog, Nova on KVM or other hypervisors, Glance for images, Cinder with pluggable backends, Neutron as the SDN layer with many vendor plugins, and Horizon as the operator portal. Ceph is described as a software cluster with monitors, configurable replication on pools, and tuning through tiering and caching. Networking coverage emphasizes Neutron plus Open vSwitch—DHCP, distributed L3 routing to avoid a single network bottleneck, security groups, load balancers—and a reference HA layout using virtual IPs, load balancing in front of controllers, and Galera for the database.

Takeaways stress cloud-native operations: no reliance on virtual CD-ROM workflows, provisioning through cloud-init and configuration management, and health checks that exercise OpenStack APIs so the platform is validated as a whole. A brief live instance launch illustrates the path from image to console. Questions at the end address when simple VLAN networking is enough versus full SDN, integration with operator switches, collecting the large log volume instance builds create, and stretching Ceph across datacenters for backup-oriented disaster recovery.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Making It Rain: Crowdfunding Stories (K. Boladz, M. Furtak, A. Targosz, S. Tam)
talks.teaser: A discussion shows how crowdfunding platforms and DIY sites turn nos into validation, customer insight, and funding for products and art.
talks.summary:
The session opens with an Indiegogo representative describing crowdfunding as a practical answer to chronic rejection from banks, investors, and advisors. He argues that campaigns deliver value beyond cash: early customer dialogue, packaging and pricing experiments, proof of demand for controversial hardware, and stories where cause-driven projects funded high-visibility media in days. He outlines how a large open platform operates globally, surfaces merit-driven momentum, offers flexible funding options, and expects founders to run active month-long outreach rather than passive pages.

Panel members add contrasting paths. A 3D printer company representative recalls a Kickstarter that far exceeded a six-figure target, shifting the firm from a handful of prototypes to mass production while exposing gaps in pre-launch marketing. A musician describes crowdfund­ing a studio budget through a hand-built bilingual site, a single bundled perk price, and traffic drawn only from existing fan channels, with optional creative fan engagement instead of broad paid ads.

Audience questions probe promotion tactics, whether backers face fatigue as platforms grow, how bands with tight timelines can still build audience, and how repeat campaigns differ for artists versus product firms. Closing contrasts highlight learning-oriented platform features, buying multiples for retail interest, and hosting mirrored campaign pages on a custom domain. The through-line for practitioners is to define success as validation and relationships, invest sustained marketing during the live window, and apply backer feedback before locking design and packaging.

talks.title: JDD2014: Import allegro.tech.internal.* czyli budowanie zaplecza technologicznego (A.Dubiel)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in JDD2014: Import allegro.tech.internal.* czyli budowanie zaplecza technologicznego (A.Dubiel).

talks.title: JDD2014: The Mythical 10x Developer (M.Gruca)
talks.teaser: Walks through practical productivity habits for developers, from desk setup and Pomodoro focus to imposter syndrome.
talks.summary:
The talk questions the idea of the mythical 10x developer, the programmer who seems far more productive than everyone else, and asks what it takes to become one. M.Gruca starts with the workspace: keep the desk tidy, invest in good hardware such as an SSD, a solid keyboard and an adjustable desk, and automate builds, deployments and dependency management instead of doing them by hand. He also stresses ergonomic seating and how to set up a chair properly.

The middle of the talk covers procrastination, which he links to the brain's preference for instant rewards, and distractions such as news feeds and social notifications. He shares a capture-and-review workflow adapted from David Allen's GTD: write everything down in a trusted place, review it weekly, and finish any task that takes about two minutes straight away. His toolset includes a paper notebook, a calendar, Evernote, Pocket and Trello. He describes Pomodoro sessions of 25 minutes, the flow state, and quiet hours that protect focus. For habits, he used a bullet-journal style chain calendar and later an RPG-style habit app, and he cut his daily reading goal to a single page to keep it sustainable. He also suggests tracking time and batching email.

The closing part covers health, such as limiting coffee and energy drinks and switching off screens before bed. He then discusses imposter syndrome and the Dunning-Kruger effect, encouraging developers who have delivered real value to recognise their skills. His final message is that sharing knowledge through blogs, user groups and talks makes a developer more valuable, and that a team of capable developers scales like a 10x developer.

talks.title: JDD2014: Effective refactoring (W. Krakowski)
talks.teaser: Blends live IDE refactoring on a rental-pricing example with habits that help teams sustain code quality under delivery pressure.
talks.summary:
The session frames refactoring as a disciplined way to balance shipping working software with keeping the codebase readable, testable, and extensible. Stories about a goose that lays golden eggs, a press run without maintenance, and the split between product and production capability warn that chasing output alone eventually erodes the asset that produces it.

Most of the running time is live coding on the familiar movie-rental pricing example in Java. With tests green, a long customer statement method is broken apart through extract-method, inlining, signature changes, and moves onto rental and movie types. Pricing logic lands in a calculator class and interface so new movie types and strategies add less duplication. The presenter stresses running tests after each step, knowing when to stop for a fire drill, and climbing a pyramid where renames and small extracts happen often while patterns stay rare.

The narrative links these mechanics to an effectiveness mindset drawn from Covey’s habits: act in your circle of influence, begin refactors with a clear goal and safety net, treat cleanup as important rather than merely urgent, pursue win-win with the business, understand teammates before pushing design, use reviews for joint improvement, and pause to sharpen skills. Brainstorming answers shift from listing management prerequisites to concrete actions individuals can take so refactoring becomes habitual rather than a postponed backlog item.

talks.title: JDD2014: 10 things I'd tell my younger self about (Java) Web Development (M. Kwaśniewski)
talks.teaser: Shares ten lessons on choosing Java web libraries, covering HTTP abstraction, concurrency, dependency injection, templates and testing.
talks.summary:
The speaker revisits his early years as a Java web developer, when he chose frameworks mostly by book reviews and narrow options. His first rule is that a web library should not hide HTTP: status codes, headers and request objects should be first-class, and developers should learn HTML, CSS and JavaScript properly. He then compares the thread-per-request model with the single-threaded event loop used by Node.js, suggesting event-driven designs suit I/O-heavy orchestration while number crunching does not belong on that loop.

Dependency injection, embedded servers and tooling come next. Containers are optional, he argues, since explicit argument passing works for most applications, except for onboarding into a large monolith or writing a reusable library. He suggests separating object wiring from scope, and recommends embedded web servers started from a main method, which keep development and production identical and let functional tests run in the commit build. He also favours logic-less templates that can be tested without a container, logs written to standard output, and tests that send request objects directly to the application.

He closes with dependency hygiene. Every jar on the classpath becomes the team's problem, so dependencies should be chosen deliberately, and he suggests a small resolver that avoids transitive dependencies. His final message is to question why each library is used and what problems it actually solves. He encourages developers to look under the hood of attractive projects and to learn from people who do things differently.

talks.title: JDD 2014: Jak wciągnąć eksperta domenowego w wir modelowania - techniki DDD (S. Sobótka)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for JDD 2014: Jak wciągnąć eksperta domenowego w wir modelowania - techniki DDD (S. Sobótka).

talks.title: JDD2014: Java.util.concurrent czyli wielowątkowość z różnych perspektyw (T. Łabuz)
talks.teaser: Shows how java.util.concurrent pools and server-managed concurrency keep overloaded Java applications stable under load.
talks.summary:
This talk covers multithreading in Java applications, from the java.util.concurrent package to threading inside Java EE application servers. The speaker starts with the practical problem: many simultaneous users overload a server, exhausting database connections, CPU and memory, so the application slows down or stops responding. He notes that extra hardware does not always fix this, citing a system where four servers were added to two without improvement because the design was the bottleneck.

For standalone Java code, the talk covers ExecutorService pools with a fixed size, Callable and Future for collecting results without blocking, and the Fork/Join framework with RecursiveTask for splitting large computations across cores. In Java EE the speaker advises against creating raw threads, since the server should manage them. The server-side options include pooled EJB instances with size and timeout settings, singleton beans guarded by read and write locks, and the managed executor services added in Java EE 7, which let the server track threads and keep transaction and security context.

A live load test compared unbounded threads, where 60 concurrent tasks ran the server out of memory, with a capped executor, where the server stayed up and extra tasks waited in the queue. For long-running reports, results can be written to a database or a return queue so users retrieve them later. The takeaway is to limit concurrent work to what the machine can sustain and to let the container manage threads.

talks.title: JDD2014: Real Life Lambdas (P. Lawrey)
talks.teaser: Walks through real migrated code to show which Java 8 lambda and stream patterns work well and which to avoid.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at lambdas in production code rather than toy examples. The speaker describes a client project that was porting a C# application of about 25,000 lines to Java 8, where roughly 2,000 lines were lambda-based. Many lambda examples seen earlier seemed contrived, so the focus is on code that came out of this translation, including parts that looked elegant and parts that looked awkward.

The patterns that worked well include a one-line check for whether any element matches a predicate, composing comparators across several fields in a single chain (including reversed ordering), and grouping map values with filters. Problem cases included side effects inside lambdas, such as altering a map passed in from outside or throwing an exception from a lambda. Reduce was used to sum BigDecimal values, which needed a second method to support parallel streams. Anti-patterns covered collecting to a list only to stream it again, sorting before grouping into a HashMap that does not keep order, and chaining several sorts where one composed comparator is clearer. A word-frequency example combined flatMap, groupingBy with counting, parallel and a limit of 20.

Optional was often unwrapped straight back into null checks, which defeats its purpose. In questions, the speaker suggested utility helpers for common filter, sum and split patterns, pointed to Guava as an existing source of helpers, and warned that parallel streams require thread-safe collections. Tooling that flags these mistakes was described as still limited.

talks.title: JDD2014: Spring 4, Java EE 7 or Both? (I. Grimstad)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD2014: Spring 4, Java EE 7 or Both? (I. Grimstad).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at JDD 2014, consultant Ivar Grimstad compares Spring Framework 4 and Java EE 7, analyzing their evolution, feature sets, architectural differences, and how they interact when combined in enterprise applications. The talk walks through the historical trajectory of both ecosystems—from the early complexities of J2EE to the developer-friendly improvements in Java EE 5 through 7, alongside Spring's rise as an alternative that has now reached version 4. Grimstad presents live code examples to demonstrate the mechanics and pitfalls of integrating Spring components inside a Java EE application, as well as incorporating Java EE components within a Spring-based application.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Enterprise Java and Spring**: A review of J2EE's initial complexity, the emergence of Spring in 2002–2004, and the modernization of Java EE (culminating in Java EE 7) focused on developer productivity, HTML5 support, and enterprise features.
- **Spring 4 Features**: Overview of improvements including enhanced documentation on spring.io, Java 8 compatibility (supporting `@Repeatable`, lambda expressions, and method references via callback interfaces), core container updates with generic injection qualifiers, `@RestController` for REST endpoints, WebSocket and STOMP messaging support, and caching enhancements.
- **Java EE 7 Capabilities**: Updates highlighting lighter configuration without mandatory `web.xml` or `beans.xml`, simplified EJBs, JMS 2.0 API cleanups, batch processing, JSON processing, and WebSocket support across certified application servers (GlassFish 4.0.1, WildFly 8.1, and TmaxSoft).
- **Architectural Contrasts**: Java EE relies heavily on the underlying application server container to implement specifications, while Spring packages its context and container directly inside the application artifact.
- **Cross-Framework Integration**: Hands-on techniques using CDI producers to expose Spring-managed beans within Java EE, and conversely using `@EJB` annotations or Spring bean definitions to ingest Java EE components into Spring.

### Technical Details
Grimstad demonstrates both frameworks using simple REST counter applications:
- **Integrating Spring into Java EE**: When adding a Spring component with `@Autowired` dependencies into a Java EE application, a CDI producer (`@Produces`) must not simply instantiate the object directly via `new`. Direct instantiation bypasses Spring's lifecycle, causing autowired dependencies to fail or produce incorrect results. Instead, the producer must initialize an `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext`, register the configuration class, refresh the context, and retrieve the bean explicitly so that Spring manages the dependency graph.
- **Integrating Java EE into Spring**: When bringing a Java EE component (such as an EJB) into a Spring application, injecting it requires accessing the container using `@EJB` or configuring a Spring bean definition. If an EJB does not rely on enterprise container services, Spring can manage it as a standard bean; however, if the bean strictly relies on EJB container-provided functionality (such as transaction management), letting Spring take over can break expected container behavior.

### Takeaways
Grimstad emphasizes that while Spring 4 and Java EE 7 solve similar problems and have substantial feature overlap, mixing both frameworks in a single project should generally be avoided. Java EE provides leaner WAR packaging and faster deployments due to shared container dependencies, whereas Spring offers portability by packaging its own context. If integration is unavoidable, Grimstad advises hosting Spring components inside a Java EE application rather than injecting Java EE components into Spring, and always ensuring that beans remain managed by their native runtime context.

talks.title: JDD2014: REST API Versioning Practice: From Header to Model (Ł. Wierzbicki)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of JDD2014: REST API Versioning Practice: From Header to Model (Ł. Wierzbicki).
talks.summary:
### Overview
Łukasz Wierzbicki presents a practical engineering perspective on REST API versioning, drawing directly from experiences at Kontakt.io. Facing a rapidly evolving startup environment where new API versions had to be delivered every three to four weeks while supporting thousands of external clients with production mobile apps, the company needed an architectural approach that avoided breaking contracts and minimized code duplication.

### Key Topics
- **API Versioning Challenges in Fast-Paced Startups**: Balancing rapid iterations (delivering updates every 3–4 weeks) with backwards compatibility guarantees for third-party client applications published in app stores.
- **Core Architecture Assumptions**: Keeping core business logic version-agnostic (avoiding sprawling `if`/`switch` statements inside business rules), versioning at the controller level, and keeping object-to-view serialization transparent.
- **Architectural Approaches Considered**:
  1. *Top-to-Bottom Duplication*: Duplicating controllers, services, repositories, and models across versions. Simple to understand for newcomers, but leads to massive, unsustainable code duplication.
  2. *Single Model with Explicit Converters*: Maintaining a single backend model and using explicit converter classes to map models to versioned view object hierarchies. While reducing model code, it introduces high maintenance overhead for class hierarchies when fields are removed or modified.
  3. *Dynamic Proxies (View Factory)*: Using runtime dynamic proxies (e.g., via `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`) with annotations and providers to map fields and inject synthetic view properties not present in the backend model.
  4. *Map-Based View Factory (Chosen Solution)*: Employing a lightweight factory that transforms domain models directly into structured maps based on version configurations. The resulting map is serialized into JSON/XML transparently by serializers like Jackson.
- **Pragmatic API Design vs. Pure REST**: Intentionally diverging from pure RESTful design and HATEOAS by relying strictly on `GET` (for fetching data) and `POST` (for operations/verbs in URLs like `/update` and `/delete`).

### Technical Details
- **Header-Based Versioning**: Versioning metadata is passed through the HTTP `Accept` header rather than via URL paths.
- **Configuration Options in Map View Factory**:
  - *Includes*: Specifying explicit lists of fields (including dot-notation traversal of nested objects) to copy from domain model to map.
  - *Excludes*: Omitting specified fields, though noted as risky when maintaining numerous versions since newly added model fields might accidentally leak into older API versions if not explicitly excluded.
  - *Generated Fields (Providers)*: Creating view-specific computed fields directly at response generation time without polluting domain entities.
  - *Field Renaming/Mapping*: Aliasing model property names to match client expectations for a specific version.
- **Partial Resources**: Allowing clients to request only the specific fields they need (e.g., asking for 3 fields out of 15), reducing response payloads.

### Takeaways
- Versioning strictly via header or URL is often an aesthetic or operational choice, though URL-based routing can simplify external reverse proxying and caching.
- Minimizing redundant class hierarchies via dynamic map-based view generation drastically reduces maintenance burden.
- Adding fields to payloads without a version bump is not always backwards compatible, as poorly configured client deserializers (such as unconfigured Jackson mappers) can fail on unexpected fields.
- Maintain clean boundaries between versions in the codebase so that obsolete versions can be cleanly deprecated and deleted without complex refactoring.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Taking Your Startup To The Next Level (M.Sadowski)
talks.teaser: Delivers a playbook for scaling a Polish SaaS startup globally with viral video, Twitter, remote sales, and practical acquisition tools.
talks.summary:
The presenter, CEO of a social media monitoring company, describes building a profitable Polish customer base of nearly 500 paid accounts since a 2011 launch, then expanding with an Asian offering and a recent worldwide product release. He argues that breaking through advertising noise requires memorable campaigns, citing a customer welcome video that reached roughly 200,000 views and drove inbound interest.

The middle of the talk emphasizes engagement on Twitter as the main channel for international signups, turning users into unpaid advocates, and keeping pitches short. He contrasts costly U.S. travel that yielded no immediate sales with forty new global subscribers acquired remotely in the first two months, and recommends YouTube and SlideShare for discoverable educational content alongside a subscription revenue model.

Closing sections recommend Gmail plugins for tracking opens and enriching leads, live chat and in-product messaging for conversion, and a more open startup culture. He cites Polish firms and the WhatsApp founder story to encourage founders to pursue global ambitions despite skepticism.

talks.title: JDD2014: What you won't read in books about implementing rest services (J. Kubryński)
talks.teaser: Validated caching, hypermedia links, header-based versioning, and OWASP parser hardening show why tutorial REST APIs fail in production.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by assuming the audience already knows REST constraints and the Richardson maturity model, then contrasts formal rules with practices that actually govern maintainable APIs. He walks through POST versus PUT and PATCH, including partial updates with Jackson in Spring MVC, and explains why cache-control semantics matter more than legacy pragma headers. A DevSkiller story shows how missing cache headers left Internet Explorer serving stale AngularJS results after deployments, and why copying Stack Overflow values can mark authenticated responses as public and leak data through CDNs.

Hypermedia comes next: Spring HATEOAS link builders, location headers on 201 responses, meaningful 4xx bodies, hiding stack traces, and logging Spring MVC mapping failures through a custom ResponseEntityExceptionHandler. He argues against version segments in URLs, favors Accept headers for representations, and suggests modeling complex searches as POST-created search resources with cacheable IDs for pagination. He also reframes “stateless” as avoiding business context in sessions while noting Spring’s default session creation and the cost of per-request password hashing.

The closing segment ties REST choices to OWASP-class risks: HQL injection despite Hibernate, CSRF on state-changing GETs, careless CORS with wildcard origins, and XXE entity expansion that can read files or exhaust memory on current WildFly defaults. The takeaway is that tutorial-grade APIs are not production-ready; teams must validate caching, headers, sessions, and parser behavior before shipping.

talks.title: JDD2014: Scala, approachable functional programming (T.Bjerkestrand)
talks.teaser: Shows how Scala eases into functional programming through pure functions, immutable data and a quicksort rewritten functionally.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Scala as a gentle route into functional programming, since it blends object-oriented and functional styles and lets developers start with code that looks much like Java. The speaker covers its strong static type system, collection library, pattern matching, expression-oriented syntax, and its ability to run on the JVM so that existing libraries and build tools still work. Pure functions are defined as functions with no observable side effects, and referential transparency is illustrated with a substitution example. A contrasting case with a mutable string buffer shows how in-place state changes break that property.

The speaker advises favouring vals, immutable collections and case classes, and keeping I/O, exceptions and console output at the edges of a program around a pure core. Much of the session is a live rewrite of an imperative quicksort. The comparator is turned into a function type, and the loops are replaced with filter and recursive calls. Folding, reduce, map and flatMap are compared using a minutes-counting example, showing when foldLeft is needed instead of reduce.

The final section introduces algebraic data types through a sealed trait for comparison results, so the partition step can walk the collection once using pattern matching on tuples. The closing part points to where to learn more, including a free online course from Scala's creator, the official project site, and a note that Scala jobs are becoming more common.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Standard 802.11e, a usługi multimedialne w sieciach bezprzewodowych (S.Pasternacki)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in PLNOG13: Standard 802.11e, a usługi multimedialne w sieciach bezprzewodowych (S.Pasternacki).
talks.summary: Sebastian Pasternacki contrasts pre-2005 Wi-Fi without WMM against IEEE 802.11e mechanisms: AIFS, arbitration interframe spacing, four access categories mapped to DSCP, and transmit opportunities that favor voice queues. He live-reads Wireshark WMM elements from PLNOG’s own WLAN, warns that multicast at absurd mandatory rates breaks HD streaming, and ties admission control to protecting voice under load.

talks.summary: Krzysztof Otrębski shares Ocado lessons splitting HTTP, vendor, and application logs, using mapped diagnostic context to disentangle parallel requests, and building the open-source Lox log viewer with grep-friendly filtering, colored formatting, IntelliJ jump-to-code, and bookmarked investigation sessions for legacy systems without tests.

talks.title: JDD2014: Continous Delivery: Capitalizing High Quality Automated Tests (Sz. Faber)
talks.teaser: Shows how the Mockito project moved from releases every two years to automatic release on every push.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why a well-tested open-source mocking library was released only about every two years, and how its maintainer set out to make releases automatic. The core idea is continuous delivery as a mindset: each build should be treated as a potential release, and a change has no real value until it reaches users. Strong test code alone was not enough, because writing release notes was slow and the manual release steps kept getting postponed.

The approach described uses GitHub for source control, Travis CI for builds, and Gradle to orchestrate the build and publish binaries to Bintray. Each push to the main branch produces a new version, with release notes and documentation generated from commit messages and issue titles. Travis builds run on fresh, stateless machines, so credentials are stored as encrypted variables in the configuration file. A recent change skips publishing when the binaries are unchanged. The speaker also showed how a contributor's fix could be reviewed and released entirely from a browser.

The second half covers Gradle, which ships a release roughly every two months and runs nightly builds that do not go through the full validation cycle. The main challenges are slow feedback from a very large test suite, flaky tests, identifying which change broke a build, and selecting which tests to run. The speaker suggests a pragmatic stance on flaky tests, measuring how often they fail for the wrong reason, dry-running changes against dependent projects, and modelling dependencies across an organisation. The closing takeaway is to adopt these practices gradually, since code delivers no value until it is released.

talks.title: JDD2014: Agile Transformation in Real World (O. Rashid)
talks.teaser: A SaaS engineering group explains how it moved from waterfall releases to Scrum, with metrics and repeatable transformation patterns.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by asking how far the audience has moved toward agile, then frames the emotional mix of excitement and anxiety when leadership mandates a process change. He describes Oracle’s Taleo Business Edition talent-management SaaS: large customer base, high weekly transaction volume, single shared version, and a distributed team. The pre-transformation flow was waterfall-like, with late QA, a crunch from code complete to code freeze, split focus across releases, frequent post-release patches, and burned-out teams.

The team adopted Scrum with a deliberately sequenced release model: product development sprints for risky work with PM, dev, and QA aligned from the start; a dedicated bug-fix sprint for backlog defects; a product release sprint for integration and advanced testing; and a release stabilization sprint before the next cycle. Reported outcomes include far fewer production patches, fewer defects per patch, reduced priority-one defects, lower support incident spikes after releases, and improved customer satisfaction trends.

Closing guidance stresses selling holdouts with prepared objections, shared training, a cross-functional transition team that dogfoods Scrum while designing the blueprint, documented rationale for process choices, pragmatic compromises, real empowerment over commitments, and measured before-and-after metrics. The speaker notes the effort took on the order of two years from convincing upper management to operating in the new model.

talks.title: JDD2014: Co Twój kod mówi do Ciebie (M. Sieraczkiewicz)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of JDD2014: Co Twój kod mówi do Ciebie (M. Sieraczkiewicz).

talks.title: JDD2014: Game of throneware (J. Nabrdalik)
talks.teaser: Recounts a developer's move into management, covering office politics, team layout, decisions and communication.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a developer with more than ten years of coding experience, describes moving into a management role about nine months before the talk. He opens with a former lead who was younger than him but well suited to the job and was dismissed within two weeks, to show that managers should expect sudden change. The talk is presented as a set of practical, anecdote-based lessons from an engineer's point of view rather than a how-to guide.

The middle covers politics and communication. Engineers should steer proposals toward the group's shared goal instead of rejecting ideas outright, and ask whether a new technology fits the situation or whether a proof of concept could test it. One example shows a security team that blocked developers from installing tools on Windows laptops; the dispute was eased by an intermediary server that let developers reach production data without broader access. Team layout matters too: the speaker prefers team clusters with desks facing inward, and notes that a system tends to mirror the structure of the organisation that builds it. For decisions, he presents problems to engineers rather than prescribing answers, builds trust through honesty and transparency, and gives people authority along with responsibility.

The closing section covers self-organising teams. They still need a team lead to handle interpersonal conflicts, break ties and make calls when the group is stuck. Retrospectives help leaders find blockers, and time for innovation has to be protected. The speaker also suggests managers keep their own goals and find ways to stay motivated when they lose the deep focus of coding. The overall takeaway is to manage with honesty, clear reasons and deliberate structures.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Monitorowanie jakości usług w sieciach IP (P. Głaska)
talks.teaser: Network operators learn how probe results drive automated failover, backup DHCP, and adaptive bandwidth on carrier routers.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames service-quality monitoring in IP networks as something operators already know in outline—synthetic probes such as Huawei NQA, familiar from IP SLA or RPM elsewhere—and then shifts attention to what to do with the measurements. After a short recap of layered tests, including simple reachability checks and delay or jitter measurements that need cooperation on the far end, the speaker emphasizes policy actions on routers.

Those actions include bringing a standby interface online when a tracked path fails, shifting VRRP priorities, temporarily enabling local DHCP address pools when the real server stops answering probe requests, and switching DNS forwarding targets when resolvers go slow or silent. Further examples cover unreliable 3G dongles, adaptive shaping when loss crosses defined thresholds, SmartLink-style path selection, and mobile setups that prefer failing over tunnels before swapping SIM registration. The talk also contrasts synthetic probes with iPCA, which marks live traffic to expose per-device and per-path loss that customers feel even between probe intervals, and sketches newer control-plane collection plus a small USB measurement device for wider deployment.

Practitioners should leave with concrete patterns for binding measurements to automation rather than only to graphs, plus awareness of precision limits on the control plane, hardware-assisted probing where available, and the trade-off between synthetic tests and in-band telemetry when judging real user experience.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Be Early Adopter (Katarzyna Kalinowska)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Bitspiration 2014: Be Early Adopter (Katarzyna Kalinowska).

talks.title: PLNOG 13: NFV czyli wirtualizuj sieci albo zgiń - głos realisty (R. Ślaski)
talks.teaser: Surveys NFV adoption trade-offs, contrasting operator hype with data-plane limits, vendor sprawl, and licensing realities.
talks.summary:
The session is framed as a skeptical counterpoint to earlier NFV presentations at the same conference. Rather than teaching basics, it deepens the dilemmas operators face when moving from appliances toward virtualized network functions.

The speaker walks through typical adoption motives—lower cost, faster delivery, elasticity, and operational simplicity—and compares application virtualization to composing real network services. ETSI NFV materials, hype-cycle dynamics, and audience answers surface recurring themes: fashion, scale, and time-to-market. Gaps remain in open multi-vendor stacks, orchestration, and clickable service models. Buying a virtual router can mean four separate problem domains—hardware, hypervisor, VNF software, and integration—plus a different performance and staffing model than classic operations.

Much of the talk focuses on the data plane versus control and management planes. Workloads that lean on specialized silicon for forwarding, security, or timing often degrade on generic CPUs and hypervisors; lighter or edge cases may suit proof-of-concept virtualization better. Appliance pricing is dissected into support, branding, documentation, and intellectual property, including performance licenses on virtual routers. The closing message favors deliberate adoption: use virtualization where flexibility wins, retain hardware expertise where throughput and predictability matter, and avoid discarding network engineering when handing systems to developers. A second part was announced for nearer-term implementation topics.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: How Akamai scales to serve the largest events on the Internet (J. Kretchmar)
talks.teaser: Explains how a global content delivery network distributes live video to millions of viewers and absorbs sudden traffic spikes.
talks.summary:
James Kretchmar, CTO for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Akamai, explains how the company serves very large live events. He starts with the scale involved: the Sochi Winter Olympics streamed 98 events to a global audience, with a US-Canada hockey game peaking at 3.5 terabits per second and more than 2 million simultaneous online viewers. He then describes the FIFA World Cup, which reached 6.9 terabits per second at peak, with 5.3 million simultaneous viewers in the US alone for one match. Traffic at these events arrives in sharp spikes at kickoff, and the event sizes have grown sharply over just a few years.

The core of the talk is why scale depends on a highly distributed deployment. He compares a centralized data center, a moderately distributed setup of around 30 sites, and a deep deployment of thousands of servers placed inside many end-user networks, which avoids congested peering points. He explains why IP anycast alone falls short, since it does not measure real performance or account for congestion. Instead, DNS-based load balancing uses real-time measurements of latency, loss and load to steer each user to the best server, allowing utilization to approach full capacity and letting traffic be rerouted around network problems.

He argues that reliability and scalability are effectively the same problem. Servers built from commodity hardware share storage, use consistent hashing to reassign content when machines fail, and let neighbouring machines take over a failed server's address, so small failures do not cascade. He closes with future directions, including client SDKs, a hybrid HTTP and UDP protocol, multicast, and pre-positioning video-on-demand content before peak viewing times. The takeaway is that handling huge live audiences requires deep distribution together with a system that continuously measures and acts on network conditions.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Internet Traffic-Engineering with LISP (L. Iannone, W. Shao)
talks.teaser: Edge operators learn how LISP mapping beats BGP limits for inbound path quality and transit load balancing.
talks.summary:
The speakers open with two inbound traffic-engineering problems seen on a real edge network with dual transits. In the first case, BGP asymmetry sends much traffic over a slower transit, adding on the order of 80 milliseconds of delay for some remote autonomous systems and affecting hundreds of gigabytes of incoming volume; bubble charts highlight many remote prefixes paying more than ten milliseconds extra delay. Selective announcement, more-specific routes, and AS prepending are shown as blunt or unreliable BGP levers.

The second case pairs the same two transits with matching committed data rates while realtime and 95th-percentile utilization pin one link against its contract even though the other transit still has headroom; BGP again offers little safe way to shift only part of the load. A concise LISP primer follows: separating edge identifiers from core locators, on-demand mapping instead of global prefix flooding, and policy-driven associations that can follow delay, drops, or volume.

Applied examples use remote-prefix and group-specific mappings, locator priorities with failover, and load-balancing weights across transits or data-center paths. The close points to a French LISP lab, testing with Border 6, and OpenLISP on FreeBSD, with Q&A on explicit locator path drafts, working-group activity, and upcoming platform features.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Handling high-bandwidth-consumption applications in a modern DC design (A. Dacquay)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for PLNOG 13: Handling high-bandwidth-consumption applications in a modern DC design (A. Dacquay).

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Centralized Traffic Enginnering (J. Lucek)
talks.teaser: Contrasts centralized and distributed MPLS traffic engineering and outlines PCEP, BGP-LS, and a real-time controller design.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting shortest-path routing, distributed traffic engineering, and a centralized controller that sees the full demand matrix. Distributed computation hides competing reservations from other ingress routers, which produces classic LSP blocking, suboptimal hop counts under contention, and unpredictable path changes after maintenance events.

Centralized path computation is argued to enable global optimization, latency-aware cost functions, dynamic LSP splitting as volumes change, strict path diversity for point-to-point and point-to-multipoint services, bandwidth calendaring, and make-before-break maintenance workflows. The speaker then reviews protocol building blocks: Path Computation Element Protocol for computation, reporting, delegation, updates, and instantiation, including RSVP and SPRING signaling; and BGP Link State for real-time TE topology beyond IGP areas instead of per-area IGP peering or CLI scraping.

The closing section sketches a NorthStar-style controller with discovery, path computation, and provisioning pillars, analytics-driven feedback on traffic matrices, and northbound APIs for topology, computation, and provisioning. Practitioners should treat standards-based visibility plus control as the foundation for operable centralized TE, not optimization algorithms alone.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Running a 2 Tbps global IP network using Open Source tools (B.van der Sloot)
talks.teaser: Shows how a hosting network operator runs global backbone monitoring, capacity planning, and attack detection with open source tools.
talks.summary:
Fibering, the Dutch group behind the hosting brand LeaseWeb, presents its global IP network, which carries roughly 2.5 Tbps across locations in Amsterdam, Frankfurt, the US coasts and Singapore. The backbone is built on more than 10 transit providers, over 500 peers and connections at around 30 internet exchanges. A network design engineer explains four operational challenges the team faced and why it chose open source tools, given that it has no dedicated infrastructure staff.

For monitoring, the team combines Opsview and Nagios for alarms with custom RRDtool graphs and scripts that check BGP and IGP state. Aggregate graphs now hit file-handle limits because of the number of 10G interfaces. For capacity planning, NetFlow is collected with pmacct into MongoDB and queried through an in-house interface focused on destination traffic, which supports peering and cost decisions as traffic grows by about 120 Gbps a month. For attack detection, small distributed collectors write NetFlow dumps every 60 seconds, so the operations centre can use nfdump to find attack sources and destinations within minutes. Configuration backup moved from RANCID to Oxidized, with changes committed to GitLab so that git blame shows who edited a device.

The speaker is candid that these tools need constant hands-on work, such as disks filling almost daily. Planned next steps include time series databases such as InfluxDB, better log visualisation, more automation and a possible new network management system. The closing point is that a team of under 15 engineers can run an efficient global network, but finding people who understand both networking and programming is the hard part.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: IPv4 Transfers (A. Wolski)
talks.teaser: Explains how IPv4 address blocks are distributed and transferred in the RIPE region, from IANA history to today's exhausted pool.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how IPv4 address space reached the regional registries, starting with a single person handing out blocks in the early days of the internet and moving to a framework of five regional internet registries. It explains that RIPE NCC, a non-profit based in Amsterdam, carries out policies set by its community, and how the region's pool shrank to a final, limited allocation of a /22 per local internet registry.

The middle section looks at how organisations can still obtain space. Three routes are covered: mergers and acquisitions, where resources follow the business; transfers of allocations between LIRs, which can be permanent or temporary and are published by the registry; and legacy space, which sits outside the normal rules and needs contact with the registry to update its maintainer. Brokers and a transfer listing service that matches offers with requests are described, with the documents each route requires. The speaker notes that the registry checks who the parties are but does not judge the price paid, and that criminals forge paperwork to take over blocks, so hijacks are a real risk.

The closing part covers policy work in progress, including proposals for transfers between registries and for transferring provider independent space. The practical takeaway is to verify the current holder in the registry before buying space, to use brokers that have signed the registry's agreement, and to keep registry records current so that route objects still work after a change. Attendees are invited to bring policy ideas to the community through the policy development process.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Jak Akamai i Prolexic radzą sobie z atakami (D)DoS (P. Kuśmierski)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding PLNOG 13: Jak Akamai i Prolexic radzą sobie z atakami (D)DoS (P. Kuśmierski).

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Bezpieczeństwo Data Center w 2014 (G. Mikołajczyk)
talks.teaser: Reviews 2014 data center defenses: clustered firewalls, symmetric flows, and policy-driven application-centric networks.
talks.summary:
The session situates enterprise data center security in 2014 against a backdrop of lengthening breach detection times and widely publicized flaws in foundational protocols. The presenter frames security as a continuum spanning hardening before an incident, response while traffic is under attack, and retrospective cleanup once compromise is discovered—including the risk that virtualized desktops and private cloud become malware launch pads toward mission-critical zones.

The technical core addresses north–south protection for large, geographically spread facilities. Geographically clustered stateful firewalls (described at scales up to sixteen nodes) rely on a control plane, a director for session state, and deliberate flow symmetry so stateful inspection and intrusion modules see both directions of a connection. The talk walks through symmetric and asymmetric routing tricks, failure and recovery behavior, transparent layer-two deployment, and performance figures from live testing (connections per second and HTTPS inspection throughput). Integration of advanced threat and IPS capabilities onto the same platform is highlighted, along with design references for end-to-end data center blueprints.

The closing arc introduces application-centric, software-defined data center control: abstract contracts chain firewall, load balancing, and deep inspection without classic per-box wiring, including ideas for richer metadata on service paths and east–west filtering between workloads. Practitioners should leave with a concrete picture of why segmentation must be policy- and context-driven rather than purely VLAN-oriented, and how clustered edge firewalls and programmable fabrics fit a before–during–after security lifecycle.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Architektura nowoczesnego Centrum Danych (A. Gmaj)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of PLNOG 13: Architektura nowoczesnego Centrum Danych (A. Gmaj).
talks.summary:
### Overview
Prezentacja wygłoszona na konferencji PLNOG 13 koncentruje się na architekturze nowoczesnych centrów danych (Data Center) z perspektywy technologii sieciowych. Prelegent omawia dynamiczną ewolucję środowisk DC, w których tradycyjne, statyczne podejście ustępuje miejsca wysokiej elastyczności, dużej skali oraz wszechobecnej wirtualizacji zasobów i separacji wielu klientów (multi-tenancy). Głównym motywem wystąpienia jest wykorzystanie nakładkowych sieci wirtualnych (VXLAN) oraz architektur typu fabric (np. MetaFabric) do rozwiązania ograniczeń tradycyjnych przełączników L2.

### Key Topics
- **Wyzwania nowoczesnych Data Center**: Konieczność obsługi tysięcy portów, ograniczenie tradycyjnego standardu 802.1Q (zaledwie 12 bitów, czyli 4096 VLAN-ów), separacja ruchu wielu najemców oraz masowa migracja maszyn wirtualnych.
- **Technologia VXLAN**: Enkapsulacja ruchu i 24-bitowy identyfikator VNI (Virtual Network Identifier), który umożliwia tworzenie ponad 16 milionów sieci wirtualnych i odciąża tablice MAC fizycznych przełączników transportowych.
- **Koncepcja sieci Fabric**: Budowa struktur sieciowych typu single-hop (np. matryce Clos, Virtual Chassis Fabric), eliminujących wieloskokowe przełączanie i skalujących się do tysięcy portów.
- **Bramy integracyjne (VXLAN Gateway)**: Rola urządzeń łączących świat wirtualny z fizycznym oraz obsługa translacji L2/L3 przy użyciu dedykowanych układów ASIC (np. chipset Trio w routerach Juniper MX).
- **Fuzja sieci SAN i LAN**: Wyzwania związane z koegzystencją Fibre Channel (FC) oraz Fibre Channel over Ethernet (FCoE).

### Technical Details
- **VXLAN i kontrola ruchu**: Wykorzystanie enkapsulacji ethernetowej z 24-bitowym nagłówkiem. Zarządzanie mapowaniem maszyn wirtualnych do fizycznych hostów realizowane jest przez płaszczyznę sterowania (control plane) za pośrednictwem protokołów takich jak OVSDB (w rozwiązaniach VMware NSX) lub OpenFlow (w rozwiązaniach Contrail).
- **Ograniczenia sprzętowe**: Wielu dostawców opiera swoje przełączniki na chipsetach handlowych (merchant silicon), które miewają problemy z pełną translacją VXLAN na poziomie L3. Prelegent wskazuje routery Juniper z rodziny MX oraz dedykowany chipset Trio jako wydajne rozwiązanie do obsługi bramek VXLAN L2/L3.
- **Architektura Fabric i MetaFabric**: Przełączniki (takie jak Juniper QFX5100) wspierają różne typy struktur: od wirtualnego łączenia w pojedynczy logiczny przełącznik po routing IP Fabric oparty na siatce spine-leaf (Clos), zapewniając stałą liczbę przeskoków między dowolnymi portami.
- **Bezpieczeństwo i inspekcja pakietów**: Zwrócenie uwagi na konieczność stosowania wirtualnych firewalli aplikacyjnych zdolnych do dynamicznego podążania za migrującymi maszynami wirtualnymi (service chaining), zamiast statycznych zapór filtrujących jedynie porty L4.

### Takeaways
Nowoczesne centrum danych nie może być projektowane w sposób statyczny. Architektura musi zakładać ciągłą obecność urządzeń nielastycznych/fizycznych (konieczność stosowania gatewayów VXLAN i FC/FCoE) oraz dynamiczną orkiestrację ruchu przez SDN. Kluczowymi filarami skalowalnego i bezpiecznego centrum danych pozostają technologie VXLAN oraz architektury Fabric pod kontrolą centralnych systemów zarządzania i telemetrii.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: EVPN - rozwiązanie nie tylko dla Data Center (E. Gągała)
talks.teaser: Explains how EVPN replaces VPLS with BGP-driven MAC learning, active-active multihoming and VM mobility beyond data centers.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits a presentation the speaker gave three years earlier, when the technology was still called MAC-VPN and drew only a handful of listeners. EVPN is presented as a way to carry Layer 2 traffic across an IP network. It is compared with VPLS, which already provides full-mesh Layer 2 transport but relies on data-plane MAC learning and handles active-active links poorly.

The middle section walks through the protocol as if the audience were drafting a new standard. EVPN moves MAC learning into BGP, and four BGP route types carry auto-discovery, MAC and IP advertisement, multicast handling and Ethernet segment information. The Ethernet segment identifier enables multihoming, with loop prevention through designated forwarder selection and faster convergence through segment-level withdrawal. Further examples cover a distributed default gateway with ARP proxy, host routes for virtual machines, and MAC mobility signalled through sequenced updates, so traffic to and from a moved VM stays on an optimal path.

The speaker argues that EVPN is not limited to data centers. Many operator networks that offer Layer 2 VPN services can use it for their own transport or for customers, and it can interconnect data centers over MPLS, VXLAN or other encapsulations. The closing comparison places EVPN beside VPLS, showing how BGP gives operators finer control over routing and VPN policy. The practical takeaway is that EVPN is a viable option for service providers as well as data center operators.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: DNSSEC - Kryptografia w służbie bezpiecznego DNS (A. Obszyński)
talks.teaser: Explains how DNSSEC uses public-key signatures to authenticate DNS data, and why validation remains rare in practice.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces DNSSEC as a way to add cryptographic signatures to DNS data, so that resolvers and end users can check that records really come from the zone owner. The speaker starts from the weaknesses of classic DNS, which runs over UDP without verification and is easy to spoof or poison. DNSSEC does not encrypt anything, and its larger signed responses bring their own costs, including possible amplification in denial-of-service attacks.

The middle of the talk covers how the system works in practice. Zones are signed with a zone-signing key, which is itself signed by a key-signing key, and trust is anchored at the root and passed down through DS records. Authenticated denial of existence relies on NSEC and NSEC3 records, and plain NSEC can let anyone enumerate a zone. The speaker walks through how a signed zone grows, how keys are rolled over by pre-publishing new keys or signing twice, and why a DS update at the registrar can cause an outage. Test domains were used to show how a validating resolver fails on broken signatures, and browser plugins, the short-lived validation feature in Chrome and adoption figures for several countries were also discussed.

The closing part gives practical advice. Operators should enable validation on their own resolvers, make sure TCP 53 and larger DNS responses are not blocked, keep NTP running, and confirm how their registrar handles DS changes. The speaker's main point is that adoption is still low, so teams that deploy DNSSEC should test it and monitor its failures.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Rola informacji w nowoczesnych systemach bezpieczeństwa (P. Kędra)
talks.teaser: Maps network-centric warfare concepts onto firewall evolution, shared threat intelligence, and richer perimeter decision-making.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing network defense as an arms race between attack and protection, then borrows military ideas such as network-centric operations and power to the edge to argue that modern defenders need broad situational awareness, not isolated point controls. It walks through how firewalls evolved from packet filters to stateful devices and next-generation platforms that understand applications and users, often via directory integration, while also absorbing IPS, web filtering, and antivirus roles that once lived on separate appliances.

The middle section stresses that no single product stops complex, multi-vector attacks, cites limitations of relying only on edge controls or antivirus effectiveness, and outlines a typical threat lifecycle from infection through command-and-control and spread. The speaker describes enriching enforcement with security intelligence: geoIP context, attack fingerprints, application honeypots, shared C&C indicators, and custom allow or deny lists, fed through a central intelligence store into dynamic firewall objects, with examples such as blocking known C&C destinations or scoring traffic by geography.

The close extends the information theme to NAC on switches, SIEM correlation across logs and vulnerability data, and big-data style user-behavior profiling, while repeating that people remain the weakest link. Practitioners should treat firewalls as one layer in a complementary stack and invest in aggregating timely intelligence to policy decisions across the estate.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Doświadczenia z budowy sieci Video Transport Network (K. Bieliński, P. Sowa)
talks.teaser: A cable operator’s team shares how it rebuilt nationwide multicast video transport with MPLS trials, staging, and phased night migrations.
talks.summary:
Multimedia Polska needed a new video transport network because expanding HD channels and future 4K on a legacy Layer‑2, one‑gigabit plant would exhaust bandwidth within months. The speakers outline business drivers, technical goals—minimal customer impact, multi‑year growth, quick regional contribution feeds, higher reliability, and aggressive sub‑fifty‑millisecond protection targets—and the choice between scaling Layer‑2 versus a routed MPLS design with multicast VPN and PIM, including a simpler PIM‑only fallback with longer switchover times.

Before procurement they ran month‑long production trials across distant sites, comparing vendor approaches and capturing pitfalls such as low multicast TTL, IGMP report handling on Juniper MX routers, incomplete cross‑team documentation, and VLANs lost during changes. A formal tender followed, then parallel construction toward sixty‑five locations, a large Warsaw staging lab with real multicast and customer gear, and exhaustive testing that exposed optics, probe, and DHCP helper quirks.

Migration used three nightly service windows per week for about three months with a small core engineering team and dozens of field partners. They recommend production trials, staging at scale, concise per‑site implementation plans with photos, disciplined documentation, and pragmatic vendor cooperation—including contract incentives—over rigid dispute escalation.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Koncepcje inżynierii ruchu WAN z użyciem optymalizacji BGP (M. Viste)
talks.teaser: Outlines a three-stage flow, probing, and policy approach to steer WAN traffic over preferred BGP transits.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames everyday WAN operations where BGP picks paths using metrics that may not match reachability, latency, cost, or circuit capacity. Against a backdrop of very large global prefix tables, the speaker argues that most enterprises only exchange traffic with a few hundred destinations, so optimization should target those prefixes rather than the full table.

The proposed method unfolds in three layers. First, collect and aggregate flow with open tools such as pmacct so SQL can reveal which remote prefixes actually matter. Second, run active probing (for example toward hosts inside each important prefix) through every transit and store round-trip times, because quality shifts over time and may even vary by time of day. Third, apply simple logic—often a script—to map each important prefix to the preferred transit and push that choice to edge routers using BGP, optionally with common open routing stacks or libraries.

In practice, the speaker reports sizable reductions in access time to key destinations, better control over transit utilization, less waste on unused capacity, and clearer visibility into why paths change. The main trade-off is sustained engineering time to automate, validate, and operate the loop; teams short on time may adopt packaged offerings that implement the same pattern.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Platforma Value Added Services (K. Baniak)
talks.teaser: Explains how carriers consolidate video optimization, parental controls, and subscriber messaging on one shared traffic-steering platform.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a recurring operator dilemma: marketing pressure to launch value-added services quickly and cheaply, while each new offering historically meant more dedicated hardware, staff, and risk to core traffic availability. The speaker contrasts bolting on a new network element per service, doing nothing, and adopting a universal in-path platform that can host many services with incremental scale rather than repeated greenfield purchases.

A reference architecture is outlined for that platform. It must sit on high-volume subscriber traffic with load balancing and dynamic routing, integrate identity and application awareness across access methods, pull or host flexible per-user policy (including interfaces such as PCRF, LDAP, or REST), report and charge without choking capacity, and expose APIs for health monitoring, automation, and custom orchestration. Implementation centers on F5 BIG-IP, with modular scaling and iRules-style programmability; identity, policy delivery, and provisioning modules are shown in logical diagrams and an admin console.

Operational pitfalls include multi-datacenter steering, hairpinning versus replicating functions at many internet exits, and sizing from real session and HTTP rates rather than guesswork. Example services cover TCP optimization, video handling, URL and malware-oriented filtering, and enterprise HTTPS inspection where contracts allow. A live walkthrough creates subscriber sessions, applies bandwidth and conditioning policies, injects on-page ads and operator info panels, and triggers urgent notifications. Closing discussion stresses that lawful use depends on tariff and contract choices, and that full SSL interception into sensitive sites is a different privacy trade-off than HTTP-level injection.
