talks.title: PLNOG 13: Konwergencja xWDM oraz GPON na potrzeby podłączania klientów biznesowych (R. Ziemba)
talks.teaser: Shows how xWDM wavelengths layered on GPON let one passive fiber network serve both residential and business customers.
talks.summary:
This talk from PLNOG 13, given in Polish, covers bringing fiber directly into subscriber premises and using one access technology, GPON with xWDM overlays, for both home users and small and medium businesses. The speaker introduces Elmat, a Polish maker of passive fiber products that also supplies active equipment from Dasan Networks, and argues that operators running a mix of access technologies carry heavy costs that a single design can reduce.

The middle section explains how a business wavelength is added to a shared passive network. A WDM filter in the customer terminal blocks wavelengths it should not receive, while a passive module drops an extra channel to a dedicated business transceiver. Up to six channels are possible, though 10GbE modules rarely work above a 24 to 26 dB budget, so single-fiber designs are typical. Other points include protection types A to D, with a switchover under 50 milliseconds for type C, in-service software upgrades on dual control cards, bandwidth limits per terminal and per port, and RADIUS-driven provisioning that keeps the last configuration if the server fails.

The closing example is a shopping centre in Rzeszów with 200 retail units, each reached by a dedicated fiber run from a single OLT location. The speaker argues this lowers maintenance and avoids the cost of rebuilding copper cabling, and presents the approach as a practical model for business and residential access on one network.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Polityka bezpieczeństwa i kontroli (P. Wojciechowski)
talks.teaser: Explores corporate security policy lifecycles, role separation, audits, and change control as networks and threats evolve.
talks.summary:
The session frames corporate security policy as a living library of written rules, not informal training or generic internet templates. Policies must stay consistent across the organization while respecting local law, cover business processes beyond pure networking, and repeat a lifecycle of assessment, drafting, communication, implementation, and revision as technology and threats shift.

From a practitioner angle, the speaker walks through representative control areas such as internet and social use, mail monitoring, physical keys, mobile devices on corporate and data-center networks, visitor access, and NDAs. He stresses role-specific awareness, separation of duties between administrators, implementers, and security officers, and regular audits—internal roughly every six months and certification-driven annually in his payment-processing environment—distinguishing compliance audits from penetration tests that probe single weaknesses.

Audit work is described in four phases: preparation and scope, goal-setting, evidence gathering including interviews and log review, and reporting. Risk analysis and business continuity tie policy to cost, reputation, and acceptable trade-offs. Closing guidance favors unified document templates, explicit accountability, risk-based writing, controlled exceptions, clear communication, defined incident response, automated enforcement of configuration standards, and reporting weak links without blaming minor findings.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: HP Moonshot (M. Grabowski)
talks.teaser: Covers HP Moonshot software-defined servers, workload-tuned cartridges, and layered switching for high-density web hosting.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens at a network specialists’ gathering by arguing that Moonshot belongs on that agenda: shared enclosure networking, separation of management traffic, and workloads such as web hosting where network behavior often dominates CPU or memory limits.

Moonshot is framed as software-defined servers built from three ideas—dense modular enclosures, system-on-chip cartridges, and scale-out by adding physical nodes instead of scaling up single boxes. The speaker contrasts buying generic servers then layering applications with first defining the service, then choosing cartridge silicon (Atom, FPGA, and similar options). A 4.3U chassis can host on the order of 45 to 180 independent nodes plus enterprise switches, with dedicated management plane, dual paths per cartridge, storage fabric, cartridge-to-cartridge links, and newer direct neighbor connectivity.

Production examples include migrating dozens of rack servers to six Moonshot enclosures for hp.com-scale HTTP, HTTPS, and FTP traffic, reporting large power reductions while preserving performance. Cartridge lines for static web, dynamic web, and remote desktop are outlined, along with OpenStack-style orchestration mapping logical designs to hardware. Practitioners gain a workload-first sizing mindset and a picture of when dense, network-rich enclosures beat traditional racks for hosting and consolidation.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Ochrona prywatności (A. Piechocki)
talks.teaser: Maps Polish civil, labor, and telecom rules on personal data, correspondence secrecy, and lawful workplace monitoring for operators.
talks.summary:
The presentation structures privacy protection around three linked areas: personal goods under the Polish Civil Code, personal data processing rules, and the secrecy of correspondence. It walks through Article 23 and related statutes on data protection, electronic services, and telecommunications, including cookie rules, and explains civil remedies such as cease-and-desist, removal of effects, and compensation.

On personal data, the speaker discusses when identifiers such as IP addresses, email addresses, and names count as personal data, the broad meaning of processing, purpose limitation and adequacy, and legal bases including explicit consent. For employers and hosting providers, it covers labor-code limits, sensitive data, processing agreements when operators can access customer data, and heightened technical and organizational requirements when systems touch the public internet.

The second half focuses on correspondence secrecy and employer oversight, citing European Court of Human Rights practice and Polish labor law. Monitoring email, web use, decryption in serious leak scenarios, and CCTV must be lawful, work-related, transparent, proportional, and non-discriminatory; written employee consent is advised. Q&A clarifies moral-harm claims, limits on blanket private-mail review, lawful access for authorities only with a defined proceeding, and documenting CCTV notices in internal rules.

talks.title: JDD2014: JVM bytecode manipulation techniques for JVM "freaks wannabe" (J. Pałka)
talks.teaser: Explains how JVM bytecode is laid out and how libraries like ASM and Javassist let developers generate and modify it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that hand-writing JVM bytecode is tedious and error-prone, yet there are cases where frameworks fall short and developers need to generate or change bytecode directly. The speaker first covers the basics: the class file layout, including the magic number, constant pool, fields, methods and attributes, and the stack-based design of the JVM. He walks through a small method's instructions, showing how values move between the operand stack and local variable slots, how the different invoke instructions resolve methods, and how exception tables and jumps work.

The middle section compares libraries for bytecode generation and manipulation. ASM is presented as a low-level, visitor-based toolkit where the developer can have the library compute frame and stack sizes automatically. Javassist is shown as a higher-level option that lets code be written as Java source strings, which are compiled into the method body. Examples generate a class in memory, call it, and write it to disk, and show how a method can be wrapped or its behaviour replaced when the class is loaded.

The final part covers the java.lang.instrument API. An agent with a premain method receives an Instrumentation object and registers a transformer that can rewrite class bytes before they are loaded, and classes can be redefined at runtime. The speaker notes limits, such as core classes like java.lang.Object not being passed to the transformer. He also mentions tools that attach to running JVMs and use instrumentation in tests to simulate failures. The takeaway is that these techniques are powerful but are best reserved for cases where regular frameworks cannot help.

talks.title: JDD2014: Behaviour driven development, BDD, with Cucumber for Java (T. Sundberg)
talks.teaser: The session demonstrates behavior-driven development with Cucumber for Java through building subscribe and unsubscribe flows.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames behavior-driven development as a way to communicate expected system behavior to mixed audiences, contrasting declarative scenarios with imperative unit tests and noting when BDD complements test-driven development. He outlines collaboration among product owners, analysts, and testers through shared examples in Given-When-Then form, then walks through Cucumber’s architecture linking feature files, step glue, and production code.

Most of the session is live coding in Maven and IntelliJ IDEA: a Cucumber-JUnit runner, feature files for email marketing subscribe and unsubscribe, step definitions with regex capture groups, and a small Subscriptions class backed by an in-memory set. The work proceeds in small test-first steps—from pending steps and minimal assertions through email validation, storage, and unhappy-path checks—with commits pushed to a public repository during the tutorial.

The closing discussion argues BDD fits complicated, well-understood domains rather than spikes or chaotic crises, and that Cucumber is primarily a communication tool, not a silver bullet. A brief Q&A covers localized messages and when framework validation belongs in unit tests instead of feature files; extended web and persistence refactors are left for the published sources.

talks.title: JDD2014: Życie po wdrożeniu, czyli utrzymanie aplikacji (M. Berkan)
talks.teaser: Explores post-deployment application maintenance from a developer view, covering pitfalls, recurring issues, and client communication.
talks.summary:
The presentation reframes application maintenance as the phase when software actually earns money for the business, unlike costly pre-launch work. It opens with a cautionary story of a 2003 e-commerce deployment left with only a short warranty and personal phone support, which kept the author tied to legacy encoding and quarterly fixes for over a decade.

It then outlines why maintenance feels dull: higher production responsibility, frozen technology choices, harder hiring, repetitive tasks, elusive intermittent bugs, and client contact driven almost entirely by failures. Practical maintenance work spans library and database upgrades, regulated changes such as currency or citizenship rules, ticket handling, safe releases, and preventive log and monitoring review.

Common pain points include rarely used features breaking, broken cascade deletes on account removal, concurrency under real load, fragile environments after restarts, upstream API changes, data growth, and basic web security issues. Recommendations emphasize clear handover criteria—automated functional and integration tests, performance testing, security audits, and a hypercare period—plus honest client communication, proactive outage notices, documented procedures, planned on-call rotations, automation, and recognizing stable operation as success.

talks.title: JDD2014: TIMTOWTDI and Java (G. Rożniecki)
talks.teaser: Links Perl's TIMTOWTDI idea to Java verbosity, lambdas, and why teams should pick conventions and stick to them.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the speaker's path from Perl and JavaScript into Java, then explains TIMTOWTDI—there is more than one way to do it—as a core Perl idea from Programming Perl, contrasted with Python's preference for one obvious approach. Football anecdotes illustrate how roles can shift in rare situations, paralleling language flexibility for edge cases versus everyday work.

Perl examples walk through several equivalent for-loops, implicit topic variables, and postfix forms, plus how the community later favored consistency. Linguistic relativity and Hopi concepts of time frame how programming languages may shape thinking. Moose, Mouse, Moo, Mo, and Bow show Perl's many OO stacks and the trade-offs among speed, dependencies, and simplicity.

For Java, the talk covers syntax verbosity versus Scala, helpers such as Objects.equals and toString, Lombok and AutoValue, arrays versus lists, JVM languages, backward compatibility, the final keyword, Effective Java-style habits, and Java 8 lambdas as another valid style when a team agrees. The closing message is that multiple approaches are fine; documented, shared consistency matters more than which option wins a holy war.

talks.title: JDD2014: Reactive Java (T. Kowalczewski)
talks.teaser: Shows how RxJava streams and operators can replace nested callbacks and blocking calls in asynchronous Java services.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces RxJava, the Java reactive extensions library that originated at Netflix, and explains why event streams suit services that must stay responsive over slow networks and serve many kinds of devices. The speaker frames the problem with a screen that needs several dependent requests: in a synchronous model the user waits until everything is ready. The alternative is to push each piece of data to the client as soon as it is available, with the client subscribing to a stream of events and able to cancel that subscription when it no longer needs the data.

Most of the session is live coding. Starting from a static stream built from a list, the speaker applies filtering, mapping and throttling operators, then subscribes to receive the values. He shows that an error terminates a stream, that a retry re-subscribes and rebuilds the stream from the beginning, and that a fallback stream can take over after a failure, for example an empty stream when a database call fails. The examples then move to a live Twitter stream parsed into Java objects, where flatMap expands each item into its own asynchronous stream. A small desktop client connects a text input to a stream so that results update as the user types.

The closing part compares the model with Future and callback patterns and notes that throttling and backpressure need deliberate design between client and server. The speaker mentions that the library is used in production at large scale and points attendees to the project repositories for the code. The practical takeaway is that operator chains can replace deeply nested callbacks in asynchronous code, although the programming model takes time to learn.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in PLNOG 13: Programmable and Application aware IP/MPLS networking (J. Tantsura).
talks.summary: A PLNOG speaker traces programmable MPLS and segment routing with centralized controllers, arguing networking is entering another industry cycle toward business-driven forwarding state via OpenDaylight-style SDN.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: The Great ‘100G Metro’ Migration (S. Adhikari)
talks.teaser: Contrasts direct-detect and coherent 100G DWDM options for operators upgrading congested metro links from 10G.
talks.summary:
Metro traffic is outpacing long haul, pushing operators from 10G toward 100G DWDM while component markets shift revenue toward hundred-gigabit gear. The speaker frames the migration dilemma: when existing 10G mux capacity is full or customers demand 100G immediately, and which transceiver flavor fits distance and access versus core needs.

The core of the presentation contrasts DWDM direct detect modules—four-by-twenty-five-gigabit wavelengths, lower power, tunable options, and roughly twenty to thirty percent of coherent cost—with coherent reception from long haul, where DSP compensates chromatic dispersion and supports single-lambda 100G at higher power and price, often still as line cards rather than pluggables. Comparisons cover spectral efficiency, dispersion limits from bit-rate scaling, forward error correction margins, port density across CFP form factors, vendor lock-in for coherent gear, and interoperability testing with mixed 10G and 100G channels.

Architectures walk through overlaying 100G on filled 10G systems, full-channel 100G upgrades with amplification and dispersion compensation blocks, and OADM drop scenarios for intermediate sites. The closing message is that metro 100G adoption is gradual; planners must balance technical reach, budget, power, flexibility, and waiting for coherent pluggables against near-term direct-detect DWDM upgrades.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Optimising TCP in today’s changing network environment (B. Salaets)
talks.teaser: Explains how inline TCP optimizers lift mobile throughput and page loads when SSL blocks legacy caching approaches.
talks.summary:
Mobile operators face shrinking performance gaps versus rivals as more traffic moves to encrypted HTTPS, which breaks traditional video optimization, web optimization, and transparent caching. The presenter argues that tuning at the TCP layer can still improve roughly 90–95% of traffic because optimization sits below SSL and application protocols.

The talk walks through connection setup, acknowledgements, and congestion control, contrasting loss-based Reno with hybrid loss-and-delay algorithms that suit high-latency radio paths. Emphasis falls on bandwidth-delay product tuning, managing buffer bloat, distinguishing random radio loss from congestion, and raising initial congestion windows to cut slow-start round trips. A transparent in-line proxy behind the packet gateway lets operators tune the mobile leg separately from the low-latency internet side. Reported field tests cite meaningful throughput and web page load gains on 3G and 4G, including incremental benefit on top of Google's multiplexed HTTPS protocol, plus a case where identical speed-test throughput still hid harmful buffer latency.

Practitioners should treat page load time as latency-driven rather than raw bitrate, validate poor-coverage scenarios where gains spike, and plan deployment so encrypted traffic is not left on legacy port-80-only optimization paths.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Handling high-bandwidth-consumption applications in a modern DC design (A. Dacquay)
talks.teaser: Explains spine-leaf underlays, VXLAN overlays, and orchestration choices for scaling high-bandwidth data center cloud traffic.
talks.summary:
Enterprise data centers often maintain separate network silos for storage, virtualization, and cloud platforms, which weakens visibility and limits where heavy workloads can run. The speaker advocates a unified design: commoditized hardware, standard routing protocols on the underlay, and end-to-end automation so orchestrators can provision networking alongside compute and storage rather than leaving ports and VLANs manually configured.

Multi-tier hierarchies impose harsh oversubscription on east-west traffic, so workloads that move between racks lose performance compared with hosts in the same cabinet. A spine-and-leaf Clos fabric scales out by adding leaves and spines while keeping local switching on the spine tier. Flat Layer Two still collides with VLAN counts, shared MAC tables, and gateway throughput, so the talk separates a pure Layer Three underlay from a VXLAN overlay where tunnel endpoints encapsulate tenant Ethernet in IP and stretch subnets across rooms or sites. VTEP placement, broadcast handling via head-end replication, and tying overlays to cloud management APIs are walked through, including tradeoffs among all-in-one vendor stacks, demanding open-source builds, and mixed hardware plus software controllers.

The closing emphasis is agility: preserve best-of-breed choices, automate at scale with tooling familiar from the server world, and match routing and gateway design to tenant counts and VRF scale. Questions address tromboning versus localized default gateways, draft metadata extensions, and why customers still insist on Layer Two despite broader Layer Three adoption.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Orchestrated VNF-supported 100G Services (U. Wagner)
talks.teaser: Multi-vendor SDN and NFV orchestration is shown cutting metro service setup from weeks to hours via automated provisioning.
talks.summary:
Carriers historically needed many touchpoints and specialist handoffs to deliver customer Layer 2 services, with one European operator citing provisioning windows of up to forty days before automation. The speaker positions Sign/Cyan around 100G packet-optical transport and, more centrally, Blue Planet as production SDN and NFV orchestration across mixed estates that include Juniper, Cisco, RAD, and other third-party gear, with intelligence centralized in controller software and open APIs for customer-built provisioning flows.

The middle of the talk contrasts manual topology work with graphical end-to-end service design: EVPL-style metro circuits computed and pushed to hardware in seconds, MEF-related API exposure, and multi-domain control that spans WAN operations plus data-center and cloud resources on OpenStack, orchestrating virtual network functions such as virtual firewalls, encryption, and packet-core workloads. A shared demo recording walks through an ETSI-oriented Planet Orchestrate scenario: drag-and-drop VNF placement for Fortinet firewall and Certes encryption on RAD NFV-capable nodes, automatic discovery and stitching of Layer 2 paths between sites, EMS-driven policy control, optional firewall-only or encryption-only combinations, and Wireshark on an NNI port showing fully encrypted Layer 2 frames.

For network operators and integrators, the through-line is service agility—hours instead of weeks, fewer truck rolls for distributed CPE functions, and one orchestration layer that can instantiate and tear down VNFs and transport circuits from the same interface when hybrid physical and virtual designs are required.

talks.title: JDD2014: How to rebuild monolithic application to micro services architecture? (T. Lelek)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning JDD2014: How to rebuild monolithic application to micro services architecture? (T. Lelek).

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Cisco Access Architectures: GPON, Ethernet, Access for business (K. Konkowski)
talks.teaser: Summarizes Cisco GPON gear, EPN validated designs, and scaled business access products for carrier deployments.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with Cisco’s relatively new GPON portfolio for residential and business access, including OLT chassis sizes, ONT options, third-party interoperability, TR-069 provisioning, redundancy modes, and support for XG-PON and varied fiber deployment models. The speaker sketches hardware density, management via built-in GUI or Prime/Agora NG, and Prime Home for subscriber-facing CPE services without dwelling on every slide-level component.

The middle section pivots to how operators should deploy these technologies using Cisco’s lab-tested design and implementation guides. Under the Evolved Programmable Network (EPN) architecture—updated quarterly and reachable via Cisco Validated Designs—teams can pick residential or business access scenarios, integrate BNG functions, and apply copy-paste configurations for GPON, active Ethernet, or mixed models such as one-to-one VLAN aggregation.

The close covers business access innovations: virtualized ASR 9k nodes, low-cost ISR 903 and ISR 920 aggregation, and Network Interface Device controllers that scale many cheap edge units from a central router using Metro Ethernet Forum XML. Practitioners should treat the talk as a map to official CVD documents and Poland-market GPON readiness rather than a full deep-dive architecture session the speaker defers to a future meeting.

talks.title: JDD2014: To nie zawsze wina aplikacji (T. Borek, J. Jagieła)
talks.teaser: Argues that application failures often come from infrastructure, and shows how developers can monitor, test and set SLAs for it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that an application is code plus the infrastructure it runs on, so failures often originate outside the code. The presenters urge developers to treat servers, networks, storage and firewalls as part of the product, to design and test them with the same care, and to set service levels in agreements when someone else runs the hardware.

Monitoring comes first. The speakers advise relying on operating system data, keeping history, and not running every tool at once; one monitoring product consumed most of the CPU on production, and a round-robin database file grew by 17 GB in 20 minutes. A throughput jump every morning at 9:30 was traced to a ticketing customer's logins, which shows why teams should know how users behave. Capacity should be estimated per session before release. In virtualized setups, CPU-ready time reveals virtual machines waiting for physical cores, and live migration can briefly drop long sessions. Network examples show that a switch's rated throughput depends on packet size and load, and that a firewall in the path can saturate.

On recovery, the talk stresses that backups need defined recovery point and recovery time objectives, that differential backups have limited lifespans, and that snapshots are not backups. Tape media age out, so copies must be rotated and stored off site, and restores must be tested. The closing advice is to script checks for infrastructure, separate production from test environments rather than sharing them, and require explicit SLAs.

talks.title: JDD2014: Code review - jak więcej zyskać niż stracić? (S. Malaca)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of JDD2014: Code review - jak więcej zyskać niż stracić? (S. Malaca).

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: How to Raise Money from Strangers? (Jaromir Dzialo)
talks.teaser: An investor explains how startups win funding by reducing risk, scaling cleanly, and making VCs excited enough to pitch them.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames fundraising as a scalable alternative to obvious one-off ways of getting cash, grounded in how venture investors actually evaluate companies. The speaker contrasts the glamorous startup myth with grueling early reality, then compares “empire building” through heavy traditional expansion versus lightweight digital scale, using familiar platform examples to argue that testing ideas cheaply has never been easier.

For investors, a startup is a hypothesis validated through A/B tests and a conversion funnel where value may be revenue or engagement time. Scalability and expansion matter: overloaded systems that fail under growth are contrasted with offerings that stay attractive under load. The financing cycle covers friends-family-fools funding, the valley of death, and renewed interest as revenue appears; capital is about removing risk and dominating a niche, not merely shipping another feature parity release.

Closing guidance urges founders to communicate like a clear, specific message: state the project, revenue expectations, financing needs, and what investors receive for their money. The goal is excitement about the product so strangers advocate and invest, not a one-sided beg. The talk also sketches a Polish business-angel network’s scale, co-investors, and portfolio wins including a fast-funded hardware crowdfunding case.

talks.title: JDD2014: GO! The one language you have to try in 2014 (A. Grzesik)
talks.teaser: Surveys Go concurrency, static deployment, and standard tooling via live demos aimed at Java-oriented developers.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by positioning Go as a concise, fast alternative to Java for teams tired of heavy build tools and runtime dependency stacks. He argues the language suits 2014-era work such as HTTP middleware, sockets, microservice glue, and tooling ecosystems where Docker already demonstrated Go’s footprint, while steering complex business logic back toward established JVM stacks.

Through console demos he walks typed syntax, compile-time rejection of unused imports, maps and structs, implicit interfaces, and goroutines with channels, select, and range iteration. He contrasts latch-like coordination and generator-style channel reads with familiar Java concurrency patterns, shows go get fetching compilable dependency source, and builds sequential versus concurrent TCP echo servers plus built-in WebSockets. Honest drawbacks include verbose JSON tagging and basic testing compared with Spock-style frameworks.

Audience questions cover native compilation and cross-target binaries, integer overflow behavior, practical adoption boundaries, eBay production middleware examples, and the built-in go test workflow. The closing message encourages trying a hello world and small network experiments rather than expecting a full language tutorial from the session.

talks.title: PLNOG 13: Lifesize - wideokonferencje w chmurze (P. Kolasa)
talks.teaser: Contrasts Lifesize cloud service with on-premises and private-cloud video setups, covering licensing, scale, recording, and administration.
talks.summary:
The session introduces two ways to run Lifesize video conferencing: a producer-hosted cloud subscription priced per user account, and customer-owned on-premises or private-cloud stacks built on virtual or appliance hardware. For cloud, each licensed account maps to a personal meeting room capped at twenty-five participants in one call, with mobile clients, a corporate gateway, shared address books, and registration of room systems so mixed vendor terminals can join the same bridge without a full hardware refresh.

The core of the presentation is a feature-by-feature contrast. On-premises allows up to one hundred five participants per conference, seamless live handoff of an active call between a room codec, laptop, and tablet, straightforward recording and streaming, richer administrator controls, LDAP integration, and deployment inside the customer network. Cloud administration is limited to adding or removing users and meeting rooms, lacks live transfer between endpoints, and often needs a hybrid server for recording or Video Center-style capture, federation, and large live audiences.

Closing points cover encrypted business-grade sessions, PIN-protected rooms, positioning against consumer tools such as Skype, building a scalable private cloud with incremental license unlocks, and operational benefits for distributed organizations. The speaker notes trial options and answers licensing questions about shared meeting rooms versus per-employee accounts, guest join, and browser-based access.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Intel Capital - Investing in the Future (Marcin Hejka)
talks.teaser: Explains how Intel Capital chooses and supports early-stage technology companies, and what its investments and exits look like.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Intel Capital, the investment division of Intel, and explains why a large corporation backs early-stage technology firms. The speaker argues that Intel's PC and server markets cannot expand much further on their own, so the company gains when the wider ecosystem grows. Deals must make financial sense, and they should also make technology more appealing to consumers or businesses.

Figures covered scale and reach. Over roughly two decades the fund reported more than 11 billion dollars invested across more than 55 countries, with offices in 25 countries and well over a hundred deals a year. Deal sizes run from 250 thousand dollars to above a billion, with no fixed limits. Most investments are in software and services rather than hardware, with focus areas including internet of things, security, wearables, data center and cloud, and smartphones. Last year 333 million dollars went into 146 companies, about half in the United States and a quarter in Europe.

The speaker described the support given to portfolio companies, including marketing, engineering, product optimisation, sales channels and introductions to international customers. Intel Capital technology days connect startups with decision makers at large companies, and the speaker reported a follow-up rate above 70 percent. Exit results were also cited, including over 200 IPOs and around 350 acquisitions among roughly 1200 companies invested in. The takeaway is that corporate investors can offer market access that startups struggle to get elsewhere.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Music Industry And it's Digital Facelift (A. Navin, Ł. Targosz, P. Kabaj)
talks.teaser: Panelists detail how technology, piracy battles, and streaming services transformed music production and sales worldwide.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with a Polish composer describing how digital workstations replaced costly orchestral recording cycles that once took half a year or more, and why opening a commercial studio marked his shift from session guitarist to full-time creation. He ties Poland’s post-1989 political opening to easier access to computers, the internet, and platforms such as iTunes and Spotify, while noting that democratized tools mean craft and originality still separate professional work from sample-driven output.

A longtime label executive follows with market statistics: CD-era wholesale peaks near twenty-five billion dollars, last year’s rebound despite Japan’s physical decline, and digital share that still varies sharply by country. He recounts industry resistance to the internet in the late nineties, the Napster fight, the rise of subscriptions, Spotify’s royalty pressures, Nordic streaming growth paired with less piracy, Poland’s lagging broadband coverage, smartphone uptake, and expectations around in-car connected listening.

The former BitTorrent commercialization lead explains early lossless concert-trading communities, why MP3 collections overtook CDs on convenience, and parallels with downloadable video. The panel closes on practical global strategy for Polish artists—niche excellence, social proof abroad, English versus dubbed media, playback culture on television, whether any service can rival YouTube’s investment, and how Shazam-style listening data feeds promotion decisions.

talks.title: JDD 2014: Sławomir Sobótka
talks.teaser: Polish interview with a Java architect and trainer about the developer market, community groups and emigration of IT talent.
talks.summary:
In this short interview recorded at JDD 2014 in Kraków, Sławomir Sobótka, a software architect and trainer at Bottega IT Solutions, explains how the conference chooses its speakers and topics. He says he watches candidate speakers on video or at other conferences to see how they present, and that the programme looks for cross-cutting themes alongside solid fundamentals.

He then turns to the Java community in Poland. He describes an older generation of programmers who have become less active while newer people join, and he mentions the reactivation of the Lublin Java User Group after a year-long break. The aim is to draw local companies that struggle to hire, and he notes that senior developers often share their experience for free at community meetings.

Toward the end he discusses a shortage of mid-level talent. He recalls an HR manager's view that a few exceptional students always exist, but the broad middle group is thin, and he sees emigration as one contributing reason, though he feels the first wave of departures has passed. The interview suggests that local meetups and mentoring are practical ways to grow the pool of developers.

talks.title: JDD 2014: Pablo Barros
talks.teaser: An Oracle applications architect discusses JDD, static code analysis practices, and upcoming multi-tenant search design considerations.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens at JDD in Kraków with Pablo Barros, an applications architect for Oracle’s Taleo Business Edition platform, describing how he oversees architecture for the product after Oracle’s acquisition and coordinates with a local development team when he visits.

He reflects on why he returns to JDD, praising Kraków’s eager learning culture and architect–engineer community. He summarizes the morning session on static code analysis in architecture: teams often underuse it, and he points listeners toward tooling that improves visibility into work. He previews the next day’s lecture on multi-tenant search—what to weigh when combining multi-tenancy with search and which patterns apply—and recommends another agenda item, Atomic’s architecture track. The close turns to agile’s value for cross-role transparency and a brief case for students learning Java alongside newer languages.

talks.title: JDD 2014: Michael Hunger
talks.teaser: Interview details JDD 2014: Michael Hunger.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this interview at the JDD 2014 conference, Michael Hunger discusses his background with Neo Technology, the neo4j graph database, and his conference session focused on analyzing source code structure using neo4j. The conversation covers the core capabilities of graph databases for interconnected data, practical applications in software development, the pre-conference hackathon, and his impressions of the JDD event.

### Key Topics
- **neo4j and Graph Databases**: Designed specifically for storing and quickly querying connected data where traditional databases struggle with rich connections.
- **Analyzing Source Code**: Using a simple source code scanner to import software structural elements into neo4j, enabling developers to query the codebase using the Cypher query language.
- **JDD Hackathon**: A pre-conference coding challenge organized by Jarek at SmartRecruiters focused on implementing a source code management (SCM) and version control system with neo4j.
- **Conference Atmosphere**: Reflections on the developer-centric community spirit, organization, and networking value of the JDD conference.

### Technical Details
- **Data Ingestion**: Developers can scan source code to import entities such as classes, types, interfaces, inheritance relationships, composition, fields, and methods into neo4j.
- **Querying Code with Patterns**: Using simple graph patterns in the query language (referred to in the transcript as Cypher/server), developers can query the graph once to discover code smells and extract software metrics.
- **Graph Enhancement & CI Integration**: Teams can enrich the graph model with custom concepts and constraints, allowing the entire analysis workflow to be integrated directly into automated build processes.
- **SCM Implementation Challenge**: During the hackathon, participants tackled building a version control system on top of a graph database following an introductory session on neo4j and graph concepts.

### Takeaways
- Graph databases provide a low-risk, fast-value entry point for developers looking to understand and enforce rules across complex, interconnected software codebases.
- Integrating graph-based code analysis into continuous build processes helps detect code smells and monitor architectural constraints automatically.
- JDD is recommended for developers looking to move beyond their comfort zone, learn new paradigms, and approach software problems differently.

talks.title: JDD 2014: Katarzyna Mrowca
talks.teaser: An agile business analyst discusses feature gluttony, visual communication workshops, and what sets JDD apart.
talks.summary:
In this short conference interview, an agile business analyst explains her role: she works with clients and gathers requirements, shaping how software should look before it is built. She describes feature gluttony as the constant pressure to deliver more features, faster and cheaper, while keeping quality high. Her lecture at the conference explored whether that pressure is good or bad and how teams can handle it.

She also runs a workshop on visualization-based communication, which applies simple schemas, diagrams and basic text formatting to everyday exchanges between developers and managers. She argues that people often already know these principles but do not apply them, and that doing so can make teams more successful. On agile work, she names close cooperation with clients as the best part, since it lets a team understand the business domain well and build good software.

Asked to compare conferences, she finds the atmosphere at JDD distinctive, with playful themes and attendees dressed up, which makes it easier to network and talk about what people saw. She mentions an upcoming appearance at GeeCON the following week and says she had attended two lectures so far that day.

talks.title: JDD2014: Joseph W. Yoder
talks.teaser: Interview details JDD2014: Joseph W. Yoder.
talks.summary:
In a hallway interview at JDD, Joseph W. Yoder argues that agile teams should embed quality assistance throughout delivery instead of relegating QA to end-of-line gatekeeping. He contrasts manufacturing-style quality control with the collaborative pairing he advocates between testers and developers during estimation and coding.

Yoder reflects on how different regions adopt agile unevenly: Europe and the United States moved early, Japan leverages lean manufacturing heritage but still defaults to waterfall software habits, and Brazil hosts vibrant conferences such as Agile Brazil and Sugarloaf PLoP where he will keynote on pragmatic test-driven development and taming legacy mud.

He praises JDD itself for hallway tracks and spontaneous mini-talks that build community beyond slide decks. The segment is conversational promotion of culture change rather than tooling instructions.

talks.title: JDD2014: Andrzej Grzesik
talks.teaser: A conference interview covers dual conference organizing, JVM ecosystem trends, and encouraging students to explore beyond Java alone.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with Andrzej Grzesik describing his overlapping roles: organizing Geekon in Kraków (with a new Prague edition), writing software for eBay in London, and supporting the Polish Java User Group remotely. He explains community participation as fun, a way to learn, and a natural hub when people change jobs or hire.

He contrasts Geekon and JDD as similar Java-focused events that differ mainly in calendar timing—Geekon early in the year, JDD later—with comparable audiences and quality. He also promotes Atmosphere, aimed at web performance and scalability, as eye-opening for developers who rarely think beyond their application server or container.

On career advice, he argues students should not treat Java as the only path: the JVM now hosts multiple languages, and DevOps, Docker, and broader systems thinking matter. Passion and experimentation beat grinding only on safe corporate stacks. He closes by naming a recommended JDD session on languages to learn in 2014 and praising another speaker’s development-insights talk as especially memorable.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Wywiad z Andrzejem Targoszem
talks.teaser: The organizer discusses the conference’s growth, program priorities and plans for local meetups and youth education.
talks.summary: The interview covers how the conference has grown and how its program is shaped by participant interests, including a focus on network security and changing network technologies. The organizer describes plans to add educational activities for young people and hold local meetups between the main events, shaped with help from regional partners.

talks.title: JDD 2014: Enforcing architecture patterns with static code analysis (P. Barros)
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn to enforce Java layer boundaries via static analysis, view SonarGraph Pet Clinic demo, and embed checks in daily builds.
talks.summary:
Growing applications suffer architectural decay: relationships between modules blur, frameworks like Spring only cover part of the story, and distributed teams introduce conflicting decisions. The presentation frames architecture agility—keeping structure visible through agile delivery—with dependency analysis supporting estimates, quality work, and technical debt choices before refactors become expensive.

Organizing code matters as much as declaring rules. Horizontal layers and vertical feature modules can be arranged package-by-layer or module-first; Eclipse walkthroughs contrast three sample layouts and argue for module-first naming so static rules can target consistent layer names across features. Enforcement goes beyond compilers: tools such as FindBugs and Coverity excel at unit-level issues, while architecture-oriented products including SonarGraph and Structure101 let teams define allowed and forbidden dependencies.

A live SonarGraph import of the Spring Pet Clinic Maven project maps service, model, DAO, and web tiers, exposes an undeclared model-to-web cycle through an owner model referencing a clinic controller, and surfaces the same violation in Eclipse once rules activate. Practitioners should embed these checks in continuous builds, designate owners for rule changes, choose severity deliberately, grandfather legacy debt while blocking new breaches, and expect on the order of twenty seconds of overhead per hundred thousand lines for routine scans.

talks.title: JDD 2014: Systematyczny architekt na drodze ku planowanemu postarzaniu (J. Pałka)
talks.teaser: Argues that software ages through leaky abstractions and lost context, and suggests design habits to resist it.
talks.summary:
The talk compares software aging to planned obsolescence in hardware, such as phone batteries that cannot be swapped and devices that stop being repairable. The speaker argues that teams age their own code through constant rewrites to new frameworks, languages and incompatible APIs, while organisations delay modernisation, and big-bang rewrites tend to overrun.

The middle section looks at code-level causes. A method that takes a generic string says less than a typed parameter, forcing readers into implementations to learn what the author meant. Constructors that do real work, long lists of overloaded constructors and business classes tangled with framework plumbing each mix responsibilities. Exposing internal collections through getters and setters breaks encapsulation, which he defines as how the whole system is structured rather than just private fields. He suggests keeping lower layers dense and decomposing systems along business boundaries, such as separating a candidate from an applicant.

He closes by asking engineers to write code that a successor can rewrite, to stop asking permission for obvious fixes, and to enforce architectural rules with code review and static analysis during the build. In the Q&A he notes that many systems outlive their creators.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Nadciągają smoki! Otwarcie konferencji (A. Targosz)
talks.teaser: Opening remarks trace PLNOG's growth, youth education efforts, and upcoming regional meetups for network practitioners.
talks.summary:
The session launches the thirteenth PLNOG gathering in Krakow, stressing record attendance, a fantasy-themed atmosphere, and strong encouragement for newcomers to ask questions during both days. The presenter revisits how the event grew from a small Wawel meeting in 2008 into a major meeting point for people who built and still operate Polish internet infrastructure, mixing veterans with first-time participants.

Much of the middle covers community programs rather than packet diagrams: past PLNOG for Edu financial and material help to schools, the shift toward hands-on PLNOG for Kids workshops where children act out routers and DNS, and a call for volunteers as Warsaw adopts the kids format. Organizers invite attendees to shape half-day meetups in cities such as Wrocław, Gdańsk, Katowice, and Rzeszów, and they acknowledge ongoing struggles to keep mailing lists alive as lively forums.

The close turns reflective. Network engineers remain visible mainly when something breaks, even as phones, wearables, and home automation multiply unpredictable load. Closed vendor protocols echo early internet silos, so standardization and operator skill matter more. Practical tips cover crowded lunches and after-parties, partner booths, and a handoff to the next lecture while thanking organizers and sponsors.

talks.title: PLNOG13: Peering vs Tranzyt - Czy peering jest naprawdę szybszy? (G. Janoszka)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for PLNOG13: Peering vs Tranzyt - Czy peering jest naprawdę szybszy? (G. Janoszka).

talks.title: Atmosphere 2014: Go, go, go - the one language to try in 2014 (Andrzej Grzesik)
talks.teaser: A live-coded walkthrough shows how Go’s toolchain, goroutines, and channels help build small, fast concurrent servers.
talks.summary:
The speaker urges the audience to try the Go language in 2014, after years of moving among C++, Java, Ruby, and other stacks. He frames Go as fast to compile, statically linked, open source, and shipped with a single `go` command for build, format, dependency fetch, and cleanup—avoiding heavy JVM installs and long Maven-style setup fights.

Through live compilation he covers packages and imports, unused-import enforcement, basic types, maps, structs, methods, implicit interfaces, goroutines, buffered and unbuffered channels, `select`, range over channels, and a latch-style worker start pattern. He contrasts a blocking echo server with a concurrent version using one extra keyword, demos `go get` and a short WebSocket listener, and cites rewriting a Java Spring Tomcat service at eBay into Go at roughly one-eighth the line count while keeping features.

Practitioners should treat the session as motivation plus syntax snapshots, not a full language reference. He nudges newcomers toward golang.org browser tutorials, a hello world, a tiny HTTP server, and experimenting with concurrency primitives rather than hand-rolled mutex-heavy threading.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2014: Optimising and Automating your Front End Workflow
talks.teaser: Walks through npm, Bower, Grunt and Gulp for automating front-end builds, plus a live demo of asset versioning and live reload.
talks.summary:
Szymon Przybylski, a developer at Allegro, frames the talk around front-end ops, a role described in a Smashing Magazine piece about a year earlier as browsers taking on more application logic. He lists the duties such a person might cover: deciding which HTTP requests a page should make, keeping dependencies updated, watching client-side JavaScript errors and tracking how fast pages render and load.

The talk then turns to tooling. Npm handles Node modules, while Bower manages client-side libraries such as jQuery so that vendor code does not sit in repositories. He compares Grunt, which is configured through a file of tasks, with Gulp, which is written as code and pipes results between steps without temporary files. Typical task groups include linting with JSHint and unit testing with Jasmine, Mocha or QUnit. The build chain covers compiling CoffeeScript, Sass or Less, concatenation, minification and versioning. He warns that Less, which processes files asynchronously, produced different MD5 hashes for identical source across machines, so that behaviour had to be turned off.

The demo shows a serve task with live reload for development, and a distribution build that minifies code and appends content-based hashes so browsers can cache files safely. In the Q&A he suggests keeping the front end separate from the back end and talking to it through RESTful APIs. He adds that Allegro has used Grunt for about two years alongside PHP Symphony pages, and that its image hashing relies on a custom plugin. He closes by encouraging teams to automate as many front-end tasks as possible.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Irish startups rock the stage: Huggity, Greenletterbox, Musicband
talks.teaser: Irish startup founders pitch digital postboxes and stadium fan-engagement platforms, with adoption metrics and Q&A.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a brief introduction from Ireland’s Enterprise Island agency, which backs startups and helped bring several companies to the event. Nick Keegan then presents Green Letterbox, an Irish–Polish venture offering a free digital mailbox tied to each home address. Senders such as banks and utilities submit the same print files they use for paper mail; consumers verify residency via a code sent by traditional post, then receive PDF correspondence in one inbox with bill pay, reminders, and bank-grade encryption. He cites EU letter volumes, sender cost savings up to 90%, and digital-mail adoption in Denmark, Australia, Singapore, France, and Sweden, plus integration and partner-acquisition questions from the audience.

Michael from Huggity (FanPix) follows with a sports and live-event product that stitches crowd photos into shareable, brand-overlaid images within 24 hours. He describes scale metrics—millions of fans photographed, large tag counts at Manchester United and Celtic matches—and how shared posts multiply impressions beyond stadium capacity. Gamification, channel partners, email capture, and privacy blurring for tagged faces come up in discussion, along with why events above roughly 15,000 attendees fit the model best.

Time runs out before the third listed company presents; the host closes with Enterprise Island brochures and founder testimonials about export support.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Internet of things
talks.teaser: A panel maps Internet of Things economics, smart-city cases, connected-home patterns, and data-sharing stakes for software startups.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens by framing the Internet of Things as hyper-connection among everyday objects and comparing its layered stack—nodes, gateways, routers, and ultimately services—to the classic human-centric internet. Panelists describe an accelerated evolution rather than a single sudden hype cycle, pointing to around 2008 when cheap radio silicon made it practical to separate power delivery from software-defined sensing and control, and to wider wireless coverage that favors many small connected devices over one large system.

On the industry side, they cite European smart-city and port logistics examples where sensor networks, traffic, lighting, and energy data feed optimization and savings. For residences, they argue most homes remain largely analog while phones and routers are digital islands, and outline behavioral modes—active, asleep, and away—with scenarios such as pre-arrival ventilation tied to navigation and pumps that react to presence inferred from phones and motion sensors. They also stress that connectivity alone is insufficient until home platforms enable services the way the wired internet eventually enabled major web services.

The conversation turns to analytics across vertical silos, brokers mediating information flows, and cross-sector data such as mobile operators versus financial institutions. A facilitated example explores insurers pricing policies using lifestyle telemetry from the home, raising opt-in versus coercion concerns. Closing at a startup-oriented event, they urge founders to think from the future backward, invent sellable end-user use cases, and treat IoT primarily as an opportunity for software innovators rather than network operators or hardware makers alone.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Interview with Dan Bragiel
talks.teaser: Gives startup founders advice on pitching, fundraising and getting into Silicon Valley, drawn from years of angel investing.
talks.summary:
Recorded at the Bitspiration festival in Krakow, this short interview features Dan Bragiel, an angel investor and partner at an accelerator program who has made close to 30 investments. He explains that his work is mostly evaluating companies and writing checks, then addresses Silicon Valley, which he describes as a central place that can take a business to its next level through clients and funding, while cautioning that it is hard work rather than a dream.

The middle of the conversation covers advice for founders, especially international teams such as Polish startups. He says founders often underestimate how long fundraising takes, since it can absorb all of their time, and that a company should build a product people want instead of what it thinks investors want to hear. He recommends lining up many meetings so several investors compete, which can speed up a raise and improve terms. For newcomers, he suggests starting at meetups in their own field, and he discusses hackathon pitches, where he looks for an intuitive, exciting idea over a full business problem.

He closes by saying the CEO should usually front the pitch as the visionary, with the CTO focused on building the product, and that charisma and strong storytelling matter alongside good numbers. The interview ends with him praising the festival venue and mentioning upcoming travel to Brazil before returning to San Francisco.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: When You Realize Your Band Is A Business
talks.teaser: A panel maps band life to startup discipline: roles, Polish market data, budgets, revenue streams, and daily work habits.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting the fantasy of gigs and glamour with the reality that most musicians in the room do not earn a living from music alone. One panelist frames a band as an institution with overlapping jobs—members, management, booking, touring, design, PR, and tech—and argues that early groups must share those duties even when one person wears many hats.

The middle section grounds planning in Polish listening habits, radio, downloads, streaming, and shifting physical versus digital sales. Panelists walk through treating the band like a startup: solid music as product, one- to five-year goals, audience analytics from Spotify and YouTube, revenue from live shows, streams, merch, ads, and licensing. They stress realistic budgets, acceptable early spending, creative low-cost merch, instrumental stems for commercials, libraries and supervisors abroad, and overcoming shame about money and “selling out.”

The close urges daily professional routines—social media, rehearsal, maintenance, calls, promotion—and audience Q&A on data tools, delegation, festival support, streaming payouts, premium listeners, and reaching global markets from day one rather than waiting on Poland alone.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Venture Capital Funnel (Bartłomiej Gola)
talks.teaser: Explains why Central European venture funds chase rare huge exits and why startups should plan for global markets early.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at early-stage venture capital in Central and Eastern Europe through the idea of the "black swan": one exit large enough to return an entire fund. The speaker, who runs a young Polish early-stage fund with about 35 portfolio companies, opens with Facebook's 2012 purchase of Instagram for a billion dollars. He explains that limited partners expect large multiples on their money, so fund returns determine how much capital later reaches startups.

Using a hypothetical 50 million zloty fund with 20 holdings, he works out that a single black swan would need a 250 million zloty exit. Checking the Warsaw Stock Exchange, he counts 164 listed companies above that valuation, but only 10 of them are technology firms. He notes that about half of early-stage investments fail and that most returns come from roughly a tenth of a portfolio. He contrasts the Silicon Valley model of hunting rare huge outcomes, citing Y Combinator, where two companies, Airbnb and Dropbox, make up 76 percent of the value, with a lower-risk approach that accepts smaller returns.

His conclusion is that Polish funds need black swans to attract private institutional money, and that founders should think globally from the first day, focusing on niche markets rather than copying American products. In the question round he advised founders to build early traction with Polish money and then seek foreign partners. He also questioned how EU-funded programmes affect private investment in the sector.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Designing The Emotional Connection (Andreas Connellan)
talks.teaser: Explains how a design consultancy uses emotion, research and scenarios to shape technology products and brands.
talks.summary:
This talk from a design consultancy looks at what the design process brings to new business and technology development. The speaker opens with a client case: an established antivirus maker had released no product for about three and a half years, and a smaller competitor loved by younger gamers took much of its revenue. The client asked the firm to inject emotion into its product, and the work later grew into overall brand communication.

The middle of the talk sets out the firm's approach. Researchers recruit participants and visit their homes, aiming to build lasting relationships with them rather than collect survey counts. Early on, the team builds scenarios and storyboards, then moves to prototypes that help gauge emotional reaction. The project is distilled into a few brand values and constraints that guide later decisions. The speaker also sketches a technology trajectory, from remote control to action at a distance and then to context-aware, anticipatory products, and discusses the pressure that wearables and growing data volumes place on users.

The closing advice treats design as a set of tools for making decisions. Practitioners should keep a few essential constraints fixed, set aside other opinions, and bring clients into the research so they see user reactions first-hand. Startups can buy a short early session with a consultancy rather than commit to a full process.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Building The Entrepreneurial Eco-system in Krakow (Richard Lucas)
talks.teaser: Assesses Kraków's startup support landscape and offers ten practical steps anyone can take to strengthen local entrepreneurship.
talks.summary:
The presentation evaluates Kraków's startup and entrepreneurship support environment from the perspective of someone who has promoted enterprise in Poland since the early 1990s. The speaker argues that the city has made genuine progress on cooperation and trust: community venues host cross-promotion among peers, and internationally known firms founded locally show that success is possible without constant publicity.

The middle of the talk contrasts those strengths with persistent weaknesses. Available investment capital remains limited compared with Western Europe, partly because hyperinflation in 1989 destroyed household savings in ways most EU countries never experienced. Professional services such as banking and law rarely accommodate startups on equity-friendly terms, and some flagship programs are relocating to Warsaw. The speaker invites the audience to name additional gaps.

The closing section lays out a ten-part action plan centered on personal responsibility rather than waiting for institutions. Recommendations include returning to schools to promote entrepreneurship, pressing employers—especially Polish ones—to host student programs, widening the community beyond programmers, favoring participatory formats over lecture-only events, treating entrepreneurship as broader than venture-backed startups, demanding transparency from banks and law firms, and aligning recurring meetups with a practical curriculum covering finance, sales, and management. The talk ends with examples of low-cost school projects and a call for attendees to act individually so collective effort can offset structural capital constraints.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Raspberry Pi Powered Home Robots Controlled From a Cloud (Marek Sadowski)
talks.teaser: Presents a Raspberry Pi based home vacuum robot managed over the internet, with a crowdfunding pitch.
talks.summary:
Marek Sadowski, a founder of the robotics company Robotics Inventions, presents a home robot built on a robotic vacuum platform that the company designed. The robot is driven by cloud services, so it can be managed over the internet. The company builds robot prototypes and autonomous-robot software for industry, space and military customers, and says that earlier work on a floor-servicing robot for office underfloor spaces led to this consumer product.

The talk frames the problem around family life: parents with little time, households affected by allergies, and the need to clean up small toys. The design answers these with stronger dust extraction, a UV-C lamp to sanitise floors, and a Lego-friendly cleaning mode that avoids sucking up small bricks. A Raspberry Pi board is included as an open platform, so hobbyists can add a webcam or other parts and tweak the robot to their needs.

The presenter then covers pricing tiers for a regular and an extended edition, plus an optional subscription for internet control, and announces a Kickstarter campaign with pre-orders. A working robot was brought on stage for demonstration, and attendees were invited to see it at the company's stand. The main takeaway is how a commercial robot can be opened up to makers while still being managed remotely through a cloud service.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Enrich Your App With Real Life Context in 1 Hour (M. Klimek)
talks.teaser: The session shows how context awareness, beacons, and a mobile SDK help apps react to where users are.
talks.summary:
Martin Klimek frames context as what connected apps and Internet of Things setups need so services can act without constant user prompts. He walks through everyday product ideas—todo helpers, sleep trackers, venue and music apps, and location-based games—to show how knowing place, activity, and company changes what the software should do next.

He contrasts high-friction approaches such as NFC and QR codes with always-on beacon broadcasts, describes Estimote hardware with sensors like accelerometers and temperature probes, and explains Apple’s proximity UUID, major, and minor fields as layered precision for venues and rooms. Monitoring behaves like geofencing for beacon regions; ranging supplies nearby beacon detail and immediate, near, and far distance zones. A short SDK walkthrough covers entry and exit callbacks, and a roughly 70-line demo switches on-screen art as he moves between beacon-labeled paintings.

Practitioners hear that beacons emit identifiers while phones map IDs to context in the cloud-backed platform, that Android support exists beside iOS, and that battery readouts on dev kits can mislead until settings are tuned. The takeaway is to prototype context-driven UX quickly rather than hard-coding static location logic.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2014: Cheffing the department, one dev at a time
talks.teaser: Andrzej Grzesik (ebay) details Atmosphere 2014: Cheffing the department, one dev at a time.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At Atmosphere 2014, speaker Andrzej discusses the practical realities, human dynamics, and technical hurdles of introducing Chef and Infrastructure as Code (IaC) to a newly formed department at eBay. Distributed across London, Zurich, and Berlin, the department comprised between 50 and 100 primarily Java-oriented developers who needed rapid production and staging environments without relying on slow waterfall processes or corporate platform-as-a-service constraints.

### Key Topics
- **Transitioning Developers to Infrastructure**: Encouraging Java developers to manage environments beyond application containers like Tomcat or Node, moving away from unscalable Bash scripts and manual configuration.
- **Overcoming Tooling and Mindset Friction**: Transitioning Java developers to writing Chef recipes and DSLs in Ruby, as well as handling copy-pasting unverified cookbooks from public repositories like GitHub.
- **Human and Cultural Dynamics**: Managing interpersonal conflict, avoiding "rat race" friction during code reviews, and applying techniques from Linda Rising’s book (including sharing sweets like cupcakes and muffins) to build rapport and psychological safety.
- **Infrastructure Patterns and Local Testing**: Utilizing Vagrant for fast local testing and adopting the Phoenix pattern (disposable servers) rather than applying ad-hoc manual hotfixes on running instances.

### Technical Details
- **Chef Solo vs. Chef Server**: The team initially adopted a Chef Solo approach with a single shared repository on a single master branch to avoid broken commits impacting everyone's machines simultaneously, later experimenting with Chef Server as maturity grew.
- **Dual Execution Model**: Managing Chef’s two-phase compile/materialize and converge/execution model, which surfaced unexpected behaviors and required tools like Chef Zero and local testing.
- **Quality and Linting**: Enforcing pair programming, code reviews (initially using Review Kiwi), Foodcritic for linting, and ChefSpec for unit tests, followed by validation inside Vagrant virtual machines running on OS X and Linux.
- **Cloud Environment and Scale**: Running virtual machines provisioned on eBay's private internal cloud (typically up to 20 boxes per project), serving test and staging environments alongside automated mobile testing infrastructures (utilizing tools such as Selendroid, Selenium iOS driver, and physical device walls).

### Takeaways
- Implementing IaC is predominantly a human communication challenge rather than merely a technical one; building trust and allowing developers to make controlled mistakes is essential.
- Simplicity should take precedence over complex architectures: start with localized, low-blast-radius tooling (such as Chef Solo and Vagrant) before introducing central servers or elaborate pipelines.
- Disposable infrastructure enforces discipline, ensuring all environment configurations remain strictly versioned in code.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2014: Lockless programming
talks.teaser: Explains lock-free programming with atomic operations and memory barriers, then builds a lock-free queue and its pitfalls.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the cost of lock-based parallel code on multi-core hardware. Threads that wait on a lock leave cores idle, and locks bring problems such as deadlock, priority inversion and convoying. Lockless programming is presented as an alternative in which threads use atomic operations to exchange data without blocking one another, which matters most for real-time workloads.

The middle of the talk covers the building blocks. The speaker describes atomic compare-and-swap and fetch-and-add, and the four basic memory barrier types (load-load, load-store, store-load and store-store) plus the full barrier. Sequential consistency is defined as all threads agreeing on a memory order that matches the programmer's intent, and reordering by compilers, CPUs and the JVM is the reason barriers are needed. A lock-free FIFO queue attributed to John D. Valois serves as the worked example. Its enqueue needs a compare-and-swap loop to keep the tail consistent when threads are descheduled, and dequeue must retry under contention. A stack example shows the ABA problem, with tagged references, intermediate nodes and load-link/store-conditional offered as remedies. The speaker notes that load-link/store-conditional exists on PowerPC, ARM and MIPS but not on x86.

The talk ends with language support: GCC intrinsics, the C++11 atomic template, and Java's atomic classes including stamped and marked references. The main takeaway is that lockless code is much harder to analyse and design than lock-based code, so wait-free approaches should be avoided unless the problem demands them. In the questions, the speaker reported roughly three times the throughput of a standard implementation on a 24-core workload with short bursts of processing.

talks.title: PLNOG12: Architektura tradycyjna vs. architektura w chmurze. (Maciej Kuźniar)
talks.teaser: Explores how infrastructure-as-a-service reshapes application design through autoscaling, tiered disks, and managed object storage.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing cloud computing not as a single new technology but as a mindset shift: applications should stop being tied to individual servers and instead treat compute, memory, and disks as managed components, much like databases or other services. On infrastructure-as-a-service, resources can grow or shrink during operation—disk tiers can jump from thousands to hundreds of thousands of I/O operations per second without restart, and changes can be driven manually, through autoscaling, or via APIs.

The middle section walks through vertical and horizontal autoscaling, including roughly twenty-minute decision windows, limits such as 64 GB RAM per instance, and the session-stickiness problems that appear when traffic spreads across clones. The speaker contrasts sticky load-balancer workarounds with stateless or shared-session designs, then moves to data: cloning servers duplicates block storage and causes drift, so static assets belong in object storage while mutable shared data may use shared block volumes or object APIs with token-based authorization.

The close ties fast proprietary storage—Infiniband-backed nodes, SRP, and tiers delivering on the order of 3.5 GB per second—to cost stories: a database quoted at six large-memory servers reduced to one smaller instance with a top disk tier, and dozens of file-serving machines consolidated to a few compute instances plus object storage. Practitioners are urged to enable autoscaling for hourly billing savings, lift static content to object stores when possible, and right-size memory once storage stops throttling CPUs.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Always on, Always listening: The New Era of Ambient Computing (Ashwin Navin)
talks.teaser: Defines ambient computing within IoT and shows why TVs need contextual awareness instead of another smart-TV platform wave.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames ambient computing as a slice of the Internet of Things: always-on, connected, context-sensing devices woven into daily life, distinct from PCs and phones that demand full attention. He walks through decades of rising device counts at home, then contrasts failed “revolution” plays—smart TVs treated like app phones, Google TV inventory writedowns—with behavior that still favors linear broadcast and entrenched cable economics.

He maps the traditional TV value chain, where manufacturers often lose money on sets while distributors and advertising earn steady margins, and argues disruption works better when it augments offline habits (place-shifting with Sling, personal recording) than when it tries to replace the bundle outright. Ambient computing, in his terms, sits beside existing viewing—like discovery apps beside restaurants—rather than overthrowing the living-room screen.

The closing focus is technology that understands everything displayed on the TV—cable, consoles, tuners, apps—to power discovery, on-screen metadata, and quantified interest. The stated business direction is richer, real-time viewership insight than panel-based Nielsen-style sampling, while audience questions touch smart-TV connectivity, phone-to-TV casting, BitTorrent hardware risk, and why true à-la-carte channel bundles stall on programmer bundling deals.

talks.title: PLNOG11: Best Current Operational Practices
talks.teaser: Outlines how regional operator communities build trusted BCOP documents to cut deployment clutter for IPv6 and related technologies.
talks.summary:
The session reports progress on best current operational practices: practical deployment guidance written by experienced network operators, distinct from IETF BCP documents that anyone may author. Operators already exchange know-how through lists, forums, and conference talks, yet finding trusted material for tasks such as ISP IPv6 rollout still means wading through unreliable search results.

After RIPE and other communities rejected a heavy global repository with central committees, Internet Society Deploy360 shifted to regional BCOP efforts. A simple web page now links what each region is doing, without imposing top-down structure. Travel and outreach have engaged Africa, Latin America, North America via NANOG, Europe via RIPE, the Middle East, and future work targets Asia. Volunteers are needed to draft identified topics; one example in progress covers generic IPv6 help-desk troubleshooting, with contributors from large U.S. cable deployments and ideas for a help-desk-oriented variant of test-ipv6.com.

The presenter stresses that operators should own the process while Deploy360 facilitates. BCOP work tends to start at larger NOGs and RIR meetings, with duplication avoided through cross-regional coordination. Questions close on whether every NOG should run BCOP or focus stays on regional hubs.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Silicon Valley Checklist(Piotr Wilam)
talks.teaser: Presents a seven-element checklist for winning Silicon Valley funding, drawn from trips and a founder's fundraising case.
talks.summary:
The speaker describes how, in 2011, they concluded that Polish startups were cut off from the global tech community, relying on local money, advisors and customers. Their response was to build a bridge to Silicon Valley, beginning with a first trip at the end of 2011 with two founders. Cold emails and introductions led to meetings, and pitching to people there brought feedback that changed how the founders thought about networking.

Over several visits the speaker built a checklist of elements needed to win funding there: a leader who is passionate, competent and communicates well; a big vision tied to market size and long-term advantage; a precisely defined customer and a product that solves an important problem; traction, with growth benchmarks such as 20 percent a month; a roadmap; a complete team of co-founders; and credibility. A case study followed a UX design company that raised money after roughly eight months of fundraising, during which its vision changed three times and its product and target segment were reworked.

The talk closes with two ways to engage with the Valley: a short, well-prepared two-week trip for feedback and know-how, or a deeper commitment that involves hiring, selling and raising there. The speaker argues that meeting all seven elements makes investor conversations far easier, urges European founders to be professional, and states a hope for ten Polish-American companies within two years. In the questions, the focus shifts to keeping ties with the home ecosystem through returning founders, and to building credibility through networks, press and accelerators.
