talks.title: PLNOG12: The latest innovations in DWDM space (David Bianchi)
talks.teaser: Explores flex-spectrum DWDM, terabit super-channels, and software-defined optical restoration that cuts carrier capital spending.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames how communication is shifting from person-to-person traffic toward devices, video, and cloud-oriented services, and why that growth forces backbone operators to pursue more flexible, programmable networks. It outlines service-provider pressures to raise utilization, contain capital and operating costs, and compete as traffic patterns and customer demands change.

The technical core covers evolving dense wavelength division multiplexing: flex-spectrum reconfigurable add-drop multiplexers that let operators assign spectrum and wavelengths in software, super-channels that aggregate capacity toward terabit-class links, and selectable modulation formats that balance distance against bandwidth. It also treats converged layer-one to layer-three platforms, silicon photonics integration, and a generalized multiprotocol label switching control plane aware of optical impairments, together with coordinated restoration across service and photonic layers.

Practitioners hear how multi-layer protection strategies—optical bypass, optical restoration, and packet restoration—can free router ports and reduce spend in ring, mesh, and extended-core designs. Referenced carrier and vendor studies illustrate multi-year capital savings scenarios, and the close emphasizes accelerating adoption of these restoration and bypass combinations across operator networks.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2014: Centralized log management based on Logstash and Kibana
talks.teaser: Shows how centralized log management can be built with Logstash and Kibana for security monitoring.
talks.summary:
This Polish-language talk from Atmosphere 2014 covers how to build a central logging setup using Logstash and Kibana. It begins with the difficulty of working with logs scattered across many servers and applications, each producing its own format. The speaker weighs how monolithic systems and microservice designs generate logs differently, and why that matters when collecting them.

The middle of the session moves to the stack itself. Log events are gathered and passed to a central point, where filters parse and reshape them before they are indexed. Kibana then serves as the interface for searching and viewing the stored data. Security monitoring is named as a key use case, and the speaker walks through configuration of the components.

The closing message for practitioners is that a single searchable store, with parsing rules applied before queries, makes logs from varied systems far easier to use for monitoring and investigation.

talks.title: Bitspiration 2014: Valleywood - reflections of VC in Warsaw (Krzysztof Kowalczyk)
talks.teaser: A venture investor maps Polish startup culture to Hollywood glamour against Bay Area funding scale and accelerator subsidies.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes an early-stage fund rooted in Warsaw that has placed more capital with partners in London and Texas than at home, with individual checks topping out around $200,000. A running discount code during the session is meant to show how unnatural it would be for a serious portfolio company to drive sales from the stage in a mature market; the figure reported after Q&A is zero, echoing a prior festival attempt.

The core argument is that technology in Central and Eastern Europe often behaves like entertainment: festivals, celebrity founders, and press can overshadow revenue and durable exits. Polish engineering shows up in large corporate acquisitions and global productions, yet the region still lacks home-grown software outcomes comparable to the largest global benchmarks. Charts compare venture activity in the Bay Area, the United States, and Europe, emphasize dry powder concentration, and question whether copying Silicon Valley locally is rational when the numbers differ by orders of magnitude. Easy public accelerator money may encourage playing it safe rather than building deep ICT businesses.

The fund plans to stop sub-pre-seed work after a second close and target roughly one to two and a half million euro rounds for teams with traction and prior backers. Founders are told to respect venture math, show product and revenue, stay focused, keep decks simple, and seek warm introductions from existing portfolio companies. A short question about the Showroom fashion marketplace stresses team chemistry, sector growth, and metric-driven operations over novelty of the idea alone.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2014: Hadoop: Challenge accepted!
talks.teaser: Shows Hadoop basics through hands-on demos: Flume ingestion, Streaming jobs, Mahout recommendations and Elasticsearch dashboards.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the claim that only a small share of company data is ever analyzed. The speakers blame partly the fact that application and system logs are often never gathered into a central store and are simply lost during log rotation. They then introduce Hadoop as a scalable platform that runs on commodity hardware. HDFS provides distributed storage with built-in replication, and YARN acts as the resource layer that runs jobs on the nodes where the data already sits. Access control through Kerberos and the absence of a single point of failure in recent releases are also covered.

The middle section is a set of live-style examples. Flume, with a source written by Cloudera, streams Twitter data directly into HDFS. A Hadoop Streaming job written in Python then counts per day how many tweets mention Hadoop, using a mapper and a reducer. Mahout produces user recommendations from a small user-item example. A larger run analyzes the link structure of a Wikipedia dump, proposing new links for about 11 thousand articles. The speakers checked two of the proposals by hand and found them plausible, having given the algorithm no prior knowledge of the data. A tweet-clustering run then grouped hashtags into topics such as fitness, Linux and mobile games.

The final part shows how results reach users. Hive queries aggregate tweets by date, hashtag and language, and the output is exported to Elasticsearch. A dashboard then surfaces trends that appear in one period but not in the earlier one. The main takeaway is that open Hadoop tooling lets an administrator move from raw data to visualization with little custom code.

talks.title: PLNOG12: Solving the LTE Backhaul Challenges (Ezra Mizrahi)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning PLNOG12: Solving the LTE Backhaul Challenges (Ezra Mizrahi).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at PLNOG12, Ezra Mizrahi from MRV addresses the network challenges associated with LTE mobile backhaul deployment. With mobile operators facing explosive bandwidth demand driven by video acceleration, gaming, and location-based services, the transition to LTE focuses on maximizing user quality of experience (QoE) while preserving the average revenue per user (ARPU). Mizrahi reviews the shift from legacy 2G/3G infrastructures to flat, all-IP Carrier Ethernet architectures, evaluating the requirements for transport, synchronization, security, and quality of service.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Mobile Backhaul Architecture**: The move from 2G (TDM) and 3G (ATM/Ethernet with central radio network controllers) to LTE's flat all-IP architecture. LTE introduces direct base station-to-base station communication across the X2 interface alongside the S1 interface to the Evolved Packet Core (EPC).
- **Front-Haul and Small Cells**: Alternative infrastructure approaches including Wi-Fi offload, Cloud RAN (using the Common Public Radio Interface / CPRI for front-hauling), and small cell deployments (femtocells, picocells, microcells) to expand capacity and coverage.
- **Standardization and MEF Specifications**: The role of MEF 22.1 and MEF 22.2 standards in defining Ethernet mobile backhaul requirements, link and service OAM, quality of service performance objectives (QPO), and multi-class of service models supporting wholesale access.
- **Timing and Synchronization**: Transitioning from legacy TDM or GPS timing to packet-based network synchronization using IEEE 1588v2 and Synchronous Ethernet (SyncE) for frequency, phase, and time-of-day alignment.

### Technical Details
- **Core Interfaces & Control Protocols**: LTE relies on the S1-C interface between the base station (eNodeB) and Mobility Management Entity (MME) for control and signaling, S1-U to the Serving Gateway (SGW) for user traffic, and X2-C/X2-U between base stations for rapid handovers and low-latency coordination.
- **Quality of Service (QoS)**: Implemented through Quality of Service Class Identifiers (QCI), managing parameters like Guaranteed Bit Rate (GBR) for time-sensitive services, Non-GBR for best-effort traffic (e.g., FTP), and Maximum Bit Rate (MBR).
- **Scale and Security**: Scaling requires E-LAN multipoint-to-multipoint topologies and IPv6 as an eNodeB can communicate with up to 32 neighbor base stations. Unlike 3G's encrypted cellular channels, the all-IP LTE nature exposes vulnerability to untrusted networks, requiring IPsec tunnels that introduce packet overhead and potential latency.
- **Protection and Testing**: Multi-layer protection spans Layer 1 (loss of signal), Layer 2/MPLS, and Layer 3 (using BFD and VCCV alongside Ethernet OAM). Network SLA verification utilizes built-in test features moving from RFC 2544 to ITU-T Y.1564.

### Takeaways
Operators deploying LTE must modernize their transport to high-capacity, multi-class Carrier Ethernet networks with rigorous end-to-end OAM and multi-layer protection. MRV highlights solutions such as their OptiSwitch product family and Pro-Vision management software, illustrating real-world implementations including an early Nordic LTE E-LAN deployment using packet synchronization and a North American 3G/small cell wholesale network.

talks.title: PLNOG11: Slaying the Two-Headed Beast: Challenges and Triumphs of DNSSEC (panel)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of PLNOG11: Slaying the Two-Headed Beast: Challenges and Triumphs of DNSSEC (panel).
talks.summary:
### Overview
At PLNOG 11, Dan York (Internet Society Deploy360) moderated a panel titled "Slaying the Two-Headed Beast: Challenges and Triumphs of DNSSEC," addressing the operational challenges, advantages, and deployment strategies of DNSSEC. The panel featured experts Frederick (StatDNS), Krzysztof Olejniczak (NASK / .pl registry), and Patrik Wallström (.se / OpenDNSSEC). The discussion explored the dual nature of DNSSEC—signing zones on the authoritative side and validating responses on the resolving side—while examining emerging standards such as DANE and real-world deployment lessons from ccTLD registries.

### Key Topics
- **Signing vs. Validating**: DNSSEC relies on public-key cryptography where authoritative nameservers publish digital signatures alongside DNS records, and validating recursive resolvers verify signatures up to the root zone.
- **Automation and Key Management**: Manual signing and static key management carry significant operational risks. Software like OpenDNSSEC was developed to automate zone signing, policy enforcement, and key rollovers. NASK developed automated scripts and wrappers around DNS software to sign the .pl zone three times daily.
- **Registry Incentives & Adoption**: The .se ccTLD initially charged extra for DS record publication, which hindered adoption; reversing policy to make signed domains cheaper significantly drove uptake, resulting in roughly one-third of the .se zone being signed.
- **DANE (RFC 6698) and Certificate Validation**: DANE enables domain owners to bind SSL/TLS certificates or certificate fingerprints to DNS via TLSA records secured by DNSSEC, mitigating reliance on hundreds of certificate authorities. While browser adoption remains slowed by concerns over latency and packet sizes, DANE is actively being tested in SMTP, XMPP, and VoIP/SIP.
- **Resolver Deployment and Failure Modes**: DNSSEC does not have a user-facing failure mode; validation failures typically return `SERVFAIL`, causing applications to fail silently without explicit error details. Major milestones like Comcast and Google Public DNS enabling validation increased global validation percentages from around 3% to 8%.

### Technical Details
- **Hardware Security Modules (HSMs)**: NASK integrated tamper-proof HSMs utilizing the PKCS#11 standard to protect cryptographic signing keys for the .pl zone, requiring testing to ensure software compatibility and sufficient throughput. The panelists noted that while HSMs are critical for high-impact TLDs and enterprises, smaller domain owners can sign without dedicated hardware.
- **Resource Demands**: Validating resolvers require additional CPU and memory capacity to process cryptographic validations, along with larger network pipes to accommodate DNSSEC responses that are 4–5 times larger than traditional DNS responses.
- **Packet Fragmentation & Home Gateways**: Large DNS packets containing DNSKEY and TLSA records can fail to traverse older consumer home routers and gateways, prompting ongoing standardization work in IETF home networking groups.
- **Operating System Integration**: Modern Linux distributions and BSD releases (such as FreeBSD 10 bundling Unbound instead of BIND, as well as Fedora and Debian initiatives) increasingly enable validating resolvers by default.

### Takeaways
Network operators are encouraged to activate DNSSEC validation on recursive resolvers immediately—often requiring only a single configuration line in software such as Unbound or Windows Server. The panel stressed that mastering zone signing and automated key rollover early carries far less operational risk while adoption is still growing, rather than waiting until widespread validation turns configuration errors into catastrophic user outages.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2014: Scalability and Websockets: Creating a Websocket CDN with DIASP.
talks.teaser: Explains how a WebSocket proxy was built to scale live sports updates to large numbers of mobile and browser clients.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the difficulty of pushing live updates from a server to browsers and phones. WebSockets became a widely supported standard, but before them the options were polling, long polling, or plugin-based sockets, and only very large companies could afford them at scale. The speaker's team found that WebSocket traffic cannot be cached by typical reverse proxies such as Varnish or Squid, and that long-lived connections fit poorly into frameworks built around short request and response cycles.

The case study covers a live-score application for a Polish sports portal. Real traffic far exceeded the estimates, and the middleware that handled every client connection could not keep up. The fix was a WebSocket proxy module, called ASP, that holds a single upstream connection to the middleware and fans messages out to many clients, so the backend no longer manages sockets itself. The speaker showed a live demo in which a pushed message reached connected clients within roughly 20 milliseconds. Load testing reached around 30,000 concurrent connections, at which point the test traffic saturated the office routers. A single instance needed about 300 MB of RAM and little CPU, and failover across several app servers used round-robin.

The talk closes with current limitations and next steps. Plain WebSocket support was still being fixed, and the team planned better handling of multiple connection types and easier configuration through a server controller. The proxy was published on npm for others to try, and the speaker invited companies with similar needs to contact them for support.

talks.title: CONFidence 2014: Xtraction Point
talks.teaser: A conference game mixes lock picking, alarms, shooting, and live memory key extraction inside a thirty-minute facility raid.
talks.summary:
The session describes Extraction Point, a challenge course offered at CONFidence that combines physical security skills with offensive cyber tasks. Early rounds cover shooting, lock picking, and bypassing alarm systems by hacking wiring. The main event adds stress: teams move through an unfamiliar facility, face guards and simulated hazards, and never know how sharply performance will drop once adrenaline hits.

The fictional mission sends teams inside to seize an encrypted hard drive that lists other manufacturing sites. They must disable alarms, open real locks, pass marksmanship checks, and run live attacks against computers, including extracting encryption keys from memory. Only half an hour is allowed to finish and escape; in the storyline, failure means capture.

Organizers frame the game as a bridge from conference discussions about exploits and weak controls to something participants physically attempt. Trial runs left players drenched in sweat but grinning, highlighting how excitement and uncertainty change outcomes when techniques leave the slide deck and enter a staged operational setting.

talks.title: OpenContrail jako wtyczka do OpenStack (Bartosz Górski Paweł Banaszewski)
talks.teaser: Maps OpenContrail as an OpenStack Neutron plugin, from control-plane roles through packet forwarding and peering with physical routers.
talks.summary:
The presenters frame private cloud operations around network virtualization: tenants need isolated address spaces and connectivity without exposing physical topology or carrying one tenant’s misconfiguration into the fabric. They introduce OpenStack as the orchestration layer, highlight Neutron’s network–subnet–port API, and place backend plugins between the API and hypervisor implementations.

OpenContrail’s lineage runs from Contrail Systems through Juniper’s open-source release under Apache 2.0. The talk centers on the config node, control node, and vrouter, with analytics mentioned only briefly. Config translates higher-level intent via REST; control distributes state with XMPP and can align across hosts using BGP, including sessions toward physical routers. The vrouter enforces security policies, mirroring, and banning while forwarding at the hypervisor.

Integration is walked through creating a VM in Horizon: Nova allocates the instance, Neutron notifies OpenContrail, and configuration propagates until the vrouter programs forwarding. A second compute host learns shared virtual network membership only when matching labels appear locally. Egress uses MPLS over GRE by default; vrouters intercept ARP and DHCP to limit broadcast load. Multicast follows an optimizer tree rather than flooding every server. Practitioners hear tradeoffs against Open vSwitch and Linux Bridge, plus minimal hardware requirements, and planned BFD support for faster reachability detection.

talks.title: PLNOG11: Global IPv6 Tournament: Who will take the IPv6 Crown? (panel)
talks.teaser: Operators compare regional IPv6 rollout, security gaps, and practical lessons for building resilient native and transitional networks.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with short operator updates on how IPv6 is actually landing in Poland, Germany, North America, and mobile networks. Academic backbones and cities such as Poznań have carried v6 for years, yet content uptake, firewall mismatches, and client stacks still cause friction; residential markets lag when customer-premises gear lacks v6 or replacement cycles stall deployments.

Discussion then turns to resilience and security expectations. European operator surveys found little belief that IPv6 alone hardens networks, while practitioners warn that immature implementations, uneven firewall parity, and transition tunnels can expose v4-only environments to v6-shaped threats. Panelists cite pilot pain points, sparse but real attack data, legal-intercept scaling choices, and the chance to embed anti-spoofing and cleaner routing policy in greenfield designs rather than copy legacy mistakes.

Closing themes stress attrition-driven rollout tied to fiber, DOCSIS upgrades, and handset defaults; training help desks not to disable v6 as a fix; and testing before scale. Initiatives such as deployment readiness guidance and compliance checks are urged so teams can measure stack maturity and keep deploying while issues are found and fixed.

talks.title: 4Dev2014: Jakie umiejętności niezbędne są w UX? Wywiad z Emilią Maj
talks.teaser: The conversation covers teachable UX skills, cultural interface patterns, designer-developer teamwork, and women in IT.
talks.summary:
A Warsaw 4developers sit-down opens with reflections on a small but engaged UX session and programmer questions about designer–developer tension. The guest argues conflict is avoidable with strong collaboration and frames user experience as a broad discipline spanning layout, naming, graphics, and code.

The middle centers on whether UX is learnable versus innate talent, highlighting logical thinking, clear labeling, and empathy. Drawing on multi-country client work, she contrasts interface norms—minimalism in German-speaking markets versus dense, link-heavy Asian designs—and notes patterns cultures repeat across products.

The close turns to gender in technology: skill parity at equal roles, stereotypes and classroom messaging as real barriers, and active promotion of girls through community events such as one-day coding workshops. She praises the conference for mixing industries and backgrounds so practitioners exchange perspectives they rarely hear elsewhere.

talks.title: 4Dev 2014: Hermetyczność branży IT. Prawda czy fałsz? Wywiad z Michałem Bartyzelem.
talks.teaser: An interview explores whether IT workers are socially closed off and why linguistic skills matter for programmers.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens at a Warsaw developers conference on the Soft Skills track, questioning whether people in IT are socially closed off and fit the nerd stereotype. The guest, who trains soft skills and also programs, rejects the cliché while explaining how teams sometimes lean into labels like nerd or gamer to feel safer and distinct from business counterparts.

He argues that linguistic skill matters deeply for software work, tying everyday conversation to ideas such as ubiquitous language and modeling a client’s business reality that lives in people’s heads. Generic soft-skills courses often feel too vague for technical audiences; framing communication as repeatable patterns or algorithms can land better. He describes conversation patterns as practical, repeatable ways for programmers to surface concrete needs from business stakeholders.

In his practice, developers care about outcomes and engage readily once recurring business–IT misunderstandings are addressed. He notes that IT often drives initiatives to improve collaboration. The piece closes with brief praise for the conference’s concentrated one-day format and sponsor-driven tracks as an innovative model.

talks.title: CONFidence 2014: Exploring treasures of 77FEh
talks.teaser: Explains how a proprietary setup port on Lantronix device servers leaks passwords and allows security resets.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Lantronix serial-to-Ethernet device servers, small bridges built into alarm, air conditioning, pool and sprinkler systems that expose a serial port over TCP/IP. The speaker explains that physical access to these devices gives full control, that the web interface and Telnet prompt are common entry points, and that a proprietary setup protocol on port 77FE (hexadecimal for 30718) is the main focus.

Through that protocol, one request returned the simple password in plaintext when one was set, and other requests leaked most of the configuration. The enhanced password, which the vendor documents as 16 characters, could not be read directly, but the speaker found a write request that overwrote the security record and reset it. The record layout was pieced together from older online material and trial and error. The talk also covers how broadcast queries reveal devices on a subnet, and how automated scanning can corrupt setup records.

The speaker shares a Perl tool on GitHub that queries simple passwords, resets security records, and backs up configuration. Recommendations include disabling the port where possible, placing devices behind a VPN or SSL tunnel, and filtering access to allowed hosts. The speaker notes that vendors point to documentation rather than fixing defaults, which makes disclosure difficult, and leaves firmware handling and the plaintext web applet for further research.

talks.title: CONFidence 2014: SCADA deep inside: protocols and security mechanisms
talks.teaser: Surveys industrial protocols and walks through Siemens PLC flaws, from weak password hashes to predictable web session cookies.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an overview of industrial control systems and explains why many vendor protocols were designed decades ago without authentication or encryption. The speaker surveys widely deployed protocols, including Modbus, DNP3, PROFINET DCP, MMS, IEC 60870-5-101/104 and the fault-tolerant Ethernet used in some control networks. For each one he covers the basic frame structure, the available dissectors and scanning tools, and the weak or missing security. Several demonstrations stand out. A crafted PROFINET DCP set request that zeroes the controller's network settings puts the device into defect mode, and a similar write packet can change the speed setpoint of a turbine during a penetration test.

The middle of the talk focuses on Siemens products and vulnerabilities. TIA Portal project files retained earlier password hashes, which were first stored with SHA-1 and later switched to MD5 after the vendor was notified. The speaker showed how those hashes can be brute-forced, how the challenge-response login on the PLC can be captured and cracked offline, and how a low-entropy random number generator in the controller's web interface led to predictable session cookies. Forging a valid cookie depended on the controller's start time, which could be inferred from SNMP and a default community string, and on a limited login counter. The speaker noted that the vendor patch took about a year.

The closing part describes his method for reverse engineering the proprietary S7 protocol by analysing hex dumps and captures with small Python helper scripts. The main takeaway is that protocol knowledge helps both attackers and defenders identify devices and monitor control traffic, since many of these protocols remain unsecured by design. The speaker said he planned to release his scripts and packet captures later.

talks.title: CONFidence 2014: On the battlefield with the Dragons -- G. Coldwind, M. Jurczyk
talks.teaser: Walks through Dragon Sector's CTF challenges, from Python sandbox escapes to a custom-architecture VM and TLS key recovery.
talks.summary:
This talk is a tour of capture-the-flag challenges solved by Dragon Sector, a Polish CTF team that has played together for about a year and a half and taken first place at several events. The speakers outline the CTF format, where tasks span cryptography, web, steganography and exploitation, and point to CTFtime as a source for event listings and archived write-ups.

The middle of the talk walks through specific challenges. A Mumble voice capture was decoded by spotting bursts of packets in a traffic graph and reading the short and long bursts as Morse code. Python sandbox tasks were escaped in two ways: one reached file objects through the class hierarchy to overwrite a libc entry, the other swapped a function's code object so it ran with globals it should not reach. A custom-architecture virtual machine was reversed by trial and error, building an assembler from observed behaviour, and a serial-port task on an unreal-mode system was solved through a heap bug and a writable descriptor alias to the code segment. Other tasks covered recovering a TLS master key from a core dump, brute-forcing keys from memory, and hiding data in base64 padding bits.

The speakers also described techniques they use repeatedly. These include abusing stack protector error output to leak memory when stderr is reachable over a socket, building a symbol corpus of common libc builds to resolve addresses quickly, and using instrumentation to change instruction behaviour without patching the binary. They closed by saying that a diverse team helps, that unintended bugs are common in CTF tasks, and that any working solution is a valid one.

talks.title: CONFidence 2014: Preventing violation of memory safety in C/C++ software
talks.teaser: Shows how an LLVM-based compiler extension adds spatial and temporal memory checks to C programs, with a FreeBSD port.
talks.summary:
The talk covers memory safety bugs in C and C++, including buffer overflows, integer overflows and use-after-free, which are grouped as spatial and temporal violations. The speaker argues that common defences fall short: randomisation and stack canaries can be bypassed, and object-based memory debugging tools miss overflows that stay inside a larger allocation, such as a buffer embedded in a struct.

The core of the talk is SoftBound with CETS, an LLVM-based instrumentation that stores base and bound metadata for pointers in a separate table, so struct layouts stay intact. Temporal checks use a key and lock scheme that is invalidated on free. The walkthrough covers pointer arithmetic, narrowing bounds for struct members, globals, memcpy and function pointers, and cases such as XOR-linked lists that the approach cannot handle. The reported slowdown is roughly a factor of two, and multithreaded code is a weak spot because the metadata updates are not thread safe.

The port to FreeBSD, which builds its whole system with LLVM, shows the approach working: a small demonstration program with an overlong command-line argument is stopped with a memory safety violation rather than overflowing silently. Open gaps include C++ code with virtual table calls, which the prototype could not yet compile, the extra memory used for pointer metadata, and kernel interface calls that need manual checks. The takeaway is that compiler-inserted checks offer stronger guarantees than debugging sanitizers, at a cost in speed and porting effort.

talks.title: CONFidence 2014: Asymmetric Defense "Using your home-field advantage"
talks.teaser: Shows defenders how to use their own network knowledge, logs and team to hunt intruders who should not be there.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that defenders hold an asymmetric edge because they know their own networks, while attackers must work that out from outside. Framed as a home-field advantage, the presenter lays out three points: understand your environment, study your opponent, and actively hunt for intruders who should not be there. He stresses building a team that mixes hands-on scripting skill with strategic thinking, since no one knows everything.

On environment, individual log sources can look harmless alone but become meaningful when correlated, such as an administrator logging into a machine while not badged into the building housing it. He separates logs into white noise, indicators and actionable intelligence, and notes that mismatched time sources can break Kerberos in ways that only log review reveals. He advises planning responses in advance, including who to notify and any compliance duties, and keeping management informed. On the adversary side he argues that financial motive drives serious attacks, so the most valuable data deserves focus first, and he points to blind spots such as encrypted traffic leaving through a proxy as reasons to justify better tooling.

For hunting, he suggests starting with basics like comparing autostart entries and executable hashes across all systems, then moving to advanced techniques without disrupting production services such as Exchange. He recommends administering from an isolated virtual machine and using non-interactive remote execution so credentials are not exposed. He closes by urging defenders to build relationships across siloed departments.

talks.title: CONFidence 2014: Protecting Big Data at Scale
talks.teaser: Argues that big data platforms need familiar security controls adapted to scale, using Hadoop as the main case.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that security models built for small, bounded networks break down when datasets and nodes number in the millions. The speaker argues that analysts must judge threats from accumulated patterns and graded risk scores rather than simple good-or-bad rules. Analogies such as stoplights, Hume's doorknob example, and shark hunting frame the argument, and public datasets on weather, floods, voting and wastewater drug traces show how much knowledge large collections can produce.

The middle of the talk turns to controls in Hadoop. Services commonly run under one shared user, so a single recursive delete command run as that user can wipe a whole file system, and one mistake by a new data scientist can halt operations for days while data is restored. Authentication, authorization, audit logging and confidentiality are described as scattered or missing, and many deployments leave services open because logging and checks are seen as performance costs. The speaker compares failing nodes to cattle rather than pets, calling for routine treatment backed by records and daily evaluation, and cites the Ariane 5 failure as a reminder that software faults matter.

The closing takeaway is to map classic controls onto big data stacks. Practical steps include multi-tenancy awareness, access control lists on file systems, Kerberos authentication, which the speaker considers weak, redundancy that keeps the name node and data nodes from being single points of failure, and classification-based access such as Accumulo labels or least-authority file systems. The speaker notes these tools are still being built, so practitioners should share lessons early rather than reinvent them.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2014: Let's build a solid base for a scale
talks.teaser: Traces how Allegro built a shared microservice bootstrap to replace a 15-year-old codebase, including the mistakes along the way.
talks.summary:
Krzysztof Debski, an Allegro developer, architect and product owner of the bootstrap, describes how the company's auction platform, about 15 years old and roughly 6 million lines of code, moved toward microservices. Early attempts at SOA and an ambitious plan for fully automated services fell short, so the team switched to a working-skeleton approach, building small pieces and deploying them quickly.

The shared bootstrap began with Gradle, Spring and an external Jetty server, then moved to embedded servers so each service ran as one package. It added Jersey and Swagger for REST endpoints and documentation, ZooKeeper for registering instances, and a discovery service that tells callers where to send requests. API versions were chosen through the Accept header, and configuration came from ZooKeeper with local property overrides. Mutation testing, Logstash and Graphite integration, and a multi-module layout completed the kit, while service authentication and Docker support were still in progress.

The lessons were practical. Upgrading Gradle cut long waits for missing jars on the Nexus repository, and a CI environment that downloaded the Gradle wrapper on every build was changed. Unclear parameters, such as magic numbers that really belonged in headers, made some APIs hard to use. The main advice was to adopt current tools, keep APIs stable while internals change, and invite developers from other teams to contribute to the open source project.

talks.teaser: A Q&A covers front-end shifts, modern build tools, and why slow UIs undermine back-end scalability efforts.

The segment begins at the Atmosphere conference with brief remarks on the event’s second edition and the guest’s front-end presentation that day. The interviewer asks how front-end work today differs from roughly five years earlier. The guest answers that far more business logic now lives in the browser, producing complex client-side applications that were uncommon only a few years before.

Discussion moves to tooling beyond familiar Chrome and Firefox debuggers. The guest emphasizes build tools and task runners that preprocess, optimize, and automate front-end workflows as the ecosystem matures. On scalability, he describes the UI as the meeting point between users and infrastructure, warning that slow, heavy interfaces prevent customers from benefiting from back-end optimization.

The interview ends by asking whether DevOps practitioners should care about front-end performance. The guest says both layers matter equally because the front end is where technology meets users. He closes by outlining his full-stack work at Allegro—provisioning cloud machines, deploying applications, writing PHP or Java back-end code, and handling HTML and CSS on the client.

talks.title: 4Dev 2014: Is PHP Dying? Interview with Mariusz Gil.
talks.teaser: Examines whether PHP is fading, comparing its standing in Europe and the US with rival languages and why conferences matter.
talks.summary:
The interview opens with the question of whether PHP is fading. Mariusz Gil, a member of the programme committee who handled the PHP track at this 4Developers edition, explains how talks were picked: the aim was a mix covering the PHP ecosystem, front-end work and quality tools rather than one narrow theme, so most attendees find a few sessions they love. He argues PHP is still the mainstream choice for web development, even as Python, Ruby, .NET and Java gain ground.

He describes a regional split. In Europe, PHP is enjoying a revival, driven by the Symfony team and a wave of tools built around the ecosystem, Composer among them. In the United States the trend has reversed: Silicon Valley startups often pick Python or Ruby for fast clickable prototypes, then run into problems and move to other languages. Twitter, which began on Ruby, now runs on the JVM, he notes.

On the conference itself, he says it offers two things: direct access to speakers, many of them working at well-known companies, and networking with people already known from social media and blogs. The event has grown from small hotels to fill three floors and a whole hotel, and it has widened beyond developers to include project managers, testers and cloud people. He closes by urging attendees to join local meetups and user groups, or to start their own event if none exists nearby.

talks.title: CONFidence 2014: NSA for dummies ...methods to break RSA
talks.teaser: Walks through how RSA and Diffie-Hellman work and the factoring methods that threaten them, with a small Sage demo.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the motivation for public-key cryptography, covering the Diffie-Hellman key exchange and the discrete logarithm problem it relies on. It then moves to RSA, its key generation, and why its security depends on factoring being hard. Basic number theory follows, including congruences and Euler's totient, which underpin the attacks discussed later. A short Sage script builds a toy 1024-bit RSA key pair, encrypts a message, and decrypts it, so the mechanics can be seen step by step.

The middle section surveys factoring methods. Trial division suits very small primes, Pollard's rho uses a random walk and collisions to find moderate factors, and Pollard's p-1 method only works when a factor has smooth p-1 structure. The elliptic curve method and the quadratic sieve handle larger numbers, and the number field sieve is presented as the current state of the art. The speaker recalls public factoring challenges, including the 1977 RSA challenge and a 1990s collaborative effort, and notes recent progress on discrete logarithm algorithms.

The closing part argues that practical risk often comes from poor implementations rather than cryptanalytic breakthroughs. Weak randomness can let two keys share a prime, which a GCD calculation exposes quickly. Cost estimates suggest that keys above a certain size stay out of reach for now, while quantum computers are named as the main long-term threat. The takeaways are to avoid textbook RSA, rely on vetted cryptographic libraries, and replace weakly seeded network devices.

talks.title: CONFidence 2014: Scaling Security
talks.teaser: Robert Kiss explores CONFidence 2014: Scaling Security.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At CONFidence 2014, members of the Prezi security team—Mishi, Robi, and Attila—presented practical approaches to scaling security in a fast-growing startup environment. Operating with over 40 million users, more than 400 AWS instances, over 400 Git repositories, and 15+ programming languages, Prezi deploys software over 100 times per week with more than 80 engineers. With only a three-person security team, traditional blocking security controls (such as mandatory pre-deployment sign-offs or blocking code reviews) are impossible. Instead, the team prioritizes influence, culture, non-blocking monitoring, automated alerting, and iterative learning.

### Key Topics
- **DevOps Culture & Agile Security:** Integrating security into full-stack engineering where developers own code and infrastructure. Critical incidents trigger a 'Prior 1' mode where developers rally to fix issues within 30 minutes.
- **Static Code Analysis with RepoGuard:** A custom Python-based tool that fetches Git repositories and applies regular expressions to detect risky code changes without blocking deployments.
- **Infrastructure Auditing with Red Alert:** Built around Netflix’s open-source tool Edda (and libraries like Boto), Red Alert tracks near-real-time changes across AWS environments and triggers alerts on risky infrastructure modifications.
- **Logging and Fast Search:** Transitioning from slow Hadoop queries to Elasticsearch for near-real-time log indexing and correlation, complemented by host-level monitoring like auditd.
- **Bug Bounty Program & Feedback Loops:** Leveraging external security researchers to identify real-world attack vectors, followed by blameless post-mortem investigations that produce new detection rules.

### Technical Details
- **RepoGuard:** Because market static analysis tools did not support Prezi's 15+ diverse languages, the team developed RepoGuard. It runs pattern-matching regexes across code commits and chef repositories (e.g., detecting newly exposed virtual hosts or insecure ORM usage such as Django's `get_by_secondary_key`). Although initially generating overwhelming false positives, the rule set was refined to over 70 rules, yielding roughly 20 manageable alerts per day.
- **Red Alert & AWS Tracking:** Netflix's Edda polls AWS APIs and stores environment state snapshots in a local database, allowing diffing without incurring heavy AWS API costs. Prezi built Red Alert as an extensible plugin framework on top of Edda and Boto. Red Alert monitors security groups (e.g., catching accidentally exposed ports like 9080/TCP), elastic load balancers, and user creation. The team open-sourced Red Alert at the conference.
- **Vulnerability Insights & Bug Bounty:** Prezi instituted a bug bounty program that generated nearly 1,000 unique submissions and over 60 paid issues in its first eight months, requiring around five hours weekly just for email triage. Notable findings included an SSRF/local file read in an offline conversion service where an external researcher bypassed theoretical defenses by querying the AWS link-local metadata service to extract bootstrap secrets. Subsequent fixes were subjected to further community review, exposing subtle issues like DNS rebinding.
- **Post-Mortem Process:** Following critical outages or security findings, teams produce detailed post-mortem documents and hold open review meetings to implement multi-layered prevention rules rather than one-off patches.

### Takeaways
Defenders often theorize about attack vectors that differ from what attackers actually exploit. Rather than relying on generic out-of-the-box tools (such as unmodified Suricata), organizations should tailor detection systems to their specific architecture. By adopting non-blocking automated detectors like RepoGuard and Red Alert, fostering open communication with developers, and actively learning from external researchers via bug bounties, a small security team can effectively protect an agile, cloud-native enterprise.

talks.title: PLNOG 12: How much does DDoS cost from the perspective of a cybercriminal and a victim of an attack
talks.teaser: Weighs the financial damage of DDoS attacks against the cheap DDoS-for-hire services sold to criminals.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a refresher on denial-of-service attacks and why distributed variants are hard to stop. It focuses on reflection and amplification attacks, where spoofed UDP requests sent to open DNS and other servers produce much larger responses aimed at a victim. The speaker points to measurements showing that many networks still allow address spoofing, and to recent attacks that reached roughly 300 Gbit/s by abusing tens of thousands of DNS servers.

The middle of the talk covers costs. Victims face incident handling, lost sales, call-center load, reputation damage, contractual penalties and lost staff productivity, with hourly estimates varying widely by industry. Examples include a Polish ISP where a quarter of customers lost internet access during a 60 Gbit/s attack, and an attack on a major Polish e-commerce group that moved from one service to the next. A bank case shows DDoS used as cover for a theft of about $900,000. The speaker then walks through DDoS-for-hire storefronts, with hourly packages, free short tests, refund guarantees and live support, priced at a small fraction of the losses described earlier.

The closing section gives defensive advice. Teams should restrict exposed services such as NTP monlist queries, add rate limits, and prepare a written action plan with clear decision owners. Other recommendations include templated customer communication that does not mislead, arranging provider help before an incident, patching devices, segmenting services, and blocking spoofed traffic from leaving the network.

The discussion turns to OWASP as a global community that ships tools and ideas, including a Polish chapter and meetups tied to other security events. On the conference theme of scalability, the guest describes Node.js scaling as straightforward thanks to built-in clustering, and points to Docker containers as another practical way to grow workloads without deep CPU internals knowledge.

The closing segment highlights open-source work alongside a day job and family life, especially Fedora efforts such as Dockerfile examples for learning containers, peripheral contributions to the Fedora Account System, and hands-on support for monitoring projects when contributors hit install or configuration snags.

The middle centers on life in London at eBay while staying tied to Polish developer communities. He explains stepping back from some local groups after relocating, yet continuing remote involvement—mailing lists, speaker outreach, and pride in the sixth edition of a large Polish developer conference run entirely remotely, with more than 1100 attendees finishing just before the interview. He frames support for Poland as sentimental advocacy, comparing London meetups with Kraków’s active startup scene and arguing the Polish community should promote itself more openly.

Toward the end he previews a separate session on Go in 2014: concise syntax, speed, and strong HTTP libraries. He describes an eBay experiment that rewrote an ordinary Java Spring application in Go, yielding about one-eighth the code with the same behavior and easier readability. He closes with thoughts on moving the conference from Kraków toward Wrocław as a practical, travel-driven venue choice.

talks.teaser: A short interview explores how a presentation company scales its backend, adopts DevOps, and plans a move to Amazon cloud infrastructure.

The conversation opens at a DevOps-focused conference in Poland, where a backend engineer from Prezi reflects on the venue and his prior visits to the region. The interviewer asks how widely DevOps is understood in Hungary; he notes smaller firms often blend development and operations for practicality, while many large organizations still treat the idea as novel.

He describes Prezi’s growth past roughly four million users and the pressure to scale further within one or two years. Infrastructure began with a handful of on-premise servers and now spans hundreds of machines, with a shift toward Amazon’s cloud. The team uses Chef, Jenkins, monitoring and paging tools, homemade utilities, and pilot work with Docker while wrestling with splitting a long-lived monolith before the full cloud move.

Practitioners hear a preview of his separate session on continuous delivery and making DevOps workable at both small and large scale. For attendees who missed the hall, the exchange also frames the conference as a strong DevOps gathering in an appealing city.

He frames DevOps as culture rather than a job title, praises Undead Labs for adopting Berkshelf before he arrived, and teases online features built with repeatable promotion pipelines that aim to shrink maintenance windows.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2014: Interview with Phil Dibowitz from Facebook
talks.teaser: The conversation covers human-centric configuration scaling, empowered small teams, and impressions of a European operations conference.
talks.summary:
An on-stage interview opens with a recap of a separate presentation on scalability challenges inside a large social network’s operations organization. The guest argues that configuration management should optimize for how many engineers and teams can reason about the estate, not only how many nodes can register with Chef or similar control planes. He describes a pattern where a shared baseline defines what a standard server should look like, while product and service owners declare only deltas from that norm, shrinking total policy volume and letting specialists own the pieces they care about while a central group keeps the overall management model coherent.

The middle of the conversation shifts to workplace culture: small teams with broad latitude, fringe benefits on campus, and examples of fixing broken LDAP synchronization and later driving a multi-month migration away from CF Engine 2 toward Chef, often without formal approval gates. A four- or five-person team grew around that configuration work as interest spread.

Closing topics include personal travel and concert habits, brief comparisons of Warsaw visits, and encouragement for future attendees to try a conference that the guest says is less famous in the United States but already feels well run and conversation-rich on day one. Practitioners hear a people-scaling frame for infra automation plus anecdotes about autonomy and incremental adoption of new tooling.

talks.title: Atmosphere 2014: Really large scale systems configuration
talks.teaser: Shows how Facebook replaced CF Engine with a Chef-based system that lets service owners manage their own configuration deltas.
talks.summary:
Phil Dibowitz explains why Facebook moved its configuration management from CF Engine 2 to Chef and the design principles behind that move. The goal was to manage very large heterogeneous fleets while letting service owners adjust only the settings they care about. He argues these ideas apply at almost any size. The core requirements were a distributed, deterministic system that is extensible without forking the tool, and one that treats configuration as data merged from small hashes and arrays.

One example is CIS control settings, which had 151 stale copies under the old setup. With a single template rendering a merged hash of defaults, each team overrides only its own values, and removing those lines reverts the setting cleanly. Node data was another problem: the default Chef node save sent multi-megabyte objects every 15 minutes, so a whitelist cut each check-in to under a kilobyte. Scale tests reached 17,000 nodes with about 82% CPU idle on the back end once a rewritten Chef server was in use.

Delivery relied on a service that synced cookbooks from version control to back ends every minute. Testing combined food critic linting, ChefSpec and a local Chef Zero tool that pushed a developer's code to a production host. The takeaways: express only the delta, prefer full programming languages over restrictive DSLs, wrap complex logic in functions, and test against real systems, because only production shows what a change will really do. Several of the tools were open-sourced.

talks.title: PLNOG12: The Phantom Menace or IPv6 DS-Lite at Neostrada
talks.teaser: Walks through Orange Polska's DS-Lite rollout on Neostrada, covering CGN design, port allocation, redundancy and pitfalls.
talks.summary:
Monika Antoniak-Lewandowska and Krzysztof Kwiecień of Orange Polska describe how their fixed-line Neostrada service was moved to DS-Lite, an IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnelling approach with carrier-grade NAT. They start with the IPv4 address shortage that led the operator to begin its IPv6 program around 2010. They then compare options: dual-stack NAT44, dual-stack lite and NAT64 with DNS64. DS-Lite was chosen because customer equipment needs IPv6 support only, the access link carries a single protocol, and it fit the group's strategy. The talk also covers the N+1 CGN topology with BGP local preference for failover, changes to the BNG and DHCPv6 prefix delegation, and the need to fit the design into the existing network.

The middle of the talk covers testing with a student dormitory and real traffic, which exposed problems that the lab could not. The team settled on a block of 8000 ports per user, a public address kept for at least 24 hours, and a limit of three simultaneous tunnels per subscriber prefix. They also described raising MTU on some devices, implementing PCP for port forwarding with its security risks, and tuning timeouts, which had no published best practice. Traffic statistics showed that around 20% of traffic from IPv6-only clients was native IPv6, with the rest going through the CGN.

The takeaway is that DS-Lite at scale needs parameters tuned on live traffic, and those values must be revisited as usage changes. Users who need IPv4 can return to the old service by removing a suffix from their login. Operators should expect long integration work between CGN and CPE vendors, and should plan for logging and retention requirements from the start.

talks.title: PLNOG12: The use of FlexVPN to provide carrier network security
talks.teaser: Shows how Flex VPN's IKEv2-based IPsec design covers multi-tenant remote access, spoke-to-spoke tunnels and MPLS virtualization.
talks.summary:
The session introduces Flex VPN, an overlay IPsec framework built on IKEv2 that consolidates earlier approaches such as Easy VPN, DMVPN and legacy crypto maps under one CLI. Its advantages over IKEv1 include a standardized RFC, EAP and hybrid authentication, and protection against half-open session floods. Virtual templates are instantiated into per-peer virtual-access interfaces, and AAA can drive authorization for each peer.

Four use cases are walked through with short configurations. In single-customer remote access, each user's virtual-access interface is placed into the correct VRF, with QoS and firewall zones applied from RADIUS attributes. A multi-customer design uses separate profiles so each customer's users authenticate against that customer's own AAA server, while the provider keeps control of VRF and bandwidth settings. A mixed deployment places clients and branches on one profile, enabling per-peer spoke-to-spoke tunnels and pushing static route sets from AAA so no routing protocol is needed. The last case carries BGP VPNv4 prefixes for several VRFs over one IPsec tunnel, with dynamic BGP neighbors on the hub and VPN label resolution between spokes.

The main takeaway is that moving policy into the AAA backend keeps configurations short and makes changes such as subnet updates a server-side task rather than a router edit. The speaker points to recorded sessions and the Cisco configuration guide for deeper detail on remote access clients, EAP and MPLS overlays.

The talk presents a practical way for an ISP to automate customer service handling, from sales and technical survey through to activating network services. The presenters explain that their UNIBOX back-office application, written in Java on the jPALIO portal technology, hands orders to Juniper Junos Space, a vendor management system that understands the device software and builds the services on the routers.

The live demo covered creating a customer, choosing business parameters, adding two endpoints and an SLA, and publishing a multipoint service to a lab Juniper MX device. The team described integration challenges. Junos Space operations are not atomic, so they built a rollback mechanism around its API, and a removed service could not be recreated with identical parameters for a couple of seconds. They also noted gaps in the documentation and small differences between what the API accepts and what Junos Space itself allows.

The presenters argued that keeping the application team and the network operations team separate lets each focus on its own work, and that a process which often takes weeks at larger operators can be cut to minutes. They closed by inviting interested ISPs to their booth, noting that the tool is now sold commercially.

talks.teaser: A presenter outlines why Java Developers Days in Krakow helps practitioners learn what peers build and the problems they face.
talks.summary:
Kirk Pepperdine opens with a brief personal introduction and notes that long involvement in the Java space led to his invitation to Java Developers Days in Krakow. He frames the conference as a chance to meet attendees in person rather than only consume sessions from afar.

He emphasizes conversations with participants: learning what they are working on, which problems dominate their day-to-day work, and how they apply the shared technology that connects the community. That feedback loop, he suggests, is what makes the gathering worthwhile.

He closes on a forward-looking note, hoping future editions bring even more people together to share techniques and experiences. The segment is introductory in nature and does not walk through tools, exploits, or a defined technical agenda.

talks.title: PLNOG12: Wywiad z Rafałem Szewczykiem (Infoblox)
talks.teaser: A vendor representative covers rising network complexity, outsourced DDoS threats, and DNS protection priorities for operators in Poland.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with how enterprise and administrator awareness of network complexity is expected to grow over the next five years, and why forums that swap experience between vendors and customers matter for future network management. The guest describes a near-term focus on launching advanced DNS protection after widespread DDoS incidents affecting clients globally and in Poland, and argues that full network automation is unrealistic even though partial automation can shrink or surface problems faster.

The middle turns to DDoS mechanics at a high level: attacks can be bought anonymously, often with cryptocurrency, with motives ranging from hacktivism to commissioned disruption among competitors or unclear parties. Detection of such crime remains weak, so organizations are left to harden availability. Awareness among banks and large Polish services still lags Western markets, yet smaller operators now report DDoS as an acute issue rather than a problem only for tier-one carriers.

The close ties PLNOG’s record attendance to curated, practitioner-heavy programming and outlines a year-round security network working group to share defensive good practices. The guest endorses that initiative and frames repeated conference participation as relationship-building that flows into client work, not a one-off marketing appearance.

talks.title: JDD09 Mark Richard Sztuka Messagingu
talks.teaser: Explains JMS basics, queue design pitfalls, and RESTful JMS, with live Java and Groovy ActiveMQ demos.
talks.summary:
The presentation begins by arguing for messaging as a way to achieve asynchronous communication, guaranteed delivery, and load balancing. It illustrates heterogeneous integration between Java and other stacks, relieving processing bottlenecks with multiple listeners, speeding up long reports through fire-and-forget requests, and keeping architecture agile when components are removed or replaced while messages wait in queues.

The middle section reviews JMS point-to-point and publish-subscribe models, message headers, properties, and body types, warning against object messages that re-tighten coupling across deployments. The speaker codes a minimal Java sender and Groovy receiver against ActiveMQ, then shifts to design choices: persistent versus non-persistent delivery and benchmarked throughput, the common single-queue router pattern and its concurrency downsides, and why separate queues for book orders, status, and cancels beat relying on message priority when batch and web orders compete for the same listeners.

The close contrasts in-firewall messaging with web services for external clients, outlines RESTful JMS challenges such as idempotent GET semantics, demonstrates HTTP-to-JMS bridging in ActiveMQ, and invites a hands-on day covering pub/sub, transactions, and acknowledgements while pointing listeners to slides, sample code, and an updated O’Reilly Java Message Service second edition.

talks.title: JDD09 Piotr Walczyszyn
talks.teaser: Attendees see how Flex, Flash Catalyst, and LiveCycle Data Services build a data-driven rich internet app via model-driven development.
talks.summary:
The session begins with rich internet applications and a quick history of user interfaces from text terminals and thick clients to early HTML and browser apps that aim for desktop-grade interaction. The speaker positions Adobe runtimes—Flash Player, AIR for desktop distribution, and the Flex stack of MXML, ActionScript, and SWF—and explains how clients talk to servers over HTTP, SOAP, or compact AMF into Java via LiveCycle Data Services and the open BlazeDS line.

The core middle section walks through LiveCycle Data Services capabilities: data management and offline sync, configurable paging and lazy loading, exposing Java services as RPC or HTTP endpoints, JMS-style messaging with RTMP or automatic HTTP fallback, transactional delete confirmation across unreliable networks, pause-and-resume for large record sets, network transparency behind firewalls, and client-side data throttling under load. Flash Catalyst is introduced as a designer-oriented path from Illustrator artwork to components, states, and transitions without hand-coding every control.

The closing live demo builds a multi-state UI in Catalyst, imports it into Flash Builder, reverse-engineers HSQL tables into an object model deployed to Tomcat, binds a generated data grid with server paging, and adds a model variant that shows or hides fields when a boolean flag is set. Beta tooling limits some Catalyst-to-list wiring, but the flow illustrates model-driven development shrinking bespoke client and server code for a simple conference attendee example.

talks.title: JDD09 Scot Davis Testowanie z Groovy
talks.teaser: Demonstrates Groovy for JVM unit tests, behavior-driven stories with easyb, and closure-based mocks with gmock.
talks.summary:
Scott Davis frames Groovy as a JVM language that augments Java rather than replacing it, and argues that adoption can start safely in the test suite before production use. He walks through why organizations still undertest, cites industry pressure toward high coverage, and contrasts writing tests after large Java beans with a test-first style that shapes better models.

Live coding moves from a Java Car class and JUnit-style tests into GroovyTestCase, showing terse asserts, optional visibility on members, and reflection-style access that makes it practical to force inconsistent state and expect specific exceptions. He briefly covers behavior-driven development with easyb using scenario, given, when, and then blocks tied to user wording, plus pending stories in generated reports.

The session closes with gmock, comparing closure-based expectation blocks to familiar Java mocking libraries so tests avoid live databases and services. Practitioners should leave seeing Groovy as a low-friction path to richer unit, BDD, and mock testing against existing Java code.

talks.title: JDD09 Tom Baeyens and Joram Barrez
