talks.title: Adam Bien "EJB 3.1..." Part 6
talks.teaser: Answers audience questions on testing EJBs, container startup times, dependency injection and integration tests against real databases.
talks.summary:
This closing part of an EJB 3.1 session is a question-and-answer round in which the speaker describes how he handles dependency injection, testing and deployment in his own projects. He keeps the architecture to a few thin layers such as service, facade and domain, and says a couple of field injections are not a major concern. For wiring outside a container he suggests reflection, OpenEJB, Pitchfork, or starting the embeddable container in a test setup method.

On testing, he avoids mocking the persistence layer so that named queries are really exercised. He mocks only view classes in unit tests and treats facade-level tests as integration tests. For databases he describes an embedded file-system Derby instance that is deleted after each run, and for larger projects virtual machines running an application server and Oracle that are discarded after each test, which allows parallel runs. He argues that tests should also run on a continuous integration machine so that results do not depend on one developer's laptop.

Asked about deployment speed, he says a project with about 200 entities and 30 facades took 15 seconds to fully redeploy, while later EJB 3.1 redeployments took roughly 40 to 60 milliseconds. Major refactorings still call for a full server restart. He also recounts a rich internet application built on an Eclipse client that embedded the container. His takeaway is that EJBs suit transactional, concurrent business systems such as insurance and banking, though they may be too heavy for real-time trading systems.

talks.title: Corneliu Vasile Creanga "Flex and Java..." Part 1
talks.teaser: Introduces the Adobe Flex graphical framework for the Flash platform and its declarative MXML approach to building interfaces.
talks.summary:
The session opens a two-part series on using Adobe Flex with Java, and this first part is a primer for listeners who have never worked with the framework. The speaker traces the history of the Flash Player, which began in the late 1990s mainly for simple movies and advertising, and explains why the Flash authoring tool was a poor fit for building applications. Macromedia began work on Flex in 2004, and the speaker presents it as a graphical library for the Flash platform, comparable to Swing in the Java world, that uses the ActionScript 3 language.

The middle of the talk is a live walkthrough of the free Tour de Flex application, which lists the built-in components, from input controls and advanced data grids to layouts called containers, effects, formatters, validators and charting. The speaker also points to sample code for connecting to web services such as Amazon and eBay, and notes that developers can contribute their own components. Loading some of the component samples was slow because of the network connection.

The talk closes with the idea that Flex uses two languages: ActionScript for logic and MXML, a declarative XML-based language for layout. The speaker shows an MXML file in the Flex IDE and explains that declarative markup makes visual interfaces easier to build and suits design tools, while very complex or highly dynamic interfaces may be better written in code. The second part is said to cover integration with Java frameworks.

talks.title: Adam Bien "EJB 3.1..." Part 5
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Adam Bien "EJB 3.1..." Part 5.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Adam Bien discusses Enterprise JavaBeans (EJB) configuration, migration strategies, and developer workflow across EJB 2, EJB 3.0, and EJB 3.1. Addressing common criticisms regarding EJB complexity, the session focuses on debunking myths about configuration verbosity, simplifying migration from legacy EJB 2 architectures, and demonstrating how minimal modern EJB implementations can be.

### Key Topics
- **Configuration Precedence:** How conventions, Java annotations, and XML deployment descriptors interact, highlighting the ability to override configurations per environment.
- **Dependency Injection and Alternatives:** Injecting primitive data types, limitations in EJB 3, upcoming changes in EJB 3.1, and using frameworks like Guice (Juice) or databases for bean configuration.
- **Spring Integration:** Mention of SpringSource's Pitchfork container providing EJB 3.0 support and project Matisse bringing EJB 3.1 support.
- **EJB 2 to EJB 3 Migration:** Overcoming legacy J2EE 1.4 XML dependencies, leveraging backward compatibility, replacing service locators, and using annotations like `@LocalHome`.
- **Vendor Neutrality:** The strategic and financial motivations driving companies away from proprietary application servers due to licensing costs.
- **Minimal EJB Development:** The development simplicity of modern stateless session beans without deployment descriptors or complex build tooling.

### Technical Details
- **Configuration Hierarchy:** EJB relies first on conventions (predefined defaults), which can be overridden by Java annotations. Annotations can further be overridden by XML deployment descriptors. Bien demonstrates using XML strictly for testing overrides and omitting it in production.
- **XML and Injection Improvements:** EJB 3 allows configuring and injecting primitive types via XML, though it requires specifying an injection target. In EJB 3.1, the injection target becomes optional or can be removed, reducing verbosity.
- **Migration Strategy:** Migrating directly between J2EE 1.4 platforms is complicated by XML configurations. Because EJB 3 is backward compatible with EJB 2, developers can deploy EJB 2 beans in an EJB 3 container. By using annotations such as `@LocalHome`, teams can eliminate XML deployment descriptors, remove legacy service locators via dependency injection, and preserve underlying business logic. Once migrated, teams can incrementally refactor, replacing home interfaces with business interfaces and removing up to 80% of legacy boilerplate code.
- **Modern EJB Simplicity:** The simplest modern EJB requires only a class with a default constructor annotated with `@Stateless`. Compiling requires only the stateless annotation on the classpath, packaging into a standard JAR, and dropping it into an application server like GlassFish or JBoss for auto-deployment, without requiring deployment descriptors or code generation wizards.

### Takeaways
- EJB 3.x simplifies enterprise Java by prioritizing convention over configuration and making XML completely optional.
- Backward compatibility allows safe, incremental modernization of legacy EJB 2 systems while maintaining enterprise vendor independence.
- Modern stateless session beans offer a lightweight, boilerplate-free alternative that can be packaged and auto-deployed into standard application servers or integrated within Spring environments.

talks.title: Adam Bien "EJB 3.1..." Part 4
talks.teaser: Explains why Java EJB 3.1 reduces complexity in distributed applications and how it integrates with web frameworks.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that the real complexity of distributed applications comes from shared state, concurrency and synchronization rather than from the framework. Unit tests on plain objects run single-threaded and miss these problems, which appear under heavy load when threads contend for a shared resource such as the database. The speaker says EJB provides declarative transactions and concepts that teams otherwise rebuild by hand. He recounts a team that wrapped a home-built context in thread-local filters and then suffered resource leaks because developers forgot to close resources, and another team that later deployed OpenEJB into Tomcat to gain transactions.

On the practical side, he covers integration and operations. EJBs can be injected directly into JSF backing beans and servlets, though stateful beans cannot be injected into stateless servlets. He exposes EJBs through servlets so JMeter can load test them. Every bean is exposed through JMX under the JSR 77 management specification, so tools such as JConsole or VisualVM can monitor the server without extra work, while hand-built POJO servers often add this later.

For legacy classes without source code, he shows a proof of concept that injects a Swing table model as a transactional bean, stressing that it is not a best practice. With EJB 3.1, a no-interface view makes such injection simpler. His takeaway is to understand the distributed concepts first, then let the container handle transactions, concurrency and management instead of rebuilding them.

talks.title: Adam Bien "EJB 3.1..." Part 3
talks.teaser: Measures EJB session bean overhead against plain POJOs and discusses memory, scalability and stateful session handling.
talks.summary:
The talk takes on the common belief that Enterprise JavaBeans are slow. The speaker describes a test in which the same class first ran as a plain object called from a servlet, then as a session bean. The difference came to about 3 percent, or roughly two milliseconds, which he argues is negligible next to any database access. He attributes that overhead to the dynamic proxy the container wraps around the bean.

On memory, he reports little difference between beans and plain objects, since containers may create several proxies per instance. He says the bigger memory risk is cached JPA entities, and recommends profilers such as the NetBeans profiler, YourKit or TPTP when usage gets high. On scalability, he explains that each request gets its own bean instance bound to one thread for the whole call, which avoids synchronization concerns and scales much like a prototype-scoped bean. Stateful beans scale through session affinity at the load balancer, while synchronous state replication is costly.

He closes with a create-read-update-delete load test of a GlassFish application on modest test machines, which reached about 500 transactions per second without any tuning. His takeaway is to measure rather than assume, since the real bottlenecks in most systems are persistence, locking and caching rather than the session beans themselves.

talks.title: Adam Bien "EJB 3.1..." Part 2
talks.teaser: Part two covers in-process EJB testing, cross-vendor portability in Java EE, and wiring Guice beans into EJB facades via interceptors.
talks.summary:
The speaker continues a walkthrough of real migration work on a crowded online-store-style codebase, where introducing an EJB service boundary and entities removed roughly eighty percent of custom layering built over years. He argues EJB 3.x components are plain annotated POJOs that unit tests can target directly, with reflection filling private dependencies where needed, and warns against rolling a bespoke embedded container when EJB 3.1 already supports in-process boot via the standard API—often about a second on his setup, sometimes less.

He highlights global JNDI naming in EJB 3.1 as the missing piece for portable lookups across local, remote, or no-interface views, contrasting older vendor-specific naming schemes. Compared with J2EE 1.4, where vendors extended persistence and locking differently and migrations between WebSphere, WebLogic, and GlassFish often failed, Java EE 5 standardized behavior so the same deployment descriptors can move between commercial and open-source servers. He notes strategic leverage for licensing and that vendor XML overlays largely disappear, while production still demands persistence-provider testing because OpenJPA, Hibernate, and TopLink diverge in behavior.

The closing segment shows a proof-of-concept Guice integration: a method interceptor builds a Guice injector, binds a message provider, and injects non-EJB dependencies into an EJB facade on each invocation—similar in spirit to how Seam handled scopes behind interceptors. Practitioners should leave able to test EJBs in-process, reason about portability limits, and extend beans with external DI when the spec alone is not enough.

talks.title: Adam Bien "EJB 3.1..." Part 1
talks.teaser: Debunks common myths about Enterprise JavaBeans weight, XML, POJOs, and testing using hands-on project experience.
talks.summary:
The presentation reframes longtime objections to Enterprise JavaBeans by walking through the first items on a longer list of misconceptions, shaped by feedback from prior conference appearances and day-to-day architecture work on client projects. The opening focuses on the claim that EJBs are heavyweight. The speaker challenges teams to define what heavyweight means, contrasts that label with Spring and similar stacks that still rely on containers and proxies, and cites measurable footprint figures for GlassFish early-access packaging and the EJB 3.1 API surface, arguing that modern annotations and removed deployment descriptors make the programming model lean.

The middle of the session ties misconceptions to persistence configuration, built-in transaction and security behavior through declarative aspects, and the idea that plain old Java objects in production are always container-managed regardless of framework branding. A short workshop anecdote illustrates building service-oriented, domain-driven applications quickly without XML-heavy setup.

The segment on testing addresses review cultures that reward coverage percentages without meaningful assertions, then shows concrete unit-test scaffolding that boots JPA inside tests and exercises a service bean with a handful of lines. Practitioners are invited to question blanket rejection of EJBs and to compare size, annotations, and testability on equal terms with alternative stacks.

talks.title: Neal Ford "The Productive Programmer..." Part 7
talks.teaser: Explores growing one-off automation into tested tooling, ROI timeboxing for managers, and the yak-shaving trap in side quests.
talks.summary:
This segment continues a case where automating a recurring file-generation task initially took five times longer than doing the work by hand. Because the underlying file kept changing, the team ran the job many more times, and the automated approach eventually paid off in repeated effort.

The presenter recommends building such helpers in a real programming language rather than a one-off hack, so the solution can grow unit tests, mock objects, refactoring, and IDE support as it becomes part of the project. He argues that manual repetition steals concentration even when it looks faster on a spreadsheet, while automation pushes clearer design. For managers, he suggests timeboxing automation experiments and weighing current manual duration against how often the task must run, framing automation as both time savings and risk mitigation.

He closes with a cautionary chain—needing a Subversion visualization tool, then Apache, Linux, kernel, and video-driver changes—illustrating “yak shaving,” where developers lose sight of the original goal amid nested side problems.

talks.title: Neal Ford "The Productive Programmer..." Part 6
talks.teaser: Outlines CI as team priority, strict version control, and automation from packaged stacks through Selenium to bespoke scripts.
talks.summary:
The segment argues that continuous integration should be the top priority for teams still building only on individual machines. A dedicated integration host becomes the sole official build, running tests and continuously producing artifacts such as schema documentation, which ends reliance on “works on my machine” claims.

Version control is treated as mandatory: commented-out code should disappear because history already preserves old lines. Automation is split into three approaches—adopting packaged stacks like Buildix for repositories and build servers in minutes, repurposing tools such as the Selenium IDE to record and replay long web wizards (including export to JUnit or Ruby for command-line runs), and writing small bespoke utilities. Examples include a bash pipeline to bulk-add new Subversion files and a Ruby script that split a 38,000-line SQL file into thousand-line syntactically valid chunks in roughly fifty minutes instead of manual slicing.

Practitioners are urged to favor real scripting languages over fragile shell one-offs when problems recur, and to invest minutes in jigs and scripts the way a craftsperson would. QA can record failing browser sessions for playback, cutting repetitive navigation during debugging and clarifying reproduction steps.

talks.title: Neal Ford "The Productive Programmer..." Part 5
talks.teaser: The segment shows how canonical data sources and Groovy build scripts eliminate duplication across ORM mappings and Java DTOs.
talks.summary:
Ford opens with a maintenance nightmare: database schema, ORM XML, and plain Java objects all carried overlapping structure, while external DBAs kept making subtle schema tweaks that broke application code. The team treated the live database as the single source of truth and used Groovy against JDBC metadata—including a Sybase trick that returns column types from an empty result set—to emit iBatis SQL map files via the language’s XML builder.

A companion class builder script then generated matching DTOs with fields, getters, and setters so the Java layer stayed aligned with both the schema and the mapping configuration. He contrasts this with approaches like letting XML drive generation through tools such as XDoclet, then pivots to distributed teamwork across Chicago, New York, and Bangalore.

Rather than rely on end-of-day wiki discipline, they hooked Subversion commits to dated wiki pages and paired RSS readers on workstations so developers—and eventually the project manager—could scan only unseen updates. Exporting that wiki to static HTML yielded a searchable check-in history. The closing emphasis is automation: a healthy project must build from one checkout with one command.

talks.title: Neal Ford "The Productive Programmer..." Part 4
talks.teaser: Offers practical tips for cutting desktop distractions, searching instead of navigating, and keeping project knowledge in one place.
talks.summary:
This part of Neal Ford's Productive Programmer session, given at a Polish developer conference, looks at mechanics that protect a programmer's concentration at the desk. Ford argues that pop-up balloon tips, flashing copy dialogs and other random notifications break a developer's flow. He suggests moving nuisance dialogs off the edge of the screen and using a screen dimmer that fades the background to black while the active window stays in full color. He names Jedi Concentrate for Windows and Do Dim for the Mac as examples.

Next, Ford argues that search beats navigation in deep file hierarchies. Desktop search is built into modern operating systems and can be added to Windows XP through Google Desktop search. He recommends configuring the indexer to cover source and configuration file types only, so that typing a Java class name opens the file directly. He also describes the rooted view: an Explorer window started from a shortcut that shows only one project directory and its children. He says the same idea works by dragging a folder to the Mac dock and on GNOME under Linux, and that it leaves other Explorer windows unaffected.

The final section covers canonicality, which Ford describes as the don't-repeat-yourself principle applied to everything in a project, including schemas and documentation. His example is a mapping setup using tools such as iBatis or Hibernate, where the database schema, the XML configuration and the Java class all restate the same information and must be kept in sync by hand. The takeaways are to reduce interruptions, rely on search over deep navigation and keep one authoritative representation of each fact.

talks.title: Neal Ford "The Productive Programmer..." Part 3
talks.teaser: Covers IDE shortcuts, live templates, OS-level text expansion, and attention habits that reduce repetition and protect developer flow.
talks.summary:
The session continues a tour of editor mechanics aimed at doing less typing while staying inside the code. It shows how abbreviated navigation can jump to classes and symbols even when only fragments of names are remembered, and how refactoring assists can infer types and avoid clashing variable names in the current scope. Escalating selection is demonstrated as one repeating shortcut that grows the highlight word by word and block by block until a whole method is selected without reaching for the mouse.

The middle portion stacks acceleration habits: downloadable shortcut references, live templates with parameter substitution in major IDEs, and a rule to templatize anything typed a third time. Macro utilities at the operating system level extend the same idea beyond the editor, including snippets for hard-to-spell terms, repeated phrases, and automatically inserted dates and times.

The close ties tooling to concentration. Drawing on ideas about locus of attention and flow, the speaker argues that interruptions cost roughly fifteen to twenty minutes to recover from and that both workspace and computer setup should minimize trivial breaks in focus. The practical takeaway is to externalize shortcuts and repeated text so the brain stays on the problem instead of ceremony.

talks.title: Neal Ford "The Productive Programmer..." Part 2
talks.teaser: Part two covers shell integration in file managers, keyboard-first habits, and IDE plugins that drill shortcut mastery.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with Windows and Mac utilities that marry graphical file browsing to shells: Microsoft PowerToys’ “command prompt here,” Cygwin’s “Bash here,” and third-party Explorer integrations that keep a terminal’s working directory aligned with the folder being viewed, with Pathfinder offering a similar drawer on macOS.

The speaker argues that developers resemble heads-down data entry workers who lose time whenever they reach for a mouse, then walks through concrete ways to internalize IDE shortcuts. Tactics include dismissing menus to force shortcut use, a pairing rule that makes offenders redo mouse actions via the keyboard three times, on-screen key display during pairing, and free IntelliJ and Eclipse plugins such as Key Prompter and Mousefeed that nag or even disable menus until shortcuts stick. A companion wiki hosts flash cards for lunch-time drills.

The close ties shallow keyboard navigation to huge modern trees: deep package folders make mouse-driven expansion wasteful when names are already known. Go-to-class style jumps via Ctrl+N and abbreviated camel-case letter patterns locate types such as shopping-cart memento classes without traversing the hierarchy visually.

talks.title: Neal Ford "The Productive Programmer..." Part 1
talks.teaser: Productivity mechanics demonstrate acceleration via keyboard navigation, clipboard history, and command-line efficiency.
talks.summary:
Ford traces how The Productive Programmer evolved from early conversations with David Boach about developers who grew up on graphical systems and needed stronger command-line habits. After leaving Pragmatic Press for O'Reilly, the book shipped in two halves—mechanics and practices—and this segment addresses mechanics only. He frames productivity around four principles: acceleration, focus, automation, and canonicity, with Java-flavored examples because the session belongs to a Java track.

The acceleration portion targets habitual slowdowns. Ford contends that expanding project trees with a mouse mostly tests hand-eye coordination when you already know a target name, and that a single system clipboard creates painful alt-tab copy cycles or ad hoc scratch buffers. He recommends OS-wide clipboard history on Windows via ClCL and on macOS via paid iClip or the Jumpcut utility he uses, which exposes history through a menu-bar icon or hotkey. He also contrasts graphical explorers, useful for seeing structure, with command lines that often complete file work in fewer keystrokes.

Although focus, automation, and canonicity are named up front, the visible segment concentrates on acceleration illustrations. Listeners gain concrete swaps—navigation by typing, richer clipboards, and selective CLI use—rather than a giant recipe dump, matching Ford’s pivot from scattered tricks toward repeatable productivity patterns for working programmers.

talks.title: JDD09 Scott Davis talk 1 PART6
talks.teaser: Explains how Atom standardizes syndication beyond RSS and why platforms like Google and Twitter expose REST-style programmatic access.
talks.summary:
The segment closes a longer discussion of web APIs by positioning Atom alongside RSS. RSS and early feed wars motivated an IETF effort led in part by Tim Bray to standardize syndication. RSS works well for pulling entries but does not fully specify creating, updating, or deleting them, which leaves a gap compared with typical application CRUD needs.

Atom is described as a stable, standardized syndication format that supports resource-oriented access with familiar HTTP verbs. The speaker ties this to organizational choices between SOAP-style service orientation and REST-style resource orientation, citing OpenLogic’s use of Atom and Google’s shift away from legacy SOAP APIs toward GData and Atom-driven calendar operations, including authenticated private feeds versus public read-only RSS-style access. Twitter search over Atom is offered as another example of the same RESTful request pattern used earlier with geocoding and weather feeds.

The closing argument is pragmatic rather than dogmatic: neither SOAP nor REST is declared universally superior, but public web platforms have broadly moved toward RESTful interfaces. Listeners are encouraged to read published API documentation—especially calendar APIs with auth models—and to decide whether their organizations should invest in older RPC-oriented stacks or APIs aligned with current web practice.

talks.title: JDD09 Scott Davis talk 1 PART5
talks.teaser: The segment contrasts SOAP and REST, then explains syndication through RSS and Atom with Rome and live weather-feed examples.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with a brief return to Grails REST handlers, where switching on HTTP verbs yields only a few lines per method—a low-ceremony pattern the speaker positions as suitable for serious, high-availability systems like those at large web companies.

The core shift is architectural: REST as resource-oriented design versus SOAP as an SOA implementation, argued as style-versus-style or implementation-versus-implementation rather than confused labels. Syndication becomes the organizing idea—RSS as one flavor among several, with Atom illustrating chronology plus multiple MIME types so administrators, automated clients, and even gzip binaries can share one feed. Blogging permalinks, subscribe buttons, and familiar syndication logos tie everyday web behavior to HTTP and URIs; the Rome Java library is introduced as practical RSS and Atom support.

RSS history underscores competing definitions and parallel version numbers from Netscape and Dave Winer. A planned live walkthrough uses a zip-code weather request returning RSS channel data; connectivity fails, but the intended lesson is that time-sensitive updates fit syndication-shaped REST calls. Practitioners gain a clearer map from SOAP, REST, and syndication standards to patterns they already use in production integrations.

talks.title: JDD09 Scott Davis talk 1 PART4
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of JDD09 Scott Davis talk 1 PART4.

talks.title: JDD09 Scott Davis talk 1 PART3
talks.teaser: Contrasts verb-heavy SOAP RPC with noun-oriented REST resources, using Groovy MOP and geographic URL examples practitioners can reuse.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with Groovy’s meta object protocol: adding a rhyme method to String’s metaclass so ordinary code can call capabilities the type does not ship with, illustrating how small language features change what feels natural in code.

The core shift is SOAP as a concrete specification versus REST as architectural principles coined in Roy Fielding’s dissertation. SOAP-style SOA emphasizes remote procedure calls and arbitrary method names such as getUser, addUser, or removeUser, so each service effectively needs its own contract. REST promotes resource-oriented design aligned with familiar web URLs.

A hierarchical location service demonstrates the model: GET on paths like country, region, and city returns representations, while shortening the path yields broader lists—city, then country, then world. The lesson for practitioners is that well-shaped resources and HTTP verbs can make integrations predictable without custom WSDL wisdom for every endpoint.

talks.title: JDD09 Scott Davis talk 1 PART2
talks.teaser: Contrasts SOAP hype with real-world REST adoption and demos simple HTTP/XML geocoding and rhyming lookups.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that SOAP never became the ubiquitous, low-friction integration layer its advocates promised. Invoking Dave Winer, the speaker describes SOAP as a failed equalizer that was supposed to fade into everyday use, including fanciful visions of casual publishers. Tim O’Reilly’s Amazon example anchors the critique: the retailer exposes SOAP and REST with comparable functionality, yet more than eighty-five percent of traffic uses the REST interface. Despite corporate promotion, books, and articles, SOAP has not caught fire the way simpler XML-over-HTTP approaches have.

Against that backdrop, the speaker favors plain XML web services with low ceremony—no constant battles over APIs, versions, and stacks. Live demonstrations call public REST endpoints: a geocoder returns latitude and longitude for addresses such as Krakow, Poland, verified in Google Maps. The same interaction is rebuilt in Groovy using Java’s URL class, pulling XML via HTTP and parsing latitude and longitude with Groovy’s XML slurper. A REST rhyming dictionary shows another pattern: pass a word in the URL and receive rhyming results without SOAP envelopes or headers.

The closing message is that effective web services should be trivial to invoke and invisible in application code. RESTful HTTP requests embody the adoption developers already demonstrate in production, replacing the hoped-for SOAP ubiquity with interfaces that stay out of the way.

talks.title: JDD09 Scott Davis talk 1 PART1
talks.teaser: Explores why web services matter beyond SOAP, focusing on RESTful, resource-oriented design for the modern web.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at where software development is heading, focusing on web services, and specifically RESTful services built on a resource-oriented architecture. The speaker treats these as high-level ideas that apply across programming languages, with the choice of language being only an implementation detail. The framing draws on the book Small Pieces Loosely Joined, which describes the web as pages assembled from many separate parts.

The middle section contrasts early web pages with web 2.0 sites that mix outside services such as payment processing, mapping and embedded video. The speaker cites eBay, where over 66 percent of revenue reportedly comes through its web services, and Twitter, where 85 percent of traffic arrives via its services. A show of hands on SOAP use is followed by the point that SOAP is only one implementation of web services, dating from the late 1990s, and that Dave Winer, a creator of XML-RPC and RSS, has been critical of it.

The closing comparison is with HTTP, which is so widely used that few people track its version, unlike SOAP, where versions cause friction. The takeaway is to keep web services separate from any single protocol and to design around the data a system exposes, not only the pages it serves.

talks.title: JDD09 Tomasz Skutnik PART5
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD09 Tomasz Skutnik PART5.

talks.title: JDD09 Tomasz Skutnik PART4
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD09 Tomasz Skutnik PART4.
talks.summary:
### Overview
W tej części prezentacji Tomasz Skutnik kontynuuje omawianie zaawansowanych aspektów obsługi błędów i wyjątków w aplikacjach Java, skupiając się na mechanizmach serwletów, spójności pamięci podręcznej i bazy danych, projektowaniu stron błędów oraz bezpiecznym zarządzaniu zasobami JDBC i JMS.

### Key Topics
- **Model wyjątków w serwletach i filtry**: Domyślne wyłączenie filtrów podczas obsługi wyjątków (od wersji 1.4 możliwa deklaracja) oraz problem z utratą pierwotnej przyczyny błędu przy opakowywaniu w `ServletException`.
- **Interakcja transakcji z pamięcią podręczną (Cache)**: Rozbieżności danych wynikające z wyczyszczenia i ponownego załadowania zmodyfikowanych danych do cache w trakcie transakcji, która kończy się błędem i wycofaniem (rollback).
- **Projektowanie przyjaznych i użytecznych stron błędów**: Konieczność zachowania spójności graficznej, generowania unikalnych identyfikatorów błędów (np. 20 losowych znaków) korelowanych z logami oraz ułatwiania zgłoszeń (np. automatyczny JavaScript wysyłający raport).
- **Obsługa JDBC i JMS oraz podwójne błędy**: Pułapki związane z zamykaniem zasobów (`ResultSet`, `Statement`, `Connection`), utrata pierwotnych wyjątków, brak domyślnego wypisywania `SQLState` i `SQL Error Code` przez `SQLException`.
- **Biznesowe błędy i wyjątki od reguły szybkiego wywracania**: Wznawianie transakcji przy zakleszczeniach (deadlocks) oraz traktowanie naruszenia więzów integralności (np. unikalny login) jako normalnego przepływu biznesowego.

### Technical Details
Prelegent omawia mechanizm obsługi wyjątków w serwletach, gdzie obsługa zachowuje się jak forward, lecz domyślnie wyłącza filtry, co bywa mylące dla programistów. Wskazuje również, że `ServletException.printStackTrace()` nie wypisuje stosu przyczyny (`root cause`), przez co generyczny kod musi jawnie wyłuskać pierwotny wyjątek.

W kontekście bazodanowym `SQLException` nie drukuje automatycznie kodów `SQLState` ani kodów błędów bazowych, co utrudnia diagnozę naruszenia ograniczeń integralności czy błędów składni. Prelegent przedstawia rozwiązanie oparte na klasie pomocniczej `JdbcUtil` oraz wzorcu funktora za pomocą interfejsu `ConnectionOp` (z implementacją np. `QueryOp` i metodą `invoke`). Metoda główna `withDataSourceConnection` odpowiada za pobranie połączenia, wykonanie operacji, a w sekcji `finally` za bezpieczne zamykanie `ResultSet`, `Statement` i `Connection`. Aby uniknąć zjawiska „podwójnego błędu” (gdy wyjątek podczas zamykania zasobu przesłania pierwotny błąd wykonania), stosuje się dedykowany wyjątek opakowujący, który zachowuje pierwotną przyczynę.

### Takeaways
- Zawsze należy czyścić cache przy wycofywaniu transakcji (rollback), aby zapobiec serwowaniu nieaktualnych lub wycofanych danych.
- Strony błędów powinny prezentować unikalny identyfikator błędu tożsamy z wpisem w logach serwera oraz jasno instruować użytkownika o charakterze awarii.
- Zamykanie zasobów JDBC i JMS powinno być enkapsulowane w reużywalnych klasach narzędziowych chroniących przed podwójnymi błędami i utratą pierwotnych wyjątków.
- Nie każdy błąd bazodanowy oznacza awarię krytyczną – sytuacje takie jak deadlocki mogą wymagać ponowienia transakcji, a naruszenia unikalności (np. równoległa rejestracja loginu) stanowią standardowy element logiki aplikacji.

talks.title: JDD09 Tomasz Skutnik PART3
talks.teaser: Covers resilient production practices, simple exception paths, network timeouts, and structured logging for faster incident recovery.
talks.summary:
The segment argues that teams should plan for fast reaction when things fail rather than trying to predict every failure mode. Production workflows should favor frequent deploys, quick restarts, and rapid patches, while exception handling stays deliberately simple so a failure in the error path does not create a harder-to-trace double fault. Integrations with mail, databases, and external web services need timeouts and safe failure behavior so hung network calls do not freeze the whole application server.

Operational habits matter as much as code. A rotating “coroner” role puts developers on production log review and postmortems so they see how the system actually breaks. When throwing exceptions, the speaker stresses answering what broke, where, and why, using domain-specific types, rich context in messages, and detailed logging—including HTTP headers, cookies, and session state when an error page is shown—so incidents can be replayed without manualUI reproduction. Log infrastructure itself needs monitoring, illustrated by a silent failure when a log file exceeded two gigabytes on a commercial Unix web stack.

The closing framework favors centralized error handling for web apps, helper libraries that wrap external resources, and narrow catch clauses for deliberate recovery instead of empty or overly broad catches. A final note warns that HTTP session state may persist even when a request transaction rolls back, leaving inconsistent session data after errors.

talks.title: JDD09 Tomasz Skutnik PART2
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD09 Tomasz Skutnik PART2.

talks.title: JDD09 Tomasz Skutnik PART1
talks.teaser: Explains how production Java teams accept unpredicted failures, organize incident response, and why checked exceptions fail in practice.
talks.summary:
The session opens by arguing that exceptional situations are the norm for live systems: features change, hardware is replaced, and something is always breaking, so teams should plan to recover quickly instead of predicting every failure mode. How outages are handled shapes user trust and contract obligations, so production incident handling needs a deliberate internal process.

A concrete outage illustrates the point: after four days on production, a generic JavaScript action error suggested an application server fault, yet PostgreSQL was healthy from the command line. Step-by-step investigation showed the transaction manager partition had run out of disk space—nothing obvious in the error message pointed there.

The speaker outlines recurring elements of an incident process: external monitoring beyond application logs, polished maintenance and error pages, operator tools for fast recovery at night, automated snapshots and log preservation during stress, and calm post-mortems to drive fixes. The segment then turns to Java exception policy, contending that declared checked exceptions rarely survive real maintenance pressure, that many failures cannot meaningfully continue, and that whether execution can proceed should be decided above the code that throws.

talks.title: JDD09 Mark Richards PART6
talks.teaser: Clarifies REST idempotency against JMS queue behavior and shows servlet-backed GET and POST bridging into ActiveMQ.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with design tensions between REST and messaging semantics. On a queue, it is unclear whether GET consumes the next message or only inspects it, given the expectation that GET must not change resource state, while messaging operations routinely do. DELETE raises a parallel ambiguity: removing the queue versus dequeuing a single message.

The presenter notes that ActiveMQ and WebSphere currently expose REST-oriented JMS access, then walks through a minimal browser form wired to a Groovy listener. A posted message returns almost immediately, illustrating how provider servlets translate HTTP GET and POST into underlying JMS calls without custom client plumbing. Mapping details and sample code are referenced as available from the speaker’s site alongside the slide deck.

Closing remarks sketch a fuller hands-on agenda—pub/sub, binary payloads, transactions, acknowledgements, durable subscribers, request-reply, and common pitfalls—and point practitioners to the second edition of the O’Reilly Java Message Service book, updated for Spring and RESTful JMS, with sources and slides hosted online.

talks.title: JDD09 Mark Richards PART5
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of JDD09 Mark Richards PART5.

talks.title: JDD09 Mark Richards PART4
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of JDD09 Mark Richards PART4.

talks.title: JDD09 Mark Richards PART3
talks.teaser: Hands-on code shows Java and Groovy clients exchanging JMS text on ActiveMQ through JNDI lookups and direct TCP connections.
talks.summary:
The segment continues a hands-on introduction to Java Message Service by building the smallest possible sender in plain Java, without Spring or enterprise message-driven beans. The presenter loads JNDI from a classpath properties file, looks up a queue connection factory and a queue named q1, opens a connection and session, creates a text message saying hi jdd, sends it, and closes the connection. They note that integration stacks such as Spring, Mule, Camel, and EJB message-driven beans usually hide this wiring while leaving the same underlying flow.

Attention then shifts to consumption. A Groovy synchronous receiver connects straight to ActiveMQ on localhost port 61616 instead of JNDI, which highlights how broker-specific factories differ from portable JNDI access. The physical queue name jms.q1 replaces the shorter JNDI alias. After factory, connection, session, queue, and receiver are in place, the connection starts and a blocking receive loop waits for messages rather than implementing a message listener callback.

The presenter contrasts JMS providers with multi-language brokers such as ActiveMQ, which can bridge JMS sends to many other client APIs. For practitioners, the takeaway is the explicit send and receive sequence every higher-level framework automates, plus when direct broker connection is acceptable versus when JNDI indirection keeps vendor swapping feasible.

talks.title: JDD09 Mark Richards PART2
talks.teaser: A walkthrough of JMS messaging models, message anatomy, API usage, and ActiveMQ demos that send Java messages and receive them in Groovy.
talks.summary:
The session opens by gauging audience experience with messaging, then moves into the two core JMS delivery models. Point-to-point covers fire-and-forget work versus request-reply over paired queues, along with the rule that many competing consumers can listen yet only one receives each message. Publish-subscribe is framed as broadcast over topics, with an example where application exceptions are published once and multiple subscribers react differently for metrics, filtering, and email alerts.

The middle section decomposes a JMS message into standard header fields, custom properties beside the payload, and the body. Text messages suit strings and XML; object messages are discouraged because they tie producers and consumers to Java and shared class definitions, undoing decoupling. Map, stream, and byte variants are noted briefly, with a joking aside about binary payloads left for a later session.

The closing portion maps the specification interfaces for connections, sessions, producers, and consumers, contrasting JMS pooling of sessions with JDBC-style connection pooling. Queue and topic APIs are lined up side by side, then the speaker prepares live coding: ActiveMQ as the broker, a Java producer, and a Groovy consumer to show heterogeneous clients on the same middleware.

talks.title: JDD09 Mark Richards PART1
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of JDD09 Mark Richards PART1.

talks.title: JDD09 Tom Baeyens and Joram Barrez PART4
talks.teaser: The segment shows JUnit testing, Eclipse debugging, console prototypes, and an SMS ticket flow on the jBPM Java stack.
talks.summary:
The presentation continues a developer-focused walkthrough of jBPM after a business analyst hands a process model to a Java developer. Because the engine is implemented entirely in Java rather than as a monolithic proprietary server, business processes can be validated with ordinary unit tests: deploy the definition, start an instance, and assert outcomes with familiar JUnit patterns, then use standard Eclipse debuggers to step through decision logic such as comparing a quoted price to a customer balance.

The speaker shifts to agile prototyping using the jBPM console and lightweight task forms written as simple HTML or FreeMarker templates. A train-ticket scenario illustrates how form fields become process variables, how role switching mimics different users, and how stakeholders can exercise a credible end-to-end flow in hours without a finished production UI.

The closing demo registers users in a small Seam application, funds an account, and drives the process through a phone emulator that exchanges text messages with an EJB3 service on JBoss. Accepting a quoted fare updates balances and completes the ride-booking narrative, with full source available for download.

talks.title: JDD09 Tom Baeyens and Joram Barrez PART5
talks.teaser: Shows jBPM monitoring, BI reports, live BAM dashboards, and a timed all-in-one install in under one minute.
talks.summary:
The session picks up after earlier demos by positioning the GPM console as an operational view, not only a modeling playground. The presenter walks through process instances for a travel-ticket flow from Brussels, variable storage, and waiting on a mobile accept message, then refreshes views as messages complete. Business intelligence comes through BIRT-based reports behind the console, with counts of active instances and export options managers expect, such as PDF, Excel, and Word.

The middle segment introduces business activity monitoring aimed at executives: a Seam application fed by Esper complex event processing over GPM history drives Flash charts that update as events arrive. One chart tracks an SLA requiring customer response within one second; others show revenue across recent time windows plus average and standard deviation. Sending and accepting messages from the demo phone nudges response-time metrics and registers payment on the dashboards. The speaker notes this monitoring UI was built in roughly two hours.

The close is a speed install using a shipped script: Eclipse, Sinatra-related components, the GPM console, an in-memory database, example processes, Tomcat, and related pieces come up with an official timer stopping near fifty-seven seconds. Wrap-up contrasts free open source on jboss.org with JBoss Enterprise bundles, subscription binaries, and a services-led support model including production response targets.

talks.title: JDD09 Tom Baeyens and Joram Barrez PART 3
talks.teaser: Covers jBPM transactions and timers, SMS rail-ticketing, and browser BPMN modeling that exports deployable process definitions.
talks.summary:
The session continues a multi-part look at jBPM, focusing on how state management, transactions, and timers live in the process definition rather than scattered through application code. The speakers describe XML-driven control of reminders, long-running task escalations, and timeout handling, positioning the engine to juggle those concerns so developers can concentrate on domain logic.

They walk through a fictional train-ticket flow triggered by SMS between Krakow and Warsaw: account registration, credit checks, price quotes returned to the phone, acceptance or silent timeout, and conductor validation tied to the payer’s number. They stress binding jBPM steps to application entities such as tickets inside a single database transaction so business updates and process moves succeed or roll back together.

A pre-recorded demonstration shows business analysts modeling in a browser-based Signavio workspace with BPMN shapes, saving GPDL, and handing the model to developers via an Eclipse plug-in that preserves the diagram. Scenarios include insufficient balance with cancellation, successful quote and charge paths, and timed cleanup of stale process instances.

talks.title: JDD09 Tom Baeyens and Joram Barrez PART 2
talks.teaser: Explains how jBPM embeds in Java apps, binds transactions, records process history, and exposes one API across Spring, Seam, and plain JDK.
talks.summary:
The session continues a walkthrough of jBPM as a process engine layered on a shared process virtual machine that backs several workflow languages. It contrasts classic BPM suites with engines such as BPEL, which the speakers frame as integration technology for composing web services rather than tooling for non-technical analysts.

The narrative follows a typical Java delivery path: a business analyst supplies a boxes-and-arrows diagram, and the developer enriches that abstract model with executable detail in XML or an IDE, then deploys it beside application code on Tomcat, JBoss, or a plain JDK runtime. jBPM is presented as a library that participates in the application's transactions and rolls back with the host app, unlike monolithic standalone BPM servers. Running processes gain automatic history suitable for audits and operational statistics on claims, hiring, or expenses-style flows.

Technical mechanics include APIs to start instances, wake waiting activities with external events, and query tasks and history. jBPM 4 is described as offering one configuration and execution style familiar to Hibernate users, with Ant or programmatic deployment of example decision processes such as evaluate document branching on good, bad, or ugly outcomes. The closing point is that embedding the engine offloads multi-step state and wait handling that would otherwise require extensive custom Java plumbing.

talks.title: JDD09 Tom Baeyens and Joram Barrez PART 1
talks.teaser: Introduces business process management and the jBPM open source framework for Java developers, with a focus on process languages.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining a business process as an organised way of doing things to reach a goal, usually making money. The speakers trace the idea through Adam Smith's pin factory, Henry Ford's assembly lines and W. Edwards Deming's quality methods, then give everyday examples such as filing taxes, borrowing library books and paying for parking by phone. They explain that management is what gets people to follow a shared process, and that key performance indicators are simply metrics, such as whether a task finishes within an hour.

The focus then moves to software. The audience, mostly Java developers, is asked about daily work and prior workflow experience, and roughly a fifth had used BPM before. Tom Baeyens describes how a business process management system takes a diagram plus technical details as input, which is deployed and then executed as a running process. jBPM supports several process languages. jPDL is presented as developer-friendly, with readable XML and human tasks that produce task lists for users. BPMN 2 is a standard aimed at collaboration between business and non-technical staff, but it is less convenient for developers.

The takeaway is that BPM bridges non-technical stakeholders and IT, and that the right process language depends on whether shared diagrams or developer convenience matters more. The session is the first part of a longer presentation, and a demo built around a train ticket system is planned for later.

talks.title: JDD08 Neal Ford part2
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD08 Neal Ford part2.
talks.summary: Neal Ford continues a JDD talk arguing Java is framework-oriented, not purely object-oriented: teams ship libraries and configure strategies (mainframe-style record readers) instead of single classes. He revisits Dijkstra on goto, Simula predating Smalltalk by 13 years, and proposes domain-specific languages as the next layer paving over aspect-oriented complexity, using readable jargon like Starbucks drink orders to motivate language as the right abstraction.

talks.title: JDD08 Neal Ford Part5
talks.teaser: Contrasts essential and accidental complexity and argues Java teams should move framework configuration from XML into code-driven DSLs.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by borrowing Aristotle’s split between essential and accidental complexity and applying it to modern software, especially the Java ecosystem. The speaker argues that XML became the default external DSL for late-bound framework configuration because parsers were ubiquitous and grammars were free, then catalogs how that choice aged poorly: weak refactoring, copy-paste reuse, and configs that frighten non-developers. Ant is treated as the gateway habit; anecdote notes ant’s author publicly distancing himself from ant and Tomcat.

The middle focuses on Struts-style XML and why expressing relationships—such as keeping a connection pool maximum four greater than its minimum—forces manual discipline XML cannot enforce. A Groovy builder example is shown emitting the same Struts XML while using variables so one change propagates. Struts’s attempt at variables inside XML is contrasted unfavorably with Rails-style context-aware validation.

The close demonstrates a small Ruby DSL modeling farms, cows, and properties: class-level property declarations build an internal hash and dynamically define accessors. Practitioners are steered to keep behavior in code, treat XML configuration as deprecated for frameworks, and prefer internal or embedded DSLs where context and rules live with the program.

talks.title: JDD08 Neal Ford part4
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD08 Neal Ford part4.
talks.summary: Neal Ford continues a Java Developers Day fluent-interface tour, framing semicolons as sentence endings so chained calls read as complete thoughts. He cites Hamcrest, jMock, Rhino Mocks, and easyb behavior-driven tests, then contrasts Java limits with Groovy and Ruby metaclass extensions that add grams and pounds to integers. The talk closes on why frameworks still rely on XML configuration when Ruby-style internal DSLs could express wiring more clearly.

talks.title: JDD08 Neal Ford part3
talks.teaser: Explores how domain jargon and DSLs reduce repetitive code so business stakeholders can read application logic more clearly.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with the Waffle House hash-brown ordering scheme—eight verbs instead of narrating every cooking step—as a stand-in for how programming often over-explains tasks to machines. The speaker links that idea to jargon in music, gaming slang, sports, and industry domains, and argues that business vocabulary is itself a domain-specific language developers should echo so non-developers have a chance to read what code is for.

Drawing on Martin Fowler’s definitions, the talk distinguishes domain-specific languages from general APIs, contrasts noisy imperative Java with more declarative examples such as SQL and Ruby on Rails validations, and outlines language-oriented programming built around multiple DSLs. It then splits DSLs into internal forms hosted on flexible base languages and external ones you parse yourself, focusing on internal patterns—especially fluent interfaces.

A rail-car leasing example illustrates the payoff: elaborate rules such as tankers that hauled tar no longer being eligible for milk were buried in Java that analysts rejected as noise. Reshaping setters into a fluent chain—dropping repeated “set” prefixes and returning `this`—stripped enough ceremony that the same logic became readable to them without new frameworks.

talks.title: JDD08 Neal Ford part1
talks.teaser: A keynote connects art-era abstraction styles to Java frameworks, XML, aspects, and growing interest in domain-specific languages.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing domain-specific languages as a long-building trend rather than hype, citing ongoing patterns work at Thoughtworks and posing familiar Java developer puzzles: pervasive XML configuration, aspects, and sustained excitement around Ruby on Rails compared with quieter enterprise frameworks.

The speaker pivots to a long analogy from classical, Renaissance, Enlightenment, and neoclassical art, treating each period as an abstraction style—fixed subjects and techniques later reused with better materials. That metaphor maps onto programming: durable styles such as C-shaped syntax versus short-lived ones like Ada, and the habit of keeping useful ideas—variables, scoping, garbage collection—as newer layers appear.

For Java, frameworks become the dominant abstraction layer, to the point that object orientation is questioned as the defining trait. The first part ends by teeing up Edgar Dijkstra’s inflammatory 1968 ACM talk as the next step in that argument, setting up a shift beyond frameworks toward language-oriented programming.

talks.title: JDD08 Adam Bien part6
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD08 Adam Bien part6.
talks.summary: Adam Bien fields JDD08 audience questions on Java EE 6: Comet long-poll behavior, annotation-driven stateless beans versus Spring-style interceptors, and why developers moved to lighter Java EE 5 stacks without EJB jar ceremony.

talks.title: JDD08 Adam Bien part5
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding JDD08 Adam Bien part5.

talks.title: JDD08 Adam Bien part4
talks.teaser: A walk through JPA, REST, DTO trade-offs, and pragmatic alternatives to heavyweight J2EE layering in enterprise Java.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with lightweight integration patterns: JAXB as a wrapper for serializing JPA entities to XML or JSON, and REST conventions that replaced SOAP in some projects. It critiques classic J2EE patterns as spec-driven abstractions that rarely matched production reality, arguing that depending on JPA alone is enough to swap providers such as Hibernate and TopLink without rewriting application code.

The middle focuses on persistence ergonomics. Entity Manager is framed as the modern Domain Store: a thin DAO can wrap generic create, find, update, and list operations, with fluent query helpers and inheritance-based reuse for pragmatic teams. Testing is described with separate persistence units for JTA production versus JDBC-backed tests. DTOs are challenged as mere data structures that duplicate entities; generators and reflection copy utilities are warned against, with exposure of domain objects to the UI preferred where frameworks allow.

The close maps the Domain Store UML pattern to Entity Manager semantics, recommends starting from JPA rather than a single vendor implementation, and compares JSF to alternatives such as Wicket, stressing that JSF without visual design tooling imposes heavy XML and manual page work.

talks.title: JDD08 Adam Bien part3
talks.teaser: Shows EJB 3 as annotated POJOs, auto-deploy web services, and Jersey REST resources mapped from URLs with minimal XML.
talks.summary:
The session continues a walkthrough of enterprise Java after the shift from EJB 2’s verbose configuration toward EJB 3’s convention-over-configuration model. The presenter deploys a small JDD-related EJB as a JAR through auto-deploy, exposes a hello-style web service without interface boilerplate when desired, and wires remote access through injection so only the interface is required at the injection point while implementations remain swappable.

He contrasts the older mindset—teams insisting on XML or image-based crypto diplomas that fail after day one—with EJB 3 metadata derived from annotations and reflection. The GlassFish V3 container footprint (~300 kilobytes) and a notebook benchmark frame EJB 3 and plain POJO performance as effectively equivalent at thousands of requests per second on the demo hardware. The full EJB API is described as roughly 40 kilobytes with about ten annotations, leaving room for familiar unit-test tooling.

The closing segment pivots to REST via JSR 311 and the Jersey reference implementation bundled with NetBeans: a customers resource class with GET parameters, POST handling, and path templates that bind IDs from well-formed URLs returning XML or JSON. The takeaway for practitioners is leaner EJB 3 services, optional migration toward Spring because everything hinges on interfaces, and REST resources addressed through annotations rather than sprawling deployment descriptors.

talks.title: JDD08 Adam Bien part2
talks.teaser: A walkthrough of EJB 3 conveniences—from singleton startup ordering and async methods to WAR deployment and standardized JNDI names.
talks.summary:
The speaker continues a Java EE-focused session by arguing that EJB 3 makes web applications easier to build than rolling comparable transaction, filter, and resource-management plumbing by hand or through large alternate stacks. He walks through POJO-style injection and chaining over enterprise beans, notes that local call overhead is negligible for his tests, and highlights container-managed entity managers as a practical win.

Midway he covers singleton lifecycle control with startup ordering, asynchronous methods returning futures (including cancellation), embeddable containers for unit tests, and deploying enterprise beans inside a WAR without a separate EJB JAR—useful for incremental deploy-on-save workflows with NetBeans, Eclipse, Wicket, and JavaServer Faces. He explains standardized global JNDI names, briefly contrasts REST (JSR 311) with SOAP-style web services, and describes exposing EJB remote interfaces through CORBA for lightweight C++ integration in embedded settings.

He closes with a live GlassFish demonstration: a minimal stateless session bean exposing a remote hello service from Poland, shown as ordinary Java with little ceremony. The practical takeaway is that naming, packaging, and integration choices matter as much as the APIs when selling EJB 3 to teams and managers.

talks.title: JDD08 Adam Bien part1
talks.teaser: Shows how trimming layered Java EE architectures and leaning on EJB 3 container services can keep applications simpler and fast.
talks.summary: Adam Bien opens JDD08 explaining his Java Champion freelance work, Java EE 6 expert-group advocacy, and why European architects obsess over five JDBC-to-UI layers that inflate cost without adding isolation.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in JDD08 Ted Neward part6.

talks.title: JDD08 Ted Neward part7
talks.teaser: Covers strategies for introducing JVM dynamic languages and DSLs, from faster unit tests to domain-specific user input over SMS.
talks.summary:
The segment continues a longer discussion of programming languages by revisiting how object-relational mapping and query layers relate to SQL, then arguing that relations are best handled as tables, sets, and tuples rather than forced object shapes. After that buildup, the speaker frames management approval as the main obstacle, describing stereotypical executives who lack software-building experience yet treat their opinions as authoritative.

Two pragmatic adoption paths follow. One sells genuine value: dynamic languages such as Groovy or JRuby make unit tests and upper-stack UI work far easier, so teams can start in testing cycles before deploying on frameworks like Grails. The other leans on opacity: many alternate languages compile to familiar class files and JARs, and teams might even relabel unfamiliar source extensions while gradually migrating Java sources toward more dynamic code.

The closing material champions a broader language renaissance on the Java virtual machine, points to large catalogs of JVM languages, and warns that domain-specific languages should stay simpler than full programming languages per Martin Fowler’s guidance. It also describes language-oriented programming with parser generators for rich validation, and SMS-style micro-syntax for tasks such as stock orders, arguing that domain experts can safely author behavior when given constrained textual languages instead of endless bespoke UI features.

talks.title: JDD08 Ted Neward part5
talks.teaser: Connects POJOs, aspect-oriented programming, and multi-core CPUs to why thread-safe concurrency remains an unsolved pain for Java teams.
talks.summary:
The segment opens by tying Rod Johnson’s POJO and dependency-injection story to Spring’s transaction-oriented style, arguing that neither classic enterprise Java nor Spring is deeply object-oriented in the purist sense. Ted Neward then recounts Gregor Kiczales’s work at the University of British Columbia: constrained meta-object programming, bytecode emission, and the emergence of AspectJ and aspect-oriented programming as a wake-up call for developers who had settled into POJOs and transactional containers after mastering inheritance and object design.

He contrasts object-oriented and functional mindsets, noting Lisp’s recurring influence on mainstream languages through ideas such as conditionals, recursion, and garbage collection. The narrative shifts to hardware limits: clock speeds stalling near roughly 2.5–3 GHz, Intel hitting signal-propagation constraints, and the industry pivot to multi-core chips such as Core Duo. That shift exposes fragile application threading—only rarely thread-safe code can exploit extra cores, so perceived performance gains evaporate when mutable shared state is handled poorly.

The close frames concurrency as the defining problem for the next decade, with vendors still searching for better answers than widespread use of synchronized blocks. Practitioners should treat multi-core machines as a forcing function to revisit architecture and synchronization rather than assuming free speedups from new hardware alone.

talks.title: JDD08 Ted Neward part4
talks.teaser: Surveys JVM parser generators, bytecode kits, and IDE tooling so new languages reuse the runtime without rebuilding execution layers.
talks.summary:
The session opens from the language designer’s angle: targeting Java bytecode buys garbage collection, threading, serialization, RMI, and class loading without reimplementing a platform. That framing motivates a tour of the Java tooling stack that everyday developers already rely on—IDEs with completion and codegen, static analyzers such as FindBugs for concurrency defects, debuggers, profilers, and logging—contrasted with the comparatively primitive early days of println debugging.

The middle shifts to front-end and back-end machinery for creating languages. Classic lex-and-yacc style generator pain gives way to ANTLR and similar generator-oriented workflows, parser combinators in functional languages, and grammar debuggers that reduce hand-written parser tests. On execution, the talk contrasts Microsoft’s Dynamic Language Runtime with JVM bytecode helpers like Javassist, ASM, and BCEL, arguing that mature libraries make experimenting with language ideas practical.

The close uses enterprise Java history as a cautionary lens: late-1990s object orthodoxy collided with transaction processing needs, producing EJB shapes that prioritized containers and transactions over intuitive object models. The takeaway for practitioners is that runtime and toolchain maturity now frees designers to choose paradigms that fit the problem—especially when the domain is transactional rather than nominally object-oriented.

talks.title: JDD08 Ted Neward part3
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in JDD08 Ted Neward part3.
talks.summary:
Ted Neward examines the essential role of feedback loops in language design, using a driving metaphor to illustrate how developers and language designers rely on continuous feedback to identify problems and improve. He traces object-oriented programming's evolution from its emergence in Simula and Smalltalk (late 1960s) to mainstream adoption with C++ in the early 1990s—approximately 25 years later. Java, released in 1995, rapidly became the mainstream business language by 1998, effectively replacing COBOL.

Neward identifies four converging forces creating a 'perfect storm' that will shape future programming languages. He focuses extensively on the first force: virtualization. The Java Virtual Machine exemplifies virtualization's power by eliminating low-level programming concerns that plagued C++ developers: worrying about integer size and endianness, managing binary data exchange across different platforms, and most significantly, manual memory management. While resource management issues like closing result sets still require attention, the JVM handles the vast majority of low-level infrastructure.

Virtualization enables sophisticated runtime capabilities that form the foundation of modern Java development: automatic object serialization, Remote Method Invocation, class loaders for loading multiple class versions simultaneously, and hot deployment features. These capabilities are essential to application server architecture. Reflecting on his 1995 transition from C++ to Java, Neward notes that Java's language syntax itself is relatively unremarkable—'a crippled C++'—but the virtual machine's runtime introspection abilities and full access to object fields represent genuine innovation. This abstraction layer benefits not only developers but also language designers, who no longer need to implement low-level platform-specific details.

talks.title: JDD08 Ted Neward part2
talks.teaser: Contrasts academic language research with industry needs, arguing rapid feedback matters as much for platforms as for agile projects.
talks.summary:
The segment continues a contrast between software practitioners and academics, using a hypothetical “fibers” language that avoids shared mutable state as something practitioners want but cannot adopt for real systems. Integrations for relational databases, XML, serialization, and cross-process calls are missing or immature, and garbage collection stalls once programs grow—unlike the JVM, where HotSpot and related work absorbed decades of sustained engineering after acquisitions such as StrongTalk.

The speaker argues that professors optimize for novel language theory—pi calculus, lambda calculus, and similar ideas—not the grind required for production readiness. Practitioners download experimental runtimes, experiment briefly, then set them aside until they are “prime time,” which can mean nine- or eighteen-month gaps before useful feedback arrives.

The closing thread maps that delay onto methodology: agile and Scrum emphasize weekly user feedback to correct course, while waterfall and long release cycles starve improvement. The takeaway for builders is to treat platforms like products that need the same rapid feedback loops that make application projects succeed.

talks.title: JDD08 Ted Neward part1
talks.teaser: Argues that programming languages are in a renaissance, contrasting working developers' needs with academic language research.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the question attendees usually bring to conferences: where the field is heading next. Ted Neward suggests that programming languages are in the middle of a renaissance, with growing interest in using languages in everyday work, building custom languages, domain-specific languages, and language-oriented programming.

He splits the language world into two camps. Practitioners write software to get business work done under deadlines and demands from managers, while academics focus on abstract ideas such as type systems and on the tools themselves rather than the problems programmers face. He contrasts this with medicine and law, where university teachers are usually respected for recent hands-on experience, and jokes that in computer science people who have not done real work for decades end up in teaching roles.

The part ends on that critique of academic hiring, with the wider discussion of the language renaissance left for later.
